- **kind:** Circular
- **exact title:** FPI Participation in Exchange Traded Commodity Derivatives (ETCDs)
- **reference number:** HO/47/16/13(17)2026-MRD-POD1/I/26650/2026
- **addressed to / applies to:** The Managing Directors / Chief Executive Officers, All Recognized Stock Exchanges/Clearing Corporations having Commodity Derivatives Segment
- **official URL (detail page):** https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/circulars/nov-2026/fpi-participation-in-exchange-traded-commodity-derivatives-etcds-_105989.html
- **official PDF URL:** https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/nov-2026/1795778944519.PDF
- **effective date:** June 01, 2027
- **local text file name:** SEBI-105989.txt

```text
CIRCULAR



HO/47/16/13(17)2026-MRD-POD1/I/26650/2026  November 27, 2026



To,



The Managing Directors / Chief Executive Officers,



All Recognized Stock Exchanges/Clearing Corporations having Commodity

Derivatives Segment



Sir / Madam,

Sub: FPI Participation in Exchange Traded Commodity Derivatives (ETCDs)



1. In terms of Para 4.2 of Chapter 4 of SEBI Master Circular for Commodity Derivatives

    Segment dated Aug 04, 2023, Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) are currently

    permitted to participate in the commodity derivatives segment of recognised stock

    exchanges only through cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivative contracts

    and indices comprising such commodities.



2. Based on representations received from stakeholders, deliberations of the Commodity

    Derivatives Advisory Committee (CDAC), and public comments received on the

    consultation paper on this subject, and with the objective of deepening institutional

    participation and liquidity in the commodity derivatives segment, it has been decided

    to permit FPIs to participate in non-cash (physically) settled non-agricultural

    commodity derivative contracts, subject to the safeguards specified in this circular.

    Accordingly, following provisions contained in Paragraph 4.2 of the aforesaid circular

    stand revised as under:

         2.1 Para 4.2.2.(i) shall be revised as under:



                  4.2.2.(i) FPIs are allowed to participate in non-agricultural commodity

                  derivative contracts (except in option in goods) and indices comprising non-



                                                         Page 1 of 8

agricultural commodity derivatives. Further, FPI participation in non-cash

settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives shall be subject to following

conditions:



         (a) FPIs are allowed to participate up to the commencement of the

         tender/ staggered delivery period. Further, FPIs shall unwind/roll

         over their open positions, if any, prior to the commencement of the

         tender/ staggered delivery period.



         (b) Three trading days prior to the commencement of the

         tender/staggered delivery period, no fresh positions that result in an

         increase in the FPI's existing positions in the expiring futures contract

         shall be allowed; however, positions arising from the devolvement of

         options on futures on expiry shall not be treated as fresh positions

         for this purpose.



         (c) Any open (residual) positions of the FPI at the end of the day

         preceding the start of the tender period shall devolve upon the

         designated TM/TCM as prescribed under ‘Operational Framework

         for FPI Participation in Non-Cash Settled Contracts’ in this Circular.



         (d) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in the Master

         Circular for Commodity Derivatives Segment and Master Circular for

         Foreign Portfolio Investors, Designated Depository Participants and

         Eligible Foreign Investors; the devolvement of position from the FPI

         to TM/TCM on account of FPI's failure to voluntarily square off or roll

         over non-cash settled non-agriculture commodity futures contract

         prior to the tender period under the special arrangement shall not be

         treated as OTC derivatives, nor shall the extant regulations with

         respect to transfer of positions between client codes applicable to

         non-institutional transfer of positions, error accounts or off market

         transfer related provisions be applicable to the said arrangement.



                                     Page 2 of 8

                  Such devolvement shall be considered as a trade with applicable

                  statutory levies.



2.2 Para 4.2.2.(iii)(c) shall be inserted as under:



         4.2.2.(iii)(c) Due to post close devolvement of futures positions from FPI to

         the designated TM/TCM, there is a possibility that positions recorded in the

         TM's/TCM's proprietary account solely due to operation of the safeguard

         mechanism may exceed their permissible position limits for futures

         contracts. For such members, the exchanges may permit maximum up to

         two trading days to reduce their futures positions to bring them within the

         permissible position limits. The mere recording of such positions in the

         proprietary account shall not by itself result in such positions being regarded

         as voluntarily assumed proprietary positions.



2.3 Para 4.2.3 titled ‘Operational Framework for FPI Participation in Non-Cash

     Settled Contracts’ shall be inserted as under:



         4.2.3 Operational Framework for FPI Participation in Non-Cash Settled

         Contracts



         (i) Onboarding of FPI:



         (a) An FPI shall enter into a tripartite agreement with the Clearing Member

         (CM) and Trading Member(TM), or a bipartite agreement with the Trading

         Cum Clearing Member(TCM) (or any other nomenclature used by the

         exchanges in this regard) as per their membership structure. The TM/TCM

         entering into such agreement, only for the purpose of devolvement of open

         positions, shall henceforth be called as designated TM/TCM.



         (b) The Clearing Member of FPI shall inform the Exchange and Clearing

         Corporation(CC) of the agreement referred above, prior to facilitating the

         FPI to trade in the relevant deliverable commodity derivative contracts. The

         Exchange shall allow trading for the FPI client only upon confirmation of

         such agreement by the CM to the CC.



                                               Page 3 of 8

(c) Thereafter, the FPI may trade in non-cash settled commodity derivatives

through multiple trading members; however, there shall be only one

designated TM/TCM, as specified below:



      I. One designated TM/ TCM across all exchanges and commodities; or

     II. One designated TM/ TCM per exchange; or

    III. Within each exchange, one designated TM/ TCM per commodity or



                  group of commodities



(ii) Voluntary Square-off / Rollover – Primary Obligation:



(a) The FPI shall be free to square off or roll over its open position(s) at any

time up to the close of market hours on the day preceding the start of the

tender period. This voluntary square-off or rollover is, and shall remain, the

primary mode of exit for FPIs from such expiring contracts.



(iii) Safeguard Mechanism: Compulsory Square-off / Devolvement of FPI

Positions Before Tender Period in futures contracts



(a) Where an FPI has not voluntarily squared off or rolled over its open

position by the close of market hours on T-1, where T denotes start of the

Tender Period, the FPI positions shall be devolved upon the proprietary

account of the designated TM/TCM automatically post closure of market

hours of the T-1 day (the day prior to the start of Tender Period), before

start of EOD activities of the clearing corporation.



(b) To enable the designated TM to arrange adequate margins ahead of the

devolvement, the Clearing Member of FPI shall, by end-of-day on T-2,

inform the designated TM of the FPI's open position that is liable to devolve

under the Safeguard Mechanism.



(c) Under this arrangement, the devolvement of the open position of the FPI

shall be executed at the Closing Price/Daily Settlement Price, as declared

by the Exchange on the day of devolvement of the position. Such



                                     Page 4 of 8

devolvement shall be treated as Normal Market trades for all purposes,

including for applicability of statutory levies.



(d) Upon execution of the devolvement, the FPI's open position in the

contract shall be treated as closed, and the FPI shall cease to have any

further right, title, obligation, or exposure in respect of such position,

including in relation to the tender/delivery process. All rights and obligations

in respect of the devolved position shall thereafter vest solely in the

designated TM/TCM.



(e) From T-3 day, the clearing member shall not accept or clear any trade

that results in an increase of an FPI's open position in the near-month

deliverable futures contract. The clearing member shall ensure adequate

risk management measures such that FPI positions are either squared off

or devolved upon the designated TM/TCM by closure of T-1 day.



(f) The manner in which the positions of the FPI shall be handled, including

the squaring off of the FPI positions or devolvement of such positions at the

end of T-1 market hours, shall be governed as per the agreement between

the FPI and the TM/TCM.



(iv) Designated TM/TCM as Risk-Management Intermediary:



(a) The designated TM/TCM shall act as a risk-management intermediary

under the current framework and, where applicable, accept responsibility

for management of devolved positions pursuant to the regulatory

arrangement. The TM/TCM may charge an agreed fee for providing risk-

management, execution, monitoring, compliance and operational services

under the safeguard framework. For the avoidance of doubt, the acceptance

of a devolved position shall not be construed as a business activity involving

assumption of commodity exposure, or proprietary trades of the TM/TCM.



                                     Page 5 of 8

(v) Post-Devolvement Position-Limit Reduction:



(a) Where the said devolvement of FPI positions to TM/TCM results in the

designated TM's/TCM's proprietary account exceeding position limits

otherwise applicable to it, the TM/TCM shall be permitted a period up to two

trading days from the date of devolvement to reduce such position to within

the prescribed limits, in a manner analogous to the treatment of devolved

option positions as prescribed under Para 6.1.9.iii of the SEBI Master

Circular for Commodity Derivatives Segment. During this period, the

position so devolved shall not be treated as a violation attracting penal

action under extant position limit violation norms.



(vi) Risk Absorption Charge:



(a) The onboarding agreement may incorporate a pre-agreed ‘Risk

Absorption Charge', payable by the FPI to the designated TM/TCM where

the FPI's open position is devolved under the safeguard mechanism on

account of the FPI's failure to voluntarily square off or roll over such position

by T-1. The Risk Absorption Charge is intended to compensate the

designated TM/TCM for the risk, margin, and position-limit burden it absorbs

on account of the functions undertaken under the safeguard mechanism,

and shall be over and above any service fee agreed between the parties.



The quantum and manner of computation of the said charge shall be

disclosed to, and agreed by, the FPI at the time of onboarding and shall be

without prejudice to any penalty leviable by the Exchange/Clearing

Corporation under the extant framework.



(vii) Standardisation and Post-Closure Window:



(a) The Exchanges/Clearing Corporations having commodity derivatives

segment shall, in consultation with each other, standardise the format and

material terms of the onboarding agreement, so as to ensure consistency



                                     Page 6 of 8

                  in the safeguards and disclosures applicable to FPIs across

                  exchanges/clearing corporations.



                  (b) The Exchanges/Clearing Corporations shall notify detailed scheme /

                  guidelines of the post-closure window between the designated TM and FPI

                  for open positions held by the FPI (one day prior to the start of the tender

                  period) after normal market hours at Closing Price/Daily Settlement Price in

                  Commodity Derivatives Market Segment.



                  (c) The Exchanges/Clearing Corporations shall ensure that the designated

                  TM/TCM has adequate visibility of the FPI's positions liable to devolve, and

                  of the consequent margin obligation, so that it can arrange the required

                  margins in time.



         2.4 Para 6.2.7.(iii) shall be inserted as under:



                  6.2.7.(iii) Penalty for short-collection/non-collection of margins due to

                  increase in initial margins resulting from trade involving devolved positions

                  of FPI upon its designated trading member for mandatory closure of

                  positions of FPI may not be levied by clearing corporations for the first day.



3. The circular shall come into effect from June 01, 2027.

4. The MIIs are advised to:



         4.1 take necessary steps and put in place necessary systems for implementation

              of the above.



         4.2 make necessary amendments to the relevant bye-laws, rules and regulations,

              wherever required, for the implementation of the above; and,



         4.3 bring the provisions of this circular to the notice of the market participants

              (including investors) and disseminate the same on their website.



5. This circular is issued in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 11(1) of the

    Securities and Exchange Board of India Act 1992, read with Regulation 51 of the

    Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations)



                                                         Page 7 of 8

    Regulations, 2018, to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote

    the development of, and to regulate the securities market.

6. The Circular is issued with the approval of the competent authority.

7. This Circular is available on SEBI website www.sebi.gov.in under the category

    "Circulars" and "Info for Commodity Derivatives".



                                                                                                 Yours faithfully,

                                                                                                  Neetika Rajpal

                                                                                    Deputy General Manager

                                                                            Market Regulation Department

                                                                                Email: neetikar@sebi.gov.in

                                                                        Phone Number: +91-22-26449628



                                                         Page 8 of 8
```

```text
November 26, 2026



Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Security Council 1267(1999) ISIL (Da’esh)

and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee amends its Sanctions List



1. Clause 54 of the SEBI Master Circular, “Guidelines on Anti-Money Laundering (AML)

    Standards and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT)/ Obligations of Securities

    Market Intermediaries under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and rules

    framed thereunder” dated June 06, 2024, inter-alia, states that ‘The Stock exchanges and the

    registered intermediaries shall ensure that in terms of Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities

    (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA) and amendments thereto, they do not have any accounts in the

    name of individuals/ entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of

    having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations

    Security Council (UNSC)’.



2. In this regard, United Nations Security Council Committee established pursuant to

    resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al-Qaida and

    associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities on the Sanctions List of individuals

    and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1

    of Security Council Resolution 2610 (2021) has issued the following notifications.



             2.1. Note SC/16515 dated November 20, 2026 regarding the amendment of 1 entry, in

                   UNSC's 1267 (1999) ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions list (Annexure 1) and

                   notifications for the same is available at'

                   https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16515.doc.htm



             2.2. Note SC/16516 dated November 20, 2026 regarding the amendment of 81 entries,

                   in UNSC's 1267 (1999) ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions list (Annexure 2) and

                   notifications for the same is available at'

                   https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16516.doc.htm



2. An updated list of individuals and entities which are subject to various sanction measures such

    as freezing of assets/ accounts, denial of financial services etc., as approved by the Security

    Council Committee established pursuant to various United Nations' Security Council

    Resolutions (UNSCRs) can be accessed at its website at

    https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/content/un-sc-consolidated-list



    The updated list issued by the UNSC Committee established pursuant to resolution 1267 (1999)

    of individuals and entities linked to ISIL (Da'esh) and Al Qaida can be accessed at URL -

    https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/sanctions/1267/aq_sanctions_list



    The updated list issued by the UNSC Committee established pursuant to resolution 1988 (2011)

    of individuals and entities linked to Taliban can be accessed at URL -

    https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/sanctions/1988/materials



                                                         Page 1 of 6

3. As per the instructions from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), any request for delisting

    received by any Regulated Entity (RE) is to be forwarded electronically to Joint Secretary

    (CTCR), MHA (email: jsctcr-mha@gov.in) for consideration. A copy of the same may be marked

    to Joint Secretary (UNP), Ministry of External Affairs (e-mail id: jsunp@mea.gov.in). Individuals,

    groups, undertakings or entities seeking to be removed from the Security Council’s Sanctions

    List can submit their request for delisting to an independent and impartial Ombudsperson who

    has been appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General. More details are available at the
```

```text
CIRCULAR



HO/38/14/(25)2026-MIRSD-POD3            November 25, 2026



To,



Intermediaries registered with SEBI under Section 12 of the Securities and

Exchange Board of India Act, 1992;

Recognised Stock Exchanges;

Recognised Clearing Corporations; and

All Depositories



Sir/ Madam,



Subject: Simplification of client on-boarding and rationalisation of risk

            management framework at KYC Registration Agencies



1. SEBI vide Master Circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/SECFATF/P/CIR/2023/169 dated

    October 12, 2023 (‘KYC Master Circular’), inter-alia, specifies the Know Your Client

    (KYC) norms to be followed by intermediaries and KYC Registration Agencies

    (KRAs)1 in the securities market.



2. A working group was constituted comprising of market participants, Market

    Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs), KRAs and members of industry associations, with

    the objective of reviewing the existing risk management framework at KRAs and

    streamlining the client on-boarding process.



3. Based on the recommendations of the working group, the suggestions received in

    the public consultation process and deliberations with KRAs, in order to ease the



1 KYC Registration Agencies as per SEBI (Know Your Client Registration Agencies) Regulations, 2011;



                                                            Page 1 of 11

    process of on-boarding for clients and intermediaries, it has been decided to make

    certain modifications in the KYC process, as mentioned below:



    3.1. Centralisation of supplementary client information: Some of the

          supplementary information being submitted by a client in Part – II of the

          account opening form (AOF), which is common across intermediaries shall

          now be centralised at KRA level. This will ease out the on-boarding process

          when the client approaches another intermediary. Additionally, information viz.

          Central Know Your Customer Identifier (CKYC ID)2 and Digital Postal Index

          Number (DIGIPIN)3, if available, and the expiry/ validity date of Officially Valid

          Document (OVD)4, shall also be uploaded by the intermediary in the KRA

          system. Accordingly, the following changes will be made in the KYC Master

          Circular:



          3.1.1. The paragraph5 6 of the KYC Master Circular, shall be replaced with the

                  following:



                  “In Part II of the AOF, the intermediary collects information specific to the

                  nature of service being provided to the client. Additionally, the

                  intermediary shall collect the following information:

                  a. Central Know Your Customer Identifier (CKYC ID), if available;

                  b. Digital Postal Index Number (DIGIPIN), if available;

                  c. Expiry date of Officially Valid Document (as applicable)”.



          3.1.2. The paragraph 84 of the KYC Master Circular, shall be replaced with the

                  following:



2 The unique number or code assigned to a client by Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCRR);

3 10-character alphanumeric geo-coded addressing system developed by the Department of Posts;

4 OVD as defined under Rule 2(1)(d) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005;

5 paragraph 6 of the Section 1: Know Your Client (KYC) Requirements for the Securities Market



                                                            Page 2 of 11

             “After performing the initial KYC of a new client, the intermediary shall,

             within three working days from the date of completion of the KYC

             process, upload the below mentioned information on KRA:

             b. The following information from Part II of AOF:



                    i. Income range [i) 0 – 5 lakhs ii) 5 – 10 lakhs iii) 10 – 50 lakhs iv)

                      50 lakhs – 1 crore v) 1 – 2 crores vi) > 2 crores];



                   ii. Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and Common

                      Reporting Standard (CRS) related information (as specified in

                      SEBI Circular HO/38/14/(18)2026-MIRSD-POD-2/I/25560/2026

                      dated November 11, 2026); and



                  iii. Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) status;

                  iv. Occupation;

                   v. CKYC ID, if available;

                  vi. DIGIPIN, if available;

                 vii. Expiry date of OVD (as applicable)”.



     3.1.3. A paragraph 104A shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular, as

             given below:



             “KRA shall tag the records that it independently verifies and validates

             including information given under paragraph 84 b.”



3.2. Update of the KYC records: The intermediary shall update the KYC records of

     clients upon receiving updates from KRA and CKYCRR to avoid duplication of

     efforts and simplify the client on-boarding process. The intermediary shall

     provide option to the clients to confirm the update in their KYC records.

     Accordingly, the following change will be made in the KYC Master Circular:



                                                      Page 3 of 11

     3.2.1. A paragraph 89A shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular, as

             given below:



             “The intermediary shall update the KYC records of its clients based on

             the information received from the KRA in terms of Regulation 15(f) of the

             SEBI KYC Registration Agency (KRA) Regulations, 2011 and from

             CKYCRR in terms of Rule 9 (1-H) of the PML Rules. In this regard, the

             intermediary may seek additional information from client, as per its due

             diligence. The intermediary shall provide option to the clients to confirm

             the update in their KYC records.



3.3. Verification of Aadhaar seeded mobile number: The verification of mobile

     number shall be optional for the intermediary while on-boarding a client, if the

     mobile number available in the KRA system is already verified and tagged as

     seeded with Aadhaar. Accordingly, the following change will be made in the

     KYC Master Circular:



     3.3.1. A paragraph 104B shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular, as

             given below:



             “If the client mobile number is tagged by KRA as seeded with Aadhaar

             and verified, verification of such mobile number shall be optional for the

             intermediary accessing the information from the KRA database.”



3.4. Intimation of account closure/ non-association with client:



     3.4.1. Intimation of account closure/ update by the intermediary (other than

             Mutual Funds): In order to ensure that client KYC information is being

             shared with intermediaries only for clients which are having account-

             based relationship with it, the intermediary shall be required to inform

             the KRA, within five working days from the date of account closure of a

             client. Further, the intermediary shall within three months from the date

             of issuance of this circular, inform KRA(s) about account closures for

       records, within two working days from the date of receipt of updated

       information or modification request from intermediary. Accordingly, the

3.4.1.1. A paragraph 89B shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular,

3.4.1.2. A paragraph 104C shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular,

3.4.2. Intimation of zero balance folio account by Mutual Funds: Mutual Fund

       shall within three months from the date of issuance of this circular, inform

       be made in the KYC Master Circular:

  3.4.2.2. A paragraph 104D shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular,

3.4.3. Intimation of non-association by intermediaries: When an intermediary

       Accordingly, the following change will be made in the KYC Master

       Circular:



                                               Page 6 of 11

          3.4.3.1. A paragraph 89D shall be incorporated in the KYC Master Circular,

                     as given below:



                     “After download of a KYC record from the KRA, if a client account is

                     days, send intimation to KRA. Upon receipt of such information, KRA

                     shall within two working days, delink the relevant KYC record”.



    3.5. Overseas address proof optional for resident Overseas Citizen of India (OCI)6

          card holder and foreign national: The requirement of overseas address proof

          shall be optional for an OCI card holder and foreign national who is “resident”

          such client submitting proof of address for residing in India, to the intermediary.

          Accordingly, the following change will be made in the KYC Master Circular:

                  requirement of overseas address shall be optional, provided the client

    3.6. Documents required for change of name of client: In order to ease

          documentation, a client shall no longer be required to submit proof of name

          change to an intermediary if he/ she has already got the necessary change

          affected in PAN and Aadhaar. In case the name change has not been updated

          in PAN and Aadhaar, the client shall be required to submit to the intermediary,

          copy of Marriage Certificate issued by the State Government, copy of Passport

change of name. However, in case of state of Karnataka and Punjab, where

no official gazette is possible for change in name in case of private individuals,

    3.7. Ease on portability of KYC records: In order to ease the process of account
```

```text
===== [attached PDF] =====
Consultation paper on Early Pay Out (EPO) of funds for Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs)



  Objective

  1. The objective of this consultation paper is to seek public comments on the proposal to review



       the existing settlement framework for exchange transactions with a view to permitting early

       payout of funds for Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), subject to appropriate safeguards,

       while ensuring that settlement discipline, market integrity, and systemic stability are not

       compromised.



  Background

  2. Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) play an important role in aggregating agricultural



       produce of small and marginal farmers and facilitating their access to organised markets,

       including exchange-based trading platforms. Exchange traded commodity derivatives markets

       provide avenue for hedging and price risk management while ensuring transparent price

       discovery and assured settlement. At the same time, the standard settlement cycle results in a

       time lag between execution of trades and receipt of funds by selling FPOs.



  3. When FPOs deposit stocks in accredited warehouses for sale on the exchange, they have to

       wait till the contract expiry for realisation of funds from that sale transaction. Due to this, FPOs

       face a liquidity crunch till their funds are realised and hence have to operate with limited liquidity.

       While aggregating produce, FPOs pay farmers almost immediately but have to wait for the

       stocks to be sold to realize payments, to enable fresh aggregations. Most FPOs operate with

       limited working capital and are required to make prompt payments to member farmers. Delays

       in realisation of funds may adversely affect their liquidity position, farmer confidence, and

       participation in exchange-based markets.



  4. In this regard, various FPOs had also raised concerns that the waiting period from deposit to

       receiving money is substantial and they are without any funds in the interim period. Accordingly,

       the FPOs have also requested SEBI to consider reducing the timelines of release of payments

       to the FPOs post deposit of goods. Subsequently, SEBI has also received representations from



                                                               Page 1 of 9

    Clearing Corporations to facilitate Early Pay-Out of funds for FPOs when Early Pay-In of goods

    has been marked by them.



Recommendations of the Working Group and Commodity Derivatives Advisory Committee

(CDAC)

5. The proposal was deliberated in the meeting of the Working Group (WG) on ‘Review of current



    regulatory framework of delivery and settlement applicable to Agricultural Commodity

    Derivatives Segment’, wherein, based on deliberations/ discussions, the WG recommended that

    Early Pay-Out of funds prior to contract expiry by members may be permitted subject to

    incorporation of appropriate/required guardrails, for example, FPO-wise or commodity-wise or

    member-wise concentration limits, for the purpose of implementation of this proposal in order to

    mitigate any additional risk to the system.



6. Further, the recommendation of the WG was also placed before the Commodity Derivatives

    Advisory Committee (CDAC) meeting held on Feb 26, 2026, wherein the CDAC was broadly in

    agreement with the same.



7. Subsequently, the matter was discussed with Clearing corporations for the safeguards to be put

    in place.



8. In view of the above, a draft circular has been prepared for introducing the Early Pay-Out

    framework for Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) in the Commodity Derivatives Segment.

    The said circular is placed at Annexure - A.



Request for Public Comments:

9. With reference to the aforementioned draft circular at para 8 above, public comments, along



    with rationale, are invited on:

  9.1. The proposed framework (detailed in the said circular placed at Annexure – A) for



          facilitating Early Pay-Out (EPO) for FPOs.

  9.2. Any other safeguards/ guardrails that should be included in the EPO facility.



                                                            Page 2 of 9

Public Comments on this Consultation Paper:

10. Public comments are invited on the draft circular on “Early Pay Out (EPO) of funds for Farmer



    Producer Organisations (FPOs)”. The comments/ suggestions should be submitted latest by

    December 16, 2026, through the online web-based form which can be accessed using the

    following link:

    https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/publiccommentv2/PublicCommentAction.do?doPublicC

    omme nts=yes

11. In case of any technical issue in submitting your comment through the web based public

    comments form, you may contact the following through email to neetikar@sebi.gov.in,

    rashmis@sebi.gov.in and mrd_consultation@sebi.gov.in with the subject: “Public comments

    on - Early Pay-Out (EPO) of funds for Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs)”.

Issued on: November 25, 2026



                                                            Page 3 of 9

              Annexure - A



              CIRCULAR



SEBI/HO/MRD/MRD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2026/___  December xx, 2026



To,



The Managing Directors / Chief Executive Officers,

All Recognised Clearing Corporations having Commodity Derivatives Segment



Sir / Madam,



Sub: Early Pay-Out (EPO) of funds for Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs)



1. Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) play an important role in the Indian Agri Commodity

    Derivatives Segment. FPOs aggregate agricultural produce of small and marginal farmers and

    facilitate their access to organised markets, including exchange based trading platforms. In case

    of spot/ physical markets, FPOs can get the funds for their goods immediately on execution of

    trade. On the other hand, exchange traded commodity derivatives provide avenue for hedging

    and price risk management while ensuring transparent price discovery and assured settlement.

    At the same time, the standard settlement cycle results in a time lag between execution of trades

    and receipt of funds by selling FPOs.



2. In this regard, SEBI has received representations from Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs)

    and market participants stating that in order to facilitate participation and ease of doing business

    for FPOs in the Commodity Derivatives Segment, a mechanism for early release of funds to

    FPOs may be explored, subject to certain guardrails.



3. Based on the representations received from stakeholders, recommendation of the Working

    Group on Review of Current Regulatory Framework of Delivery and Settlement applicable to

    agricultural commodity derivatives segment and Commodity Derivatives Advisory Committee

    (CDAC), and with the objective of facilitating Ease of Doing Business for FPOs, it has been

    decided to introduce the framework of “Early Pay-Out (EPO) of funds for Farmer Producer

    Organisations (FPOs)”.



4. The key elements of the Framework are as under:

  4.1 Early Pay-Out (EPO): Early pay-out refers to pay-out/ release of funds to an FPO client by

         the trading member before the expiry of the derivatives contract, thereby reducing the time



              Page 4 of 9

between the deposit of goods towards the sale of derivatives contract on the exchange

platform and realisation of sale proceeds by the FPO client.



4.2 Subject to the conditions specified in this circular, the members may provide the facility of

      early pay-out of funds to their FPO clients.



4.3 Conditions for Early Pay-Out of Funds:

  4.3.1 This facility shall be available only to FPO clients who are dealing in agri commodities

           derivatives segment on the exchange platform.

  4.3.2 An FPO client would be eligible to avail the facility of Early Pay-Out of Funds only if it

           has made Early Pay-In (EPI) of goods in respect of sale transactions of derivatives

           contracts executed by it on the exchange platform.

  4.3.3 EPO of funds may be made by the member only up to 30 days prior to the expiry of the

           derivatives contract in respect of which EPI has been made by the FPO client.



4.4 Eligibility requirements for trading members to provide EPO facility to FPO clients:

  4.4.1 Only corporate trading members (TM) with a net worth of at least Rupees Three crore

           shall be eligible to offer facility of EPO of funds to their FPO clients.

  4.4.2 The “net worth” for the purpose of this facility shall be calculated as per the net worth

           formula prescribed under SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026.



4.5 Process Flow for EPO: The process flow for EPO facility is as follows:



4.5.1 Timeline: Once EPI has been marked, the FPO client may place the request for early

         pay-out of funds up to 30 days prior to expiry of the commodity derivatives contract i.e.

         E-30 days (where E: expiry day of the contract).



4.5.2 Request placement and verification:

4.5.2.1 The request for early pay-out of funds may be made by the FPO client through its



             TM.



4.5.2.2  Trade Verification: The TM shall verify the request placed by the FPO client vis-à-

         vis the trade executed on the exchange platform.



4.5.2.3 EPI Verification:

    4.5.2.3.1 The TM shall verify from the Clearing Corporation system that EPI has been

                  marked.

    4.5.2.3.2 The TMs shall then inform the Clearing Members about the request.

                  Subsequently, the Clearing Members shall inform the Clearing Corporation about

                  such request.



         Page 5 of 9

4.5.3 Release of Funds: The TMs may then release early pay-out to FPO clients against the

         goods marked for EPI and for which the sale transactions of derivatives contracts has

         been executed by the FPO client on the exchange platform.



4.5.3.1  A maximum of 80% of the value of the sale transaction of the derivatives contract

4.5.3.2  executed on the exchange, may be released as early pay-out to the FPO clients.

         TMs may levy some charges for extending the early pay-out facility to the FPO client

         for the period until the pay-out is settled upon expiry of the derivatives contract. Such

         charges and other terms and conditions relating to the EPO facility should be clearly

         informed to the FPO client in advance and consent from the FPO client should be

         obtained before release of early pay-out.



4.5.4 Settlement: At the time of settlement of the derivatives contracts, the TM shall adjust

         from the payout, the funds released as EPO to the FPO client and any accrued charge,

         and then release the balance settlement amount to the FPO client.



4.5.5 The detailed mechanism of the EPO is provided below:



         Page 6 of 9

4.6 Source of Funds:



4.6.1  For the purpose of providing EPO facility to FPO clients, the TM may use own funds or

4.6.2  borrow funds from scheduled commercial banks and/ or NBFCs regulated by the

4.6.3  Reserve Bank of India, borrow funds by way of Commercial Papers (CPs), by way of

       unsecured long term loans from their promoters and directors and/ or through issuance

       of listed Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) or any other debt instruments.

       The borrowing by way of issuance of CPs/ debt securities shall be subject to compliance

       with appropriate RBI Guidelines. The borrowing by way of unsecured long term loans

       from the promoters and directors shall be subject to the compliance with appropriate

       provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.

       Under no circumstances should funds belonging to other clients be used for the purpose

       of providing EPO facility by the TM.



4.7 Maximum allowable exposure of the TM:



4.7.1 The maximum allowable exposure of the TM towards this facility shall not exceed three

         times of its “net worth”, calculated as per the prescribed guidelines specified in this

         circular.



4.8 Margin related provisions:



4.8.1  The margin exemptions for initial margins, etc., and all other terms and conditions which

4.8.2  have been prescribed for FPO clients availing EPI, shall be applicable as per the extant

       prescribed guidelines.

       Mark-to-Market Margin Handling: With respect to Mark to Market Margin, CCs shall

       continue to compute obligations at clearing member level as per the extant prescribed

       guidelines. Upon final settlement of the contract, the net amount funded by CC towards

       MTM shall be adjusted from the balance pay-out due to the FPO client.



4.9 Restriction on Squaring Off and responsibility of TMs and Stock Exchanges/ Clearing

      Corporations:



4.9.1  The FPO clients after receiving early pay out shall not be permitted to square off such

4.9.2  positions.

4.9.3  The TMs shall ensure that positions where early pay-out has been made are not

       squared off by the FPO clients.

       The Stock Exchange/ Clearing Corporation shall put in place suitable mechanism to

       ensure that the positions where early pay-out is released under this facility are not

       squared off.



                                Page 7 of 9

  4.10 Maintenance of Records:



     4.10.1 The TM shall maintain separate client wise accounts of the FPOs who have availed the

              facility of early pay-out.



     4.10.2 The trading members to maintain records of the funds utilised for the purpose of

              providing EPO to the FPOs. The said records should contain details w.r.t the amount

              released to each client, the source of the funds used for early pay-out, etc.



     4.10.3 The books of accounts and such records w.r.t the details of FPOs availing early payout

              shall be subject to audit. SEBI and stock exchange/s shall have the right to inspect the

              books of accounts and/ or any other documents maintained by the TM w.r.t the early

              pay-out.



  4.11 Due diligence and disclosure:



     4.11.1 A TM should take adequate care and exercise due diligence before providing early

              payout facility to any FPO client.



     4.11.2 The TM shall disclose to the stock exchange/s, the details on gross exposure including

              name of the client, Unique Client Code, name and details of the contract/ commodity on

              which early pay-out of funds request has been made, on or before 12 noon on the

              following day of such request.



     4.11.3 The stock exchanges shall also put in place a suitable mechanism to capture and

              maintain all relevant details including member-wise, client-wise, commodity-wise

              information and source of funds of the TMs, pertaining to early pay-out of funds on their

              exchange, both on daily as well as on cumulative basis.



5. The circular shall come into force within three months from the date of issuance of this circular.



6. The stock exchanges/ clearing corporations are advised to:



  6.1 Make necessary amendments to the bye-laws, rules and regulations for the implementation

         of the above decision immediately.



  6.2 Prepare a detailed SOP setting out the operational guidelines including disclosure formats for

         the EPO facility



  6.3 Bring the provisions of this circular to the notice of the trading members/clearing members of

         the Exchange and also to disseminate the same on the website for easy access to the

         investors/ clients.
```

```text
Media & Notifications

 Advisory Regarding Unregulated Pre-listing Premium often called as Grey Market Premium (GMP) for Upcoming Initial Public Offers (IPOs)

Nov 23, 2026

PR No.: 
76/2026

Advisory Regarding Unregulated Pre-listing Premium often called as Grey Market Premium (GMP) for Upcoming Initial Public Offers (IPOs)

===== [attached PDF] =====
                                                                                                 PR No.75/2026



  Advisory Regarding Unregulated Pre-listing Premium often called as Grey Market

                   Premium (GMP) for Upcoming Initial Public Offers (IPOs)



It has come to the notice of SEBI that Unregulated Pre-listing Premium often called as Grey

Market Premium figures for upcoming IPOs are being widely published across various

websites, digital platforms, newspapers and some SEBI registered intermediaries and

market participants, where they are portrayed as indicators of the likely listing price or

anticipated returns upon listing.



Investors are hereby cautioned that such pre-listing premium figures are unofficial,

unverified, and unregulated at which shares are supposedly traded before they are formally

listed on a recognized stock exchange. These transactions are executed outside the

exchange framework, are not subject to regulatory oversight, carry no settlement guarantee

or investor protection, and follow no formal price-discovery process.



The publication of such pre-listing premium figures may be detrimental to the interests of

investors and contrary to the core principles of transparency and accountability in the

securities market.



In order to safeguard the interest of the investors and maintain transparency and integrity

in the securities market, the publication, display, circulation or dissemination of such



                                                                                                     Page 1 of 2

Unregulated Pre-listing Premium often called as Grey Market Premium through any mode

or platform may be discontinued across the securities market.



All SEBI-registered intermediaries and market participants are advised to refrain from

publishing, displaying, or broadcasting GMP figures for IPOs on their websites, platforms,

or any other communication channels-including email, SMS, and social media.



While investing in the securities market, investors are advised to:



     Not treat GMP as an indicator of listing price or expected returns;

     Refrain from engaging in any GMP-linked transactions, as they fall entirely outside



         the regulatory framework; and

     Transact in IPOs exclusively through SEBI-registered intermediaries and



         authorized platforms.



Non-Availability of Dispute Redressal Recourses



Investors should note that in the event of any dispute arising from or relating to GMP

transactions, none of the following regulatory recourses will be available:



     Investor protection benefits under SEBI or Stock Exchange jurisdiction; and

     Investor grievance redressal mechanisms administered by Stock Exchanges, ог the



         Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) portal administered by Exchanges/Depositories

         (smartodr.in).

Mumbai

November 23, 2026



                                                                                                     Page 2 of 2


```

```text
Nov 23, 2026

76/2026

                                                                                                 PR No.76/2026



 Caution to investors regarding impersonation of SEBI registered intermediaries on

                           closed user groups of social media platforms



It has come to the notice of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) that many

WhatsApp groups are impersonating SEBI registered intermediaries on closed user groups

of social media platforms.

It has been observed that fraudsters are impersonating SEBI registered intermediaries by

creating an impression of legitimacy and inducing investors to open trading accounts.

Investors are being lured to participate in purported institutional trading opportunities by

portraying international stock markets as being more lucrative vis-a-vis Indian stock

markets. These fraudsters are providing recommendations on shares/stocks/indices listed

in international stock markets /Indian stock markets. Investors are being directed to register

on unauthorised trading platforms and transfer funds to designated bank accounts which

are held in the names of unregistered entities.

You may also refer to earlier press releases issued by SEBI cautioning investors regarding

impersonation of SEBI by visiting the link: https://www.sebi.gov.in/media-and-

notifications/press-releases/sep-2025/caution-to-the-public-regarding-impersonation-of-

sebi_96449.html and cautioning against Stock Tips offered through Invitation-only

Whatsapp Groups by visiting the link: https://www.sebi.gov.in/media-and-

notifications/press-releases/oct-2026/caution-to-investors-against-stock-tips-offered-

through-invitation-only-whatsapp-groups_105389.html



                                                                                                     Page 1 of 3

Given below are the red flags that investors should be cautious of, of such fraudsters on

closed user groups include (but are not limited to):



    1) Invitation links: Invitations to join closed user groups (like WhatsApp/ Telegram

         etc.) are sent from unknown sources on social media platforms.



    2) Admin numbers of closed user groups: Admins of the closed user groups may

         usually have mobile numbers with international codes like +44, +65 etc., or may

         also have Indian mobile nos. starting with +91.



    3) Strategy: Investors are enticed through fraudulent claims like ‘Recover your Indian

         portfolio loss from investments in foreign markets’, ‘Off-Market Negotiated Block

         Trades’, ‘Institutional Trades’ and ‘Steady Growth opportunities to recover losses’.



    4) Fake Institutional trading accounts’: Investors are misled into trading through

         fake ‘institutional trading accounts’ by impersonating SEBI registered intermediary.



    5) Stock recommendations: Free recommendations of stocks listed in international/

         Indian securities market are provided



    6) Third Party bank accounts: Investors are enticed to transfer money to third party

         bank accounts which do not belong to SEBI registered entities.



    7) Fraudulent Apps: Investors are given access to download fraudulent apps that

         display the supposedly invested funds transferred by investors and their portfolio.



    8) False sense of legitimacy: Misuse of SEBI website screenshots showing that

         entity is SEBI registered while these fraudsters are impersonating SEBI registered

         entities.



    9) Unauthorized use of SEBI Letter head: Fake SEBI letter heads and fake SEBI

         stamps are used to certify fraudulent bank accounts



    10)Connection with SEBI: Fraudulently state connection with SEBI employees.

    11)Fresh invitation to join closed user group: If a group is suspended, a fresh



         invitation link may be sent to join new closed user groups.

In this regard, investors are advised to:



    1) Verify SEBI registration status: Check SEBI registered entities from the following

         link: https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/other/OtherAction.do?doRecognised=yes



    2) Avoid investments that claim sure shot returns: Exercise caution against

         investment opportunities from unauthentic sources involving institutional

         trades/assured returns/investment in international markets.



                                                                                                     Page 2 of 3

    3) Avoid unverified trading platforms: Refrain from opening accounts on unverified

         trading platforms or transferring funds to bank accounts communicated by unknown

         persons.



    4) Avoid downloading unverified apps: Investors are advised to check ‘verified’

         badge while downloading trading apps from the Play Store.



    5) Check the authorised trading applications: Check authorised mobile apps of

         SEBI registered intermediaries through the following link:

         https://investor.sebi.gov.in/Investor-support.html



    6) Verify the authenticity of bank account details provided: Check bank

         accounts/UPI IDs from the following link:

         https://siportal.sebi.gov.in/intermediary/sebi-check



    7) Avoid joining closed user groups: It is advised to refrain from joining unverified/

         unknown closed user groups via invitation from unknown individuals.



SEBI urges investors to remain vigilant and verify the SEBI registration status before

engaging with any entity offering investment advisory related services on closed user

groups.



Mumbai

November 23, 2026
```

```text
Reports : 
Reports for Public Comments

 Click here to provide your comments " allowfullscreen webkitallowfullscreen>Consultation Paper on proposal to review the Additional Disclosure Framework for Foreign Portfolio Investors. Click here to provide your comments

===== [attached PDF] =====
Consultation Paper on proposal to review the Additional Disclosure Framework

for Foreign Portfolio Investors



1. OBJECTIVE

1.1. To improve ease of doing business for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) by



       reviewing the Additional Disclosure Framework to provide a more investor

       friendly regulatory framework, aligned with global standards and thereby making

       India a preferred investment destination.



2. BACKGROUND

2.1. Foreign capital has been an important constituent in India's economic expansion



       especially since the 1991 liberalization reforms. Foreign capital helps in bridging

       the gap between domestic savings and investment requirements and also

       provides vital foreign exchange to support a growing economy.



2.2. However, the opportunities that such foreign capital provides also come with their

       attendant risks. Mitigation of such risks demands that adequate safeguards are

       in place. Identification of beneficial ownership in the financial system is an

       important mandate emerging from the need to prevent, control and combat

       money laundering, terrorism financing and other related threats for the integrity

       of the international financial system.



2.3. Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is the international policy making body

       established in 1989 to lead global action to tackle money laundering, terrorist and

       proliferation financing. Currently, 40 countries/jurisdictions (including India) are

       members of FATF and more than 200 countries and jurisdictions have committed

       to implement the FATF’s standards. FATF Recommendations provide a

       comprehensive framework of measures to help countries tackle illicit financial

       flows. Recommendation 10 requires financial institutions to undertake Client Due

       Diligence (CDD) and identify the Beneficial Owner (BO) of their clients. While

       FATF has provided respective jurisdictions the flexibility to prescribe their own

       thresholds to determine ownership of client based on ownership interest, it has

       recommended that such threshold should not exceed 25%.



                                                       Page 1 of 7

2.4. In India, ‘The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002’ (PMLA) has been

       enacted to, inter alia, prevent money-laundering. Prevention of Money

       Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (PMLR), provides for

       identification of BO of clients on the basis of controlling ownership interest and

       control. In terms of Rule 9(3) of PMLR, the current threshold for controlling

       ownership interest is 10% /15% depending on the legal form of the client.



2.5. For accessing Indian securities market, Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) register

       with SEBI and also enter into an account based relationship with a custodian,

       bank, depository participant and stock broker as a client. Thus, the PMLR

       requirements related to CDD norms including identification of BO as per the

       extant 10%/15% ownership threshold are applicable to FPIs as well.



2.6. A comparative analysis of global practices adopted for identification of BOs

       indicates that several emerging markets which are FATF members adopt a

       relaxed ownership threshold (typically 25%). Further, developed markets such as

       USA, UK, Canada, Luxembourg, Belgium, Portugal, Netherlands, France,

       Germany, Singapore, Japan and Hong Kong also follow a norm of 25% threshold,

       with lower threshold applicable in some jurisdictions only for high-risk entities.

       Thus, going by global standards, India follows a more stringent regime for

       identification of BOs. There may be a need to review the PMLR, 2005 to make it

       consistent with other jurisdictions. However, this is under the jurisdiction of

       Ministry of Finance.



2.7. Over and above the aforementioned requirement of BO identification, SEBI has

       prescribed an Additional Disclosure Framework (ADF)1. ADF, inter alia, provides

       the criteria for identification of FPIs that are required to submit granular details of

       all entities holding any ownership, economic interest, or exercising control in the

       FPI, on a full look through basis, upto the level of all natural persons, without any

       threshold. The criteria provided under ADF are as follows:



1 Through insertion of Regulations 22(6) and 22(7) in SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 and issuance of

circular dated August 24, 2023, amended from time to time. The said circulars have been subsequently

subsumed into SEBI’s Master circular for FPIs dated May 30, 2024.



                                                       Page 2 of 7

       2.7.1. Concentration criteria: FPI holding more than 50% of their Indian equity

                Assets Under Management (AUM) in a single Indian corporate group



       2.7.2. Size criteria: FPIs, individually or along with their investor group, hold more

                than INR 50,000 crore of equity AUM in the Indian markets. [original limit

                was INR 25,000 crore, increased to INR 50,000 crore vide circular dated

                April 09, 2025]



       2.7.3. Exemption criteria: Certain FPIs, including those having a broad based,

                pooled structure with widespread investor base or those having ownership

                interest by Government or Government related investors have been

                exempted from such additional disclosure requirements, subject to

                conditions.



2.8. An industry-wide Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) has also been adopted in

       consultation with SEBI, for implementation of the ADF.



3. NEED FOR REVIEW of SEBI’s ADF

3.1. In today’s global financial landscape, capital is highly mobile and responsive.



       Investors have access to a vast universe of markets and securities, and their

       allocation decisions are shaped by a range of factors. For any investee

       jurisdiction, many of these determinants remain exogenous and beyond direct

       control. In such times, any measure that increases the compliance burdens may

       reduce the attractiveness of Indian capital markets for foreign investors.



3.2. As stated earlier, the granular disclosure requirements under ADF have been

       prescribed by SEBI over and above the BO identification requirements specified

       under PMLR. Further, such granular disclosure requirements under the ADF are

       unique to India.



3.3. Such disclosure requirements have to be weighed against the prevailing

       requirements in our own jurisdiction as well as other jurisdictions competing for

       the same pool of global monies. Disclosure requirements that are not in line with

       globally accepted practices could potentially place India at a competitive

       disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory

       requirements.

                                                       Page 3 of 7

3.4. India has experienced large FPI outflows which have exerted severe pressure on

       the foreign exchange market and value of INR. FPIs have been net sellers in the

       Indian equity markets for a sustained period starting late 2024, with an exodus

       accelerating through 2025 and early 2026. During the period between October

       2024 and October 2026, FPIs have pulled out more than ₹5.61 lakh crore ($62.24

       billion) from Indian equity market.

3.5. While there may be several factors behind such FPI outflows, the relatively

       onerous rules regarding BO identification and disclosures required as per ADF

       as compared to most of the FATF compliant countries (both developed and

       emerging) necessitate a review of existing processes and rules.



3.6. Policymaking involves a careful balancing act of minimising both Type I errors

       (over-regulation that stifles innovation and market efficiency) and Type II errors

       (under-regulation that may expose the system to risks). Continuous evaluation of

       policy outcomes, informed by stakeholder feedback and evolving market

       conditions, is therefore essential. Accordingly, regulatory fine-tuning has to be an

       ongoing process.



4. ISSUES UNDER CONSIDERATION

4.1. SEBI has received constant feedback from FPIs and other market participants



       regarding the stringent disclosure requirements especially when no such

       disclosure requirements are present in other competing jurisdictions. It is



                                                       Page 4 of 7

       observed that ADF is giving rise to several practical challenges, including the

       following:



         a) FPIs are required to identify and collect information from significantly larger

             number of underlying investors for their Indian investments as compared to

             investments in other jurisdictions.



         b) A global fund which invests in different countries is forced to set up a different

             fund for its Indian investments as compliance levels are different, resulting in

             additional operational and compliance costs.



         c) In case of pooled investment vehicles such as hedge funds, investor holdings

             may change frequently due to subscriptions and redemptions, necessitating

             repeated identification exercises and periodic updates.



         d) Many investors may not be accustomed to providing information beyond

             what is required in their home jurisdictions, leading to practical difficulties in

             obtaining the requisite information and documentation.



         e) In case of FPIs with complex structures, such as ‘fund of fund’ arrangements

             and segregated portfolios, tracing ownership through multiple layers to

             identify natural persons for the purpose of regulatory compliance can be

             time-consuming and costly.



4.2. Many foreign investors looking to invest in India consider the granular disclosure

       requirements as additional compliance burden. Rather than investing in India and

       be subject to granular disclosures, many investors may instead choose to avoid

       investing in India. Therefore, the disclosure requirements for breach of

       ‘concentration criteria’ have practically become an entry barrier for FPIs looking

       to invest in India. In any case, even if an FPI holds a concentrated position in a

       listed entity, such investment is capped at 10% of the shareholding of the listed

       entity.



4.3. Further, specifically with regard to ‘size criteria’, it may be noted that PN3, inter

       alia, provided that an entity or a citizen of a country which shares land border with

       India, or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is a citizen of any

       such country, can invest only under the Government route. While the conditions

       prescribed under PN3 were not made applicable to investments made by FPIs,



                                                       Page 5 of 7

       considering the potential for misuse of the FPI route for circumventing the

       stipulations of PN3, SEBI had included the ‘size criteria’ under the ADF.



4.4. It may be noted that, in absence of a clear definition of BO under PN3, the term

       was purported to include any ownership directly or indirectly. Therefore, even a

       small stake by a person from land bordering countries used to come under the

       purview of conditions placed by PN3. Vide Press Note 02 of 2026 (PN2) dated

       March 15, 2026, Government of India reviewed the FDI Policy and modified the

       investment conditions prescribed via PN3. The definition of ‘beneficial owner’ has

       now been clarified to include only those persons who hold more than the

       thresholds prescribed under PMLR.



4.5. As mentioned earlier, FPIs are also required to provide details of the BOs as per

       the thresholds prescribed under PMLR. Therefore, as far as identification of BO

       is concerned, the position under PN3 (as clarified by PN2) is similar to

       requirements already specified for FPIs. Therefore, the additional requirement

       under ADF to identify all entities holding any ownership or economic interest or

       control in the FPI in case of breach of ‘size criteria’, may not be required.



5. PROPOSAL

5.1. Considering the challenges faced by foreign investors and the change in FDI



       policy as mentioned above, it is proposed to remove the Additional Disclosure

       Framework for FPIs.



5.2. Since the requirements under ADF are also applicable to subscribers of Offshore

       Derivative Instruments (ODIs) and segregated portfolio(s) maintained by FPI, the

       provisions under ADF, applicable to ODI subscribers and segregated portfolio(s)

       of FPI, are also proposed to be removed.



         Question for public comments

         1. Do you agree with proposal to remove Additional Disclosure Framework



             for FPIs?



                                                       Page 6 of 7

6. PUBLIC COMMENTS

6.1. Considering the implications of the aforementioned matters on the market



       participants, public comments are invited on the above proposals. The

       comments/ suggestions should be submitted latest by December 11, 2026,
```
