```text
Consultation Paper on Strengthening the Governance of Market Infrastructure

                                           Institutions (MIIs)



1. Objective



1.1. The objective of this consultation paper is to seek comments / suggestions

         from the public and stakeholders on the proposals relating to strengthening

         the governance of recognised stock exchanges, recognised clearing

         corporations (including Limited Purpose Clearing Corporations) and

         depositories (collectively referred to as “Market Infrastructure Institutions”

         or “MIIs”) under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges

         and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018 (“SECC Regulations”) and

         the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Depositories and Participants)

         Regulations, 2018 (“D&P Regulations”).



2. Background



2.1. Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs), namely stock exchanges, clearing

         corporations and depositories, are the backbone of the securities market.

         They provide the platforms on which securities are traded, cleared, settled

         and held. They are governed by the Securities Contracts (Regulation)

         (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018 (SECC

         Regulations) and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Depositories

         and Participants) Regulations, 2018 (D&P Regulations).



2.2. MIIs perform a first-line regulatory role over their members, participants and

         issuers. Public trust in the market therefore depends on the independence,

         competence and periodic renewal of their governing boards and senior

         leadership. The governance framework under the SECC Regulations and

         the D&P Regulations rests on three pillars: Public Interest Directors (PIDs),

         who hold a quasi-regulatory position on the board; a Managing Director

         (MD) and Executive Directors (EDs) who run the institution; and statutory

         committees through which the board discharges its oversight functions.



2.3. In view of the above, this consultation paper seeks comments / suggestions

         from the public and stakeholders on the following proposals related to the

         governance of MIIs:



2.3.1.  Proposal 1: Reduction in the age limit of PIDs from 75 years to 70

        years and the upper limit on number of terms across MIIs from 3 to

        2.



2.3.2. Proposal 2: Revised limits on the term and tenure of MDs and EDs

          of MIIs.



                                              Page 1 of 14

2.3.3. Proposal 3: Extension of the restriction on simultaneous

          directorships of PIDs to associates of MIIs.



2.3.4. Proposal 4: Reduction in the cap on the number of statutory

          committees on which a PID may be a member, to four.



2.3.5.  Proposal 5: Permitting the Chief Executive of the Association of

        Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), ex officio, to be appointed on the

        governing board of a recognised Limited Purpose Clearing

        Corporation (LPCC), subject to conditions including safeguards

        against conflicts of interest.



3. Proposal 1: Reduction in the age limit of PIDs from 75 years to 70 years and

    the upper limit on number of terms across MIIs from 3 to 2



3.1. Current Framework: A PID may be appointed subject to the maximum age

         limit of 75 years. The PID can be appointed for the term of 3 years. The

         said term is extendable by further term of 3 years in the same MII, or a third

         tenure of 3 years in another MII. The total limit is therefore 3 terms of 3

         years each across MIIs.



3.2. Proposed Framework: A PID may be appointed subject to the maximum

         age limit of 70 years. The PID shall be appointed for the term of 3 years. A

         PID may serve one tenure of 3 years, a second tenure of 3 years on

         reappointment in the same MII or appointment in another MII. The total limit

         is, therefore, proposed to be of 2 terms of 3 years each across MIIs.



3.3. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



3.3.1.  Quasi-regulatory role. A PID is not an ordinary independent director. The

        PID sits on the board of an institution that performs first-line regulatory

        functions and is expected to safeguard the interests of the securities

        market and its investors, rather than those of any shareholder. The role

        therefore carries obligations that are closer to those of a regulator than of

        a company director.



3.3.2.  A more demanding role than an ordinary non-executive role. PIDs meet

        separately among themselves, lead or sit on several statutory committees,

        take part in structured performance reviews and report on matters that

        may involve conflicts of interest for the MII or an impact on the market.

        The workload, time commitment and sustained alertness required are

        materially higher than for a non-executive director of a typical company.

        The age limit should reflect these demands.



        Page 2 of 14

         3.3.3. Change in landscape and skill set requirement. MIIs operate in an

               environment of faster, technology-intensive and more interconnected

               markets, wider product ranges and greater expectations on resilience and

               risk management. The skills expected of a PID now include familiarity with

               rapidly changing technology, cyber and operational risk, and investor-

               protection practices, in addition to experience in law, finance, regulation or

               public administration. An age limit of 70 years supports a PID cohort whose

               experience and skills remain current and who can serve a full term with

               undiminished engagement.



         3.3.4. Stops a narrow pool from recycling. Because a PID may serve up to 3

               terms across MIIs, a small group of individuals can move from one MII to

               another over many years. A lower age limit and a lower term limit brings

               about periodic renewal of the PID cohort, opens the position to a wider and

               more diverse set of professionals and strengthens the independence of

               the board from long-standing familiarity. It also brings new ideas and

               initiatives.



4. Proposal 2: Revised limits on the term and tenure of MDs and EDs of MIIs



         A. Managing Directors



    4.1. Current Framework: The framework is as below:



         4.1.1. The first tenure of an MD can be upto extendable upto 5 years.



         4.1.2. An MD may serve a maximum of 10 years in a single MII. The person

               may then become MD of another MII for on similar terms again, totalling a

               maximum of 10 years.



         4.1.3. There is no limit on the total term across MIIs. The maximum age limit is

               65 years.



    4.2. Proposed Framework: It is proposed that:



         4.2.1. a single term of an MD shall not exceed 5 years;



         4.2.2. an MD may serve a maximum of 2 terms, for a maximum period of 8

               years, in a single MII;



         4.2.3. an MD may serve 3 terms across MIIs; and



         4.2.4. the total period as MD across the MIIs shall not exceed 12 years.

               However, for an individual already serving as an MD as on the date of



                                                      Page 3 of 14

          commencement of this amendment, the overall period as an MD across

          MIIs shall not exceed 15 years, to provide for smooth transition.



4.3. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



    4.3.1. Key man risk and risk of entrenchment: The MD is the most influential

          executive of an MII. A long continuous tenure, followed by a similar tenure

          at another MII, can concentrate institutional knowledge, relationships and

          decision-making in one individual. Over time this raises the risk that the

          institution depends on a single person and that the MD becomes

          entrenched in a way that weakens the checks exercised by the board and

          by SEBI. A defined ceiling on tenure addresses this risk in advance.



    4.3.2. Capping influence over the ecosystem: At present nothing limits the

          total period for which a person may head MIIs. A person can lead one MII

          for 10 years and then another for a further 10 years, and so on. As MIIs

          are interconnected through clearing, settlement, depository and market-

          data linkages, an individual who heads several of them in succession may

          carry a disproportionate influence over the whole ecosystem. Thus, total

          ceiling of 12 years across MIIs may keep that influence within a defined

          limit.



    4.3.3. First-line regulatory nature of MIIs: MIIs frame and enforce rules for

          members and participants, and SEBI relies on them to detect and address

          problems at the first instance. The head of such an institution should hold

          office for a period that preserves objectivity and the ability to take

          unpopular decisions, and should not be positioned for an open-ended

          association with the institution or the industry it oversees.



    4.3.4. Scope for evolution and new ideas: A fixed ceiling ensures regular

          leadership renewal. New leaders bring fresh perspectives, different

          mindsets and new approaches to technology, risk management and

          investor service, which supports continued evolution of the institution.



     B. Executive Directors



4.4. Current Framework: The term and tenure of EDs are aligned with those of

     MDs.



4.5. Proposed Framework:



    4.5.1. a single term of an ED shall not exceed 5 years;



                                                 Page 4 of 14

4.5.2. as ED, a person may serve an aggregate of not more than 8 years in a

        single MII and not more than 16 years across MIIs; and



4.5.3. as ED and MD taken together, a person may serve an aggregate of not

        more than 20 years across MIIs, subject to a maximum of 12 years (as

        ED and MD together) in a single MII.



Position held         Single term Maximum in a single MII  Maximum      across

                                                           MIIs

ED                    Up to 5 years 8 years                16 years

ED and         MD Up to 5 years 12 years                   20 years

together



4.6. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



4.6.1. Preventing EDs from becoming a successor channel across MIIs: If

      EDs are subject to the same terms as MDs, the position of ED can become

      a standing pipeline through which the same individuals move from ED to

      MD, and from one MII to another, for very long periods. The cap on

      aggregate service as ED, and on combined service as ED and MD,

      ensures that the ED position does not defeat the tenure limits proposed for

      MDs.



4.6.2. Support for succession and continuity planning: The ED position is

      a natural step in the development of future MDs. Defined aggregate limits

      give each MII a predictable framework to plan its leadership pipeline, to

      groom successors internally and to time transitions without sudden gaps

      in leadership.



4.6.3. Balance between key man risk and the growth expectations of the

      workforce: Limits on MD tenure address key man risk. At the same time,

      staff of MIIs who aspire to senior executive positions should see a credible

      and orderly path to growth. A ceiling of 8 years as ED in a single MII, with

      a combined ceiling of 12 years as ED and MD, allows a career path to the

      top while keeping all executive tenures within known bounds.



4.6.4. The outer limit of 20 years across MIIs, as ED and MD together, ensures

      that the total period for which an individual may hold executive

      directorships across the MII ecosystem is finite and predictable.



               Page 5 of 14

4.7. For the proposals 1 and 2, a PID, MD or ED holding office on the date of

     commencement of these amendments shall continue to hold office till the end

     of the ongoing term, as per the terms on which they were appointed.



5. Proposal 3: Extension of the restriction on simultaneous directorships of

    PIDs to associates of MIIs



5.1. Current framework: Under Regulation 24(4) of the SECC Regulations and

     Regulation 25(4) of the D&P Regulations, a PID on the board of an MII shall

     not act simultaneously as a director on the board of its subsidiary, on the board

     of any other MII or on the board of a subsidiary of such other MII. The restriction

     does not extend to associates of MIIs.



5.2. Proposed Framework: It is proposed that the restriction be enhanced so that

     a PID shall not hold simultaneous directorships on the boards of any MII, its

     subsidiaries or its associates.



Entities on whose boards a PID cannot simultaneously be a Current  Proposed

director



Subsidiaries of the MII on whose board the PID sits  Yes           Yes



Any other MII                                        Yes           Yes



Subsidiaries of any other MII                        Yes           Yes



Associates of the MII on whose board the PID sits    No            Yes



Associates of any other MII                          No            Yes



5.3. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



    5.3.1. An associate is a connected entity in substance. An associate is an

          entity which holds a significant control or voting power on an MII. In

          substance, such an entity is connected to the MII, and the interests of the

          two are closely aligned.



    5.3.2. It closes the structuring gap. A restriction confined to MIIs and their

          subsidiaries can be avoided by placing an activity or investment in an

          associate, rather than in a subsidiary. Therefore, the the restriction needs

          to be extended to associates.



    5.3.3. It protects the PID’s oversight role. A PID is expected to give

          independent, undivided and un-conflicted attention to the MII on whose

          board the PID sits. Simultaneous directorships in connected entities can

          divide the PID’s time and may also create conflict of interest. A wider



                                                 Page 6 of 14

restriction safeguards the independence of the PID and the credibility of

the oversight role in the eyes of the market.



6. Proposal 4: Reduction in the cap on the number of statutory committees on

    which a PID may be a member, to four



    6.1. Current Framework: An MII has 6 statutory committees in total as per SECC

         Regulations. A PID may be a member of at most 5 committees. The provision

         does not clearly state whether this limit applies to all committees of the board

         or only to statutory committees. If it applies to all committees, it is restrictive. If

         it applies only to statutory committees, a PID can be a member of 5 out of the

         6 statutory committees.



    6.2. Proposed Framework: It is proposed that the cap be fixed clearly at 4

         statutory committees, that is, a PID may be a member of not more than 4

         statutory committees of an MII.



    6.3. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



         6.3.1. Clarity. A cap stated expressly in terms of statutory committees removes

               the present uncertainty about whether non-statutory committees count

               towards the limit, and gives MIIs and PIDs a single, clear standard to

               follow.



         6.3.2. Meaningful participation. Statutory committees take decisions of

               regulatory importance, and PIDs are expected to take an active part in

               them. A PID who is a member of five of the six committees may leave very

               little scope to prepare for, attend and contribute to each of them. A cap of

               4 allows more time and attention for each committee.



         6.3.3. Distribution of oversight. A lower cap leads to wider participation by

               all PIDs in committee work, avoids reliance on a few PIDs for most

               committees and results in a more balanced allocation of responsibilities

               within the board.



7. Proposal 5: Permitting ex-officio representative of the Association of Mutual

    Funds in India (AMFI), to be appointed on the governing board of a

    recognised Limited Purpose Clearing Corporation (LPCC)



7.1. Background and Current Framework



7.1.1.  In its board meeting held on September 29, 2020, SEBI had approved

        the proposals for amendments to the SECC Regulations and the

        relevant circulars to facilitate the setting up of a LPCC for clearing and

        settlement of repo transactions in corporate bonds. Mutual funds, being

        major lenders in the repo market and the dominant participants in the

        secondary market for corporate bonds, were considered to have the



        Page 7 of 14

        desired incentive for setting up the LPCC and AMCs were accordingly

        expected to contribute to its capital.



7.1.2.  The memorandum placed before the SEBI Board on September 29,

        2020 had, inter alia, proposed that a representative of AMFI for a fixed

        term and a representative of one of the top three public sector issuers

        of debt securities on a rotational basis, be permitted on the governing

        board of the LPCC in the category of shareholder directors. The

        rationale then given was that active participation of the stakeholders of

        the repo market on the governing board could be valuable, particularly

        in the initial years and that a representative of AMFI, a non-profit body

        representing the entire body of AMCs, would avoid the difficulty of

        accommodating representatives of individual AMCs.



7.1.3.  The SEBI-Board approved the proposals with the following

        modification: “The representative of AMFI shall not be appointed on the

        governing board of the LPRCC.” The provision for the representative of

        public sector issuers was notified and presently forms sub-regulation

        (2) of Regulation 22C of the SECC Regulations.



7.1.4.  Pursuant to the decision of the SEBI-Board, AMCs contributed Rs. 150

        crore towards the share capital of the AMC Repo Clearing Ltd., the first

        LPCC, in proportion to their average AUM of open-ended debt oriented

        schemes for FY 2020-21, in terms of SEBI circular SEBI Circular No.

        SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2021/17 dated February 02, 2021. Total of

        37 AMCs contributed to the capital. AMC Repo Clearing Limited

        (ARCL) was granted recognition as an LPCC and commenced

        operations in July 2023.



7.1.5.  In terms of the Directions for Central Counterparties (CCPs) issued by

        RBI a CCP is required to have a minimum net worth of Rs. 300 crore.

        The net worth of ARCL stood at Rs. 138.98 crore as on June 30, 2026.

        In the absence of QCCP status granted by RBI, banks and primary

        dealers are required to hold significantly higher capital against their

        exposure to ARCL, which limits their participation. Further, no other

        entity including entities regulated by RBI are mandated to contribute to

        the capital of ARCL. Therefore, the ARCL is in risk of de-recognition if

        it fails to raise capital to comply with net worth requirement of RBI..



7.1.6.  The proposal for representation of AMFI was considered by the SEBI-

        Board in 2020, before the LPCC was set up. Since then, the

        circumstances relating to the LPCC have changed materially, as

        brought out below, which warrant a fresh consideration of the matter:



        Page 8 of 14

7.1.6.1.  ARCL is operational and growing. The traded value of tri-party

          repo cleared by ARCL rose from Rs. 33,778 crore in FY 2023-

          24, its first year of operations, to Rs. 8.19 lakh crore in the first

          half of FY 2026-27 alone. The average daily value rose from Rs.

          211 crore to Rs. 6,656.79 crore over the same period..



7.1.6.2.  Mutual funds are the principal users of the ARCL platform. In

          August 2026, mutual funds accounted for 98.49% of the lending

          value and 97.38% of the lending trades on ARCL. The repo rates

          on ARCL have been observed to be 15 to 25 basis points higher

          than the corresponding TREPS rates, and this benefit accrues

          to the investors in debt schemes.



7.1.6.3.  While ARCL requires further capital, no other market participant

          has shown any concrete interest in significant capital

          contribution. The primary reason is that an investment in ARCL,

          a clearing corporation that bears counterparty risks, carried no

          dividend and exit until early 2027, and also its shares are not

          listable. In such a scenario, to prevent the functioning of an

          important MII from coming to a stop, AMCs are expected to

          contribute again. At the same time, there is no provision in the

          SECC Regulations for the AMCs, as a body, to be represented

          on its governing board.



7.1.6.4.  The urgency of the capital requirement has increased as the

          timeline of compliance is nearing and ARCL also needs capital

          for development of its own clearing and settlement system,

          required to address RBI’s concerns on outsourcing.



7.1.6.5.  Since contribution of further capital is required, representation of

          the owners would bring business interest and expenditure

          control for required activities in the governing board. The AMCs,

          as the owners of ARCL, have a direct interest in its commercial

          viability, cost structure, product development and growth in

          volumes. Their representation would complement the focus of

          the public interest directors on regulatory and risk management

          matters.



7.1.6.6.  Further, governance standards of MIIs have been significantly

          enhanced since 2020. The functions of an MII are now

          segregated into three verticals under Part C of Schedule II of the

          SECC Regulations: critical operations; regulatory, compliance,

          risk management and investor grievance functions; and other



          Page 9 of 14

                        functions including business development. The first two verticals

                        are headed by executive directors who are key management

                        personnel and are required to perform their functions in the

                        interest of the securities market, without revenue-oriented

                        objectives. This segregation, together with an independent

                        internal audit, gives effect to three lines of defence within the MII:

                        operations as the first line, risk management and compliance as

                        the second line, and internal audit as the third line. Oversight is

                        further exercised through the statutory committees of the

                        governing board and through the performance review of public

                        interest directors and the statutory committees. In this

                        framework, the presence of one non-independent director

                        representing the owners on the governing board of an LPCC is

                        adequately counterbalanced.



7.2. Proposed Framework: It is proposed as follows:



    7.2.1. The Chief Executive of AMFI, ex officio, may be appointed on the

          governing board of a recognised LPCC, notwithstanding the restrictions

          under sub-regulations (6) and (7) of Regulation 23 of the SECC

          Regulations.



    7.2.2. Such appointment shall be subject to such conditions as may be

          specified by the SEBI, including those relating to contribution by AMCs to

          the share capital of the LPCC.



    7.2.3. The Chief Executive of AMFI so appointed shall be deemed to be a

          nominee director and, in terms of the proviso to sub-regulation (1) of

          Regulation 23 of the SECC Regulations, shall be treated as a non-

          independent director. The requirement that the number of public interest

          directors shall not be less than the number of non-independent directors

          shall continue to apply.



    7.2.4. The appointment shall be with the prior approval of SEBI under

          Regulation 24(1) of the SECC Regulations and subject to the fit and proper

          criteria. The director shall cease to hold office on the governing board of

          the LPCC upon ceasing to be the Chief Executive of AMFI.



    7.2.5. Safeguards to prevent conflict of interest. As mutual funds are the

          principal trading participants on ARCL, the representation of AMFI on its

          governing board could give rise to conflicts of interest in matters such as

          risk parameters and default management. These are proposed to be

          addressed through the safeguards set out below by way of a circular:



                                                Page 10 of 14

         7.2.5.1. the Chief Executive of AMFI as a Non-Independent Director shall

                 not be a member of the Risk Management Committee, the Members

                 Committee or the Regulatory Oversight Committee of the LPCC;



         7.2.5.2. the Chief Executive of AMFI shall recuse from decisions of the

                 governing board relating to risk management parameters, the Core

                 Settlement Guarantee Fund, default management and matters

                 relating to specific participants; and



         7.2.5.3. the Chief Executive of AMFI shall not have access to data relating

                 to individual participants.



    7.2.6. The safeguards above are additional requirement proposed in view of

          the position of mutual funds as the principal participants on the LPCC.



7.3. Rationale: The proposal is based on the following considerations:



    7.3.1. Representation through AMFI rather than individual AMCs. The capital

          of ARCL is held by 37 AMCs. Representation of individual AMCs would

          either be impracticable or would result in the larger AMCs being

          represented to the exclusion of others. AMFI, a non-profit body

          representing all AMCs, provides a collective voice for the shareholders, as

          recognised in the memorandum of 2020.



    7.3.2. Representation through the Chief Executive of AMFI. The Chief

          Executive of AMFI is a full-time professional appointed by AMFI and is not

          an employee of any AMC. On the other hand, the Chairperson and the

          Vice-Chairperson of AMFI are serving heads of AMCs, whose mutual

          funds are participants on ARCL. Representation through the Chief

          Executive, ex officio, therefore avoids a conflict of interest at the level of

          an individual AMC and provides continuity, as the seat is attached to the

          office rather than to an individual directly linked to a particular AMC.



    7.3.3. Linkage with further capital contribution. Linking the representation with

          further contribution by AMCs aligns the voice of the owners in governance

          with their capital commitment and provides an incentive for the capital

          infusion required by ARCL. Specifying the conditions by way of a circular

          would allow the SEBI to calibrate them to the capital requirement of the

          LPCC from time to time.



                                                Page 11 of 14

Sr.         Current                 Proposed Framework Rationale for change
```

```text
November 19, 2026



Implementation of Security Council Resolution on Democratic People‘s Republic of Korea

(Amendment) Order, 2021: Security Council 1718 Sanctions Committee Updates One Entry

on Its Sanctions List



1. Clause 54 of the SEBI Master Circular, “Guidelines on Anti-Money Laundering (AML)

    Standards and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT)/ Obligations of Securities

    Market Intermediaries under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and rules

    framed thereunder” dated June 06, 2024, inter-alia, states that ‘The Stock exchanges and the

    registered intermediaries shall ensure that in terms of Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities

    (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA) and amendments thereto, they do not have any accounts in the

    name of individuals/ entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of

    having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations

    Security Council (UNSC)’.

    1718 (2006) concerning the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), enacted the
```

```text
*Pending complaints also include complaints wherein entities, Designated Bodies have submitted their Action Taken reports to the investors

within the stipulated time and complaints are kept pending giving opportunity for the investors to escalate in case of dissatisfaction.

Workflow for SCORES 2.0



     As per SCORES 2.0, complaints are automatically forwarded to entity and entity has 21 days to submit the ATR to investor.

     Investor can opt for 1st level review within 15 days if not satisfied with the ATR. The complaint is shown in pending list for 15 days



         despite ATR is submitted by entity.

     If investor does not opt for review, then the complaint is disposed. In case if investor opts for 1st level review then Designated body will



         take up the complaint and submit ATR.

     Investor again has time of 15 days to opt for 2nd level review if not satisfied with the ATR submitted by Designated Body. The complaint



         is shown in pending list for 15 days despite ATR is submitted by Designated Body.

     If investor does not opt for review, then the complaint is disposed.

     In case if investor opts for 2nd level review then SEBI will take up the complaint and submit ATR.

     Complaint is also treated as disposed if investor opts for Online Disputes Redressal (ODR) mechanism.
```

```text
Media & Notifications
 Media & Notifications▼ 

 SEBI hosts IOSCO’s Asia-Pacific Regional Committee Regulatory Roundtable on Market Infrastructure Institutions

Nov 19, 2026

PR No.: 
74/2026

SEBI hosts IOSCO’s Asia-Pacific Regional Committee Regulatory Roundtable on Market Infrastructure Institutions

===== [attached PDF] =====
                                                                                            PR No.74/2026



        SEBI hosts IOSCO’s Asia-Pacific Regional Committee Regulatory

                    Roundtable on Market Infrastructure Institutions



The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), on November 16-17, 2026,

hosted the IOSCO’s Asia-Pacific Regional Committee (APRC) Regulatory

Roundtable on Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs) in Mumbai. The

programme brought together securities market regulators, market infrastructure

institutions and other stakeholders from across the Asia-Pacific region.



SEBI Symposium on Technology Solutions for the Securities Market



The programme commenced with a SEBI Symposium on Technology Solutions for

the Securities Market that featured demonstrations of technology solutions and

systems developed by SEBI in the areas of Supervisory Technology (SupTech) and

Artificial Intelligence (AI) for applications relating to the securities market. The

demonstrations provided participants with insights into how technology and data-

driven approaches can support regulatory supervision, surveillance and market

oversight. The Symposium also featured a demonstration by Nasdaq on the use of

Artificial Intelligence in Market Surveillance.



Joint APRC-WFE Session



A joint APRC-World Federation of Exchanges (WFE) session provided an

opportunity for Regulators and Exchanges to share perspectives on the evolving

role of exchanges and market infrastructure institutions in modern capital markets,

the regulatory considerations underpinning their functioning, and the importance of

developing robust, efficient and resilient market infrastructure.



                                                                                            Page 1 of 2

APRC Regulatory Roundtable



The programme concluded with a Regulatory Roundtable focused on two key areas

of contemporary relevance to securities markets viz. Accelerating Settlement: T+1

and Tokenization.



The session on T+1 settlement explored the experiences of regulators and markets

in transitioning towards shorter settlement cycles, benefits of accelerated settlement

and the challenges associated with such transitions.



The session on Tokenization examined the potential applications and benefits of

distributed ledger technology and tokenization in securities markets. Discussions

included potential efficiencies in issuance, trading and settlement, as well as the

evolving regulatory, technological, legal and risk considerations related to these

technological developments.



SEBI Chairman Mr. Tuhin Kanta Pandey, Vice-Chair of the APRC, acknowledged

the support of IOSCO, APRC and WFE members in making the Roundtable a

success.



Mumbai

November 19, 2026



                   Page 2 of 2


```

- **addressed to / applies to:** The Managing Directors / Chief Executive Officers, All Recognized Clearing Corporations having Commodity Derivatives Segment
- **official URL (detail page):** https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/circulars/nov-2026/review-of-margin-framework-for-commodity-derivatives-segment_105799.html
- **official PDF URL:** https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/nov-2026/1794917100786.PDF
- **effective date:** December 01, 2026
- **local text file name:** SEBI-105799.txt

```text
CIRCULAR



HO/47/16/14(3)2026-MRD-POD1/I/25885/2026        November 17, 2026



To,

The Managing Directors / Chief Executive Officers,

All Recognized Clearing Corporations having Commodity Derivatives Segment



Sir / Madam,



Sub: Review of Margin Framework for Commodity Derivatives Segment



1. The norms relating to margin framework in the commodity derivatives segment are

    prescribed under Chapter 9 of SEBI Master Circular for Commodity Derivatives

    segment dated Aug 04, 2023.



2. Based on representations received from stakeholders, recommendations by the

    Working Group(WG) on 'Review of current regulatory norms applicable to Agri

    Commodity Derivatives Segment' and Risk Management Review

    Committee(RMRC), it has been decided to revise the minimum Initial Margin (IM)

    and minimum Margin Period of Risk (MPOR). Accordingly, the Para 9.1.3.I.a(iv)

    regarding “Minimum value for Initial Margin and minimum MPOR” of Chapter 9 of

    the aforementioned Master Circular stands revised as under:



    (iv) Based on volatility category, minimum initial margin (IM) and minimum MPOR

    shall be as under:



Volatility Category of  Minimum IM                 Minimum MPOR

      Commodity                                 Non-Agri Agri



                        Non-Agri          Agri



  Low                   6%                6%    2  2

Medium

                        8%                8%    2  2

  High

                        10%               10%   3  3

3. The circular shall come into force from December 01, 2026.



4. This circular shall be applicable for a period of one year from the date of issuance

    of this circular. Provided that the Board may, if considered necessary, extend this

    period, by way of a separate circular issued in this regard.



5. The MIIs are advised to:

    5.1. take necessary steps and put in place necessary systems for implementation

         of the above.

    5.2. make necessary amendments to the relevant bye-laws, rules and regulations,

         wherever required, for the implementation of the above; and,

    5.3. bring the provisions of this circular to the notice of the market participants

         (including investors) and disseminate the same on their website.



6. This circular is issued in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 11(1) of

    the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act 1992, read with Regulation 51 of

    the Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing

    Corporations) Regulations, 2018, to protect the interests of investors in securities

    and to promote the development of, and to regulate the securities market.



7. The Circular is issued with the approval of the competent authority.



8. This Circular is available on SEBI website www.sebi.gov.in under the category

    "Circulars" and "Info for Commodity Derivatives".



                                                                                             Yours faithfully,



                                                                                              Neetika Rajpal

                                                                               Deputy General Manager

                                                                        Market Regulation Department

                                                                            Email: neetikar@sebi.gov.in

                                                                   Phone Number: +91-22-26449628
```

```text
PR No.73/2026



SEBI Constitutes a Sub-Group of PMAC to Review Specified Provisions of the SEBI

                                          (ICDR) Regulations, 2018



The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has constituted a Sub-Group of the

Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) to review Chapters II, IIA, IV, V and VI of

the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 (“ICDR

Regulations”), along with the relevant Schedules and related regulatory directions.



The review aims to identify opportunities to facilitate ease of access to the capital market

for eligible issuers, simplify and rationalise regulatory requirements, eliminate duplicative

disclosures and procedures, and improve regulatory clarity and consistency, while

maintaining adequate disclosures, investor protection and market integrity.



The Terms of Reference of the Sub-Group are as follows:



1. Review of Eligibility Conditions: Review of eligibility conditions applicable to issuers

    under the relevant modes of capital raising, including conditions governing IPOs, FPOs,

    preferential issues and QIPs, as applicable.



2. Review of Lock-in Provisions: Review of lock-in requirements applicable to promoters,

    pre-issue capital, securities allotted under preferential issues and other relevant

    categories, as applicable to the respective modes of capital raising.

                                                                                                     Page 1 of 4

3. Review of Application, Allocation and Allotment Mechanism: Review of the application

    process, allocation methodology and allotment mechanism applicable to the respective

    modes of capital raising, including related procedural requirements.



4. Review of Disclosure Requirements: Review and rationalisation of disclosure

    requirements applicable to IPOs, FPOs, preferential issues and QIPs, including

    disclosures in offer documents and other relevant documents prescribed under the ICDR

    Regulations and the relevant Schedules.



5. Review of Pricing and Price Discovery Framework: Review of pricing requirements and

    the applicable price discovery framework, including determination and disclosure of the

    price or price band, floor price and other related requirements, as applicable to the

    respective modes of capital raising.



6. Review of Due Diligence Requirements: Review of the format, content and requirements

    relating to due diligence certificates and other due diligence submissions by lead

    manager(s) and other relevant intermediaries, as applicable.



7. Review of Related Regulatory Directions: Review of relevant SEBI circulars, advisories,

    general orders and other directions or instructions issued in relation to the aforesaid

    provisions, with a view to identifying the need for their consolidation, modification or

    alignment with the ICDR Regulations.



8. Review of Other Related Requirements: Examination of other regulatory and procedural

    requirements under the aforesaid Chapters and Schedules, including inconsistencies,

    ambiguities, duplicative requirements and implementation-related issues, and

    recommendation of appropriate changes, wherever necessary.



9. Other Matters: Examination of any other matter incidental or relevant to the above, as

    considered necessary by the Sub-Group.



                                                                                                     Page 2 of 4

The composition of the Sub-Group is as follows:



S. No.                 Name and Designation              Capacity

   1.                    Shri Ashish Chauhan             Chairman

   2.                                                     Member

   3.    Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer,     Member

   4.      National Stock Exchange of India Limited       Member

   5.                Shri Gopalan S Raghavan              Member

   6.                      Executive Director             Member

   7.                          BSE Limited                Member

   8.                  Shri Prasanna Kumar D              Member

   9.                           President                 Member



        The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India      Page 3 of 4

                    Shri Pawan Kumar Chandak

                                President



        The Institute of Company Secretaries of India

                            Shri J. N. Gupta



                Co- Founder & Managing Director

               Stakeholder Empowerment services

         CII National Committee on Financial Markets

The Sub-Group may co-opt additional members or invite subject matter experts and

other relevant stakeholders for its deliberations, as considered appropriate.



The Sub-Group shall be supported by the concerned team of SEBI for providing

necessary secretarial and technical assistance in its deliberations.



The recommendations of the Sub-Group will be placed before PMAC for consideration.
```

```text
                                             PART B — DETAILED APPLICATION



1. Brief background of the Applicant and eligibility under the Scheme



1.1 Navigant Corporate Advisors Limited (the “Applicant™) is a company incorporated under the Companies

Act, 1956 and holds a valid Certificate of Registration as a Merchant Banker granted by the Securities and

Exchange Board of India (“SEBI” / “Board”) under the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992 (the “MB

Regulations”). The Applicant is duly compliant with all applicable provisions of the MB Regulations.



1.2 Being an intermediary registered with the Board, the Applicant is eligible to seek informal guidance under

Paragraph 6(a) of the Scheme.



1.3 The application relates to the Applicant’s own, existing and continuing business activities. The Applicant

therefore has a direct and proximate interest in the subject matter of the application, and the application does

not involve any hypothetical situation.



2. Purpose of this application



2.1 The Applicant seeks an Interpretive Letter under Paragraph 7(b) of the Scheme on the interpretation and

applicability of Regulation 13A of the MB Regulations, as amended, specifically in relation to valuation

activities carried out by the Applicant under:



       (a) the Income-tax Act, 1961 and/or the Income-tax Act, 2025, read with the Income-tax Rules

       (collectively, the “IT Act”); and



       (b) the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 framed under the Foreign

       Exchange Management Act, 1999 (the “NDI Rules”).



2.2 The guidance is sought so as to enable the Applicant to determine, with regulatory certainty, whether such

valuation assignments must be concluded within the transitional period prescribed under Regulation 13A(4) of

the MB Regulations, or whether they may lawfully be continued as permissible activities under Regulation

13A(2)(iii).



3. Regulatory framework— Regulation 13A of the MB Regulations



3.1 The SEBI (Merchant Bankers) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (the “Amendment Regulations™) were

notified on December 03, 2025 and came into force on January 01, 2026. Regulation 13A of the MB Regulations

was substituted thereby. The relevant sub-regulations are reproduced below for ready reference.



3.2 Regulation 13A(2) — Permissible activities:



       “4 merchant banker may also undertake —



       (i) other activities regulated by the Board in accordance with the respective regulations made by the

      Board by obtaining the relevant certificate of registration; and/or



       (ii) activities which fall under the purview of any other financial sector regulator or an authority specified

       by the Board, in accordance with the regulations or guidelines, if any, issued by such financial sector

       regulator or authority; and/or



       (iii) activities that do not fall under the purview of the Board or any other financial sector regulator or

       authority, which shall be fee-based, non-find based and pertain to the financial services sector;



       on an arms-length basis through separate business units of such merchant banker, in such manner and

       subject to such other conditions as may be specified by the Board.”



3.3 Regulation 13A(4) — Transitional provision for valuation activities:



       “The merchant banker that does not possess the registration for valuation related activities from the

       relevant regulatory authority shall conclude the existing valuation assignments undertaken by it within a

      period of nine months from the date of coming into force of the Securities and Exchange Board of India

       (Merchant Bankers) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025.”

4. Nature of the valuation activities carried out by the Applicant



4.1 The Applicant presently undertakes valuation assignments in the following two distinct regulatory contexts.



4.2 Valuation under the IT Act (IT Act Valuation). The Applicant determines the fair market value (FMV)

of unquoted equity shares and other assets as required under various provisions of the IT Act, including the

provisions corresponding to Section 56(2)(x) and Section S0CA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with Rules

11U, 11UA and 11UAA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 (and the equivalent or successor provisions under the

Income-tax Act, 2025). These valuations are required for fiscal purposes such as computation of income,

determination of deemed consideration and the anti-abuse provisions relating to transfer of property for

inadequate consideration.



4.3 Valuation under the NDI Rules (FEMA Valuation). The Applicant undertakes valuations for the purposes

of pricing of equity instruments in transactions involving foreign direct investment, issue of equity instruments

to persons resident outside India, and transfer of equity instruments between persons resident in India and

persons resident outside India, in compliance with the pricing guidelines prescribed under Rule 21 of the NDI

Rules read with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.



4.4 In each case the activity is advisory and certification-based in character: it is fee-based, non-fund based, and

pertains to the financial services sector. The Applicant does not assume any principal position, does not deploy

its own funds, and does not undertake any fund-based exposure in connection with such assignments.



5. Position under the IT Act and the NDI Rules regarding eligibility of the valuer



5.1 The Applicant respectfully submits that neither the IT Act nor the NDI Rules prescribes a separate

registration, licence or authorisation as a pre-condition for undertaking the valuation assignments described in

Paragraph 4 above. In particular:



       (i) neither framework requires such valuations to be undertaken only by a person registered as a “registered

       valuer” with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India under Section 247 of the Companies Act,

       2013 read with the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017, nor by a person registered

       in any other authority in a valuation-specific capacity; and



       (ii) there is accordingly no “registration for valuation related activities™ issued by any “relevant regulatory

       authority™ that the Applicant could obtain in respect of these particular assignments.



5.2 On the contrary, both frameworks expressly recognise a SEBI-registered Merchant Banker as an

eligible valuer for these purposes. Under the relevant Income-tax Rules, the fair market value of unquoted

equity shares determined under the discounted free cash flow method is required to be determined by amerchant

banker. Similarly, Rule 21 of the NDI Rules requires the price of equity instruments to be worked out in

accordance with any internationally accepted pricing methodology on an arm’s length basis, duly certified by

a Chartered Accountant, a SEBI-registered Merchant Banker or a practising Cost Accountant. The

Applicant’s certificate of registration as a Merchant Banker granted by the Board is therefore itself the

qualification that the applicable frameworks recognise for the performance of these assignments.



6. Legal analysis and submissions



6.1 Regulation 13A(4) is, on its plain language, a transitional provision addressed to a specific class of merchant

bankers, namely those that do not possess “registration for valuation related activities from the relevant

regulatory authority™. The provision presupposes the existence of (a) a relevant regulatory authority, and (b) a

registration granted by that authority for valuation related activities.



6.2 Where the applicable law does not contemplate any such registration for the valuation in question, the

condition that triggers Regulation 13A(4) is not satisfied, and the nine-month wind-down obligation would, on

a purposive and harmonious construction, not be attracted. A contrary reading would produce the anomalous

result that a merchant banker must discontinue an activity which the applicable law expressly permits it to

perform in its capacity as a merchant banker, and for which no registration is available to be obtained.

6.3 The valuation activities described in Paragraph 4 above are not regulated as a distinct or separately registered

financial activity by the Board or by any other financial sector regulator or authority. While the Income-tax Act

and the NDI Rules prescribe the circumstances in which valuations are required and recognise a SEBI-registered

Merchant Banker as an eligible valuer, they do not require the valuer to obtain any separate registration, licence

or authorisation for undertaking such valuation assignments. These activities are advisory and certification-

based in nature, are fee-based and non-fund based, and pertain to the financial services sector. Accordingly, the

Applicant is of the prima facie view that such activities fall within the scope of Regulation 13A(2)(iii) of the

MB Regulations.



6.4 The Applicant is, in the premises, of the prima facie view that such valuation activities may be continued

under Regulation 13A(2)(iii), through a separate business unit and on an arm’s-length basis, subject to

compliance with the conditions prescribed thereunder and with such manner and conditions as may be specified

by the Board, without attracting the transitional obligation under Regulation 13A(4). The Applicant seeks the

Board’s interpretive guidance to confirm this understanding.



6.5 The Applicant confirms that it will, in any event, conduct such activities through a separate business unit on

an arm’s-length basis and in compliance with all conditions that may be specified by the Board in this regard.



7. Query / clarification sought



The Applicant respectfully submits that the interpretation set out above reflects its bona fide understanding of

the applicable legal provisions, and seeks the Board’s guidance in order to obtain regulatory certainty. In view

of the foregoing, the Applicant seeks an Interpretive Letter on the following queries:



Query 1: Whether Navigant Corporate Advisors Limited, a Merchant Banker registered with SEBI, is permitted

to continue carrying out valuation activities under the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Income-tax Act, 2025 (including

FMV-based valuations for fiscal purposes) and under the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt

Instruments) Rules, 2019 (including pricing-related valuations for foreign direct investment and resident-non-

resident transfer transactions), in the absence of any mandatory registration requirement for such valuation

activities under the said laws, without being subject to the nine-month wind-down obligation prescribed under

Regulation 13A(4) of the MB Regulations.

Query 2: Whether such valuation activities, in the absence of any requirement of registration under the

applicable statute or rules, qualify as permissible activities under Regulation 13A(2)(iii) of the MB Regulations

— being fee-based, non-fund-based activities pertaining to the financial services sector which do not fall under

the purview of the Board or of any other financial sector regulator or authority — subject to compliance with

the conditions prescribed thereunder.

8. Statements required under the Scheme



8.1 The application is not general in nature and completely and sufficiently describes the factual situation

(Paragraph 11(a) of the Scheme).



8.2 The application does not involve any hypothetical situation; it relates to valuation assignments actually

undertaken and presently being undertaken by the Applicant (Paragraph 11(b)).



8.3 The Applicant has a direct and proximate interest in the subject matter of the application (Paragraph 11(c)).



8.4 All applicable legal provisions have been cited in Part A and in Paragraphs 3 to 6 above (Paragraph 11(d)).



8.5 To the best of the Applicant’s knowledge and belief, no No-action Letter or Interpretive Letter has been

issued by any Department of the Board on a substantially similar question involving substantially similar facts

(Paragraph 11(e)).



8.6 No investigation, enquiry, adjudication or other enforcement action has been initiated against the Applicant

in relation to the subject matter of this application (Paragraph 11(f)), and no connected issue is pending before

any Tribunal or Court or is otherwise sub judice (Paragraph 11(g)).



8.7 Confidentiality: The Applicant does not seek confidential treatment under Paragraph 15 of the Scheme.

9. Supporting documents

The following documents are enclosed with this application:



       (a) Copy of the Certificate of Registration as Merchant Banker issued by SEBI — Annexure I;

       (b) Copy of the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Applicant — Annexure IT;

       (c) Duly signed undertaking-cum-declaration of the Applicant — Annexure III; and

       (d) Proof of payment of fee together with payment particulars in the format prescribed under Paragraph

       8(c) of the Scheme — Annexure IV.

10. Fee

The fee of 350,000/ (Rupees Fifty Thousand only), together with applicable GST, prescribed under Paragraph

8(c) of the Scheme has been paid. Proof of payment and the payment particulars in the prescribed format are

enclosed as Annexure IV. A copy of the payment confirmation has also been sent to tad@sebi.gov.in in the

format prescribed under Paragraph 8(c).

11. Conclusion

The Applicant respectfully requests the Board to consider this application and to issue an Interpretive Letter on

the queries raised herein at the earliest, so as to enable the Applicant to conduct its business in a compliant and

certain regulatory environment, particularly having regard to the transitional period prescribed under Regulation

13A(4).

The Applicant remains available to furnish any further information or clarification that the Board may require

in connection with this application, and undertakes to respond to any clarification sought within the timelines

prescribed under Paragraph 10 of the Scheme.



Thanking you,



Yours faithfully,



For Navigant Corporate Advisors Limited



      Q



Sarthak Vijlani

Managing Director

DIN: 05174824



Date: 05.08.2026

Place: Mumbai



Encl.: AnnexuresI to IV, as above.
```

```text
PR No.72/2026



        Inauguration of SEBI’s Pavilion at the IITF, 2026 by Chairman, SEBI



The 45th India International Trade Fair (IITF), the annual multi-product exhibition

organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO) under the Ministry of

Commerce and Industry, Government of India, is being held at Bharat Mandapam,

New Delhi, from November 14–27, 2026.



As part of its continued efforts to showcase India’s well-regulated securities market

and to promote investor awareness and education, the Securities and Exchange

Board of India (SEBI), in association with NSE, BSE, MCX, MSEI, NCDEX, CDSL,

NSDL, KFin Technologies, CAMS, OBPP Association, CPAI, IRA, BIA, AMFI and

NISM, has set up a pavilion titled “Bharat Ka Share Bazaar” in Hall No. 4 at the fair.



In keeping with the overall IITF theme “Vikas aur Virasat”, this year’s Pavilion

presents India’s securities market, whose roots go back over 150 years, as a key

enabler of the nation’s journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047.



The Pavilion was inaugurated on November 14, 2026, by Shri Tuhin Kanta Pandey,

Chairman, SEBI, in the presence of SEBI officials, dignitaries from the participating

institutions and participants from across the securities market ecosystem.



In his address, the Chairman appreciated the joint effort of SEBI and the participating

institutions to promote investor awareness and education and expressed happiness

that the Pavilion has expanded since last year, with new participants. Chairman urged

the institutions to pay close attention to the discussions with the visitors to identify

processes that can be simplified and services that can be improved. He also

highlighted SEBI’s campaign “Samajh Se Investing Simple” under Project Jagrook

and the “Check, Validate and Verify” safety message, and advised investors to



                                                                                            Page 1 of 2

understand an investment, check its authenticity and consider its risks before making

a decision.

The Pavilion showcases SEBI’s continuous efforts toward investor protection and

market integrity while making financial education interactive and experiential. It

features an AI Zone and an Investor Facilitation Camp (IFC), where visitors can

interact directly with officials and learn about safe investment practices.

Quizzes and games with exciting prizes will be held throughout the fair. These

initiatives aim to make investor education engaging, experiential and inclusive, while

also cautioning the public against illegal money mobilisation schemes, unregistered

entities and fraudulent investment offers, including those on social media and

messaging platforms.

The “Bharat Ka Share Bazaar” Pavilion truly embodies the spirit of “Vikas aur

Virasat”, bringing together the legacy of India’s securities market and its modern,

technology-driven present. It invites every citizen, from students and first-time

investors to senior citizens, to participate in the nation’s growth journey as informed

and protected investors.

Mumbai

November 15, 2026
```

- **official URL (detail page):** https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/circulars/nov-2026/reporting-requirement-under-foreign-account-tax-compliance-act-fatca-and-common-reporting-standard-crs-revised-through-income-tax-act-2025-read-with-income-tax-rules-2026_105705.html

```text
CIRCULAR



HO/38/14/(18)2026-MIRSD-POD2/I/25560/2026  November 11, 2026



To,

All Intermediaries registered with SEBI

All Stock Exchanges

All Depositories



Dear Sir/Madam,



Sub: Reporting requirement under Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and

Common Reporting Standard (CRS) revised through Income-Tax Act, 2025 read with

Income-Tax Rules, 2026



1. SEBI, vide Circular no. CIR/MIRSD/2/2015 dated August 26, 2015, Circular no.

    CIR/MIRSD/3/2015 dated September 10, 2015 and Circular no.

    SEBI/HO/MIRSD/SECFATF/P/CIR/2024/12 dated February 20, 2024, informed all

    intermediaries registered with Board regarding reporting requirements and due diligence

    under Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (“FATCA”) and Common Reporting Standards

    (“CRS”). The aforesaid circulars were issued in terms of Section 285BA of the Income-Tax

    Act, 1961, read with Rule 114F to 114H, and Form 61B of the Income-Tax Rules, 1962.



2. With recent changes in the Income Tax regime, the Income Tax Act, 2025, read with the

    Income Tax Rules, 2026 (hereinafter referred to as “IT Rules, 2026”), has replaced the

    Income Tax Act, 1961, read with the Income Tax Rules, 1962, with effect from April 1,

    2026. The reporting requirements under the Automatic Exchange of Information (“AEOI”)

    framework for reportable accounts under FATCA/CRS reporting have been revised in

    terms of Section 508 of the Income Tax Act, 2025, read with Rules 238, 239, and 240, and

    Form 166 of the IT Rules, 2026.



3. In terms of Rule 239(12)(a) of the IT Rules, 2026, the regulator is required to issue

    instructions or guidelines to its regulated financial institutions to incorporate the reporting

    and due diligence procedures specified under Rules 238 to 240, prescribe the manner and

    procedure for maintaining account information, and ensure its availability to satisfy

    reporting obligations.



4. The reporting obligations apply to entities that qualify as Reporting Financial Institutions

    (“RFIs”). "RFI" is defined in Rule 238(8) of the IT Rules, 2026, and "Financial Institution"

    is defined in Rule 238(3) of the IT Rules, 2026."



5. Accordingly, all registered intermediaries, who are RFI, shall take the necessary steps to

    ensure compliance with Rules 238 to 240 of the IT Rules, 2026, and are advised to refer

    to the Guidance Note on FATCA and CRS issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes.



    5.1. IT Rules, 2026 are available at https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/income-tax-rule-

          2026



                 Page 1 of 2

5.2. Guidance Note on FATCA and CRS dated July 24, 2026, providing guidance to



Reporting  Financial    Institutions  (RFIs),  is  available                      at



https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/e-book-crs-and-fatca-



guidance-note-faqs-pdf



6. Registered intermediaries shall incorporate AEOI reporting and due diligence

    requirements into their customer onboarding and Know Your Customer (KYC) frameworks,

    and maintain the information required to meet their obligations under the IT Rules, 2026.

    Registered intermediaries shall, inter alia, review and update the following in accordance

    with the IT Rules, 2026:



6.1. Self-certification collection procedures to capture the validity indicator;



6.2. Controlling Person identification systems to capture roles (settlor/trustee/

     protector/beneficiary/other);



6.3. Account classification systems to capture account type and pre-existing/new status;



6.4. Form 166 XML generation software to include all new mandatory fields. Failure to

     include required fields will result in validation errors on the Income Tax portal.



7. Registered intermediaries shall upload the FATCA and CRS certification obtained from

    clients onto the systems of the KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs).



8. The onus of obtaining and reporting the FATCA and CRS certification and related

    compliances shall lie solely with the respective intermediaries.



9. This circular is issued in exercise of powers conferred under Section 11(1) of Chapter IV

    of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 read with Rule 239(12)(a) of the

    Income-tax Rules, 2026, to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote

    the development of, and to regulate the securities markets.



10. This circular is available on SEBI website at www.sebi.gov.in under the category: ‘Legal

      → Circulars’.



                                                   Yours faithfully,



                                                           Bhumika Kanojia

                                               Deputy General Manager

                                               Tel no.: +91- 22-2644 9202



                                                     bhumikak@sebi.gov.in



                        Page 2 of 2
```

```text
===== [attached PDF] =====
   Consultation paper on Introduction of Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the

    Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) Certification requirement for Principal Officer



1. Objective

    1.1. The objective of this consultation paper is to seek comments/suggestions from the

          public and stakeholders on the proposal relating to introduction of Anti-Money

          Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) certification

          requirement for Principal Officer of all intermediaries registered with SEBI under

          Section 12 of the SEBI Act, 1992.

    1.2. The proposed certification is intended to strengthen the knowledge, competence and

          professional capacity of Principal Officers responsible for implementation of AML/CFT

          compliances in the securities market.



2. Background

    2.1. The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (“PMLA”) and the Prevention of

          Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (“PML Rules”), inter-alia

          prescribe obligations for reporting entities, including intermediaries registered with

          SEBI.

    2.2. As per Rule 2(f) of the PML Rules, the ‘Principal Officer’ has been defined as ‘an

          officer designated by a registered intermediary; provided that such officer shall be an

          officer at the management level’.

    2.3. SEBI has issued the Master Circular dated June 06, 2024 on ‘Guidelines on Anti-

          Money Laundering Standards and Combating the Financing of Terrorism / Obligations

          of Securities Market Intermediaries under the PMLA and Rules framed thereunder’.

          The Master Circular inter-alia provides for appointment of a ‘Principal Officer’ by

          registered intermediaries, including the following responsibilities of a Principal Officer:

         2.3.1. To timely report suspicious transactions to the authorities (FIU-IND);

         2.3.2. To record reasons for treating any transaction or a series of transactions as

                   suspicious

         2.3.3. To act as a central reference point in facilitating onward reporting of suspicious

                   transactions;

         2.3.4. To play an active role in the identification and assessment of potentially

                   suspicious transactions.

    2.4. Further, the Master Circular provides that registered intermediaries should give due

          regard to risk of money laundering and terrorist financing while hiring and ensuring

          existing personnel taking up key positions are fully suitable and competent to perform

          their duties. Additionally, registered intermediaries should conduct ongoing employee



1|Page

          training programmes covering AML/CFT procedures and sensitizing their clients

          about regulatory requirements under AML/CFT framework.



3. Proposals for consideration

    3.1. Proposal 1: Certification for Principal Officer: The role and responsibilities of the

          Principal Officer include overseeing and ensuring overall compliance with the

          regulatory guidelines on AML/CFT framework. The Principal Officer is expected to

          have adequate understanding of :

           3.1.1. the provisions of the PMLA, 2002 and PML Rules, 2005;

           3.1.2. SEBI's AML/CFT framework;

           3.1.3. Customer due diligence and Beneficial ownership requirements;

           3.1.4. Risk-based classification of clients;

           3.1.5. Enhanced due diligence;

           3.1.6. Identification and assessment of suspicious transactions;

           3.1.7. Reporting requirements to FIU-IND;

           3.1.8. Confidentiality and prohibition against tipping-off;

           3.1.9. Targeted financial sanctions under UAPA;

           3.1.10. Requirements relating to proliferation financing under the WMD Act;

           3.1.11. FATF high-risk jurisdictions;

           3.1.12. Transaction monitoring systems;

           3.1.13. Maintenance and retrieval of records; and

           3.1.14. Emerging ML/TF risks, including risks arising from new products, technologies

                     and delivery mechanisms.

    3.2. The effective implementation of the AML/CFT framework depends on Principal Officer

          possessing adequate knowledge and competence to discharge their responsibilities.

    3.3. At present, the Master Circular issued by SEBI provides for mandatory appointment

          of the Principal Officer at the management level. However, the said Circular does not

          prescribe any AML/CFT related certification requirement for the Principal Officer.

    3.4. So, the level of AML/CFT knowledge/expertise of Principal Officers may vary across

          intermediaries.

    3.5. SEBI prescribes various NISM certifications for persons engaged or employed by

          securities market intermediaries under Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Certification of

          Associated Persons in the Securities Markets) Regulations, 2007. Currently, there are

          a total of 28 NISM certifications mandated for different categories of persons engaged

          or employed by intermediaries. A few of these certifications are listed below:



2|Page

Sl. NISM certification                     Certificate Mandated For

No.



1 NISM-Series-III-A:    Securities Compliance officer of an Intermediaries

                                           of mutual fund products.

                                           related to investor funds, the redressal

        Adviser (Level 1) and NISM-Series- investment advisory services.

        Issue and Share Transfer Agents – listed companies or mutual funds at an



        Corporate and NISM-Series-II-B: RTA.

        Transfer Agents - Mutual Fund



3.6. Considering the central role performed by Principal Officers in ensuring compliance



with AML/CFT framework, it is proposed that AML/CFT related certification may be



introduced for the Principal Officers.



Proposal 1

Whether AML/CFT certification be made mandatory for every Principal Officer

of a SEBI-registered intermediary?



3.7. Proposal 2: Certification Institute: As part of SEBI’s ongoing efforts to strengthen

     the capital market, SEBI has been organising outreach programs on Anti-Money

     Laundering (AML) and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) framework for the

     benefit of securities market intermediaries. Towards this objective, the certification

     course on AML/CFT Provisions in Securities Market Certification Examination, has

     been conceptualized and developed by SEBI in collaboration with NISM.



3.8. Vide communique dated February 07, 2025, NISM announced the launch of NISM-

     Series-XXIV: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism

     Provisions (AML and CFT) in Securities Market Certification Examination w.e.f. Feb

     28, 2025. The Certification examination covers various aspects related to Anti Money



3|Page

          Laundering (AML), Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) and Proliferation

          Financing (PF), requirements under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002

          (PMLA) and PML Rules, 2005, Scheduled Offences, AML and CFT Guidelines issued

          by SEBI, KYC Guidelines, PMLA related cases etc.

    3.9. This certification examination seeks to create a common minimum knowledge

          benchmark for the employees of securities market intermediaries about AML/CFT

          Provisions in Securities markets.

   3.10.In view of the above, it is proposed that the above NISM certification conducted by

          National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) may be mandated for Principal

          Officers.



            Proposal 2

            Whether NISM-Series-XXIV: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the

            Financing of Terrorism Provisions (AML and CFT) in Securities Markets

            Certification Examination be mandated for Principal Officers?



 3.11. Proposal 3: Timeline for acquiring the certification: To ensure that Principal

         Officers possess an adequate understanding of their statutory obligations under Anti-

         Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) framework

         through formal certification, it is proposed that all Principal Officers shall successfully

         complete the prescribed certification course within the following specified timelines.

         3.11.1. For existing Principal Officers: Within a maximum period of six (6) months

                     from the date of issuance of this requirement.

         3.11.2. For newly appointed Principal Officers: Within a maximum period of six (6)

                     months from the date of their official appointment.



 3.12. A Principal Officer shall continuously hold and maintain the validity of the said

         certification at all times throughout their tenure while discharging their official duties

         and responsibilities under the SEBI Guidelines on Anti-Money Laundering (AML)

         Standards and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) / Obligations.

            Proposal 3

            Whether the timeline of six (6) months for compliance with the certification

            requirement should be mandated for both existing and newly appointed

            Principal Officers?



4|Page

4. Public Comments

    4.1. Public comments are invited on the proposals 1 to 3 as mentioned above and

          draft Circular in the matter placed at Annexure A. The comments / suggestions along

          with rationale should be submitted no later than November 27, 2026, through the

          following link of web based form:

                   https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/publiccommentv2/PublicCommentAction.do?

                   doPublicComments=yes

          It may be noted that the comments/suggestions should be mandatorily

To,

         and Exchange Board of India Act, 19922.

Dear Sir/Madam,



Subject: NISM Certification for Principal Officer under AML/CFT Guidelines



1. In terms of Paragraph 76 of SEBI Master Circular no.

    SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSDSECFATF/P/CIR/2024/78 dated June 06, 2024,

    registered Intermediaries are required to appoint a Principal Officer to fulfill

    compliance obligations under the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance

    of Records) Rules, 2005 (PML Rules) and SEBI Guidelines on Anti-Money

    Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT).



2. To ensure that Principal Officers possess an adequate understanding of their

    statutory obligations under Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing

    of Terrorism (AML/CFT) framework and effectively discharge their obligations, it

    has been decided that all Principal Officers of registered Intermediaries shall hold

    a valid certification of "NISM-Series-XXIV: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating

    the Financing of Terrorism Provisions (AML and CFT) in Securities Markets

    Certification Examination" conducted by the National Institute of Securities Markets

    (NISM).



3. A Principal Officer shall continuously hold and maintain the validity of the aforesaid

    certification at all times throughout their tenure while discharging their official duties

    and responsibilities.



4. The Principal Officer shall successfully complete the course within six (6) months

    from the date of issuance of this circular, or from the date of their appointment as

    such, as the case may be.



5. All registered intermediaries shall ensure strict compliance with these provisions.

    Further, apart from the Principal Officer, other employees handling AML/CFT-



6|Page

    related activities for the registered intermediaries may also be encouraged to

    undergo the aforementioned certification examination.

6. This circular is issued in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 11(1) of

    Chapter IV of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Rule

    7(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005

    and Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Certification of Associated Persons in the

    Securities Markets) Regulations, 2007, to protect the interests of investors in

    securities and to promote the development of, and to regulate the securities

    market.

7. This circular is available on SEBI website at www.sebi.gov.in under the category:

    ‘Legal → Circulars’.



                                                                                             Yours faithfully,

                                                                                                     XXXXXX



7|Page


```
