- **official URL (detail page):** https://ifsca.gov.in/Legal/Index?MId=IX858BVgwwE=
- **official PDF URL:** https://ifsca.gov.in/CommonDirect/DownloadFile?id=850da50e42b9c192894a42a7d2d02cc3&fileName=FAQs_on_Banking__Nov_5___approved_1_20261105_0649.pdf
- **local text file name:** IFSCA-1105-13.txt

```text
               Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

                                       On



IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020 (as amended), IFSCA

Banking Handbook and the Circulars on Internet Banking.



                                                     Page 1 of 8

                                            Section – I (General)



I. Establishment of Banking unit



 1. What are the permitted legal forms for setting up of Bank in IFSC



 At present, a Banking Unit in the IFSC may be established as a branch of the parent

 bank. Such branch is referred to as an IFSC Banking Unit (IBU).



 2. What are the Licensing requirements for setting of a Banking Unit :



 Banks shall require licence from the Authority to set up a Banking Unit in an

 International Financial Services Centre. An application for setting up a Banking Unit

 shall be made by the Parent Bank on the Single Window IT System portal of IFSCA

 (https://swit.ifsca.gov.in/EntityRegLogin/Index).



 As per regulation 3 of the IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020 (as amended) and

 module 1 on Licensing of Banking Units in IFSCA Banking Handbook: General

 Directions, the applicant shall satisfy the following requirements for grant of licence by

 the Authority to set up a Banking Unit:



 a) The Parent Bank shall undertake to maintain necessary regulatory capital for the

 operations of the IBU, subject to a minimum of USD 20 million or such other level of

 capital that may be specified by the Authority. Such capital shall be maintained at the

 Parent Bank in the manner as specified by the Authority.



 b) The Parent Bank shall obtain a No Objection Letter from its Home Regulator

 regarding setting up of the Banking Unit in the IFSC.



 c) The Parent Bank shall submit an undertaking to the Authority to the effect:



  (i) it shall ensure that the IBU shall have access to liquid assets and financial

 resources which are adequate in relation to the nature, size and complexity of the

 business of the IBU to ensure that there is no significant risk that liabilities cannot be

 met as and when they fall due.



 (ii) it complies and shall continue to comply with its home regulator's prudential

 requirements;



 (iii) it will share with the Authority reports pertaining to capital adequacy, liquidity risk

 and leverage ratio that it submits to its home regulator, within such time as may be

 specified by the Authority.



 (iv) in case of breach of prudential requirements relating to Capital to Risk Weighted

 Asset Ratio (CRAR), Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio

 (NSFR) and Leverage Ratio (s) set by its home regulator, it shall notify the Authority

 forthwith with relevant documents.



 d) Any other requirement as may be specified by the Authority.



                                                        Page 2 of 8

   3. Can a Bank, which does not have a presence in India set up an IBU



   Yes. A Banking company not having a presence in India may apply to the Authority to

   set up an IBU. The applicant bank, in addition to satisfying the requirements stated at

   2 above, shall meet the requirement of section 22(3A) of the Banking Regulation Act,

   1949... The Authority may seek the opinion of the Government of India or any body

   set up the Government of India before deciding on such an application. Further, the

   Banking Company not having presence in India, submitting an application to the

   Authority to set up an IBU shall also satisfy the additional conditions specified under

   para 6 of the IFSCA Banking Handbook: General Directions.



II. Banking Handbook:



   4. Where are guidelines for operation of Banking Units in IFSC be found ?



   .The detailed guidelines for IFSC Banking Units, in the form of IFSCA Banking

   Handbook, can be accessed on Authority’s website at the following path: about us>

   Legal framework> Circular.



    The Banking Handbook consists of three components viz. a) General Directions b)

   Conduct of Business Directions and c) Prudential Directions.



        a) General directions (GEN): It deals with licensing of IBUs, defines the 'controlled'

            and 'designated' functions and the requirements from 'approved/ authorized

            individuals' who can carry out such functions. It also lays out the broad

            principles for banking business and provides information about IFSCA's

            supervisory functions.



        b) Conduct of Business directions (COB) : it aims at ensuring that IBUs (and other

            financial institutions operating in IFSC, wherever made applicable) meet the

            minimum standards of conduct expected, particularly with regard to the

            treatment of their clients, their dealings with counterparties and other market

            participants and contribute to fostering and maintaining the integrity of the

            financial markets in IFSC.



        c) Prudential directions (PRU): Prudential guidelines of the Home Regulator of the

            Banking Companies setting up IBUs shall apply – unless otherwise specified

            by the Authority. The Banking Handbook provides the minimum non-

            quantitative prudential requirements that shall be applicable for the IBUs in

            addition to those applicable on them as a branch of the Banking Company

            under the respective Home Regulations.



 III. Governance of an IFSC Banking Unit:



   5. What does governing body of the IBU mean ?



                                                          Page 3 of 8

   a) The Governing Body refers to the structure responsible for oversight of the IBU’s

   operations. The composition of governing body of the IBU is laid down in para 2(1) of

   module 2 of the IFSCA Banking Handbook: General Directions (as amended).



   b) The Banking company shall, prior to the commencement of the IBU’s operations,

   appoint a Governing Body of the IBU and inform the Authority about the same in

   writing. The governing body of an IBU shall have at least 3 members. The duties of

   Governing body of the IBU are stated in para 5 of the module 2 of the IFSCA Banking

   handbook: General Directions (as amended).



   6. Applicability of domestic laws of India to IFSC:



   Unless specifically exempted, all domestic laws of India apply to IFSC. Banks may

   consider obtaining legal opinion on the applicability of individual laws to the IBU.



   Transactions with persons resident in India shall be subject to the provisions of the

   Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA).



   7. What does approved individuals of the IBU mean



   Approved individual refers to an employee of the IBU, working out of IFSC, who has

   been approved by the Authority to carry out specific functions mentioned in General

   Directions. Following positions with respect to an IBU are to be held by an Approved

   Individual at all times :



        a) CEO/ Head-IBU

        b) Compliance officer

        c) such other role or function as the Authority may direct from time to time



   For more information, please refer to the sub-point (a) of point (i) of para 3 of Module

   no. 3 titled “Controlled and Designated Functions” of General Directions of IFSCA

   Banking Handbook (as amended)



   IV. Permissible Activities



   8. What are the permissible activities of an IBU



   A Banking Unit may undertake any or all the activities mentioned under clause (e) of

   sub-section (1) of Section 3 of the IFSCA Act, 2019 and Section 6 of the Banking

   Regulation Act, 1949, except those which are explicitly prohibited either by the Home

   Regulator of the Parent Bank of the IBU or by the Authority, subject to compliance with

   such terms and conditions or guidelines as may be specified by the Authority.



   9. Are there any guidelines on outsourcing applicable on IBU



   Yes, the guidelines on outsourcing are specified in para 3 of module on Systems and

   Controls in General Directions of the Banking Handbook.



V. Prudential Requirements for IBU



                                                          Page 4 of 8

10. What are prudential requirements mandated for an IBU



The extant IFSCA regulations and the handbook have specified the requirement for

compliance with certain prudential regulatory requirements for IBUs, such as Liquidity

Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) and Leverage Ratio (LR).

As the regulations also permit retail banking business by IBUs, an additional

requirement in the form of Retail Deposit Reserve Ratio (RDRR) has been prescribed.

These prudential rules applicable to IBUs are as under:



LCR and NSFR: IBUs are required to maintain on a standalone basis LCR and NSFR

at a level that is higher of the minimum ratio prescribed by the home regulator of the

banking company (of which the IBU is a branch) or as specified by the Authority from

time to time. IBUs are permitted to maintain LCR at the parent level subject to

permission from the Authority. At present, the Authority has not specified the

requirement for NSFR while the minimum LCR prescribed is 100 per cent.



Leverage Ratio (LR): A minimum LR, as defined under the Basel Framework, for an

IBU is required to be maintained by its banking company, subject to the regulations

specified by the respective home regulator, unless otherwise specified by the Authority.

IBUs are required to submit a quarterly certificate to this effect signed by an authorized

official of its parent bank.



RDRR: IBUs are required to maintain RDRR on daily basis at 3 per cent of the deposits

raised from individuals, outstanding at the end of the previous working day. The RDRR

may be maintained in any specified foreign currency and in the form of balance in the

nostro account of the IBU or as holdings of sovereign debt securities (including T-bills)

rated investment grade or above by at least two rating agencies of international

standing.



IBUs are required to submit a copy of the prudential reports being submitted to the

home regulator, to the Authority also and comply with the prudential reporting

requirements, as specified under the guidelines/ directions/ circulars issued from time

to time. The prudential reporting formats may be accessed on the Authority’s website

in the following path: Downloads > Banking.



VI. Fee Structure



11. What are the various kinds of fees applicable for a Banking Company

intending to set up as an IBU, and where should the fees be remitted?



The Banking Company is subject to three categories of fee:



    a) One time application fee to be paid along with the application to set up an IBU

    b) One time License fee to be paid post the receipt of In-principle approval

    c) Recurring fee to be paid annually based on the annual turnover of the IBU.



The details of fee applicable to the IBU are specified in the circular ‘Fee structure for

the entities undertaking or intending to undertake permissible activities in IFSC or



                                                      Page 5 of 8

persons seeking guidance under the Informal Guidance Scheme’ dated March 2,

2026.

VII. AML-CFT/KYC

12. What are the Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML)

measures applicable to IBUs

IBUs are required to comply with the IFSCA (Anti Money Laundering, Counter-Terrorist

Financing and Know Your Customer) Guidelines, 2022 (as amended) (“the

guidelines”).

13. Can IBUs rely on third party for KYC?

Yes. An IBU may rely on third party for KYC to the extent and subject to such conditions

as specified in the guidelines. Please note that Chapter VI of the IFSCA (AML, CFT

and KYC) guidelines, 2022 deals with the third-party reliance on Customer Due

Diligence measures.



VIII. Global Administrative Office

14. What is Global Administrative Office

GAO is a financial institution set up in IFSC by a Banking Company that :

a. manages, administers, or coordinates the operations of the Parent Bank or any of

the Group entities either in IFSC or outside IFSC;

b. provides support services to Parent Bank or any of the Group entities for execution

of the permitted activities in IFSC or outside IFSC.

For more information, please visit Module No. 17 on Global Administrative Office in

Conduct of Business Directions of IFSCA Banking Handbook.

15. Can GAO operate on same premises as that of IBU

The GAO of a Bank shall be located in IFSC, but not on the same or contiguous

premises as the branch of the same bank, unless specifically permitted by the

Authority. In case of an existing IBU of the banking company intending to set up GAO,

the entity is required to seek approval for broad banding of the activities of the existing

SEZ Unit (i.e. IBU).

Further, the resources provided for the GAO, including the Head-GAO and other

personnel, shall be kept separate and distinct from that of the IBU (if any) or the

Representative Office (if any) of the Banking company in IFSC.



IX. Representative Office

16. What is Representative Office (RO)



                                                      Page 6 of 8

A Banking company incorporated in India or outside India is permitted to set up RO in

IFSC vide section 3(9) of the IFSCA (Banking) Regulation, 2020 (as amended). A RO

is permitted to undertake activities as specified under para 6 of the module 12

(‘Representative Office’) of the IFSCA Banking Handbook: Conduct of Business

Directions. ‘



             Section -II (Internet banking services for the clients of the IBU)



(Please refer to the Circular on Internet banking services to clients of IBUs dated

April 2, 2024 and the Circular on Internet banking services to clients of IBUs –

Review dated December 29, 2025 (as amended))



1. Whether the display of live market rates for currency conversions, including

    the applicable spread offered to customers, on the customers’ digital

    dashboard also includes the display of card rates.



    The ability to view live market rates for currency conversions, including the

    applicable spread offered to customers, implies that internet banking platforms shall

    display prevailing market rates along with the spreads applied and does not include

    card rates. The intent of this requirement is to enhance transparency by providing

    customers with information on market rates. The actual rates offered to customers

    may vary from the prevailing market rates depending on the applicable spread.



    Further, reference is drawn to the para 4 of the Amendment to the Circular titled

    “Internet banking services to clients of IBUs –Review” dated June 30, 2026, the

    ability to view live market rates for currency conversions including the applicable

    spread offered to its customers has been made non mandatory.



2. Whether the formats for viewing and downloading account statements by the

    clients of the IBU is limited to CSV, JSON and XML



    No. CSV, JSON, and XML are illustrative sample formats only. Account statements

    provided by the IBU for viewing and download may be made available in any other

    machine-readable format apart from the above. The requirement of the customer/s

    would be the guiding principle behind this requirement.



3. What does ability to provide white-listing options for IBU’s fintech partners

    mean?



    If the IBU partners with a fintech entity, the IBU may provide access to selected

    APIs for fintech partners for specific purposes like account verification, payments

    etc.,



4. What does ability to initiate auto-schedule payouts including one-time, date

    based, recurring, rule-based executions mean



                                                        Page 7 of 8

    Ability to initiate auto-schedule payouts by customer’ means that the customer shall

    be provided with the facility to set up an automated payout schedule. The IBU may

    proceed with the transaction subject to applicable verification and other prescribed

    procedures.

5. What does “Validation tools to identify incorrect account numbers to the

    extent feasible, currency mismatches, or regulatory non-compliance for e.g.

    the account is in a FATF compliant jurisdiction etc., before execution” mean

    It is expected that IBUs, to the extent feasible, may avail services from third parties

    that provide validation tools to identify issues such as incorrect account numbers,

    currency mismatches (the beneficiary account is denominated in a different

    currency than the transaction currency) etc.,

6. With respect to corporate customers holding current accounts, what

    principles shall govern the operation of user access management, including

    Master User access.

    The operation of user access management including Master user access may be

    according to bank’s policy.

7. Whether obtaining explicit consent by the IBU from their customers for

    registering/de registering internet banking services applies to new customers

    or only existing customers

    The obtaining of consent for registering/deregistering internet banking services

    applies only for existing customers.



          __________________****************___________________



                                                        Page 8 of 8
```

```text
        अधिधियम की अिुसूची VI [ताधिका: क्र.सं. 11] के तहत छूट के धिए पात्र िाभांश आय देय है; और



   (ख) इस तरह के धववरण-सह-घोर्णा को उस कर वर्ि के धिए उि प्रपत्र मंे धिर्दिष्ट तरीके से प्रस्तुत और

              सत्याधपत ककया िाएगा धिसमंे उि अधिधियम की अिुसूची VI [ताधिका: क्र.सं. 11] के तहत छूट के

              धिए पात्र िाभांश आय देय है;



   (2) भुगतािकता-ि



   (क)  भुगतािकत्ताड से उि प्रपत्र मंे धववरण-सह-घोर्णा की प्रधत प्राप्त होिे की तारीख के बाद ऐसे िाभांश



        (आदाता) के प्राप्तकताि को ककए गए या िमा ककए गए भुगताि पर कर की कटौती िहीं करेगा; तथा



   (ख) आयकर धियम, 2026 के धियम 219 के साथ पठित उि अधिधियम की िारा 397(3)(ख) में धिर्दिष्ट

              कर की कटौती के धववरण में इस अधिसूचिा के मद्देििर ऐसे िाभांश के प्राप्तकताि को ककए गए सभी

              भुगतािों का धववरण प्रस्तुत करेगा, धिस पर कर कटौती िहीं की गई है।



2. आयकर के प्रिाि महाधिदेशक (धसस्टम्स) या आयकर महाधिदेशक (धसस्टम्स), िैसा भी मामिा हो, डेटा के

सुरधित कैप्चर और प्रसारण और दस्तावेिों को अपिोड करिे के धिए प्रकियाओं, प्रारूपों और मािकों को धििािठरत करेंगे

और उनपर उपयुि सुरिा, अधभिेखीय और पुिप्रािधप्त िीधतयों को तैयार करिे और िागू करिे की भी जिम्मेिारी होगी।



स्पष्टीकरण - इस अधिसूचिा के प्रयोिि के धिए, -



   (क) "एअर क्राफ्ट्स" का वही अथि होगा िो उि अधिधियम की अिुसूची VI के िोट 3 मंे इसे दिया गया है;



   (ख) "अंतरािष्ट्रीय धवत्तीय सेवा केंद्र" का वही अथि होगा िो धवशेर् आर्थिक िेत्र अधिधियम, 2005 (2005 का

          28) की िारा 2 के खंड मंे दिया गया है; तथा



   (ग) "इकाई" का वही अथि होगा िो इसे धवशेर् आर्थिक िेत्र अधिधियम, 2005 (2005 का 28) के खंड 2

          (िेडसी) में दिया गया है।



3. यह अधिसूचिा 1 अप्रैि, 2026 से िागू मािी िाएगी।

                                                      MINISTRY OF FINANCE

                                             (CENTRAL BOARD OF DIRECT TAXES)



                                                            NOTIFICATION



                                                  New Delhi, the 4th November, 2026



                                                              INCOME TAX



          S.O. 6016(E).— In exercise of the powers conferred by section 400(1) read with Schedule VI [Table: S.No.

11] of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (30 of 2025) (hereinafter referred to as the said Act), the Central Government hereby

specifies that no deduction of tax shall be made under section 393(1)[Table: S.No. 7] of the said Act from any income

in the nature of dividend paid by any unit of an International Financial Services Centre, primarily engaged in the business

of leasing of an aircraft (hereinafter referred to as the payer) to a company, being a Unit of an International Financial

Services Centre primarily engaged in the business of leasing of an aircraft (hereinafter referred to as the payee) subject

to the following, namely:-



1. (1) The payee shall,—



    (a) furnish a statement-cum-declaration in the Form No.1(N) annexed to this notification (hereinafter

              referred to as the said Form) to the payer giving details of the tax year in which the dividend income

              eligible for exemption under Schedule VI [Table: S.No. 11] of the said Act is payable; and



    (b) such statement-cum-declaration shall be furnished and verified in the manner specified in the said

              Form for the tax year in which the dividend income eligible for exemption under Schedule VI [Table:

              S.No. 11] of the said Act is payable;



    (2) The payer shall,—



    (a) not deduct tax on payment made or credited to the recipient of such dividend (payee) after the date of

            receipt of copy of statement-cum-declaration in the said Form from payee; and



    (b) furnish the particulars of all the payments made to the recipient of such dividend on which tax has not

            been deducted in view of this Notification in the statement of deduction of tax referred to in section

            397(3)(b) of the said Act, read with the rule 219 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026.



2.  The Principal Director General of Income-tax (Systems) or the Director General of Income-tax (Systems), as



the case may be, shall lay down procedures, formats and standards for ensuring secure capture and transmission of data



and uploading of documents and they shall also be responsible for evolving and implementing appropriate security,



archival and retrieval policies.



Explanation.— For the purpose of this notification,—



    (a) "aircraft" shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in Note 3 of Schedule VI to the said Act;

    (b) "International Financial Services Centre" shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (q)



              of section 2 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 (28 of 2005); and

    (c) "Unit" shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause 2(zc) of the Special Economic Zones



              Act, 2005 (28 of 2005).
```

```text
         सा.का.जन. 968(अ).— केन्द्रीर् सरकार, कंपनी अजधजनर्म, 2013 (2013 का 18) की धारा 469 के साथ पठित

करना) जनर्म, 2024 का और आगे संिोधन करने के जलए जनम्नजलजखत जनर्म बनाती है, अथायत् :-



1. (1) इन जनर्मों का संजिप्त नाम (अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरताओं में साधारण िेर्र सूचीबद्ध करना) संिोधन जनर्म, 2026

है।



(2) र्े जनर्म रािपत्र मंे इनके प्रकािन की तारीख को प्रवृत्त होंगे।



2. संपूणय कंपनी (अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरताओं मंे साधारण िेर्र सूचीबद्ध करना) जनर्म, 2024 में (इसमें इसके पश्चात मूल

जनर्म के रूप मंे जनर्ियष्ट), में िहां भी ‘िेर्र’ िब्ि आता है, उसके स्ट्थान पर ‘‘इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स’’ िब्ि रखा िाएगा।



3. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 2 के उप-जनर्म (1) मंे, खंड (ख) के बाि, जनम्नजलजखत खंड िोडा िाएगा, अथायत्:-



8398 GI/2026                    (1)

‘(खक) ‘‘इदिटी इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स’’ से, भारतीर् कंपनी द्वारा िारी दकए गए इदिटी िेर्र, पठरवतयनीर् जडबेंचर, अधीमानी िेर्र

अजभप्रेत है;’



4. मूल जनर्मों के जनर्म 3--



    (i) खंड (क) मंे, ‘‘कंपजनर्ों’’, िब्ि के बाि, ‘‘अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर् सेवा कंेरों की अजधकाठरता मंे, सावयिजनक कंपनजर्ों

              के अलावा’’, िब्ि अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे;



    (ii) खंड (ख) के पश्चात, जनम्नजलजखत खंड अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकर्ा िाएगा, अथातय् -



    ‘‘(ग) अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर् सेवा केंर की अजधकाठरता मंे गैर-सूचीबद्ध सावयिजनक कंपजनर्ां, िहां तक वे अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर्

    सेवा कंेर प्राजधकरण अजधजनर्म, 2019 (2019 का 50) के प्रावधानों और उसके अधीन बनाए गए जनर्मों के अनुसार

    हंै।’’



5. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 4 में, िोनों स्ट्थानों पर आने वाली ‘‘मौिूिा िेर्रधारकों’’ िब्िों के स्ट्थान पर ‘‘मौिूिा धारक’’ िब्ि

प्रजतस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे।



6. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 5 मंे,



    (i) खंड (घ) मंे, ‘‘जिसका जनवल मूल्र् ऋणात्मक है’’ िब्िों के पश्चात जनम्नजलजखत परंतुक अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकर्ा िाएगा,

    अथायत् :-



             "बिते दक नकारात्मक जनवल मूल्र् वाली कंपनी भी सूचीबद्ध होने के जलए अपने इदिटी इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स िारी करने

             के जलए पात्र होगी, र्दि िारीकताय इस जनर्म के प्रर्ोिन के जलए अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरता में संबंजधत प्रजतभूजत

             बािार जनर्ामक द्वारा इस संबंध मंे बनाए गए जनर्मों के अनुसार र्ोग्र् संस्ट्थागत खरीिारों को िुद्ध पेिकि का

             कम से कम पचहत्तर प्रजतित आवंठटत करने का वचन िेता है।"



   (ii) खंड (ङ) मंे, परंतुक मंे, िब्ि "िो वर्"य के जलए, "छह माह से अजधक" िब्ि प्रजतस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे।

G.S.R. 968(E).— In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (3) of section 23 read with section 469 of the

Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013), the Central Government hereby makes the following rules further to amend the

Companies (Listing of equity shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules, 2024, namely:̶

6  THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY                             [PART II—SEC. 3(i)]



1. (1) These rules may be called the Companies (Listing of equity instruments in permissible jurisdictions) Amendment

Rules, 2026.



   (2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.



2. Throughout the Companies (Listing of equity shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules, 2024 (hereinafter referred

to as the principal rules), for the word “shares”, wherever it occurs, the word “instruments’ shall be substituted.



3. In the principal rules, in sub-rule (1) of rule 2, after clause (b), the following clause shall be inserted, namely: -



’(ba) “equity instruments” means equity shares, convertible debentures, preference shares issued by an Indian

Company;’



4. In the principal rules, in rule 3,-



(i) in clause (a), after the word, “companies”, the words, “other than public companies in the International Financial

Services Centres jurisdiction”, shall be inserted;



(ii) after clause (b), the following clause shall be inserted, namely:–



“(c) unlisted public companies in the International Financial Services Centres jurisdiction, in so far as they are in

accordance with the provisions of the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50 of 2019) and

with the regulations framed thereunder.”.



5. In the principal rules, in rule 4, for the words “existing shareholders” occurring at both the places, the words “existing

holders” shall be substituted.



6. In the principal rules, in rule 5,



      (i) in clause (d), after the words “has a negative net worth” the following proviso, shall be inserted, namely: -



                     “Provided that a company having a negative net worth shall be eligible to issue its equity

               instruments for listing, if the issuer undertakes to allot at least seventy-five per cent. of the net offer

               to qualified institutional buyers in accordance with the regulations framed in this regard by the

               respective securities market regulator in permissible jurisdiction for purpose of this rule.”.



(ii) in clause (e), in the proviso, for the words “two years”, the words, “more than six months” shall be substituted;



(iii) in clause (g), after the words “specified period”, the words “and such default has not been made good” shall be

inserted;
```

```text
         सं. आईएफएससीए/िीएन/2026/017.— केंद्र सरकार ने 14 दिसंबर, 2021 की अजधसूचना एस.ओ. 5199

(ङ) के तहत, अंतरराष्ट्रीय जित्तीय सेिा कंेद्र प्राजधकरण द्वारा जनर्ििष्ट उत्पािों या उपकरणों के 'पररचालन पट्टे'

(जिसमंे पररचालन और जित्तीय पट्टे का कोई भी िणि-संकर रूप िाजमल है) को 'जित्तीय उत्पाि' के रूप मंे

अजधसूजचत दकया;



         अंतरराष्ट्रीय जित्तीय सेिा केंद्र प्राजधकरण, उक्त अजधसूचना और 'अंतरराष्ट्रीय जित्तीय सेिा केंद्र प्राजधकरण

अजधजनयम, 2019' (2019 का 50) की धारा 12 द्वारा प्रित्त िजक्तयों का प्रयोग करते हुए, एतद्द्वारा "ग्रादफक्स

प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाइयां" और "परस्ट्पर संयोजित डेटा संेटर उपकरणों" को उक्त अजधसूचना के उद्देश्यों के जलए

'उपकरण' के रूप मंे जनर्ििष्ट करता है।



स्ट्पष्टीकरण - इस अजधसूचना के प्रयोिनार्ि, -



(i) "ग्रादफक्स प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाइयों" का तात्पयि —



         (क) ऐसी ग्रादफक्स प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाइयों से है, चाहे इनमंे एक ही ढांचे में जनम्नजलजखत प्रकार की इकाइयों

         अर्ाित भंडारण इकाइयों, इनपुट इकाइयों या आउटपुट इकाइयों मंे से एक या िो िाजमल हों अर्िा नहीं।



8257 GI/2026                    (1)

2  THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY                [PART III—SEC.4]



   इसमें जिजभन्न प्रकार की भंडारण इकाइयाँा और उनसे िुडे पुिे ि सहायक उपस्ट्कर िाजमल हंै। सार् ही,

   इसमें सामान्य प्रयोिन की ग्रादफक्स प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाइयां, कृजिम बुजिमता गजतिधिक, टेंसर या तंजिका

   प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाई, त्िररत संगणक उपकरण और इसी तरह की अन्य संगणन या गजतिधिक तकनीक

   िाजमल हंै; और



   (ख) रैक-स्ट्तरीय कृजिम बुजिमता प्रणाजलयों से है, चाहे उनकी दकसी एकीकृत प्रणाली के रूप में आपूर्ति

   या इनिॉइस की गई हो या नहीं। इसमें एक ही रैक के भीतर एकीकृत संगण रे, जस्ट्िच रे, सीपीयू और

   इनपुट या आउटपुट इकाइयाँ,ा जिन्हंे प्रणाली के रूप मंे प्रस्ट्तुत दकया िाता है, िाजमल हंै;



(ii) "परस्ट्पर संयोजित डेटा सेंटर उपकरण" का तात्पयि -



   (क) प्रोसेसर और कंरोलर सजहत इलेक्रॉजनक इंटीग्रेटेड सर्कि ट से है, चाहे िे मेमोरी, कन्िटिर, लॉजिक

   सर्कि ट, एम्पलीफायर, क्लॉक और टाइममंग सर्कि ट या अन्य सर्कि ट के सार् संयोजित हों अर्िा नहीं;



   (ख) सििर जिद्युत आपूर्ति इकाइयों सजहत सिरि , स्ट्टोरेि, नेटिर्कंि ग, इंटरकनेक्ट और पािर उपकरण तर्ा

   डेटा संेटर में उपकरणों को लगाने या उनके संचालन के जलए आिश्यक कजतपय अन्य उपकरणों से है; और



         (ग) उपयुिक्त के पुिों और सहायक उपस्ट्करों से है, लेदकन इनमें समग्र डेटा संेटर की फेजसजलटी के काम

         आने िाले उपकरण िाजमल नहीं हैं;

         ये जििेष रूप से ग्रादफक्स प्रसंस्ट्करण इकाइयों के जलए हंै और सीधे तौर पर उनसे िुडे हुए हैं।

2. यह अजधसूचना िासकीय रािपि में प्रकाजित होने की तारीख से प्रभािी होगी।



                                                        डॉ. प्रिीण जििेिी, कायिकारी जनिेिक

                                                       [जिज्ञापन-III/4/असा./408/2026-27]



                        INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL SERVICES CENTRES AUTHORITY



                                                            NOTIFICATION



                                                 Gandhinagar, the 22nd October, 2026



          No. IFSCA/GN/2026/ 017.— The Central Government vide notification S.O. 5199 (E) dated 14th December,

2021, notified operating lease including any hybrid of operating and financial lease of such product or equipment as

may be specified by International Financial Services Centres Authority, as financial product;



          In exercise of the powers conferred by the said notification read with section 12 of the International Financial

Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50 of 2019), the International Financial Services Centres Authority hereby

specifies “Graphics Processing Units” and “connected data centre equipment” as equipment for the purposes of

the said notification.



Explanation. - For the purposes of this notification, -



(i) "Graphics Processing Units " means—



(a) graphics processing units, whether or not containing, in the same housing, one or two of the following types of

units: storage units, input units or output units, including various types of storage units and allied parts and

accessories, and includes general-purpose graphics processing units, artificial intelligence accelerators, tensor or

neural processing units, accelerated computing equipment and comparable computing or acceleration technologies;

and

[भाग III—खण्ड 4]  भारत का रािपि : असाधारण                                                                                                                                              3



(b) rack-scale artificial intelligence systems, whether or not supplied or invoiced as one integrated system or

otherwise, including compute trays, switch trays, CPU and input or output units integrated within a single rack, and

presented in the form of systems;



(ii) “connected data centre equipment” means-



(a) electronic integrated circuits comprising processors and controllers, whether or not combined with memories,

converters, logic circuits, amplifiers, clock and timing circuits or other circuits;



(b) servers, storage, networking, interconnect and power equipment including server power supply units and any other

equipment required for the deployment or operation of the equipment in a data centre; and



(c) parts and accessories of above, but does not include equipment serving the data centre facility as a whole;



in so far as the above equipment are dedicated to and directly associated with Graphics Processing Units.



2. This notification shall come into force on the date of publication in the Official Gazette.
```

```text
              Conference on Consumer Awareness on Protection in the Digital Era | 2026 | Post Event Report



Introduction and Conference Overview



The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) organised a full-day

conference titled “Consumer Awareness and Protection in the Digital Era” on 6

October 2026 at GIFT City Club, GIFT City, as part of the 10th edition of IOSCO World

Investor Week (WIW) 2026.

The conference brought together senior officials from IFSCA, the Reserve Bank of India

(RBI), the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the Insurance Regulatory

and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), along with representatives from market

infrastructure institutions, banks, insurance companies, fintech enterprises, educational

institutions and law-enforcement agencies.

The conference focused on consumer protection across financial services, with particular

emphasis on digital frauds, risks associated with artificial intelligence (AI), institutional

safeguards and grievance redressal, in line with the WIW 2026 themes of “Investor

Resilience, Digital Deception and Scams.”

The increasing use of mobile applications, online platforms and AI-enabled services has

made financial services more accessible and convenient. However, these developments

have also given rise to new risks, including impersonation of regulated entities,

misleading investment information, deepfakes, account compromise, manipulative

digital interfaces and social-engineering frauds. Against this backdrop, the conference

provided a platform for regulators, financial institutions, technology providers and law-

enforcement agencies to share their perspectives on emerging risks, preventive

Special Session: How to Combat Digital Frauds in the Era of AI

by Mr. Hardik Makadia, Assistant Commissioner of Police

(ACP), Cyber Crime, Ahmedabad



Mr. Hardik Makadia, ACP, Cyber Crime, Ahmedabad, delivering his special session



Mr. Hardik Makadia delivered a special session on emerging digital financial frauds,

highlighting the methods adopted by cybercriminals and preventive measures for

consumers. He stated that reported financial frauds in India had reached approximately

₹23,000 crore in 2024, representing a fivefold increase since 2019. He also highlighted

the involvement of organised cybercrime networks operating from Southeast Asia and

referred to domestic cybercrime hotspots such as Jamtara and Mewat.

Common Digital Frauds and Their Modus Operandi

Mr. Makadia explained various types of digital frauds through examples drawn from

cybercrime investigations:



    • Digital Arrest Scams: Fraudsters impersonate police or other law-enforcement

         officials, use fabricated legal documents and video calls to intimidate victims, and

         persuade them to transfer funds to purported verification accounts.



    • Fraudulent Investment and Romance Scams: Scammers use social media

         advertisements, WhatsApp and Telegram groups, and fraudulent investment

         applications to gain victims' trust. They display fictitious investment returns and

         subsequently prevent withdrawals or demand additional payments.



    • Task-Based Scams: Individuals are offered payments for completing simple

         online tasks, such as reviewing hotels or liking videos. He explained that payments

                                               Page 16 of 35

              Conference on Consumer Awareness on Protection in the Digital Era | 2026 | Post Event Report



         may originate from other victims' accounts, potentially resulting in the freezing of

         recipients' bank accounts.

    • Executive Impersonation and WhatsApp Hijacking: Fraudsters circulate

         malicious files to compromise WhatsApp Web sessions and impersonate senior

         executives, subsequently directing employees to make unauthorised fund

         transfers.

    • Fraudulent Loan Applications: Unverified loan applications may access users'

         contacts and personal information, which can subsequently be misused for

         harassment, blackmail and financial exploitation.

Preventive Measures

Mr. Makadia emphasised the importance of digital awareness and basic cyber security

practices. He advised consumers to regularly check devices linked to their WhatsApp

accounts, enable two-factor authentication, avoid downloading files or applications from

unverified sources and independently verify suspicious communications or payment

requests.

He concluded by reiterating the message “Stop, Verify and Take Advice”, encouraging

consumers to exercise caution before responding to suspicious financial requests.

increasing accessibility of algorithmic trading tools to retail investors.

He also highlighted the shift in cyber threats towards investors' personal devices and the

risks associated with regulated entities relying on third-party AI applications. He

emphasised that outsourcing technology does not absolve regulated entities of their

Shri Arjun Prasad, Chief General Manager, IFSCA, delivering his special session



Mr. Arjun Prasad, Chief General Manager, IFSCA, delivered a special session on

international standards relating to financial consumer protection and the initiatives

undertaken by IFSCA to strengthen consumer awareness and grievance redressal in GIFT

IFSC.

International Standards on Consumer Protection

Mr. Prasad outlined the international regulatory principles and standards relevant to

consumer protection, including those developed by the International Organization of

Securities Commissions (IOSCO), International Association of Insurance Supervisors

(IAIS), Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) and G20/OECD.

He highlighted IOSCO's 38 Principles of Securities Regulation and its Multilateral

Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU) and Enhanced MMoU (EMMoU), which facilitate

regulatory cooperation, information-sharing and cross-border enforcement. He also

referred to the work of IOSCO Committee 8 on Retail Investors, including its report

identifying nine good practices relating to complaint handling by financial institutions.

Consumer Protection Initiatives Undertaken by IFSCA

Mr. Prasad discussed the initiatives undertaken by IFSCA to strengthen consumer

protection across financial services in GIFT IFSC.



                                               Page 21 of 35

              Conference on Consumer Awareness on Protection in the Digital Era | 2026 | Post Event Report



He highlighted the IFSCA (Complaint Handling and Grievance Redressal) Circular,

effective from 1 April 2025, which specifies a common grievance redressal process for

regulated entities across banking, capital markets, insurance and other financial services.

The Circular requires regulated entities to adopt a Board-approved complaint handling

policy, designate officers for complaint handling and escalation, and provide consumers

with an internal grievance redressal process before approaching IFSCA.

Mr. Prasad further highlighted IFSCA's initiative on the Consumer Charter, under which

regulated entities have been encouraged to adopt charters setting out the rights and

responsibilities of consumers and the commitments of financial institutions towards

them.

Key Suggestions for Regulated Entities

Mr. Prasad outlined five measures that regulated entities could undertake to strengthen

consumer protection:



    1. Dedicated Website Information: Maintain dedicated webpages providing clear

         information on financial products, services and complaint handling procedures.



    2. Effective Compliance: Implement regulatory requirements in their true spirit

         rather than adopting a checklist-based approach.



    3. Monitoring Digital Impersonation: Use AI-based monitoring tools to identify

         fraudulent websites, social media profiles and communications impersonating

         regulated entities or their officials.



    4. Consumer Awareness: Conduct regular awareness programmes to educate

         consumers about financial products, associated risks and digital frauds.



    5. Investor Relations: Consider appointing dedicated Investor Relations Officers to

         facilitate communication with retail investors and address their concerns.



The session provided an overview of IFSCA's consumer protection initiatives and

highlighted the role of regulated entities in ensuring transparent practices, accessible

grievance redressal and greater consumer awareness in GIFT IFSC.

1. Digital Payment Fraud Detection and Information Sharing



Mr. K. Satyanarayana Raju highlighted the scale of digital payments in India, noting that

monthly UPI transactions had reached approximately 24–29 billion, alongside a

significant increase in reported cyber fraud complaints.



He discussed the Digital Payment Intelligence (DPI) Platform, operationalised on 1

September 2026, which facilitates information sharing among participating banks to

identify suspicious accounts and prevent fraudulent transactions. He explained that the

initial phase involves sharing fraud-related identifiers to detect mule accounts, while the

subsequent phase envisages AI-based risk scoring of originating and beneficiary accounts

to identify suspicious transactions before funds are transferred.



2. Banking Challenges and Customer Identification



Mr. Shiv Bajrang Singh highlighted challenges faced by banks in identifying fraudulent

accounts, including inconsistencies in customer identity documents, misuse of accounts

and the changing geographical concentration of mule-account networks.



He emphasised the need for common customer identifiers, improved Know Your

Customer (KYC) processes and greater information sharing among financial institutions

to strengthen fraud prevention and facilitate timely identification of suspicious accounts.



3. AI-Based Fraud Detection in Insurance



Mr. Abhay Tewari discussed the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning

in insurance operations, particularly for identifying fraudulent claims and assessing

emerging risks.



He referred to the use of technologies such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)

and autoencoders for developing simulated risk scenarios and improving risk

assessment. He also highlighted the importance of independent verification of high-value

claims through reliable sources, including hospitals and other service providers, to

reduce fraudulent claims while avoiding unnecessary inconvenience to genuine

policyholders.



4. Consumer Protection in Fintech Platforms



Mr. Ashish Kashyap discussed the importance of incorporating security and compliance

requirements into the design of digital financial products. He highlighted safeguards

adopted by INDmoney, including multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring

of fraudulent websites and digital profiles impersonating legitimate financial service

providers.



He further emphasised that consumer protection should not remain confined to

compliance departments. Product managers, software developers and user-experience

designers must also understand regulatory requirements and incorporate appropriate

safeguards while developing digital financial services.



                                               Page 26 of 35

              Conference on Consumer Awareness on Protection in the Digital Era | 2026 | Post Event Report



5. Emerging Technology Risks and Industry Collaboration

Mr. Siddarth Pai discussed the growing risks associated with AI-generated deepfakes,

digital impersonation and advances in computing technologies. He highlighted the

importance of strengthening cryptographic safeguards, including preparedness for post-

quantum cryptography.

He also advocated greater industry collaboration through mechanisms for sharing

anonymised fraud-related information, enabling financial institutions to identify

emerging fraud patterns and respond more effectively. He further highlighted the need

to adapt consumer education initiatives to changing digital consumption patterns,

including the use of short-form digital content to reach younger audiences.

Key Takeaways

The panel emphasised the need to shift from reactive fraud management towards

predictive and preventive measures, supported by AI-based detection systems,

stronger identity verification, timely information sharing and appropriate safeguards

before financial transactions are completed.

The discussion also highlighted that consumer protection must be incorporated into the

design and delivery of financial products, with responsibility extending beyond

compliance teams to technology developers, financial institutions and other

stakeholders. Consumer education, clear disclosures and timely digital alerts were

identified as important complementary measures for strengthening protection against

emerging digital frauds.



                                               Page 27 of 35

resilience.

Special Session: Corporate Frauds – Case Studies by Shri

Pradeep Ramakrishnan, Executive Director, IFSCA



Shri Pradeep Ramakrishnan, Executive Director, IFSCA, delivering his special session



Shri Pradeep Ramakrishnan, Executive Director, IFSCA, delivered a special session on

corporate frauds, drawing upon historical financial scandals, real-world case studies and

examples from popular films to explain how fraudulent practices develop within

organisations. He highlighted the role of weak internal controls, inadequate oversight and

organisational structures in facilitating financial misconduct.

Understanding Corporate Frauds and Organisational Weaknesses

Shri Ramakrishnan discussed the Satyam corporate fraud case, highlighting how a major

financial fraud involving an organisation with approximately 50,000 employees was

orchestrated by a small group of individuals. He explained that frauds can remain

undetected when organisational departments, including finance, sales, procurement and

internal audit, operate in isolation with limited information sharing and cross-functional

oversight.

He emphasised the importance of strong internal controls, effective communication

across departments and institutional accountability in preventing and detecting

fraudulent activities.



                                               Page 32 of 35

              Conference on Consumer Awareness on Protection in the Digital Era | 2026 | Post Event Report



Historical Fraud Schemes and Lessons

Referring to the history of financial frauds, Shri Ramakrishnan discussed Ponzi schemes

and how similar fraudulent structures have repeatedly emerged over time. He cited

examples of plantation investment schemes and Emu farming scams in India, where

promises of unusually high returns attracted investors despite substantial underlying

risks.

He observed that such schemes often exploit expectations of high returns and limited

public awareness of earlier financial frauds, underscoring the importance of financial

literacy and investor vigilance.

Regulatory Oversight and Institutional Resilience

Shri Ramakrishnan also discussed the limitations of relying solely on legislation to

prevent financial misconduct. He observed that attempting to address every possible

form of fraud through increasingly restrictive regulations could adversely affect

legitimate business activities.

He emphasised that effective fraud prevention requires a combination of

appropriate regulation, strong enforcement, sound internal controls and

continuous institutional vigilance. He also highlighted the importance of

organisational resilience, including the ability to contain fraud-related incidents, respond

effectively and maintain business continuity.

The session highlighted that understanding regulatory requirements, strengthening

internal governance and encouraging accountability across organisational functions are

essential for preventing corporate frauds and protecting stakeholders.
```

```text
                                      भारतीय ररज़र्व बैंक           November 12, 2026

                               RESERVE BANK OF INDIA



DoR.CO.BCG(MCS).No.S6464/01.01.008/2026-27



The Chairpersons / Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officers

All Banks and NBFCs



Madam / Dear Sir



                        Appointment of Arbitrators for Resolution of Disputes



Please refer to the order passed by the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi dated September 30, 2026

in FAO (COMM) 91/2025 & CM APPL. 20542/2025 (Shikha Ghosh v Axis Bank & Anr.) on the

captioned subject (copy enclosed).



2. The Hon’ble High Court of Delhi has examined the issue of unilateral appointment of

arbitrators by a bank in a large number of disputes and expressed serious concerns regarding

the independence and impartiality of arbitrators appointed repeatedly by a single party. It also

referred to the relevant provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the judicial

pronouncements governing the neutrality and independence of arbitrators. It also directed the

Reserve Bank of India, being the sectoral regulator, to caution all banks in this regard, so that

any remedial measures required to be undertaken by banks and financial institutions in respect

of unilateral appointments of arbitrators may also be examined and appropriate guidance

issued.



3. Accordingly, it is advised that banks and NBFCs shall take note of the observations made by

the Hon’ble Court in respect of unilateral appointment of arbitrators and ensure that the

appointment of arbitrators in disputes is undertaken in accordance with the provisions of the

Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the applicable judicial pronouncements governing

the independence, impartiality and neutrality of arbitrators.



4. Banks and NBFCs shall report the action taken to their respective supervisor/Senior

Supervisory Manager (SSM).



Yours faithfully



(Sukhjinder Saini)

Deputy General Manager



Encl.: As above

$~36



* IN THE HIGH COURT OF DELHI AT NEW DELHI



                                       Date of decision: 30th September, 2026.

                                           Uploaded on: 5th October, 2026.



# CNR No. DLHC010190212025



+     FAO (COMM) 91/2025 & CM APPL. 20542/2025



      SHIKHA GHOSH                     .....Appellant



                             Through:  Mr. Vishal Gupta, Mr. Ratneswar Das,

                                       Ms. Barnali Deka Das and Ms. Swati

                             versus    Singh, Advs.

      AXIS BANK LTD. & ANR.

                                                              .....Respondents

                             Through:  Mr. Dayan Krishnan, Sr. Advocate

                                       with Mr. Sanjay Kumar, Adv.

                                       Mr. Ramesh Babu, Senior Adv. Along

                                       with Ms. Manisha Singh, Advocate for

                                       RBI



       CORAM:

       JUSTICE PRATHIBA M. SINGH

       JUSTICE DINESH BHATT

Prathiba M. Singh, J. (Oral)

1. This hearing has been done through hybrid mode.

2. The issue that has arisen in this case is with respect to enforcement of

Awards wherein the Respondent has not been properly served as also

unilateral appointment of the same arbitrators made by Banks in thousands of

disputes.

3. The present appeal has been filed challenging the impugned order dated

30th January, 2025 passed by the ld. District Judge (Commercial Court)-05,

Tis Hazari, Delhi. Vide the impugned order the petition under Section 34 of



FAO (COMM) 91/2025                              Page 1 of 10

the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereinafter “the ACA, 1996”) has

been dismissed on the ground of limitation.

4. The brief facts of the case are that sometime in January, 2019 the

Respondent Bank had disbursed a loan for a sum of Rs. 16,66,795/- to the

Petitioner. The said loan was allegedly not repaid by the Appellant and

accordingly the Respondent Bank initiated arbitration proceedings after

communicating the same to the Appellant on 18th January, 2023. However,

receipt of this communication is disputed by the Appellant.

5. On 6th February, 2023, the ld. Sole Arbitrator is stated to have accepted

the reference of dispute to arbitration and allegedly issued notice to the

Appellant. The receipt of this notice is, again, disputed by the Appellant.

Accordingly, the matter proceeded ex-parte as against the Appellant in terms

of order dated 16th May, 2023 passed by the ld. Sole Arbitrator.

6. Thus, the case of the Appellant is that the Award dated 26th May, 2023

was passed without the knowledge of the Appellant as to the existence of the

said arbitral proceedings.

7. A copy of the said Award was received by the Appellant on 2nd June,

2023 and upon the award coming to the knowledge of the Appellant, a petition

under Section 34 of the ACA, 1996 was filed before the Commercial Court.

8. This petition was dismissed vide the impugned order as being time

barred.

9. The present appeal was considered on 7th April, 2025, on which date

notice was issued and the TCR was called for. Thereafter, on 5th August,

2025, upon joint submission of the parties the matter was referred to the Delhi

High Court Mediation and Conciliation Centre for amicable resolution



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 2 of 10

through mediation, but the same did not fructify.

10. On 3rd September, 2026, after hearing some arguments in this matter,

the Court had put the following queries to the Respondent Bank:



            “2. The Court has considered the matter and heard the

            ld. Counsels for the parties. Before proceeding further.

            Respondent Bank is directed to file an affidavit giving

            the following information:

            i) Whether there is any proof of service of the Appellant

            in the arbitral proceedings?



            ii) Whether Shri. Vikrant Bhardwaj, who was the Sole

            Arbitrator, is connected to the Respondent Bank in any

            manner?



            iii) Number of arbitrations handled by Shri. Vikrant

            Bhardwaj, the Sole Arbitrator on behalf of the

            Respondent Bank.



            iv) Whether any declaration in terms of Schedule VI and

            VII of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was

            given by the said Arbitrator.”



11. Thus, an affidavit was directed to be filed by the Respondent Bank in

respect of the above queries. The said affidavit has been filed by the

Respondent Bank answering the queries raised by the Court as under:



            “3. In compliance with the above directions, the

            Respondent No.1, respectfully submits its answers to

            each of the queries as under:



            a. Query (i) Proof of Service:



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 3 of 10

It is respectfully submitted that there exists clear and

sufficient proof of service of the Appellant in the arbitral

proceedings. The Ld. Sole Arbitrator, in the Award

dated 26.05.2023, specifically recorded that notices of

the arbitral hearings were issued to the Appellant at her

last known address, service was held sufficient, and

despite such service the Appellant failed to appear,

resulting in her being proceeded against ex-parte.

Significantly, the address reflected in the arbitral

proceedings is the very same address repeatedly

disclosed and admitted by the Appellant in her pleadings

and documents filed before the courts.

Further, the Appellant has herself admitted receipt of

the arbitral award at the same address and thereafter

addressed applications to the Ld. Sole Arbitrator

seeking copies of the arbitral record. At no stage in

those communications did she raise any grievance

regarding non-service of notices during the arbitral

proceedings. The plea of non-service has therefore been

raised belatedly and is contrary to both the record and

the Appellant's own conduct.



b. Query (ii): Arbitrator's connection with the Bank:



That Shri Vikrant Bhardwaj, the Sole Arbitrator who

adjudicated the said arbitral proceedings, is not

connected to Respondent No.1/Axis Bank Ltd. In any

manner whatsoever, whether by way of employment,

engagement, consultancy, retainership, financial

interest, or any other relationship of the nature

contemplated under the Seventh Schedule to the

Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.



c. Query (iii): Number of arbitrations handled for the

Bank:



As per the records maintained by Respondent No. 1 -



FAO (COMM) 91/2025                                            Page 4 of 10

            the number of Arbitrations conducted by Shri Vikrant

            Bharadwaj, over the span of 04-05 years, is 4155.



            Presently there are no arbitration proceedings pending

            or being handled by Shri Vikrant Bharadwaj in which

            he has been appointed as the Sole Arbitrator by, or on

            behalf of, the Respondent Bank.



            Accordingly, there is no subsisting or continuing

            appointment of Shri Vikrant Bharadwaj as an arbitrator

            in any matter on behalf of the Respondent Bank as on

            date.



            It is further submitted that the Respondent Bank has

            discontinued the practice of initiating arbitration

            proceedings through unilateral appointment of

            arbitrators.



            d. Query (iv): Schedule VI and VII declaration:



            Yes. Shri Vikrant Bhardwaj had given the requisite

            declarations.



            4. That the present affidavit is filed bona filed and in the

            interest of justice, and no part of it is false, and nothing

            material has been concealed or suppressed therefrom.”



12. A perusal of the affidavit, as extracted above, would show that there is

no proof of service except what is recorded by the ld. Sole Arbitrator in the

Award dated 26th May 2023. Further, in respect of the ld. Sole Arbitrator -

Shri Vikrant Bhardwaj the Respondent Bank claims that he does not have any

relationship with the Bank of the nature as provided under Schedule 7 of the

ACA, 1996. However, upon querying the official of the Respondent Bank,

who is present in Court, it is stated that the said Arbitrator was paid his fees



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 5 of 10

through the concerned lawyer for the Respondent Bank.

13. The most shocking aspect uncovered from the affidavit of the

Respondent Bank is that in a span of four to five years the said Arbitrator -

Shri Vikrant Bhardwaj has acted as an arbitrator in a whopping 4155 cases

concerning the Respondent Bank.

14. This would clearly be in violation of various provisions of the ACA,

1996, especially those introduced through amendments in 2015 via the

Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2015. It is a matter of fact

that Section 12 of the ACA, 1996 was amended in order to deal with such a

situations, albeit the scale of conflict contemplated under the Fifth Schedule

was of a far lower level than what has been unearthed here. Under the Fifth

Schedule to the ACA, 1996, in total 34 grounds/circumstances have been

mentioned which would give rise to a justifiable doubt as to the independence

or impartiality of the arbitrator. The said grounds have been categorised under

the following heads:



   (i) Arbitrator’s relationship with the parties or counsel;

   (ii) Relationship of the arbitrator to the dispute;

   (iii) Arbitrator’s direct or indirect interest in the dispute;

   (iv) Previous services for one of the parties or other involvement in the



           case;

   (v) Relationship between an arbitrator and another arbitrator or counsel;

   (vi) Relationship between arbitrator and party and others involved in the



           arbitration; and

   (vii) Other circumstances.

15. It is seen that the grounds/circumstances mentioned in respect of the



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 6 of 10

category (iv) above i.e., previous services for one of the parties or other

involvement in the case, the following have been expressly contemplated by

the Legislature:



           “22. The arbitrator has within the past three years

           been appointed as arbitrator on two or more occasions

           by one of the parties or an affiliate of one of the parties.



           xxx



           24. The arbitrator currently serves, or has served

           within the past three years, as arbitrator in another

           arbitration on a related issue involving one of the

           parties or an affiliate of one of the parties.”



16. The above amendments came into effect from 23rd October, 2015,

however, the Court has been informed that up until 2023 such unilateral

appointments were continued to be made by the Respondent bank.

17. Mr. Dayan Krishnan, ld. Senior Counsel appearing for the Respondent

Bank submits that the Bank concedes that such arbitral awards, where the

Respondent Bank had made unilateral appointment of arbitrators, are void ab

initio, in view of the settled principle of necessity of neutrality at all stages of

arbitration as settled by the Supreme Court in Perkins Eastman Architects

DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd., (2020) 20 SCC 760 and Central Organisation

for Railway Electrification v. ECI SPIC SMO MCML (JV), (2025) 4 SCC

641.

18. In fact, in similar matters, this Court has also rendered judgments

setting aside arbitral awards on the ground of unilateral appointment of

arbitrators, including in M/s. Satyaprakash and Brothers (P) Ltd. v. Union



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 7 of 10

of India [2025:DHC:6615-DB], M/s. Sidharth Construction Co. v. Indian

Tourism Development Corporation & Anr. [2025:DHC:2313-DB]. In

addition, the Coordinate Bench of this Court in Ram Kumar and Anr. v.

Shriram Transport Finance Co. Ltd., [2022 SCC Online Del 4268] has also

held similarly.

19. Mr. Krishnan, ld. Senior Counsel further concedes that out of the 4155

cases, where Shri Vikrant Bhardwaj was an arbitrator, in almost 65 per cent

of the awards settlements have been effected, i.e., the disputes have been

resolved in about 2700 cases. Further, in about 1264 cases no execution

petition has been filed and no fresh arbitral appointment has also been made.

20. On instructions from the bank, it is further submitted that from 2023 no

unilateral appointment has been made and upon being queried, it is submitted

that there are a total of 76,000 awards which have been passed by such sole

arbitrators pan India concerning the Respondent Bank.

21. Heard. The clear impression that the Court gathers from the above is

that this is nothing but the tip of an iceberg.

22. Arbitrators who were appointed in thousands of matters like this

without filing proper declarations cannot be said to be independent and

impartial arbitrators. Even judging by the unamended Section 12(1) of the

ACA, 1996, handling thousands of the arbitrations by the very same arbitrator

appointed by one single party would give rise to justifiable doubts as to

independence and impartiality. Clearly, such lawyers who are appointed as

arbitrators cannot be considered as lacking bias. Repeated appointments of

the same arbitrators in thousands of cases goes against the core of Neutrality

which is at the soul of any arbitral process.



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 8 of 10

23. The Respondent Bank - Axis Bank which is the party in the present

case is answerable as to how this situation could be permitted and the Bank

also requires to take some remedial measures without doubt.

24. Accordingly, let a fresh affidavit be filed by the Respondent Bank

giving the reasons as to why thousands of arbitration cases were being given

to the same arbitrator. The Bank shall also file an affidavit as to what is the

future course of action that the bank wishes to adopt in respect of such awards

which have been passed by unilaterally appointed arbitrators, including

enforcement of such awards and steps taken for recovery of loan amounts.

25. Banks being the custodian of the public money cannot avail remedies

which are contrary to law to recover loans. There can be no doubt that the

defaulting borrowers also cannot be allowed to go scot free.

26. Notwithstanding the public interest in recovery of the loans, the route

adopted by the Respondent Bank for the same which is in complete lack of

adherence to statutory provisions has come as a double blow to the

Respondent Bank – on the one hand Awards which are passed in unilateral

appointments are void and unenforceable, while on the other hand the

Respondent Bank’s hands are tied as it cannot enforce such awards or recover

such monies. Thus, the Respondent Bank is totally in a fix as to how to recover

the monies or even invoke fresh arbitration.

27. A solution would need to be carved at an institutional level in a

centralised manner by the Respondent Bank failing which substantial amounts

of public money will go unrecovered and a significant number of awards

would be rendered void and unenforceable.

28. Under these circumstances, let a fresh affidavit be filed as to the manner



FAO (COMM) 91/2025  Page 9 of 10

in which the Respondent Bank wishes to proceed in such cases.

29. Notice was issued to the Reserve Bank of India which is today

represented before the Court. The RBI being the sector regulator, shall also

caution all banks in this regard, so that if any remedial measures need to be

taken by other banks and financial institutions in respect of unilateral

appointments, the same can also be looked into and some guidance issued in

respect thereof.

30. The RBI also to file its affidavit by 16th November, 2026.

31. Coming to the merits of this case, since on behalf of the Respondent

Bank the stand is that the award is void ab initio, therefore, it is declared that

the award dated 26th May, 2023 is unenforceable against the Appellant.

32. The appeal accordingly succeeds, however, in order to take this issue

to a logical conclusion, let the Respondent bank file its affidavit by 16th

November, 2026.

33. In respect of recovery of the loan disbursed to the Appellant, the

Respondent Bank is free to take steps afresh, in accordance with law, if so

permissible.

34. List on 17th November, 2026.

35. This matter shall be treated as part-heard.



                                                              PRATHIBA M. SINGH

                                                                         JUDGE



                           DINESH BHATT

                                JUDGE



SEPTEMBER 30, 2026/ss/msh



FAO (COMM) 91/2025         Page 10 of 10
```

```text
         सा.का.जन. 968(अ).— केन्द्रीर् सरकार, कंपनी अजधजनर्म, 2013 (2013 का 18) की धारा 469 के साथ पठित

धारा 23 की उपधारा (3) द्वारा प्रित्त िजिर्ों का प्रर्ोग करते हुए, कंपनी (अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरताओं में साधारण िेर्र सूचीबद्ध

करना) जनर्म, 2024 का और आगे संिोधन करने के जलए जनम्नजलजखत जनर्म बनाती है, अथायत् :-



1. (1) इन जनर्मों का संजिप्त नाम (अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरताओं में साधारण िेर्र सूचीबद्ध करना) संिोधन जनर्म, 2026

है।



(2) र्े जनर्म रािपत्र मंे इनके प्रकािन की तारीख को प्रवृत्त होंगे।



2. संपूणय कंपनी (अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरताओं मंे साधारण िेर्र सूचीबद्ध करना) जनर्म, 2024 में (इसमें इसके पश्चात मूल

जनर्म के रूप मंे जनर्ियष्ट), में िहां भी ‘िेर्र’ िब्ि आता है, उसके स्ट्थान पर ‘‘इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स’’ िब्ि रखा िाएगा।



3. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 2 के उप-जनर्म (1) मंे, खंड (ख) के बाि, जनम्नजलजखत खंड िोडा िाएगा, अथायत्:-



8398 GI/2026                    (1)

2                            THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY  [PART II—SEC. 3(i)]



‘(खक) ‘‘इदिटी इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स’’ से, भारतीर् कंपनी द्वारा िारी दकए गए इदिटी िेर्र, पठरवतयनीर् जडबेंचर, अधीमानी िेर्र

अजभप्रेत है;’



4. मूल जनर्मों के जनर्म 3--



    (i) खंड (क) मंे, ‘‘कंपजनर्ों’’, िब्ि के बाि, ‘‘अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर् सेवा कंेरों की अजधकाठरता मंे, सावयिजनक कंपनजर्ों

              के अलावा’’, िब्ि अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे;



    (ii) खंड (ख) के पश्चात, जनम्नजलजखत खंड अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकर्ा िाएगा, अथातय् -



    ‘‘(ग) अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर् सेवा केंर की अजधकाठरता मंे गैर-सूचीबद्ध सावयिजनक कंपजनर्ां, िहां तक वे अंतरायष्‍टरीर् जवत्तीर्

    सेवा कंेर प्राजधकरण अजधजनर्म, 2019 (2019 का 50) के प्रावधानों और उसके अधीन बनाए गए जनर्मों के अनुसार

    हंै।’’



5. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 4 में, िोनों स्ट्थानों पर आने वाली ‘‘मौिूिा िेर्रधारकों’’ िब्िों के स्ट्थान पर ‘‘मौिूिा धारक’’ िब्ि

प्रजतस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे।



6. मूल जनर्मों में, जनर्म 5 मंे,



    (i) खंड (घ) मंे, ‘‘जिसका जनवल मूल्र् ऋणात्मक है’’ िब्िों के पश्चात जनम्नजलजखत परंतुक अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकर्ा िाएगा,

    अथायत् :-



             "बिते दक नकारात्मक जनवल मूल्र् वाली कंपनी भी सूचीबद्ध होने के जलए अपने इदिटी इंस्ट्ूमेंट्स िारी करने

             के जलए पात्र होगी, र्दि िारीकताय इस जनर्म के प्रर्ोिन के जलए अनुज्ञेर् अजधकाठरता में संबंजधत प्रजतभूजत

             बािार जनर्ामक द्वारा इस संबंध मंे बनाए गए जनर्मों के अनुसार र्ोग्र् संस्ट्थागत खरीिारों को िुद्ध पेिकि का

             कम से कम पचहत्तर प्रजतित आवंठटत करने का वचन िेता है।"



   (ii) खंड (ङ) मंे, परंतुक मंे, िब्ि "िो वर्"य के जलए, "छह माह से अजधक" िब्ि प्रजतस्ट्थाजपत दकए िाएंगे।



   (iii) खंड (छ) मंे, िब्िों "जनर्ियष्ट अवजध" के पश्चात, "और ऐसी चूक की भरपाई नहीं की गई है" िब्ि अंतःस्ट्थाजपत दकए

   िाएंगे;



7. मूल जनर्मों में, जद्वतीर् अनुसूची में, प्ररूप लीप-1 के जलए जनम्नजलजखत प्ररूप प्रजतस्ट्थाजपत दकर्ा िाएगा, अथायत्:-

Companies (Listing of equity shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules, 2024, namely:̶

1. (1) These rules may be called the Companies (Listing of equity instruments in permissible jurisdictions) Amendment

Rules, 2026.

2. Throughout the Companies (Listing of equity shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules, 2024 (hereinafter referred

to as the principal rules), for the word “shares”, wherever it occurs, the word “instruments’ shall be substituted.

Company;’



4. In the principal rules, in rule 3,-



(i) in clause (a), after the word, “companies”, the words, “other than public companies in the International Financial

Services Centres jurisdiction”, shall be inserted;



(ii) after clause (b), the following clause shall be inserted, namely:–



“(c) unlisted public companies in the International Financial Services Centres jurisdiction, in so far as they are in

accordance with the provisions of the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50 of 2019) and

with the regulations framed thereunder.”.



5. In the principal rules, in rule 4, for the words “existing shareholders” occurring at both the places, the words “existing

holders” shall be substituted.
```
