                     INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA



[Authority delegated by the Central Government vide notification no. GSR 1316(E) dated

18.10.2017 under section 458 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with rule 2(1)(b) of the Companies

(Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017]



IBBI/Valuation/Disc./44/2026                26 November 2026



                              ORDER



This Order disposes, afresh, the Show Cause Notice (SCN) No. RV-13012/3/2024-IBBI/401 dated

06.05.2025 issued to Mr. R Vaidyanathan (RV) under rule 17 read with rule 15 of the Companies

(Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017 (Valuation Rules), pursuant to the directions of the

Appellate Authority in its Order No. IBBI/Valuation/Disc.(A)/07/2025 dated 07.01.2026 (Appellate

Order). Mr. R Vaidyanathan is registered with Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) as

a valuer of Securities or Financial Assets (SFA) with the Registration number

IBBI/RV/03/2018/10049.



1. Background, issuance of the SCN and proceedings on remand.



1.1. Rule 17(1) of the Valuation Rules provides that, based on material available on record, if the

        authorised officer is of the prima facie opinion that sufficient cause exists to cancel or

        suspend the registration of a valuer, it shall issue a SCN to the valuer.



1.2. IBBI had taken cognizance of the valuation report dated 12.09.2022 submitted by Mr. R

        Vaidyanathan in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s Uniply

        Industries Limited, Corporate Debtor (CD), and of the clarifications submitted by him vide

        email dated 06.05.2024. Several contraventions of the provisions of the Valuation Rules

        were observed with respect to his assignment in the CIRP of the CD and accordingly the

        SCN dated 06.05.2025 was issued to him. The SCN alleged the following three

        contraventions:



        a) Non-inclusion of brand name/trademarks/licenses/intellectual properties in the valuation

            report;



        b) Issue regarding assigning zero value to the investment of the CD; and

        c) Issue regarding assigning Fair Value and Liquidation value for the assets of the CD as



            ‘0/Not Determinable’.



1.3. Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted his reply to the SCN on 31.05.2025, availed the opportunity

        of personal hearing through virtual mode on 11.09.2025 and submitted his additional

        response vide email(s) dated 17.09.2025. This Authority, vide Order No.

        IBBI/Valuation/Disc./32/2025 dated 27.11.2025 (Earlier Order), examined the

        contraventions alleged in the SCN vis-à-vis the reply and additional submissions made by

        Mr. R Vaidyanathan and suspended his registration for a period of three months.



                              Page 1 of 15

1.4. Mr. R Vaidyanathan preferred an appeal against the Earlier Order under rule 17(9) of the

        Valuation Rules. The Appellate Authority, after hearing him on 17.12.2025 and considering

        his submissions dated 10.12.2025, 19.12.2025 and 22.12.2025, passed the Order dated

        07.01.2026. The Appellate Authority, inter alia, observed and directed as under:



        a) there was no infirmity in the procedure of issuance of the SCN and no misalignment

            between the findings in the Earlier Order and the contraventions alleged in the SCN; the

            assignment of zero and ‘not determinable’ to several assets gave an impression of

            arbitrary assignment of values without justifiable reason (para 3.1 and 3.2);



        b) under regulation 27 read with regulation 35 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process

            for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 (CIRP Regulations), registered valuers are

            expected to determine the fair value and liquidation value of all the assets of the CD,

            including intangible assets which were not valued on the ground that intangibles were not

            part of the scope of work communicated by the Resolution Professional (RP) (para 3.3);



        c) Mr. R Vaidyanathan, by assigning zero value, completely decimated the value of financial

            assets having a book value of around ₹960 crore; even cash and cash equivalents of

            around ₹1.06 crore were stated to be ‘Not Determinable’, which should have called for

            greater scrutiny and independent due diligence (para 3.5);



        d) Mr. R Vaidyanathan failed to adhere to the International Valuation Standards (IVS),

            including IVS 200 (Businesses and Business Interests) and IVS 210 (Intangible Assets),

            which he claimed to have adopted, and failed to ensure compliance with regulation 35

            read with regulation 27 of the CIRP Regulations (para 4.3);



        e) the punishment of suspension for three months was grossly insufficient given the gravity

            of the misconduct, and the matter was remanded for fresh consideration of the

            contraventions alleged in the SCN, with liberty to Mr. R Vaidyanathan to submit his

            explanations afresh. The Authority was also requested to consider afresh the other issues

            not raised in the appeal (para 4.4); and



        f) Mr. R Vaidyanathan would not be entitled to take any new assignment of valuation till

            disposal of the SCN (para 4.5).



1.5. Pursuant to the Appellate Order, Mr. R Vaidyanathan made a detailed submission dated

        16.10.2026, forwarded the correspondence exchanged with the RP (along with attachments)

        vide emails dated 13.11.2026, and made a further submission dated 19.11.2026. This

        Authority has considered afresh the SCN, the valuation report dated 12.09.2022, the replies

        and submissions made by Mr. R Vaidyanathan at every stage before this Authority and the

        Appellate Authority, and the other material available on record.



2. Preliminary submissions of Mr. R Vaidyanathan.



2.1. Mr. R Vaidyanathan has submitted that he had preferred the appeal as an “aggrieved person”

        under rule 17(9) of the Valuation Rules, seeking to set aside the Earlier Order, and that an

        appellant should not be placed in a worse position merely because he exercised his right of

        appeal. He placed reliance on the doctrine of reformatio in peius. Mr. R Vaidyanathan further



                                                    Page 2 of 15

        submitted that in the Earlier Order dated 27.11.2025, accepted his submissions in respect of

        the first two contraventions. However, with respect to the third contravention, it was

        observed that, in view of the unavailability of adequate documents/information and

        considering the effect of the limitation period, assigning a ‘zero’ value to the trade

        receivables without due justification was not appropriate. Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted

        that the SCN, in respect of the first two contraventions, does not allege any violation of

        valuation standards, rules, regulations, bye-laws or the Code of Conduct. Further, the Earlier

        Order dated 27.11.2025, did not find any violation in respect of these two contraventions on

        merits. Accordingly, no violation of any rules, regulations, bye-laws, etc., was established

        in respect thereof. Thus, only the third alleged contravention survived, wherein the authority

        in its Earlier Order dated 27.11.2025 found him lacking in due diligence in terms of Clauses

        3 and 6 of the Code of Conduct. He has further submitted that the observations in the

        Appellate Order relating to regulations 27 and 35 of the CIRP Regulations and compliance

        with the IVS were not framed as contraventions in the SCN and were recorded without his

        submissions being asked on those aspects. He has requested that the fresh consideration be

        confined to the contraventions alleged in the SCN, that the findings, reasoning and evidence

        considered in the Earlier Order be given due weight, that he be given an effective opportunity

        to respond on any ground not expressly framed in the SCN, and that the matter be disposed

        of expeditiously since he has been restrained from accepting new assignments since

        07.01.2026.



2.2. In compliance with the directions of the Appellate Authority, this Authority has considered

        afresh each of the contraventions alleged in the SCN, along with the observations made in

        the Appellate Order, after affording Mr. R Vaidyanathan the opportunity to submit his

        explanations afresh, which he has availed through his submissions dated 16.10.2026 and

        19.11.2026. The fresh consideration has been confined to the contraventions alleged in the

        SCN, and the findings and reasoning in the Earlier Order, together with the material on which

        they were based, have been duly taken into account.



3. Fresh examination of the contraventions alleged in the SCN.



        The contraventions alleged in the SCN, the response of Mr. R Vaidyanathan and the findings

        of the Authority are summarised as follows:



3.1. Non-inclusion of Brand Name/trademarks/licenses/intellectual properties in the

        Valuation Report.



3.1.1.  It was noted in the SCN that vide letter dated 20.11.2021, Mr. R Vaidyanathan was appointed

        as registered valuer to determine the fair value and liquidation value of the financial assets

        of the CD. There was a brand license agreement dated 01.10.2017 between Uniply Industries

        Limited (CD/Licensor) and UV Boards Limited (Licensee), granting the use of trade name

        ‘UNIPLY’ and other trademarks/licenses/intellectual properties by the Licensor to the

        Licensee for a consideration of ₹75.00 crore over 10 years as per point 5.3 (royalty payment)

        under Article 5 of that agreement. Annexure A of the valuation report dated 12.09.2022

        acknowledged the existence of this agreement. Despite having knowledge of the same, Mr.



        Page 3 of 15

        R Vaidyanathan has not assigned any value to the brand ‘UNIPLY’ and other

        trademarks/licenses/intellectual properties.



3.1.2.  In the Earlier Order, this Authority had accepted the explanation of Mr. R Vaidyanathan on

        this allegation, after observing that the scope of valuation, as per the appointment letter dated

        20.11.2021, was limited to the financial assets mentioned in the balance sheet of the CD,

        that the ‘brand’ was not mentioned in the appointment letter and that, the ‘brand’ being

        internally generated, was not recognised as an intangible asset in the balance sheet in terms

        of para 63 of Ind AS 38. The Appellate Authority, however, observed that under regulation

        27 read with regulation 35 of the CIRP Regulations registered valuers are expected to

        determine the fair value and liquidation value of all the assets of the CD, including intangible

        assets, and that a conjoint reading of IVS 200 and IVS 210 indicates that intangible assets

        must be considered where relevant.



        Submissions of Mr. R Vaidyanathan.



3.1.3.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan reiterated his earlier submissions (recorded in paras 2.1.5 to 2.1.10 of

        the Earlier Order) and submitted that the issue about the scope of work in respect of the

        assets to be valued had been examined in para 2.1.11 to 2.1.14 of the Earlier Order dated

        27.11.2025.



        Mr. R Vaidyanathan has referred to the following observation mentioned in para 3.3 of the

        Order of the Appellate Authority with respect to the valuation of brand UNIPLY:



        “….The valuation report also reflects the valuer’s ignorance to the provisions of the Code

        and the regulations made thereunder. Under Regulation 27 read with Regulation 35 of the

        IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016, the registered valuers are expected to determine the fair

        value and liquidation value of the assets of the CD which should comprise all assets of the

        CD including intangible assets. The valuer cannot shirk off his duty to conduct a full and

        complete valuation of all assets of the CD merely on the ground that intangibles were

        probably not part of the scope of work communicated by the Resolution Professional which

        in any case cannot be contrary to the statutory requirements.”



3.1.4.  In this regard, he has submitted that the observations in the Appellate Order relating to

        regulations 27 and 35 of the CIRP Regulations were not framed as contraventions in the

        SCN and were therefore beyond the scope of the SCN. He has further submitted that there

        were three registered valuers who were assigned the valuation of different assets of the CD.

        First for ‘Land & Building”, Second for “Plant & Machinery” and third for “Securities &

        Financial Assets”. He was given the valuation of “Securities & Financial Assets”. Even for

        the valuation of the assets under the head “Securities & Financial Assets”, the same was not

        mentioned in a general manner. Rather specific list of items which corresponded to the line

        items in the Balance Sheet along with the corresponding book value were referred for

        valuation. Hence, it is very clear from the reference made that he was asked to value specific

        items which were only a small part of all the items in the Balance Sheet while the other

        valuers were also asked to value other items in the balance sheet. In this scenario, if anyone



        Page 4 of 15

        can be set to have a whole picture about the items to be valued is the IP who knows which

        items have been referred for valuation by which valuer. So, if a valuation of a particular item

        was missing, it was the duty of the IP to point out the same and only then can it be said that

        he did not value that item. Since all the items which were referred for valuation were valued

        by him and no discrepancy and query was ever made till the time.



3.1.5.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted that he was never asked by the IP about the valuation of the

        brand UNIPLY. However, on perusal of the DC order dated 04.03.2025, in the matter of

        Lingumgunta Venkata Shyam Sundar, he became aware that the IP had mailed the other two

        valuers valuing “Securities & Financial Assets” assets class about the valuation of the brand

        UNIPLY. It is pertinent to note the query was raised by the IP only when SCN was issued

        to the IP, Mr. Lingumgunta Venkata Shyam Sundar by the Board on 10.04.2024 and even at

        that time the IP did not ask him but asked the other two valuers the following "Pursuant to

        the valuation report received, we request you to confirm whether any value is ascertained

        for the brand UNIPLY. If so, we request you to share the same with us” without giving the

        reference to the SCN issued to the IP. It is clear, therefore, that even at the later stage no

        query whatsoever, was made from him by the IP in respect of the brand.



3.1.6.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan also submitted that the conduct in question related to the valuation

        exercise, at a time when only specified assets had been referred to him, and that he had

        valued all those assets. He contended that this issue had been examined in detail by this

        Authority in the Earlier Order, which correctly recorded the relevant facts, whereas the

        Appellate Authority had introduced a new finding that he had failed to value all the assets of

        the CD, including intangible assets. He submitted that he could not be faulted for not valuing

        an asset that was not included in the specific list of assets referred to him by the RP.



3.1.7.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted that the duty of a valuer is defined by the scope of work, and

        under IVS 101 (Scope of Work) the engagement is fixed by the asset to be valued, the

        purpose, the basis of value, the valuation date and the nature and limits of the work. The

        appointment letter dated 20.11.2021 did not refer to "Securities and Financial Assets" in a

        general manner. It is reiterated that the IP had listed specific line items with their book

        values, namely trade receivables, other current assets, cash and cash equivalents,

        investments, other non-current assets and other financial assets, under Regulation 35 of the

        CIRP Regulations. This Authority in its earlier order recorded this in paras 2.1.11 and 2.1.12

        of its order dated 27.11.2025, noting that the scope was limited to the financial assets in the

        balance sheet and that the "brand" of the CD was not mentioned in the appointment letter.

        Every item referred to him was valued, and the Appellate Authority has not identified a

        single referred item that was left unvalued.



3.1.8.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted that the RP was at all times empowered and, in a position, to

        amend or expand the scope of work initially agreed upon under the Engagement Letter dated

        20th November 2021, including the addition of any requirement for the valuation of

        Engagement Letter dated 20th November 2021, executed between the Interim Resolution

        Professional and Mr. R Vaidyanathan, expressly provides for the possibility of amendment



        Page 5 of 15

        or modification of the agreed scope of work. However, no such modification was made to

        the scope of work by the RP.



3.1.9.  Mr. R Vaidyanathan has further submitted that the definition of ‘fair value’ in regulation

        2(1)(hb) of the CIRP Regulations, as it stood on the valuation date and the report date, did

        not contain any reference to all assets including tangible and intangible assets. The

        Explanation clarifying that the estimated realizable value is to be computed after taking into

        account all the assets of the CD, including tangible and intangible assets along with their

        underlying synergies, was inserted only with effect from 25.02.2026. Therefore, his

        engagement must be assessed under the framework applicable on the valuation date.



3.1.10. Mr. R Vaidyanathan has further referred to the following observation mentioned in para 4.3

        of the Order of the Appellate Authority with respect to applicability of valuation standards:



        “It is pertinent to note that the International Valuation Standards under IVS 210 Intangible

        Assets recognises ‘intangible asset’ as “non-monetary asset that manifests itself by its

        economic properties. It does not have physical substance but grants rights and/or economic

        benefits to its owner”. Further, IVS 200 Businesses and Business Interests stipulate that

        valuation of business includes “the sum of the recorded and unrecorded net tangible and

        identifiable intangible assets of the business””. Therefore, conjoint reading of IVS 200 and

        IVS 210 clarifies that intangible assets may derive value independently or in combination

        with other assets and must be considered where relevant. Consequently, this Appellate

        Authority finds that Mr. R. Vaidyanathan failed to adhere to the International Valuation

        Standards (IVS), despite his explicit assertion in his valuation report that such standards

        were adopted and followed by him. In the present case, the material available on record,

        Mr. R Vaidyanathan miserably failed to carry out his assigned duty…..”

        ‘Land and Building’, ‘Plant and Machinery’ and ‘Securities or Financial Assets’, and that he

        had been engaged only for the last category. He submitted that each asset class is governed

        by its own applicable standards: ‘Land and Building’ by IVS 400 (Real Property Interests)

        and, where applicable, IVS 410 (Development Property), and ‘Plant and Machinery’ by IVS

        300 (Plant and Equipment). He contended that he was not required to apply these standards

        and value these assets as they did not relate to the assets which had been referred to him for

        valuation. Similarly, he was not required to apply IVS 200 (which applies to valuation of

        business and business interests) and IVS 210 (which applies to intangible assets), as neither

        he had been engaged to value the CD as a going concern nor were intangible assets referred

        to him for valuation.



3.1.12. Mr. R Vaidyanathan further submitted that the statement in the valuation report that IVS had

        been adopted meant that the standards applicable to the assets within the scope of work had

        with reference to the standards relevant to this engagement, namely IVS 101, 102, 103, 104,

        105 and 500. He therefore submitted that the Appellate Authority’s observation that, despite

3.1.14. This Authority notes that the scope of valuation of Mr. R Vaidyanathan was confined to

        specified financial assets, identified by line items and book values as appearing in the

        balance sheet of the CD. The ‘brand’ of the CD did not find mention in the appointment

        letter. The ‘brand’ of the CD in the present case is internally generated, has not been acquired

        through any business combination and is, therefore, not reflected in the balance sheet of the

        CD, in terms of para 63 of Ind AS 38, which provides that “Internally generated brands,

        mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance shall not be

        recognized as intangible assets”.



3.1.15. This Authority again after detailed perusal of the scope of work, notes that the engagement

        letter provided a mechanism for amending the scope of work, which was never invoked by

        the RP to include the brand or any other intangible asset. This Authority notes that

        submission of the RV that the RP, having appointed separate valuers for different asset

        classes, was in the best position to identify any asset of the CD which had not been referred

        for valuation, and the record does not show that the RP ever raised any query with Mr. R

        Vaidyanathan regarding the brand. The reference to the trademark licence agreement in

        Annexure A of the valuation report was a reproduction of the list of agreements furnished

        by the RP, accompanied by a disclosure in para 11.5 of the report that the agreements were

        not necessarily related to the scope of the valuation.

        by these standards was to be valued by him merely because he followed IVS.

        books of account of the CD, cannot by itself be regarded as conclusive evidence of the

        existence, validity, recoverability or realisable value of that asset as on the valuation date.

        Book values are accounting balances, and their reliability for valuation purposes must be

        examined having regard to the underlying records, the nature of the asset, the period for

        which the balance has remained outstanding, subsequent movements, recoveries, supporting

        documentation and other relevant circumstances. He submitted that this was particularly

        significant in the present case, where several balances had been carried forward from earlier

        financial periods without corresponding movements or supporting evidence being made

        available for independent verification. For instance, the cash balance of approximately ₹1.03

        crore reflected in the audited financial statements for FY 2019–20 was significantly higher

        than the cash balances reported in the preceding financial years.

        underlying balances rather than their automatic acceptance at their recorded book values.

        Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted that adopting the book values without examining their

        underlying substance, existence and recoverability would itself have resulted in an

        unsupported valuation. Accordingly, the book values were considered as an important

        starting point for the valuation exercise, but could not, in the absence of adequate

        corroborative evidence, be treated as determinative of the fair value or liquidation value of

        the respective assets.



3.3.15. Mr. R Vaidyanathan submitted that the conclusions recorded in the valuation report were

        based on the evidence and records made available to him, the independent examination and

        verification undertaken wherever feasible, and the professional assessment that could

        reasonably be carried out in the circumstances prevailing as at the relevant valuation date.

        The expressions ‘Zero’ and ‘Not Determinable’ were used to reflect the distinct evidentiary

        and valuation circumstances of the respective assets, and not as a substitute for undertaking

        the valuation exercise.



        Findings of the Authority.



3.3.16. This Authority has perused the valuation report, which sets out in detail, asset-wise, the

        valuation process adopted, the information sought, the information received and the reasons

        for the values assigned (as summarised in para 2.3.10 of the Earlier Order). It is noted that

        Mr. R Vaidyanathan sought specific information from the RP through emails dated

        09.01.2022, 10.01.2022, 18.01.2022, 19.01.2022, 31.01.2022 and 24.02.2022, and that the

        RP, in his written representation dated 15.06.2022, recorded that the CD had not produced

        bank statements for any of the bank accounts as on or after the insolvency commencement

        date, that no physical cash had been produced before him during the CIRP, and that no

        further information in terms of ageing, invoices or confirmation of balances was available.



3.3.17. As regards cash and cash equivalents, this Authority finds merit in the submission of Mr. R

        Vaidyanathan. He in his email dated 19.01.2022 raised flags about the handling large cash

        balances which is not a usual business practices, made specific enquiries in this regard, and

        obtained the RP’s representation that no physical cash had been produced. In these

        circumstances, assigning a positive value would have implied the existence of cash that

        could not be verified, while assigning zero would have implied a confirmed nil balance. The

        use of ‘Not Determinable’, with the reasons disclosed in the report, cannot be said to be a

        failure of due diligence or a misrepresentation. The same reasoning applies to the bank

        balances.



3.3.18. This Authority also accepts the submission of Mr. R Vaidyanathan that the book value of an

        asset, by itself, is not conclusive of its realisable value, and that the aggregate book value of

        ₹960.45 crore cannot be the measure of undervaluation in the absence of information

        establishing the existence and recoverability of the underlying assets. In respect of other

        current assets, other non-current assets and other financial assets, the report records the

        information sought, the information not received and the reasons for the conclusion, and the

        explanation of Mr. R Vaidyanathan on these assets is accepted. Further, the valuation report

        discloses the scope, approaches, methods, inputs, assumptions, limitations and principal

        reasons for the conclusions reached and, read with the contemporaneous correspondence,

        this Authority accepts his submission regarding compliance with the reporting requirements.



                                                    Page 13 of 15

3.3.19. However, this Authority notes that the position with respect to trade receivables (other than

        those from KKN) is different. It is noted from the valuation report that the RV did not have

        adequate documents/information for valuation of the trade receivables, as captured in the

        report itself (“Adequacy of Information - NOT ADEQUATE”). In such a scenario of

        inadequate documents/information, according ‘zero’ value to the receivables is not

        appropriate. With respect to cash and cash equivalents, other non-current assets and non-

        current other financial assets, and even the trade receivable from KKN, in the absence of

        necessary documents/information Mr. R Vaidyanathan reported the value as ‘Not

        Determinable’. It is not clear as to why, with respect to the other trade receivables, he

        accorded ‘zero’ value when the same situation of unavailability of adequate

        documents/information persisted. Mr. R Vaidyanathan has himself submitted that a value of

        ‘Zero’ conveys an affirmative conclusion which ought to be supported by adequate evidence;

        no such evidence of irrecoverability has been brought on record in respect of these trade

        receivables.



3.3.20. Further, the valuation report states that the dues are not less than 26/27 months old. Thus, by

        his own admission, the CD still had the right to recover the dues as the limitation period of

        three years had not expired on the valuation date. It is also noted that the last audited financial

        statements of the CD for FY 2019-20, relied upon by Mr. R Vaidyanathan, describe the trade

        receivables as ‘considered good’. While this Authority agrees that legal enforceability is not

        by itself determinative of economic value, the absence of collections during the CIRP and

        the non-availability of records do not, by themselves, establish that the receivables had no

        realisable value. The fact that no recovery was made up to the liquidation commencement

        date is an event subsequent to the valuation date and does not justify the conclusion reached

        as on 04.10.2021.



3.3.21. This Authority notes that in light of unavailability of adequate documents/information and

        considering the effect of the limitation period, assigning of ‘zero’ value to the trade

        receivables (other than those from KKN), without due justification, is not appropriate and is

        in contravention of clause 6 of the Code of Conduct.



4. Order.



4.1. The valuation report is based on the professional opinion of the valuer backed by his

        expertise and skills. Based on the valuation report, various critical decisions are taken during

        the CIRP and liquidation process, such as approving a resolution plan for the CD or fixing

        the base price for auction of the assets of the CD. A valuation report is inherently subjective

        in nature, and its reliability decreases with increase in subjectivity. Therefore, it is necessary

        for a valuer to exercise a high degree of due diligence while preparing the valuation report.



4.2. On fresh consideration of the contraventions alleged in the SCN, this Authority has accepted

        the explanation of Mr. R Vaidyanathan on the allegations relating to non-inclusion of brand

        name/trademarks/licenses/intellectual properties and non-valuation of the investment in

        Artmatrix Technology Sdn Bhd, as well as on the assignment of ‘Not Determinable’ values

        to cash and cash equivalents and the other assets. However, the assignment of ‘zero’ value



                                                    Page 14 of 15

        to trade receivables of about ₹161.90 crore, without due justification, has been found to be

        in contravention of clause 6 of the Code of Conduct. This Authority has also taken note of

        the observation of the Appellate Authority regarding the adequacy of the punishment, the

        significance of the trade receivables in the assets of the CD, the fact that Mr. R Vaidyanathan

        has been restrained from accepting new valuation assignments since 07.01.2026 in terms of

        para 4.5 of the Appellate Order, and that there is no allegation of mala fide or personal gain

        against him.



4.3. In view of the foregoing, after considering the allegations made in the SCN, the replies and

        submissions of Mr. R Vaidyanathan, the Appellate Order and the material available on

        record, the Authority, in exercise of powers conferred vide notification of Central

        Government no. GSR 1316(E) dated 18.10.2017 under section 458 of the Companies Act,

        2013 and in pursuance of rule 15 and rule 17 of the Valuation Rules, considers that the

        suspension of registration of Mr. R Vaidyanathan (Registration No.

        IBBI/RV/03/2018/10049) for a period of three months as given in the earlier order was

        justified.



4.4. Further, this authority notes that an appeal was filed by Mr. R Vaidyanathan on 10.12.2025

        against this earlier order dated 27.11.2025 wherein no interim relief was granted to him.

        Thereafter, the Appellate Authority in its Order dated 07.01.2026 directed for disposal of the

        SCN afresh and also restrained Mr. R Vaidyanathan from taking any fresh assignment till

        disposal of the SCN afresh. Now the SCN is being disposed of afresh in this order wherein

        suspension for a period of three months as given in the Earlier order is being considered

        justified. However, since this order is being made after a period of almost one year from the

        date of the earlier order, during which period he has suffered the consequences of suspension

        of his registration; the punishment already undergone by him is being considered sufficient

        and no further punishment is being imposed on him.



4.5. In terms of para 4.4, this Order shall come into force immediately.



4.6. A copy of this Order shall be forwarded to ICSI Registered Valuers Organisation, where Mr.

        R Vaidyanathan is enrolled as a member.



4.7. Accordingly, the show cause notice is disposed of.

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India



                                          No. IBBI/PR/2026/19

                                          26th November, 2026



Press Release



Shri Rahul Madan takes charge as Chairperson of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of

India



Shri Rahul Madan assumed charge as Chairperson of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of

India in New Delhi on 25th November, 2026.



Shri Rahul Madan is a Chartered Accountant, Cost and Management Accountant and qualified

Insolvency Professional. Prior to joining the IBBI as Chairperson, he served as the Managing

Director of the Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals of ICAI (IIIPI) for over 6 years.

Prior to that, he had an extensive career spanning over 24 years in the banking and financial

services sector, having served with institutions including the State Bank of India, Kotak

Mahindra Bank and ICICI Bank. During his professional career, he has worked in diverse areas,

including corporate banking, credit and risk management, investment banking, debt advisory,

structured finance and institutional wealth management.

INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA

                    (Disciplinary Committee)



No. IBBI/DC/353/2026                13 November 2026



                                                     ORDER



This Order disposes of the Show Cause Notice (SCN) No. IBBI/C/2024/01132/883/488 dated

30.07.2024, issued to Shri Alok Kailash Saksena, an Insolvency Professional registered with the

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI/Board) with Registration No. IBBI/IPA-

001/IP-P00056/2017-18/10134, who is a Professional Member of the Indian Institute of

Insolvency Professionals of ICAI.



1. Background



1.1 The National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, (AA) vide its order dated

        26.10.2018, admitted an application filed by M/s. Oriental Bank of Commerce under

        Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code) for initiating Corporate

        Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s. Associate Decor Limited (CD) and Shri

        Alok Kailash Saksena was appointed as Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) in the

        matter and later he was appointed as the Resolution Professional (RP) of CD.



1.2 The Board received a complaint dated 17.05.2024 against Shri Alok Kailash Saksena

        about certain irregularities in the CIRP of the CD. The Board vide emails dated

        06.06.2024 and 11.07.2024 sought reply from Shri Alok Kailash Saksena on the

        allegation raised in the complaint. In response to the said emails, replies were received

        by the Board from Shri Alok Kailash Saksena on 12.06.2024, 18.07.2024 and 24.07.2024.

        The Board examined the allegations in the above complaint vis-a-vis the reply to the same

        and based on such examination and material available on record, the Board formed a

        prima facie opinion that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena had contravened provisions of the

        Code and Regulations made thereunder and issued the SCN to Shri Alok Kailash Saksena.

        Shri Alok Kailash Saksena provided his response to the SCN on 23.08.2024.



1.3 The SCN, along with the response of Shri Alok Kailash Saksena to the SCN, was referred

        to Disciplinary Committee (DC) for disposal. The personal hearing of Shri Alok Kailash

        Saksena before the DC was initially scheduled for 21.03.2025, and an email in this regard

        was sent to Shri Alok Kailash Saksena on 12.03.2025. The link for joining the personal

        hearing was subsequently shared with him vide email dated 20.03.2025. On the same day,

        Shri Alok Kailash Saksena requested that the personal hearing be rescheduled on account

        of a family emergency.



1.4 Thereafter, the Board, vide email dated 29.05.2025, sought certain clarifications and

        documents from Shri Alok Kailash Saksena in relation to the alleged contraventions. In

        response, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena, vide email dated 18.06.2025, provided certain

        submissions and sought additional time to furnish the requisite documents. He further



                      Page 1 of 41

        submitted that the issues raised in the complaint before the Board were identical to the

        issues raised by the suspended director in IA No. 10 of 2022, which had been heard and

        reserved for orders by the AA. On 30.06.2025, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena furnished

        certain documents and sought time until 10.07.2025 to provide the remaining documents.

        On 10.07.2025, he furnished additional submissions and stated that the AA had informed

        on 08.07.2025 that the order in IA No. 161 of 2020 would be pronounced on 30.07.2025.

        Subsequently, vide email dated 02.08.2025, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena informed to the

        Board that on 30.07.2025, the AA had informed that the order was not ready and had

        adjourned the matter to 26.08.2025 for orders.



1.5 Thereafter, vide email dated 14.08.2025, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that the

        issues raised in the complaint and the SCN were identical to those raised by the ex-

        promoter and the complainant before the AA in IA No. 10 of 2022. He further stated that

        the said application had been fully heard by the Bench and was reserved for orders on

        26.08.2025. Accordingly, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena requested that the personal hearing

        before the DC be scheduled after the pronouncement of the order in IA No. 10 of 2022.

        He also stated that he would inform the Board immediately upon pronouncement of the

        order. Thereafter, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena vide his email dated 03.09.2025 informed

        to Board that on 26.08.2025 also, the AA had stated that the order was not ready and had

        accordingly posted the matter to 24.09.2025. Ultimately, on 06.02.2026, Shri Alok

        Kailash Saksena furnished a copy of the order dated 12.01.2026 passed by the AA in IA

        No. 10 of 2022, whereby the said application was dismissed. He also made additional

        submissions in the matter.



1.6 Thereafter, the DC scheduled the personal hearing of Shri Alok Kailash Saksena before

        the DC for 18.02.2026. On 17.02.2026, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena requested that the

        personal hearing be rescheduled to another date as he was travelling. Subsequently, vide

        communication dated 21.02.2026, he submitted that the question of approval of the

        Resolution Plan was being considered by the third member of the Bench, who had posted

        the matter to 23.02.2026 for resolving the difference of opinion in relation to the

        pronouncement of the order on the Resolution Plan. He further stated that he would be

        occupied with the said matter for some time and would communicate a convenient date

        for the personal hearing. Thereafter, the DC fixed the personal hearing for 21.07.2026.

        However, vide email dated 14.07.2026, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena informed to the DC

        that he was travelling to Udaipur and, in support thereof, enclosed a copy of his air tickets.

        He accordingly requested that the personal hearing be rescheduled. The personal hearing

        was thereafter rescheduled to 06.08.2026. Shri Alok Kailash Saksena again vide email

        dated 30.07.2026 requested that the hearing be further rescheduled, stating that his

        Advocate, Shri Ashish Makhija, was not available, and requested that it be fixed on

        07.08.2026, 10.08.2026 or 11.08.2026.



1.7 Accordingly, the DC, vide email dated 06.08.2026, rescheduled the personal hearing to

        07.08.2026. Shri Alok Kailash Saksena availed the opportunity of personal hearing before

        the DC through virtual mode on 07.08.2026, along with his Advocate, Shri Deep Tarun



                                              Page 2 of 41

        Bisht. Pursuant to the personal hearing, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted additional

        written submissions vide emails dated 17.08.2026 and 24.08.2026.



2. Preliminary Objections raised by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena.



2.1 Forum shopping by the complainant and prevailing orders of the AA



2.1.1.  Before going into the merits of the instant SCN, the DC notes that in his reply to SCN

        and in various emails sent to the Board, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena has at length submitted

        that the complainant has raised materially identical allegations before the AA (IA 10/2022

        & IA 161/2020), Hon’ble Karnataka High Court (WP 483/2023), and the Supreme Court

        (Civil Appeal No. 48 of 2025 arising out of SLP (C) No. 11599 of 2024), which amounts

        to forum-shopping and an abuse of process, and that judicial prudence requires these

        proceedings be kept in abeyance pending outcomes elsewhere. The DC finds it

        appropriate to deal with this issue first.



        Examination by the DC



2.1.2.  The DC has gone through the orders passed in the above mentioned court proceedings.

        The DC notes that Hon’ble Supreme Court vide judgment dated 03.01.2025 in the matter

        of Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd. v. Farooq Ali Khan & Ors. (Civil Appeal No.

        48 of 2025 with Civil Appeal Nos. 49 and 50 of 2025, 2025 INSC 25) had set aside the

        order of Hon’ble Karnataka High Court in WP 483/2023 dated 22.04.2024, and observed

        as under: -



        “11. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion that the last point taken

        by Mr. Shyam Divan, that there is no delay in approaching the High Court, must be

        rejected. The reason is this. The CIRP proceedings commenced on 26.10.2018. The sheet

        anchor of Mr. Divan submission and also the justification for the High Court to assume

        jurisdiction on the ground that principles of natural justice were violated, when

        respondent no.1 was not given a notice before the 19th COC meeting, occurred way back

        on 11.02.2020. However, the jurisdiction of the High Court was invoked only on

        04.01.2023. The time gap between these two events is almost three years. The initiation

        and continuation of proceeding by Swamitva Consortium before the Adjudicating

        Authority, NCLT or the Supreme Court cannot lend any justification whatsoever in

        approaching the High Court so late.



        12. Further, it is also an admitted fact that on 06.10.2022, respondent no. 1 moved an

        interlocutory application before the Adjudicating Authority seeking rejection of the

        resolution plan filed by the appellant. The grounds taken in the interlocutory application

        are the same as those in this appeal. It is not as if the High Court was unaware of

        respondent no. 1 availing the statutory remedy under the Code. At least on this ground,

        the High Court should have relegated respondent no. 1 to the procedure under the Code

        and permitted him to continue the remedy that he has chosen to adopt. We may hasten to

        add that it is not necessary for us to enter into the merits of the matter to examine the



                               Page 3 of 41

        amounts offered by respondent no. 1 and to contrast with the offer made by the

        applicant.



        13. The jurisdiction and power of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5)(c) has

        already been reiterated by this Court in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd.

        v. Satish Kumar Gupta and Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited v. Amit Gupta. It is

        important to note that CIRP proceedings commenced on 26.10.2018, six years ago, and

        the resolution plan of the appellant was approved in 2020, four years back. The

        importance of concluding the CIRP proceedings was highlighted by this Court, on a

        number of occasions. In a recent order in Committee of Creditors of KSK Mahanadi

        Power Company Ltd. v. M/s Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd (supra), this Court

        has observed that an unjustified interference with the proceedings initiated under the

        Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, breaches the discipline of law.



        14. In view of the delay in approaching the High Court, particularly when respondent

        no.1 himself has initiated proceedings under the Code by filing interlocutory applications

        seeking similar relief, we are of the opinion that the High Court committed an error in

        entertaining the writ petition.



        15. Apart from delay and laches, High Court should have noted that Insolvency and

        Bankruptcy Code is a complete code in itself, having sufficient checks and balances,

        remedial avenues and appeals. Adherence of protocols and procedures maintains legal

        discipline and preserves the balance between the need for order and the quest for justice.

        The supervisory and judicial review powers vested in High Courts represent critical

        constitutional safeguards, yet their exercise demands rigorous scrutiny and judicious

        application. This is certainly not a case for the High Court to interdict CIRP proceedings

        under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.



        16. In view of the above, we allow these appeals and set aside the final judgment and

        order passed by the High Court in Writ Petition No. 483 of 2023 (GM-RES) dated

        22.04.2024. We further direct that the Adjudicating Authority will now commence the

        proceedings from where it was interdicted by the High Court and complete the same as

        expeditiously as possible, which is also the spirit of the Code.



        17. There shall be no order as to costs.”



2.1.3.  Accordingly, the DC observes that the Hon’ble Supreme Court had set aside the judgment

        of the Hon’ble Karnataka High Court on the ground of delay and because the suspended

        director had already pursued his remedy under the Code by approaching the AA. The

        Hon’ble Supreme Court did not go into the merits and had directed the AA to resume the

        proceedings from where it was interdicted by the Hon’ble High Court and to complete

        them expeditiously.



2.1.4. The DC further notes that there were two applications which were filed before the AA.

        The first application was IA 10/2022 which contained matters related to some of the

        contraventions of the instant SCN. Although the matter was dismissed by the AA, there



                                              Page 4 of 41

        were two separate orders i.e., one by the Hon’ble Technical Member and the other by

        Hon’ble Judicial Member. The Hon’ble Judicial Member dismissed the matter on all

        parameters raised in the application and recorded that “In conclusion, based on

        aforegoing reasons, the Application is dismissed on all parameters raised therein and

        observing that the [sic] it is yet another spoke in the wheel of adoption of Resolution Plan

        submitted by SRA which got approval with 100% voting strength of CoC and that this

        Plan is languishing all these years because of the manoeuvrability of suspended

        director.” The Hon’ble Technical Member dismissed the application as not maintainable

        on the grounds of lack of locus standi and the conduct of the suspended directors during

        the CIRP. Some of the issues forming part of the contraventions in the SCN were raised

        in the application, though they were not specifically discussed in the analysis portion of

        the orders.



2.1.5. In the second application bearing IA 161/2020 filed before the AA for approval of the

        Resolution Plan, two separate orders were passed on 12.01.2026 by Hon’ble Judicial and

        Hon’ble Technical Member. The Hon’ble Technical Member observed as under: -



        “1. From the Documents available on record, it appears that the Audited Financial

        Statements are not included in the Information Memorandum nor were they made

        available to the Prospective Resolution applicants.



        In this regard, it is necessary to refer to the Regulation 36 of the CIRP Regulations



        …



        Form G itself requires: “Financial statements, including audited financial statements for

        last two financial years of the corporate debtor...” The use of the word “shall” in

        Regulation 36 makes it clear that providing audited financial statements in the IM is

        mandatory, not discretionary.



        1.2 In the present case: CIRP commenced on 26.10.2018. The RP should have prepared

        the IM with audited financials by 19.12.2018 (54 days from CIRP commencement).

        However, the RP did not appoint a statutory auditor until September 2019, nearly 11

        months into the CIRP. The EOI was issued on 23.08.2019, even before the auditor was

        appointed.



        1.3 The Information Memorandum issued in June-August 2019 contained only

        provisional/unaudited financial statements. Audited financial statements were provided

        to stakeholders only on 03.02.2020, nearly 15 months into the CIRP and well after the

        last date for submission of resolution plans, by which time most of the PRAs withdrew.



        1.4 The RP seeks to justify this by claiming that



            a. The books of account were not available with the RP.



            b. The RP acted on a “best efforts” basis.



            c. The Corporate Debtor was to be resolved “as is where is.”



                                              Page 5 of 41

        1.5 I find these justifications to be wholly improper and contrary to law. Section 19 of the

        IBC provides:



        …



        1.5.3. By proceeding with a defective IM, the RP has:



            a. Reduced competition in the bidding process.



            b. Violated the fundamental principle of transparency in the CIRP process.



            c. Deprived creditors of better recovery and guarantors of protection from invocation.



        1.6. The RP’s argument that there is no concept of “best efforts” under the Code is

        correct, but it applies to the RP himself. The Code imposes strict statutory duties on the

        RP. There is no provision allowing the RP to discharge duties on a “best efforts” basis.

        The RP must comply with statutory requirements, failing which appropriate action must

        be taken



        1.7. Similarly, the concept of “as is where is” in Clause 1.10.5 of the RFRP does not stop

        or holdback the RP from complying with Regulation 36. The phrase “as is where is”

        means that the resolution applicant takes over the corporate debtor with all its assets and

        liabilities as they exist. It does not mean that the RP can provide incomplete or inaccurate

        information. Even for “as is where is” sale, the seller (in this case, the RP) must provide

        full and accurate information to enable buyers to make informed decisions.



        Thus, the First Violation that occurred in the CIRP process is the Violation of Regulation

        36.”



2.1.6. Furthermore, the Hon’ble Technical Member rejected the resolution plan and ordered for

        liquidation of the CD by making following observations: -

        13. DECISION:



        13.1. Based on the above detailed analysis, I arrive at the following conclusions:



        A. The Resolution Plan dated 11.02.2020 submitted by METL and approved by the CoC

        suffers from multiple fundamental and incurable defects, both procedural and

        substantive.



        B. The CIRP process leading to approval of the Resolution Plan was vitiated by material

        irregularities including violation of Regulations 19, 21(3), 36, 36B(4A), 39(3) and 39(4)

        of the CIRP Regulations.



        C. The Resolution Plan violates Section 24, 30, 30(2)(c), (d), (e) and (f) of the Insolvency

        and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and thus, is not satisfactory.



         D. The Resolution Plan is conditional in nature and cannot be effectively implemented,

        contrary to the principles laid down in Ebix Singapore (supra).



                                              Page 6 of 41

        E. The Resolution Applicant and Acquisition SPV through which the plan is to be

        implemented does not satisfy the requirements specified in the Resolution Plan itself and

        has not provided Section 29A compliance.



        F. The proposed merger violates the Companies Act, 2013 and the Competition Act, 2002.



        G. The proposed assignment of debt violates the SARFAESI Act and RBI guidelines.



         H. The Resolution Plan dated 11.02.2020 is not viable and feasible.



         I. The Resolution Professional failed to maximize the value of the Corporate Debtor by

        excluding the VAT Loan eligibility of Rs.205 crores from the valuation, issuing

        Information Memorandum without audited financial statements and conducting a CIRP

        process that resulted in withdrawal of 21 out of 23 prospective applicants.



        The defects are so fundamental and incurable that the Resolution Plan cannot be

        approved and must be rejected under Section 31(2) of the IBC.



        The CIRP process is not a game where parties can cut corners, violate regulations, and

        hope to escape on technicalities. It is a serious process with serious consequences for all

        stakeholders. It must be conducted with utmost fairness, transparency, and adherence to

        law.



        13.2. I also note that certain actions of the Resolution Professional in this case raise

        serious questions about his conduct and deserve investigation by the Insolvency and

        Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI). In particular:



            a. The issuance of Information Memorandum without audited financial statements in

            violation of Regulation 36.



            b. The tabling of an amended Resolution Plan dated 11.02.2020 for approval without

            evaluation matrix.



            c. The submission of Compliance Certificate and Form H for the wrong plan dated:

            10.02.2020.



            d. The filing of I.A. 161/2020 before receipt of Performance Bank Guarantee.



        These actions, viewed cumulatively, suggest either gross incompetence or worse,

        deliberate misconduct in collusion with the Resolution Applicant. The Registry is directed

        to forward a copy of this order to the IBBI for such action as it deems appropriate against

        the Resolution Professional.”



2.1.7. However, the Hon’ble Judicial Member through his separate order approved the

        resolution plan and observed as under:



        “16. In view of the discussions, the law thus settled and for the aforesaid reasons, the

        incumbent application bearing I.A. No. 161 of 2020 in CP (IB) 51/2018 meets the

        requirements of Section 30(2) of the Code and Regulations 37, 38, 38 (1A) and 39 of the

        CIRP Regulations, 2016 and the Resolution Plan is not in contravention of any of the



                                              Page 7 of 41

        provisions of Section 29A of the Code and is Resolution Plan, the Resolution Plan dated

        11.02.2020 bearing I.A. No. 161 of 2020 , submitted by MeTL, is hereby approved.”



2.1.8.  Since there was a difference of opinion between the Hon’ble Judicial and Hon’ble

        Technical Member, the matter was referred to the President, NCLT for referring the

        matter to a third member. The relevant excerpts are as follows:

        “1. Having heard the submissions advanced on behalf of the parties in various

        Interlocutory Applications on multiple dates and perusing material available before the

        Bench, the Members of this Bench had a difference of opinion in passing the Order. While

        the Member (Judicial), upon considering the facts and circumstances of the case, has

        concluded to Approve the Resolution Plan submitted by SRA, the Member (Technical) has

        deemed it as a fit case for Rejection of the Resolution Plan and accordingly has appointed

        a Liquidator from the Panel of Resolution Professionals submitted by the IBBI.



        2. Consequently, the Members have passed two separate and independent Orders

        authored by them.



        3. In the circumstances, a request letter with necessary annexures be sent to the Hon’ble

        President, NCLT, New Delhi for necessary order/directions regarding constituting a

        Bench of the Third Member as envisaged in Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013

        read with Rule 60(3) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to consider the following legal point.

        “Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the Resolution Plan submitted by the

        SRA is liable to be approved or Rejected under Section 31 of the IBC, 2016?



        4. The Registry to take immediate necessary steps in this behalf. Parties will be

        accordingly notified in due course.”



2.1.9.  In view of the above, the matter was referred to a Third Member i.e., Hon’ble Justice

        Jyotsna Sharma, Member (Judicial), sitting as Special Bench, who after hearing all the

        parties, passed the order on 30.09.2026. The Hon’ble Third Member has rendered her

        opinion on each of the issues where there was a difference of opinion between the

        members, except on the issue of conditional nature of the resolution plan. The relevant

        extract of the order is as under: -



        “13. K. Concluding Para: Cumulative effect of procedural violations, if any, on

        approval of Resolution Plan



        (i) All the points of difference between the members of the regular bench have been dealt

        with in the above paras in seriatim. The points of difference can be divided into two

        categories: some are procedural and other points are not.



        (ii) As far as the procedural violations are concerned, they may be in the nature of

        irregularities, deficiencies or misapplication. They may further fall into two broad

        categories First are those which may cause prejudice to the interest of the stakeholder.

        The second category may consist of the procedural violation of such nature which may

        not cause any real prejudice to any of the stakeholders. Considering from this point of



                                             Page 8 of 41

        view, each and every case may have its own peculiar facts and circumstances for reaching

        to the right conclusion. In general whenever a procedure is prescribed it should be

        followed as it is. The word of caution is that minor violations which are trivial in nature

        or not substantive, may not call for any interference. The old adage is that procedure is

        handmaids to justice. Such procedural violations or irregularities which do not

        prejudicially affect the right of any party or do not have any direct or indirect bearing on

        the objective sought to be achieved and where principles of fairness have not been

        ignored may not be treated as vitiating the process.



        …



        (vi) All the points of difference have been dealt with in the preceding paras. Certain

        procedural violations have been committed, however, none of them has been found to be

        material enough so as to vitiate the whole process and therefore reject the resolution

        plan.



        The point discussed under the head “F. Conditional nature of Resolution Plan” requires

        special consideration in view of peculiarity of facts and circumstances.



                                                         ORDER



         I. Accordingly, the opinion(s) of the Special Bench in the capacity of a third member is

        pronounced.



        II. The matter be placed before the Original Division Bench (NCLT Bengaluru Bench)

        for passing appropriate orders in terms of the majority opinion under Section 419(5) of

        the Companies Act, 2013.



        III. This order alongwith the order passed under section 419(5) of the Companies Act,

        2013 dated 29.01.2026, be placed before the Hon’ble President, NCLT, for appropriate

        action.”



2.1.10. The DC observes that the Third Member, Hon’ble Justice Jyotsna Sharma, sitting as

        Special Bench, has given her opinion on all the points of difference except the conditional

        nature of the Resolution Plan. She has held that this point requires special consideration

        and directed that the matter be placed before the original Division Bench for orders in

        terms of the majority opinion. As on the date of this order, the AA has not passed a final

        order approving or rejecting the plan.



2.1.11. The DC notes that the jurisdiction of the AA and that of the DC are totally different,

        although there might be similar set of facts to be considered by both the authorities. The

        AA examines whether the CIRP was running as per the provisions of the Code and

        Regulations and whether the Resolution Plan should be approved under Section 31 of the

        Code. However, the present proceedings under Section 220 of the Code has a different

        scope of consideration to examine as to whether the Insolvency Professional has complied

        with the Code, the Regulations and the Code of Conduct. These two separate proceedings



                                              Page 9 of 41

        operate in separate fields. Neither the pendency of proceedings before the AA, nor the

        fact that the complainant raised similar grievances before other fora, prevents the Board

        from examining the conduct of the Insolvency Professional. Likewise, the dismissal of

        IA 10/2022, whether on merits or on the ground of locus and conduct, does not take away

        the statutory power of the Board to monitor the performance of the Insolvency

        Professional. The Board’s power is irrespective of either the identity or the conduct of

        the complainant.



2.1.12. The DC observes that insofar as Contravention V of the SCN with respect to the failure

        to consider the Resolution Plan in accordance with applicable provisions of the Code is

        concerned, it rests on several grounds i.e., the details of the resolution applicant,

        disclosures under Section 29A, the source of funds, the conditional nature of the plan,

        and the alleged undue haste in its approval. Of these, only the question of whether the

        Resolution Plan dated 11.02.2020 was conditional in nature remains unsettled and has

        not yet been finally decided by the AA. Accordingly, the DC has refrained from recording

        any finding at this stage and the Board will be at liberty to reexamine the Contravention

        V appropriately, based on the order of the AA.



2.1.13. The DC further notes that even though the Hon’ble Third Member has observed that none

        of the procedural violations has been found to be material enough so as to vitiate the

        whole process and reject the resolution plan. Such observation is to be seen in the context

        of the adjudicatory proceedings before the AA. That observation was made in the context

        of the CIRP and the approval of the Resolution Plan and it does not dispense with or

        dilute the independent statutory obligation of an Insolvency Professional to comply with

        the requirements prescribed under Code and Regulations made thereunder. This

        supervisory and disciplinary function lies squarely within the mandate of the Board. The

        DC accordingly proceeds to examine the contraventions on their own merits.



2.2. Validity of SCN in absence of formal investigation report under Section 219 of the

        Code and Regulation 10A of Inspection and Investigation Regulations.



2.2.1.  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that the SCN purportedly issued under Section 219

        of the Code read with regulations 11 and 12 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India

        (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017 (Inspection and Investigation

        Regulations) is not tenable and unauthorised. He submitted that in terms of Regulation

        11 of Inspection and Investigation Regulations, before issuance of any show-cause notice,

        the IBBI is required to form a prima facie opinion that sufficient cause exist to take

        actions against the Insolvency Professional. However, in the instant case, the prima facie

        opinion does not exist because there was no investigation report.



2.2.2.  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena further submitted that Regulation 10A is inconsistent with the

        provisions of the Code, particularly regarding the handling of complaints against

        insolvency professionals. The Code does not grant any suo motu power to IBBI to refer

        a matter to the DC without first conducting an inspection or investigation. Therefore,

        Regulation 10A is ultra vires the Code, and the present notice is liable to be quashed.



        Page 10 of 41

        Examination by the DC.



2.2.3.  The DC notes that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena has raised a preliminary objection with

        respect to the provisions of Sections 218 and 219 of the Code not being followed prior to

        issuance of the SCN. However, it is pertinent to note that the present SCN has been issued

        in terms of the Regulation 11(2) read with Regulation 10A of the Inspection and

        Investigation Regulations, 2017 which empowers the Board to issue SCN if after the

        consideration of the investigation report on the basis of material available on record, the

        Board is of the prima facie opinion that sufficient cause exists. The said regulation is as

        hereunder:



        “11. Consideration of Report.



        (1) The Board shall consider the inspection report received under regulation 6 or

        investigation report received under regulation 10, as the case may be, expeditiously.



        (2) If the Board, after consideration of the report under sub regulation (1) or on the basis

        of material otherwise available on record, is of the prima facie opinion that sufficient

        cause exists to take actions under section 220 or sub-section (2) of section 236, it shall

        issue a show-cause notice in accordance with regulation 12 to the service provider or an

        associated person and in any other case, close the inspection or investigation, as the case

        may be”



2.2.4.  Further, the DC notes that in terms of Regulation 10A of the Inspection and Investigation

        Regulations, the processing of a complaint or grievance or material available on record,

        is deemed to be investigation and the processing papers in this regard are deemed to be

        investigation report. The said Regulations is as hereunder:



        10A. Investigation during disposal of complaint or grievance.



        Notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter III, the processing of a complaint or

        grievance or material available on record under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of

        India (Grievance and Complaint Handling Procedure) Regulations, 2017, shall mean

        investigation under this regulation and in such case the processing papers shall mean the

        investigation report under regulation 10:



        Provided that nothing in this regulation shall restrict the Board to appoint an inspecting

        authority under Chapter-II or an investigating authority under Chapter-III.



2.2.5. Therefore, the DC is of the considered view that the present SCN has been issued in terms

        of the statutory framework and is therefore proper and can be adjudicated by this DC in

        terms of the provisions of the Code.



2.3. Non-supply of the complaint and its annexures alleged violation of natural justice



2.3.1. Shri Alok Kailash Saksena has submitted that he was only served with the Form A of the

        complaint filed by the complainant with the Board. However, the five volumes attached



                                              Page 11 of 41

        to in complaint and referred to in complaint was never supplied to him. Therefore, he

        never had the access to entire complaint and the documents referred to by the

        complainant.



        Examination by the DC.



2.3.2.  The DC notes that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena was provided with the gist of the complaint,

        which runs to 42 pages and sets out each allegation in detail. Further, the relevant

        documents which was relied upon by the Board to form a prima facie opinion for issuance

        of SCN was shared with Shri Alok Kailash Saksena alongwith the SCN.



2.3.3.  Accordingly, the DC is of the view that the instant SCN has been validly issued in terms

        of the applicable statutory provisions and Shri Alok Kailash Saksena has been provided

        a full and fair opportunity to explain his conduct on the allegations mentioned in the SCN.

        Nonetheless, apart from written submissions, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena has also been

        provided with repeated opportunities of personal hearing before this DC to defend his

        actions and also allowed Shri Alok Kailash Saksena to submit multiple additional

        submissions.



3. Alleged contraventions in the SCN, submissions of Shri Alok Kailash Saksena and

        findings of the DC



        The contravention alleged in the SCN, submissions by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena and

        findings of the DC are summarized as follows:



3.1 Contravention – I: Failure to Include the Audited Financial Statements of the CD in

        the Information Memorandum (IM).



3.1.1   It was observed by the Board that the CIRP of the CD was initiated vide order of AA

        dated 26.10.2018 and as per the procedure prescribed under the Code and rules and

        regulations made thereunder, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena was required to prepare the IM

        according to Regulation 36 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate

        Persons) Regulations, 2016 (CIRP Regulations) and provide it to the members of the

        CoC.



3.1.2   It was further observed by the Board that Regulation 36(2)(c) of CIRP Regulations

        mandates the RP to include audited financial statements of the CD for the last two

        financial years and provisional financial statements for the current financial year made

        up to a date not earlier than fourteen days from the date of the application. It was observed

        that only the provisional balance sheet as on 31.03.2017, and 2018 have been included in

        the IM and Shri Alok Kailash Saksena failed to provide the audited financial statements

        for the year ending 31.03.2017 and 31.03.2018 as provided under Regulation 36(2)(c) of

        the CIRP Regulations.



3.1.3 Thus, the Board held a prima facie view that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena had contravened

        Section 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 36(2)(c) of CIRP Regulations,



                                Page 12 of 41

       Regulation 7(2)(a) and 7(2)(h) of the IP Regulations read with Clause 14 of the Code of

       Conduct for Insolvency Professionals provided under First Schedule to IP Regulations

       (Code of Conduct).



       Submissions by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena.



3.1.4  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that complainant was engaged in forum shopping

       and the issues raised in the complaint were exactly the same as those raised by the

       complainant in application bearing I.A No. 10 of 2022, which was pending adjudication

       before the AA and in Writ Petition No. 483 of 2023 filed before Hon’ble High Court of

       Karnataka.



3.1.5  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena further submitted that the pattern of raising the same issues

       before multiple forums suggested a deliberate attempt to create undue pressure on him.

       He also submitted that the issues raised in the present complaint were already before the

       AA in I.A 10 of 2022, which was then awaiting adjudication, and the matter was therefore

       sub-judice. He further pointed out that IBBI was made a party in WP 483 of 2023 before

       adjudication and in SLP no. 11599/2024 filed before the Hon’ble Supreme Court which

       had been filed against the order of Hon’ble High Court in WP 483 of 2023. The

       complainant has dragged IBBI in legal proceedings with the oblique objective.



3.1.6  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that the issue related to ‘audited financial statement’

       of the CD was raised in multiple forums, including the High Court, NCLAT, and the

       Supreme Court by one of the unsuccessful Prospective Resolution Applicant (PRA) and

       by the complainant in their individual capacity. The Hon’ble NCLAT, Chennai Bench had

       already dealt with this specific issue in an appeal bearing Company Appeal (AT)(Ins.)

       No. 173/2021 filed by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena, wherein the Hon’ble NCLAT observed

       that there was no violation of the CIRP. The relevant extract of the NCLAT order dated

       19.09.2022 is reproduced hereunder:



       39. The Respondents failed to establish that the RP violated the ‘CIRP’ process. It is

       only the case of the Respondents such averments allegations have been made and the

       ‘Adjudicating Authority’ without going into the reality simply ratified the submissions

       of the Respondents, which this Tribunal highly deprecate the said stand.



3.1.7  Subsequently, Hon’ble Supreme Court vide its order dated 25.11.2022 upheld the above-

       said order of the Hon’ble NCLAT. Further, the complainant also raised the similar

       allegations before the Hon’ble Karnataka High Court in WP 483/2023. There were no

       adverse observations of the Hon’ble High Court on the issue of non-updation of books of

       accounts and non-furnishing of audited accounts in the Information Memorandum and

       violation of Regulation 36 of the CIRP Regulations.



3.1.8  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that in the present case, due to mismanagement of

       the CD (where the complainant himself was the managing director of CD) prior to

       initiation of ‘CIRP’, its accounts had remained unaudited from FY 2015-16 onwards and



       Page 13 of 41

        the auditor appointed by the erstwhile management had also resigned on the date of

        initiation of the ‘CIRP’. Therefore, in absence of the audited financial statements, he had

        included the provisional financial statements of the CD for the FY 2016-17 and FY 2017-

        18 in the Information Memorandum. Further, Shri Alok Kailash Saksena took appropriate

        steps to have the books of accounts updated and to appoint a statutory auditor to have the

        financial statements audited while keeping the CoC informed of the steps taken.



3.1.9   Shri Alok Kailash Saksena further submitted that fire break out at Mumbai office of the

        CD just approximately 2 months before the initiation of CIRP had damaged the server

        where the books of accounts were stored, and considerable effort was made to recover
