```text
        “Page 8 of IM: The CD has reported that there was a fire in its office and the server on

        which books of accounts were stored was damaged in the fire. The process of recovery

        from the damaged hard disk was entrusted to a specialized agency. The agency took

        considerable time and recently delivered the complete tally for the year 1 April 2015 to

        the date of the fire. Such recovered books of accounts are now available for due diligence.

        The provisional accounts are based on such recovered tally. The provisional and

        unaudited annual financial statement as on 26 October 2018 prepared from the Tally

        backup received is given in Annexure A (i).”



3.1.10 Shri Alok Kailash Saksena submitted that he took all necessary efforts to recover the

        accounts from the damaged hard disk, prepare provisional accounts, and make them

        available for due diligence. Therefore, the allegations against him are unfounded, and the

        complainant’s lack of action in preparing these accounts should also be noted by the

        Board.



3.1.11  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena further submitted that the issue relating to Regulation 36(2)(c)

        of the CIRP Regulations was first raised before the AA by Svamitva Landmarks

        (Consortium), one of the PRAs, in I.A 227/2020, and the complainant had also filed an

        impleadment application bearing I.A. 228 of 2020 in support of that application. Though

        the AA initially observed that the IM should have contained the audited financial

        statements, the Hon’ble NCLAT, on appeal, overturned this observation, holding that the

        resolution process was conducted on an “as is where is basis” with the data and resources

        available, as provided in the RFRP, and that he had complied with the rules. According

        to Shri Alok Kailash Saksena, since the IM clearly disclosed the reasons for the non-

        availability of the audited accounts and the issue has already been examined and settled

        by the judicial forums, it should not be re-opened by the Board.



        Analysis and findings of the DC.



3.1.12 The DC notes that the requirement of Regulation 36 (2)(c) of CIRP Regulation is as

        below: -



        “36. Information memorandum



        …

                                             Page 14 of 41

        (2) The information memorandum shall highlight the key selling propositions and contain

        all relevant information which serves as a comprehensive document conveying significant

        information about the corporate debtor including its operations, financial statements, to

        the prospective resolution applicant and shall contain the following details of the

        corporate debtor-



        ..



        (c) audited financial statements of the corporate debtor for the last two financial years

        and provisional financial statements for the current financial year made up to a date not

        earlier than fourteen days from the date of the application;”



3.1.13  The DC notes that Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations requires the IM to contain

        the audited financial statements of the CD for the last two financial years. In the instant

        matter the CIRP of the CD had commenced on 26.10.2018. The IM therefore had to

        contain the audited financial statements for FY 2016-17 and FY 2017-18. However, the

        IM contained audited financial statements only up to FY 2014-15. For FY 2015-16 to FY

        2017-18 it contained only provisional, unaudited statements. Shri Alok Kailash Saksena

        did not dispute this fact. The Third Member of the AA also recorded this fact in her order

        dated 30.09.2026 and described it as "an irregularity as far as stipulated procedure is

        concerned".



3.1.14  The DC notes that this matter was also one of the issues where there was a difference of

        opinion and where findings were given by the Third Member vide order dated 30.09.2026.

        It was observed that this issue was earlier litigated before the NCLAT in Alok Kailash

        Saksena, the RP v. Svamitva Landmarks and Ors, Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins.) No.

        173 of 2021, which was decided on 19.09.2022, where the NCLAT allowed the RP’s

        appeal and had set aside the AA’s order directing RP to place Svamitva’s plan (one of the

        PRAs) before the CoC, holding that the AA had exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering

        with the CoC’s commercial wisdom.



3.1.15 The DC further notes that the Third Member of the AA, in its order dated 30.09.2026 had

        recorded that there was no dispute that the IM contained audited financial statements only

        up to FY 2014-15, that all prospective resolution applicants had access to the same

        material, and that the non-availability of audited statements for the subsequent two years

        was disclosed both at the 1st CoC meeting and in the IM itself. On this basis, it held that



          “My opinion is that non-availability of audited financial statements for the last two

          financial years was an irregularity as far as stipulated procedure is concerned.

          However, I cannot ignore that the deficiency in complying with procedural

          requirements has been a point in issue before the Hon’ble NCLAT and their

          observations have a binding effect. My opinion is that every procedural deficiency, non-

          adherence or even violations, if trivial in nature, may not be fatal in nature. As pointed

          out earlier, every prospective resolution applicant had the same material before them

          hence, it cannot be said that unavailability of the audited financial statements of

          preceding two financial years caused prejudice to any party or was unfair, therefore



                                              Page 15 of 41

        the procedure is vitiated. However, the issue of procedural irregularities and violations,

        their legal impact on the ultimate decision given or to be given by the adjudicating

        authority shall be again dealt with in the concluding para of this order.”



        In concluding paragraph, it was observed that:



        “All the points of difference have been dealt with in the preceding paras. Certain

        procedural violations have been committed, however, none of them has been found to

        be material enough so as to vitiate the whole process and therefore reject the resolution

        plan.”



3.1.16  Shri Alok Kailash Saksena sought to explain this lapse by submitting that the accounts of

        the CD had remained unaudited since FY 2015-16 under the erstwhile management and

        the statutory auditor appointed by them had resigned on the date of commencement of

        the CIRP, that a fire in the office of the CD about two months before the commencement

        of the CIRP had damaged the server on which the books of account were stored, and that

        the non-availability of the audited financial statements was disclosed to the members of

        the CoC in the 1st CoC meeting and was also mentioned in the IM. He further placed

        reliance on the order of the Hon’ble NCLAT in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins.) No.

        173 of 2021, which did not find any material irregularity in the CIRP, and on the order of

        the Third Member, which held that no prejudice was caused to any party on this account.



3.1.17  However, the DC notes that Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations uses the word

        "shall", so the requirement of providing the audited financial statements of the corporate

        debtor for the last two financial years was mandatory. The defaults of the earlier

        management can explain why audited accounts were not available when the CIRP began,

        however it does not explain why Shri Alok Kailash Saksena did not get the accounts

        audited before he issued the IM. As examined in Contravention II in later paragraphs, the

        DC found that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena did not start the process of appointing an auditor

        in time.



3.1.18  The DC further notes that the minutes of the 3rd CoC meeting held on 26.02.2019 record

        that the CD had not provided access to its books of account (Tally data) and that the

        members of the CoC had directed Shri Alok Kailash Saksena to give one last opportunity

        to the CD, failing which he could seek legal remedy. In such a situation, Section 19(2) of

        the Code specifically enables the IRP/RP to make an application to the AA for necessary

        directions where the personnel of the CD do not extend the required cooperation.

        However, there is nothing on record to show that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena had

        approached the AA under Section 19(2) of the Code for getting access to the books of

        account or for getting the accounts updated and audited, and he has also not made any

        submission to this effect either in his reply to the SCN or during the personal hearing.



3.1.19 As regards the submission of Shri Alok Kailash Saksena that the non-availability of the

        audited financial statements was disclosed in the 1st CoC meeting and in the IM, the DC

        is of the view that such disclosure cannot be treated as a substitute for compliance with

        Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations. The very purpose of the IM is to enable a

                                              Page 16 of 41

        prospective resolution applicant to form a fair and informed assessment of the CD, and a

        disclosure that certain information is not available only informs the prospective resolution

        applicant to know about the gap only but does not help in taking informed decision. The

        audited financial statements carry the assurance of an independent auditor, and absence

        of any such information lead to a situation of information asymmetry in which the

        prospective resolution applicants are left to rely upon figures which had not been verified

        through an audit process as required under the Code. This may have affected both the

        level of participation in the process and the value offered in the resolution plans which

        have a direct ramification on the value maximization objective of Code.



3.1.20  The DC also notes that the reliance placed by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena on the order of

        the Hon’ble NCLAT and on the order of the Hon’ble Third Member does not come to his

        rescue. The Hon’ble NCLAT was examining whether the AA was right in directing that

        the resolution plan of Svamitva Landmarks be placed before the CoC, and the Hon’ble

        Third Member was examining whether the procedural irregularities in the CIRP were

        material enough to vitiate the process or to reject the resolution plan. Neither of these fora

        has held that the requirement of Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations was

        complied with in the present case. On the contrary, the Hon’ble Third Member has

        categorically held that the non-availability of the audited financial statements for the last

        two financial years was an irregularity as far as the stipulated procedure is concerned.

        The question before the DC is not whether the CIRP stands vitiated, but whether Shri

        Alok Kailash Saksena has discharged his duties as the RP in the manner required under

        the Code and the Regulations.



3.1.21  In view of the above, the DC is of the view that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena failed to

        include the audited financial statements of the CD for the last two financial years in the

        IM, as mandated under Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations, and has thereby

        contravened Sections 208(2)(a) and 208(2)(e) of the Code, Regulation 36(2)(c) of the

        CIRP Regulations and Regulations 7(2)(a) and 7(2)(h) of the IP Regulations read with

        Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct.



3.2 Contravention - II: Inordinate delay in Appointment of Statutory Auditors.



3.2.1   It was observed by the Board that the financial statements of the CD were not audited and

        books of accounts of the CD were incomplete, after Shri Alok Kailash Saksena took over

        as the RP of the CD. In pursuance of the same, Mr. Alok Kailash Saksena discussed the

        same with the CoC in the 1st and 3rd CoC meeting held on 26.12.2018 and 26.02.2019

        respectively. However, despite such discussion regarding the non-availability of the

        audited financial statements of the CD being held with the CoC as early as the 1st and the

        3rd CoC meeting, the discussion on appointing an auditor for conducting an audit of the

        provisional financial statements was raised by Shri Alok Kailash Saksena only during the

        9th CoC held on 20.08.2019.



3.2.2 It was noted by the Board that by this time, the IM was already submitted to the CoC on

        04.05.2019. The statutory auditor was eventually appointed after conclusion of 10th CoC



        Page 17 of 41

       meeting held on 06.09.2019 and as noted from minutes of 19th CoC meeting, the audited

       report was submitted on 03.02.2020. Due to such delay in the appointment of statutory

       auditors, the requirement of providing audited financial statements of the CD in the IM

       as per Regulation 36(2)(c) of the CIRP Regulations was not fulfilled.



3.2.3  Thus, the Board held a prima facie view that Shri Alok Kailash Saksena had contravened

       Section 208(2)(a), 208(2)(e) of the Code, Regulations 7(2)(a) and 7(2)(h) of IP
```

```text
INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA



                      (Disciplinary Committee)



No. IBBI/DC/352/2026                            12 November 2026



                      ORDER



This Order disposes of the Show Cause Notice (SCN) No. COMP-11011/180/2025-

IBBI/1921/328 dated 30.03.2026, issued to Mr. Soumitra Lahiri, who is an Insolvency

Professional (IP) registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI/Board)

with Registration No. IBBI/IPA-001/IP-P00734/2017-2018/11232 and a Professional Member

of the Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals of ICAI (IIIPI).



1. Background



1.1. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s Manglam Fiscal Services

        Private Limited (CD) was initiated by the order of the National Company Law Tribunal,

        Kolkata Bench (AA) dated 03.10.2023 on the application filed by State Bank of India under

        Section 7 of the Code. The Liquidation process of the CD commenced vide order dated

        16.01.2025 of the AA and Mr. Vasudeo Agarwal was appointed as Liquidator.

        Subsequently, vide order dated 24.04.2025, Mr. Vasudeo Agarwal was replaced and Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri was appointed as the Liquidator in the matter.



1.2. The Board received a complaint against Mr. Soumitra Lahiri with regard to his assignment

        as Liquidator in the Liquidation proceedings of the CD. The Board in exercise of its powers

        under Section 218 of the Code read with Regulations 7(2) and 7(3) of IBBI (Inspection and

        Investigation) Regulations, 2017 (Inspection and Investigation Regulations) appointed an

        Investigating Authority (IA) to conduct investigation in the matter of CD in reference to the

        complaint. The IA served upon Mr. Soumitra Lahiri, the notice of investigation dated

        27.10.2025 as per Regulation 8(1) of the Inspection and Investigation Regulations and in

        response thereof, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted his reply on the even date. After

        considering reply of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri, the IA submitted the Investigation Report (IR) to

        the Board. On examination of the IR, the Board formed a prima facie opinion that Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri has contravened provisions of the Code and Regulations made thereunder

        and issued SCN to Mr. Soumitra Lahiri on 30.03.2026. Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted his

        reply to the SCN on 13.04.2026.



1.3. The SCN and its response by Mr. Soumitra Lahiri was referred to the Disciplinary

        Committee (DC) for disposal. Mr. Soumitra Lahiri availed the opportunity of personal

        hearing before the DC through virtual mode on 18.08.2026. Thereafter, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri

        submitted additional written submissions on 21.08.2026. By email dated 13.10.2026, Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri was requested to furnish certain documents and information, which he



                                                      Page 1 of 22

        furnished on 14.10.2026 and 22.10.2026. The DC has considered the SCN, the reply to SCN,

        oral and written submissions of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri and the documents furnished by him

        and proceeds to dispose of the SCN.



2. Alleged Contravention, submissions of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri and findings of the DC.



2.1. Contravention-I: Arbitrary revision of claim of the financial creditor resulting in

        alteration of voting share.



2.1.1  Section 39 of the Code requires the liquidator to verify the claims submitted under Section

       38 within such time as specified by the Board. Further, under Section 40, the liquidator is

       required to admit or reject claims (in whole or in part) after verification. It further provides

       that where the liquidator rejects a claim, he shall record reasons in writing and communicate

       them to the creditor. Regulation 30 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016

       (Liquidation Regulations) states that "the liquidator shall verify the claims submitted within

       thirty days from the last date for receipt of claims and may either admit or reject the claim,

       in whole or in part, as the case may be."



2.1.2  Further, as per Regulation 31 of the Liquidation Regulations, the liquidator is required to

       file the list of stakeholders with the AA within forty-five days from the last date for receipt

       of the claims. Furthermore, in terms of Regulation 31(3) of the Liquidation Regulations, the

       liquidator may apply to the AA to modify an entry in the list of stakeholders filed with the

       AA, when he comes across additional information warranting such modification, and shall

       modify the entry in the manner directed by the AA.



2.1.3  It was observed that the State Bank of India (SBI) had filed its claim amounting to

       Rs.19,80,41,869/- during the CIRP of the CD. Thereafter, upon Liquidation of the CD,

       erstwhile liquidator admitted the claim amount of Rs.19,80,41,869/- and later on, Mr.

       Soumitra Lahiri, admitted the claim amount of Rs.24,39,20,845.30/-, appreciated on account

       of interest accrued during the CIRP period, as against the amount claimed of

       Rs.8,65,09,94,392.47/-. This resulted in modification of the list of stakeholders and increase

       in the voting share of SBI from 4.61% to 5.62% in the stakeholders’ consultation committee

       (SCC). While Mr. Soumitra Lahiri proceeded to conduct the third meeting of the SCC on

       19.05.2025 with the reconstituted composition, however, there is no material on record

       indicating that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri applied to the AA for carrying out such modification of

       the list of stakeholders.



2.1.4  Thereafter, on 21.05.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri revised the admitted claim of SBI to

       Rs.8,65,09,94,392.48/-, including additional claim on account of corporate guarantee

       executed by CD for loan accommodations extended by SBI to Shree Mahalaxmi

       Corporation Private Limited (SMCPL), acknowledging the co-extensive liability of the

       corporate guarantor with that of the principal borrower. This resulted in modification of the

       list of stakeholders and increase in the voting share of SBI from 5.62% to 67.87% in the

       SCC. While Mr. Soumitra Lahiri proceeded to conduct the fourth and fifth meetings of the



       Page 2 of 22

       SCC on 04.06.2025 and 01.07.2025, respectively with the reconstituted composition,

       however, there is no material on record indicating that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri applied to the

       AA for carrying out such modification of the list of stakeholders.



2.1.5  However, on 08.07.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri reduced the claim of SBI to Rs.

       24,39,20,845.30/- excluding the aforesaid claim submitted by SBI on account of corporate

       guarantee without obtaining the requisite directions of the AA for such modification. This

       resulted in modification of the list of stakeholders and reduction of the voting share of SBI

       from 67.87% to 5.62% in the SCC. After carrying out such modification of the list of

       stakeholders, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri went ahead and conducted sixth meeting of the SCC on

       02.01.2026



2.1.6  In view of the above, it was observed that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri initially modified the claim

       of SBI by including the claim amount towards accrued interest during the CIRP period and

       gave effect to the same by modifying the list of stakeholders, resulting in an increase in its

       voting share in the SCC from 4.61% to 5.62%. Thereafter, in May 2025, upon

       acknowledging the co-extensive liability of the corporate guarantor with that of the principal

       borrower, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri further modified the claim of SBI by including the

       component on account of corporate guarantee executed by CD for loan accommodations

       extended by SBI to SMCPL, resulting in a substantial increase in its voting share from

       5.62% to 67.87%. It was observed that in both instances, there was no material on record to

       indicate that Mr, Soumitra Lahiri applied to the AA for modification of the list of

       stakeholders under Regulation 31(3) of the Liquidation Regulations. In the meantime, Mr.

       Soumitra Lahiri proceeded to conduct the third, fourth and fifth meetings of the SCC based

       on such modified composition.



2.1.7  It was further noted that in July 2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri modified the claim of SBI by

       excluding the component relating to the corporate guarantee, resulting in a substantial

       reduction in its voting share in the SCC from 67.87% to 5.62%. Thereafter, it was noted that

       Mr. Soumitra Lahiri also conducted sixth meeting of the SCC on 02.01.2026 without

       obtaining directions of the AA regarding such modification.



2.1.8  In view of the foregoing, the Board held a prima facie view that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri had

       contravened Regulation 31(3) of the Liquidation Regulations read with Clause 14 of the

       Code of Conduct specified in First Schedule to IBBI (Insolvency Professionals)

       Regulations, 2016 (IP Regulations).



       Submissions by Mr. Soumitra Lahiri.



2.1.9  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted that SBI has already filed IA No. 1259 of 2025 under Section

       42 of the Code before the AA, specifically challenging decision of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri to

       disallow its additional claim of Rs. 840,70,73,547.18/- on account of a purported corporate

       guarantee given by the CD in respect of its group entity, Shree Mahalaxmi Corporation

       Private Limited. The petition and its supporting pleadings substantially overlap with the

        factual allegations and issues set out in Point No. 1 and Point No. 2 of the SCN and is under

        consideration of the AA under Section 60(5) of the Code.



2.1.10  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted that SBI filed its claim of Rs. 19,80,41,869/- during CIRP

2.1.11  and intentionally did not claim the amount due on account of Corporate Guarantee of Shree

        Mahalaxmi Corporation Private Limited.

        He submitted that in case a resolution plan would get approved under Section 31 of the Code

        in the matter of CIRP of Manglam Fiscal Services Private Limited, SBI would have been

        eligible to receive resolution amount commensurate with the claim filed which was only Rs.

        19,80,41,869/-.



2.1.12  He submitted that SBI took this calculated risk because it was more than certain that no

        resolution will happen in the case of Manglam Fiscal Services Private Limited and the

        opportunity of recovery would only arise at the time of Liquidation, and thus, it would be

        wise to inflate the claim during Liquidation to maximize gain. In other words, SBI did not

        initiate CIRP of Manglam Fiscal Services Private Limited with clean hands. The initiation

        of CIRP was solely for the purpose of recovery, which was an abuse of the law and frankly

        speaking attract section 65 of the Code.



2.1.13 He submitted that from the documents handed over by the erstwhile Liquidator, he noticed

        the claim documents received from Financial Creditors and Operational Creditors but there

        was no record of any report being filed with the AA under sub regulation (2) of regulation

        31 of the Liquidation Regulations, 2016. However, an email dated 19.04.2025 from the

        erstwhile Liquidator addressed to all creditors informing them about their respective claim.



2.1.14 He submitted that in the 3rd SCC meeting held on 19.05.2025, SBI drew his attention to the

        claim submitted by them in Form D dated 21.03.2025 which showed total amount claimed

        as under:



        Due from Manglam Fiscal Services Private Limited: Rs. 24,39,20,845.30

        Due on account of Corporate Guarantee executed by the corporate debtor pertaining to

        Shree Mahalaxmi Corporation Private Limited: Rs. 840,70,73,547.18

        Totaling: Rs. 865,09,94,392.48



2.1.15  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted that he reconstituted the claim admission and informed all

        the creditors vide email of 21.05.2025. With this revision, the claim of SBI increased to

        Rs.8,65,09,94,392.47/-., He submitted that SBI's Form D had included claim of corporate

        guarantee for facilities availed by Shree Mahalaxmi Corporation Pvt. Ltd. He was bound to

        re-verify the claim under Regulation 30 of Liquidation Regulation and ARCIL has raised

        no objection; and that a guarantor's co-extensive liability with the principal borrower is well

        settled by Hon’ble Supreme Court and Hon’ble NCLAT.



2.1.16 Thereafter, the claim reduced back to Rs.24,39,20,845.30/- on 08.07.2025. He submitted

        that this was necessitated by NCLAT's judgement dated 03.07.2025 in Moneywise Financial



                                                      Page 4 of 22

        Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Arunava Sikdar, wherein it was held that even where a guarantee exists,

        the claim can be rejected, if the right to enforce it has not been crystallized, or if admitting

        it would result in unjust enrichment or procedural abuse and a financial creditor cannot be

        allowed to enforce the same claim in multiple CIRPs without proper adjustment or

        coordination. He submitted that this judgement having not been challenged in Supreme

        Court, hence it attained finality.



2.1.17  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri has filed additional submissions dated 21.08.2026 and reiterated that

        the matter is sub judice and placed on record copy of IA filed by SBI before the AA which

        is pending. He submitted that the DC may consider the pendency of such proceedings before

        AA and avoid a situation where conflicting factual findings are recorded on the same matrix

        and prayed that the DC dispose of the SCN, subject to his undertaking to keep the DC

        apprised of developments in the pending applications before the AA in CP (IB) No.

        157/KB/2022.



2.2 Contravention-II: Refusal to include agenda of replacement of liquidator as requested

        by majority stakeholder and time gap in conducting SCC meetings.



2.2.1   Regulation 31A(11) of the Liquidation Regulations provides that the SCC may, by a vote of

        not less than sixty-six per cent and after recording reasons, propose replacement of the

        liquidator and file an application before the AA. Further, Regulation 31A(6) stipulates that

        the liquidator shall convene subsequent meetings of the SCC within thirty days of the

        previous meeting, unless extended by the SCC, and that at least one meeting shall be held

        in each quarter.



2.2.2   It was noted that the SBI holding 67.87% of the voting share requested for inclusion of an

        agenda item for replacement of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri as liquidator on 20.06.2025 and

        subsequently communicated reasons for the same on 25.06.2025. However, despite such

        request, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri proceeded to conduct the fifth meeting of the SCC on

        01.07.2025 without placing the said agenda item for deliberation and voting. Instead, Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri, in his reply, stated that in the said SCC meeting “I asserted that since I

        had countered / challenged each of State Bank of India’s allegations, let the Hon’ble

        Adjudicating Authority sagaciously decide as to whether the Liquidator should hold the post

        or step aside.”.



2.2.3   It was further noted that at the time of the fifth SCC meeting, SBI continued to hold majority

        voting share of 67.87% in the SCC. Thereafter, the sixth meeting of the SCC was convened

        on 02.01.2026, i.e., after a gap of more than six months, which is not in consonance with

        the timelines prescribed under Regulation 31A(6). In the intervening period, the voting share

        of SBI was reduced from 67.87% to 5.62%. It was noted that the agenda relating to

        replacement of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri as liquidator was placed in the sixth SCC meeting,

        however, by that time, the voting share of SBI was substantially reduced, thereby affecting

        the efficacy of such request.

       contravened Regulations 31A(6) and 31A(11) of the Liquidation Regulations read with

       Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in First Schedule to IBBI (IP Regulations).



2.3 Submissions by Mr. Soumitra Lahiri.



2.3.1  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted that from the documents received by erstwhile Liquidator

       during handover, he found one certificate from erstwhile RP stating that he was holding

       control and custody of the premises of the corporate debtor at Panagarh, District West

       Burdwan. Mr. Soumitra Lahiri visited the premises on 09.05.2025 and found that the front

       gate was painted in bold stating that the property belongs to State Bank of India. He entered

       the premises which was initially denied by the guards of SBI. On 15.05.2025, he received

       email from SBI stating that “First and foremost, please be informed that the premises of

       Mangalam Fiscal Services Private Limited, located at Village – Beldanga, P.O. – Paschim

       Gangarampur, District – Paschim Bardhaman, are under the control and custody of SBI.

       Accordingly, I request an explanation as to how you entered the premises without obtaining

       prior permission from SBI."



2.3.2  In third and fourth meetings of the SCC, he mentioned that security guards will be deployed

       and that the matter came under the absolute jurisdiction of the Liquidator. On 20.06.2025,

       he appointed M/s Dayal Security and emailed the work order to them marking a copy to SBI

       and ARCIL. He submitted that this lead to email from SBI on 20.06.2025 requesting to

       include agenda for "Removal of Liquidator" on the 5th SCC meeting. He replied the same

       day asking SBI to provide reasons for removal as it is contemplated by the proviso to

       Regulation 31A(11), and to allow him an opportunity to respond. On 25.06.2025, SBI

       furnished nine allegations to which he submitted a point-wise rebuttal on 28.06.2025. At the

       5th SCC meeting held on 01.07.2025 he stated that, having countered each allegation, let the

       AA decide as to whether the Liquidator should hold the post or step aside.



2.3.3  He further submitted that Liquidation cost was not paid for a long time and it was paid only

       after filing contempt petition before AA and there was personalized vengeance against the

       Liquidator. On the six-month gap from 5th meeting of SCC held on 01.07.2025 to 6th meeting

       of SCC held on 02.01.2026, he cited unavailability of books of account, untraceable

       promoter directors, denial of control/custody of the liquidation estate, non-payment of

       liquidation costs. He further stated that since the matters is under consideration of the AA,

2.3.4  He submitted that as directed by AA vide its order dated 18.12.2025, he convened the sixth

2.4 Analysis and Findings of the DC



2.4.1  The DC has considered the SCN, the reply of Mr. Soumitra Lahiri, his oral submissions

       made during the personal hearing on 18.08.2026, his additional written submissions dated

       21.08.2026, and the documents furnished by him on 14.10.2026 and 22.10.2026 in response

       to the information sought from him on 13.10.2026.



2.4.2  The two contraventions alleged in the SCN arise out of the same set of events and within

       the same period. Contravention-I concerns the revisions of the admitted claim of SBI and

       the consequent alteration of its voting share in the SCC. Contravention-II concerns the non-

       placement of SBI’s request for replacement of the Liquidator before the SCC and the failure

       to convene meetings of the SCC for six months. The voting share of SBI, which is the subject

       matter of the first contravention, determined whether SBI could carry a proposal for

       replacement of the Liquidator under Regulation 31A(11), which is the subject matter of the

       second contravention. It will be easier to appreciate the two contravention together as they

       are interlinked. The DC has, therefore, examined both the contraventions together by tracing

       the events in the order in which they occurred, and has recorded its findings on each

       contravention at the stage at which it arises.



       Preliminary objection: pendency of proceedings before the AA



2.4.3  Mr. Soumitra Lahiri, in his reply and in his additional submissions dated 21.08.2026,

       contended that the subject matter of the SCN was under consideration of the AA in IA No.

       1259/2025 filed by SBI under Section 42 of the Code, and requested the DC to dispose of

       the SCN subject to his undertaking to keep the DC apprised of the developments. The DC

       notes that the AA, vide order dated 11.09.2026, has dismissed IA No. 1259/2025 as

       infructuous, recording as under:



       “a. It is submitted by Ld. Counsel appearing for the SBI that the application has

       become infructuous, since the claim has been admitted in full by the liquidator.

       b. Accordingly, this application is dismissed as infructuous.”



2.4.4  The ground of pendency, therefore, no longer survives. Further, the question of professional

       conduct falls within the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Board. The DC, accordingly,

       proceeds to examine the matter on merits.

2.4.6 The DC now examines the events in the order in which they occurred.



            Page 11 of 22

       (A) Claims at the commencement of liquidation and the first list of stakeholders

       (January – May 2025)



2.4.7  SBI had initiated the CIRP of the CD and had filed a claim of Rs.19,80,41,869/- as a

       financial creditor of the CD as principal borrower. It did not raise any claim on account of

       the corporate guarantee given by the CD for the loans extended by SBI to SMCPL. Upon

       commencement of liquidation, SBI, on 21.03.2025, submitted its claim in Form D for

       Rs.865,09,94,392.48, comprising Rs.24,39,20,845.30 due from the CD as principal

       borrower and Rs.8,40,70,73,547.18 on account of the corporate guarantee. The erstwhile

       Liquidator, by email dated 19.04.2025, informed the creditors of the admitted claims, in

       which the claim of SBI was shown at Rs.19,80,41,869/- with a voting share of 4.61%. Mr.

       Soumitra Lahiri, who took charge as Liquidator pursuant to the order of the AA dated

       24.04.2025, has stated that no list of stakeholders had been filed with the AA by the

       erstwhile Liquidator, and nothing on record indicates otherwise.



2.4.8  On 13.05.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri filed before the AA a report on compilation of the list

       of stakeholders in conformity with Regulation 31 of the Liquidation Regulations, in which

       he admitted the claim of SBI at Rs.24,39,20,845.30, being the amount due from the CD

       including the interest accrued during the CIRP period, while leaving out the guarantee

       component. The voting share of SBI became 5.62%. The AA took the report on record in

       IA No. 864/2025 vide order dated 23.05.2025. The 3rd SCC meeting held on 19.05.2025 was

       conducted on the basis of this list.



2.4.9  The SCN treats this as the first revision of the claim of SBI made without approaching the

       AA. Regulation 31(3) of the Liquidation Regulations provides as under:



              “(3) The liquidator may apply to the Adjudicating Authority to modify an entry

              in the list of stakeholders filed with the Adjudicating Authority, when he comes

              across additional information warranting such modification, and shall modify

              the entry in the manner directed by the Adjudicating Authority.”



2.4.10 The provision governs the modification of an entry in a list of stakeholders already filed

        with the AA. Since no list had been filed by the erstwhile Liquidator, the list filed by Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri on 13.05.2025 was the first list of stakeholders before the AA, and the

        admission of the claim of SBI at Rs.24,39,20,845.30 was an entry in that list and not a

        modification of an entry in an earlier one. The email of the erstwhile Liquidator dated

        19.04.2025 was not a list filed with the AA. The DC, therefore, does not find a contravention

        of Regulation 31(3) in respect of the first revision.



2.4.11 The DC also notes that dispute arose between Mr. Soumitra Lahiri and SBI over the control

        and custody of the land of the CD at Panagarh. He visited the premises on 09.05.2025,

        asserted by his email dated 12.05.2025 that the land has to be in the control and custody of

        the Liquidator, SBI objected to his entry on 15.05.2025, and he responded on 16.05.2025



                                                      Page 12 of 22

        asking SBI to refrain from such aspersions to avoid serious legal consequences. The DC

        does not examine the merits of this dispute, which is not the subject matter of the SCN, but

        notes it as the backdrop against which the relationship between the Liquidator and SBI

        deteriorated in the weeks that followed.



        (B) Admission of the guarantee claim: the second revision (May – June 2025)



2.4.12 In the 3rd SCC meeting held on 19.05.2025, SBI pressed for admission of the guarantee

        component of its claim. Two days later, on 21.05.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri informed all

        the stakeholders through email that the claim of SBI had been recasted to

        Rs.865,09,94,392.48, on the ground that the liability of a guarantor is co-extensive with that

        of the principal borrower. The voting share of SBI rose from 5.62% to 67.87%, giving SBI,

        on its own, more than the sixty-six per cent of the voting share required under Regulation

        31A(11) to propose replacement of the liquidator. The 4th SCC meeting was held on

        05.06.2025 with this composition.



2.4.13 Mr. Soumitra Lahiri has submitted that this modification was duly reported to the AA. The

        record shows that his application under Regulation 31(3), which is dated 29.05.2025, was

        e-filed on 09.06.2025, and the AA took the admitted claims on record in IA No. 941/2025

        vide order dated 12.06.2025. The application itself states that the Liquidator was “praying

        before the Adjudicating Authority to modify an entry in the list of stakeholders”. The

        modification had, however, already been communicated to the stakeholders on 21.05.2025

        and acted upon at the 4th SCC meeting on 05.06.2025, before the application was even filed.

        Regulation 31(3) contemplates the reverse sequence, namely, an application to the AA first

        and modification thereafter in the manner directed by the AA. To this extent, the second

        revision did not conform to Regulation 31(3). The DC, however, notes that the application

        followed shortly thereafter and that the AA took the revised list on record on 12.06.2025,

        so that when the 5th SCC meeting was held on 01.07.2025, the list on which SBI held 67.87%

        of the voting share was the list on the record of the AA.



2.4.14 The DC also notes that, in his reply, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri has stated that the sudden

        appreciation of the claim of SBI did not appear to him commercially ethical and has

        contended that SBI deliberately kept the guarantee claim out of the CIRP, which he termed

        an abuse of process attracting Section 65 of the Code. Yet he admitted the claim after

        verification and conducted the 4th and 5th SCC meetings on that basis. If he held such

        reservations, the proper course was to reflect them in his decision on the claim or to seek

        directions of the AA at that stage, rather than to admit the claim and reverse it later.



                                                      Page 13 of 22

        (C) SBI’s request for replacement of the Liquidator and the 5th SCC meeting (June –

2.4.15 The 5th SCC meeting which was originally convened for 19.06.2025 was deferred to

        25.06.2025 at the request of ARCIL. On 20.06.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri issued a work

        order to a security agency for deployment of guards at the premises of the CD, marking a

        copy to SBI and ARCIL. On the same day, SBI, then holding 67.87% of the voting share,

        requested that the item “Replacement of Liquidator” be included in the agenda of the 5th

        SCC meeting and that the meeting be held on 26.06.2025. Mr. Soumitra Lahiri replied the

        same day asking SBI to state its reasons, citing Regulation 31A(11) of Liquidation

        Regulations. SBI furnished nine reasons on 25.06.2025, including deficit of trust between

        the liquidator and lenders, liquidator not acting fairly, unilateral deployment of security

        guards at a disputed/ED-attached property, disproportionate liquidation-cost claims (with

        reference to the Space Matrix account), acting against stakeholder interest, use of

        defamatory language, filing of litigation without SCC consultation, and a proposal for a

        common liquidator across the Shree Mahalaxmi Corporation Pvt Ltd group of accounts. On

        26.06.2025, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri termed them as “allegations” and adjourned the meeting

        to 01.07.2025, declining SBI’s request to hold it on the same day or the next day. On

        28.06.2025, he sent a point-wise rebuttal, in which he also stated: “Had State Bank of India

        politely requested me to move out of being the Liquidator of Manglam Fiscal Services

        Private Limited, I might have agreed to its request. But causing hindrance to the liquidation

        process and casting baseless allegations do not display a behavior becoming the stature of

        a bank like State Bank of India.”



2.4.16 In the 5th SCC meeting held on 01.07.2025, the proposal was not placed before the SCC for

        deliberation and vote. The minutes prepared by Mr. Soumitra Lahiri record, under the item

        “any other matter”, that “Since State Bank of India cast allegations, the liquidator raised

        objections to the proposal of Replacement of Liquidator and declined to alter the agenda as

        suggested by State Bank of India.” The minutes further record that both sides “agreed to

        move forward to reach an amicable settlement post 08th July 2025”. SBI, by email dated

        05.07.2025, sought incorporation of following in the minutes: -



        “After the call of participants introduced themselves and the meeting started the liquidator

        immediately informed the lenders that since he is the Chairman of the meeting, he has

        decided not to have any discussion on the issue of his removal/ replacement of liquidator

        proposed by the SBI (vide mail dated 20.06.2025). The representatives of SBI then enquired

        about the provision which authorizes the liquidator to not to include as an agenda proposed

        by a SCC member, particularly one creditor who is having majority voting share (67.87%)

        and say in the meeting. To this liquidator simply reiterated his earlier stand that Regulations

        provide that liquidator will be chairman of the meeting and as chairperson he has right to

        decide what to discuss and what not to discuss. The Ld. Liquidator also informed the house



                                                      Page 14 of 22

        that he has written many books on IBC and he knows how to handle a meeting under the

        Code. He also advised the members of SCC that they were free to challenge his decision as

        per law.



        At one point in the meeting, it was enquired by the representatives of SBI that why

        applications are being filed by liquidator against SBI and its officials without first

        deliberating the issues in SCC, particularly when Regulations provide that SCC shall be

        consulted before institution of a legal proceeding. To this liquidator did not give clear

        answer and dropped some section of IBC to intimate the house that the consultation of SCC

        is in any manner not binding on liquidator.



        Representative of SBI informed the house that they would not bear expenses for any

        litigation brought by liquidator (particularly against SBI). To this liquidator informed that

        matter will be decided by Ld. Tribunal where applications have been filed”



        However, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri declined the request to modify the minutes on 08.07.2025.



2.4.17 Regulations 31A(6) and 31A(11) of the Liquidation Regulations provide as under:

                “31A. Stakeholders’ consultation committee.

                ….

                (6) The liquidator shall convene the first meeting of the consultation committee

                within seven days of the liquidation commencement date and may convene other

                meetings, if he considers necessary, on a request received from one or more

                members of the consultation committee:

                Provided that when a request is received by the liquidator from members,

                individually or collectively, having at least thirty three percent of the total voting

                rights, the liquidator shall mandatorily convene the meeting.

                Provided further that the liquidator shall convene subsequent meetings within

                thirty days of the previous meeting, unless the consultation committee has

                extended the period between such meetings:

                Provided further that there shall be at least one meeting in each quarter.

                ….

                (11) The consultation committee, after recording the reasons, may by a majority

                vote of not less sixty-six per cent., propose to replace the liquidator and shall

                file an application, after obtaining the written consent of the proposed liquidator

                in Form AA of the Schedule II, before the Adjudicating Authority for

                replacement of the liquidator:

                Provided that where a liquidator is proposed to be replaced, he shall-

                (a) continue to work till his replacement; and

                (b) be suitably remunerated for work performed till his replacement.”



                                                      Page 15 of 22

2.4.18 Regulation 31A(6) of Liquidation Regulations provides for convening of meeting, on a

        request received from SCC members individually or collectively, having at least 33 per cent

        voting share. Regulation 31A (11) further provides that the consultation committee, after

        recording the reasons, by a majority vote of not less sixty-six per cent, replace the Liquidator

        and the final decision rests with the AA. The liquidator, who convenes and chairs the

        meetings, has no role in deciding whether such a proposal deserves to be considered or not.

        Under the first proviso to Regulation 31A(6), a request from members holding at least thirty-

        three per cent of the voting rights obliges the liquidator to convene a meeting. In this case,

        since a member holding 67.87% of the voting share requested the Liquidator to convene a

        meeting to place an agenda of replacement, the Liquidator was duty bound to place that

        agenda in the meeting. The requirement of “recording the reasons” is a requirement for the

        SCC when it votes. In any case, SBI had furnished its reasons on 25.06.2025, six days before

        the meeting. However, the Liquidator termed these reasons as allegations and furnished

        replies to these reasons and did not place the agenda in the meeting. Regulation 31A(6) does

        not require the stakeholder to furnish any reasons for placing an agenda. Further, even at the

        time of voting by the SCC, although reasons are to be recorded for replacement of the

        liquidator, it is not open to the liquidator to judge the sufficiency of such reasons. The DC

        notes that a liquidator is free to place his objections before the SCC when it deliberates on

        the proposal, and before the AA when the application for replacement is considered. The

        right to object, however, does not extend to keeping the proposal off the agenda. By deciding

        for himself that the reasons were “allegations” and declining to alter the agenda, Mr.

        Soumitra Lahiri effectively decided a question that the regulations leave to the SCC and the

        AA and did so on a proposal for his own replacement, in which he was personally interested.

        The DC, accordingly, finds that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri failed to comply with Regulation

        31A(11) read with Regulation 31A(6) of the Liquidation Regulations.



        (D) Exclusion of the guarantee claim: the third revision (July 2025)



2.4.19 The DC notes that Mr. Soumitra Lahiri himself, on 21.05.2025, modified the list of

        stakeholders by admitting the guarantee component of SBI’s claim, and increased SBI’s

        voting share from 5.62% to 67.87%. The law on the liability of a guarantor was already well

        settled by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India and

        Another, Civil Appeal No. 2734 of 2020, decided on 26.03.2021, where it was held as under:



        “19. Indubitably, a right or cause of action would enure to the lender (financial creditor)

        to proceed against the principal borrower, as well as the guarantor in equal measure in

        case they commit default in repayment of the amount of debt acting jointly and severally. It

        would still be a case of default committed by the guarantor itself, if and when the principal

        borrower fails to discharge his obligation in respect of amount of debt. For, the obligation

        of the guarantor is coextensive and coterminous with that of the principal borrower to

        defray the debt, as predicated in Section 128 of the Contract Act.”



                                                      Page 16 of 22

2.4.20 As stated above, the liability of the guarantor is coextensive with that of the principal

        borrower. The Hon’ble Supreme Court further held in Maitreya Doshi v. Anand Rathi

        Global Finance Ltd. and Another, Civil Appeal No. 6613 of 2021, decided on 22.09.2022,

        as under : -



        “ 37. If there are two borrowers or if two corporate bodies fall within the ambit of corporate

        debtors, there is no reason why proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be initiated

        against both the Corporate Debtors. Needless to mention, the same amount cannot be

        realised from both the Corporate Debtors. If the dues are realised in part from one

        Corporate Debtor, the balance may be realised from the other Corporate Debtor being the

        co-borrower. However, once the claim of the Financial Creditor is discharged, there can

        be no question of recovery of the claim twice over”



2.4.21 In view of the above judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the law is well settled that a

        financial creditor may proceed against both the principal borrower and the guarantor, the

        safeguard being that the amount realised does not exceed the total claim. Further, the law

        does not bar filing of guarantee claim before the principal borrower as well as guarantor. It

        only prevents realisation beyond the claim amount. In the present case, nothing on record

        indicates any realisation in the process of SMCPL, so no occasion for double recovery had

        arisen. In view of this settled position of law, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri himself first admitted the

        guarantee component of the claim filed by SBI.



2.4.22 On 03.07.2025, the Hon’ble NCLAT delivered its judgment in Moneywise Financial

        Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Arunava Sikdar, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 310 of 2024. On

        08.07.2025, the very date after which the parties had agreed at the 5th SCC meeting to

        explore an amicable settlement, and on the same day on which he declined SBI’s request to

        correct the minutes, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri revised the claim of SBI back to Rs.

        24,39,20,845.30, excluding the guarantee component, relying on the said judgment. The

        voting share of SBI fell from 67.87% to 5.62%. With this, SBI, which a week earlier held

        on its own the majority required under Regulation 31A(11) for replacement of liquidator,

        was unfairly prevented by the liquidator from proceeding with the same.



2.4.23 On 09.07.2025, a day after giving effect to the revision, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri filed an

        application before the AA under Regulation 31(3), being IA No. 1135/2025. The AA did

        not pass any direction on the application during his tenure. It was disposed of on 14.10.2026,

        after the claim of SBI had been again revised and admitted by his successor on 14.10.2026.

        In the meantime, Mr. Soumitra Lahiri conducted the 6th SCC meeting on 02.01.2026 and

        the 7th SCC meeting on 19.02.2026 on the basis of the reduced voting share of SBI. Thus,

        the modification of voting shares was given effect to before any directions were passed by

        the AA on the application filed for modification of claim.



2.4.24 The relevant Regulation 31(3) of Liquidation Regulations is reproduced as under: -



                                                      Page 17 of 22

        “31. List of stakeholders



        …



        (3) The liquidator may apply to the Adjudicating Authority to modify an entry in the list of

        stakeholders filed with the Adjudicating Authority, when he comes across additional

        information warranting such modification, and shall modify the entry in the manner directed

        by the Adjudicating Authority.”



2.4.25 The Liquidator has to apply to the AA to modify an entry in the list of stakeholders when

        he comes across additional information warranting such modification and shall modify the

        entry only in the manner directed by the AA. In the present case, the liquidator has modified

        the entry on his own without seeking the direction of AA to modify the entry. He has given

        effect to the modification even before the AA has taken on record the revised list of

        stakeholders.



2.4.26 Mr. Soumitra Lahiri submitted that the judgment in Moneywise constituted additional

        information warranting modification under Regulation 31(3). The DC has perused the

        judgment. It arose from an appeal under Section 61 of the Code against the dismissal of an

        application seeking admission of a claim of Rs. 14.59 crore against a corporate guarantor in

        its CIRP. The Hon’ble NCLAT rejected the claim as no guarantee deed or board

        authorisation was produced, the guarantee was never invoked, the claim was filed 388 days

        after the last date and after the CoC had approved the resolution plan, and the identical claim

        had already been admitted in the CIRP of the principal borrower without disclosure or

        adjustment. It observed that a financial creditor cannot enforce the same claim in multiple

        CIRPs without proper adjustment or coordination, and that simultaneous claims are

        permitted to the extent double recovery is avoided. Mr. Soumitra Lahiri has not been able

        to show how the facts of the present case relate to Moneywise. The judgment does not deal

        with Regulation 31(3) and nowhere holds that a liquidator may modify an entry in the list

        of stakeholders without the direction of the AA. There, the claim failed because the

        guarantee itself was not established, was never invoked, and was filed 388 days late after

        indicates any realisation in the process of SMCPL that could give rise to double recovery.

        multiple proceedings without adjustment or coordination. This is the position already settled

        by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Laxmi Pat Sur
```

```text
             INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA

                                  (Disciplinary Committee)



No. IBBI/DC/351/2026                                                             09 November 2026



                             ORDER



This  Order    disposes  of  the    Show   Cause                                 Notice  (SCN)



No. IBBI/C/2024/01059/1812/1355 dated 11.09.2025, issued to Shri Venkata Sivakumar, who is an



Insolvency Professional (IP) registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India



(IBBI/Board) with Registration No. IBBI/IPA-001/IP-P00184/2017-18/10852 and a Professional



Member of the Indian Institute of Insolvency Professionals of ICAI (IIIP-ICAI).



1. Background



1.1. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s The Jeypore Sugar Company

        Limited (Corporate Debtor/CD) commenced vide order dated 25.02.2019 passed by the National

        Company Law Tribunal, Chennai Bench (AA) under Section 7 of the Insolvency and

        Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC/Code) on an application filed by M/s IDBI Bank Limited.

        Shri Venkata Sivakumar was appointed as Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) who was later

        confirmed as Resolution Professional (RP). The AA ordered the liquidation of the CD vide its

        order dated 29.05.2020 and Shri Venkata Sivakumar was appointed as the Liquidator. Later, Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar was replaced as the liquidator by the AA vide its order dated 01.07.2022 and

        Mr. Subburengan Hari Karthik was appointed as the Liquidator.



1.2. The Board received a complaint dated 18.01.2024 against Shri Venkata Sivakumar in the matter

        of the CD. The Board, in exercise of power conferred under Section 218 of the Code read with

        Regulation 7(1) and 7(2) of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017

        (Investigation Regulations) vide order dated 07.02.2024 appointed an Investigating Authority

        (IA) to conduct the investigation on the issues raised by the complainant.



1.3. The IA in terms of Regulation 8(1) of the Investigation Regulations, served notice to Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar on 21.02.2024 and in response to the said notice Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        submitted partial reply on the same date. The IA again sought clarification vide an email dated

        13.12.2024 on all the issues raised in the complaint. In response, Shri Venkata Sivakumar vide

        email dated 15.12.2024, stated that he had given all the required details in the form of recordings

        of the Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC) meetings. However, specific reply to the

        allegations raised in the complaint was not provided to the IA. The IA repeatedly requested Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar to provide his reply to all the allegations contained in the complaint, but in

        response Shri Venkata Sivakumar instead raised queries and questions to the Board and chose

        not to submit reply/comments on the allegations mentioned in the complaint. Constrained by his

        non-cooperative attitude and despite being provided multiple opportunities to submit his

        reply/comments on the allegations in the complaint, the IA, after considering his partial reply

        and material available on records, submitted the Investigation Report (IR) to the Board.



1.4. On perusal of the IR, the Board formed a prima facie view that Shri Venkata Sivakumar had

        contravened the provisions of the Code and the Regulations made thereunder and issued an SCN



                             Page 1 of 25

        to him on 11.09.2025. The SCN alleged contraventions of several provisions of the Code, the

        IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 (Liquidation Regulations) and the IBBI

        (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016 (IP Regulations). The reply of Shri Venkata

        Sivakumar to the SCN was received by the Board on a piecemeal basis on 12.09.2025,

        13.09.2025, 15.09.2025 and 17.09.2025.



1.5. The SCN and the replies of Shri Venkata Sivakumar to the SCN were referred to the Disciplinary

        Committee (DC) for disposal. Shri Venkata Sivakumar availed an opportunity of personal

        hearing before the DC on 12.08.2026 through virtual mode. Shri Venkata Sivakumar provided

        additional written submissions on 11.08.2026 and 12.08.2026 which was also placed before the

        DC for consideration.



2. Examination of Preliminary Objections raised by Shri Venkata Sivakumar.



2.1. Locus of IDBI Bank as complainant.



2.1.1 Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that IDBI Bank had no locus standi as a complainant as it

        was not a member of the stakeholders' consultation committee, owing to its failure to surrender

        its security interest. He further submitted that IDBI Bank did not obtain prior permission from

        the AA before ordering any enquiry, which was a serious irregularity. Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        submitted that he had requested a copy of the E&Y report, but it had not been provided, making

        it impossible for him to address specific details, particularly as the vouchers were in the

        possession of the new liquidator.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.1.2 The DC observes that Section 217 of the Code as quoted below is unambiguously clear:

        “Any person aggrieved by the functioning of an insolvency professional agency or insolvency

        professional or an information utility may file a complaint to the Board in such form, within such

        time and in such manner as may be specified.”



2.1.3 Further, Regulation 2(1)(j) of the IBBI (Grievance and Complaint Handling Procedure)

        Regulations, 2017 provides that “‘stakeholder’ means a debtor, a creditor, a claimant, a service

        provider, a resolution applicant and any other person having an interest in the insolvency,

        liquidation, voluntary liquidation, or bankruptcy transaction under the Code.”



2.1.4 Whether or not IDBI Bank relinquished its security interest, it remains a secured creditor of the

        CD and hence has an interest in the ongoing liquidation process of the CD. Hence, it is covered

        under the definition of the stakeholder and has locus to file the complaint. Whether or not IDBI

        Bank obtained the permission of the AA before getting the forensic audit conducted by E&Y has

        no bearing on the statutory power of the Board to order an investigation on a complaint.

        Moreover, the DC notes that the copy of the E&Y report was provided to Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        by the IA on 16.12.2024 and Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted his comments on the same on

        23.01.2025.



                                                       Page 2 of 25

2.2. Recording of reasons before ordering investigation.



2.2.1.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that it was mandatory under Sections 218 and 219 of the Code

        that reasons be recorded before ordering an investigation, which was a condition precedent, and

        that the action of the Board in ordering the investigation without recording reasons is void ab

        initio. He also submitted that the RTI reply provided by the Central Public Information Officer

        of the Board made it clear that reasons for ordering the investigation were not recorded, which

        was sine qua non.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.2.2. Section 218(1) of the Code provides as follows:



        “Where the Board, on receipt of a complaint under Section 217 or has reasonable grounds to

        believe that any insolvency professional agency or insolvency professional or an information

        utility has contravened any of the provisions of the Code or the rules or regulations made or

        directions issued by the Board thereunder, it may, at any time by an order in writing, direct any

        person or persons to act as an investigating authority to conduct an inspection or investigation

        of the insolvency professional agency or insolvency professional or an information utility.”



2.2.3.  Accordingly, under Section 218(1) of the Code, the Board may order an investigation on either

        of two independent grounds. The first is the receipt of a complaint under Section 217 and the

        second is where the Board has reasonable grounds to believe that an insolvency professional has

        contravened the provisions of the Code. Where a complaint has been received, the complaint

        itself forms the basis for ordering the investigation. Neither Section 218 nor the Regulations

        made thereunder require the Board to record reasons before ordering an investigation.



2.2.4.  The DC notes that in the present case, the Board had received a complaint dated 18.01.2024 from

        IDBI Bank Limited and thereafter appointed the IA through an order in writing dated 07.02.2024.

        The investigation was therefore validly ordered under Section 218(1) of the Code. The said order

        itself records that the Board had reasonable grounds to believe that Shri Venkata Sivakumar had

        contravened the provisions of the Code or the regulations made thereunder, and specifies the

        allegations contained in the complaint dated 18.01.2024 as the scope of the investigation.

        Further, the RTI reply dated 23.04.2024 relied upon by Shri Venkata Sivakumar does not state

        that no reasons were recorded. It states that no minutes of correspondence of officers or of a

        Board meeting exist on the subject, and furnishes the file noting on the basis of which the

        investigation was ordered. In any case, since the law does not require reasons to be recorded

        separately, the absence of such reasons would not vitiate the investigation. The DC accordingly

        finds no merit in the submission.

        validity of the liquidation cost incurred by the Liquidator and therefore the DC is not going into

        the question as to whether the costs incurred were after deliberation with the SCC, or whether

        seeking expert advice would come under liquidation cost or not. Further, the DC finds that the

        requirement under Regulations 42 to 44 of the Liquidation Regulations that distribution shall not

        commence until liquidation costs are met does not give right to any Liquidator to transfer any

        amount to an account in his own name and that too after his replacement as the Liquidator.

        Further, the DC notes that Regulation 2A and Regulation 44 of the Liquidation Regulations do

        not specifically give power to a Liquidator to set aside liquidation costs and transfer it to his own

        account before distributing the proceeds to the stakeholders.

        Venkata Sivakumar was aware that he had been replaced as Liquidator. An insolvency

        professional must maintain integrity by being honest, straightforward, and forthright in all

        professional relationships. An IP cannot misrepresent any facts or situations and should refrain

        from being involved in any action that would bring disrepute to the profession. He must not

        conceal any material information or knowingly make a misleading statement to the Board and

        the AA.
```
