3.2. Failure to appoint a second valuer and exclusion of asset of CD in the Asset Memorandum.



3.2.1.  Regulation 35(2) of the Liquidation Regulations states that in cases not covered under sub-

        regulation (1) or where the liquidator is of the opinion that fresh valuation is required under the

        circumstances, he shall within seven days of the liquidation commencement date, appoint two

        registered valuers to determine the realisable value of the assets or businesses under clauses (a)

        to (f) of Regulation 32 of the Liquidation Regulations, of the CD. It was observed that Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar got fresh valuation of Land & Building and Plant & Machinery conducted

        during the liquidation process of the CD. However, apparently, Shri Venkata Sivakumar did not

        appoint the two valuers for each asset class, as required under Regulation 35(2) of the



        Page 11 of 25

        Liquidation Regulations. The Hon'ble NCLAT in paragraph 126 of its order dated 16.01.2024

        noted this. In the absence of specific reply by Shri Venkata Sivakumar to the various issues raised

        in the complaint, the IA was constrained to hold from the material available on record that Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar failed to appoint a second valuer for each asset class i.e. for Land & building

        and Plant & Machinery.



3.2.2. Further, it was observed from the order of Hon’ble NCLAT dated 16.01.2024 that the Raygada

        property was excluded from the valuation. The Hon'ble NCLAT vide its order dated 16.01.2024

        observed as under:



        "140. To be noted, merely because in respect of the 'Title of the property', if a 'Corporate Debtor

        'has no valid or any marketable title, ipso facto, the 'value of the property' cannot be described

        as Zero. No wonder, the Liquidator, holding the 'Liquidation Estate', in the interest and for the

        benefit of 'stakeholders', is to take into consideration as to which/what are all the properties? do

        form part of the 'Liquidation Estate'. By adhering to the ingredients of Section 36(3) of the I&B

        Code, 2016, the 'Registered Valuers', are to 'value' the property.



        141. In the instant case, the Erstwhile Liquidator had not obtained the valuation from the second

        valuer and that the liquidation value was arrived at only by one value. Also that the erstwhile

        liquidator had gone for a fresh valuation which clearly points out that Regulation 35(2) of IBBI

        (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 was not followed. The stakeholders ‘plea/request to go

        for a fresh set of valuations was not acceded to by the Erstwhile liquidator."



3.2.3.  As per Section 36(3)(e) of the Code, the liquidation estate shall comprise all assets which shall

        also include the assets subject to the determination of ownership by the court or authority.

        However, it was observed that the Raygada property was not included in the liquidation estate

        of the CD as the same was valued at zero merely by reason that the asset was under "lis" which

        was prima facie a contravention of Section 36(3)(e) of the Code. The relevant extract of

        observations of the Hon'ble NCLAT in this regard is as under:



        "125. The Erstwhile Liquidator, who had filed the Asset Memorandum on 21.09.2020, had not

        included the 'Raygada Property Assets' but arrived at a 'realisable value' of 217.52 crore.



        126. The valuation of the Raygada Property with a market value of more than Rs. 1000 crore as

        mentioned by the Liquidator/7th Respondent was valued at Rs. Zero by the erstwhile liquidator

        without adhering to the mandatory requirement of Regulation 35 of IBBI (liquidation process)

        Regulations, 2016. Even the second value report secured by the 7th Respondent / liquidator does

        not exhibit the compliance of the Regulations because of the fact that in the instant case the

        liquidator / 7th Respondent had only obtained one Report on the plant and machinery and

        another report on the land and building which is in negation of the procedure as specified under

        the Regulations. In short, the said valuation was made, without including a vital asset of the

        Corporate Debtor.



        128. In reality, the valuer in the initial report had assessed the value of Raygada lands to be

        Rs.1087.98 crore, later based on the information furnished by the 7th Respondent / liquidator

        and resting upon the opinion furnished by the Learned Advocate, the liquidator came to the

        conclusion that the value of the Raygada lands should be decided as zero. Resultantly, based on



        Page 12 of 25

        the opinion of advocate, coming to the zero valuation was not approved by the Committee of

        Creditors /Stakeholders Consultation Committee.



        130. A cursory glance of Section 36(3)(e) of the Code clearly exhibit that the Assets subject to

        the determination of ownership by the Court or authority shall form part of the Liquidation Asset,

        meaning thereby inclusive of the 'Lands of the Corporate Debtor at Raygada.”



3.2.4. It was noted from the above-stated observations of the Hon'ble NCLAT that Rayagada property

        of the CD was not included in the asset memorandum and the only one valuer appointed by Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar for land and building category valued the said asset at zero on his advice.



3.2.5.  In the absence of Shri Venkata Sivakumar’s reply to the allegation, the Board held prima facie

        view that, his conduct in not including the Rayagada property of the CD in the asset

        memorandum and appointing only one valuer for each asset class, was in contravention of

        Sections 36(3)(e), 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulations 35(2) of the Liquidation

        Regulations, Regulations 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations read with Clauses 14, 18 and 19

        of the Code of Conduct and Section 230(2) of the Companies Act.



        Submissions by Shri Venkata Sivakumar.



3.2.6.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that there was no need for referring to the order in

        IA/815/2020, when the Hon'ble Supreme Court had already set aside all adverse findings. He

        also submitted that there was no necessity of referring to the order of the Hon'ble NCLAT in

        CA/302/2021, which had already been considered in the earlier investigation report, on which

        the Hon'ble Madras High Court had granted a stay.



3.2.7.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that both valuers were appointed simultaneously after

        consulting the SCC. The JLF also actively participated in the deliberations, as confirmed in

        paragraph 3 of the order in IA/815/2020. The first valuer conducted the inspection in time, but

        immediately thereafter, the Covid-19 lockdown was announced, preventing the second valuer

        from proceeding. Meanwhile, the compromise scheme under Section 230 was to be completed

        within 90 days from 01.06.2020.



3.2.8.  He further submitted that there were more than seven resolution applicants who were willing to

        negotiate for a higher price. However, IDBI Bank filed IA/255/2021 raising objections on issues

        which had already been deliberated upon and approved by them. He submitted that the IA

        selectively relied on portions of the orders, refused to examine the minutes of the SCC and JLF

        meetings and merely reproduced stray observations from orders which might itself be based on

        an erroneous appreciation of facts.



3.2.9.  With regard to the exclusion of the Rayagada property, Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that

        it was the decision of the CoC to value the Rayagada land at nil value after he had got it valued

        at Rs.1078 crore, because the land belonged to the Government of Odisha (OLR proceedings

        were ongoing), and that it was IDBI Bank which directed the appointment of another legal expert

        to give an opinion, pursuant to which he conducted the affairs accordingly.



        Page 13 of 25

        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



3.2.10. The DC notes that in response to the instant alleged contravention, Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        raised two preliminary objections which need to be addressed first. The first objection is that the

        Board ought not to have relied on the order of the AA in IA/815/2020, since the Hon’ble Supreme

        Court had set aside all the adverse findings recorded against him. The DC notes that the AA,

        vide order dated 01.07.2022 in IA/815/2020, had replaced Shri Venkata Sivakumar as the

        Liquidator of the CD. His appeal against that order was dismissed by the Hon’ble NCLAT vide

        order dated 20.12.2022. When he challenged the order of the Hon’ble NCLAT before the Hon’ble

        Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 1614 of 2023, he stated that he was not interested in

        continuing as the Liquidator of the CD. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, vide order dated

        22.10.2024, took this statement on record and, only in view of that statement, set aside the

        adverse findings recorded against him in the said two orders, without going into the merits of the

        appeal.



3.2.11. The DC further observes that as noted earlier in paragraph 2.4.3 of this order, the present

        allegation does not rest on the order of the AA dated 01.07.2022 in IA/815/2020 or on the order

        of the Hon’ble NCLAT dated 20.12.2022. The reference in the SCN is to the order of the Hon’ble

        NCLAT dated 16.01.2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 302 of 2021, which arose

        out of a different application, namely IA/255/2021 filed by the secured creditors of the CD, and

        which was not the subject matter of the proceedings before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. The DC

        further notes that the Review Application No. 02 of 2024 filed by Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        against the said order was withdrawn by him on 28.03.2024, and the order has, therefore, attained

        finality. The first objection is accordingly rejected.



3.2.12. The second preliminary objection raised by Shri Venkata Sivakumar is that the referred order

        dated 16.01.2024 of the Hon’ble NCLAT had already been considered in the earlier investigation,

        the outcome of which has been stayed by the Hon’ble High Court of Madras. The DC notes that

        the earlier SCN dated 03.07.2023 was based on an investigation report dated 21.02.2023 and

        was disposed of by another DC vide order dated 09.04.2024. That investigation report was

        submitted nearly eleven months before the Hon’ble NCLAT passed its order dated 16.01.2024

        and, therefore, could not have considered that order. Further, the earlier proceedings concerned

        the disclosure of the valuation of the CD to a prospective scheme proponent, whereas the present

        allegation concerns the non-appointment of a second registered valuer and the exclusion of the

        Rayagada property from the Asset Memorandum. The present SCN is based on a separate

        investigation ordered on 07.02.2024 on a separate complaint. The stay granted by the Hon’ble

        High Court of Madras vide order dated 06.06.2024 on the DC order dated 09.04.2024 does not,

        therefore, come in the way of the present proceedings. The second objection is also rejected.



3.2.13. The DC now proceeds to examine the merits of the allegation. The DC notes that the CD owned,

        among other assets, sugar factories and lands in Andhra Pradesh and a large parcel of land at

        Rayagada in Odisha (Rayagada property). As recorded by the Hon’ble NCLAT in paragraphs

        122 to 124 of its order dated 16.01.2024, a registered valuer, in his report dated 25.09.2019

        obtained during the CIRP, had valued the Rayagada lands at Rs.1087.98 crore, out of a total fair

        value of about Rs.1368.78 crore for all the assets of the CD. Thereafter, Shri Venkata Sivakumar



                                                      Page 14 of 25

        obtained a fresh legal opinion from an advocate at Rayagada. The opinion stated that the lands

        were the subject matter of proceedings under the Odisha Land Reforms Act (OLR proceedings)

        pending before the Revenue Officer, Rayagada, and that the said proceedings had been stayed

        by the Hon’ble High Court of Orissa, and that the lands could neither be sold nor mortgaged.

        Relying on this opinion, the valuer, at the request of Shri Venkata Sivakumar, revised his report

        on 28.10.2019 and valued the Odisha assets at zero. As stated by the valuer and recorded by the

        Hon’ble NCLAT, when the fresh valuation was carried out after the commencement of

        liquidation on 29.05.2020, the Odisha assets were not taken up for valuation at all. The Asset

        Memorandum filed by Shri Venkata Sivakumar on 21.09.2020 accordingly showed a realisable

        value of Rs.217.52 crore, without including the Rayagada property.



3.2.14. The DC notes that Section 36(3)(e) of the Code provides that the liquidation estate shall include

        “assets subject to the determination of ownership by the court or authority”. In simple terms,

        where the ownership of an asset of the corporate debtor is under dispute before a court or an

        authority, the asset does not drop out of the liquidation estate; rather, it remains a part of the

        estate of the CD.. A dispute over title may be a factor in arriving at the value of an asset, but it

        cannot be a ground for leaving the asset out of the liquidation estate and the Asset Memorandum

        altogether. The Hon’ble NCLAT, in paragraphs 130, 139 and 140 of its order dated 16.01.2024,

        has taken the same view. The DC also notes that, as recorded by the Hon’ble NCLAT in its order

        dated 16.01.2024, the Hon’ble High Court of Orissa, vide order dated 16.03.2022 in W.P.(C) No.

        4490 of 2015, held that the CD had a right to compensation in respect of its ceiling surplus land

        at Rayagada. This shows that the Rayagada property carried value for the stakeholders.



3.2.15. The DC further notes that Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that the decision to value the

        Rayagada land as nil was taken by the CoC and that it was IDBI Bank which directed the

        appointment of another legal expert. The DC does not find merit in this submission for the

        following reasons. Firstly, the Hon’ble NCLAT, in paragraph 128 of its order dated 16.01.2024,

        has recorded that the zero-valuation based on the opinion of the advocate was not approved by

        the CoC/SCC. Secondly, it was the secured creditors, led by IDBI Bank, who had objected to the

        valuation by filing IA/255/2021 before the AA, and in the appeal arising out of that application,

        the Hon’ble NCLAT held that the Rayagada property is to be valued and included in the

        liquidation estate. The duty to take into custody all the assets of the CD and to include them in

        the liquidation estate and the Asset Memorandum is a statutory duty of the liquidator, and he

        cannot shift that responsibility to the creditors.



3.2.16. The DC also notes that Regulation 35 of the Liquidation Regulations, as it stood at the relevant

        time, gave the liquidator two options. Under sub-regulation (1), the liquidator can consider the

        average of the values arrived at by the registered valuers during the CIRP. Further, under sub-

        regulation (2), if the liquidator is of the opinion that a fresh valuation is required, the two

        registered valuers are required to be appointed within seven days of the liquidation

        commencement date to determine the realisable value of the assets. The decision whether to go

        for a fresh valuation was thus left to the liquidator. However, once he chose a fresh valuation,

        the appointment of two registered valuers was mandatory. The purpose of requiring two

        independent valuations is to guard against error or bias in a single estimate and to give the

        stakeholders a reliable basis for their decisions. Since registered valuers are registered for



                                                      Page 15 of 25

        specific asset classes, such as land and building or plant and machinery, two registered valuers

        are required for each asset class.



3.2.17. In the present case, Shri Venkata Sivakumar chose to get a fresh valuation of the land and

        building and the plant and machinery of the CD during the liquidation process. The relationship

        disclosures filed by him with IIIP-ICAI on 21.12.2020, a copy of which he has himself placed

        on record, shows that he had appointed only one valuer Shri R. Chandran for the asset class of

        ‘Land and Building’ and one valuer Shri R. Santha Kumar for the asset class of ‘Plant and

        Machinery’, on 06.06.2020. Hon’ble NCLAT, in paragraphs 126 and 141 of its order dated

        16.01.2024, has also observed that only one report was obtained on the plant and machinery and

        one on the land and building, and that the liquidation value was arrived at on the basis of the

        report of a single valuer. Shri Venkata Sivakumar has neither named a second valuer for either

        asset class nor produced the report of any such valuer.



3.2.18. The DC notes that Shri Venkata Sivakumar submitted that both the valuers were appointed at the

        same time, but that the COVID-19 lockdown, announced soon after the first valuer completed

        his inspection, prevented the second valuer from proceeding. The DC is unable to accept this

        explanation. The nationwide lockdown came into force on 25.03.2020, about two months before

        the liquidation commencement date of 29.05.2020, and the restrictions were being progressively

        relaxed from 01.06.2020. The valuers were appointed on 06.06.2020 and the Asset Memorandum

        was filed only on 21.09.2020, more than three months later. Nothing has been placed on record

        to show that a second valuer was appointed for each asset class or that any effort was made

        during this period to obtain a second valuation. The DC also finds that the submission by Shri

        Venkata Sivakumar that the scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 was to be

        completed within 90 days, cannot be accepted as a valid justification for non-appointment of

        second valuer. As held by the Hon’ble NCLAT in paragraph 129 of its order dated 16.01.2024,

        the requirement of Regulation 35 of the Liquidation Regulations is separate from the process

        under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, and the timeline for the latter cannot be used to

        bypass the former.



3.2.19. Shri Venkata Sivakumar has also submitted that more than seven resolution applicants were

        willing to negotiate for a higher price, and that the IA relied selectively on portions of judicial

        orders without examining the minutes of the SCC and JLF meetings. The DC has independently

        examined the material on record, including his replies and the documents relied upon by him.

        The willingness of a prospective applicant to offer a higher price does not dispense with the

        statutory requirements of including all the assets in the liquidation estate and obtaining two

        valuations. On the contrary, a proper valuation that included an asset as significant as the

        Rayagada property was essential for the stakeholders to judge as to what extent the offer reflected

        fair value of the liquidation assets.



3.2.20. In view of the above, the DC finds that Shri Venkata Sivakumar excluded the Rayagada property

        from the liquidation estate and the Asset Memorandum and conducted a fresh valuation of the

        assets of the CD without appointing two registered valuers for each asset class. The DC,

        therefore, holds that Shri Venkata Sivakumar has contravened Sections 36(3)(e), 208(2)(a) and



                                                      Page 16 of 25

        208(2)(e) of the Code, Regulation 35(2) of the Liquidation Regulations and Regulations 7(2)(a)

        and 7(2)(h) of the IP Regulations read with Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct.



3.3. Bringing the Scheme of Arrangement without approval of the CoC.



3.3.1.  It was observed that Shri Venkata Sivakumar did not secure the approval of the Committee of

        Creditors (CoC) or the SCC to bring to an effect the 'scheme' under Section 230 of the Companies

        Act, 2013 which provides for the consent of secured creditors to the extent of 75%. Section

        230(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 states as under:



        "2) The company or any other person, by whom an application is made under sub-section(1),

        shall disclose to the Tribunal by affidavit-



        …



        (c) any scheme of corporate debt restructuring consented to by not less than seventy-five per

        cent. of the secured creditors in value,..."



3.3.2. The Hon'ble NCLAT vide order dated 16.01.2024 held the following:



        "144. There is no two opinion of the vital fact that the Liquidator has not secured the 'Approval

        of the Creditors' to bring to an effect the 'scheme' under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013.

        In this connection, this Tribunal quite significantly points out that the procedure mentioned in

        Section 230(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is to be adhered to and the same is not in exemption

        of any other Law, inclusive of the I&B Code, 2016."



3.3.3.  In view of the above, the Board held prima facie view that conduct of Shri Venkata Sivakumar

        was, in violation of Sections 36(3)(e), 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulations 35(2) of the

        Liquidation Regulations, Regulations 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations read with Clauses 14,

        18 and 19 of the Code of Conduct and Section 230(2) of the Companies Act read with Section

        35(1)(m) of the Code.



        Submissions by Shri Venkata Sivakumar.



3.3.4.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar has submitted that the issuance of the present SCN was based solely on

        an observation made by the Hon'ble NCLAT, which itself was factually and legally incorrect,

        and was made without considering the actual record of the proceedings. The Hon’ble NCLAT

        order merely recorded the contention of the IDBI Bank, not a finding based on evidence or

        verified facts.



3.3.5.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar further submitted that pursuant to directions from the AA, he was asked

        to explore the possibility of a compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies

        Act, 2013. Accordingly, deliberations with the SCC were duly recorded. The SCC directed that

        negotiations be held with potential promoters/applicants, and this was done twice in presence of

        the SCC members. These deliberations were recorded in the Joint Lenders Forum (JLF) minutes,

        which were also shared with the stakeholders. Based on the SCC inputs and deliberations, he

        shortlisted one proposal and filed a First Motion application before the AA seeking directions to

        convene the meeting of stakeholders under Section 230(1) of the Companies Act.



        Page 17 of 25

3.3.6.  Shri Venkata Sivakumar further submitted that Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, read

        with Rule 3 of the Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules, 2016,

        clearly allows the liquidator to file a first motion seeking directions from the AA. The

        Stakeholder approval is sought after the AA permits convening of meetings and not before. No

        provision in the Code or Companies Act, 2013 mandates prior written "approval" of the SCC

        before filing a first motion under Section 230 of the Companies Act.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



3.3.7.  The Liquidation Regulations allow for compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the

        Companies Act, 2013 even after a company goes into liquidation, so that the company may be

        revived as a whole instead of its assets being sold. Under Regulation 2B of the Liquidation

        Regulations, as it then stood, such a compromise or arrangement was required to be completed

        within 90 days of the order of liquidation. The DC notes that, after the CD went into liquidation

        on 29.05.2020, Shri Venkata Sivakumar held deliberations with the SCC and the lenders,

        shortlisted one proposal and filed an application (first motion) before the AA under Section

        230(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking directions to convene the meetings of the

        stakeholders. The secured creditors, led by IDBI Bank, objected to the scheme and to the

        valuation on which it was based by filing IA/255/2021 before the AA. The matter eventually
