```text
INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA

                     (Disciplinary Committee)



No. IBBI/DC/350/2026                03 November 2026



                      ORDER



This Order disposes of the Show Cause Notice (SCN) No. COMP-11011/75/2025-IBBI/1840/1762

dated 21.11.2025, issued to Shri Pathukasahasram Raghunathan Raman (P.R. Raman), who is an

Insolvency Professional (IP) registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India

(IBBI/Board) having Registration No. IBBI/IPA-002/IP-N00295/2017-18/10896 and a Professional

Member of the ICSI Institute of Insolvency Professionals.



1. Background



1.1. The corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) of Hallmark Infrastructure Private Limited

        (Corporate Debtor/CD) commenced vide order of the National Company Law Tribunal,

        Chennai Bench (AA) dated 23.08.2024 on an application filed by Bank of India under Section

        7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code). Shri P.R. Raman was appointed as

        Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) in the matter and was later confirmed as the Resolution

        Professional (RP).



1.2. IBBI received a complaint from Shri T. Ranganathan, Authorised Representative of the

        homebuyers of the CD, against Shri P.R. Raman regarding his conduct as RP in the CIRP of

        the CD. IBBI sought reply from Shri P.R. Raman on the complaint who submitted his replies

        vide emails dated 30.05.2025 and 04.08.2025. IBBI examined the allegations in the above

        complaint vis-à-vis the replies of Shri P.R. Raman and based on such examination, IBBI formed

        a prima facie opinion that Shri P.R. Raman had contravened provisions of the Code and

        Regulations made thereunder and accordingly issued the SCN to Shri P.R. Raman on

        21.11.2025. Shri P.R. Raman submitted his reply to the SCN on 04.12.2025.



1.3. The SCN and its response by Shri P.R. Raman were referred to the Disciplinary Committee

        (DC) for disposal. Shri P.R. Raman availed the opportunity of personal hearing before the DC

        through virtual mode on 21.08.2026. The DC has considered the SCN, the reply to the SCN,

        oral and written submissions of Shri P.R. Raman, and proceeds to dispose of the SCN.



2. Alleged Contravention, submissions of Shri P.R. Raman and analysis and findings of the

        DC.



2.1 Failure to appoint Registered Valuers for the Asset class - Securities or Financial Assets.



2.1.1 Regulation 27(1) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons)

        Regulations, 2016 (CIRP Regulations) provides that, “The resolution professional shall, within

        seven days of his appointment but not later than forty-seventh day from the insolvency

        commencement date, appoint two registered valuers to determine the fair value and the

        liquidation value of the corporate debtor in accordance with Regulation 35.”



                      Page 1 of 16

2.1.2  In the present matter, as observed from the Form CIRP-3 filed by Shri P.R. Raman, two

       registered valuers were appointed for the asset class "Land & Building'' on 08.10.2024. The

       provisional financials as on the insolvency commencement date (ICD) indicated value of the

       total assets of the CD to the tune of Rs.49.64 crore including financial assets under the heads

       such as Non-Current Investments, Long term loans and advances, Trade receivables etc. In the

       5th CoC meeting held on 18.02.2025, the Authorised Representative of homebuyers informed

       the CoC that the homebuyers had unanimously proposed for the valuation of the financial

       assets. However, despite existence of such assets in financial statements of the CD and request

       made by the homebuyers, no registered valuer was appointed for the asset class ''Securities or

       financial assets".



2.1.3 In response, Shri P.R. Raman submitted that one of the CoC members, viz., Bank of India (FC)

        requested to defer the discussion on valuation of these assets to the next meeting and that there

        was no further communication in this regard. This explanation is not consistent with the

        mandate of the Code. It is the duty of the RP to appoint registered valuers to secure

        determination of the fair value and liquidation value of the assets of the CD, as valuation is

        fundamental to the CoC's consideration of the resolution plans.



2.1.4 In view of the above, the Board had formed a prima facie view that Shri P.R. Raman had

        contravened the provisions of Sections 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 27(1) of CIRP

        Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of IP Regulations, read with Clause 14 of the Code of

        Conduct as specified in First Schedule of the IP Regulations.



        Submissions by Shri P.R. Raman.



2.1.5 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the CIRP of the CD commenced pursuant to the order of the

        AA dated 23.08.2024 and the copy of the said order was received by him by e-mail on

        27.08.2024. He visited the registered office of the CD on the same day, where he met the

        director of the suspended board, Shri Anand Jain. During the said visit, he observed that the

        CD had not carried out any business operations since 2013, its books of account had not been

        audited for the Financial Year 2023-24, there were no employees, the premises were severely

        infested with termites due to prolonged closure, the physical records had been damaged and

        the Tally backup was found to be corrupted.



2.1.6 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that he handed over a list of documents required for

        conducting the CIRP and requested the erstwhile management to furnish the same on the

        following day. He thereafter followed up the request through the e-mail reminders. Despite

        such repeated follow-ups, the financial statements for FY 2023-24 were furnished by the

        erstwhile management only on 02.12.2024. Shri P.R. Raman submitted that upon examination

        of the financial statements, it appeared that the CD did not have any actual or tangible financial

        assets, except an equity investment in M/s. Hallmark Living Space Private Limited (“HLSPL”)

        which was undergoing liquidation. Shri P.R. Raman submitted that a claim in respect of the

        said investment had already been submitted in the liquidation proceedings of HLSPL and the

        amount was awaited from the Liquidator in accordance with Section 53 of the Code. He further



       Page 2 of 16

        submitted that the other financial assets reflected in the financial statements had, owing to the

        prolonged inactivity of the Corporate Debtor, effectively become bad and doubtful debts and

        were not written off from the books of account.



2.1.7   Shri P.R. Raman submitted that, in the 1st CoC meeting held on 23.09.2024, it was resolved to

        open a CIRP account with Bank of India, being the only financial institution and one of the

        Financial Creditors with which the CD had maintained a current account. However, despite

        repeated requests, Bank of India delayed the opening of the CIRP account on account of

        operational difficulties, and the account was ultimately opened only on 29.12.2024, i.e., nearly

        four months after the commencement of the CIRP. Shri P.R. Raman submitted that, during this

        period, no contribution was made by the CoC members/Financial Creditors, resulting in paucity

        of funds for conducting the CIRP and making payments to the professionals proposed to be

        appointed.



2.1.8   Shri P.R. Raman submitted that, in the 10th CoC meeting, he proposed the appointment of the

        registered valuers for the asset class “Securities or Financial Assets”. However, the

        representative of Bank of India requested that the matter be deferred as internal approval was

        required. Thereafter, no further response was received from Bank of India and no other CoC

        member including the Authorised Representative of the homebuyers, who raised the present

        complaint, sought to revisit the matter.



2.1.9 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that the financial assets reflected under the heads “Non-

        current Investments”, “Long-term Loans and Advances”, “Trade Receivables”, etc., in the

        balance sheets appeared to exist only as book entries, as the CD had not undertaken any

        business activity for approximately ten years. Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that the

        position was further compounded by the non-availability of the books of account, including the

        soft copies of the accounts, which, according to the erstwhile management, had been

        damaged/destroyed due to termite infestation. Further, the aforesaid circumstances were duly

        brought to the notice of the AA in his report immediately upon assuming charge.



2.1.10 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the investment in HLSPL, which was undergoing liquidation,

        had already been claimed before the Liquidator, while the remaining financial assets appeared

        to be bad and doubtful debts which ought to have been written off. However, these assets

        continued to be reflected in the books of the CD. In the absence of the books of account and

        supporting records, the existence and value of such assets could not be independently verified.



2.1.11  Shri P.R. Raman also submitted that, in view of the apparent non-existence of the assets, non-

        availability of supporting documents for inspection and verification by the valuers, paucity of

        funds, and the limited time available for completion of the CIRP, obtaining valuation reports

        for the asset class “Securities or Financial Assets” would not have served any meaningful

        purpose. Therefore, considering the facts and circumstances prevailing at the relevant time,

        registered valuers for the said asset class were not appointed.



        Page 3 of 16

        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.1.12 Regulation 27(1) of the CIRP Regulations read as follows:-



        “27. Appointment of Professionals.

        (1) The resolution professional shall, within seven days of his appointment but not later than

        forty seventh day from the insolvency commencement date, appoint two sets of registered

        valuers to determine the fair value and the liquidation value in accordance with regulation

        35.”



2.1.13  In the instant matter, the CIRP of the CD commenced on 23.08.2024 and, accordingly, the

        registered valuers were required to be appointed not later than the forty-seventh day, i.e. by

        09.10.2024. The DC notes that although the financial statements of the Corporate Debtor

        reflected financial assets under various heads, including investments, loans and advances and

        trade receivables, no registered valuer was appointed for the asset class “Securities or Financial

        Assets” within the prescribed period. The issue of valuation of such financial assets was

        considered only in the 5th CoC meeting held on 18.02.2025, wherein the Authorised

        Representative of the homebuyers informed the CoC that the homebuyers had unanimously

        suggested that the financial assets be valued. Thus, the issue of appointment of valuers was

        taken up for consideration after the expiry of the statutory period prescribed under Regulation

        27(1).



2.1.14  The DC further notes that during the 5th CoC meeting, Shri P.R. Raman explained the process

        of valuation of financial assets. The representative of Bank of India thereafter requested that

        the discussion on valuation be deferred to the next CoC meeting. However, there is nothing on

        record to indicate that, thereafter, Shri P.R. Raman took any effective step to appoint the

        registered valuers for the said asset class or to place the matter before the CoC again for

        consideration. The DC notes that in terms of the provisions of the afore-mentioned regulations,

        it is the statutory duty of the resolution professional to appoint registered valuers and he cannot

        escape from his duty citing deferment of issue by a CoC member. The DC also observes that

        even after the issue of valuation was specifically raised and the necessity of valuation was

        brought to the his attention, Shri P.R. Raman did not appoint the registered valuers.



2.1.15  The DC notes the submissions of Shri P.R. Raman that the financial assets were apparently only

        book entries, that the books and supporting records were not available, that the investment in

        HLSPL was already subject to liquidation proceedings, and that there was paucity of funds for

        conducting the CIRP. The DC also notes his submission that, in the prevailing circumstances,

        obtaining valuation reports for the financial assets would not have served any meaningful

        purpose.



2.1.16  The DC notes that the aforesaid circumstances cannot absolve Shri P.R. Raman from

        compliance with the specific statutory requirement under Regulation 27(1). The obligation to

        appoint registered valuers within the prescribed period is cast upon the RP and is not made

        contingent upon the prior availability of physical possession of the assets, availability of

        complete supporting documents, availability of CIRP funds, or an assessment by the RP as to

        whether the valuation would ultimately be useful. The issues relating to the existence, nature,



                                          Page 4 of 16

        recoverability or value of the financial assets were matters which could appropriately be

        examined in the course of the valuation exercise. The absence of supporting records or Shri

        P.R. Raman’s own assessment regarding the utility of valuation cannot, be treated as a ground

        for not undertaking the statutory process.



2.1.17  The DC further observes that the CIRP framework prescribes definite timelines for various

        actions to be undertaken by the RP. The requirement of timely valuation is intended to ensure

        that the fair value and liquidation value of the Corporate Debtor are determined in a structured

        and objective manner and are available for consideration during the CIRP. In the present case,

        the appointment of valuers for the relevant asset class was not undertaken within the prescribed

        period and the issue was considered only at a much later stage. Even thereafter, no effective

        follow-up action was taken for appointment of the registered valuers.



2.1.18  In view of the foregoing, the DC finds that Shri P.R. Raman did not appoint the registered

        valuers for the asset class “Securities or Financial Assets” at any stage of the CIRP, much less

        within the period prescribed under Regulation 27(1) of the CIRP Regulations. Accordingly, the

        DC holds Shri P.R. Raman in contravention of provisions of Section 208(2)(a) and (e) of the

        Code, Regulation 27(1) of the CIRP Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP

        Regulations read with Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in the First Schedule of the

        IP Regulations.



2.2 Failure to facilitate meeting of the CoC with the Registered Valuers.



2.2.1 The proviso to Regulation 35(1) of CIRP Regulations provides that the resolution professional

        shall facilitate a meeting wherein registered valuers shall explain the methodology being

        adopted to arrive at valuation to the members of the CoC before computation of estimates.



2.2.2   It was observed that in the 5th CoC meeting held on 18.02.2025, Shri P.R. Raman informed the

        CoC members that once the Information Memorandum (IM) and valuation reports were

        circulated, a meeting with the valuers shall be scheduled for discussion. Further, the minutes of

        the 10th CoC meeting held on 04.07.2025 recorded that the valuation report was pending for

        sharing with Bank of India due to non-submission of the confidentiality undertaking by the

        creditor. Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that he had proposed a presentation by the

        registered valuers before the CoC, however no such meeting could be facilitated as the CoC

        members did not show interest. Regulation 35(1) casts a clear duty upon the RP to facilitate a

        meeting of the CoC with the registered valuers for explaining the valuation methodology prior

        to computation of estimates. The objective of this provision is to ensure that the CoC is apprised

        of the methodology adopted by valuers before valuation figures are finalised. There is no

        requirement under the Code or Regulations to obtain confidentiality undertakings for arranging

        meeting with the registered valuers for explaining the methodology adopted by the valuers for

        computing the estimates. Further, there was no material on record to indicate the efforts taken

        by Shri P.R. Raman to facilitate such a meeting even after circulation of the valuation reports.



2.2.3 In view of the above, IBBI had formed a prima facie view that Shri P.R. Raman had contravened

        the provisions of Sections 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, proviso to Regulation 35(1) of CIRP



        Page 5 of 16

       Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of IP Regulations, read with Clause 14 of the Code of

       Conduct specified in IP Regulations.



       Submissions by Shri P.R. Raman.



2.2.4  Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the valuation reports were available as early as 26.12.2024 and

       were communicated to all members of the CoC during the 3rd CoC meeting held on 27.12.2024.

       Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that the Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) format for

       obtaining the valuation reports was circulated to all CoC members by e-mail on 27.12.2024.

       However, the CoC members did not promptly execute the NDA to get the valuation reports.

       The Authorised Representative (AR) of the homebuyers submitted the NDA on 15.01.2025 and

       obtained the valuation reports on 24.04.2025, whereas Bank of India, the applicant and sole

       financial institution in the CoC, submitted its NDA only on 03.07.2025.



2.2.5 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that, at the time of their appointment, he had informed the

        registered valuers that they would be required to present their valuation methodology before

        the CoC members as and when invited. However, since the time available for completion of

        the CIRP was running out and there was a lack of enthusiasm on the part of the CoC members,

        the meeting of the valuers with the CoC could not be facilitated. He submitted that the non-

        appearance of the registered valuers before the CoC did not cause any prejudice to the

        resolution process of the CD, as both valuers were experienced professionals and had prepared

        the valuation reports with due expertise.



2.2.6 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that in the aforesaid circumstances, he made an informed decision

        not to facilitate the appearance of the registered valuers before the CoC and that such decision

        was taken in good faith and in the interest of the CIRP.



       Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.2.7 The proviso to Regulation 35(1) of the CIRP Regulations requires the Resolution Professional

        to facilitate a meeting of registered valuers with the CoC where the registered valuers would

        explain to the members of the CoC the methodology they are adopting for valuation, before the

        estimates are computed. The purpose is to give the CoC an opportunity to understand, and if

        necessary question, the valuation methodology. The fair value and the liquidation value bear

        directly on the CoC's evaluation of resolution plans and its commercial decisions, so the

        requirement is substantive. The provision uses the word "shall" and therefore it places the

        obligation squarely on the RP.



2.2.8  The DC has considered Shri P.R. Raman's submission that the meeting could not be held

       because the CoC members delayed in executing the NDA, lacked enthusiasm, and because the

       time available in the CIRP was running out. However, he did not produce any email,

       communication to the valuers or the CoC minutes showing that a date was fixed for the meeting,

       that the CoC members or the valuers were invited, or that any member declined to attend. On

       the contrary, the minutes show that Shri P.R. Raman assured the CoC at the 2nd CoC meeting

       held on 03.12.2024 and again at the 5th CoC meeting held on 18.02.2025 that the valuers would

       be called upon to present before the CoC, but no such meeting was ever held. He was, therefore,



                                         Page 6 of 16

        conscious of the requirement. As regards the NDA, a confidentiality undertaking is a condition

        for a CoC member to receive the fair value and liquidation value; it is not a pre-condition for a

        meeting in which the valuers explain the methodology to be adopted. Even if some members

        were not interested, the RP's duty to facilitate the meeting remained, since a statutory duty

        cannot be set aside by the indifferent attitude of the CoC members who are expected to be the

        beneficiary of such meeting.



2.2.9   The DC has also considered the plea that the meeting could not be held for want of time, and

        the submissions that the omission caused no prejudice and that the valuers were experienced.

        The DC notes that a mere shortage of time cannot justify dispensing with a mandatory step.

        The registered valuers were appointed on 08.10.2024. The minutes of the 2nd CoC meeting held

        on 03.12.2024 recorded that one of the two valuation reports had already been received by then,

        and Shri P.R. Raman submitted that both the reports were available by 26.12.2024. The meeting

        contemplated by the proviso was therefore required to be held between 08.10.2024 and the

        computation of the estimates. No CoC meeting was convened between the period of

        appointment of the valuers and computation of the valuation by the valuers. The opportunity

        contemplated under the proviso to Regulation 35(1) of the CIRP Regulations was lost once the

        valuation estimates were computed without first discussing the valuation methodology with the

        CoC members. Shri P.R. Raman also stated in his reply that he decided not to facilitate the

        appearance of the valuers before the CoC, which shows a conscious choice not to comply with

        a mandatory requirement under the CIRP Regulations. Good faith is no defence to the breach

        of an express regulatory obligation, and the reasons offered do not show reasonable care and

        diligence.



2.2.10  In view of the above, the DC holds that Shri P.R. Raman failed to facilitate a meeting of the

        CoC with the registered valuers before computation of the estimates of fair value and

        liquidation value, as mandated by the proviso to Regulation 35(1) of the CIRP Regulations.

        Accordingly, the DC holds Shri P.R. Raman to be in contravention of Sections 208(2)(a) and

        (e) of the Code, the proviso to Regulation 35(1) of the CIRP Regulations, and Regulation

        7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations, read with Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in

        the IP Regulations.



2.3 Failure to form opinion on avoidance transactions.



2.3.1 Regulation 35A read with Regulation 40A of CIRP Regulations provides that on or before the

        seventy-fifth day of the ICD, the RP shall form an opinion whether the CD has been subject to

        any transaction covered under Sections 43, 45, 50 or 60 of the Code and where the RP is of the

        opinion that the CD has been subjected to any transactions covered under these provisions, then

        he shall make a determination before the one hundred fifteenth day of ICD and file an

        application before AA for appropriate relief on or before the one hundred and thirtieth day of

        ICD.



2.3.2   In the present matter, the issue of conducting forensic audit and forming opinion on avoidance

        transactions was first discussed in the 10th CoC meeting held on 04.07.2025, wherein Shri P.R.

        Raman apprised the CoC that forensic audit was proposed by him in an earlier CoC meeting

        but the decision was deferred on the request of Bank of India. Shri P.R. Raman also assured the



        Page 7 of 16

       CoC that this agenda would be placed again in the forthcoming CoC meeting. However, no

       such discussion was found recorded in the minutes of the subsequent CoC meetings.



2.3.3  It was further noted from the minutes of the 2nd CoC meeting held on 03.12.2024 that while

       discussing the financial statements for the year 2023-24, Shri P.R. Raman apprised the CoC

       that diamonds worth Rs.8 crore were reflected as stock-in-hand, whereas there were no such

       diamond in possession of the CD or its erstwhile directors. The representatives of the CD could

       not offer any explanation on this issue. Instead of initiating steps to identify potential avoidance

       transactions, Shri P.R. Raman informed the CoC of his instructions to write off the said amount

       in the provisional financial statements as on the ICD, purportedly to reflect the correct picture

       to the prospective resolution applicants. Thus, Shri P.R. Raman chose to write off the amount

       without offering any cogent reasons for not examining the possibility of avoidance transactions.

       It was further noted that Shri P.R. Raman had not filed Form CIRP 6 / CIRP 8 pertaining to the

       intimation of his opinion, determination and filing of applications in respect of the avoidance

       transactions.



2.3.4 In view of the above, IBBI had formed prima facie view that Shri P.R. Raman had failed to

        form his opinion and determination on avoidance transactions needed for filing application

        before the AA for the appropriate relief. Hence, Shri P.R. Raman had prima facie contravened

        the provisions of Sections 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 35A read with Regulations

        40A and 40B of CIRP Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of IP Regulations, read with

        Clause 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in IP Regulations.



       Submissions by Shri P.R. Raman.



2.3.5 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the diamonds in question had been continuously reflected as

        trading stock in the books of account of the CD since FY 2011–12. He further submitted that,

        upon examination of the available records and discussions with the auditors, it could not be

        established that any funds of the CD were utilised for purchase of the diamonds. The diamonds

        had been procured from Israel through an agent, who raised the invoice on the CD and handed

        over the diamonds for approval by the prospective buyer, which, as submitted, was an industry

        practice. He further submitted that, in the present case, the diamonds were stated to have been

        supplied to a high-profile political leader of Tamil Nadu for approval but were neither returned

        nor paid for after the stipulated period. The erstwhile director had allegedly pursued the

        payment and had also lodged a criminal complaint in this regard. However, no further action

        could be pursued as the person named in the auditor’s report, Shri Adyar Mohan, had

        subsequently passed away.



2.3.6 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that, in view of the above circumstances, he could not form

        a conclusive opinion regarding initiation of application in respect of preferential, undervalued

        or fraudulent transactions, or for fraudulent or wrongful trading, against the erstwhile directors

        in relation to the diamonds. He submitted that the involvement of the funds of the CD in the

        purchase of the diamonds could not be established beyond doubt; no invoice had been raised

        by the CD upon any buyer in respect thereof; and a criminal complaint had already been lodged

        by the erstwhile director, which was subsequently disposed of by the police authorities. He

        further submitted that the erstwhile management had admitted that the diamonds were not



                                        Page 8 of 16

        physically available and that the details thereof had been disclosed in the explanatory notes

        forming part of the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor.



2.3.7 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that, in his considered opinion, the diamonds, which had neither

        been purchased from the funds of the CD nor physically formed part of its stock, ought not to

        have continued to be reflected as trading stock in the books. Accordingly, the same were

        permitted to be written off when the books of account were first audited during the CIRP. He

        further submitted that the existence and nature of the other bad and doubtful debts reflected

        under various heads, including non-current investments, long-term loans and advances and

        trade receivables, could not be conclusively established owing to the non-availability of

        ledgers, books and other underlying records for verification.



2.3.8 Shri P.R. Raman also submitted that a CBI investigation had already been initiated on the

        complaint of the financial creditor, Bank of India, against the erstwhile director in relation to

        the alleged diversion of funds. He submitted that, in the circumstances, initiation of separate

        applications in respect of the alleged avoidance transactions or fraudulent and wrongful trading,

        in the absence of sufficient records and evidence, would not have been productive and could

        result in duplication of proceedings in respect of the same underlying transactions.



2.3.9 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that no failure could be attributed to him for not filing

        applications in respect of avoidance transactions or fraudulent and wrongful trading, as he had

        formed a considered opinion that such applications could not be effectively pursued in the

        absence of the relevant books, ledgers and records necessary to establish the transactions. Shri

        P.R. Raman submitted that the decision was taken on the basis of his professional experience

        in dealing with avoidance transactions of various CDs and with reasonable caution and

        prudence, keeping in view the circumstances of the case and without causing prejudice to the

        ongoing CIRP.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.3.10 Regulation 35A of the CIRP Regulations requires the RP to form an opinion on avoidance

        transactions on or before the 75th day of the ICD, to make a determination before the 115th day



        if such transactions exist, and to report through Form CIRP 6 / CIRP 8 under Regulation 40B.



2.3.11 The DC notes the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that he proposed a forensic audit in an earlier

        CoC meeting, but the decision was deferred at the request of Bank of India. At the 10th CoC

        meeting on 04.07.2025, he assured the CoC that the agenda would be placed again. However,

        the DC notes that no such discussion appears in the minutes of any subsequent meeting.



2.3.12  The DC notes that the duty under Regulation 35A rests on the RP and does not depend on the

        CoC's approval for conducting a forensic audit. The CoC's deferral for appointment of

        transaction auditor did not stop Shri P.R. Raman from examining the CD's transactions on the

        records available, forming an opinion, recording it and reporting it. Even after it came to light

        that diamonds worth Rs.8 crore reflected as stock-in-hand were not in the possession of the CD

        or the directors of the suspended board, no opinion or determination was recorded in the CoC

        minutes, and no Form CIRP 8 was filed. The claim of a considered opinion appears for the first



                                          Page 9 of 16

        time in the reply to the SCN and finds no support in the contemporaneous record. The reply is

        also internally inconsistent as at one place Shri P.R. Raman stated that he could not form any

        opinion on filing applications in respect of the diamonds in view of the circumstances that no

        utilisation of the CD’s funds for their purchase could be established from the available records,

        while in the same reply at other place he claims to have formed an opinion that such

        applications would be a futile exercise in view of the CBI investigation.



2.3.13 The DC notes the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that a CBI investigation had already been

        initiated against the erstwhile director in relation to alleged diversion of funds, accordingly,

        filing a separate application would not be productive. The DC notes that the pending CBI

        investigation does not release him from his statutory duty under the Code and regulations.



2.3.14  The DC notes that in the 2nd CoC meeting held on 03.12.2024, Shri P.R. Raman informed the

        CoC that diamonds worth Rs.8 crore were shown as stock-in-hand although neither they were

        in possession of the CD nor the directors of the suspended board could explain this. The DC

        notes that Shri P.R. Raman on his own informed the CoC of his own instructions to write off

        the amount in the provisional financial statements as on the ICD. Although the minutes

        recorded that the CoC members agreed, the concurrence of the CoC does not discharge the

        RP’s independent duty under Regulation 35A to examine whether the loss of the asset arose

        from a transaction covered under the Code.



2.3.15  The DC notes that the unexplained whereabouts of diamonds worth Rs. 8 crore was a matter

        calling for examination under Sections 43, 45, 50 or 66 of the Code. A mere write-off of the

        asset from the books does not explain how it was taken out of the CD’s possession. Although

        the diamonds had been reflected in the books since FY 2011-12, the transactions under Section

        66 of the Code prescribe no look-back period, and the age of the transaction was therefore no

        ground for not examining it. The DC further notes that Shri P.R. Raman offered no cogent

        reason for not examining this possibility before writing off the asset. The closure of a police

        complaint filed by the erstwhile director also did not relieve the RP of his duty. The DC notes

        the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that the stated purpose of the write-off was to reflect the

        correct picture to prospective resolution applicants. However, the DC notes that the purpose

        was defeated by the write-off itself, since the resolution applicants and the CoC were deprived

        of any assessment of whether the loss arose from an avoidable transaction.



2.3.16  In view of the above, the DC finds that Shri P.R. Raman failed to form an opinion and

        determination on avoidance transactions within the prescribed timelines and further he

        permitted the write-off of diamonds worth Rs. 8 crore without examining possible avoidance

        transactions. Accordingly, the DC finds Shri P.R. Raman in contravention of Sections

        208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 35A read with Regulations 40A and 40B of the CIRP

        Regulations, and Regulations 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations, read with Clause 14 of the

        Code of Conduct.



        Page 10 of 16

2.4 Delay in publication of Expression of Interest (Form G).



2.4.1 Regulation 36A (1) of CIRP Regulations provides that, “The resolution professional shall

        publish brief particulars of the invitation for expression of interest in Form G of the Schedule-

        I at the earliest, not later than sixtieth day from the insolvency commencement date, from

        interested and eligible prospective resolution applicants to submit resolution plans.” Further,

        Form G is inter-alia required to be published on the website, if any, designated by the Board

        for the purpose.



2.4.2 In the present matter, the CIRP of the CD commenced on 23.08.2024. Accordingly, in terms of

        Regulation 36A (1) read with Regulation 40A of CIRP Regulations, invitation for expression

        of interest in Form G was required to be published by 22.10.2024. However, Form G was

        published only on 31.12.2024 i.e. with a delay of approximately 70 days.



2.4.3  Shri P.R. Raman submitted in his response that delay in finalization of audited financials for

       the year 2023-24 led to delay in publication of Form G and that the matter was duly informed

       to the CoC members. It was noted that in the 2nd CoC meeting held on 03.12.2024, Shri P.R.

       Raman apprised the CoC that the audited financials for the year 2023-24 had been received and

       that Form G would be published immediately after preparation of the IM. It was only in the 3rd

       CoC meeting held on 27.12.2024 that the draft Form G was placed before the CoC for its inputs.

       It was observed that publication of Form G could have been undertaken without awaiting

       completion of the information memorandum.



2.4.4 In view of the above, it was observed that there was delay of approximately 70 days in

        publication of Form G. Hence, Shri P.R. Raman had prima facie contravened the provisions of

        Sections 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 36A(1) read with Regulation 40A of CIRP

        Regulations, Regulations 7(2)(a) and (h) of IP Regulations, read with Clause 13 and 14 of the

        Code of Conduct specified in IP Regulations



       Submissions by Shri P.R. Raman.



2.4.5 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that immediately upon commencement of the CIRP, he had

        inspected the registered office of the Corporate Debtor and found the premises completely

        vacant, with no records, furniture or staff present. He further submitted that the premises had

        remained locked for considerable period and, owing to prolonged closure, the entire office was

        severely infested with termites, resulting in the destruction of files, books, ledgers and

        computer hard disks, notwithstanding the pest control measures subsequently undertaken.

        Accordingly, no records or documents were available for his inspection or for taking into

        custody. He submitted that these facts were duly reported in the report filed vide I.A. No.

        IA(IBC)/1902(CHE)/2024 in CP/IB/1208(CHE)/2018 on 11.09.2024, which was taken on

        record by the AA vide its order dated 20.09.2024.



2.4.6 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that, during the course of the CIRP, it was ascertained that

        the accounts of the CD had not been audited for the immediately preceding financial year, i.e.,

        FY 2023–24. Further, owing to the limited and selective cooperation extended by the erstwhile

        management, the Information Memorandum could not be prepared within the stipulated



                                        Page 11 of 16

        timeline, which consequently resulted in delay in publication of Form G. The Information

        Memorandum could be finalised only on the 129th day of the CIRP and Form G was thereafter

        published on the 132nd day.



2.4.7 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the delay in completion of the aforesaid CIRP requirements

        was attributable to factors beyond his control and that he should not be held responsible for

        such delays.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.4.8 The DC notes that the timeline under Regulation 36A(1) is mandatory. The DC notes that the

        CIRP of the CD commenced on 23.08.2024. In terms of Regulation 36A(1) read with

        Regulation 40A of the CIRP Regulations, Form G was required to be published at the earliest,

        and not later than the sixtieth day from the insolvency commencement date, i.e. 22.10.2024.

        The draft Form G was placed before the CoC only on 27.12.2024 and was published on

        31.12.2024. This delay of nearly 70 days was not satisfactorily explained. The Regulation 36A

        does not make the publication of Form G contingent upon finalisation of the IM.



2.4.9   The DC notes the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that no records or documents were available

        for his inspection or for taking into custody, and that these facts were reported vide I.A. No.

        IA(IBC)/1902(CHE)/2024 in CP/IB/1208(CHE)/2018 on 11.09.2024, which the AA took on

        record through the order dated 20.09.2024. The DC notes that the given factor may have

        affected the collection of information and financials. However, they do not explain the delay in

        publishing Form G. Further, the minutes of the 1st and 2nd CoC meetings do not reflect that the

        difficulties that are now pleaded before the DC, were placed before the CoC also. Further, Shri

        P.R. Raman did not approach the AA under Section 19(2) of the Code for non-cooperation by

        the suspended management.



2.4.10  The DC notes that, by failing to publish Form G within time, Shri P.R. Raman did not exercise

        the reasonable care and diligence expected of an IP, and failed to plan his actions so as to adhere

        to the time limits prescribed under the CIRP Regulations, The DC finds Shri P.R. Raman in

        contravention of Section 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 36A(1) read with

        Regulation 40A of the CIRP Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations, read

        with Clauses 13 and 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in the First Schedule to the IP

        Regulations.



2.5 Acceptance of EoI beyond last date.



2.5.1 The Regulation 36A(3) (b) of CIRP Regulations provides that Form G shall provide the last

        date for submission of expression of interest which shall not be less than fifteen days from the

        date of issue of detailed invitation for expression of interest. Regulation 36A(6) of CIRP

        Regulations provides that the expression of interest received after the time specified in the

        invitation under clause (b) of sub regulation (3) shall be rejected.



2.5.2 In the present matter, Form G dated 31.12.2024 issued by Shri P.R. Raman provided for the last

        date of submission of EoI as 15.01.2025. It was noted that Shri P.R. Raman received four EOIs,



                                          Page 12 of 16

        including one EOI jointly from Shri Anand Jain, director of the suspended board and

        shareholder of CD and three other shareholders of the CD. In the 4th CoC meeting held on

        07.02.2025, Shri P.R. Raman informed the CoC that pursuant to the objection raised by

        homebuyers as regards eligibility of Shri Anand Jain, the EoI submitted by him was withdrawn,

        and a new EoI dated 04.02.2025 was submitted jointly by the remaining three shareholders of

        the CD, viz., Ms. A. Aarthi, Ms. A. Poonam and Ms. A. Anitha, which was beyond the last date

        of submission of the EoI, i.e., 15.01.2025. It was further stated that after deliberations, the CoC

        decided to permit all four applicants who had submitted EoI to submit their resolution plans.



2.5.3 While addressing the objection raised by homebuyers on considering belated EoI, Shri P.R.

        Raman stated that belated EoI dated 04.02.2025 was treated as a substitution for the earlier EoI

        of Shri Anand Jain, submitted along with three shareholders. Regulation 36A(6) of CIRP

        Regulations clearly provides for rejection of EoI submitted after the last date. It was therefore

        incumbent on Shri P.R. Raman to draw the CoC’s attention to the statutory requirement and its

        implications before allowing acceptance of any belated submission. The CoC’s purported

        approval cannot, in itself, cure non-compliance with the mandatory requirements of IBBI

        Regulations.



2.5.4 In view of the above, it was observed that Shri P.R. Raman had prima facie contravened the

        provisions of Sections 208(2)(a) and (e) of the Code, Regulation 36A(6) of CIRP Regulations,

        Regulations 7(2)(a) and (h) of IP Regulations, read with Clauses 11, 13 and 14 of the Code of

        Conduct specified in IP Regulations.



        Submissions by Shri P.R. Raman.



2.5.5 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the EOI dated 14.01.2025 was initially submitted within the

        prescribed timeline and was subsequently resubmitted by three shareholders of the CD after

        removing the name of the director of the suspended board of the CD, Shri Anand Jain, whose

        inclusion had been objected to on the ground that he had been declared a wilful defaulter. Shri

        P.R. Raman was of the considered view that the timeline for submission of EOIs was directory

        in nature and, particularly in the absence of any prejudice or harm being caused to any

        stakeholder, the EOI could be placed before the CoC along with other EOIs for consideration

        on merits.



2.5.6 Shri P.R. Raman further submitted that by placing the said EOI before the CoC, he sought to

        provide an opportunity to the shareholders of the CD, being an MSME, in view of the special

        treatment contemplated under the Code for MSMEs. Accordingly, the EoI was placed before

        the CoC along with other EoIs with the sole objective of maximising the value of the CD, while

        leaving the final decision entirely to the commercial wisdom of the CoC.



2.5.7 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that his approach was subsequently supported by the interim order

        dated 24.06.2025 passed by the Hon’ble Madras High Court in W.P. No. 22339 of 2025 and

        W.M.P. No. 25160 of 2025, whereby the declaration of Shri Anand Jain as a wilful defaulter

        was stayed, thereby permitting his eligibility to submit a resolution plan. He further submitted

        that, following the rejection of the EOI by the CoC, when the representatives of the



                                                     Page 13 of 16

        shareholders raised the issue in a subsequent CoC meeting, he advised them to approach the

        AA for appropriate relief.



2.5.8 Shri P.R. Raman submitted that the shareholders thereafter approached the AA challenging the

        decision of the CoC to disallow their EoI on the ground of late submission. The application has

        been numbered as I.A. (IBC)/1204(CHE)/2025 in CP (IB)/1208(CHE)/2018 and is presently

        sub-judice. He further submitted that the resolution plan is already in place and under the

        approved resolution plan, the homebuyers are stated to realise 99.39% of their shelter-related

        entitlements, with completion of the plan scheduled within 15 months from the date of its

        approval by the AA.



        Analysis and Findings of the DC.



2.5.9 The Regulation 36A(3)(b) of the CIRP Regulations requires Form G to specify the last date for

        submission of EoI, which shall not be less than fifteen days from the date of issue of the detailed

        invitation. Regulation 36A(6) provides that an EoI received after the time specified in the

        invitation "shall be rejected".



2.5.10  The DC notes that in the present matter, Form G dated 31.12.2024 fixed 15.01.2025 as the last

        date for submission of EoI. Shri P.R. Raman received four EoIs, including a joint EoI from Shri

        Anand Jain, director of suspended board and shareholder of the CD, and three other

        shareholders. The DC notes that following the homebuyers' objection to the eligibility of Shri

        Anand Jain being one of the directors of the suspended board, the EoI was withdrawn, and a

        fresh EoI dated 04.02.2025 was submitted jointly by Ms. A. Aarthi, Ms. A. Poonam and Ms. A.

        Anitha, which was about 20 days after the last date of submission of EoI. Shri P.R. Raman

        placed this belated EoI before the CoC along with the other EoIs for consideration.



2.5.11  The DC notes the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that the Hon'ble Madras High Court by the

        interim order dated 24.06.2025 stayed the wilful defaulter declaration against Shri Anand Jain.

        However, the DC also observes that the EoI dated 04.02.2025 was not a mere resubmission,

        since the earlier joint EoI including Shri Anand Jain had been withdrawn and the later one was

        submitted without Shri Anand Jain, after the last date of submission of EoI. The DC notes that

        the EoI dated 04.02.2025 was, in substance, a fresh EoI received after the last date of

        submission of EoI, i.e., 15.01.2025. Further, Shri P.R. Raman himself described it at the 4th

        CoC meeting as “a new application”. The DC notes that Regulation 36A(6) provides that, ‘the

        expression of interest received after the time specified in the invitation under clause (b) of sub-

        regulation (3) shall be rejected’, and the CIRP Regulations contain no provision for

        “substitution” of an EoI after the last date. Further, Shri P.R. Raman also invoked Section 240A

        of the Code on the ground that the CD is an MSME. In this regard, the DC notes that in respect

        of MSMEs only clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A is not applicable for determining the

        eligibility of a resolution applicant and does not relax the timelines stipulated under Regulation

        36A.



2.5.12 The DC notes the submission of Shri P.R. Raman that the EoI was rejected by the CoC on

        ground of late submission. This decision of CoC for rejection of EoI was challenged by the

        resolution applicant before the AA where it is sub-judice. The DC notes that the core issue of



                                          Page 14 of 16

        examination in the instant disciplinary proceedings is the conduct of Shri P.R. Raman as to

        whether by allowing a new application after the due date, he has contravened the provisions of

        the Code and Regulations. The pendency of matter with AA regarding rejection of EoI by the

        CoC is a separate issue and has no impact on the present contravention alleged.



2.5.13  The DC notes that it was the duty of Shri P.R. Raman to draw the CoC's attention to Regulation

        36A(6) and its consequences, which Shri P.R. Raman failed to do. Further, the Hon’ble High

        Court's order dated 24.06.2025 staying the wilful defaulter declaration, was passed long after

        the last date of submission of EoI and does not address the timeline for EoIs. The pendency of

        I.A. (IBC)/1204(CHE)/2025 before the AA preferred by the shareholders of the CD challenging

        the decision of the CoC disallowing their EoI on the ground of late submission, does not bar

        the present proceedings, which concern only the conduct of Shri P.R. Raman as RP. The

        subsequent approval of a resolution plan by the CoC also does not cure the non-compliance.

        Therefore, the submissions of Shri P.R. Raman are not tenable.



2.5.14  Accordingly, the DC holds that Shri P.R. Raman treated a belated EoI as a “substitution” and

        placed it before the CoC without apprising the CoC of the statutory requirement under

        Regulation 36A(6) and thereby did not exercise the reasonable care and diligence expected of

        an IP. In view of the above, the DC finds Shri P.R. Raman in contravention of Sections 208(2)(a)

        and (e) of the Code, Regulation 36A(6) of the CIRP Regulations, Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of

        the IP Regulations, read with Clauses 11, 13 and 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in the

        First Schedule to the IP Regulations.



3. Order.



3.1. In view of the findings recorded in the foregoing paragraphs 2.1 to 2.5, the DC holds that Shri

        P.R. Raman, as the RP of the CD: (i) did not appoint registered valuers for the asset class

        “Securities or Financial Assets” at any stage of the CIRP, even though the financial statements

        of the CD reflected such assets and the homebuyers had sought its valuation; (ii) did not

        facilitate a meeting in which the registered valuers were required to explain the valuation

        methodology to the CoC before computation of the estimates; (iii) did not form an opinion or

        make a determination on avoidance transactions within the prescribed timelines, did not file

        Form CIRP 8, and directed the write-off of diamonds worth about Rs.8 crore without examining

        whether their loss arose from an alleged fraudulent transaction covered under the Code; (iv)

        published Form G on 31.12.2024 against the due date of 22.10.2024, i.e. with a delay of about

        70 days; and (v) treated an EoI received on 04.02.2025, after the last date of 15.01.2025, as a

        “substitution” and placed it before the CoC without apprising the CoC of the requirement of

        Regulation 36A(6). Shri P.R. Raman has therefore contravened Section 208(2)(a) and (e) of

        the Code; Regulation 27(1), the proviso to Regulation 35(1), Regulation 35A read with

        Regulations 40A and 40B, Regulation 36A(1) read with Regulation 40A, and Regulation

        36A(6) of the CIRP Regulations; and Regulation 7(2)(a) and (h) of the IP Regulations read

        with Clauses 11, 13 and 14 of the Code of Conduct specified in the First Schedule to the IP

        Regulations.



3.2. Accordingly, the DC in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 220 of the Code read

        with Regulation 13 of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017 hereby



        Page 15 of 16

        suspends the registration of Shri Pathukasahasram Raghunathan Raman for a period of two

        years. Further, in terms of Section 206 of the Code, Shri Pathukasahasram Raghunathan Raman

        shall not be eligible to continue his existing assignments.



3.3. This Order shall come into force on expiry of 30 days from the date of its issue.



3.4. A copy of this order shall be sent to the CoC of all the corporate debtors in which Shri P.R.

        Raman is providing his services. The CoC of the respective corporate debtors shall replace Shri

        P.R. Raman with another Resolution Professional/Liquidator.



3.5. A copy of this order shall be forwarded to ICSI Institute of Insolvency Professionals where

        Shri Pathukasahasram Raghunathan Raman is enrolled as a member.



3.6. A copy of this order shall also be forwarded to the Registrar of the Principal Bench of the

        National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, for information.



3.7. Accordingly, the show cause notice is disposed of.
```

- **local text file name:** PIB-2336151.txt

```text
Ministry of Electronics & IT

 Consent Manager Registration Framework Comes into Effect; MeitY Secretary Launches Online Registration Portal

Eligible Indian Companies Can Now Apply For Registration As Consent Managers Through dpbi.gov.in; Minimum Net Worth 
Requirement Set At ₹2 Crore

 Posted On:
 14 NOV 2026 12:41PM by PIB Delhi

 The registration framework for Consent Managers under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, came into effect on 13 November 2026. As part of this phase of implementation, Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), launched the online portal https://dpbi.gov.in to enable eligible companies to apply for registration as Consent Managers.

The framework marks an important step towards operationalising a system that enables Data Principals to exercise greater control over consent relating to their personal data. It forms part of the phased implementation of the DPDP framework and enables eligible entities to seek registration and prepare to offer consent management services.

Role and Accountability of Consent Managers

A Consent Manager is an entity registered with the Data Protection Board of India (Board) that enables Data Principals to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform. The framework seeks to strengthen trust and accountability in the digital ecosystem, with Consent Managers being accountable to the Data Principals.

Eligibility and Registration Process

Companies incorporated in India with adequate technical, operational and financial capacity, including a net worth of not less than ₹2 crore, may seek registration as Consent Managers. These requirements are intended to ensure that registered entities have the resources and capabilities to provide secure, reliable and accountable services.

Eligible companies may apply to the Board for registration through the newly launched portal. The Board will assess applications against the applicable requirements and may register qualifying companies. The list of registered Consent Managers will be made publicly available on the Board’s website.

Other key provisions concerning the rights of Data Principals, the obligations of Data Fiduciaries, and the Board’s inquiry and penalty processes are scheduled to come into effect on 13 May 2027.

Further information on the DPDP Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025 is available on the Ministry’s website at https://www.meity.gov.in/. For related queries, the email address secretary[at]dpbi[dot]gov[dot]in may be contacted.

For more details on the Consent Manager Registration Framework, click here.

****

Vinod Kumar / Kanishk Sharma

 (Release ID: 2336151)
 Visitor Counter : 5111
```

```text
National Stock Exchange of India Limited



Circular



Department: SURVEILLANCE                           Date: November 25, 2026

Download Ref No: NSE/SURV/ 77600

Circular Ref. No: 903/2026



To All NSE Members



Sub: Reversal Trade Cancellation Mechanism (RTCM)



This is with reference to NSE circular no. NSE/SURV/62493 dated June 18, 2024 regarding Reversal Trade

Cancellation Mechanism (RTCM).



Trading members are requested to make a note of methodology of shortlisting the symbols for which the

RTCM shall be made applicable.



RTCM will be applicable for the series (i.e. EQ, BE, BZ, SM, ST & SZ) pertaining to the symbols in the file

provided “CM_RTCM_dec2026.csv”. The symbols list on which RTCM shall be applicable will be excluding

of the following securities



    1. Approved securities list published by NSE Clearing Ltd

    2. Constituents of Nifty 500 index

    3. ETF’s



Members may note that the file “CM_RTCM_dec2026.csv” containing the list of symbols (based on the

aforesaid methodology) on which RTCM shall be applicable for the month of December 2026, has been

made available on the extranet path: /common/Surveillance/RTCM.



Please note that RTCM is a facility provided by Exchange (NSE/SURV/62493 dated June 18, 2024) to help

prevent incidence of reversal trades between two PANs if certain thresholds are breached. However, the

facility of RTCM does not absolve the Trading Members of their obligation to adhere to the provisions of

circular NSE/INVG/46662 dated December 16, 2020.



In case of any further queries, members might write to us on surveillance@nse.co.in.

National Stock Exchange of India Limited



 For National Stock Exchange of India Limited

 Mayank Rathod

 Chief Manager
```

```text
National Stock Exchange of India Limited                        Date: November 25, 2026



Circular



 Department: Member Compliance

 Download Ref No: NSE/COMP/77602

 Circular Ref. No: 103/2026



To All Members,



Sub: Submission of Action taken report (ATR) for observations reported during

inspection of Authorised Persons



This has a reference to Exchange circular ref. no. NSE/INSP/70751 dated October 10, 2025,

and Exchange circular ref. no. NSE/COMP/75878 dated August 21, 2026, regarding the

indicative disciplinary actions to be applied by trading members against their Authorised

Persons (APs) in case of non-compliance identified during AP inspections and requirement of

submission of ATR along with status of closure of observation to Exchange.



Members are hereby informed that the functionality is provided on ENIT (Electronic NSE

Interface for Trading Members) portal for reporting of ATR for observations reported during

inspection of Authorised Persons.



Members are advised to submit ATR for observations reported during inspection of Authorised

Persons to Exchange. Timelines for submission of ATR are mentioned below:



Inspections undertaken during the FY   Due date for submission  Due date for

                                       of AP inspection report  submission of ATR

Inspections done during the Quarter-1

(April-June)                                     July 31st         September 30th

Inspections done during the Quarter-2

(July-September)                               October 31st        December 31st

Inspections done during the Quarter-3

(October-December)                             January 31st           March 31st

Inspections done during the Quarter-4

(January-March)                                 April 30th             June 30th



Accordingly, ATR along with status of closure of observation reported during AP inspections

for quarter ended September 30, 2026, shall be submitted by December 31, 2026, and onwards

as per above timelines.



Details for accessing the ENIT portal and reporting of ATR are enclosed as under:



Annexure A: The user manual for submission of AP inspection report and ATR

Annexure B: List of validations applicable for uploading ATR file on ENIT



Inspections of APs undertaken during each quarter shall be reported within one month from

end of the said quarter. In case no inspection is undertaken during a particular quarter, the

Members may submit a "NIL" declaration for that quarter through the ENIT portal. All reports

shall be submitted through the online system in ENIT.

All Members are advised to take note of the same and ensure compliance.



For any support, please reach out to the helpdesk on 1800 266 0050 (Select IVR option 3) or

email at memcompliance_support@nse.co.in.



For and on behalf of

National Stock Exchange of India Limited



Swati Sopare

Chief Manager

Annexure A: The user manual for submission of AP inspection report and ATR



                         User manual

                              For



        Submission of AP Inspection Report and

                    Action Taken Report



Disclaimer:



“This document/user manual summarizes the queries relating to the above topic in a concise manner for the

Member’s ease of understanding. The information and/ or content (collectively ‘Information’) provided herein

is general information only and NSE has issued detailed circulars to that effect from time to time, as referred

herein. While reasonable care has been exercised to ensure that the Information is adequate and reliable, no

representation is made by NSE as to its accuracy or completeness and NSE, its affiliates and subsidiaries accept

no liability of whatsoever nature for any direct or consequential loss, including without limitation any loss of

profits, arising from reliance on this Information. The readers are expected to undertake their own diligence and

are advised not to solely rely on this document. Any such reliance shall be at the reader’s own risk. Nothing

stated herein shall bind NSE, in any manner whatsoever

Summary

Part 1: Steps for submission of Authorized Person Inspection Report

Part 2: General Guidelines for submission of AP Inspection Action Taken Report (ATR)

Part 3: Steps for submission of ATR

Part 1- Steps for Authorized Person Inspection Report Submission

Step 1: Log In to the ENIT Member Portal

Log in to the ENIT Member Portal using valid member credentials.

Step 2: Navigate to the AP Inspection Page

From the main menu, follow this navigation path:

ENIT → Compliance → Authorized Person → Applications → Inspection of Authorized

Person New

Step 3: Download and Fill File Template



    1. Download the file template provided ENIT portal as shown in below screenshot.

    2. Save file with the name “AUTH_PERSON_INSP_ (Member Code)” to local drive.



         Do not change file format or add or delete any column.

    3. Fill data in all relevant fields in the downloaded template.

Step 4: Upload of file on ENIT portal

     1. On ENIT at path ENIT → Compliance → Authorized Person → Applications →



         Inspection of Authorized Person New select the relevant quarter for the AP

         Inspection from the drop-down menu.



     2. Upload the file in the format prescribed.

     3. File will be validated at the time of uploading on ENIT portal.

     4. In case of any Error, message will be displayed as “Error file generated – Check



        comments and rectify”. Error file can be downloaded at path ENIT → Compliance →

        Authorized Person → Applications → Inspection of Authorized Person New



                                                                                                                          .

Sample Error file:



     5. Refer General guidelines and Validation sheet to resolve errors mentioned in Error file.

     6. All Errors shall be resolved before uploading file again on ENIT portal.

     7. On Successful validation, message will be displayed as “File uploaded successfully –



        the file has been accepted”



Part 2: General Guidelines for submission of AP Inspection Action Taken Report (ATR)

1. Submission of ATR is mandatory for the members if any “Not Complied” reported in any



   of the criterion during quarterly AP Inspection reporting.

   (Please note that template will be available only if there is any non-compliance reported in

   respective quarter for any of the Authorised Person inspection reporting)

2. Member shall review non compliances reported/observed during AP inspection and shall

   take necessary action against AP within reasonable time. Also, member shall ensure that non

   compliances are rectified/ complied before submission of ATR to Exchange i.e. within 60

   days of the due date for submission of AP inspection report with the status of compliance.

3. The ATR template will be made available for download at ENIT portal in the following

   path: ENIT → Compliance → Authorized Person → Applications → Action on Non-

   Compliance in AP Inspection Report

4. Below details shall be provided in the downloaded template.

   • Type of Action Taken as prescribed under Exchange circular Ref No: NSE/INSP/70751



       dated October 10, 2025

   • If type of action selected as Others, then please specify

   • If action taken by member is not in line with action prescribed in Exchange circular Ref



       No: NSE/INSP/ 70751, then specify reason

• Date of Action Taken (DD-MM-YYYY)

• Compliance status of the non-compliance observed



5. Under the column “Type of Action Taken” in ATR Template, select indicative actions as

   prescribed in circular NSE/INSP/70751 dated October 10, 2025, from the dropdowns

   available for each criterion where non-compliance was marked against the AP in AP

   Inspection Reporting for the quarter.



These actions may include, but are not limited to:



Violation           Indicative Action

Category

           Termination on Disciplinary grounds, informing all clients of the AP, withhold

    A      money due to the AP, and public notification. (for violations mentioned in point

           no. 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 of Annexure A of the circular NSE/INSP/70751 dated

    B      October 10, 2025, it is mandatory to file police complaint for termination of

    C      AP on disciplinary grounds).

           Issuance of a warning Letter, with instruction to avoid repeat violations, with

           termination on disciplinary grounds in case of repeated offenses.

           Issuance of an Advisory Letter, with instruction to avoid repeat violations. In

           case of repeat violation, warning letter to be issued.



 6. If “Others” is selected in the “Type of Action” column, it is mandatory to provide the required

     details in the column “If type of action selected as Others, then please specify”.



 7. If the action is not in line with the prescribed Indicative action in the above table, it is

     mandatory to provide the reason under the column, “If action taken by member is not in line

     with action prescribed in Exchange circular Ref No: NSE/INSP/ 70751, then specify reason”



 8. Date of Action Taken should be captured in the DD-MM-YYYY format.

 9. All observations shall be acted upon and complied before submission of ATR to Exchange.



     In the exceptional cases where compliance status is not closed/completed, member shall

     report ATR with Type of action “In Progress” and compliance status as “open” within due

     date for submission of ATR.

10. ATR submission window will be available till due date for submission of ATR. In case of

     any discrepancy in ATR submitted to Exchange, same can be rectify by resubmission of

     entire file again. The ATR submitted for respective quarter will be overwritten with the latest

     submission. The option of resubmission of ATR will be available only till the due date of

     filing of ATR.

Part 3-Steps for Submission of ATR



Step 1: Navigate to the ATR submission page



Log in to the ENIT Member Portal and follow this navigation path:



ENIT → Compliance → Authorized Person → Applications → Action on Non-Compliance

in AP Inspection Report



STEP 2 Download ATR Template

    1. Select the relevant quarter for the AP Inspection from the drop-down menu.

    2. Download the file template from the page.

         (Please note that template will be available only if there is any non-compliance

         reported in respective quarter for any of the Authorised Person inspection reporting)



Step: 3 Fill in the details of action taken and status of closure of non-Compliance in the

template and upload on ENIT

The required information should be provided in file downloaded from ENIT and should be

uploaded back on the ENIT at Path: Compliance -> Authorized Person -> Applications ->

Action on Non-Compliance in AP Inspection Report

Step 4: Verify Upload Status

After uploading, one of the following messages will appear:

• For Successful submission: “File Uploaded Successfully – The file has been accepted”.



   Or

• On identification of Error: “Error File Generated – Check Comments and Rectify”. The



   file contains errors that must be corrected.

Message on successful submission



Message on identification of Error:



Error Excel file:



STEP 5: Rectify and Re-upload (If Errors Occur)

If an error message is displayed, follow these steps to resolve the issue:



    1. Click the OK button and download the error file that is generated.

    2. Open the error file and review the comments to identify the issues.

    3. Refer general guidelines and validation sheet available on the page to assist in



         correcting the data.

    4. After rectifying all errors, re-upload the corrected file.

Step 6: Downloading of report for submission on Action on Non-Compliance in AP

Inspection



Once the ATR submitted to Exchange, report will be available on ENIT. Find below the steps

to download.



    1. From the main menu, follow this navigation path:

         ENIT → Compliance → Authorized Person → Applications → Action on Non-

         Compliance in AP Inspection MIS



    2. Select the relevant quarter for the AP Inspection from the drop-down menu.

    3. Download the file from the page.
```

```text
NSE Clearing Limited              Date: November 25, 2026



  Department: COMPLIANCE

 Download Ref No: NCL/CMPL/77605

 Circular Ref. No: 38/2026



All Members



Sub: Reminder for Submission of Half Yearly Networth Certificate as on September 30, 2026.



This has reference to our circular ref no. NCL/CMPL/76751 issued on October 06, 2026 Submission of

Half Yearly Networth Certificate as on September 30, 2026.



In view of the above, members are hereby advised to submit the Half Yearly Networth Certificate as

on September 30, 2026 as per prescribed formats on or before November 30, 2026.



Members may note that as per Chapter X of the SEBI (Stockbrokers) Regulations, 2026, Net worth

requirement for members shall be Base Net worth or Variable Net worth, whichever is higher.

Members are further advised to refer to NCL Circular ref no. NCL/CMPL/55460 dated February 01,

2023 and NCL/CMPL/72712 dated February 09, 2026 for clarification on ascertaining Net worth as

per SEBI Gazette Notification No. SEBI/LAD- NRO/GN/2022/73 dated February 23, 2022.



It is reiterated that as per SEBI PR No.58/2026 dated September 17, 2026 and NCL circular no.

NCL/CMPL/76430 dated September 18, 2026 regarding “Samuhik Prativedan Manch- A Technology

based sharing mechanism of common submissions extended to Members of Clearing Corporations”,

Clearing/Self Clearing Members of the Clearing Corporation who are also registered with NSE will be

required to submit their Half Yearly Net worth Certificate to NSE only. NSE in turn will share the Half

Yearly Net worth Certificate (including data/documents) of the Common Clearing/Self Clearing

Members with the Clearing Corporation(s).



Submitting data to NSE alone will be treated as submission to the Clearing Corporation and the same

will be in compliance of the regulatory requirements for such Members.



It may further be noted that, Clearing/Self Clearing Members of NCL who are not registered with NSE

for submissions and Professional Clearing members registered with NCL are required to make

submissions directly to NCL through the NCL portal at link

(https://ims.connect2nsccl.com/NCLMemberPortal/).



                                  Confidential

submit a revised Net worth certificate along with the original Net worth certificate as on September

April 30, 2026, administrative circular ref no. NCL/CMPL/67927 dated May 8, 2025 and

NCL/CMPL/70806 dated October 14, 2025.
```

```text
trading issued by Exchange’ – Tech-savvy Retail Investors



This has reference to SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/0000013 dated

February 04, 2025, BSE Notice No. 20250723-41 dated July 23, 2025, and SEBI circular No.

SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/132 dated September 30, 2025, related to ‘Safer

participation of Retail investors in Algorithmic trading issued by the Exchange’. The Retail Algo

framework was implemented with effect from April 01, 2026.



As per Exchange Notice No. 20250723-41 dated July 23, 2025 (Annexure A, Para 14), it is

mandated that "all the strategies shall be run on the brokers servers. The order messages shall

be originated from brokers server." This requirement is central to ensuring the broker's control

over risk management and data confidentiality. However, Tech Savvy client is required to host the

Algo using a static IP at their end where Algo logic resides instead of hosting the Algo on Trading

Member’s cloud server.”



Post April 01, 2026, i.e. the commencement of Retail Algo framework, Exchanges have been

receiving complaints from market participants regarding the misuse of Static IP facilities by

certain Exchange empaneled Algo Providers. The Exchange has also noted that some Algo

Providers are providing Static IPs to retail clients, under the guise of them being ‘Tech-savvy’ retail

clients, which is in violation with SEBI/Exchange guidelines issued for Safer participation of Retail

investors in Algorithmic trading.



Accordingly, the Exchange hereby informs all market participants that:

    1. The Static IP is intended only for ‘Tech-savvy Retail Investors’ who develop their own algos

         using programming knowledge (As per SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-

         PoD/P/CIR/2025/0000013 dated February 04, 2025)

    2. Trading Members and Algo Providers must not, under any circumstances, provide Static

         IP access to retail clients who do not fall under the category of ‘Tech-savvy Retail

         Investors’ for Algorithmic Trading. Any such case of misclassification or misuse of ‘Static

         IPs’ will be treated as a violation of SEBI and Exchange guidelines.

    3. Trading Members who are registering such “Tech Savvy Client” shall take an undertaking

         from such clients that “such clients meet the requirements of the SEBI definition of ‘Tech-

         savvy’ Retail clients i.e. they are Retail clients who develop their own algos using

         programming knowledge.”

    4. The undertaking shall further state that “As a “Tech Savvy Client” since we are developing

         our own algos using programming knowledge, we shall have no recourse to the Investor

         Grievance mechanism of the Exchange in the event of losses incurred on account of the

         logic of ALGO used.”

The Exchanges will closely monitor compliance of Trading Members and Algo Providers with the

above guidelines and in the event of any violations shall take following actions:



• Non-Adherence on part of Trading Members - Initiate following penal action on the Trading

    Member (s) concerned.



Details of Contravention         Action in case of first  Action in case of repeat

                                 instance                 instance

Undertaking not obtained by      Rs. 5,000/- per client,  2nd time - 50% escalation

Trading Member for ‘Tech-        subject to maximum       3rd Time & Onwards-

savvy Retail Client’ in case of  penalty of Rs. 1 lakh    100% Escalation

Retail Algo



• Non-Adherence on the part of Algo Providers - The empanelment status of the Algo

    Provider shall be subject to review and may be suspended or revoked.



All concerned Algo Providers and Trading Members are advised to ensure strict adherence to the

above guidelines and take necessary corrective actions immediately, wherever applicable.



This circular shall be applicable with immediate effect.



For and on behalf of BSE Ltd.



Vandana Vania                                             Sandhya Sapaliga

Assistant Vice President                                  Manager

Enforcement                                               Enforcement


```
