Per: Justice N. Seshasayee, Member (Judicial)

       These instant Company appeals have been filed by Mr. Debashis Bose



and Ms. Pragya Jhunjhunwala, both of who are the suspended directors



of the corporate debtor, M/s. India Power Corporation Limited



(hereinafter would be referred to as IPCL). IPCL has provided corporate



guarantee for the financial facilities availed by M/s. Meenakshi Energy



Ltd., the principal borrower herein MEL), and it challenges the Order of



the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT), Hyderabad, dated 15.05.2026 in



                                              3

       CP/IB/205/2021, admitting IPCL to CIRP under Sec.7 IBC in a petition

       which the first respondent SBI had instituted.



1.2 This is the second innings this case is undergoing. Earlier, when the

       matter was before the Adjudicating Authority, and the pleadings were

       required to be completed, SBI had filed its rejoinder belatedly, and it filed

       I.A.1547 of 2022 to take its rejoinder on record. The Adjudicating

       Authority allowed it partially and had held that while it would take the

       rejoinder on record, it still would not consider it. This was challenged

       both by SBI and IPCL before this tribunal in Company Appeal (Ins) 87 of

       2023 and (Ins) 69 of 2023 and vide its Order dated 04.10.2023 both were

       dismissed. SBI chose to challenge the judgement in Civil Appeal No. 8178

       of 2023 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. In the meantime, the

       Adjudicating Authority dismissed the very company petition filed under

       Sec.7 IBC, vide its Order dated 30.10.2023, on the ground that the debt

       claimed is not payable since the deed of corporate guarantee is void

       under Sec.23 of the Contract Act,1872. This order was challenged by

       the SBI in Company Appeal (Ins) 53 of 2024. While it was pending, the

       C.A.8178 of 2023 came up before the Hon’ble Supreme Court, and vide

       its judgment dated 14.02.2025 it was disposed of the same as below:



               “13. As we have set aside the order passed by the NCLAT, the

               matter should now go back to the NCLT for fresh consideration of

               Section 7 application.

               14. In this regard, the NCLAT shall pass appropriate order in the

               pending appeal filed by the State Bank of India keeping in mind

               our observations in this order.

               15. However, we clarify that we have otherwise not expressed

               any opinion on the merits of the case.



                                                                                                                          4

               16. The Section 7 application of the bank shall now be decided

               by the NCLT afresh strictly in accordance with law on its own

               merits.”

       In view of the same, this tribunal vide its Order dated 24.02.2025, closed

       the Company Appeal (Ins) 53 of 2024 filed against the Order dismissing

       the petition under Sec.7 IBC. Thereafter, the Adjudicating Authority

       heard the matter de novo, and this time, it chose to allow the petition

       and initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor. It is this Order which

       is now in challenge before us.



1.3 The quintessential point raised by IPCL is as to the validity of the deed of

       corporate guarantee. While it carried conviction with the Adjudicating

       Authority in the first instance, post remand, it took the opposite view.



2. A brief narration of material facts that provide the context for this appeal

       is provided as below:



       a) IPCL is an electricity distribution licensee in the State of West Bengal

          since 1920s and is engaged in its business for over a century. It is now

          governed by the Electricity Act, 2003, and the Regulations framed by

          the West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission (Licensing and

          conditions of License) Regulations, 2013 (hereinafter referred to as

          WBERC).



       b) Be that as it may, a certain Meenakshi Energy Private Limited (MEL),

          came to be promoted by M/s Engie Global Developments B.V (Engie)

          a Dutch subsidiary of a French company, and incorporated for

          engaging in the business of thermal electricity generation. It was

          proposed to be done in two phases.



                                                                                                                          5

c) For financing Phase I, comprising 270MW power project, on

   10.07.2009, MEL executed a Common Loan Agreement with a

   consortium of lenders (hereinafter referred as Phase I CLA) with the

   consortium led by State Bank of India (SBI). Subsequently, on

   01.10.2010, MEL executed a Common Loan Agreement for financing

   Phase II, comprising a 700 MW thermal power project (henceforth

   would be referred to as Phase II CLA) with the consortium led by Rural

   Electrification Corporation Limited (REC). Both these loan agreements

   underwent certain amendments which are not very germane to this

   appeal.



d) While things stood thus, IPCL opted to takeover MEL, and on

   25.02.2016, IPCL and Engie entered into a share purchase agreement

   for the transfer of Engie’s 95.07% shareholding in MEL to IPCL, while

   simultaneously agreeing to infuse approximately USD 300 million into

   MEL.



e) It appears on 18.05.2016, SBI, the lead bank of the consortium gave

   its approval to the proposed transfer of shares of MEL to IPCL, but

   added a rider that IPCL must offer corporate guarantee to the

   outstanding loans of MEL. (This correspondence is not on record, but

   it is referred to in some other correspondence placed before us. It,

   however, is not very material for the disposal of this appeal.)



f) On 29.07.2016, IPCL addressed a letter to REC recording the in-

   principal approval for the share transfer by SBI vide letter dated

   18.05.2016, and its agreement to pledge 100% of its shareholding in

   MEL, but raised its objections/concerns vis-à-vis a condition

   stipulated by the lenders requiring IPCL to provide corporate

                                                                                                                  6

   guarantee. IPCL’s principal ground of objection has been that in terms

   of Regulation 5.13.2 of the West Bengal Electricity Regulation

   Commission (Licensing & Distribution) Regulations (hence forth

   WBERC Regulations or just Regulations) no corporate guarantee could

   be given.

g) Thereafter, between 08.09.2016 and 13.09.2016 and also on

   19.09.2016 legal opinions were obtained by the lenders on the

   applicability of Regulation 5.13.2 of the WBERC Regulations which in

   essence is to the effect that there would be no bar for IPCL to provide

   corporate guarantee with its non-regulated assets.

h) Based on these legal opinions, on 14.09.2016, IPCL addressed a letter

   to REC in which it stated that no specific WBERC approval was

   required for providing a corporate guarantee in respect of its non-

   regulated assets and the surplus funds generated from the regulated

   asset. On 22.09.2016, REC confirmed it.

i) Against this backdrop, on 23.09.2016, IPCL executed two documents

   in favour of SBICAP Trustee Company Limited for the benefit of the

   lenders: (i) an Unattested Share Pledge Agreement pledging 100% of

   its shareholding in MEL and (ii) a deed of Corporate Guarantee

   restricting recourse to its Non-Regulated Assets and Surplus Amounts

   under Clauses 2.1, 2.2 and 2.7 of the said deed. Also, on the same

   day, IPCL executed deed of undertaking and indemnity in favour of

   REC. It is to be underscored here that this Corporate Guarantee was

   executed without obtaining the permission of WBERC. Besides, Mr.

   Asok Kumar Goswami, a Director of IPCL, had also executed an

   affidavit dated 23.09.2016, stating that IPCL was not required to



                                                                                                                  7

   obtain the prior consent of WBERC for issuing the Corporate

   Guarantee in accordance with its terms.

j) Subsequently, on 17.08.2017, IPCL filed an application before WBERC

   in Case No. OA-260/17-18, seeking, inter alia, approval for issuing

   Corporate Guarantees in favour of lenders for businesses acquired or

   proposed to be acquired. This is the first of the three applications made

   to the WBERC. On 09.11.2017, WBERC rejected this application to

   WBERC, holding that the enforcement of the Corporate Guarantee

   could adversely affect the interests of the consumers within its

   licensed area and, therefore, disallowed IPCL from issuing Corporate

   Guarantees to funding agencies or any other agencies. What however,

   is significant is that IPCL had not disclosed about the execution of the

   deed of guarantee which it had earlier executed.

k) On 22.11.2017, IPCL addressed letters to REC and SBI informing them

   of the First WBERC Order, dated 09.11.2017, and asserting that the

   Corporate Guarantee was non-est, unenforceable and incapable of

   being given effect to. But REC stood its ground, and on 01.12.2017,

   REC, in response to IPCL’s letter dated 22.11.2017, asserted that

   WBERC’s consent was not required since the Corporate Guarantee

   was restricted to IPCL’s Non-Regulated Assets and Surplus Amounts,

   and maintained that the Corporate Guarantee remained valid,

   subsisting and enforceable. But vide its correspondence dated

   13.12.2017, IPCL maintained that it had executed the Corporate

   Guarantee relying on REC’s assurances and legal opinions obtained

   by the lenders and that the Guarantee had been structured in

   accordance with the legal advice shared by the lenders. REC was



                                                                                                                  8

    unflinching in its reaction when it vide its response dated 11.01.2018,

    REC insisted that the First WBERC Order had not invalidated the

    Corporate Guarantee and alleged that IPCL had induced the lenders

    to extend financial assistance by representing that the guarantees

    were valid and enforceable.

l) IPCL and MEL would now institute Commercial O.S. 266 of 2017

    before the Commercial Court, Hyderabad, seeking a declaration that

    the deed of guarantee that it had executed on 23.09.2016 is illegal,

    arbitrary and void.

m) In the meantime, on 28.10.2017, MEL’s loan account was classified as

    NPA due to its default in repaying the debt. On 20.12.2017, SBICAP

    Trustee Company Limited issued the First Demand Certificate,

    demanding approximately ₹93.57 Crores from IPCL and invoking the

    pledge over 100% of IPCL’s shareholding in MEL. On 02.05.2018, the

    pledged shares were transferred to SBICAP Trustee Company Limited

    as the beneficial owner.

n) In these circumstances, on 15.05.2018, IPCL filed its second

    application before WBERC in Case No. OA-274/18-19, seeking

    approval for issuing Corporate Guarantees to lenders specifically in

    relation to MEL (Second WBERC Application). And as in the first

    instance, for yet another time IPCL did not choose to disclose the

    execution of deed of guarantee. On 07.08.2018, WBERC rejected

    IPCL’s Second WBERC Application yet again, holding that its financial

    position did not permit it to extend a Corporate Guarantee for MEL’s

    project outside its licensed area, and it would create a charge over

    assets dedicated to supplying electricity to consumers in West Bengal.



                                                                                                                   9

o) While things stood thus, on 02.04.2019, IPCL withdrew the

   Commercial O.S. 266 of 2017 (referred above), but without liberty to

   file a fresh suit.



p) On 03.07.2019, SBI initiated recovery proceedings against MEL and

   IPCL before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, Hyderabad, in OA No.

   444/2020. And on 07.11.2019, vide an Order of the Adjudicating

   Authority in CP (IB)/184/7/HDB/2019, CIRP was initiated against

   MEL.



q) Undeterred by two successive rejections of its applications for

   permission by the WBERC under Regulation 5.13.2, on 26.10.2021,

   IPCL filed its third application No. OA-382/21-22, under Regulation

   5.15.1 before the Regulatory Commission Case seeking a

   determination as to whether prior approval under Regulation 5.13.2 of

   the WBERC Regulations was mandatory before issuance of the

   Corporate Guarantee (Third WBERC Application). On 22.12.2021,

   WBERC passed an order determining that its prior consent under

   Regulation 5.13.2 of the WBERC Regulations was mandatory before

   execution of the Corporate Guarantee and issued a show-cause notice

   to IPCL as to why action under Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003,

   should not be initiated against it (Third WBERC Order).



r) On 07.02.2020, SBICAP Trustee Company Limited issued the Second

   Demand Certificate, demanding approximately ₹.967.21 Crores from

   IPCL, purportedly outstanding as on 31.01.2020. On 26.02.2020, SBI

   filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC against IPCL before the

   Adjudicating Authority. It appears that recovery proceedings that it

   had initiated against IPCL before the DRT was not placed before the

                                                                                                                 10

          Adjudicating Authority. IPCL filed its Counter/objection and its

          fundamental defence was that the deed of corporate guarantee was

          executed not of its own volition but on the legal opinion which the

          lenders have provided and inasmuch as the said guarantee-deed

          contravenes Regulation 5.13.2 of the WBERC Regulations, it is not

          enforceable. SBI had filed its Rejoinder dated 13.06.2022, and what

          had happened thereafter have been captured in paragraph 1.2 above.

       s) After re-hearing the matter a second time, on 15.05.2026, the

          Adjudicating Authority admitted SBI’s Section 7 application against

          IPCL, commencing CIRP against it.

       t) The next fact to be stated is that on 03.01.2022, IPCL instituted a

          Money Suit No.1 of 2022 before the Commercial Court, Alipore where

          in it sought an interim injunction against the lenders from exercising

          the rights of recovery of debts from it. While an ex parte order of

          injunction was initially granted by the trial court, it came to be vacated

          later. And, on 16.05.2023 this was confirmed by the Calcutta High

          Court in F.M.A. No. 1370 of 2022. This money suit is pending.

       u) The last of the relevant fact is that on 10.08.2023, the Adjudicating

          Authority had approved the Resolution Plan submitted for MEL in IA

          156 of 2023 in C.P.(IB)184 of 2019.



3. The line of reasoning of the Adjudicating Authority in admitting IPCL to

       CIRP is that:



          a) The Corporate Guarantee was consciously executed by IPCL as part

              of the commercial arrangement and the same cannot be



                                                                                                                        11

   subsequently avoided because the transaction resulted in financial

   liability.

b) the absence of prior approval under Regulation 5.13.2 of the

   WBERC Regulations by itself will not render the Corporate

   Guarantee void or unenforceable under Section 23 of the Indian

   Contract Act, 1872 since neither the provisions of the Electricity Act

   nor the WBERC Regulation has expressly or impliedly render the

   deed guarantee as void merely because it was executed without the

   prior approval of WBERC. Also, such non regulatory compliances do

   not render the whole contract void.

c) IPCL had earlier challenged the validity of the Corporate Guarantee

   in Commercial O.S No. 266 of 2017, which was withdrawn without

   liberty to institute fresh proceedings. Further, its conduct and

   admissions in earlier proceedings acknowledged the subsistence of

   the debt, validity of the Guarantee and its liability as Corporate

   Guarantor, and therefore the IPCL is estopped.

d) The invocation and transfer of pledged shares did not, by

   themselves, extinguish the underlying debt by placing reliance on

   PTC India Financial Services Ltd. vs Venkateswarlu Kari and

   another [(2022) 9 SCC 704]. The debt and default of MEL stood

   established. The Corporate guarantee had been duly invoked,

   demand notices had been issued and IPCL had failed to discharge

   its liability and the existence of financial debt and default stood

   established.

e) Turning to limitation, by reckoning the period of limitation from the

   date of the failure to comply with the demand notice dated



                                                                                                             12

              20.12.2017 by IPCL, the petition filed by the SBI under Sec.7 IBC

              on 26.02.2020 was within the prescribed period of limitation. The

              requirements of existence of financial debt, occurrence of default

              and completeness of the application under Section 7 of the IBC were

              therefore satisfied.



Arguments



4. The learned counsel for the appellants argued that:

       a) the deed of Corporate Guarantee dated 23.09.2016 which IPCL in

          favour of the lenders of MEL is void and unenforceable for want of prior

          written consent of the WBERC, as mandatorily required under

          Regulation 5.13.2 of the WBERC (Licensing and Conditions of License)

          Regulations, 2013 under Sec. 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,

          since its object or consideration is forbidden by law or would defeat

          the provisions of law. Consequently, no enforceable debt could arise

          against IPCL within the meaning of Sec. 3(11) and 3(12) of the IBC,

          and thus the essential requirement for admission of an application

          under Sec. 7 would remain unsatisfied. Reliance was placed on

          Innoventive Industries Ltd. Vs ICICI Bank [(2018) 1 SCC 407]; M.

          Suresh Kumar Reddy Vs Canara Bank, [(2023) 8 SCC 387]; and

          Power Trust Vs Hiranmaye Energy Ltd., [(2026) 5 SCC 38]. This

          apart admission of MEL into CIRP could establish only MEL’s liability

          and could not, by itself, establish the validity or enforceability of IPCL’s

          Corporate Guarantee.

       b) WBERC had, through its orders and subsequent proceedings, affirmed

          the requirement of prior consent for execution of the Corporate



                                                                                                                        13

   Guarantee. The lenders did not challenge the said determination

   before the appropriate appellate forum under the Electricity Act, 2003.

   Therefore, the determination had attained finality and could not be

   collaterally questioned before the Adjudicating Authority under Sec.

   60(5) of the IBC. Reliance was placed on Embassy Property

   Developments Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Karnataka, [(2020) 13 SCC

   308]; Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. vs. Amit Gupta, [(2021) 7 SCC

   209]; Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. vs. Vishal Ghisulal Jain,

   [(2022) 2 SCC 583]; State Bank of India vs. Union of India , [2026

   SCC OnLine SC 202]

c) the Electricity Act, 2003, together with the regulations framed

   thereunder, constitutes a special statutory framework governing

   electricity distribution licensee. The regulatory safeguards and prior-

   consent requirements applicable to IPCL cannot be disregarded merely

   by invoking the overriding provision under Section 238 of the IBC.

   Indeed, there is no irreconcilable conflict between the two enactments

   warranting the application of the overriding clause and that both

   statutes ought to be harmoniously construed. While the Adjudicating

   Authority relied on the decisions in Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran

   Nigam Ltd., vs. Raman Ispat (P) Ltd., [(2023) 10 SCC 60], and

   Duncans Industries Ltd., vs. A.J. Agrochem, [(2019) 9 SCC 725],

   the same are distinguishable on facts and the context in which those

   decisions were rendered.

d) the affidavit furnished by IPCL’s Director, the representations made

   during negotiations, or any alleged admission on the part of IPCL

   cannot validate an agreement which is otherwise prohibited by law.



                                                                                                                 14

   The affidavit dated 23.09.2016, the Indemnity Deed and Clause 2.4 of

   the guarantee deed thereof, cannot cure the absence of mandatory

   statutory consent and make the Corporate Guarantee enforceable

   contrary to Sec. 23 of the Contract Act. Where a party aware of a

   statutory prohibition cannot seek the aid of the Court to enforce a

   contract made in its violation. Reliance was placed on Loop Telecom

   and Trading Ltd. vs. Union of India, [(2022) 6 SCC 762].

e) the withdrawal of Commercial Suit No. 266 of 2017, without

   adjudication on merits, cannot operate as a bar against IPCL

   questioning the validity of the Guarantee.

f) The Appellants contended that the requirement of prior approval

   under Regulation 5.13.2, being mandatory and backed by statutory

   penalties, amounts to a prohibition. Reliance was placed on Asha

   John Divianathan Vs Vikram Malhotra, [AIR 2021 SC 2932] and

   Mannalal Khetan Vs Kedar Nath Khetan, [(1977) 2 SCC 424]. Any

   contract entered into in breach of such statutory prohibition is void or

   unenforceable, even in the absence of an express provision declaring

   it so. Consequently, the Corporate Guarantee executed without the

   requisite approval cannot be enforced in law.

g) Alternatively, and at any rate, without prejudice to their primary

   contention regarding the invalidity of the Corporate Guarantee, Clause

   2.7 of the deed of Guarantee itself confines the contracted obligation

   of IPCL to its non-regulated assets. Indeed, the contract was drafted

   by the lenders or their legal team, and hence in terms of doctrine of

   contra proferentem, it binds the lenders. So far as the non-regulated

   assets are concerned, they were transferred by IPCL to its wholly



                                                                                                                 15

   owned subsidiary IPCL Power Ltd vide BTA dated 2.6.2025 during the

   pendency of CIRP. Reliance was placed on State of Maharashtra vs.

   M.N. Kaul, [1967 SCC OnLine SC 372], Syndicate Bank vs.

   Channaveerappa Beleri, [(2006) 11 SCC 506].

h) Even assuming the Guarantee to be enforceable, its limited recourse

   cannot justify initiation of CIRP against the entirety of IPCL, including

   its regulated electricity distribution undertaking and assets. It was

   contended that the IBC does not provide for a CIRP confined to

   specified assets and that admission of the Section 7 application would

   consequently expose assets and revenues which were never intended

   to secure the lenders’ facilities. The Resolution Professional however,

   had already assumed control over the licensed undertaking and that

   a sector-specific and modulated approach was necessary, having

   regard to the public utility character of IPCL’s business. Reliance was

   placed on S. Elangovan vs. ASREC (India) Ltd., [2022 SCC OnLine

   NCLAT 2859]; Mansi Brar Fernandes vs. Shubha Sharma, [2025

   INSC 1110]; and Gagan Tandon vs. IL&FS Financial Services Ltd.,

   [2026 SCC OnLine NCLAT 16].

i) the IBC is a mechanism for insolvency resolution and not a substitute

   for ordinary recovery proceedings. Where the very validity and

   enforceability of the Corporate Guarantee are seriously disputed and

   require adjudication, the insolvency process cannot be invoked merely

   as a means of recovery. Reliance was placed on Dhanlaxmi Bank Ltd.

   vs. Mohammed Javed Sultan, [2026 SCC OnLine SC 820], Swiss

   Ribbons (P) Ltd. vs. Union of India, [(2019) 4 SCC 17].



                                                                                                                 16

j) The earlier order dated 30.10.2023 had rejected SBI’s Sec. 7

   application after considering the material and legal issues arising in

   However, on remand, the Adjudicating Authority reversed its earlier

   findings on several independent questions of law, notwithstanding the

   absence of any material in the rejoinder warranting such reversal.



k) The fact regarding the indemnity, was filed by the respondent only in

   the rejoinder and not in Sec. 7 application. The effect of the same was

   not considered by the NCLT, therefore the issue of indemnity cannot

   be sustained at the appellate stage.



l) SBI had taken inconsistent positions regarding the date of default.

   While the application refers to 31.01.2020 as the date of default, the

   list of dates referred to 28.12.2017, and the rejoinder relied upon a

   treated the demand notice dated 20.12.2017 as the date of invocation

   of bank guarantee and accordingly determined the date of default,

   properly reconciling the inconsistent dates and the amounts claimed.

   Reliance was placed on Babulal Vardharji Gurjar Vs Veer Gurjar

   Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd., [(2020) 15 SCC 1]; Royal

   Construction Vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co. Ltd., [2025 SCC OnLine

   NCLAT 618], Syndicate Bank vs. Channaveerappa Beleri, [(2006)

                                                                                                                 17

            the correctness of the decision of the WBERC.

            void. Reliance was placed on Nanakram Vs Kundalrai, [(1986) 3

            PI Opportunities Fund-I Vs Financial Software & Systems (P) Ltd,

            [2025 SCC OnLine Mad 7113].



Discussion & Decision



6.1 The long narration of facts and the arguments built on them concern

       themselves principally with addressing a solitary issue: whether the deed

       of guarantee which IPCL had executed on 23.09.2016 is valid and

       establish the subsistence of an undisputed contractual relationship

       between IPCL and the SBI for holding the existence of a financial debt for

       the purposes of Sec.7 IBC, and the extent to which it creates a binding

       relationship. Looking just at this issue superficially, we do not consider

       that it is either novel or unfamiliar to this tribunal.



6.2 But this case is slightly different, for the defence which the corporate

       debtor has raised for defending the SBI’s petition for initiating CIRP

       against IPCL is alleged to be founded on a void agreement of guarantee

       under Sec.24 of the Contract Act, as its object is unlawful and opposed

       to public policy within the meaning of Sec.23 thereof. The pointed

       contention of IPCL is that it being an electricity distribution licensee, it

       is bound by the Electricity Act, 2003, and WBERC Regulations, and even

       though Regulation 5.13.2 requires prior consent of the Commission for

       executing the deed of guarantee, it has not been obtained, and hence it

       is unlawful. This leads to the next issue: how far should this tribunal



                                                                                                                        22

       engage itself with this issue, more so when the proceedings under the

       tribunal are summary in character?



6.3 This tribunal’s jurisdiction is well trimmed to fit in with the settled and

       well entrenched legal position: to ascertain whether the defence is

       bonafide and genuine, or is it a fakery. A more than a strong prima facie

       view to be obtained through the rule of preponderating probability. See

       the ratio in Deepak Raheja and another Vs Omkara Assets

       Reconstruction Private Ltd. [2026 SCC OnLine SC 2184]; Hardeep

       Singh Sawhney Vs Sawhney Builders Pvt., Ltd., [(2019)217

       Comp.Cases 506 (NCLAT)]; Progfin Pvt., Ltd., Vs Ganesh Benzoplast

       [(2026) ibclaw.in 786 (NCLAT)]. After all, in a summary proceeding for

       ascertaining the existence of debt and default, the twin criteria necessary

       for admitting a corporate debtor to CIRP, the document establishing

       contractual relationship between the corporate debtor and the financial

       creditor should either be beyond dispute, at least free of any probable

       dispute. Where the very document involved requires serious examination

       for its construction, then tribunal may not be the forum to approach.

       This therefore, leads to the next question: Whether this tribunal has

       authority to declare that the deed of guarantee which IPCL has

       indisputably executed, which SBI relies on fastening a liability – the

       financial debt, as void under Sec.24 read with Sec.23 of the Contract

       Act? This tribunal is conscious that in Umesh Kumar Vs Narendra

       Kumar Sharma [2024 SCC OnLine NCLAT 226], this tribunal has taken

       a view that it cannot go into the question of tenability or validity of a

       contractual agreement.



                                                                                                                        23

6.4 And there is an ancillary issue on limitation. But given the intricacies of

       the issue raised, this has taken the back seat.



7. As outlined earlier, the thrust of the arguments on either side is whether

       the deed of corporate guarantee is void. And the appellant also comes

       out with an alternative argument and contends that even if the deed of

       guarantee which IPCL has executed is considered valid, then its

       operation must be limited to separate business, and that it should not

       be construed as involving the entire business of the corporate debtor.



8.1. The deed of corporate guarantee came to be executed because when IPCL

       contemplated the takeover of MEL, and the lenders of MEL had set it as

       a precondition to enable it happen. IPCL did resist this idea, and on

       29.07.2016 it did inform the lenders that providing a corporate guarantee

       is prohibited by WBERC Regulations, but the lenders provided IPCL with

       a set of three legal opinions, all of which are to the effect that the

       Regulations only bar providing guarantee in respect of the ‘Regulated

       assets’ of IPCL and its ‘surplus amount’. The expressions ‘regulated

       asset’, or ‘surplus amount’ however, are coinage of those who have

       offered the legal opinion or drafted the deed of guarantee, whereas the

       WBERC Regulation employs the expressions such as Core, Non-Core,

       Other and Separate businesses or activities (to which pointed reference

       will be made in subsequent paragraphs). Here, we need to make few

       statements to the parties:



          a) We give no credence to the legal opinions which might have provided

              a context for IPCL to execute the guarantee deed, for IPCL is no child

              to complain that it was induced into executing it. It was keen on a



                                                                                                                        24

   commercial venture of acquiring MEL, and if it had felt that the pre-

   condition which the lenders of MEL had set would involve

   contravention of the Regulations and might invite complications to

   its core-business, it was free to disengage itself from its proposed

   commercial venture. It was justly ambitious with the keenness to

   expand its business, yielded to the demands of the lenders of MEL,

   and it cannot complain that it was induced by the lenders.

b) The second aspect is that, SBI also cannot plead innocence, as it

   knows before hand – before the deed of guarantee was executed that

   execution of the deed of guarantee as demanded by it would involve

   the need to obtain prior consent of WBERC before executing the

   guarantee deed.

c) Now that it is a bilateral document, both the parties have invested

   their creative intelligence or expertise to outmanoeuvre, if not to

   outsmart the provisions of Electricity Act and the statutory

   Regulations made thereunder through the backdoor usage of

   certain non-statutory expressions. Like IPCL, SBI also had its

   options: (i) either to withdraw the precondition of executing the deed

   of guarantee; or (ii) denying approval for IPCL’s takeover of MEL; or

   (iii) to wait for WBERC to apply its mind in terms of the Regulations.

   It did neither. In essence, both the parties were overdriven by

   commercial ambitions to pursue, and got into a contractual

   relationship through a consciously contrived drafting (of the

   agreement) to hoodwink the Electricity Act, its Regulations and the

   Regulator. And it is they who call themselves angel and the other

   the devil before us.



                                                                                                             25

8.2 And there are couple of facts which can be clarified straightway:

       a) Keeping the controversial deed of guarantee aside, somewhere in the

            course of the arguments, SBI, brought in a supplementary argument

            to fortify its principal argument on the validity of the guarantee deed

            through an affidavit dated 23.09.2016, executed for IPCL which was

            to the effect that executing a deed of corporate guarantee would not

            contravene the Regulations. This is least appealing for when the

            Regulations assert themselves on the strength of its statutory origin,

            it is not given to those whom the Regulations govern to stand against

            them. The affidavit lacks the strength to substitute the effect of the

            Regulations.

       b) Turning to the appellant, it has contended that when the Hon’ble

            Supreme Court in its judgement in C.A.8178 of 2023,

            dated,14.02.2025 required the Adjudicating Authority to consider the

            rejoinder of the SBI, the latter should have only tested the extent to

            which the rejoinder would impact its earlier judgement dismissing

            the petition under Sec.7 IBC dated, 30.10.2023, and by engaging in

            a de novo consideration, it has exceeded the terms of remand. This

            argument also is a distraction, since the very judgement of the

            Hon’ble Supreme Court (whose operative portion is captured in

            paragraph 1.2 above) belies it.



9. This now shifts the focus for a consideration of the core-issue. And, as

       indicated, there is an issue on the extent of our jurisdiction, and that will

       be considered alongside. On 23.09.2016, IPCL executed a Deed of

       Guarantee in favour of SBICAP Trustee Company Ltd., The material

                                                                                                                 27

               deductions and/or adjustments of any kind whatsoever, the

               amount of the Guaranteed Obligations as may be claimed by the

10. For understanding what ‘Non-Regulated assets’ and ‘Surplus Amounts’,

       mean, the definitions to these expressions as provided in Clause 1.1 of

       the guarantee-deed need to be referred to. They are as below:



               “Non Regulated Asset shall mean all assets of the Guarantor

               Regulated Asset shall mean all the revenues and receivables of

               Surplus Amounts shall mean the surplus funds generated from

11. In our endeavour, we consider it appropriate not just to confine our

       enquiry superficially to the factum of execution of the deed of guarantee



                                                                                                                        28

in contravention to Regulation 5.13.2, but also to ascertain prima facie

how specific terms thereof may come into conflict with the said

Regulation. Having said that, we do not propose to travel the entire

distance to match the jurisdiction of a civil court. It is this understanding

that would set the tone for testing the validity of the deed of guarantee

under Sec.24 of the Contract Act. And the extent to which we should

engage in this appeal. Accordingly, we deduce:



a) Non-Regulated assets are negatively defined in Clause 1.1 of the

   guarantee-deed as those which are not Regulated assets.



b) Regulated asset is defined to mean (hence not exhaustive) all the

   revenues and receivable of the business and operations of the

   Dishergarh Electric License. Therefore, ‘Regulated assets’, according

   to this definition, is mere trade receivables and other revenues of IPCL,

   and does not include the existing tangible assets with which IPCL is

   carrying its electricity distribution business.



c) This would now imply all the fixed and tangible assets of IPCL which

   are necessary for working the distribution licence has been made part

   of the definition of Non-Regulated Assets. Indeed, if the definition is

   closely read it does not exclude even the electricity distribution-license

   from the purview of Non-Regulated assets.



d) Now, turning to ‘Surplus Amounts’, by definition, it is the balance

   available after deducting few heads of expenditure from the revenue

   and receivables (which constitute Regulated assets) obtained from

   working the distribution licence.



                                                                                                                 29

12.1 While the appellant attacked the guarantee deed in terms of Regulation

       licensee, but the Act does not define, other business. As would be seen

2. The crux of the argument of the Appellant before us, as against the

14. It is this issue, which is the subject matter of consideration in the

instant Company Appeal. In order to over shadow the controversy, as to

17. It has come on record that Respondent Bank did appear before the

Adjudicating Authority and filed their response on 22.09.2021, it was placed

on record and that after the issuance of multiple notices by the Registry on

and in the reply thus filed by the Respondent, i.e., the Bank, here the claim

realized as invocation of Performance Bank Guarantee for non-payment in

respect of the facilities availed under the Packing Credit Limit. However, it is

Debtor were submitted on 01.11.2019, that was revised subsequently on

09.12.2019, which was duly verified and admitted and consequent to it a

Revised List of Creditors was submitted before the Ld. Adjudicating

Authority and the amount thus realized by the Respondent from ECGC

Limited as on 28.05.2020, after the period of determination of their claim

against the Corporate Debtor and also because of the fact that the amount

realized during the imposition of moratorium period since violating the

provisions contained under Section 14 of the I&B Code, it ought to have

been accounted as to be the property of the Corporate Debtor. The Ld.

Tribunal while determining the implication of the Security Interest, as

defined under Section 3(31) observed that the amount thus deposited would

not falling under the determination of the Security Interest.

19. The export credit that was availed by the Corporate Debtor was

exclusively covered under the ECGC and that has been taken to be an

independent and separate contract between the Bank and ECGC and it was

a third party guarantee and the records of the default also did not show that



                                                                                                               11 of 14

the default loss by the bank with ECGC which was much prior to the

initiation of the CIRP was found to be a part of the Security Interest, the

reason being that the ECGC credit cover was executed under the ECIB

export credit insurance for Bank that was issued under the pre-shipment

credit and was recorded to be the part of the Collateral Securities between

the Respondent and the ECGC. The scheme opted out of the pre and post

shipment insurance cover under letters of the comfort or Security Interest.

20. If we look into the definition of the Security Interest is extracted above

contained under Section 3(31) of the definition clause. It provides a proviso

which specifically observes that the Security Interest would not include a

Performance Guarantee under normal law of interpretation, the proviso

normally itself explanatory in nature which only qualifies the contents of the

principle provision. But the manner in which the proviso to sub-section 31

of Section 3 has been introduced is in the shape of an exception “Causing

an Exclusion”. By virtue of which the Performance Guarantee had been

brought outside the argument of the Security Interest. The guarantee that

was obtained from the ECGC is not a debt as per Section 3(11) of the Code.

For the reason that the amount obtained after invocation of Performance

Guarantee is not a debt. Rather, it is covered under any of the consortium

documents as it is a third-party guarantee provided a surety for violation

terms contained under the said guarantee and would not be covered under

the loan document, hence it could be safely inferred that the amount



                                                                                                               12 of 14

obtained from the ECGC is not a debt but obtain in lieu of non-performance

of obligation covered under the guarantee. When it is non-performance of an

obligation under the facilities availed under the credit limit, it has been

brought under outside the definition of debt, the performance guarantee has

been excluded from the Security Interest since the guarantee provided under

the said ECGC is the performance-based guarantee and it does not come

under the purview under the Security Interest.

21. On a simpliciter interpretation, the Security Interest under the Code

includes the interest that has been created in favour of the secured creditor

by a transaction, which secures of payment against performance of an

obligation but it will not include in it an obligation and that is why it

excludes the performance-based guarantee from the definition of Security

Interest. The carving out an exception under the proviso to sub-section 31 of

Section 3 of the code. In the matters of Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. Vs. M/s

J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd., it had laid down as under:



                  “Interalia held that 'the bank guarantee is irrevocable

              and unconditional and payable on demand without

              demur. The assets of the surety are separate from those

              of the corporate debtor, and proceedings against the

              corporate debtor may not be seriously impacted by the

              actions against assets of third party like surety. Bank

              guarantee can be invoked even during the moratorium.

              period issued under Section 14 of the IBC in view of the

              amended provision under Section 14(3)(b) of the Code.'”



                                                                                                               13 of 14

22. Owing to the facts which stand admitted herein the Corporate Debtor

had never deposited the said sum obtained by the Bank from ECGC, hence

it cannot be said to be assets of the Corporate Debtor and most of when it is

not Security Interest that has been created over on any valid claim. Thus,

the rejection of the application so far it pertains to handover the amount

received from the ECGC since being exclusively outside the ambit of Section

3(31) proviso and exclusively since being part of the Collateral Security

under the scheme opted for pre-shipment insurance cover will not fall to be

a Security Interest and it has been rightly denied to be granted to the

Appellant as it was prayed for Interlocutory Application preferred before the

Ld. Tribunal. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons, the Company Appeal lacks

merit and the same is accordingly dismissed.

23. All Interlocutory Applications would stand closed.

2026 INSC 1287                                      REPORTABLE



                IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

                 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION



                CIVIL APPEAL NO.                    OF 2026



                (@ S.L.P. (C) NO.38284 OF 2025)

                                            VERSUS



S. LOGANATHAN & ORS.



                JUDGMENT



  ALOK ARADHE, J.

     1. Leave granted.

     2. The present appeal raises an important question concerning the

          territorial limits of the recovery jurisdiction exercised by the

          Debts Recovery Tribunals under the Recovery of Debts and

          Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (the 1993 Act), particularly in relation to

          the execution of a recovery certificate against the property

          situated beyond the local limits of the Tribunal which issued it.



Signature Not Verified The question is of considerable practical importance and recurs

 3. This appeal takes exception to the judgment dated 22.08.2025

       passed by the High Court1 in a Writ Petition2. By the said

       judgment, the High Court partly allowed the Writ Petition filed

       by Respondent No.1 (the Borrower) and held that the recovery

       certificate3 issued by the Debts Recovery Tribunal-III, Chennai

       (DRT, Chennai) ought to be transmitted to the Debts Recovery

       Tribunal, Madurai (DRT, Madurai), which alone is vested with

       jurisdiction to execute it.

       FACTUAL BACKGROUND

       and are as follows. The Borrower and his late wife were partners

       which was renamed as M/s S. Loganathan Contractor with

       sanctioned in December 2004 was enhanced to Rs.42 lakhs on

       08.09.2005 and, on 21.06.2006, the Bank sanctioned a cash

       jurisdiction, as neither of the properties was situate within its

       territorial limits. He also contended that the recovery certificate

       had been issued against a dead person and that the proceedings

       had abated.

       THE IMPUGNED JUDGMENT



12. The High Court vide judgment dated 22.08.2025, on the basis

       of the principle that a decree is executed by the Court within

       whose jurisdiction the property is situate, held that DRT,

       Madurai alone has jurisdiction to execute the recovery

       certificate. The High Court concluded as follows: (i) the transfer

       of the original application to Chennai was at the instance of the

       Borrower, (ii) the grievance of the Borrower is not about the

       forum of adjudication but about the execution against the

       property outside the limits of DRT, Chennai, (iii) the issuance of

       the recovery certificate was well within the jurisdiction of DRT,

       Chennai, and (iv) for the execution of the recovery certificate,

       the same ought to have been transmitted to DRT, Madurai. The

       High Court, however, rejected the contention of the Borrower

IN RE: ISSUE NO. (i)

APPLICABILITY OF THE CODE TO RECOVERY PROCEEDINGS



17. We propose to deal with Issue No. (i) by adverting to the object

       and purpose of the enactment of the 1993 Act, the provisions of

       the 1993 Act and the decisions of this Court.



(a) Object and purpose of enactment of the 1993 Act :-

18. Prior to the enactment of the 1993 Act, the Banks and Financial



       Institutions were required to pursue recovery proceedings



                                                                                                                             15

       before the ordinary civil courts. The resulting delays and

       enormous pendency of litigation led to a substantial sum of

       public money remaining locked in unproductive assets, which

       adversely affected the financial system and the efficient

       utilisation of funds. The need for a specialised and expeditious

       mechanism for recovery of debts due to Banks and Financial

       Institutions had been recognised by the Tiwari Committee in

       1981, which recommended the establishment of special

       tribunals following a summary procedure. Subsequently, the

       Narasimham Committee in 1991 also emphasised the

       importance of a specialised adjudicatory forum and speedy

       recovery as an essential component of financial sector reforms.

19. The magnitude of the problem was evident from the fact that,

       as on 30.09.1990, more than 15 lakh cases filed by the public

       sector banks and about 304 cases filed by the financial

       institutions were pending in various courts. The amounts

       involved were approximately Rs.5622 crores due to the public

       sector banks and Rs.391 crores due to the financial

       institutions.

20. In this backdrop, Parliament enacted the 1993 Act with the

       principal object of establishing specialised Debts Recovery



                                                                                                                             16

       Tribunals and Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunals to ensure

       speedy adjudication and expeditious recovery of debts due to

       banks and financial institutions. The legislation was enacted to

       overcome the procedural delays inherent in ordinary civil

       litigation and to facilitate the productive circulation of public

       funds. It is not merely another forum for adjudication of the

       dues of the public sector banks and financial institutions, but

       is a specialised, expeditious and effective mechanism for

       adjudication and recovery of debts due to banks and financial

       institutions. The constitutional validity of the 1993 Act was

       upheld by this Court in Union of India v. Delhi High Court

       Bar Association11. The 1993 Act has since been amended from

       time to time to strengthen the recovery machinery, notably by

       Act No. 1 of 2000, Act No. 30 of 2004 and Act No. 44 of 2016.

       The last of these, inter alia, enlarged the modes of recovery

       available to the Recovery Officer and enabled the bank to file its

       application where the account in which the debt is outstanding

       is maintained.



11 (2002) 4 SCC 275



                                                                                                                             17

   (b) The Provisions of the 1993 Act



21. Chapter IV of the 1993 Act deals with procedure of Tribunals.



       Section 19 provides for application to the Tribunals. Section



       19(1) of the 1993 Act reads as under:-



                   “19. Application to the Tribunal.—(1) Where

                   a bank or a financial institution has to recover

                   any debt from any person, it may make an

                   application to the Tribunal within the local

                            bank or financial institution is

                            maintaining an account in which debt

                            claimed is outstanding, for the time

                      (aa) the defendant, or each of the

                            defendants where there are more than

                            one, at the time of making the

                            application, actually and voluntarily

                            resides or carries on business or

                            personally works for gain; or



                      (b) any of the defendants, where there are

                            more than one, at the time of making

                            the application, actually and

                            voluntarily resides or carries on

                            business or personally works for gain;

                            or



                      (c) the cause of action, wholly or in part,

                            arises:

                     institution may, with the permission of the

                     Debts Recovery Tribunal, on an application

                     made by it, withdraw the application,

                     whether made before or after the

                     no such action had been taken earlier under

22. By the Amendment Act No. 44 of 2016, sub-section (22A) was



       inserted in Section 19 with effect from 04.11.2016, which is



       indicative of legislative intent and provides for a legal fiction to



       treat the recovery certificate as a decree for the purposes



       mentioned therein. Section 19(22A) reads as under:-



                     “19(22A) Any recovery certificate issued by

                     the Presiding Officer under sub-section (22)

                     Court for the purposes of initiation of

                     winding up proceedings against a company

                     (18 of 2013) or Limited Liability Partnership

                     Partnership Act, 2008 (9 of 2008) or

                     individual or partnership firm under any

23. Section 22 of the 1993 Act deals with powers and procedure of



       the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal. Section 22 reads as



       under:-



                     “22. Procedure and powers of the Tribunal

                     and the Appellate Tribunal.—(1) The

                     Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal shall

                     the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of

                     of natural justice and, subject to the other

                     provisions of this Act and of any rules, the

                     Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal shall

                     (2) The Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal

                     powers as are vested in a civil court under

                     1908), while trying a suit, in respect of the

                        (c) receiving evidence on affidavits;



                        (d) issuing commissions for the

                        examination of witnesses or
