24. The scheme of the 1993 Act brings out the following



       distinguishing features: (i) the Debts Recovery Tribunal is a



       statutory adjudicatory body and not a civil court, (ii) the



       proceedings before it are initiated by way of an application and



                                                                                                                             21

       not by institution of a suit, (iii) the procedure prescribed before

       the Tribunal is neither rigid nor elaborate, and the Tribunal is

       vested with the flexibility to regulate its own procedure subject

       to adherence to the principles of natural justice, (iv) the

       Tribunal, upon adjudication of the claim of a bank or a financial

       institution, issues a recovery certificate specifying the amount

       due, and (v) the Recovery Officer proceeds to recover the amount

       due in accordance with the provisions of the 1993 Act.

       Thus, the mechanism contemplated under the 1993 Act

       comprises two distinct stages, namely, adjudication of the claim

       by the Tribunal and execution of the recovery certificate through

       the Recovery Officer.

25. This Court in Grapco Industries Ltd. (supra), while

       interpreting the expression “shall not be bound by” used in

       Section 22 of the 1993 Act, held that the Code does not denude

       the Tribunal of the power to exercise powers analogous to those

       contained in the Code; rather, the Tribunal can travel beyond

       the Code subject to the requirement of compliance with natural

       justice. A two-Judge Bench of this Court in MSTC Ltd. (supra),

       while considering Sections 20, 22 and 34 of the 1993 Act,

       reiterated the aforesaid view and held that the 1993 Act is a



                                                                                                                             22

       complete and exhaustive code and the provisions of the Code

       cannot be imported where they are inconsistent with the

       statutory scheme. It was held that Order XLVII Rule 7 of the

       Code does not apply to proceedings before the Tribunal, as

       Section 20 of the 1993 Act provides an appeal against every

       order of the Tribunal. Another two-Judge Bench of this Court

       in Satyawati Tondon (supra) held that the 1993 Act had

       created a special procedural mechanism for speedy recovery

       and had “freed” the Tribunals and the Appellate Tribunals from

       the procedural constraints of the Code.

26. Thus, by taking into account the object of the 1993 Act, the

       relevant provisions of the 1993 Act and the decisions of this

       Court, it is axiomatic that the provisions of the Code which are

       inconsistent with the scheme of the 1993 Act cannot be

       imported into the 1993 Act so as to curtail the powers of the

       Tribunal. The principles of the Code may, however, be drawn

       upon to aid and enable the Tribunal to exercise its powers in

       consonance with the purpose and provisions of the 1993 Act.

       For the aforementioned reasons, Issue No. (i) is answered by

       holding that the provisions of the Code do not apply to the



                                                                                                                             23

execution proceedings under the 1993 Act so as to restrict the



powers of the Tribunal.



IN RE: ISSUE NO. (ii)  EXECUTION:  DISTINCT  TERRITORIAL

ADJUDICATION AND

FIELDS



27. Section 19(1) of the 1993 Act governs the territorial jurisdiction



of the Tribunal for entertaining an original application



instituted by a Bank or Financial Institution for recovery of its



dues. A plain reading of the provision makes it evident that the



situs of the mortgaged property is not one of the statutory



criteria for determining the territorial jurisdiction of the



Tribunal for entertaining an original application under Section



19(1) of the 1993 Act. The territorial jurisdiction of the Tribunal



is determined by reference to statutory parameters expressly



prescribed under Section 19(1) of the 1993 Act, which include



the location of the relevant bank branch or office, the residence



or place of business of the defendant, or the place where the



cause of action arises wholly or in part.



28. There is a conscious omission of the situs of the mortgaged



property as a criterion for determining the jurisdiction under



Section 19(1) of the 1993 Act, in contrast with the jurisdiction



of the Civil Court under Section 16 of the Code, wherein the



                                             24

       location of immovable property assumes significance for

       determining the territorial jurisdiction of the Civil Court. Thus,

       Section 19(1) contemplates a situation where the Tribunal may

       be required to deal with a property situated beyond its territorial

       limits. Section 19(13) of the 1993 Act, which enables the

       Tribunal to attach the property in the circumstances specified

       therein, also does not refer to the situs of the property. Section

       19(22) provides for issuance of the recovery certificate by the

       Presiding Officer who has exercised the jurisdiction under

       Section 19(1) of the 1993 Act. The recovery certificate may,

       therefore, relate to properties of the defendant situated within

       or outside the territorial limits of the Tribunal which issues it.

29. The adjudication of the claim of a bank or financial institution

       and the execution of the recovery certificate are two distinct

       stages, though forming part of one statutory process. The

       territorial jurisdiction of the Tribunal to adjudicate the claim of

       the bank or financial institution is governed by Section 19(1) of

       the 1993 Act, whereas the execution of the recovery certificate

       by the Recovery Officer is governed by Chapter V of the 1993

       Act, and its transmission to another Tribunal by Section 19(23).



                                                                                                                             25

       This Court in Allahabad Bank v. Canara Bank12 recognised



       that the adjudication of liability and the recovery of the amount



       by execution of the certificate fall, respectively, within the



       exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal and the Recovery Officer.



       The location of an immovable property is not a relevant criterion



       while adjudicating a claim under Section 19(1) of the 1993 Act,



       whereas the same may have an impact on the execution of the



       certificate of recovery. Thus, there is a distinction between the



       territorial jurisdiction of the Tribunal in adjudicating the claim



       of the bank or financial institution and the territorial reach of



       the execution of the recovery certificate by the Recovery Officer



       of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the Issue No. (ii) is answered.



IN RE: ISSUE NO. (iii)

SCOPE OF SECTION 19(23)



30. At this stage, it is apposite to take note of Section 19(23) of the



       1993 Act, which reads as under:-



                        “19(23)-Where the Tribunal, which has

                        issued a certificate of recovery, is

                        satisfied that the property is situated

                        within the local limits of the jurisdiction

                        of two or more Tribunals, it may send

                        the copies of the certificate of recovery

                        for execution to such other Tribunals

                        where the property is situated:



12 (2000) 4 SCC 406



                                                                                                                             26

                          Provided that in a case where the

                          Tribunal to which the certificate of

                          recovery is sent for execution finds

                          that it has no jurisdiction to comply

                          with the certificate of recovery, it shall

                          return the same to the Tribunal

                          which has issued it.”

       (A) TEXTUAL FEATURES OF SECTION 19(23)

31. The provision has five textual features which bear upon its

       construction. First, the power is conferred only upon “the

       Tribunal, which has issued a certificate of recovery”. No other

       Tribunal can set the provision in motion, and the certificate

       holder cannot, by its own choice, determine whether the

       certificate is to be retained or transmitted. Secondly, the power

       arises when that Tribunal “is satisfied” as to the location of the

       property. Thirdly, what is sent are “the copies of the certificate

       of recovery”. The Tribunal issuing the recovery certificate

       retains the same and remains in seisin of the recovery

       proceeding. Transmission does not divest such Tribunal of its

       jurisdiction but enables execution to proceed, simultaneously if

       need be, in another territory. Fourthly, the certificate may be

       sent only “to such other Tribunals where the property is

       situated”. Fifthly, the proviso commands that a Tribunal to

       which the certificate is sent, if it “finds that it has no jurisdiction



                                                                                                                             27

       to comply with the certificate of recovery”, “shall return the

       same” to the Tribunal issuing the recovery certificate.

32. It is noteworthy that the expression “property” employed by the

       legislature in Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act is required to be

       read in the context of Section 13(2) of the General Clauses Act,

       1897, which provides that words in the singular include the

       plural, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or

       context. There is nothing repugnant in Section 19(23). On the

       contrary, a recovery certificate ordinarily covers several

       properties of the certificate debtors, as it does in the present

       case. The word “property” must, therefore, be read as

       “properties”.

       (B) PURPOSIVE CONSTRUCTION

33. Upon careful consideration of the statutory scheme, it is evident

       that Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act contemplates a mechanism

       for facilitating the execution of a recovery certificate in a case

       involving properties falling within the territorial jurisdiction of

       more than one Tribunal. Section 19(23) does not expressly bar

       the jurisdiction of the Tribunal which has issued the recovery

       certificate in dealing with the property situate outside its

       territorial limits. The conclusion that the local limits of the



                                                                                                                             28

       Tribunal do not by themselves circumscribe the reach of its

       recovery mechanism is also the one which furthers the object of

       the 1993 Act. This Court has held that statutory Tribunals,

       though creatures of the statute, are vested by necessary

       implication with such incidental powers as are essential to give

       full effect to the jurisdiction expressly conferred on them.13 A

       statute must be construed in the light of its scheme and

       purpose, and not in a manner which defeats them.14 Therefore,

       Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act has to be construed in a manner

       which advances the object of the legislation, namely,

       expeditious and effective recovery of debts due to banks and

       financial institutions.

       (C) “MAY” VERSUS “SHALL”

34. Now we advert to the contention whether the word “may” in

       Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act can be read as “shall”. The words

       “may” and “shall” are not to be read in isolation. Whether a

       provision which uses the word “may” is discretionary or whether

       it casts a duty depends upon the context, the object of the

       enactment and the consequences which would follow from the



13 Allahabad Bank (supra) and Income Tax Officer v. M.K. Mohammed Kunhi, AIR 1969 SC 430

14 RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd., (1987) 1 SCC 424



                                                                                                                             29

       one construction or the other.15 Ordinarily, “may” in a provision



       conferring a power signifies discretion. It is construed as “shall”



       only where the power is conferred for the benefit of a person



       who has a legal right to its exercise, so that the power is coupled



       with a duty to exercise it in a particular way. Equally, a



       provision which prescribes no consequence for its non-



       observance, and which relates to the convenience of



       administration, is ordinarily regarded as directory. In



       Bachahan Devi v. Nagar Nigam, Gorakhpur16, this Court



       summarised the position thus:



                     “18. … As a general rule, the word “may”

                     is permissive and operative to confer

                     discretion and especially so, where it is

                     used in juxtaposition to the word “shall”,

                     which ordinarily is imperative as it

                     imposes a duty. Cases, however, are not

                     wanting where the words “may”, “shall”

                     and “must” are used interchangeably. In

                     order to find out whether these words are

                     being used in a directory or in a

                     mandatory sense, the intent of the

                     legislature should be looked into along

                     with the pertinent circumstances.”



       The same principle was reiterated in Vidarbha Industries



       Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd.17, where it was held that the



15 Julius v. Bishop of Oxford, (1880) 5 App Cas 214; State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya, AIR 1961 SC 751;

Official Liquidator v. Dharti Dhan (P) Ltd., (1977) 2 SCC 166; Sharif-ud-Din v. Abdul Gani Lone, (1980) 1 SCC

403

16 (2008) 12 SCC 372

17 (2022) 8 SCC 352



                                                                                                                             30

       word “may” is ordinarily directory, but the prima facie

       presumption may be rebutted by other considerations, such as

       the scope of the enactment and the consequences flowing from

       the construction.

35. Applying these tests, we find that the word "may" in Section

       19(23) cannot be read as "shall", for the following reasons:

       (i) The legislature has used "may" in the main part and "shall"



               in the proviso. The contrast shows that Parliament used

               the two words advisedly. Where it intended compulsion, it

               said so. The proviso compels the transferee Tribunal; it

               does not compel the issuing Tribunal to transmit.

       (ii) The 1993 Act does not provide for any consequence for

               non-transmission of the certificate. Had Parliament

               intended that execution by the issuing Tribunal against

               property beyond its limits would be a nullity, it would have

               said so in clear terms.

       (iii) The object of the 1993 Act is speedy recovery. A mandatory

               reading would compel the Tribunal to split the certificate

               among several Tribunals whenever the securities lie at

               different places, irrespective of the stage of execution or

               the steps already taken. This would cause delay, multiply



                                                                                                                             31

               proceedings, expose the process to avoidable objections

               and frustrate the object of the Act. Execution proceedings,

               as this Court has emphasised, must not be permitted to

               become a means of delaying the fruits of an adjudication.18

36. At the same time, the discretion conferred by Section 19(23) is

       not unfettered. It is a judicial discretion, which must be

       exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not

       according to private opinion; according to law, and not

       humour19. It must be legal and regular, and not arbitrary, vague

       or fanciful20. It follows that the discretion vests in the Tribunal,

       that is, the Presiding Officer, and not in the Recovery Officer,

       and that it cannot be exercised by the certificate holder by the

       mere filing of an affidavit before the Recovery Officer.

       (D) DIVERGENCE OF OPINION AMONGST THE HIGH

            COURTS

37. The learned Amicus Curiae has brought to our notice the

       divergence of opinion amongst the High Courts. On one side are

       the decisions of the Gujarat High Court in Balbir Kumar Paul

       (supra) and of the Bombay High Court in Tushar P. Shah

       (supra), followed in GSL (India) Ltd. (supra). In Balbir Kumar



18 Rahul S. Shah v. Jinendra Kumar Gandhi, (2021) 6 SCC 418

19 Sharp v. Wakefield, [1891] AC 173

20 Aero Traders (P) Ltd. v. Ravinder Kumar Suri, (2004) 8 SCC 307



                                                                                                                             32

Paul (supra), a Division Bench reversed a learned Single Judge

who had held that the certificate ought to have been sent to the

Tribunal where the property was situated. The property there

was situated at Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh, wholly outside

the limits of DRT, Ahmedabad. In Tushar P. Shah (supra), the

property was situated at Vapi in Gujarat, wholly outside the

limits of DRT-II, Mumbai. The Bombay High Court in Tushar

P. Shah (supra), concurring with the view of the Gujarat High

Court, held that the word "may" in Section 19(23) is not to be

read as "shall", that the 1993 Act contains no counterpart of

Section 39(4) of the Code, that Mohit Bhargava (supra), being

a decision under the Code, does not govern the Tribunal, and

that a mandatory reading would delay execution under a statute

meant for speedy recovery. In GSL (India) (supra), which arose

under Section 17 of the 2002 Act, the Bombay High Court

reiterated that the issuing Tribunal may either execute the

certificate itself against property outside its jurisdiction or send

it to the Tribunal where the property is situated, and expressly

disagreed with the contrary view of the Delhi High Court. The

same view has been taken by the Debts Recovery Appellate



                                                                                                                   33

       Tribunal, Delhi in Sikka Papers Ltd. (supra) and by a Division

       Bench of the Madras High Court in Nathu K. Patel (supra).

38. On the other side are the decisions of the Delhi High Court in

       Amish Jain (supra), of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in

       Harjinder Singh (supra) and of the Calcutta High Court in

       Bizmart Projects Private Limited (supra), in which a view has

       been taken that the Tribunal which issues the recovery

       certificate is mandatorily required to transfer the same to the

       Tribunal within whose jurisdiction the property is situate. In

       Harjinder Singh (supra), the High Court drew upon Section

       39(4) of the Code and the decision of this Court in Mohit

       Bhargava (supra). The Madras High Court has taken two

       conflicting views, namely in the impugned judgment and in

       Nathu K. Patel (supra).

39. The decisions which treat transmission as mandatory rest

       substantially on Section 39(4) of the Code and on Mohit

       Bhargava (supra). That decision was rendered under the Code.

       This Court held that the conflict of opinion as to whether the

       court which passed a decree could itself execute it against

       property outside its jurisdiction was set at rest by sub-section

       (4) of Section 39, inserted by Act No. 22 of 2002 with effect from



                                                                                                                             34

       01.07.2002. The 144th Report of the Law Commission of India,

       placed before us by the learned Amicus Curiae, shows that the

       conflict arose because the word “may” in Section 39 had been

       read by some High Courts as permitting such execution, and

       that the Commission recommended an express provision to the

       contrary. Where Parliament intended a territorial restriction on

       execution under the Code, it enacted one expressly. No such

       provision is found in the 1993 Act and, for the reasons assigned

       while answering Issue No. (i), it cannot be imported.

40. We may also notice why the submission of the learned Amicus

       Curiae cannot be accepted without qualification. If the issuing

       Tribunal could execute against properties anywhere as a matter

       of course, without any judicial consideration of the question,

       the choice would, in practice, rest with the certificate holder,

       since the forum of adjudication under Section 19(1) is chosen

       by it. The certificate debtor, and third parties such as tenants,

       occupants, claimants and intending purchasers, might be

       compelled to contest attachment, valuation, possession and

       sale before a distant forum, before which the appeal under

       Section 30 would also lie. The Recovery Officers of metropolitan

       Tribunals, where the bulk of the applications are filed, would



                                                                                                                             35

       have to carry out local inquiries, affixation, valuation,

       possession and auction in distant districts, at a cost ultimately

       borne by the certificate debtor. There would also be a risk of

       conflicting proceedings where the same property is under

       attachment by the Recovery Officer of the local Tribunal at the

       instance of another creditor. These difficulties are avoided not

       by reading “may” as “shall”, but by recognising that the

       discretion is a judicial discretion of the Tribunal, to be exercised

       on the parameters laid down hereinafter.

41. For the foregoing reasons, Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act

       permits the Tribunal to execute a recovery certificate issued by

       it in relation to a property situate outside its local limits, and

       that the word “may” in Section 19(23) confers a judicial

       discretion on the Tribunal to retain the execution or to transmit

       the certificate, which is to be exercised on the parameters set

       out hereinafter. In the light of the construction which we have

       placed on Section 19(23) of the 1993 Act, we approve the view

       taken by the Gujarat and Bombay High Courts, subject to the

       parameters which we lay down hereinafter, and do not agree

       with the view expressed by the High Courts of Delhi, Punjab &

       Haryana and Calcutta.



                                                                                                                             36

42. Accordingly, the Issue No. (iii) is answered.

IN RE : ISSUE NO. (iv)

PARAMETERS FOR RETENTION OR TRANSMISSION



   (A) RELEVANT CONSIDERATIONS

43. In determining whether the recovery certificate should be



       transmitted to another Tribunal or whether the execution

       should be continued by the Recovery Officer attached to the

       issuing Tribunal, several relevant considerations would

       necessarily arise. The question is not merely one of territorial

       jurisdiction. It involves several practical and procedural

       considerations which may affect the efficacy of the recovery

       mechanism. For instance, the Recovery Officer attached to the

       Debts Recovery Tribunal at Delhi may face difficulties in

       proceeding against a property situated in Mumbai, especially

       when physical possession, removal of occupants and delivery of

       possession to the auction purchaser are required.

44. There is a difference between the jurisdiction of the Tribunal

       and the territorial reach of the Recovery Officers. Where

       different properties are situated in different jurisdictions,

       separate Recovery Officers may become involved, which may

       give rise to difficulties concerning the priority and sequence of

       attachment, common valuation standards, coordination of



                                                                                                                             37

       auction dates, disclosure of amounts realised, adjustment of

       partial recoveries, calculation of the outstanding balance and

       prevention of recovery exceeding the amount specified in the

       recovery certificate.

45. A property may also be subject to multiple claims and

       proceedings, includi

2026 INSC 1282                                                             REPORTABLE



                        IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

                          CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION



                        WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022



                        SUCHETA DALAL                                   …PETITIONERS

                                                                      …RESPONDENTS

                                       VERSUS



                        UNION OF INDIA & ORS..



                                                     J U D G M E N T

                        VIKRAM NATH, J.



1. The present writ petition has been filed under Article 32



                        of the Constitution of India (hereinafter referred to as the



                        “Constitution”) by the petitioner, Ms. Sucheta Dalal, in



                        public interest, raising concerns regarding the



                        substantial amounts of unclaimed money lying with



                        banks and other financial institutions and the difficulties



                        faced by depositors, nominees and legal heirs in



                        identifying and recovering such amounts. The petitioner



                        has particularly drawn attention to the funds transferred



                        to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund



                        (hereinafter referred to as “DEAF”), the Investor



                        Education and Protection Fund (hereinafter referred to as



Signature Not Verified  “IEPF”) and the Senior Citizens’ Welfare Fund (hereinafter

                        referred to as “SCWF”).

Digitally signed by

SHIPRA NARANG

Date: 2026.11.27

16:43:58 IST

Reason:



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022                                                  1

2. The petitioner seeks, inter alia, directions to the

       respondents for the creation of a centralised database

       providing information regarding unclaimed bank

       deposits, insurance proceeds and post-office deposits,

       and for simplification of the procedures governing

       settlement of claims by nominees and legal heirs so as to

       avoid unnecessary litigation. The petitioner has also

       sought directions for ensuring compliance with the

       circulars and guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of

       India (hereinafter referred to as “RBI”) concerning

       unclaimed deposits and settlement of claims.



       FACTUAL BACKGROUND



3. The facts giving rise to the present writ petition are as

       follows:



   3.1) The petitioner is a national award-winning journalist

           and the Managing Editor of Moneylife magazine, who

           has been actively engaged in matters concerning

           investor protection and financial accountability.

           Through her writings and public advocacy, she has

           consistently raised concerns regarding the

           accumulation of unclaimed deposits and investments

           with banks and other financial institutions, and the

           difficulties faced by depositors and their legal heirs in

           securing their recovery.



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  2

3.2) The present petition primarily concerns three

       statutory funds established for dealing with unclaimed

       financial assets. Their respective legal frameworks are

       briefly set out below:

       i) DEAF was established by RBI under Section 26A

               of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (hereinafter

               referred to as the “Banking Regulation Act”) and

               is governed by the Depositor Education and

               Awareness Fund Scheme, 2014. Under this

               framework, amounts lying in bank accounts

               which have remained inoperative for ten years, or

               deposits which have remained unclaimed for a

               similar period, are transferred to DEAF. Such

               transfer does not extinguish the entitlement of

               the depositor or other lawful claimant to seek

               repayment through the concerned bank.

       ii) IEPF is established under Section 125 of the

               Companies Act, 2013 (hereinafter referred to as

               the “Companies Act”) and is administered by the

               IEPF Authority under the Ministry of Corporate

               Affairs. The Fund receives unclaimed dividends,

               amounts relating to matured deposits and

               debentures, and other specified sums, while

               shares liable to be transferred under Section

               124(6) of the Companies Act are credited to the

               demat account of the IEPF Authority in

               accordance with the applicable Rules. The



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  3

               procedure for claiming refunds and restoration of

               securities is governed by the Investor Education

               and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting,

               Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016.

       iii) SCWF was established under the Finance Act,

               2015 and is administered by the Ministry of

               Social Justice and Empowerment. It receives

               specified unclaimed amounts from certain

               savings and financial instruments, including

               post-office and provident-fund accounts, subject

               to the conditions prescribed under the applicable

               statutory framework. The Fund is intended to

               support schemes promoting the welfare of senior

               citizens.

3.3) According to the petitioner, substantial amounts had

       accumulated in these funds without being claimed by

       the persons lawfully entitled thereto. It was pointed

       out that DEAF had accumulated approximately Rs.

       39,264.25 crores (Rupees thirty-nine thousand two

       hundred and sixty-four crore and twenty-five lakh) as

       on 31.03.2021, as compared to Rs. 18,381 crores

       (Rupees eighteen thousand three hundred and eighty-

       one crore) as on 31.03.2019. Similarly, the amount

       lying with IEPF was stated to have increased to

       approximately Rs. 4,100 crores (Rupees four thousand

       one hundred crore) by 31.03.2020. The petitioner

       attributed this accumulation, inter alia, to the lack of



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  4

       awareness among depositors and legal heirs regarding

       the existence of such assets and the difficulties

       involved in tracing and recovering them.

3.4) The petitioner relied upon various circulars issued by

       RBI from 2005 onwards, requiring banks to adopt

       simplified procedures for settlement of claims

       concerning deceased depositors and to take proactive

       measures for identifying holders of unclaimed

       deposits. These directions included publication of

       information regarding inoperative accounts on the

       websites of banks and periodic updating of such

       information. It was alleged that despite repeated

       regulatory directions, several banks had failed to

       implement these measures effectively.

3.5) The petitioner further contended that banks,

       depositories and other financial institutions frequently

       insisted upon succession certificates, probate or other

       judicial orders even where the entitlement of the

       claimants was undisputed, resulting in unnecessary

       litigation and financial hardship. Similar difficulties

       were alleged in accessing information and securing

       refunds from IEPF, notwithstanding the amendments

       introduced to the governing Rules, including those

       notified on 09.11.2021. It was in these circumstances

       that the petitioner approached this Court seeking a

       centralised mechanism for identifying unclaimed

       financial assets, simplification of claim procedures and



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  5

effective enforcement of the existing regulatory

directions.



RELEVANCE OF THE ISSUE AT HAND



4. We have heard Mr. Prashant Bhushan, learned counsel

       appearing for the petitioner, Mr. N. Venkataraman, learned

       Additional Solicitor General appearing for Respondent No.

       1, Union of India through the Department of Financial

       Services, and Respondent No. 3, Ministry of Corporate

       Affairs, Mr. Dama Seshadri Naidu, learned senior counsel

       appearing for Respondent No. 2, RBI, and Mr. Amarjit Singh

       Bedi, learned counsel appearing for Respondent No. 4, the

       Securities and Exchange Board of India (hereinafter

       referred to as “SEBI”). We have also perused the pleadings,

       affidavits and other material placed on record by the

       respective parties, including the subsequent developments

       brought to our notice during the pendency of these

       proceedings.



5. The issues raised in the present writ petition are of

       considerable public importance. Savings, deposits and

       investments represent the hard-earned money of

       individuals, often accumulated over several years to provide

       financial security to themselves and their families. The right

       to property, though no longer a fundamental right,

       continues to enjoy constitutional protection under Article

       300A of the Constitution, which provides that no person



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  6

       shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

       The transfer of unclaimed financial assets to statutory

       funds does not, by itself, extinguish the rights of persons

       lawfully entitled thereto. The State and its regulatory

       authorities, therefore, have an important responsibility to

       protect such financial interests and facilitate the recovery

       of these assets by their rightful claimants.

6. This responsibility must be discharged consistently with

       the constitutional principles of fairness, reasonableness

       and non-arbitrariness embodied in Article 14 of the

       Constitution. Where statutory mechanisms have been

       established for the custody, administration and recovery of

       unclaimed financial assets, the concerned authorities must

       ensure that such mechanisms remain effective, transparent

       and reasonably accessible. The existence of a statutory

       right to reclaim money would be of little practical value if

       the persons entitled thereto are unable to trace the assets

       or are confronted with unnecessarily cumbersome

       procedures for establishing their claims. The difficulties

       faced by nominees and legal heirs, particularly those who

       may be unaware of the financial assets left behind by

       deceased family members, are therefore legitimate matters

       of public concern deserving appropriate attention.

7. At the same time, the need to facilitate recovery of

       unclaimed financial assets must be balanced with

       appropriate safeguards against fraudulent or competing

       claims. The object must be to ensure that the procedures



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  7

       prescribed by financial institutions are neither

       unnecessarily burdensome nor so relaxed as to compromise

       the interests of rightful claimants. Viewed in this

       perspective, the concerns brought before this Court by the

       petitioner are both genuine and deserving of consideration.

       It is in this background that we proceed to examine the

       measures undertaken by the respondents during the

       pendency of these proceedings and the extent to which they

       address the issues raised in the present writ petition.

8. During the pendency of the present writ petition, the

       respondents have placed on record various affidavits

       detailing the steps undertaken to address the concerns

       raised by the petitioner. These measures include the

       introduction of centralised search facilities, simplification of

       procedures for settlement of claims, strengthening of

       nomination and transmission mechanisms, and initiatives

       for identifying and reaching out to the rightful owners of

       unclaimed financial assets. We consider it appropriate to

       examine these developments separately with reference to

       the measures undertaken by the respective respondents.



MEASURES UNDERTAKEN BY RBI



9. RBI, in its counter affidavit dated 27.01.2023, referred to

       the various regulatory directions issued to banks

       concerning unclaimed deposits and settlement of claims of

       deceased depositors. These included the requirement to



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  8

       publish details of unclaimed deposits on the websites of

       banks, periodically update such information, and adopt

       simplified procedures for settlement of claims. RBI further

       informed this Court that a centralised web portal was under

       development to enable members of the public to search for

       unclaimed deposits across different banks through a

       common platform.

10. Subsequently, in its additional affidavit dated 28.04.2026,

       RBI placed on record the establishment of UDGAM, a

       centralised web portal launched on 17.08.2023 for

       facilitating the identification of unclaimed deposits across

       multiple banks. The object of the portal was explained in

       the press release dated 17.08.2023 in the following terms:



    “The launch of the web portal will aid users to identify

    their unclaimed deposits/accounts and enable them

    to either claim the deposit amount or make their

    deposit accounts operative at their respective banks.”



The portal was initially launched with seven participating

banks. Thereafter, by press release dated 05.10.2023, RBI

informed the public that the search facility had been

extended to thirty banks with effect from 28.09.2023,

covering approximately ninety per cent of the unclaimed

deposits, in terms of value, lying with DEAF.



11. It was further submitted before us that UDGAM enables

       individuals as well as non-individual entities to search for



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  9

unclaimed deposits by furnishing relevant particulars

concerning the account holder. The search results provide

the name of the account holder, the concerned bank and a

unique Unclaimed Deposit Reference Number, which

facilitates identification of the deposit and enables the

claimant to approach the bank concerned. RBI has also

clarified, through its Frequently Asked Questions dated

05.03.2024, that the portal serves as a centralised search

facility and that the actual settlement of claims continues

to be undertaken by the respective banks. The relevant

clarification reads as follows:



“No, the UDGAM portal facilitates only (a) the search

of unclaimed deposits/accounts across multiple

banks at one place and (b) provides information on

claim/settlement process of each bank (which will be

available in the search result). The unclaimed

deposits can be claimed only from the respective

bank.”



12. RBI has further stated that the functioning of UDGAM has

       been improved on the basis of user feedback. Mandatory

       registration has been discontinued, the search facility has

       been made more accessible, and restrictions concerning the

       number of searches and logins have been relaxed. As on

       01.04.2026, approximately twenty lakh users were

       registered on the portal and nearly forty-four lakh searches

       had been conducted. These developments demonstrate that

       the centralised search mechanism, which was only under



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022                   10

consideration when the proceedings commenced, has since

been operationalised and made available for substantial

public use.



MEASURES UNDERTAKEN BY THE MINISTRY OF

CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND THE IEPF AUTHORITY



13. Respondent No. 3, through its counter affidavit dated

       02.03.2023, explained the statutory framework governing

       the transfer, administration and refund of unclaimed

       amounts under IEPF. It was submitted that the Companies

       Act and the Rules framed thereunder already provided for

       publication of information concerning unpaid dividends

       and unclaimed shares, identification of the persons entitled

       thereto and submission of claims before the IEPF Authority.

       The respondent also referred to the amendments

       introduced in 2019 and 2021 for simplifying the refund

       process. In particular, the amendments notified on

       09.11.2021 relaxed the requirement of succession

       certificates and probate in specified cases involving

       securities valued up to Rs. 5 lakhs (Rupees five lakh),

       replaced notarisation with self-attestation in the prescribed

       circumstances, and reduced certain requirements

       concerning affidavits and sureties.



14. In its subsequent affidavit filed on 06.05.2026, Respondent

       No. 3 has brought to our notice further improvements in the

       functioning of the IEPF Authority. It has been stated that



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  11

       the MCA21 system provides a publicly accessible search

       facility through which information furnished by companies

       in Form IEPF-2, including particulars of unclaimed and

       unpaid amounts and the concerned nodal officers, can be

       accessed. The respondent has also explained that the

       transition from Version 2 to Version 3 of the MCA21 system

       has resulted in greater digitisation and integration of the

       claims process. The salient improvements include

       electronic processing of applications, integration with

       depositories and the Public Financial Management System,

       improved verification and tracking of claims, automated

       workflows, and direct disbursement of approved amounts

       into the bank accounts of claimants.

15. More significantly, the IEPF Authority has stated that an

       integrated portal was introduced in August 2025 with the

       object of consolidating three previously separate systems

       and expediting the settlement of claims. The affidavit

       specifically records as follows:



“The integrated portal constitutes a major reform in

the claim disposal process by unifying three

previously fragmented systems.”



The respondent has further stated that the integrated

mechanism facilitates the generation and transfer of

securities and payment of dividends following approval of

claims. The affidavit also furnishes data concerning the

processing of claims up to 31.03.2026 and records that



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022                  12

approximately Rs. 52.85 crore (Rupees fifty-two crore and

eighty-five lakh) towards dividends and more than 3.58

crore shares were transferred to claimants during the

financial year 2025-2026. These figures have been stated to

be provisional. The measures placed on record thus reflect

efforts towards simplifying the process of tracing and

reclaiming unclaimed investments and reducing the

dependence upon manual procedures.



MEASURES UNDERTAKEN BY SEBI



16. SEBI has filed a detailed affidavit in May 2026 setting out

       the measures adopted for protecting investors and

       facilitating the transmission of securities to nominees and

       legal heirs. The affidavit refers to circulars issued from 2021

       onwards concerning nomination facilities for trading

       accounts, demat accounts, securities held in physical form

       and mutual fund folios. The regulatory framework has

       subsequently been revised through circulars dated

       10.01.2025 and 28.02.2025. These measures are intended

       to ensure that investors either register their nominees or

       expressly opt out of nomination, and that the relevant

       particulars of nominees are available to facilitate

       transmission of investments upon the death of the account

       holder.



17. SEBI has also undertaken measures for simplifying the

       documentary requirements governing transmission of



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  13

securities. By circular dated 18.05.2022, issued pursuant

to the amendments made to the applicable regulations on

25.04.2022, the procedure for transmission was further

simplified. The circular records as follows:



“The LODR Amendment Regulations has inter alia

enhanced the monetary limits for simplified

documentation for transmission of securities, allowed

‘Legal Heirship Certificate or equivalent certificate’ as

one of the acceptable documents for transmission

and provided clarification regarding acceptability of

Will as one of the valid documents for transmission of

securities.”



       The subsequent nomination framework also provides that,

       in cases involving transmission to registered nominees, the

       process may ordinarily be completed upon production of the

       prescribed death certificate and completion of the

       prescribed identity-verification requirements, without

       insisting upon additional affidavits, indemnities or

       notarised documents. These measures seek to reduce

       procedural difficulties while retaining the necessary

       safeguards concerning identification and entitlement.

18. Another important measure concerns the establishment of

       a centralised mechanism for reporting and verifying the

       death of an investor. By circular dated 03.10.2023, which

       came into effect on 01.01.2024, SEBI introduced a

       mechanism through Know Your Client (KYC) Registration

       Agencies (hereinafter referred to as “KRAs”) for



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022                       14

       communicating verified information concerning the death of

       an investor to the intermediaries connected with the

       concerned account. Upon verification of the death

       certificate, the relevant intermediary is required to initiate

       the prescribed modification of the investor's records and

       restrict debit transactions. The other connected

       intermediaries are thereafter informed through the

       centralised mechanism and are required to communicate

       the applicable transmission procedure to the nominee or

       person notifying the death. The object is to facilitate timely

       transmission while preventing unauthorised dealings in the

       assets of deceased investors.

19. SEBI has also issued a circular dated 19.03.2025

       concerning integration of information relating to demat

       accounts and mutual fund holdings with DigiLocker. The

       mechanism enables investors to access and preserve

       information concerning their financial holdings and

       designate a person who may obtain access to such

       information following their demise. The circular envisages

       that, upon receipt of verified information concerning the

       death of an investor, the designated DigiLocker nominee

       may be notified and permitted to access the relevant

       records. Such access is intended to assist the nominee or

       legal heir in identifying the financial assets of the deceased

       and initiating the appropriate transmission process. The

       mechanism does not dispense with the applicable legal

       requirements governing transmission of securities.



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  15

20. A further significant development is the introduction of the

       Mutual Fund Investment Tracing and Retrieval Assistant

       (hereinafter referred to as “MITRA”) platform pursuant to

       SEBI's circular dated 12.02.2025. The platform provides a

       searchable database of inactive and unclaimed mutual fund

       folios across the industry, thereby enabling investors and

       their lawful claimants to identify investments which may

       otherwise have remained unnoticed. The circular explains

       the object of the initiative in the following terms.



             “The objective of the platform is to encourage the

             investors to search for forgotten MF investments and

             update KYC as per the current norms.”



       The affidavit records that, up to April 2026, approximately

       5.77 lakh unique investors had accessed the platform and

       32,435 users had recorded successful searches. It further

       states that claims amounting to approximately Rs. 681.26

       crores (Rupees six hundred and eighty-one crore and

       twenty-six lakh) were settled during the period from

       01.04.2025 to 31.03.2026. SEBI has also referred to its

       Master Circular dated 20.03.2026, which requires the

       concerned mutual fund entities and the Association of

       Mutual Funds in India to provide information regarding

       investors having unclaimed amounts and the procedure for

       claiming such amounts, subject to appropriate

       identification and security safeguards.



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  16

21. Apart from these regulatory measures, SEBI has

       undertaken investor outreach initiatives in coordination

       with the IEPF Authority. These include the organisation of

       Niveshak Shivir programmes, commencing with events held

       at Pune on 01.06.2025 and Hyderabad on 30.08.2025, for

       assisting investors with claims relating to unpaid dividends

       and unclaimed shares, updating of records and completion

       of nomination formalities. SEBI has further stated that it

       will continue taking steps to streamline transmission of

       securities and reduce the accumulation of unclaimed

       investments in the securities market.



MEASURES UNDERTAKEN BY THE DEPARTMENT OF

FINANCIAL SERVICES



22. Respondent No. 1, through the Department of Financial

       Services, has also placed on record an updated affidavit

       dated 12.05.2026 detailing the measures undertaken in

       coordination with the financial sector regulators. It has been

       stated that the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025

       introduced provisions permitting multiple nominations, up

       to four nominees, for bank customers, with the relevant

       reform taking effect from 01.11.2025. The object of this

       amendment is to simplify succession and settlement of

       claims and thereby reduce the accumulation of unclaimed

       deposits. The affidavit further refers to the revised

       guidelines issued by RBI on 28.11.2025, providing for



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  17

       settlement of death claims within fifteen days of receipt of

       complete documentation, simplified procedures for certain

       claims involving accounts without nomination up to Rs. 15

       lakhs (Rupees fifteen lakh), and compensation in cases of

       delay.

23. The Department has also referred to the availability of

       existing digital mechanisms, including UDGAM for

       unclaimed bank deposits, Bima Bharosa for unclaimed

       insurance proceeds and MITRA for unclaimed mutual fund

       investments. It has further stated that a nationwide

       campaign titled “Aapki Poonji, Aapka Adhikar” was

       launched on 04.10.2025 with the object of assisting citizens

       in identifying and reclaiming their unclaimed financial

       assets. The campaign covered bank deposits, insurance

       proceeds, mutual funds, dividends and shares, and involved

       coordination among the concerned financial sector

       regulators. According to the affidavit, outreach and

       facilitation camps were organised across 748 districts,

       accompanied by awareness programmes and dissemination

       of information concerning the applicable claim procedures.

24. The Department has also furnished the results of the

       aforesaid campaign. It has stated that, as on 18.04.2026,

       unclaimed financial assets amounting to approximately Rs.

       6,453 crores (Rupees six thousand four hundred and fifty-

       three crore) had been returned to their rightful claimants

       through the efforts of the participating institutions and

       regulators. The reported amounts included substantial



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  18

       recoveries relating to bank deposits, mutual funds and

       insurance proceeds. The affidavit further records that the

       Government will continue taking measures for improving

       awareness, accessibility and settlement of unclaimed

       financial assets.

25. The aforesaid affidavits and the circulars and other

       documents placed on record indicate that, during the

       pendency of the present proceedings, several measures have

       been introduced or strengthened for identifying unclaimed

       financial assets and facilitating their recovery. The

       respondents have thus placed before this Court a series of

       regulatory and administrative developments which have a

       direct bearing on the principal concerns raised in the writ

       petition. We shall now consider the extent to which these

       measures address the reliefs sought by the petitioner and

       whether the remaining grievances call for any further

       directions from this Court.



CONSIDERATION OF THE REMAINING GRIEVANCES OF

THE PETITIONER AND THE NEED FOR FURTHER

DIRECTIONS



26. Having examined the measures undertaken by the

       respondents, we find that the principal concerns which

       prompted the institution of the present writ petition have

       been substantially addressed. The petitioner had

       approached this Court highlighting the difficulties in tracing



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  19

       unclaimed financial assets, the procedural obstacles faced

       by nominees and legal heirs, and the need for greater

       accountability on the part of financial institutions. The

       subsequent establishment of centralised search facilities,

       simplification of claim procedures, strengthening of

       nomination and transmission mechanisms, and

       implementation of public awareness initiatives constitute

       significant progress towards addressing these concerns.

27. Mr. Prashant Bhushan, learned counsel appearing for the

       petitioner, has nevertheless submitted that the measures

       undertaken remain inadequate. In particular, it has been

       contended that there is still no single comprehensive

       platform through which individuals or legal heirs can

       identify and reclaim financial assets held across different

       banks and financial institutions. It has further been

       submitted that unclaimed amounts relating to insurance

       policies, post-office deposits, provident funds and other

       financial instruments have not been adequately addressed.

       We have considered these submissions in the light of the

       material placed on record.

28. Insofar as unclaimed bank deposits are concerned, RBI has

       already established UDGAM, which provides a centralised

       search facility across participating banks. As stated in its

       affidavit dated 28.04.2026, the participating banks

       accounted for approximately ninety per cent of the

       unclaimed deposits lying with DEAF in terms of value at the

       relevant time. Although the facility does not cover every



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  20

       bank, it substantially addresses the demand for a common

       searchable database. The fact that claims continue to be

       settled by the respective banks does not render the

       mechanism inadequate, since the concerned banks remain

       responsible for verifying entitlement and effecting

       repayment in accordance with law. We therefore find no

       justification for directing the establishment of another

       centralised mechanism for this purpose.

29. As regards the broader demand for a single portal covering

       all categories of financial assets, we are unable to accept

       that its absence warrants further intervention by this Court.

       Banking, securities, insurance and other financial sectors

       operate under distinct statutory and regulatory frameworks,

       with different requirements concerning ownership,

       verification and transmission. While greater coordination

       between these mechanisms may be desirable, the

       establishment of a unified platform involves questions of

       regulatory policy, technical feasibility and administrative

       coordination. In the absence of any demonstrated violation

       requiring judicial intervention, we do not consider it

       necessary or appropriate to mandate the adoption of one

       particular institutional arrangement, particularly when

       substantial sector-specific mechanisms have already been

       established.

30. We are also unable to accept that the grievances concerning

       insurance proceeds and other financial assets remain

       wholly unaddressed. The Department of Financial Services



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  21

       has referred to the Bima Bharosa platform and the

       nationwide campaign launched on 04.10.2025, which has

       facilitated the recovery of substantial unclaimed amounts,

       including insurance proceeds. Similarly, SEBI and the IEPF

       Authority have introduced measures for simplifying the

       identification and transmission of investments. Although

       further improvements may be desirable, the developments

       already undertaken cannot be disregarded merely because

       the petitioner considers a more comprehensive arrangement

       preferable.

31. In relation to SCWF, we may also note that the said Fund is

       administered by the Ministry of Social Justice and

       Empowerment, as specifically stated in the affidavit filed on

       behalf of SEBI. The petitioner has, however, not impleaded

       the said Ministry in these proceedings. In the absence of the

       concerned administrative Ministry and its response, we do

       not consider it appropriate to issue any specific directions

       concerning the administration of the Fund or the settlement

       of claims relating thereto. Nevertheless, we grant liberty to

       the petitioner to approach the said Ministry with the

       grievances raised in this regard, which may be considered

       in accordance with law. In the event the petitioner remains

       dissatisfied with the action taken or response furnished by

       the Ministry, it shall be open to the petitioner to approach

       this Court separately, if so advised, in accordance with law.

32. The petitioner has also sought further simplification of the

       procedures governing settlement of claims by nominees and



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  22

       legal heirs. In this regard, the respondents have already

       introduced considerable relaxations in documentary

       requirements, enhanced monetary thresholds and

       simplified transmission procedures. Nevertheless, the need

       for appropriate verification cannot be dispensed with

       altogether, particularly where competing claims or disputes

       concerning succession arise. The objective must be to

       eliminate unnecessary procedural obstacles while

       safeguarding the interests of lawful claimants. We find that

       the measures undertaken by the respondents substantially

       address this concern.

33. We have also considered the additional affidavit filed by the

       petitioner on 05.12.2025, raising concerns regarding

       unclaimed deposits allegedly belonging to government

       bodies, welfare schemes and charitable institutions. While

       such concerns deserve appropriate regulatory attention, the

       existence of unclaimed deposits belonging to these entities

       does not, by itself, establish any illegality in their transfer to

       DEAF or failure of regulatory oversight. The statutory

       framework preserves the entitlement of lawful claimants to

       seek repayment. In the absence of sufficient material

       establishing specific illegality or regulatory failure, we do

       not consider it appropriate to direct a general investigation

       or continuing supervision in these proceedings. Any specific

       instance of non-compliance may be brought before the

       competent authority for examination in accordance with

       law. Insofar as the prayer for identifying and penalising



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  23

       banks for alleged non-compliance with RBI circulars is

       concerned, we do not consider it appropriate to issue any

       general direction in the absence of specific findings of

       regulatory violations. It remains open to RBI to examine any

       such defaults and take appropriate action in accordance

       with law.

34. Ultimately, the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 32 of

       the Constitution must be guided by the necessity for judicial

       intervention in the circumstances prevailing at the time of

       adjudication. Where substantial corrective measures have

       been undertaken and effective mechanisms established, the

       possibility of further administrative improvements cannot,

       by itself, justify continuing judicial supervision. Having

       regard to the developments placed before us, we are

       satisfied that the principal objectives underlying the present

       writ petition have been substantially fulfilled and that no

       further mandatory directions are warranted.



CONCLUSION



35. Before parting with the matter, we consider it appropriate to

       place on record our appreciation for the efforts undertaken

       by the petitioner, Ms. Sucheta Dalal, in raising and

       pursuing an issue of considerable public importance. The

       present proceedings were instituted not for securing any

       personal benefit, but with the object of protecting the

       financial interests of countless depositors, investors and



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  24

       their lawful claimants. The petitioner has consistently

       drawn attention to the difficulties faced by ordinary citizens

       in identifying and recovering their unclaimed financial

       assets. The concerns raised were genuine and the pursuit

       of appropriate institutional measures to address them

       reflects a responsible exercise of public interest litigation.

       Such bona fide efforts, directed towards improving the

       functioning of public institutions and securing the interests

       of citizens, deserve acknowledgment and appreciation.

36. We also place on record our appreciation for Mr. Prashant

       Bhushan, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner, for

       his earnest assistance in the present matter and the passion

       and perseverance with which he has consistently pursued

       causes of public interest before this Court. We equally

       appreciate the valuable assistance rendered by Mr. N.

       Venkataraman, learned Additional Solicitor General, Mr.

       Dama Seshadri Naidu, learned senior counsel, and Mr.

       Amarjit Singh Bedi, learned counsel appearing for the

       respective respondents, in placing the relevant regulatory

       and administrative developments before this Court and

       assisting in the effective resolution of the issues raised in

       these proceedings.

37. In view of the aforesaid discussion and the subsequent

       developments placed on record, we are of the considered

       opinion that the principal concerns raised in the present

       writ petition have been substantially addressed through the

       measures undertaken by the respondents. We take on



WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.185 OF 2022  25

       record the statements and assurances made in their

       respective affidavits and expect the concerned authorities to

       continue their efforts towards improving the accessibility,

       efficiency and transparency of the mechanisms for

       identifying and recovering unclaimed financial assets.

38. We find that no useful purpose would be served by keeping

       the present writ petition pending for further monitoring of

       the regulatory measures already undertaken. Any specific

       grievance concerning unclaimed financial assets may be

       pursued before the competent authority in accordance with

       law.

39. Accordingly, the writ petition is disposed of in the aforesaid

       terms.

40. All pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed

       of.

                   Mr. Kunal Kanungo, Tanushree Kanungo, Tanushree
