                                                 O R D E R

                                            (HYBRID MODE)

Per: Barun Mitra, Member (Technical)

         The present appeal filed under Section 61 of the Insolvency and

Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (‘IBC’ in short) by the Appellant-Suspended Director

of Dharan Infra-EPC Ltd. arises out of the Order dated 16.10.2026

(hereinafter referred to as the ‘Impugned Order’) passed by the Adjudicating

Authority (National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, Court-V) in

C.P.(IB)/729(MB)2025. By the said impugned order, the Adjudicating

Authority has dismissed I.A No. 166 of 2026 filed by the Interim Resolution

Professional (‘IRP’ in short) under Section 12A of the IBC seeking withdrawal

of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (‘CIRP’ in short) initiated

against Dharan Infra-EPC Ltd.-Corporate Debtor.

2. The salient facts of the present case which are relevant to be noticed for

consideration of the matter at hand is that the Corporate Debtor had been

admitted into CIRP on 12.12.2025 following a Section 7 petition filed by Tata



                                                   Page 3 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

Capital Housing Finance Ltd.-Financial Creditor. The IRP appointed for

conduct of CIRP proceedings published Form A on 15.12.2025 inviting claims

from the creditors of the Corporate Debtor. The last date to constitute the

Committee of Creditors (‘CoC’ in short) was 04.01.2026. However, before the

CoC was constituted, the Appellant offered a settlement proposal to the

Respondent No.1-Financial Creditor which settlement proposal was accepted

by the Respondent No. 1. On full and final settlement amount having been

received, Respondent No. 1 furnished Form FA to the IRP on 01.01.2026

requesting the withdrawal of CIRP of the Appellant-Corporate Debtor.

Accordingly, I.A No. 166 of 2026 was filed through the IRP on 06.01.2026

before the Adjudicating Authority seeking withdrawal of

C.P.(IB)/729(MB)2025. The Adjudicating Authority took notice that six other

financial creditors had submitted their respective claims to the IRP and also

opposed the withdrawal of the CIRP by way of filing intervention petitions. The

Adjudicating Authority declined the Section 12A proposal, and aggrieved by

the impugned order, the present appeal has been preferred by the suspended

Director.



3. Making submissions on behalf of the Appellant, Shri Shikhil Suri, Ld.

Sr. Counsel for the Appellant, submitted that in the present facts of the case,

the CIRP admission of the Corporate Debtor occurred on 12.12.2025; Form

FA was submitted by the Financial Creditor-Respondent No. 1 on 01.01.2026

and Section 12A withdrawal application vide I.A No. 166 of 2026 was filed on

06.01.2026. The CoC had not yet been constituted at the time when the

withdrawal application was filed. Furthermore, all the three events viz. CIRP



                                                   Page 4 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

admission, submission of Form FA and filing of withdrawal application had

preceded the coming into operation of the amended Section 12A. Submission

was pressed that since the settlement with the original Financial Creditor-

Respondent No. 1 had reached its logical conclusion even before the CoC was

constituted, the debt stood extinguished and there was no pending issue of

debt or default qua the Respondent No. 1.



4. It was pressed strongly that a Corporate Debtor company can be

admitted into CIRP only on a judicial finding returned by the Adjudicating

Authority of a default as defined under the IBC. In the present case, when

there is no subsisting debt and default, the Adjudicating Authority committed

an error in disallowing the Section 12A withdrawal application. Mere receipt,

verification or admission of claims of other Financial Creditors by the IRP was

not a cogent ground for rejecting the Section 12A application. Once the default

amount relied upon by the original Financial Creditor-Respondent No. 1

forming the basis of the Section 7 petition stood fully and finally settled, the

withdrawal application should have been allowed. Even if there existed

outstanding claims of other Financial Creditors which were yet to be settled,

any such purported debt and default relied upon by other objecting Financial

Creditors opposing the Section 12A withdrawal could not have been

entertained by the Adjudicating Authority for it required independent judicial

determination that atleast one of their claims constituted a default as defined

under the IBC. In the absence of an adjudicated default at the time of

consideration of the withdrawal application, the Corporate Debtor has to be

automatically released from the rigours of CIRP. It was emphatically asserted



                                                   Page 5 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

that there has to be a proper application of judicial mind by the Adjudicating

Authority for determination and consideration of the issue of subsistence of

any debt and default. It was contended that the Adjudicating Authority erred

in failing to carry out the said adjudicatory exercise and to reject the

withdrawal application.



5. Heard. We have also perused the records carefully.



6. Coming to the statutory framework, it is Section 12A of the IBC which

deals with withdrawal of applications admitted under Sections 7, 9 and 10 of

the IBC. Section 12A of the IBC was amended vide Insolvency and Bankruptcy

Code (Amendment) Act, 2026 and the amended provision came into operation

w.e.f. 26.05.2026. When we look at the impugned order, we find that it has

been duly considered by the Adjudicating Authority as to whether Section 12A

was applicable in its pre-amended version or as per the amended version in

the present matter. To arrive at its finding, the impugned order has taken

cognisance of the chronological sequence of three critical events and taken

notice that the Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 12.12.2025; the

Financial Creditor had submitted claims in Form FA on 01.01.2026 and I.A.

No. 166 of 2026 seeking withdrawal of the CIRP was filed on 06.01.2026. It

also concluded that these developments clearly preceded 26.05.2026 being

the date from which amended Section 12A came into operation. Hence, in our

considered view, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly held that the present

application is to be considered in accordance with the pre-amended Section

12A of the IBC.



                                                   Page 6 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

7. For ease of convenience, we would now like to advert our attention to

the pre-amended Section 12A which is as extracted below:



         “12A. The Adjudicating Authority may allow the withdrawal of

         application admitted under section 7 or section 9 or section 10,

         on an application made by the applicant with the approval of

         ninety per cent. voting share of the committee of creditors, in such

         manner as may be prescribed.”



8. This now brings us to the CIRP Regulation 30A which deals with

applications for withdrawal of Section 12A. In the present case, admittedly

the CoC had not been constituted at the time when the Section 12A

application was filed. The IRP had also admittedly filed Section 12A

application under CIRP Regulation 30A(1)(a) of the CIRP Regulations which is

as extracted below:



     “30A. (1) An application for withdrawal under section 12A may be made

     to the Adjudicating Authority –

     (a) before the constitution of the committee, by the applicant through the

     interim resolution professional;”

When we peruse the above CIRP Regulation 30A(1)(a), it clearly provides that

an application for withdrawal under Section 12A can be made before the

constitution of the CoC through the IRP.



9. When the pre-amended Section 12A of IBC is read in conjunction with

Regulation 30A(1)(a) of the CIRP Regulations, we have no ambiguity in our

minds that the statutory framework permits withdrawal of the CIRP through

the IRP with the approval of 90% voting share of the CoC.



10. Coming to the impugned order, we find that the Adjudicating Authority

rejected the Section 12A application on the grounds as excerpted hereunder:



                                                   Page 7 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

11.13 In the present case, six other Financial Creditors have not only

submitted their respective claims to the IRP but have also filed

Intervention Petitions opposing withdrawal of the CIRP and seeking its

continuation. The settlement in question is confined to one Financial

Creditor for Rs. 10 Crore against the claimed default of Rs.

28,04,91,115/-. The claims of the Intervenors are substantial, one of

them being approximately Rs. 183 Crore. Further, the IRP had informed

the Hon’ble NCLAT that claims aggregating to approximately Rs. 600

Crore had been received. The other Financial Creditors are not parties to

the settlement, and no material has been placed on record to establish

that their claims have also been settled or that any such settlement is

proposed. The ability of the Corporate Debtor to resolve its financial

liabilities vis-a-vis its creditors is a relevant consideration while

determining an application for withdrawal of CIRP. A settlement with

one Financial Creditor, in the wake of significant larger amount

pertaining to the other creditors remaining outstanding, does not, by

itself, establish the Corporate Debtor’s ability to resolve its financial

distress. Furthermore, it is also relevant to note that the higher threshold

of approval by 90% of the voting share of the CoC under Section 12A of

the Code is intended to safeguard the interests of the significant majority

of creditors and ensure that withdrawal of CIRP is not permitted solely

on the basis of a settlement with an individual creditor or some creditors.



12.  Having considered the facts and circumstances of the present



case, the implications of withdrawal, and the objectives of the Code, we



are of the considered opinion that the CIRP initiated by admitting Petition



No. 729 of 2025, cannot be permitted to be withdrawn solely on the basis



of a settlement with one Financial Creditor. Accordingly, I.A. No.



166/2026 is dismissed.



                                                   (Emphasis supplied)



11. Further when we peruse Para 11.11 of the impugned order, it is clear



that the Adjudicating Authority has placed reliance on the judgment passed



by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in GLAS Trust Company LLC Vs. BYJU



Raveendran & Ors. in Civil Appeal No. 9986 of 2024 wherein the Hon’ble



Apex Court had considered the issue of withdrawal of CIRP prior to



constitution of the CoC and held that that after initiation of CIRP, the



proceedings assume the character of proceedings in rem and no longer remain



                                                   Page 8 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

the preserve of the original applicant. It is also pertinent to add here that



GLAS Trust judgement is dated 23.10.2024 and hence falls in the era of pre-



amended Section 12A and therefore squarely applicable in the present case.



12. The Adjudicating Authority has thereafter at para 11.13 of the



impugned order taken notice that in the present case, six other financial



creditors submitted their respective claims to the IRP and opposed the



withdrawal of the CIRP by way of filing intervention petitions. It has also



noticed that the IRP had earlier informed this Tribunal that claims aggregating



to approximately Rs. 600 Cr. had been received by him. The Adjudicating



Authority has therefore held that CIRP cannot be permitted to be withdrawn



solely on the basis of a settlement with one Financial Creditor or some



creditors since the approval of 90% of the CoC members warranted by Section



12A is to safeguard majority of the creditors.



13. At this stage, we must advert our attention to the relevant portions of



the GLAS Trust judgement supra as reproduced below:



   “42. From this scheme of Chapter II of the IBC, it appears that the admission

   of an application is a significant event that alters the nature of the

   proceedings, and the stakeholders involved. Initially, when the petition is

   filed by the financial creditor, operational creditor or corporate applicant, as

   the case may be, the proceedings are in personam and the only relevant

   stakeholders are the applicant creditor and the corporate debtor. However,

   once the petition is admitted and CIRP is initiated, several significant

   changes take place, including the transfer of the management of the affairs

   of the corporate debtor to the IRP, the declaration of the moratorium, and the

   collation of the claims against the corporate debtor. Therefore, the

   proceedings now change character – they become in rem and are no longer

   the preserve of only the applicant creditor and the corporate debtor and even

   creditors who were not the original applicants, become necessary

   stakeholders.



                                                   Page 9 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

   63. In essence, after a series of deliberations by the legislature, the

   executive and nudges by this Court, the framework created by Rule 8 of

   the NCLT Rules and Section 12A of the IBC read with Rule 30A of the CIRP

   Regulations lays down an exhaustive procedure for the withdrawal of an

   application filed by creditors under Sections 7, 9, or 10 of the IBC.

   Withdrawal may be sought at four stages, all of which have a procedure

   prescribed under the existing framework. These may be summarized as

   follows:



       i. Before the application under Sections 7, 9 or 10 is admitted by the

       NCLT: …….



       ii. After an application under Sections 7, 9, or 10 is admitted,

       but before the CoC has been constituted: Although Section 12A

       continues to be silent on this aspect, after the decision in Swiss Ribbons

       (supra), Regulation 30A was amended to provide for this eventuality.

       An application for withdrawal in such cases may be made by the

       applicant through the IRP. The IRP will then place the application before

       the NCLT, which may pass an order either approving or rejecting the

       application. As noted above, once the application has been admitted,

       the proceedings are no longer the sole preserve of the applicant creditor

       and the corporate debtor. They are now in rem and at this stage, the

       NCLT must hear the concerned parties and consider all relevant factors

       before approving or rejecting the application for withdrawal. The NCLT

       being a quasi-judicial body, must not act as a mere post office, which

       stamps and approves every settlement agreement, without application

       of judicial mind.



   81. Even if the procedural infirmity is kept aside, once the CIRP was

   admitted, the proceedings became collective, and all creditors of the

   Corporate Debtor became stakeholders. As noted in Swiss Ribbons (supra),

   even while invoking Rule 11 to allow withdrawal, the NCLT must hear all the

   concerned parties and consider all relevant factors on the facts of each

   case……”



                                                                                    (Emphasis supplied)



14. When we peruse the GLAS Trust judgement supra, we find that the



Hon’ble Apex Court identified four different stages during which a procedure



for the withdrawal of CIRP or settlement of claims is contemplated in the IBC



framework under the pre-amended Section 12A provisions. The situation



applicable in the present case is the second stage outlined at para 63(ii) of the



                                                   Page 10 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

GLAS Trust judgement supra where the Section 7 application of a Financial

Creditor has been admitted and CIRP initiated, though, the CoC has not yet

been formed. The proceedings had clearly turned into in rem proceedings

involving all creditors as necessary stakeholders.



15. We notice that in the present factual matrix, upon admission of the

Corporate Debtor into CIRP, six other Financial Creditors had filed

intervention petitions before the Adjudicating Authority. These intervenors

had also submitted that withdrawal of CIRP be not permitted solely on the

basis of settlement between the Appellant and Respondent No. 1. It is also

noticed that the IRP had admitted that claims amounting to approximately

Rs. 600 Cr. had been received.



16. In terms of the GLAS Trust judgment, at the post-CIRP admission but

pre-CoC stage, the Adjudicating Authority is required to hear the concerned

parties, consider all relevant factors and apply its judicial mind. Once CIRP is

initiated, the proceedings change character from in personam to in rem

proceedings and are no longer the preserve of the original Section 7 Financial

Creditor- Applicant. Merely because the settlement with the original Financial

Creditor-Respondent No. 1 had materialised, does not make it incumbent

upon the Adjudicating Authority to allow the withdrawal application without

hearing the contentions of all other concerned parties including creditors who

were not original applicants but were opposed to the withdrawal. The

Adjudicating Authority after having taken cognisance of the objections of

other creditors to the withdrawal proposal, who are stake-holders in the

present proceedings which has since assumed the character of in rem



                                                   Page 11 of 12



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2062 of 2026

proceedings, no infirmity is found in the impugned order in rejecting the

application for withdrawal.



17. In result, we find the Appeal to be devoid of merit. The impugned order

does not warrant any interference. The Appeal is dismissed with no costs.

                                           JUDGMENT



      Leave granted.



2. The present batch of appeals arises from judgments of the High

      Courts of Delhi, Calcutta and Telangana. Though the matters

      spring from distinct factual settings, they converge upon a common

      question: the composition of the Adjudicating Authority (AA) under

      the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), and its

      competence to discharge its functions through a single Member,

      more particularly one who is not a Judicial Member. The same

      question is raised in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 186/2025, instituted

      under Article 32 of the Constitution by one Mr. Pavel

      Aleksandrovich Prozorov.



3. The law against money laundering is, by its nature, a law of

      pursuit. It follows money through every disguise it is made to wear,

      across accounts, entities and borders, until the proceeds of crime

      can be traced back to their source. A law of pursuit must

      necessarily be a law of reach, and the PMLA does not want for it.

      Property may be attached, premises searched, assets frozen and

      persons arrested, often upon a belief recorded in writing by a single

      officer, and well before any court has had occasion to pronounce

      upon guilt.



                                                                                                                       Page 2 of 55

4. A statute that permits the State to reach into a citizen’s estate

      before guilt is proved must, in the same breath, tell the citizen

      before whom he may answer. The PMLA operates through the AA.

      A person whose property has been attached first presents their case

      before the AA. Throughout the investigation or trial, the AA’s order

      determines whether that person retains their property or must

      surrender possession to the Union. Put simply, the PMLA casts a

      broad net and the AA must determine what that net may lawfully

      encompass.



5. The authority of such a forum is conferred by the statute. Its

      credibility, however, must be earned by the competence of those

      who sit in it. The present batch asks whether that competence is

      assured when the AA speaks through a single Member who is not

      drawn from the field of law. The answer depends on what the AA is

      actually called upon to do: whether it is merely the keeper of the

      sealed cover, or whether it must also hold the scales.



6. The present batch tests the second of these aspects. It asks whether

      the AA may discharge its functions through a single Member who

      does not have legal background. The answer, as we shall explain,

      does not lie in the text of Section 6 alone. It turns on a closer

      understanding of what the AA is actually called upon to do: whether

      it is merely the keeper of the sealed cover, or whether it must also



                                                                                                                       Page 3 of 55

        hold the scales; and, if it does both, whether the same answer must

        govern each. It is with these considerations in view that we turn to

        the facts.



 A. FACTUAL MATRIX

 A.1 The Lead Matter: Civil Appeal No. 1548/2024

 7. At the outset, and for the sake of convenience, we shall advert in



        some detail to the facts of the lead matter, being Civil Appeal No.

        1548/2024.



7.1. The lead case traces its origin to an investigation by the Income Tax

        Department into the finances of M/s SRS Mining, a partnership

        firm of which the Respondent is the Managing Partner. On

        08.12.2016 and 09.12.2016, Income Tax Officers searched several

        office premises of the firm, as well as the residential premises of its

        partners, including the Respondent. The searches yielded cash

        exceeding Rs. 132.73 crores, comprising currency notes that had

        then recently been demonetised as well as the newly introduced Rs.

        2000 notes, together with 128.495 kg of gold, then valued at Rs.

        36.72 crores.



7.2. Independently of the proceedings relating to undisclosed income

        and the consequent evasion of tax, the Central Bureau of

        Investigation (CBI) registered FIR No. RC-MAI-2016-A-0040 against

        the partners of the firm and certain unidentified bank officials. It



                                                                                                                         Page 4 of 55

        was alleged that the partner of the firm had, in connivance with

        those officials, converted large sums of unaccounted demonetised

        currency into new currency notes, in breach of the guidelines

        issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Offences under Sections 409

        and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 13(2), 13(1)(c)

        and 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 came to be

        invoked accordingly.



7.3. Treating the said FIR as the predicate scheduled offence, the

        Directorate of Enforcement (ED) registered Enforcement Case

        Information Report (ECIR) No. 19/2016 dated 19.12.2016, and

        commenced an inquiry into allegations of money laundering

        connected with the offences under investigation by the CBI.



7.4. In the course of that investigation, the Deputy Director of the ED,

        namely Appellant No. 3, issued Provisional Attachment Order (PAO)

        No. 13/2017 dated 29.05.2017 under Section 5(1) of the PMLA,

        attaching movable properties standing in the name of the

        Respondent and valued at Rs. 8.57 crores. In compliance with

        Section 5(5), the Deputy Director thereafter filed Original

        Complaint (OC) No. 780/2017 before the AA on 12.06.2017.



7.5. Acting upon the complaint, the AA issued a notice dated

        21.06.2017 to the Respondent under Section 8(1), calling upon him

        to show cause why the provisionally attached properties should not



                                                                                                                         Page 5 of 55

        be declared to be involved in money laundering, and why the

        attachment should not, consequently, be confirmed. It bears notice

        that the AA then consisted only of a Technical Member, officiating

        as its Chairperson; no Member drawn from a judicial or legal

        background was then in office.

7.6. Aggrieved by the notice dated 21.06.2017, the Respondent

        instituted Writ Petition (Civil) No. 5320/2017 before the Delhi High

        Court, (i) challenging the vires of the second proviso to Section 5(1)

        of the PMLA; (ii) assailing the issuance of a show-cause notice by a

        single-Member AA without any Judicial Member; and (iii) seeking

        the quashing of the PAO dated 29.05.2017 as well as the notice

        dated 21.06.2017.

7.7. The writ petition was heard together with several others, in which

        the petitioners had laid a similar challenge to the vires of the same

        provisions of PMLA, while also seeking relief on the facts of their

        respective cases. Given the common questions of law, the batch

        was placed before a Division Bench of the High Court, which

        confined itself to those questions and did not enter upon the facts

        of the individual cases.



                                                                                                                         Page 6 of 55

7.8. By its judgment dated 11.01.2018, reported as J. Sekar v. Union

        of India,1 the Division Bench answered those questions in the

        following terms:



        (i) The writ petitions were maintainable before the Delhi High

              Court, the AA being located at New Delhi, even though the

              underlying proceedings under the PMLA arose outside the

              territorial jurisdiction of that Court;



        (ii) The power conferred upon officers of the ED to provisionally

              attach property under the second proviso to Section 5(1) of the

              PMLA was upheld, subject to the stipulation that the ‘reasons

              to believe that the non-attachment of the property is likely to

              frustrate any proceeding under this Act’, as recorded by such

              officer, must be conveyed to the person concerned as part of

              the show-cause notice issued by the AA;



        (iii) There is no statutory bar against a sole Member discharging

              the functions of the AA, whether sitting as a Bench or in the

              absence of the other Members;



        (iv) A Judicial Member is not required to form part of the AA, or of

              a Bench thereof, for the discharge of its functions under the

              PMLA; and



1 2018 SCC OnLine Del 6523.



                             Page 7 of 55

        (v) The writ petitions were directed to be placed before a Single

              Judge of the High Court for adjudication on their individual

              facts.



7.9. The Union of India, aggrieved by the findings in the judgment dated

        11.01.2018 on the maintainability of the writ petitions before the

        Delhi High Court and on the requirement to communicate the

        ‘reasons to believe’, preferred Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.

        12865/2018 before this Court. By an order dated 04.07.2018, this

        Court issued notice and stayed the operation of the said judgment.

        Leave was subsequently granted on 31.01.2024.



7.10.In the meantime, by an order dated 04.12.2018, the High Court

        permitted the Respondent to withdraw his writ petition and to

        pursue the statutory remedy before the AA. This, it appears, is also

        why the Respondent has not entered appearance in the present

        appeal, despite service having been effected.



 A.2 The Connected Matters

 8. The connected matters differ in their particular facts. For the sake



        of completeness, however, we consider it apposite to notice their

        salient features briefly.



8.1. The Appellant in Civil Appeal No. 1549/2024 had approached the

        Delhi High Court by way of Writ Petition (Civil) No. 8521/2017,



                                                                                                                         Page 8 of 55

        challenging the vires of the second proviso to Section 5(1) of PMLA,

        as also a show-cause notice issued by an AA consisting of a single

        Technical Member. That writ petition, too, was disposed of by the

        common judgment in J. Sekar (supra), which is under challenge

        in the lead case. Unlike the lead matter, however, this appeal has

        been preferred by a private party, who assails the findings of the

        High Court on the constitutionality of Section 5(1) and on the

        validity of an AA functioning through a single, non-Judicial

        Member.



8.2. The Appellant in the Civil Appeal arising out of Special Leave

        Petition (Civil) No. 7795/2024 approached the Calcutta High Court

        by way of a writ petition, seeking the quashing, or in the alternative,

        to keep in abeyance, the adjudication pending before the AA on an

        application made by the ED under Section 17(4) of the PMLA. The

        contention, once again, was that the AA could not adjudicate

        through a single Member, much less one who was not a Judicial

        Member. That contention was rejected by a learned Single Judge,

        and thereafter by the Division Bench in an intra-court appeal, in

        R.P. Infosystems Ltd. v. Adjudication Authority, PMLA.2



8.3. The Telangana High Court, by separate judgments and orders

        passed in Writ Appeal Nos. 611/2023 and 604/2023 and in Writ



2 (2023) 2 HCC (Cal) 251.



                           Page 9 of 55

        Petition No. 40454/2025, declined to interfere with show-cause

        notices issued by the AA under Section 8(1) of the PMLA. The

        Calcutta High Court, likewise, by a common order dated

        28.01.2026, disposed of a batch of writ petitions seeking analogous

        relief. Each of these decisions substantially follows the reasoning

        in J. Sekar (supra) and R.P. Infosystems Ltd. (supra). The private

        parties aggrieved thereby have preferred the remaining Special

        Leave Petitions, which now stand converted into Civil and Criminal

        (Civil) No. 5308/2026, which assails the order dated 28.01.2026,

        this Court has stayed the proceedings before the AA.



8.4. Lastly, the Petitioner in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 186/2025, mindful

        that the questions noticed above were already pending before this

        Court, has invoked Article 32. He seeks the quashing of the PAO

        dated 03.12.2024 issued in respect of his property, and of the

        also challenge the vires of Sections 6(5)(b) and 6(7) of the PMLA,



                                                                                                                       Page 10 of 55

      insofar as they permit certain matters before the AA to be heard by

      a Bench that does not include a Judicial Member.



B. CONTENTIONS OF THE PARTIES

B.1 On behalf of the Private Appellants

9. Mr. Vikram Chaudhri, Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan, Mr. S.



      Niranjan Reddy, and Mr. Siddharth Agarwal, learned Senior

      Counsel, and Mr. Mahfooz Ahsan Nazki, Mr. Jatin Sehgal, and Mr.

      Shubhankar Nag, learned counsel, argued on behalf of the

      Appellants in all matters other than Civil Appeal No. 1548/2024,

      and for the Petitioner in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 186/2025

      (collectively, the Private Appellants). Their common refrain was

      that the AA cannot function without a Judicial Member, and that a

      single Member without a legal background cannot be permitted to

      discharge its functions. In support, they urged as follows:



      (a) The AA discharges quasi-judicial functions. It appreciates the

             facts and documents placed on record, interprets statutory

             and penal provisions, and determines whether the property in

             question constitutes ‘proceeds of crime’ and is involved in

             money laundering. Such an exercise calls for a Judicial

             Member, capable of applying settled legal standards to the

             facts of each case;



                                                                                                                     Page 11 of 55

(b) Parliament has established the AA as a necessary safeguard

      against arbitrary action by officers of the ED, by requiring that

      the material in their possession and the ‘reasons to believe’

      recorded by them be forwarded to the AA forthwith. Such a

      process empowers, inter alia, the provisional attachment of

      property, search and seizure, whether of premises or of

      persons, and arrest of accused persons. Heavy reliance was

      placed on the decision of a coordinate Bench of this Court in

      Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India,3 wherein the

      AA has been identified as the objective custodian of the reasons

      recorded in writing and the material relied upon by the ED at

      the stages of provisional attachment, search and seizure, and

      arrest. Given this role, it was urged, that a Member with a

      judicially trained mind must participate in such processes if

      the object of the legislation is to be fully realised;



(c) The decisions of the AA bear gravely upon the civil rights of the

      persons concerned, particularly their right to the possession of

      their properties. Once the AA confirms an attachment, the

      person ceases to enjoy any benefit from the asset, a position

      that continues for a period of 365 days during investigation, or

      until a final order of confiscation or detachment is passed by



3 (2023) 12 SCC 1, para 191 and 193.



                                      Page 12 of 55

      the Special Court upon the conclusion of the trial. A decision

      entailing such civil consequences, it was argued, cannot be

      entrusted to a body manned only by Administrative or

      Accounting Members without any judicial background;



(d) Section 11 of the PMLA vests the AA with powers akin to those

      of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so as

      to ensure a complete record and adherence to the principles of

      natural justice. Sub-section (3) thereof goes further and

      stipulates that its proceedings shall be treated as judicial

      proceedings. This must be read with Section 41, by which

      Parliament has barred the jurisdiction of civil courts over

      matters that the AA is empowered to determine. The AA, thus

      exercising powers which would ordinarily vest in civil courts,

      cannot function without a Judicial Member;



(e) Further, the Judicial Member must be the Chairperson of the

      AA, so as to preserve the objectivity and legal integrity of its

      determinations. This, it was urged, follows from the principles

      laid down by a Constitution Bench of this Court in L. Chandra

      Kumar v. Union of India,4 which mandate judicial



4 (1997) 3 SCC 261.



                     Page 13 of 55

      independence in Tribunals and other quasi-judicial bodies that

      oust the jurisdiction of the regular courts;



(f) The availability of an appeal against orders of the AA to the

      Appellate Tribunal (AT) under Section 26 of the PMLA, and of

      a further appeal to High Court under Section 42, does not

      detract from the adjudicatory character of the functions of the

      AA, or from the need for judicial objectivity in its decision-

      making. The mere availability of an appellate remedy before a

      judicial forum does not displace the quasi-judicial duties cast

      upon the AA; and



(g) Under Section 6(5) of the PMLA, the AA is to exercise its

      jurisdiction through ‘Benches’. Each Bench, it was contended,

      must consist of the Chairperson together with one or both of

      the other Members, and not of the Chairperson or a Member

      sitting alone. In support, reliance was placed on Regulation

      26(2) of the Adjudicating Authority (Procedure) Regulations,

      2013, which provides that “Every sheet of the order shall bear

      the signature of the Chairperson and Members constituting

      the Bench.” A Bench without the Chairperson is, therefore, not

      contemplated. On the same footing, the reference in Section

      6(7) to ‘a Bench consisting of two Members’ was said to denote

      a Bench of the Chairperson together with both the other



                                                                                                            Page 14 of 55

             Members, as distinct from a regular Bench of the Chairperson

             and one Member.



B.2 On behalf of the Union of India and the Directorate of

Enforcement

10. Mr. Anil Kaushik, learned Additional Solicitor General of India, and



      Mr. Zoheb Hossain, learned Senior Counsel, appeared for the Union

      of India and the ED. Controverting the submissions of Private

      Appellants, they contended that neither Section 6 nor any other

      provision of the PMLA forbids the functions of the AA from being

      discharged by a Bench consisting of a single Member drawn from

      an administrative or accounting background. In elaboration, they

      submitted as follows:



      (a) The language of Section 6 of the PMLA is plain and admits of

             no ambiguity. It neither requires the Chairperson to be drawn

             from the field of law, nor requires every Bench to include the

             Judicial Member;



      (b) On a true construction of clause (b) of sub-section (5), read

             with sub-section (7), a Bench would ordinarily consist of a

             single Member, and a matter may be placed before a Bench of

             two Members where circumstances of the kind contemplated

             in sub-section (7) arise. The composition of the AA as an



                                                                                                                     Page 15 of 55

      institution must not be conflated with the constitution of its

      Benches, which would ordinarily consist of one Member alone;



(c) There is no warrant for reading into the provisions a

      requirement that a Judicial Member must participate in every

      decision of the AA. Regulation 26 of the Adjudicating Authority

      (Procedure) Regulations, 2013 is purely procedural, and

      merely acknowledges that a Bench may consist of the

      Chairperson and Members. No mandate can be drawn from it;

      and, in any event, a procedural regulation cannot impose a

      restriction that the parent enactment does not contemplate;



(d) The functions of the AA are, in essence, administrative, the AA

      acting as the repository of the material relied upon and the

      reasons recorded by the officers of ED. The process of

      adjudication is also inherently an executive function and is

      entrusted to executive functionaries under various other

      enactments, such as the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic

      Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS), the Smugglers and Foreign

      Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976

      (SAFEMA), the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions

      Act, 1988 (Benami Act), and the Customs Act, 1962 (Customs

      Act). The AA cannot, therefore, be equated with ordinary



                                                                                                            Page 16 of 55

             courts or tribunals so as to require the participation of legally

             trained members; and



      (e) The allocation of cases and functions according to the expertise

             they require is best left to the wisdom of the Chairperson of the

             AA, since the demands of each case turn upon its own facts.



C. ISSUES FOR CONSIDERATION

11. We have heard learned Senior Counsel and learned counsel for the



      parties at a considerable length and have carefully perused the

      record.



12. We must note at the outset that although the Union of India has

      preferred Civil Appeal No. 1548/2024 against the judgment in J.

      Sekar (supra), specifically on the territorial jurisdiction of the

      Delhi High Court and on the legal necessity for the AA to forward

      the ‘reasons to believe’ recorded under the second proviso to

      Section 5(1), neither side has advanced substantive submissions

      on these aspects. This is all the more so because the Respondent

      in that appeal, J. Sekar, has not entered appearance before this

      Court. Moreover, since the filing of that Special Leave Petition in

      2018, this Court has upheld the vires of the second proviso to

      Section 5(1) in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (supra), with specific

      reference to J. Sekar (supra). In these circumstances, we consider

      it appropriate to refrain from expressing any opinion on these



                                                                                                                     Page 17 of 55

      issues in the present batch, while clarifying that the parties shall

      remain at liberty to raise their contentions thereon in appropriate

      proceedings.



13. The following principal issues, accordingly, arise for our

      consideration:



       i. Whether the AA can discharge its functions through a single,

             non-Judicial Member?



     ii. Whether every Bench of the AA must include a Judicial

             Member?



    iii. Whether the Chairperson of the AA must necessarily be a

             Judicial Member?



D. ANALYSIS

D.1 The Legislative Architecture of the Adjudicating Authority

14. Before we construe the provisions of the PMLA in the light of rival



      contentions, it is necessary to understand the place that the AA

      occupies within the scheme of the statute.



15. The PMLA was enacted to prevent money laundering and to provide

      for the confiscation of the monies and properties involved in it. The

      identification, securing and eventual confiscation of such property

      is, as the objects of the Act themselves make clear, central to its

      design. It is to this end that Section 6 constitutes the AA as a civil



                                                                                                                     Page 18 of 55

      adjudicatory authority, entrusted with various functions in relation



      to the properties, assets and records seized or attached by the ED



      in exercise of its powers under the same statute.



16. As originally enacted, the PMLA contemplated more than one AA,



      the Central Government being empowered to appoint ‘one or more



      Adjudicating Authorities’. The legislative design, evidently, was that



      there could be several AAs, each consisting of a Chairperson and



      two Members.



17. That design was altered by the Prevention of Money Laundering



      (Amendment) Act, 2009 (2009 Amendment), which replaced every



      reference to multiple AAs with the singular. There is, therefore, now



      only one Adjudicating Authority. Section 6, as it presently stands,



      reads as follows:



              “6. Adjudicating Authorities, composition, powers, etc.–

              (1) The Central Government shall, by notification, appoint an

              Adjudicating Authority to exercise jurisdiction, powers and

              authority conferred by or under this Act.

              (2) An Adjudicating Authority shall consist of a

              Chairperson and two other Members:

              Provided that one Member each shall be a person having

              experience in the field of law, administration, finance or

              accountancy.

              (3) A person shall, however, not be qualified for appointment as

              Member of an Adjudicating Authority,—



                     (a) in the field of law, unless he—

                            (i) is qualified for appointment as District Judge; or

                            (ii) has been a member of the Indian Legal Service and

                            has held a post in Grade I of that service;



                     (b) in the field of finance, accountancy or administration

                     unless he possesses such qualifications, as may be

                     prescribed.



                                                                                                                     Page 19 of 55

              (4) The Central Government shall appoint a Member to be

              the Chairperson of the Adjudicating Authority.

              (5) Subject to the provisions of this Act,—



                     (a) the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority may

                     be exercised by Benches thereof;

                     (b) a Bench may be constituted by the Chairperson of

                     the Adjudicating Authority with one or two Members

                     as the Chairperson of the Adjudicating Authority may

                     deem fit;

                     (c) the Benches of the Adjudicating Authority shall

                     ordinarily sit at New Delhi and at such other places

                     as the Central Government may, in consultation with

                     the Chairperson, by notification, specify;

                     (d) the Central Government shall, by notification,

                     specify the areas in relation to which each Bench of

                     the Adjudicating Authority may exercise jurisdiction.

              (6) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (5),

              the Chairperson may transfer a Member from one Bench to

              another Bench.

              (7) If at any stage of the hearing of any case or matter it

              appears to the Chairperson or a Member that the case or

              matter is of such a nature that it ought to be heard by a

              Bench consisting of two Members, the case or matter may

              be transferred by the Chairperson or, as the case may be,

              referred to him for transfer, to such Bench as the

              Chairperson may deem fit.

              (8) The Chairperson and every Member shall hold office as such

              for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon

              his office: Provided that no Chairperson or other Member shall

              hold office as such after he has attained the age of sixty-five

              years.



                                           xx xx xx xx

              (13) In the event of the occurrence of any vacancy in the office of

              the Chairperson by reason of his death, resignation or otherwise,

              the senior-most Member shall act as the Chairperson of the

              Adjudicating Authority until the date on which a new

              Chairperson, appointed in accordance with the provisions of this

              Act to fill such vacancy, enters upon his office.



                                           xx xx xx xx”

                                                                     [Emphasis supplied]



18. A plain reading of the above provision discloses the following



      design. There is to be a single AA, consisting of three Members



      drawn, one each, from the fields of (i) law; (ii) administration; and



      (iii) finance or accountancy. The AA thus has a Judicial Member,



                                                                                                                     Page 20 of 55

      an Administrative Member and a Financial Member. It is to

      function through Benches, which may consist of some or all of

      these Members, and for which territorial jurisdiction may be

      specified.



19. One of the three Members is to be appointed as the Chairperson,

      who exercises administrative superintendence over the functioning

      of the AA, including by constituting Benches and allocating cases

      and applications among the Members. Sub-sections (13) and (14)

      ensure that such superintendence continues uninterrupted where

      the office of the Chairperson falls vacant, or where the Chairperson

      is unable to discharge those functions.



20. The appointment of Chairperson and Members is governed by the

      Prevention of Money-Laundering (Appointment and Conditions of

      Service of Chairperson and Members of Adjudicating Authorities)

      Rules, 2007 (2007 Rules). Rule 3 thereof restates the eligibility

      prescribed in Section 6(3)(a) for the Member from the field of law

      and lays down the qualifications required for the other two

      Members. Rule 4 constitutes a Selection Committee for the

      appointment of Members, consisting of (i) the Revenue Secretary,

      Government of India, as Chairman; (ii) the Secretary, Department

      of Legal Affairs, Government of India; and (iii) the Chairman,

      Central Board of Direct Taxes, or the Chairman, Central Board of



                                                                                                                     Page 21 of 55

      Excise and Customs, as Members. Under Rule 5, the Selection

      Committee is further tasked with recommending one of the

      Members for appointment as the Chairperson.



D.2 The Text of Section 6: Who May Sit, and in What Number

21. The submissions of the parties proceed on two planes: the textual



      import of Section 6 of the PMLA, and the necessity of legal

      objectivity in the functioning of AA. We consider it prudent to

      address the former first, since it is the text of the statute that marks

      the outer limits within which any further inquiry must proceed.



22. Nothing in the PMLA or in the 2007 Rules requires the Chairperson

      of the AA to be drawn from the field of law. The contrast with the

      provisions that governed the AT is instructive. Section 6(3) merely

      prescribes the eligibility of the Member from the field of law, and

      Section 6(4) does not require that such Member alone be appointed

      as the Chairperson. Section 28(1), on the other hand, as it stood

      before Sections 27 and 28 were omitted by the Finance Act, 2016,

      specifically provided that only a person who has been, or is

      qualified to be, a Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court

      could be appointed as the Chairperson of the AT. Where Parliament

      intended the head of an adjudicatory body under this very Statute

      to be a judicially trained person, it has said so in categorical terms.

      Its silence in the case of the AA is, therefore, not an inadvertent



                                                                                                                     Page 22 of 55

      omission on the part of the draftsman, but a conscious and

      deliberate legislative choice.



23. As to the constitution of a ‘Bench’ under Section 6(5)(b), the Private

      Appellants have strenuously argued that the expression ‘one or two

      Members’ refers only to the other Members, and is exclusive of, and

      in addition to, the Chairperson. The Union of India and the ED, per

      contra, contend that the expression means that a Bench may

      consist of ‘one or two Members’ in all, with or without the

      Chairperson. In essence, the Private Appellants claim and the

      Official Respondents repel the submission that ‘Bench’ cannot

      mean a Single-Member Bench.



24. Such contention of the Private Appellants, however, fails to pass

      muster, both literally and contextually.



25. On the first count, we must observe that the word ‘Bench’ does not

      always signify a panel of judges. It can, in appropriate cases, also

      refer to a Single-Member Bench. The Oxford Advanced Learners

      Dictionary,5 inter alia, defines the word as “a judge in court or the

      seat where he/she sits; the position of being a judge or magistrate”.

      It is also described as “the raised area occupied by the judge in its

      official capacity” or “the court considered in its official capacity” by



5 Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary (11th edn, OUP 2026).



                                                              Page 23 of 55

      the Black’s Law Dictionary.6 The import of the term ‘Bench’,



      evidently, is towards the position and role of the Court or other



      adjudicatory body, not to plurality of judges executing such role.



      Hence, in a lexicographical sense, it cannot be said that the use of



      the expression ‘Bench’ would invariably denote multiple members



      of a Tribunal. This understanding, in the context of the Rules of the



      High Court at Patna, was approved by a coordinate Bench of this



      Court vide judgement in Rajendra Prasad Jain v. Sheel Bhadra



      Yajee,7 holding as follows:



              “2. … The first is that the word “Bench” used in the referring

              order cannot be interpreted as necessarily indicating that the

              case must be laid before two or more Judges. In this connection,

              the language of Rule 1(xi) and Rule 3 of Chapter II of the Rules of

              the High Court at Patna is significant. Under Rule 1(xi), a case

              under the Indian Companies Act is to be heard by a Single Judge;

              and Rule 3 indicates the nature of one of the orders which can

              be passed by a Bench hearing the case under Rule 1(xi). Thus,

              in Rule 3 of the Rules of the High Court at Patna itself a Single

              Judge is referred to as a Bench. In fact, it is well-known that,

              when referring to Judges of the High Court sitting to decide a

              case, the expressions frequently used are Single Bench and

              Division Bench. The word “Bench” used in the referring

              order, even in its ordinary connotation, would, therefore,

              include a Single Judge. …”



                                                                     [Emphasis supplied]



26. A contextual reading of Section 6 of the PMLA makes it further clear



      that the Bench need not necessarily include the Chairperson. The



      term ‘Member’ includes the Chairperson. Sub-section (2) of Section



      6 provides that the AA shall consist of “a Chairperson and two other



6 Black's Law Dictionary (12th edn, Thomson Reuters 2024).

7 1967 SCC OnLine SC 258.



                                                            Page 24 of 55

      Members,” while sub-section (4), read with Rule 5 of the 2007

      Rules, makes it clear that the Chairperson is one of the Members,

      appointed to that office. Sub-section (7), similarly, enables the

      transfer and assignment of a case to a Bench of at least two

      Members, leaving no doubt that a ‘Bench’ may consist of one or two

      Members. If a Single-Member Bench is of the view that the case

      assigned to it is required to be heard by a two-Member Bench, the

      Member may refer the matter to the Chairperson for transfer. The

      Chairperson may also exercise such power suo motu, if he deems

      fit. This reading also accords with the manner in which the terms

      ‘Chairperson’ and ‘Member’ of the AT are defined in Sections 2(1)(g)

      and 2(1)(o) of the PMLA.



27. Were the Chairperson to be excluded from the expression ‘one or

      two Members’, as urged by the Private Appellants, a Bench of ‘two

      Members’ sitting with the Chairperson would mean that the AA sit

      and hear cases en bloc, rending Section 6(5) of PMLA redundant.

      There is no gainsaying that such could not have been the intention

      of the legislature. The expression ‘one or two Members’ cannot,

      therefore, be read so as to place the Chairperson in a class apart

      from the Members.



28. We, thus, find greater force in the construction advanced by the

      Union of India, namely, that a Bench may consist of one Member,



                                                                                                                     Page 25 of 55

      being either the Chairperson or one of the other Members, or of two

      Members, being either the Chairperson and one other Member, or

      the two Members other than the Chairperson.



29. Equally, nothing in the text of the PMLA mandates the Member

      from a judicial or legal background to sit on every Bench.



30. The bare text of the PMLA, therefore, lends no support to the

      submissions of Private Appellants. That, however, does not

      conclude the inquiry. The Private Appellants urge, in the

      alternative, that the nature of the functions entrusted to the AA

      itself demands the participation of a Judicial Member, and that

      such a requirement must be read into the statute. It is to this

      contention that we now turn.



D.3 The Functions of the AA and the Need for a Legal Mind

31. Section 6(1) contemplates that the AA shall exercise the



      jurisdiction, powers and authority conferred upon it by or under

      the PMLA. To take a complete view, it is appropriate to enumerate

      the functions so entrusted:



      (i) Under Sections 5(2), 16(2), 17(2), 18(2), 19(2), 20(2) and 21(2),

             the AA receives a copy of the PAO or other order passed by the

             officer of the ED, together with the material in the officer’s



                                                                                                                     Page 26 of 55

      possession or the reasons recorded by the officer in writing,

      and preserves the same for the prescribed period;



(ii) Under Section 5(5), the AA receives a complaint from the officer

      of the ED, setting out the facts that led to the PAO and seeking

      confirmation of the attachment of the properties concerned;



(iii) Under Sections 17(4) and 18(10), the AA receives an

      application from the officer of the ED, seeking the retention of

      property or records seized, or the continuation of the freezing

      of any asset;



(iv) Under Section 8(1), the AA issues a notice to all persons

      concerned, calling upon them to indicate the sources of their

      income in respect of the properties in question, and to show

      cause why the attachment should not be confirmed; the

      property or record should not be retained; or the freezing of the

      asset should not be continued;



(v) Under Section 8(2), the AA affords the parties a full oral

      hearing and considers their rival submissions, before

      recording a finding as to whether or not the property in

      question is involved in money laundering;



(vi) Under Section 8(3), the AA passes an order consequent upon

      that finding, confirming the attachment, retention, freezing, or



                                                                                                            Page 27 of 55

             other action regarding the property, record, or asset, as the

             case may be;



      (vii) Under the first proviso to Section 9, the AA determines whether

             any encumbrance or leasehold interest over attached property

             was created to defeat the provisions of Chapter III of the PMLA,

             and, if so, declares such encumbrance or interest to be void;

             and



    (viii) Under Sections 20(4) and 21(4), the AA, if satisfied that the

             retention of a property or record is necessary for adjudication

             under Section 8, permits such retention beyond 180 days.



32. On a closer examination, these functions fall into two distinct

      categories. In the first, the AA receives and preserves the reasons

      recorded, and the material relied upon, by officers of the ED when

      they attach property, conduct searches and seizures, freeze assets

      or records, or arrest persons. In the second, the AA adjudicates

      upon the complaints and applications filed by the ED, and

      determines whether the property in question is involved in money

      laundering, with consequential orders following upon that

      determination. In the former, the AA is the keeper of the sealed

      cover; in the latter, it holds the scales.



                                                                                                                     Page 28 of 55

33. The Private Appellants rely heavily on both sets of functions to

      contend that the absence of a Judicial Member would render the

      objectivity of the AA nugatory. In our considered view, the two roles

      differ substantially in their nature and consequence, and the

      submissions must, therefore, be evaluated separately in relation to

      each.



D.3.1 The Custodial Function: Receiving and Retaining the

‘Reasons to Believe’ and the ‘Material Relied Upon’

34. The PMLA empowers officers of the ED to take a range of



      investigative and preventive measures in order to combat money

      laundering, including search and seizure, the search of persons,

      the freezing of intangible property, the attachment of property and

      the arrest of persons. Powers of such amplitude must, as a

      necessary concomitant, be accompanied by adequate safeguards

      against their misuse.



35. It is for this purpose that the PMLA designates the AA as an

      objective and independent body, to which officers of the ED must

      forward the relevant material whenever they exercise these powers.

36. A reading of these provisions makes it clear that the procedure for

      furnishing the reasons to believe, and the material on which that

      belief rests, calls for no active or overt step on the part of AA. The

      AA acts, rather, as the custodian of these sealed reports, the object

      being to instil accountability in the decision-making of the officers

      of the ED. By requiring that the reports be furnished immediately,

      Parliament has placed upon the ED the responsibility of

      committing its reasons, at the very moment of action, to the keeping

      of an independent body. The reasons so committed then stand as

      a contemporaneous record, against which the action of the officer

      may later be tested.



37. Notwithstanding the importance of this safeguard, we may observe

      that this role of the AA is essentially administrative in nature. In

      receiving these reports and ensuring their availability when

      required, the AA is not called upon to undertake any substantive

      decision-making involving the appreciation of competing

      submissions or the interpretation of statutes.

      persuaded that the absence of a Judicial Member would impair the

Facts



7.     Relevant facts may be briefly noted.



8.     Appellant is the proprietor of M/s Nikhra Warehouse



situated at Dabra in the district of Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh.



The warehouse was used to store agricultural produce of



farmers for which consideration was charged and paid. The



agricultural produce stored was hypothecated with the State



Bank of India, Dabra (SBI). For such hypothecation, it was



mandatory for the appellant to insure the stock of agricultural



produce stored in the warehouse. To insure the warehouse



building as well as the stock lying therein, appellant obtained



from the respondents Insurance Policy No. 1001/0066099 for



the period from 13.12.2006 to 12.04.2007 for a sum of



Rs. 50,00,000.00 covering the warehouse building and for a



further sum of Rs. 1,50,00,000.00 in respect of the stock lying



in the warehouse. Appellant had obtained another insurance



policy of equivalent amount for burglary.



9.     On 13.03.2007, at about 05:00 pm, Dabra and its



adjoining areas experienced a severe hailstorm followed by



       4

heavy rainfall. Because of the hailstorm, the asbestos sheet

roofing of the warehouse suffered extensive damage resulting in

rainwater seeping into the warehouse premises. Not only the

roofing was damaged extensively, but a part of the agricultural

produce stored in the warehouse got damaged by the rainwater.

As per the stock register maintained by the warehouse,

agricultural produce valued at Rs. 1,50,00,000.00 were stored

in the warehouse at the time of the incident. Appellant engaged

the services of a valuer M.L. Gupta who quantified the loss to

the agricultural produce at Rs. 36,83,955.00 and the damage

to the warehouse building at Rs. 6,41,268.00.



10.  The incident was reported to the respondents who



appointed M/s Cunningham Lindsey International Pvt. Ltd. as



the surveyor to assess the damage.



11.  Appellant also brought the matter to the notice of the



local revenue authorities. The Tehsildar assessed the loss



caused to the agricultural produce at Rs. 36,83,955.00 and the



damage to the warehouse building at Rs. 6,41,268.00.



     5

12.     M/s Cunningham Lindsey International Pvt. Ltd.



submitted its final survey report on 16.07.2007. The surveyor



acknowledged the damage suffered qua the warehouse building



and estimated the loss at Rs. 1,44,401.00. In so far the



agricultural produce stored in the warehouse were concerned,



the surveyor opined that the same belonged to third-parties and



were held by the appellant in trust. Therefore, the agricultural



produce which suffered damage were not covered under the



insurance policy in view of the General Exclusion Clause 5.



13.     At that stage, appellant instituted Consumer



Complaint No. 16 of 2007 before the State Commission seeking



total compensation of Rs. 50,45,223.00 with interest. The



complaint was resisted by the respondents who took the stand



that the agricultural produce stored in the warehouse and



which suffered damage were held in trust by the appellant as



those belonged to third-parties. As per the exclusion clause,



insurance claim did not cover the said damaged agricultural



stock.



        6

14.      Upon consideration of the pleadings and other

         compensated for the loss suffered in the warehouse?



         ii. whether there was loss of goods in the warehouse

         and, if so, whether the complainant was not entitled to

         any compensation as those goods were held in trust?



15.      On the first issue, the State Commission held that



the damage caused to the warehouse building stood established



and assessed the loss at Rs. 6,41,268.00. Accordingly, the State



Commission held that the appellant was entitled to



compensation to that extent.



16.      In so far the second issue is concerned, the State



Commission considered the claim in respect of the agricultural



produce stored in the warehouse. It took note of the assessment



made by the Tehsildar quantifying the loss at Rs. 36,83,955.00



as well as the stock register maintained for the SBI. The



contention of the respondents that the goods were held in trust



and were not covered by the insurance policy in the absence of



         7

payment of a special premium was not accepted. The State

Commission noted that two insurance policies were obtained

by the appellant from the respondents: one policy for

Rs. 1,50,00,000.00 for burglary covering all the stock and

another policy for the warehouse building and stocks for

Rs. 1,50,00,000.00 (sic). The two insurance policies were not

obtained in the abstract which indicated the insurer’s

awareness of the nature of the property sought to be insured,

further observing that issuance of the two policies indicated

that the insurance arrangement extended to the warehouse and

Submissions



19.  Mr. Navin Pahwa, learned senior counsel appearing

committed a manifest error in rejecting the claim of the



appellant towards damage caused to the agricultural produce



stored in the warehouse by placing reliance on General



Exclusion Clause 5 of the Standard Fire and Special Perils



Policy. He submits that National Commission failed to



appreciate the insurance policy as a whole and proceeded on



the erroneous assumption that since the agricultural produce



stored in the warehouse belonged to third-party farmers, the



same automatically fell within the expression ‘goods held in



trust’. According to him, such an interpretation defeats the very



purpose for which the insurance policy was obtained.



             10

19.1.  Mr. Pahwa submits that the National Commission

agricultural produce stored in the warehouse. It is evident that



the relationship between the appellant and the owners of the
