```text
Analysis



21.        Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties



have received the due consideration of the Court. The



judgments cited at the Bar have also been carefully perused and



analyzed.



22.        There is no dispute as to the facts. It is admitted that



there was a hailstorm followed by heavy rains on 13.03.2007 as



a result of which the warehouse and the agricultural stock



stored therein suffered extensive damage. There is also no



dispute as to the holding (existence) of insurance policy by the



appellant when the aforesaid occurrence took place. The



controversy boils down to applicability of the General Exclusion



Clause 5 to the agricultural produce stored in the warehouse,



the nature of the relationship between the appellant and the



owners of the agricultural produce, and the extent of the loss



           20

for which indemnification is payable under the insurance

policy.



23.       Therefore, the question which falls for our consideration



is whether the agricultural produce belonging to the farmers and



stored in the appellant’s warehouse should be taken as ‘goods held



in trust’ or ‘on commission’ within the meaning of the General



Exclusion Clause 5? Or, whether the relationship between the



appellant and the owners of such agricultural goods was one of



bailor and bailee arising out of a contractual bailment?



Corollary to the above question is, whether upon a proper



construction of the insurance policy, including the agreed bank



clause, the respondents-insurer are liable to indemnify the loss



suffered on account of the damage to the stored agricultural



produce?



24.       Before proceeding further, it would be useful to



examine the nature of an insurance contract or how an



insurance contract is to be interpreted. In Vikram Greentech



India Limited Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited8, a two-



8 (2009) 5 SCC 599



                                                         21

Judge Bench of this Court examined the nature of an insurance

contract and how its terms are to be interpreted in the following

manner:



       16. An insurance contract is a species of commercial

       transactions and must be construed like any other

       contract to its own terms and by itself. In a contract of

       insurance, there is requirement of uberrima fides i.e.

       good faith on the part of the insured. Except that, in other

       respects, there is no difference between a contract of

       insurance and any other contract.



       17. The four essentials of a contract of insurance are : (i)

       the definition of the risk, (ii) the duration of the risk, (iii)

       the premium, and (iv) the amount of insurance. Since

       upon issuance of the insurance policy, the insurer

       undertakes to indemnify the loss suffered by the insured

       on account of the risks covered by the insurance policy,

       its terms have to be strictly construed to determine the

       extent of liability of the insurer.



24.1.  Thus, what can be deduced from the above is that an



insurance contract is a species of commercial transactions. It



must be construed like any other contract having regard to its



terms and conditions. It is based on uberrima fides i.e. good



faith on the part of the insured. While the four essentials of an



insurance contract are: i) definition of the risk; ii) duration of



       22

the risk; iii) premium; and iv) amount of insurance, the terms

of the insurance policy would have to be strictly construed to

determine the extent of liability of the insurer.



24.2.  Proceeding further, this Court in Greentech opined



that the endeavour of the Court should always be to interpret



the words in which the contract is expressed by the parties.



Referring to earlier decisions of this Court, the Bench held that



the Court while construing the terms of a policy is not expected



to venture into extra liberalism that may result in re-writing the



contract or substituting the terms which were not intended by



the parties. The insured cannot claim anything more than what



is covered by the insurance policy. This Court held thus:



       18. The endeavour of the court must always be to

       interpret the words in which the contract is expressed by

       the parties. The court while construing the terms of policy

       is not expected to venture into extra liberalism that may

       result in rewriting the contract or substituting the terms

       which were not intended by the parties. The insured

       cannot claim anything more than what is covered by the

       insurance policy.



       23

25.  What follows is that while interpreting an insurance



contract, it has to be borne in mind that the rights and



obligations of the parties to the said contract i.e. the insurer



and the insured would have to be determined from the terms



and conditions of the policy itself. The policy has to be read as



a whole having regard to the nature of the insurance cover and



the purpose for which it was obtained. The task of the court is



neither to enlarge the contract by resorting to equitable



considerations nor to restrict its meaning by an isolated or



excessively literal reading of one or few of its stipulations. The



words of the policy must, therefore, be understood in their



proper setting so as to give meaningful effect to the contractual



undertaking of the parties.



26.  The principles governing interpretation of insurance



policies were further elucidated in Canara Bank. After referring



to earlier decisions of this Court, the Bench held as under:



     22. The principles relating to interpretation of insurance

     policies are well settled and not in dispute. At the same

     time, the provisions of the policy must be read and

     interpreted in such a manner so as to give effect to the

     reasonable expectations of all the parties including the



                             24

       insured and the beneficiaries. It is also well settled that

       coverage provisions should be interpreted broadly and if

       there is any ambiguity, the same should be resolved in

       favour of the insured. On the other hand, the exclusion

       clauses must be read narrowly. The policy and its

       components must be read as a whole and given a

       meaning which furthers the expectations of the parties

       and also the business realities. According to us, the

       entire policy should be understood and examined in such

       a manner and when that is done, the interpretation

       becomes a commercially sensible interpretation.



26.1.  Thus, what this decision tells us is that provisions of



an insurance policy must be read and interpreted in such



a manner so as to give effect to the reasonable expectations of



all the parties including the insured and the beneficiaries.



Coverage provisions should be interpreted broadly. If there is



any ambiguity, the same should be resolved in favour of the



insured. In so far an exclusion clause is concerned, it must be



read narrowly. The policy and its components must be read as



a whole and given a meaning which furthers the expectations of



the parties and also the business realities.



       25

27.  This Court in Shivram Chandra Jagarnath Cold



Storage Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited9, after



referring to earlier decisions of this Court, held that an



insurance policy must be construed only with reference to its



stipulations and no artificial meaning can be given to the words



of the policy. The exceptions to an insurance policy must be



construed strictly since they reflect the agreement between the



parties with respect to the losses that are covered by the



insurance policy. Any departure from this principle is possible



only if the terms of the policy are ambiguous or unclear. In the



event, two constructions are possible or if there is an ambiguity,



a construction that is beneficial to the insured should be



adopted consistent with the purpose of the policy. Another



instance where exception clauses may be interpreted to the



benefit of the insured is when the exception clauses are too wide



and not consistent with the main purpose or object of the



insurance policy. When the option is between taking a view



which will relieve the distress and agony of the victims or their



dependents on one hand and the equally plausible view which



9 (2022) 4 SCC 539



                                                         26

will reduce the profitability of the insurer in regard to the

occupational hazard undertaken by him by way of business

activity, there is hardly any choice. The court cannot but opt for

the former view. Even if one were to take a strict doctrinaire

approach, the very same conclusion would emerge by applying

the doctrine of ‘reading down’ the exclusion clause in the light

of the main purpose of the insurance contract so that the

exclusion clause does not cross swords with the main purpose.

The effort must be to harmonise the two instead of allowing the

exclusion clause to snipe successfully at the main purpose.



28.  Thus, what can be culled out from the above decision



is that while an exclusionary clause should not be disregarded



merely because it operates against the insurer, the task is to



ascertain the exact scope of the exclusion not only from the



language employed in the exclusion clause but from a



wholesome reading of the insurance policy itself. The exceptions



to an insurance policy has to be construed strictly. Where the



language admits of more than one interpretation, the construction which



is favourable to the insured should be preferred. It must always be borne



     27

in mind that an exclusion cannot be applied in a manner which defeats

the principal object of the insurance policy.



29.    In Texco Marketing Private Limited Vs. Tata AIG



General Insurance Company Limited10, a two-Judge Bench of



this Court examined as to how an exclusion clause in a contract



of insurance has to be interpretated and held as under:



       12. An exclusion clause in a contract of insurance has to

       be interpreted differently. Not only the onus but also the

       burden lies with the insurer when reliance is made on

       such a clause. This is for the reason that insurance

       contracts are special contracts premised on the notion of

       good faith. It is not a leverage or a safeguard for the

       insurer, but is meant to be pressed into service on a contingency,

       being a contract of speculation. An insurance contract by its very

       nature mandates disclosure of all material facts by both the parties.



29.1.  The Bench expressed the view that an exclusion



clause in a contract of insurance has to be interpreted



differently. If an insurer relies upon an exclusion clause, the



burden of establishing that such an exclusionary clause applies



to a claim rests upon the insurer. The significance of the



aforesaid principle lies in the fact that an insurer cannot escape



10 (2023) 1 SCC 428



                                                         28

liability merely by pointing out to the existence of an

exclusionary provision and placing reliance thereon. The

exclusion must be shown to govern the particular loss for which

indemnification is claimed. The responsibility of establishing

that the goods fall within the exclusion is on the insurer when

it places reliance on such an exclusionary clause, particularly

when effect of such exclusion is to deny the insurer the benefit

of the insurance coverage.



29.2.  Texco Marketing also examined the manner in which



an exclusionary provision has to be interpreted vis-à-vis



provisions of the principal contract which the Bench explained



in the following manner:



       13. An exclusion clause has to be understood on the

       touchstone of the doctrine of reading down in the light of

       the underlining object and intendment of the contract. It

       can never be understood to mean to be in conflict with

       the main purpose for which the contract is entered. A

       party, who relies upon it, shall not be the one who

       committed an act of fraud, coercion or misrepresentation,

       particularly when the contract along with the exclusion

       clause is introduced by it. Such a clause has to be

       understood on the prism of the main contract. The main

       contract once signed would eclipse the offending



                          29

     exclusion clause when it would otherwise be impossible

     to execute it. A clause or a term is a limb, which has got

     no existence outside, as such, it exists and vanishes

     along with the contract, having no independent life of its

     own. It has got no ability to destroy its own creator i.e.

     the main contract. When it is destructive to the main

     contract, right at its inception, it has to be severed, being

     a conscious exclusion, though brought either inadvertently or

     consciously by the party who introduced it. The doctrine of waiver,

     acquiescence, approbate and reprobate, and estoppel would

     certainly come into operation as considered by this Court in Union

     of India v. N. Murugesan.



30.  What emerges from Texco Marketing is that an



exclusionary provision cannot be isolated from the contract of



which it forms a part. Such a clause derives its meaning from



the policy and must operate consistently with the object and



intendment for which the parties have contracted for. The mere



fact that the insurer has incorporated an exclusion does not by



itself permit the exclusion to be construed in a manner which



defeats the very purpose of the policy. For this reason, the policy



as a whole has to be read so as to ensure that there is no conflict



between the exclusionary clause and the principal contract.



Both must align on the same trajectory.



     30

31.      Let us now turn to the terms of the insurance policy in the



present case. The policy in question is the Standard Fire and Special Perils



Policy, bearing policy No. 1001/0066099 issued by the respondent-



insurer in favour of Nikhra Warehouse. The insurance period commenced



on 13.12.2006 and continued till midnight of 12.04.2007. The incident in



question took place on 13.03.2007 and, therefore, fell within the insurance



period.



32.      The insuring clause of the Standard Fire and Special



Perils Policy provides for indemnification of the insured in



respect of loss or damage to the insured property on the



happening of any of the perils specified thereunder during the



period of insurance, which includes loss, destruction or damage



caused by storm, cyclone, typhoon, flood, inundation etc. The



liability of the insurer has to be determined with reference to



the insuring clause as well as to the schedule, conditions,



exclusions and endorsements forming part of the policy.



33.      A perusal of the schedule together with Annexure-B



shows that the policy covered both the warehouse building and



the stocks stored at the insured premises i.e. the warehouse.



The sum insured in respect of the building was Rs. 50,00,000.00 and in



         31

respect of the stock, it was Rs. 1,50,00,000.00, making the aggregate sum

insured at Rs. 2,00,00,000.00. The schedule also refers to the

hypothecation details as per Annexure-A and makes the policy subject to

clauses FA, FC, FG and FH attached thereto.



34.  The National Commission proceeded on the basis



that the sum insured in respect of the stock was



Rs. 1,00,00,000.00. However, Annexure-B to the policy shows



that the sum insured under this head was Rs. 1,50,00,000.00



which figure is also reflected in the counter affidavit filed by the



respondents before this Court. Therefore, the sum insured in



respect of the stock stored in the warehouse was Rs.



1,50,00,000.00 and not Rs. 1,00,00,000.00.



35.  There is another aspect of Annexure-B which needs



to be taken note of. It makes a separate mention of ‘stocks’ and



‘goods held in trust’. While ‘stocks’ are covered for a sum of



Rs. 1,50,00,000.00, the sum insured against ‘goods held in



trust’ is shown as nil. It is clear that the two expressions ‘stocks’



and ‘goods held in trust’ have thus been separately dealt with



in the policy.



                32

36.    Let us now turn to the General Exclusion Clause 5 of



the Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy, which reads thus:



       5. Loss, destruction or damage to bullion or unset precious

       stones, any curios or works of art for an amount exceeding

       Rs.10,000/-, goods held in trust or on commission,

       manuscripts, plans, drawings, securities, obligations or

       documents of any kind, stamps, coins or paper money,

       cheques, books of accounts or other business books,

       computer system records, explosives unless otherwise

       expressly stated in the policy.



36.1.  A reading of General Exclusion Clause 5 would



indicate that goods held in trust or on commission would stand



excluded from the insurance coverage unless otherwise



expressly stated in the policy.



37.    The National Commission relied upon the expression



‘goods held in trust or on commission’ appearing in the



aforesaid clause and held that the agricultural produce



belonging to the farmers were excluded from the insurance



cover. While doing so, the National Commission placed



considerable emphasis upon the fact that those goods did not



       33

belong to the appellant and held that the goods were held in

trust for which no premium was paid.



38.  However, as noticed supra, the exclusion clause does



not exclude all goods belonging to third parties. It specifically



refers to ‘goods held in trust or on commission’.



39.  We may now refer to clause FA in the schedule to the



policy. The schedule to the policy expressly makes the policy



subject to clauses FA, FC, FG and FH. Clause FA is the agreed



bank clause which has also been mentioned in the report of the



surveyor appointed by the respondents i.e. M/s Cunningham



Lindsey International Pvt. Ltd. Sum and substance of the



agreed bank clause is that upon any monies becoming payable



under the policy, the same shall be paid by the company



(respondents herein) to the bank (SBI herein) and such part of



any monies so paid as may relate to the interests of other



parties insured under the policy shall be received by the bank



(SBI herein) as agents for such other parties.



40.  It is the admitted position that the stocks lying in the



warehouse were hypothecated with the SBI, which mandated



the stocks to be insured. Respondents were aware of such



     34

hypothecation when the policy was issued. In the written

submissions before the State Commission, respondents had

stated that the agricultural produce belonging to various farmers were

stored in the warehouse and that the appellant charged fees from them for

such storage. Thus, the hypothecation of the stocks with the SBI

alongwith reference to clause FA in the policy schedule which is

the agreed bank clause are required to be taken into

consideration.



41.  That apart, the General Exclusion Clause 5 cannot



be considered in isolation. Annexure-B separately identifies



‘stocks’ and ‘goods held in trust’ providing an insurance cover



of Rs. 1,50,00,000.00 for the former and showing ‘nil’ against



the latter. The schedule also makes the policy subject to clause



FA identified by the respondent’s own surveyor as the agreed



bank clause. Further, General Exclusion Clause 5 itself



concludes with the expression ‘unless otherwise expressly



stated in the policy’. Therefore, the general exclusion clause has



to be read in the context of the overall policy including the



agreed bank clause. The agreed bank clause cannot be



construed de hors the policy. Similarly, the exclusion cannot be



     35

applied merely because the goods belonged to persons other

than the appellant.



42.        This boils down to the decisive question as to whether the



goods were held in trust or on commission or whether those were received



and stored in the warehouse under a contractual arrangement of



bailment?



43.        The National Commission while rejecting the claim of



the appellant in respect of the stock, proceeded substantially on



the basis that the goods belonged to farmers other than the



appellant and, therefore, the goods were held in trust within the



meaning of the General Exclusion Clause 5. In our view, such



an approach did not sufficiently examine the nature of the legal



relationship under which the goods were stored in the



warehouse. The National Commission ought to have examined



whether the goods were held in trust in the legal sense as



contemplated by the policy instead of treating third party



ownership as sufficient to attract the exclusion. The distinction



drawn in Annexure-B between ‘stocks’ and ‘goods held in trust’,



the reference to clause FA in the schedule, the effect of the



agreed bank clause and the express language of the General



           36

Exclusion Clause 5 were all relevant factors which escaped

consideration by the National Commission.



44.  The aspect regarding payment of additional premium



of Rs. 1500.00 also needs to be addressed. While appellant at



one point of time had contended that additional premium of Rs.



1500.00 was paid for the ‘goods held in trust’, respondents



denied receipt of any such premium which stand was accepted



by the National Commission. The material placed before this



Court indicates that the said amount related to an earlier policy



issued by the United India Insurance Company Limited and not



related to the present policy issued by the respondents for the



relevant period. Be that as it may, this disputed issue of



payment or non-payment of additional premium would pale into



insignificance in the teeth of the principal question which has



emerged in this case, which is, whether the goods were received



and stored in the warehouse under a contract of bailment?



45.  We may now examine the nature of the relationship



between the appellant and the farmers whose agricultural



produce were stored in the warehouse. The question is whether



such goods were held by the appellant in trust as contended by



     37

the respondents and accepted by the National Commission or

whether those goods were received and stored by the appellant

in the warehouse under a contractual arrangement of bailment?



46.     In this regard, we may refer to Section 148 of the



Indian Contract Act, 1872, which defines bailment, bailor and



bailee. Section 148 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 reads as



under:



        148. 'Bailment', 'bailor' and 'bailee' defined.—



        A 'bailment' is the delivery of goods by one person to

        another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall,

        when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or

        otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the

        person delivering them. The person delivering the goods is

        called the 'bailor'. The person to whom they are delivered

        is called the 'bailee'.



46.1.   As per the aforesaid provision, a bailment is the



delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose



upon a contract that when the purpose for which those goods



were received is accomplished, those shall be returned or



otherwise disposed of as per the directions of the person



delivering the goods. The person delivering the goods is called



        38

the bailor and the person to whom the goods are delivered is

called the bailee.



47.  Thus, the essential elements of bailment are the delivery of



goods by one person to another; such delivery being for some purpose; and



following a contract that upon accomplishment of such purpose the goods



would be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of



the person delivering the goods. Such delivery of possession of goods



does not result in transfer of ownership in the goods. The bailee



obtains possession of the goods for the purpose contemplated



by the contract and has corresponding obligation towards the



bailor. Therefore, whether a particular arrangement constitutes



bailment or not, has to be determined with reference to the



substance of the contract and the obligations of the parties.



48.  The question whether goods belonging to farmers and



kept in a cold storage would fall within the expression ‘goods



held in trust or on commission’ was examined by this Court in



Canara Bank. In that case, the insurance company had taken



the stand that since the goods were held in trust by the cold



storage, the exclusion clause would operate and, therefore, no



liability could be fastened onto the insurance company. This



     39

Court rejected the said contention of the insurance company. It

was noticed by the Court that the farmers had agreed to pay

rent for keeping their produce in the cold storage and that the

goods were delivered for possession of the cold storage under a

contractual arrangement. The relationship between the farmers

and the cold storage was, therefore, one of bailor and bailee,

with the cold storage holding the produce as bailee for

consideration. This Court held thus:



     35. In the present case, as pointed out above, the farmer

     had agreed to pay consideration to the cold store and,

     therefore, the goods were not held in trust per se but the

     goods were held by cold store as bailee of the goods for

     consideration. The possession of the farm produce was

     handed over by the bailor i.e. farmer to the cold store i.e.

     the bailee, in terms of the contract. There may be inter se

     rights and liabilities between the farmer and the cold

     store but it cannot be said that the goods were held ‘in

     trust’. The goods were also not held ‘on commission’. No

     commission was payable and only rental was paid.

     Therefore, we reject this argument on behalf of the

     Insurance Company.



49.  The decision in Canara Bank makes it clear that the



mere fact that goods belonging to another person are kept in the



custody of a warehouse or cold storage would not mean that the



     40

‘goods were held in trust or on commission’. What is required to

be examined is the nature of the arrangement under which the

goods were received and the capacity in which those were

stored. In Canara Bank, this Court noticed that the farmers had

delivered their produce to the cold storage against payment of

rent; thus, the relationship was one of bailor and bailee.



50.  Applying the above principles to the facts of the



present case, there is no doubt that the agricultural produce



belonging to the farmers were stored in the appellant’s



warehouse against payment of storage charges. The purpose of



such delivery was storage and safe custody of the produce. The



warehouse was required to retain the goods for the purpose for



which those were delivered and thereafter to release or deal with



such goods in accordance with the directions of the farmers who



had handed over the goods. Such an arrangement is consistent



with the essential elements of bailment under Section 148 of



the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The fact that ownership of the



produce continued to vest in the farmers does not alter the



character of the transaction. On the materials on record, it is



evident that the relationship between the appellant and the



     41

owners of the agricultural produce was that of a bailee and

bailor and not one of trustee and beneficiary or agent and

principal holding goods on commission.



51.  In the present case, appellant is the proprietor of



Nikhra Warehouse. Agricultural produce belonging to different



farmers were stored in the warehouse. Respondents in the



written submission filed before the State Commission admitted



that the warehouse stored goods belonging to different farmers



for which the appellant charged fees from the farmers. It thus



establishes that the goods were not merely kept in the



warehouse gratuitously or in some informal arrangement but



were received in the course of the warehouse’s business against



payment of storage charges.



52.  Ownership of the goods is therefore not determinative



of the existence of an insurable interest. A bailee may have an



insurable interest in the goods entrusted to its custody by



reason of the possession and responsibilities undertaken in



respect of the bailment. The appellant, being the proprietor of



the warehouse in which the agricultural produce were stored



for consideration, had a legally cognizable interest in the



     42

preservation of the goods and in the performance of the

obligations arising from the storage arrangement. The fact that

the goods belonged to the farmers would not by itself deny the

appellant of an insurable interest in the goods or render the

insurance cover in respect of the stored stock redundant.



53.  Respondents have relied upon to a great extent on



the expression ‘goods held in trust’ used in the consumer



complaint filed by the appellant himself. While it is true that at



the initial stage, appellant had described the goods stored in the



warehouse as ‘goods held in trust’, but according to us, that by



itself, may not be determinative of the nature of the goods stored



in the warehouse or the character of the relationship between



the owner of the warehouse i.e. the appellant and the farmers



who had stored their agricultural produce in the warehouse on



payment of charges. For a proper appreciation, the complaint has



to be read as a whole and the nature of the transaction has to be



examined in the light of the pleadings, the documents on record,



including the policy, and the surrounding circumstances. Mere



use of the expression ‘held in trust’ in the complaint would not



constitute an admission that the agricultural produce of



     43

different farmers stored in the warehouse were held in trust

when the materials on record clearly show otherwise.



54.  The question of insurable interest also brings into



focus the position of the farmers whose agricultural produce



were stored in the warehouse. At the relevant point of time, the



appropriate legislation was the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.



We may refer to Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act,



1986 which defines the expression ‘consumer’. Section 2(1)(d)



reads as follows:



     2. Definitions. — (1) In this Act, unless the context

     otherwise requires, —

     (d) ‘consumer’ means any person who, —

     (i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid

     or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under

     any system of deferred payment and includes any user of

     such goods other than the person who buys such goods

     for consideration paid or promised or partly paid or partly

     promised, or under any system of deferred payment, when

     such use is made with the approval of such person, but

     does not include a person who obtains such goods for

     resale or for any commercial purpose; or

     (ii) hires or avails of any services for a consideration which

     has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly

     promised, or under any system of deferred payment and



                   44

       includes any beneficiary of such services other than the

       person who hires or avails of the services for consideration

       paid or promised, or partly paid and partly promised, or

       under any system of deferred payment, when such services

       are availed of with the approval of the first mentioned

       person but does not include a person who avails of such

       services for any commercial purpose.



55.    The scope of the expression ‘consumer’ as defined



under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, particularly with



reference to persons who are beneficiaries of an insurance



policy without being parties to the contract of insurance, came



up for consideration before this Court in Canara Bank. This



Court explained the width of the definition of ‘consumer’ under



the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 in the following manner:



       27. The definition of ‘consumer’ under the Act is very wide

       and it not only includes the person who hires or avails of

       the services for consideration but also includes the

       beneficiary of such services who may be a person other

       than the person who hires or avails of services.



55.1.  In so far the Consumer Protection Act is concerned,



it is not necessary that there should be a privity of contract



between the insurance company and the beneficiaries. The



       45

definition of consumer is wide enough to include not only the



person who has hired or availed of the services but also includes



any beneficiary of such services. It is not necessary that those



beneficiaries should be parties to the contract of insurance.



They are consumers not because they are parties to the contract



of insurance but because they are the beneficiaries of the policy



taken out by the insured. Relevant portion of the judgment in



Canara Bank is extracted hereunder:



                28. Taking the issue of privity of contract, we are of the

                considered view that as far as the Act is concerned, it is

                not necessary that there should be privity of contract

                between the Insurance Company and the claimants. The

                definition of ‘consumer’ under Section 2(d) quoted

                hereinabove is in two parts. Sub-clause (i) of Section

                2(1)(d) deals with a person who buys any goods and

                includes any user of such goods other than the person

                who buys such goods as long as the use is made with the

                approval of such person. Therefore, the definition of

                consumer even in the first part not only includes the

                person who has purchased but includes any user of the

                goods so long as such user is made with the approval of

                the person who has purchased the goods. As far as the

                definition of ‘consumer’ in relation to hiring or availing of

                services is concerned, the definition, in our view, is much

                wider. In this part of the section, consumer includes not



                                                46

     only the person who has hired or availed of the services

     but also includes any beneficiary of such services.

     Therefore, an insured could be a person who hires or

     avails of the services of the Insurance Company but there

     could be many other persons who could be the

     beneficiaries of the services. It is not necessary that those

     beneficiaries should be parties to the contract of

     insurance. They are the consumers not because they are

     parties to the contract of insurance but because they are

     the beneficiaries of the policy taken out by the insured.



56.  Let us now examine the report of the surveyor



appointed by the insurer. However, before adverting to the report,



it would be necessary to examine the statutory provisions



governing assessment of insurance claim by an approved surveyor.



57.  For this purpose, let us examine Section 64UM of the



Insurance Act, 1938 which deals with licensing of surveyors and



loss assessors. Sub-section (2) of Section 64UM, as it stood at



the relevant time, is relevant which reads as follows:



     64-UM. Licensing of surveyors and loss assessors–



     (1) *  *      *  *                                 *



     (2) No claim in respect of a 
```

```text
1. Leave granted.



2. This appeal arises from the judgment and order dated 09.12.2025 passed by

      the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, by which the Criminal Appeal (ST)

      No. 23135 of 2025 filed by the appellant herein against the order dated

      29.09.2025 passed by the Designated Court under the Maharashtra

      Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999

      (the “MPID Act”) declining permission to the appellant to appropriate Rs.

      3.5 crore obtained upon sale of the property mortgaged and securitized under

      the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement

      of Security Interest Act, 2002 (the “SARFAESI Act”) came to be dismissed.



A. FACTUAL MATRIX

3. The State Bank of India, i.e., the appellant herein, extended credit facilities



      to the respondent no. 2 company, for which the promoters thereof, i.e., the

      respondent nos. 3 and 4 respectively mortgaged two of their properties on

      16.09.2009.



4. The appellant bank classified the loan account of the respondent no. 2 as a

      ‘Non-Performing Asset’ (“NPA”) on 31.12.2012. The amount due to the

      appellant bank by the respondent no. 2 as on the said date was estimated at

      Rs. 67.82 crore. In such circumstances, the appellant bank exercised its



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 2 of 84

      security rights under the mortgage agreement and sought to auction the

      mortgaged properties by invoking the provisions of the SARFAESI Act.



5. It came to the knowledge of the appellant bank on 16.08.2014 that the

      respondent no. 2 was involved in transactions that amounted to duping

      depositors inter alia under Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act, respectively.

      Pursuant to the charges being filed under the State enactment, the respondent

      no. 1, i.e., the State of Maharashtra, seized the two properties mortgaged

      with the appellant bank on 29.06.2014.



6. The respondent no. 1 further advised the appellant bank to obtain permission

      from the Designated Court under the MPID Act for the purpose of putting

      the mortgaged properties up for sale. Accordingly, the appellant bank

      preferred an application dated 28.11.2014 before the Designated Court

      seeking permission to proceed with the auction sale and to appropriate the

      sale proceeds. The Designated Court vide its order dated 24.03.2015

      permitted the appellant bank to proceed with the auction sale and to deposit

      the proceeds from such sale in a Fixed Deposit Receipt (FDR). However,

      the Designated Court stipulated that the appellant bank was not at liberty to

      deal with the amount in the FDR till further orders.



7. The mortgaged properties were accordingly auctioned and sold for the

      amount of Rs. 18.22 crore on 27.03.2015. The amount received for the two



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 3 of 84

      properties cumulatively amounted to Rs. 19.43 crore (principal amount

      along with interest for delayed payment).



8. Thereafter, the appellant bank, which sought to appropriate the auction

      proceeds under the SARFAESI Act, preferred an application dated

      19.12.2015 before the Designated Court wherein it was averred that Section

      34 of the SARFAESI Act bars all courts from granting injunction in respect

      of any action taken by the bank under the said Act. Further, Section 35 of

      the SARFAESI Act stipulates that its provisions shall override other laws.

      Therefore, the appellant bank prayed that it may be allowed to adjust its

      entire claim from the proceeds of the auction sale and to deposit any excess

      amount with the Designated Authority.



9. The Designated Authority permitted the appellant bank to credit the sum of

      Rs. 15.93 crore in the loan account of the respondent no. 2 and to leave Rs.

      3.5 crore in the FDR. The said amount of Rs. 3.5 crore matured into a sum

      of Rs. 5.51 crore.



10. In the meantime, the respondent no. 1, by way of Notification dated

      16.05.2016, attached the two properties in question, as provided under the

      MPID Act.



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 4 of 84

11. The respondent no. 1 received claims from 92 depositors for an aggregate

      amount of Rs. 4 crore, which was sought to be discharged from the corpus

      of Rs. 5.51 crore. The respondent no. 1 had already distributed Rs. 1.13

      crore, leaving a balance of Rs. 2.87 crore, which is yet to be paid.



12. Aggrieved by the disbursal of claims from the aforesaid corpus of Rs. 5.51

      crore, the appellant bank filed a miscellaneous application dated 21.12.2023

      before the City Civil and Sessions Court, Greater Bombay, praying that the

      appellant be permitted to appropriate Rs. 3.5 crore lying in the form of fixed

      deposit, towards the outstanding amount of the loan due and payable by the

      respondent no. 2, as the said amount was received after auctioning of the

      secured property under the SARFAESI Act.



13. The Sessions Court, vide its decision dated 29.09.2025, dismissed the

      application of the appellant by placing reliance on this Court’s judgment in

      National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Union of India, reported in (2025) 8 SCC

      393 (hereinafter referred to as “NSEL”). It was held by the Sessions Court

      that the judgment in NSEL (supra) observed that the provisions of the MPID

      Act would override the provisions of the SARFAESI Act. Since the

      appellant bank approached the court for permission to auction the properties

      in question, only after registration of the crime under the MPID Act, the

35. Mr. Shayam Mehta, the learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the

      Constitution. For this purpose, it would be necessary to determine the pith

      and substance of the State legislation, and so long as the same is found to be

      referable to the fields in List II, the State enactment would be held to be

      legislated competently, even if some provisions may incidentally transgress

      any entry provided in List I of the Schedule VII.

44. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and having gone



      through the materials on record, the following questions fall for our

      consideration:

      i. Whether there is a conflict between the provisions of the SARFAESI



            Act and the MPID Act, as regards the attachment of property secured

            under the former?



      ii. Whether the decision in NSEL (supra) requires reconsideration to the

            extent that it holds that attachment of secured property under the MPID

            Act would prevail over the rights of the secured creditors under the

            SARFAESI Act?



D. ANALYSIS

45. Before adverting to the conspectus of facts before us, it is necessary to look



      into a few relevant provisions of the MPID Act and understand its avowed

      purpose.



 I. Scope and purpose of the MPID Act.

46. The respondent State enacted the MPID Act to address the menace of



      fraudulent transactions by certain financial establishments that took deposits

      of the common people without any intention to refund the same along with

      the promised interest thereon, or to render the services guaranteed in



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 21 of 84

      exchange for such sum. This presented a law and order problem for which



      suitable action was required. The respondent State enacted the MPID Act to



      curb unscrupulous activities by such financial establishments with the



      objective of ensuring effective remedy for the depositors who may have lost



      their money to such entities. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the



      MPID Act reads thus:



               “There is a mushroom growth of Financial Establishments

               in the State of Maharashtra in the recent past. The sole

               object of these establishments is of grabbing money

               received as deposits from public, mostly middle class and

               poor on the promises of unprecedented high attractive

               interest rates of interest or rewards and without any

               obligation to refund the deposit to the investors on

               maturity or without any provision for ensuring rendering

               of the services in kind in return, as assured. Many of these

               Financial Establishments have defaulted to return the

               deposits to public. As such deposits run into crores of

               rupees, it has resulted in great public resentment and

               uproar, creating law and order problem in the State of

               Maharashtra, especially in the city like Mumbai which is

               treated as the financial capital of India. It is, therefore,

               expedient to a make a suitable legislation in the public

               interest to curb the unscrupulous activities of such

               Financial Establishments in the State of Maharashtra.”



47. The terms “deposit” and “financial establishment” respectively are defined



      in Sections 2(c) and 2(d) respectively, and read thus:

48. Section 3 of the MPID Act provides penal consequences for fraudulent



      default by a financial establishment. The provision reads thus:



               “3. Fraudulent default by Financial Establishment.—



               Any Financial Establishment, which fraudulently defaults

               any repayment of deposit on maturity along with any

               benefit in the form of interest, bonus, profit or in any other

               form as promised or fraudulently fails to render service as

               assured against the deposit, every person including the

               promoter, partner, director, manager or any other person

               or an employee responsible for the management of or

               conducting of the business or affairs of such Financial

               Establishment shall, on conviction, be punished with

               imprisonment for a term which may extend to six years and



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 24 of 84

               with fine which may extend to one lakh of rupees and such

               Financial Establishment also shall be liable for a fine

               which may extend to one lakh of rupees.



               Explanation—For the purpose of this section, a Financial

               Establishment, which commits default in repayment of

               such deposit with such benefits in the form of interest,

               bonus, profit or in any other form as promised or fails to

               render any specified service promised against such

               deposit, or fails to render any specific service agreed

               against the deposit with an intention of causing wrongful

               gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person or

               commits such default due to its inability arising out of

               impracticable or commercially not viable promises made

               while accepting such deposit or arising out of deployment

               of money or assets acquired out of the deposits in such a

               manner as it involves inherent risk in recovering the same

               when needed shall, be deemed to have committed a default

               or failed to render the specific service, fraudulently.”



                                                             (Emphasis supplied)



49. The aforesaid provision clarifies that fraudulent default occurs when the



      promise to return the deposits with interest or render service in return is



      made either with wrongful intention or is impracticable from the beginning.



      Section 3 punishes such fraudulent default by providing for imprisonment



      and fine for the persons involved in the management of the financial



      establishment, as well as fine for the financial establishment itself.



50. Section 4 of the MPID Act provides for attachment of properties on default



      of return of deposits. The provision reads thus:

               (3) The Collector of a District shall be competent to

               receive the complaints from his District under sub-section

               (1) and he shall forward the same together with his report

               to the Government at the earliest and shall send a copy of

               the complaint also to the concerned District Police

               Superintendent or Commissioner of Police, as the case

               may be, for investigaiton (sic investigation).”



                                                             (Emphasis supplied)



51. A bare textual reading of the provision referred to above indicates that where



      complaints have been received from depositors, or the government has



      reason to believe that the financial establishment is likely to default, it may



      attach the money or property of the financial establishment or its promoter,



      director, partner, or manager to protect the interests of the depositors.



52. What is discernible from the aforesaid provision is that the avowed objective



      of the MPID Act is not limited to criminal repercussions for the financial



      establishment and its management. The Act also seeks to restore the



      depositors to their original position by attaching the properties of the



      financial establishments and distributing the proceeds therefrom to the



      depositors.



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 27 of 84

53. Section 14 of the MPID Act provides that the Act shall override other laws.

      The section reads thus:



               “14. Act to override other laws.—Save as otherwise

               provided in this Act, the provisions of this Act shall have

               effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith

               contained in any other law for the time being in force or

               any custom or usage or any instrument having effect by

               virtue of any such law.”



                                                             (Emphasis supplied)



54. The scheme of the MPID Act and the relevant provisions indicate that the

      purpose of the Act is to safeguard the interests of the depositors by

      compensating them out of the properties of the financial establishments that

      defrauded them. For this purpose, the Act permits the attachment of

      properties of the financial establishment in Section 4 thereof and requires

      the Designated Court under Section 7 to make the order of attachment

      absolute so as to enable the State government to auction the property.



55. However, there is no gainsaying that the MPID Act does not provide any

      guidance for attachment of properties where the financial establishment may

      have secured the same to secured creditors under the SARFAESI Act. In

      such circumstances, we find it apposite to examine the position of law as

      regards the competing interests of the secured creditors and the depositors

      under the MPID Act and whether a reconciliation between the two is

      possible.



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 28 of 84

II. Competing interests of the secured creditors under SARFAESI Act and

      depositors under the MPID Act.

      (i) Analysis of the judgment in NSEL (supra).



56. The petitioner in NSEL (supra) was an exchange trading platform that

      defaulted in payment to its trading clients who had deposited their money

      therewith to be invested. Therefore, an FIR was filed by such persons under

      inter alia, the MPID Act. Accordingly, the State of Maharashtra attached

      movable and immovable properties of the petitioner company therein to

      ensure recovery of monies allegedly lost by genuine trading clients who

      deposited the same on the petitioner’s platform.



57. Thereafter, insolvency proceedings against the petitioner came to be

      instituted, and the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC started operating

      in respect of suits, disputes and transactions as regards the properties of the

      petitioner. After the initiation of the insolvency proceedings, the secured

      creditors of the petitioner submitted before this Court that they would have

      priority of interest over the properties attached by the State of Maharashtra

      under the MPID Act. It must be noted that it was not disputed by either side

      that the attachment under the MPID Act predated the initiation of the

      insolvency proceedings.



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 29 of 84

58. In this backdrop, this Court enquired into the question whether the secured

      creditors would have priority of interest of charge over assets already

      attached under the MPID Act.



59. The Bench observed that this Court, in Sonal Hemant Joshi & Ors. v. State



of Maharashtra & Ors., reported in (2012) 10 SCC 601, has upheld the



constitutional validity of the MPID Act, while relying on K.K. Baskaran



(supra), which had upheld the constitutionality of the TNPID Act. It was



held that the MPID Act contains similar provisions as in the TNPID Act,



and as a consequence, the former was referable to Entries 1, 30 and 32 of



List II of the Schedule VII in pith and substance. Hence, it was held that the



MPID Act does not encroach on the legislative field occupied by Entry 45



of List I of the Schedule VII. The relevant portion of the judgment in NSEL



(supra) reads thus:



“52. This Court in Sonal Hemant Joshi [Sonal Hemant



Joshi v. State of Maharashtra, (2012) 10 SCC 601 : (2013)



1 SCC (Civ) 543 : (2013) 1 SCC (Cri) 1084] had upheld



the constitutional validity of the MPID Act in view of the



decision                     in K.K.  Baskaran v. State [K.K.



Baskaran v. State, (2011) 3 SCC 793 : (2011) 2 SCC (Civ)



90], in which the Court was dealing with the identical



legislation enacted by the State of Tamil Nadu, namely, the



T.N. Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial



Establishments) Act, 1997, enacted with the object to



ameliorate the situation of the depositors from the clutches



of fraudulent financial establishments, who had duped the



investor/public by offering high rates of interest on



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026           Page 30 of 84

deposits, and committed deliberate fraud in repayment of

the principals and interests after maturity of such deposits.



53. In the said decision in K.K. Baskaran v. State [K.K.

Baskaran v. State, (2011) 3 SCC 793 : (2011) 2 SCC (Civ)

90], the Court had opined that the impugned Tamil Nadu

Act was in pith and substance relatable to Entries 1, 30

and 32 of the State List (List II) of the Seventh Schedule. It

further held that the financial institutions/establishments

as contemplated in the Tamil Nadu Act did not come either

under the Reserve Bank of India Act or the Banking

Regulation Act. It further held that the Tamil Nadu Act was

not focussed on the transaction of banking or acceptance

of deposit, but was focussed on remedying the situation of

the depositors who were deceived by the fraudulent

financial establishments. The said Act was intended to deal

with neither the banks which did the business of banking

and were governed by the Reserve Bank of India Act and

the Banking Regulation Act, nor the non-banking financial

companies enacted under the Companies Act. In the case

of the Tamil Nadu Act, the attachment of properties was

intended to provide for an effective and speedy remedy to

the aggrieved depositors for the realisation of their dues.

Hence, the Reserve Bank of India Act, the Banking

Regulation Act or the Companies Act did not occupy the

field which the impugned Tamil Nadu Act occupied,

though the latter might incidentally have trenched upon the

former. The Court in the said judgment specifically

disagreed with the Full Bench judgment [Vijay C.

Puljal v. State of Maharashtra, (2005) 128 Comp Cas 196

: 2005 SCC OnLine Bom 1069] of the Bombay High Court,

whereby the MPID Act was held unconstitutional.

Subsequently, the Court in Sonal Hemant Joshi [Sonal

Hemant Joshi v. State of Maharashtra, (2012) 10 SCC 601

: (2013) 1 SCC (Civ) 543 : (2013) 1 SCC (Cri) 1084],

specifically relied upon the said judgment in K.K.

Baskaran [K.K. Baskaran v. State, (2011) 3 SCC 793 :



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 31 of 84

               (2011) 2 SCC (Civ) 90] and upheld the constitutional

               validity of the MPID Act. The said judgment was also

               relied upon by the three-Judge Bench in State of

               Maharashtra v. 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. [State of

               Maharashtra v. 63 Moons Technologies Ltd., (2022) 9

               SCC 457 : (2023) 1 SCC (Civ) 429 : (2023) 2 SCC (Cri)

               414]



               54. In view of the above, there remains no shadow of doubt

               that the State of Maharashtra was within its legislative

               competence to enact the MPID Act, the subject-matter of

               which in pith and substance was relatable to Entries 1, 30

               and 32 of the State List (List II) of the Seventh Schedule to

               the Constitution of India.”



                                                             (Emphasis supplied)



60. Having observed that the MPID Act was in pith and substance referable to



      the State List and not Entry 45 of the Union List, this Court made the



      following observations as regards the question whether the secured creditors



      would have priority of interest in the properties attached under the MPID



      Act:



      a) First, reliance was placed on this Court’s decision in Union of



          India v. Delhi High Court Bar Assn., reported in (2002) 4 SCC 275



          wherein it was observed that the recovery of dues is an essential function



          of any banking institution. For this purpose, the Parliament is empowered



          to provide the mechanism by which the monies due to the banks would



          be recovered. In exercise of such power, the SARFAESI Act and the



          Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (“RDB Act”) respectively



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 32 of 84

were enacted, both of which provided mechanisms for banks to recover



their dues. However, merely because the SARFAESI Act had been



enacted by the Parliament in respect of Entry 45 of List I, it could not be



said that it can override the provisions of the MPID Act which is another



competently enacted legislation referable to Entries 1, 30 and 32 of List



II. Such an interpretation would violate the federal structure of the



Constitution, as it would amount to depriving the State legislatures of the



power to enact and enforce legislation within their exclusive domain. The



relevant portion of the judgment in NSEL (supra) is reproduced below:



        “57. As held by the Constitution Bench in Union of

        India v. Delhi High Court Bar Assn. [Union of

        India v. Delhi High Court Bar Assn., (2002) 4 SCC 275

        : (2002) 110 Comp Cas 141] , under Entry 45 of List I,

        it is Parliament alone which can enact a law with regard

        to the conduct of business by the banks. Recovery of

        dues is an essential function of any banking institution.

        In exercise of its legislative power relating to banking,

        Parliament can provide the mechanism by which monies

        due to the banks and financial institutions can be

        recovered.



        58. However, merely because the Sarfaesi Act and the

        RDB Act which are enacted in respect of the subject-

        matter falling in List I and having been enacted by

        Parliament, they could not be permitted to override the

        MPID Act, which is validly enacted for the subject-

        matter falling in List II — State List. If such an

        interpretation is permitted to be made, it would amount

        to denuding the State of its legislative power to enact

        and enforce legislation, which is within the exclusive



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 33 of 84

            domain of the State, and it would offend the very

            principle of federal structure set out in Article 246 of the

            Constitution of India, held to be a part of the basic

            structure of the Constitution of India.”



                                                       (Emphasis supplied)



b) Secondly, it was observed that the federal nature of the Constitution



   cannot be bypassed on the basis of the principle of parliamentary



   supremacy. In the situation where there is an incidental overlap between



   a central legislation and state legislation such that it causes conflict



   between the two, it would be apposite to determine which of the two



   enactments is the dominant legislation [See: Paragraph 94 of ITC



   Limited v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee and Ors., reported



   in (2002) 9 SCC 232]. The relevant portion of the judgment in NSEL



   (supra) reads thus:



            “61. In the said judgment Ruma Pal, J., in her

            concurring opinion observed in para 94 as under:

            (Agricultural Produce Market Committee case [ITC

            Ltd. v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee, (2002)

            9 SCC 232] , SCC p. 282)



                “94. Although Parliament cannot legislate on any of

                the entries in the State List, it may do so incidentally

                while essentially legislating within the entries under

                the Union List. Conversely, the State Legislatures

                may encroach on the Union List, when such an

                encroachment is merely ancillary to an exercise of

                power intrinsically under the State List. The fact of

                encroachment does not affect the vires of the law

                even as regards the area of encroachment. [A.S.

                Krishna v. State of Madras, (1956) 2 SCC 692 : AIR



SLP (Crl.) No. 6710 of 2026  Page 34 of 84

                1957 SC 297 : 1957 SCR 399; Chaturbhai M.

                Patel v. Union of India, 1959 SCC OnLine SC 35 :

                (1960) 2 SCR 362, 373 : AIR 1960 SC 424; State of

                Rajasthan v. G. Chawla, 1958 SCC OnLine SC 33 :

                AIR 1959 SC 544; Ishwari Khetan Sugar Mills (P)

                of pith and substance, does not amount to an

                extension of the legislative fields. Therefore, such

                incidental encroachment in either event does not

                Parliament in the second, of their exclusive powers

                incidental encroachment conflicts with legislation

                                                       (Emphasis supplied)



c) Thirdly, it was observed that the predominance of the Union list as



   provided in Article 246 of the Constitution would not prevent the State
```

```text
                     Corporation’) is condoned.



                                                 1

3. These appeals emanate from two judgments dated 07.03.2025

    passed by the High Court1 in exercise of its supervisory

    jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution of India in two

    writ petitions2. By the said judgments, the High Court has set

    aside the orders dated 08.07.2024 and 31.07.2024 in Application

    No. 51 of 2024 and Application No. 50 of 2024 respectively passed

    by the Joint Charity Commissioner-2, Maharashtra State,

    Mumbai (‘the Charity Commissioner’) according sanction for sale

    of lands of Ratanshi Premji Charitable Trust (‘the Trust’) and has

    remitted the proceedings to the Charity Commissioner for a fresh

    consideration. The High Court has also, in W.P. No. 1915 of 2025,

    annulled the registered conveyance deed dated 06.09.2024

    executed in respect of the land at village Vadavali.



4. Two appeals each have been preferred by Destini RealPro

    Developers LLP (formerly known as M/s Fenkin Infotech LLP) (‘the

    purchaser’) and the Trust, whereas one appeal has been filed by

    the Corporation, which was not a party before the High Court,

    against the judgment passed in W.P. No. 1915 of 2025. In order

    to appreciate the grievance of the appellants, relevant facts need

    mention which are stated infra.



1 High Court of Judicature at Bombay

2 W.P. No. 1915 of 2025 and W.P. No. 1877 of 2025



                                                               2

    FACTS

5. The Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950 (‘the Act’) is an Act to



    regulate and to make better provisions for administration of

    public religious and charitable trusts in the State of Bombay. The

    Trust was constituted for educational, religious, medical and

    social purposes and is registered under the Act. The Trust is the

    owner of lands situate at Villages Vadavali and Owale, Taluka and

    District Thane. Two parcels of land are involved in these appeals,

    the particulars of which are as under:

      (i) Land admeasuring 1,08,500 sq. mtrs. bearing Survey Nos.



            82/2, 83, 84, 85, 86 and 87 at village Vadavali (‘the Vadavali

            land’). Out of it, Survey Nos. 83 to 87, admeasuring 94,860

            sq. mtrs., are reserved in the development plan for ‘Shallow

            Water Park Reservation No. 3’ and parts thereof fall in CRZ-

            II and CRZ-IB zones. Survey No. 82/2 admeasures 13,640

            sq. mtrs. The Vadavali land is the subject matter of

            Application No. 51 of 2024, Writ Petition No. 1915 of 2025

            and the appeals arising out of SLP (C) Nos. 9834 and 9818

            of 2025 and Diary No. 54518 of 2025.

      (ii) Land admeasuring 1,53,173.4 sq. mtrs. at village Owale (‘the

            Owale land’), which falls in green zone, forest zone and eco-

            sensitive zone. The Owale land is the subject matter of



                                                               3

            Application No. 50 of 2024, Writ Petition No. 1877 of 2025

            and the appeals arising out of SLP (C) Nos. 9801 and 9850

            of 2025.

6. The trustees in the meeting of the Trust held on 06.05.2024,

    resolved to sell the aforesaid lands as the same were situated on

    a hilly and marshy terrain, were under encroachment by persons

    claiming to be agricultural tenants and were also the subject

    matter of litigation. The Trustees further noted that income of the

    Trust was meagre and the Trust was unable to protect and

    manage the lands. The Trustees, therefore, resolved to sell the

    lands on ‘as is where is’, ‘whatever there is’ and ‘without any

    recourse’ basis.

7. The Trust issued public notices inviting bids which were

    published on 18.05.2024 in two newspapers namely, ‘Free Press

    Journal’ and ‘Navakal’. The Trust obtained a valuation report with

    regard to the lands from Span Arch, a Government approved

    valuer. The said valuer in its report dated 22.05.2024 valued the

    Vadavali land at Rs.70,90,10,000/- and the Owale land at

    Rs.33,68,80,000/-. In response to the public notice for the

    Vadavali land, three bidders submitted their bids. The bid of the

    purchaser for Rs.75 crores was the highest, the other two bids

    were for Rs.66 crores and Rs.68 crores. In response to the public



                                                               4

    notice for the Owale land, three bids were received and therein

    also the purchaser was the highest bidder with a bid of Rs.38

    crores, the other two bids were for Rs.31 crores and Rs.33.50

    crores. On 05.06.2024, the Trust accepted the bids of the

    purchaser and on 07.06.2024 agreements for sale were executed

    in favour of the purchaser. The purchaser undertook, by way of

    indemnity bonds, to remove the encroachments at its own cost.

    APPLICATIONS UNDER SECTION 36(1)(a) OF THE ACT

8. The Trust thereafter approached the Charity Commissioner by

    filing applications under Section 36(1)(a) of the Act (Application

    No. 51 of 2024 for the Vadavali land and Application No. 50 of

    2024 for the Owale land) seeking sanction for sale of the lands in

    favour of the purchaser. The Charity Commissioner called for a

    second valuation from one Gokhale & Associates, a government

    registered valuer, who valued the Vadavali land at

    Rs.71,25,60,000/- and the Owale land at Rs.33,67,21,800/-.

    ORDERS OF THE CHARITY COMMISSIONER

9. By an order dated 08.07.2024 in Application No. 51 of 2024, the

    Charity Commissioner accorded sanction for sale of the Vadavali

    land to the purchaser for a consideration of Rs.75,05,00,000/-

    subject to the following conditions, inter alia, (a) the stamp duty

    and other expenses shall be borne by the purchaser; and (b) the



                                                               5

      sale proceeds shall be kept in a long term fixed deposit in a

      nationalised bank of which only the interest shall be utilised for

      the objects of the Trust. By an order dated 31.07.2024 in

      Application No. 50 of 2024, the Charity Commissioner accorded

      sanction for sale of the Owale land to the purchaser for a

      consideration of Rs.38,05,00,000/- on similar conditions. In both

      the proceedings, the purchaser, by filing a pursis, enhanced its

      offer by Rs.5,00,000/-. A third party who had intervened in the

      said proceedings relating to the Owale land was given an

      opportunity to submit an offer, but he withdrew his application.

10. In pursuance of the sanction granted by the Charity

      Commissioner under Section 36(1)(a) of the Act, on 06.09.2024, a

      registered conveyance deed was executed in favour of the

      purchaser in respect of the Vadavali land. Thereafter, by a

      registered indenture of transfer dated 03.02.2025, the purchaser

      surrendered the reserved portion of the Vadavali land, i.e., Survey

      Nos. 83 to 87 admeasuring 94,860 sq. mtrs., to the Corporation

      against grant of Transferable Development Rights (TDR) and

      handed over possession thereof to the Corporation. Thereafter,

      the reservation was modified from “shallow water park reservation

      No. 3 to Viewing Tower / Convention Centre / CBD”.



                                                                 6

11. After about seven months from the notices inviting bids i.e., on

      18.12.2024, respondent No. 1, a former trustee filed two writ

      petitions (W.P. No. 1915 of 2025 in respect of the Vadavali land

      and W.P. No. 1877 of 2025 in respect of the Owale land) under

      Article 227 of the Constitution of India. In the said writ petitions,

      the validity of the orders passed by the Charity Commissioner

      under Section 36(1)(a) of the Act was challenged. On 13.02.2025,

      the purchaser was impleaded as respondent no. 8 in both the writ

      petitions. The Trust was impleaded as a party to the writ petitions,

      whereas the Corporation was not.

      THE IMPUGNED JUDGMENTS



12. The High Court decided the writ petitions by two separate

      judgments delivered on the same date, that is, 07.03.2025. The

      High Court held as follows, (i) the Charity Commissioner failed to

      properly scrutinize the valuation report particularly the reduction

      in the value of the lands to the extent of 80% in the Ready

      Reckoner value in the case of the Vadavali land and to the extent

      of 50% in the case of the Owale land, (ii) the reduction of the area

      adopted as saleable, i.e., 94,860 sq. mtrs. as against 1,78,140 sq.

      mtrs. in the case of the Vadavali land, was not examined, (iii) the

      unexplained rationale behind assigning negative weightages of

      60% and 20% in the case of the Vadavali land, and of 30% and



                                                                 7

      20% in the case of the Owale land, in the valuation report should

      have been rigorously examined, and the basis of valuation of the

      TDR was unclear, (iv) the alleged topographical difficulties,

      encroachments and pending litigation in respect of subject lands

      were not subjected to a probing and evidence based enquiry, (v)

      the orders granting sanction failed to establish bona fide and

      compelling necessity justifying alienation of lands belonging to

      Trust, and (vi) the process did not demonstrate transparent and

      objective determination of fair market value. Accordingly, by both

      the impugned judgments, the orders of sanction were quashed

      and in W.P. No. 1915 of 2025 as a ‘necessary corollary’, the

      conveyance deed dated 06.09.2024 in respect of the Vadavali land

      was declared void ab initio and annulled. The proceedings under

      Section 36(1)(a) of the Act, namely, Application Nos. 51 and 50 of

      2024, were remitted to the Charity Commissioner for a de novo

      consideration, with a direction to decide them within six months.

      Hence, these appeals.

      SUBMISSIONS

13. Mr. Kapil Sibal and Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, learned senior

      counsel for the purchaser, submitted that respondent No. 1 has

      no locus to maintain the writ petitions as he ceased to be a trustee

      of the Trust on 03.12.2012 upon his resignation. It was pointed



                                                                 8

         out that father of respondent No. 1 continues to be a trustee and

         was a party to the decision taken by the Trust to alienate the

         subject lands. It was contended that respondent no. 1 is neither

         a trustee nor a beneficiary and is, therefore, not a ‘person having

         interest’ within the meaning of Section 2(10) of the Act. It was

         urged that respondent no. 1 is not a person aggrieved as he has

         not suffered any legal injury. It was submitted that the Act

         provides an efficacious remedy under Section 36(2), read with the

         proviso thereto, under which a sanction can be revoked only if it

         was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation or concealment of

         material facts. It was contended that after execution of the

         conveyance deed, the sanction could be revoked only on the

         ground of fraud practised on the Charity Commissioner. It was

         pointed out that no such plea had been raised in the writ

         petitions. It was urged that the writ petitions were decided on

         07.03.2025 without affording an opportunity to the appellants to

         file a reply and the registered conveyance deed executed in favour

         of the purchaser had been set at naught without hearing the

         appellant.

14. It was contended that the High Court, in the guise of supervisory

         jurisdiction, had re-appreciated the material and substituted its

         own view. It was urged that the finding that a transparent process



                                                                     9

    by public notice had not been followed is contrary to the record,

    as public notices had, in fact, been issued and bids had been

    invited. It was submitted that two valuation reports were placed

    before the Charity Commissioner and the bid exceeded the

    amounts mentioned in both the valuation reports. It was pointed

    out that in the valuation report, the valuers had assigned negative

    weightages to the valuation to the subject lands on account of

    reservation, CRZ-II, CRZ-IB and hazard line. It was also pointed

    out that both valuers had specifically valued the TDR potential;
```
