      ANALYSIS

18. We have considered the submissions made on both sides and

      have perused the record.

      SCOPE AND AMBIT OF SECTION 36 OF THE ACT

19. Section 36 deals with alienation of immovable property of the

      public trust. The relevant extract of Section 36 reads as under:-



               “36. Alienation of immovable property of

               public trust-

               (1)Notwithstanding anything contained in the



                   instrument of trust-



  5 Operation Asha v. Shelly Batra, (2026) 1 SCC 569; R. Venugopala Naidu v. Venkatarayulu Naidu Charities,

  1989 Supp (2) SCC 356; Swami Shankaranand v. Mahant Sri Sadguru Sarnanand, (2008) 14 SCC 642; and

  Sailesh Developers v. Joint Charity Commissioner, 2007 (3) Mh.L.J. 717 (FB)



                                                                13

   (a) no sale, exchange or gift of any immovable

       property, and



   (b) no lease for a period exceeding ten years in

       the case of agricultural land or for a period

       exceeding three years in the case of non-

       agricultural land or a building belonging to a

       public trust, shall be valid without the

       previous sanction of the Charity

       Commissioner. Sanction may be accorded

       subject to such condition as the Charity

       Commissioner may think fit to impose,

       regard being had to the interest, benefit or

       protection of the trust;



   (c) if the Charity Commissioner is satisfied that

       in the interest of any public trust any

       immovable property thereof should be

       disposed of, he may, on application,

       authorise any trustee to dispose of such

       property subject to such conditions as he

       may think fit to impose, regard being had to

       the interest or benefit or protection of the

       trust.



       Provided that, the Charity Commissioner

       may, before the transaction for which

       previous sanction is given under clause (a),

       (b) or (c) is completed, modify the conditions

       imposed thereunder, as he deems fit:



       Provided further that, if such condition is of

       time limit for execution of any contract or

       conveyance, then application for

       modification of such condition shall be made

       before the expiry of such stipulated time.



(1A) An application seeking previous sanction of

the Charity Commissioner under clause (a), (b) or

(c) of sub-section (1) shall be decided within 180

days of the filing of such application, and reasons

for delay, if any, shall be recorded by the Charity

Commissioner.



                                             14

(1B) The Charity Commissioner shall not sanction

any lease for a period exceeding thirty years under

the Act.



(2) The Charity Commissioner may revoke the



sanction given under clause (a) or clause (b) of



sub-section (1) on the ground that such



sanction   was obtained by fraud or



misrepresentation made to him or by



concealing from the Charity Commissioner,



facts material for the purpose of giving



sanction; and direct the trustee to take such



steps within a period of one hundred and



eighty days from the date of revocation (or such



further period not exceeding in the aggregate



one year as the Charity Commissioner may



from time to time determine) as may be



specified in the direction for the recovery of the



property.



   Provided that, no sanction shall be revoked

under this section after the execution of the

conveyance except on the ground that such

sanction was obtained by fraud practiced upon

the Charity Commissioner before the grant of

such sanction.



(3) No sanction shall be revoked under this

   section unless the person in whose favour such

   sanction has been made has been given a

   reasonable opportunity to show cause why the

   sanction should not be revoked.



(4) If, in the opinion of the Charity Commissioner,

   the trustee has failed to take effective steps

   within the period specified in sub-section (2), or

   it is not possible to recover the property with

   the reasonable effort or expense, the Charity

   Commissioner may assess any advantage

   received by the trustee and direct him to pay

   compensation to the trust equivalent to the

   advantage so assessed.”



           15

20. This Court in several decisions has dealt with the scope and ambit

      of Section 36 of the Act. It has been held that while exercising

      power under Section 36(1)(a) of the Act, the Charity Commissioner

      has to consider three classic requirements, namely, the interest,

      benefit and protection of the trust. The Charity Commissioner has

      to be objectively satisfied that there is necessity to dispose of the

      property in the interest of the public trust. It is also open to the

      Charity Commissioner to revoke the sanction in exercise of power

      under Section 36(2) of the Act on the ground that sanction has

      been obtained by plain fraud or misrepresentation or material

      facts have been suppressed while obtaining sanction. The power

      of revocation has been conferred on the Charity Commissioner

      with an object to subserve the interest, benefit and protection of

      the trust and its property. However, the power of revocation is

      circumscribed, in case a conveyance deed is executed. In such a

      case, the sanction can only be revoked on the ground of fraud.

      The Trustees hold the property for the benefit of the beneficiaries

      and in case the Charity Commissioner accepts the necessity of

      alienating the trust property, the beneficiaries cannot insist that

      property should be sold to a person of their choice6.



  6 Cyrus Rustom Patel v. Charity Commissioner, Maharashtra State and Others, (2018) 14 SCC 761; Shri

  Ambadevi Sanstha and Others v. Joint Charity Commissioner and Others, (2019) 17 SCC 419; and Ganesh

  Ramachandra Jadhav v. Govardhan Sanstha (Regd) Wai Pune and Others, 2021 SCC Online SC 3263



                                                                16

21. In the backdrop of the aforesaid statutory provisions and the well

      settled legal position, we may now advert to the orders passed by

      the Charity Commissioner. The Trust, along with Application No.

      51 of 2024 relating to the Vadavali land, had placed on record the

      following documents: (i) the Trust Deed, (ii) the minutes of the

      meetings of the board of trustees dated 06.05.2024 and

      05.06.2024, (iii) the public notices published on 18.05.2024 in

      ‘Free Press Journal’ and ‘Navakal’, (iv) the tender notices and the

      three tenders received, (v) the joint venture agreement, (vi) the

      undertaking-cum-indemnity bonds furnished by the purchaser,

      (vii) the agreement for sale, (viii) the statements of account of the

      Trust for the years 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 and the 7/12

      extracts, (ix) the development plan remarks dated 10.05.2024

      issued by the Corporation, (x) the approved revised development

      scheme, (xi) the letter of offer, (xii) the affidavit-in-evidence of the

      Trust and (xiii) the valuation reports of Span Arch and of Gokhale

      & Associates.



22. The Charity Commissioner, after hearing the Trust and perusing

      the said material, framed the point whether it would be suitable

      and appropriate to grant permission to sell the property.



23. On the question of necessity and the interest of the Trust, the

      Charity Commissioner noted that the objects of the Trust are



                                                                17

      educational, religious, medical and social, and that Clause 11 of

      the Trust Deed authorises the trustees to sell the property of the

      Trust. It was noted that the land is situate on an uneven hillock

      and is marshy, which renders it inaccessible, and that various

      parts of it have been encroached upon by persons claiming to be

      agricultural tenants, who have been filing cases before the

      Tahsildar, Thane. The Charity Commissioner was also of the

      opinion that the litigation is likely to continue for years and would

      impose a financial burden on the Trust. He further noted that the

      Trust owns several properties and it is inconvenient for the

      trustees to protect and supervise them, to pay the taxes and to

      pursue the litigation in respect of encroachments, and that the

      income of the Trust is extremely low. It was noted that the

      decision was taken on 06.05.2024 by the Trust on the advice of

      legal consultants and chartered accountants to sell the land on

      ‘as is where is’ basis. The said decision was taken with the object

      that the sale proceeds be kept in fixed deposit and the interest be

      used for the objects of the Trust.

24. On the question of benefit to the Trust and adequacy of the price,

      the Charity Commissioner took note of the following facts: (i) the

      valuation report of Span Arch valued the land at

      Rs.70,90,10,000/-, (ii) in order to fetch the maximum price,



                                                                18

public notices were published in an English and a Marathi

newspaper, (iii) three tenders were received for Rs.75 crores,

Rs.66 crores and Rs.68 crores, (iv) the two lower tenders did not

fulfil the terms of the tender documents, and (v) the purchaser,

whose tender was the highest and compliant, deposited earnest

money of Rs.1 crore. Not content with the valuation obtained by

the Trust, the Charity Commissioner, to ascertain whether the

price was proper, called for a second valuation from Gokhale &

Associates, a government registered valuer, who valued the land

at Rs.71,25,60,000/-. Upon comparing the two valuations, the

Charity Commissioner recorded his satisfaction that the price was

appropriate, and noted that the purchaser had further enhanced

its offer by Rs.5,00,000/- to Rs.75,05,00,000/-. He also took into

account the credentials of the associate of the purchaser, the

undertaking of the purchaser to remove the encroachers and to

bear the cost of litigation, the absence of any relationship between

the trustees and the purchaser, the development plan remarks

and the applicability of the coastal zone regulations, and relied on

two decisions of the Bombay High Court which permit sale of

encroached trust property to a purchaser who takes over the

responsibility for the encroachments.



                                                        19

25. For the protection of the Trust, the Charity Commissioner

      imposed certain conditions, namely, that (i) the sale be completed

      within six months, (ii) the stamp duty, registration fee and all

      other expenses be borne by the purchaser, (iii) the sale proceeds

      be kept in a long term fixed deposit in a nationalised bank and

      only the interest thereon be used for the objects of the Trust, (iv)

      the principal amount of the deposit shall not be utilised, nor shall

      any loan be raised against it, without the prior permission of the

      Charity Commissioner, (v) the regulations of the Maharashtra

      Coastal Zone Management Authority shall apply, and (vi) a change

      report be filed after completion of the transaction.



26. The order dated 31.07.2024 in Application No. 50 of 2024,

      relating to the Owale land comprising eleven survey numbers

      aggregating 1,53,173.4 sq. mtrs., proceeds on the same material

      and on similar reasoning. The Charity Commissioner noted the

      valuations of Rs.33,68,80,000/- and Rs.33,67,21,800/- by the

      two valuers, the three tenders of Rs.38 crores, Rs.31 crores and

      Rs.33.50 crores, and the enhancement of the offer by the

      purchaser to Rs.38,05,00,000/-. He also took note of the fact that

      an earlier attempt of the Trust to sell the Owale land, for which

      sanction had been granted on 02.02.2019 in Application No. 31

      of 2014, did not fructify as the then purchaser failed to complete



                                                                20

      the transaction. Further, a third party who had intervened in the

      proceedings was given an opportunity by the Trust to submit a

      tender, but he withdrew his application on 26.07.2024. In respect

      of the Owale land as well, the Charity Commissioner imposed

      conditions similar to those incorporated in the order granting

      sanction in respect of Vadavali land.

27. From perusal of the order dated 08.07.2024 passed by the Charity

      Commissioner in respect of Vadavali land, it is evident that the

      Charity Commissioner took the following considerations into

      account while granting sanction: (i) the topography of the lands,

      the encroachments and the pending litigation; (ii) the meagre

      income of the Trust and its inability to protect and manage the

      lands; (iii) the resolution of the trustees dated 06.05.2024; (iv) the

      publication of public notices in two newspapers and the receipt of

      three bids; (v) the valuation report of Span Arch and, in order to

      test its correctness, the second valuation report of Gokhale &

      Associates; (vi) the fact that the bid of the purchaser exceeded

      both the valuations; and (vii) the undertaking of the purchaser to

      remove the encroachers at its own cost. The Charity

      Commissioner also imposed conditions to secure the sale

      proceeds for the objects of the Trust. The order granting sanction

      in respect of Owale land proceeds on the same lines as the order



                                                                21

      passed in respect of the Vadavali land. The Charity

      Commissioner, while dealing with Owale land, in addition,

      recorded that the intervenor was given an opportunity to make an

      offer, which he did not avail.

28. Thus, it is evident that the Charity Commissioner has adverted to

      three classic requirements, namely, interest, benefit and

      protection of the trust and has objectively satisfied himself that

      there is a need to dispose of the property belonging to the Trust

      which is in the interest of the public trust. The Charity

      Commissioner on meticulous appreciation of material available

      before him, has acted in consonance with the parameters

      enunciated in Section 36(1)(a) of the Act.

      SCOPE AND AMBIT OF THE POWERS UNDER ARTICLE 227

      OF THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA

29. The scope and ambit of exercise of power under Article 227 of the

      Constitution of India has been examined and explained in a

      number of decisions of this Court. A Constitution Bench of this

      Court7 has held that power of superintendence conferred by

      Article 227 is to be exercised most sparingly and only in

      appropriate cases in order to keep the subordinate courts within

      the bounds of their authority and not for correcting mere errors.



  7 Waryam Singh & Anr. v. Amarnath & Anr., (1954) 1 SCC 51



                                                                22

    A two-Judge Bench of this Court8 has held that the exercise of

    power under Article 227 is restricted to cases of serious

    dereliction of duty and flagrant violation of principles of law of

    justice or where if the High Court does not interfere, a grave

    injustice remains uncorrected. It is trite that while acting under

    Article 227, the High Court does not exercise its power as an

    appellate court or substitute its own judgment in place of that of

    the subordinate court to correct an error which is not apparent

    on the face of record. The High Court can set aside the findings of

    an inferior court or tribunal if they are based on no evidence or

    the finding is so perverse that no reasonable person can possibly

    come to such a conclusion which the Court or Tribunal has

    arrived at. Another two-Judge Bench of this Court9 again

    considered the scope and ambit of Article 227 and summarised

    the principles on exercise of jurisdiction under Article 227.

    Similar view has been reiterated by another two-Judge Bench of

    this Court10 and it has been held that reasoned decision taken on

    an elaborate consideration of relevant facts cannot be interfered

    with in exercise of supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of

    the Constitution. The principles with regard to scope of exercise



8 Estralla Rubber v. Dass Estate (P) Ltd., (2001) 8 SCC 97

9 Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil, (2010) 8 SCC 329

10 Garment Craft (supra)



                                                              23

      of power under Article 227 of the Constitution again have been

      recently summarised by a two-Judge Bench of this Court.11

30. In the backdrop of aforesaid well-settled scope of exercise of power

      under Article 227, we may advert to the impugned judgments. The

      High Court has failed to appreciate that a reasoned decision was

      taken on an elaborate consideration of relevant facts by the

      Charity Commissioner which did not call for any interference in

      exercise of supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the

      Constitution. The High Court has virtually acted like an Appellate

      Court while examining the validity of the decision of the Charity

      Commissioner.

31. The High Court has clearly exceeded its powers under Article 227

      and the judgments passed by it suffer from the following

      infirmities: (i) it did not refer to the process adopted by the Trust

      to sell the property, namely, a well-considered decision by its

      trustees to alienate the properties, issuance of public notices, the

      multiple bids received and the valuation report obtained by the

      Trust to ascertain the market value of the properties, while

      recording a finding that the sale ought to have been conducted

      through a transparent and competitive process. The finding that

      a transparent process by public notice was not followed is



  11 Nandi Infrastructure Corridor Enterprises Ltd. (supra)



                                                                24

      contrary to the record. (ii) The High Court failed to take into

      consideration that the negative weightages applied by the valuers

      were on account of the reservation, the coastal regulation zone,

      the green zone and the forest zone, which are matters within the

      domain of experts. (iii) Insofar as the Owale land is concerned, the

      High Court proceeded on the footing that negative weightages of

      30% for green zone and 20% for litigation were applied, whereas

      the valuation report applies a negative weightage of 50% to the

      plots in green zone and of 75% to the plots in forest zone. The

      finding, therefore, does not even conform to the record. (iv) The

      High Court itself accepted that the topography of the land, the

      encroachments and the expenses of litigation might constitute

      valid considerations for sale, yet faulted the Charity

      Commissioner for not holding a probing inquiry. (v) The finding

      that the basis of valuation of TDR is unclear, is factually incorrect,

      as both the valuers have specifically valued the TDR potential of

      the land. (vi) The High Court ought to have appreciated that

      Section 36 does not contemplate a trial and the Charity

      Commissioner is required to arrive at his satisfaction on the

      material placed before him.

32. The High Court ought to have appreciated that it is neither

      exercising original jurisdiction nor an appellate jurisdiction but



                                                                25

      jurisdiction of superintendence. The High Court erred in not

      appreciating that the orders of the Charity Commissioner were

      passed by taking into account the interest of the Trust and the

      Charity Commissioner had objectively satisfied himself that there

      is a necessity to dispose of the property in the interest of the Trust.

      Thus, the High Court, in our opinion has clearly exceeded the

      scope of its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.

33. The High Court ought to have also appreciated that the registered

      conveyance deed with respect to Vadavali land was acted upon

      and the purchaser had already transferred a part of the land to

      the Corporation which was not impleaded as a respondent in the

      writ petitions. The High Court failed to appreciate that under the

      proviso to Section 36(2) of the Act, after the execution of the

      conveyance deed, a sanction cannot be revoked except on the

      ground of fraud practised on the Charity Commissioner. The

      respondent no. 1 had not taken any such plea and therefore, the

      High Court ought not to have set at naught the conveyance deed.

      The High Court ought to have appreciated that the respondent no.

      1 had a remedy under Section 36(2) to approach the Charity

      Commissioner for seeking revocation of sanction, which he did

      not avail. On this ground alone, the High Court ought not to have

      entertained the writ petitions.



                                                                26

34. Insofar as the other contentions of respondent No. 1 relating to

      non-payment of the balance consideration, dishonour of cheques,

      the nature of the guarantee, the eligibility of the purchaser, the

      constitution of the board of trustees, the title to the Owale land

      and the alleged contradictory stand of the Trust, are concerned,

      suffice it to say that the High Court has not recorded any finding

      on any of these aspects, and except the eligibility of the purchaser

      and the nature of the guarantee, the same were not even urged

      before the High Court. Therefore, we are not inclined to examine

      the same for the first time in these appeals.

      INTERLOCUTORY APPLICATIONS FOR AMENDMENT



35. I.A. Nos. 164280 and 164282 of 2026 have been filed in the

      appeals arising out of SLP (C) Nos. 9801 and 9834 of 2025

      respectively, seeking amendment of the cause title on account of

      change of name of the appellant from M/s Fenkin Infotech LLP to

      Destini RealPro Developers LLP, which has been approved by the

      Registrar of Companies with effect from 02.07.2025. The

      applications are allowed. The cause title shall stand amended

      accordingly. The address shall also stand changed to ‘A-Wing, 2nd

      Floor, Tika No.-16, C.S. No.-39, Ram Maruti Road, New English

      School, Thane-400602, Maharashtra’.



                                                                27

      CONCLUSION

36. In view of the preceding analysis, the impugned judgments dated



      07.03.2025 passed in W.P. No. 1915 of 2025 and W.P. No. 1877

      of 2025 cannot be sustained in the eye of law. They are

      accordingly quashed and set aside. The orders dated 08.07.2024

      in Application No. 51 of 2024 and 31.07.2024 in Application

      No. 50 of 2024 passed by the Charity Commissioner are restored.

      Consequently, the registered conveyance deed dated 06.09.2024

      and the indenture of transfer dated 03.02.2025 shall also stand

      restored.

37. In the result, the appeals are allowed. There shall be no order as

      to costs. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

[Per: Arun Baroka, Member (Technical)]

         The present appeals (“Appeals”) have been preferred by Mr. Balbir



Singh, the suspended Director of ESPO Developers Private Limited



(“Appellant”), under Section 61(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,



2016 (“Code”) before this Appellate Tribunal assailing the order dated



29.09.2026 (“Impugned Order”) passed by the Ld. National Company Law



Tribunal, New Delhi, Court-II (“Ld. Adjudicating Authority”) in CP (IB) No.



207/ND/2026. The application under Section 7 of the Code was filed by



Omkara Assets Reconstruction Private Limited (“Respondent No. 1”) for



initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process (“CIRP”) against ESPO



Developers Private Limited (“Corporate Debtor”) (“Insolvency Petition”), which



has been admitted by the impugned order.



2. We observe that CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1966 and 2017 of 2026 arise from

the order dated 29.09.2026 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal,

whereby the application filed by Respondent No. 1 under Section 7 of the Code

against ESPO Developers Private Limited, the Corporate Debtor, was

admitted. By the Impugned Order, I.A. No. 3396/ND/2026 filed by the

Corporate Debtor under Section 65 of the Code was rejected, which is under



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  3 of 14

challenge in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 2017 of 2026. The Appellant seeks, amongst

other reliefs, an interim order staying further proceedings arising from the

admission of the Section 7 application. At this stage, we are concerned only

with the prayer for interim protection.



3. We have heard both sides and also perused the material placed on

record by both sides. The observations herein are prima facie and shall not

affect the final decision of the appeals.



4. We observe that the dispute has its origin in the Loan Agreement dated

18.01.2019, under which, according to Respondent No. 1, a sum of ₹ 135.15

Crores was disbursed to the Corporate Debtor.



5. On 01.09.2021, an OTS letter was issued. The Appellant relies upon the

OTS letter as having confined the Corporate Debtor’s outstanding liability to

₹ 67,31,92,314/- together with interest at 11.62% per annum, payable

monthly. Respondent No. 1, on the other hand, contends that the OTS was

breached and that the loan was recalled on 10.11.2022.



6. The material on record refers to a balance confirmation dated

08.11.2022 for ₹ 39,18,14,859/- plus interest. It also refers to a recall notice

dated 10.11.2022. The Appellant asserts that the amount payable under the

OTS was thereafter paid by February/March 2023. Respondent No. 1 disputes

the effect of that payment and submits that the payment of ₹ 39.56 Crores

was made only on 24.03.2023, after the stipulated date, and was only a part-

payment.



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  4 of 14

7. On 29.03.2023, the parties executed a Settlement Agreement. The rival

submissions proceed on the basis that this agreement dealt with two sets of

obligations: (i) financial obligations relating to the loan liability; and (ii)

obligations relating to the agreement-to-sell (ATS) inventory and transactions.

The Appellant describes these as interdependent obligations forming one

composite arrangement. Respondent No. 1 also accepts that the Settlement

Agreement contained both sets of obligations, but submits that a breach of

either set attracted the consequences provided in Clauses 5 and 11, including

revival and enforcement of the original loan agreements.



8. The Settlement Agreement was followed by an Amended and Restated

Agreement to Sell dated 16.05.2023. A Second Addendum dated 22.02.2024

is also relied upon. According to the Appellant, the Second Addendum records

that the purchaser’s rights and obligations under the ATS had been assigned

to the SSL Parties. Respondent No. 1 likewise states that the ATS rights and

obligations concerning the ATS Properties were assigned to the SSL Parties.

The parties, however, differ on the legal effect of these assignments and on

the authority to terminate the Settlement Agreement.



9. On 11.07.2024, a termination notice was issued. Respondent No. 1

contends that the Settlement Agreement was validly terminated for breach

and that the original Loan Agreement consequently stood revived, making the

entire outstanding amount due and payable. The Appellant contends that the

termination notice rested solely on alleged breaches of the ATS obligations,



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  5 of 14

which had already been assigned to the SSL Parties, and that the authority

and validity of the termination are disputed.



10. The Corporate Debtor/Vatika Group thereafter invoked arbitration. The

chronology placed by the Appellant records a Section 9 application dated

18.10.2024, invocation of arbitration by notice dated 05.11.2024,

appointment of the arbitrator by consent on 02.12.2024, and commencement

of arbitral proceedings on 28.12.2024. The Appellant filed its Statement of

Claim on 06.08.2025. Respondent No. 1 and the other concerned parties

participated in the arbitral proceedings. Respondent No. 1 filed its Statement

of Defence and Statement of Counter-Claim. The SSL Parties also filed their

pleadings and sought interim protection in relation to the ATS Properties. A

status quo order concerning the ATS Properties was passed by the Arbitral

Tribunal on 09.07.2026.



11. The Section 7 application is stated to have been filed on 16.04.2026

and the NCLT admitted the application by order dated 29.09.2026.



12. The Appellant submits that the essential requirements for admission

under Section 7 of the Code are the existence of a financial debt and a default

in respect of that debt. According to the Appellant, these requirements were

not clearly established as on the date on which the Section 7 application was

filed.



13. It is submitted that the Settlement Agreement dated 29.03.2023 was

not a simple restructuring of a loan. It was a composite arrangement



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  6 of 14

containing interdependent financial obligations and ATS obligations. The

alleged liability under the original loan could arise only upon a valid

termination of the Settlement Agreement. The termination itself is disputed

and is the subject matter of the pending arbitration.



14. The Appellant further submits that the ATS rights and obligations had

been assigned to the SSL Parties. Respondent No. 1, therefore, had no

subsisting right in respect of those ATS obligations when it invoked Section

7. The Appellant also relies upon the participation of Respondent No. 1 in the

arbitration, including the filing of its defence and counter-claim. Its counter-

claim remains pending before the Arbitral Tribunal.



15. It is argued that the NCLT could not finally determine disputed

questions concerning the construction of the Settlement Agreement,

assignment of the ATS obligations, authority to terminate, and revival of the

original loan. Reliance is placed on Dhanlaxmi Bank Ltd. v. Mohammed

Javed Sultan, 2026 INSC 460; Indus Biotech Pvt. Ltd. v. Kotak India

Venture Fund, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 268; and Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima

Mandal, (2008) 17 SCC 491.



16. On interim relief, the Appellant submits that he has a prima facie case

because the existence of debt and default is seriously in dispute. The balance

of convenience is stated to favour the Appellant because Respondent No. 1’s

counter-claim is pending in arbitration. It is also submitted that irreparable

harm would be caused if the proposed Interim Resolution Professional takes



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  7 of 14

over the Corporate Debtor while the foundational contractual dispute remains

unresolved.



17. Respondent No. 1 submits that the financial debt and default stand

established. It relies upon the Loan Agreement dated 18.01.2019, the OTS

letter dated 01.09.2021, the recall notice dated 10.11.2022 and the

Settlement Agreement dated 29.03.2023. According to it, the Corporate

Debtor failed to comply with the OTS and thereafter failed to perform its

obligations under the Settlement Agreement.



18. Respondent No. 1 submits that the Settlement Agreement expressly

included the Corporate Debtor as a borrower and included its loan in

Schedule I. It contends that the financial and ATS obligations were

interdependent, and that Clauses 5 and 11 preserved the original loan

agreements and permitted their enforcement upon breach of the Settlement

Agreement. It accordingly maintains that the termination dated 11.07.2024

validly revived the original loan liability.



19. Respondent No. 1 further submits that the assignment of the financial

obligations and ATS obligations did not deprive the concerned parties of

authority to terminate or enforce the settlement. It relies upon the Sub-

Servicer Agreement dated 11.05.2023 and the subsequent chain of

assignments. It also contends that the Section 7 application was within

limitation.



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  8 of 14

20. As regards arbitration, Respondent No. 1 submits that arbitration and

insolvency proceedings operate in different fields. The pendency of arbitration

does not bar a Section 7 application where financial debt and default are

established. It relies upon Indus Biotech Pvt. Ltd. v. Kotak India Venture

Fund, (2021) 6 SCC 436, and Century Aluminium Company Limited v.

Religare Finvest Limited, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1719 of 2024.

It submits that the termination notice has not been stayed by the Arbitral

Tribunal and that the NCLT rightly admitted the Section 7 application.



21. We have considered the rival submissions. At the outset, it is necessary

to keep in view that an application under Section 7 of the Code can be

admitted only when the existence of a financial debt and the occurrence of

default are established. The insolvency jurisdiction is not intended to be used

as a substitute for adjudication of disputed contractual claims or as a means

of recovery.



22. The present matter, at least at this interim stage, cannot be viewed as

a case involving only a straightforward loan transaction. The Settlement

Agreement dated 29.03.2023 appears, from the material placed before us, to

have brought together two sets of obligations. One set related to the financial

liability. The other related to the ATS transactions and obligations concerning

the identified inventory. Both sides rely upon the interdependent nature of

these obligations, though they differ on the consequences of their alleged

breach.



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  9 of 14

23. The case of Respondent No. 1 is that the Settlement Agreement was

validly terminated on 11.07.2024 and that such termination revived the

original loan liability. The Appellant disputes the termination and contends

that the notice was founded on alleged breaches of the ATS obligations. It

further points out that the ATS rights and obligations had been assigned to

the SSL Parties. The effect of the assignment, the authority to issue the

termination notice, and the consequences of termination are all matters that

arise from the construction of the Settlement Agreement and its addenda.



24. The records show that the rights and obligations relating to the ATS

were assigned to the SSL Parties. The precise legal effect of that assignment,

including its bearing on the right to terminate the composite Settlement

Agreement and the right to claim revival of the loan, requires examination. At

this stage, we are not expressing a final view on the validity of the assignment

or the termination notice. We only note that these are substantial contractual

issues and are not merely incidental disputes.



25. It is also relevant that arbitration was invoked in November 2024 and

the arbitral proceedings commenced thereafter. Respondent No. 1 has

voluntarily participated in those proceedings. It has filed its Statement of

Defence and Statement of Counter-Claim. Its counter-claim is pending

adjudication. The arbitration concerns, amongst other matters, the rights and

obligations arising from the Settlement Agreement and the ATS transactions.

The Arbitral Tribunal has also passed an order dated 09.07.2026 concerning

status quo in respect of the ATS Properties.



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  10 of 14

26. The pendency of arbitration, by itself, does not automatically bar

proceedings under Section 7 of the Code. The question, however, is whether

the financial debt and default relied upon for admission are sufficiently clear

and established independently of the unresolved contractual issues. On the

material presently placed before us, the alleged revival of the original loan

liability depends substantially upon the validity and effect of the termination

of the Settlement Agreement. That termination is itself disputed and forms

part of the controversy pending before the Arbitral Tribunal.



27. In these circumstances, we are of the prima facie view that the existence

of the debt and the occurrence of default, as on the date of filing of the Section

7 application, are not free from substantial doubt. The matter requires closer

examination. The NCLT’s findings on the construction of the Settlement

Agreement, the effect of assignment and the validity of termination will have

to be considered at the final hearing of these appeals. We do not propose to

finally decide any of those questions while considering interim protection.



28. The principles relied upon by the parties also need to be noticed. The

Appellant relies upon the following propositions, as set out in his written

submissions:



         o In Dhanlaxmi Bank Ltd. v. Mohammed Javed Sultan, 2026

               INSC 460, the Appellant submits that the Code is a collective

               insolvency resolution mechanism, “not … a forum for the

               adjudication of individual contractual claims”, nor “a tool for

               coercion and debt recovery”. It further relies upon the proposition



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  11 of 14

               that a loan “intrinsically linked” to performance of other

               contractual obligations “cannot be viewed in isolation as a simple

               financial lending arrangement”, and that a “predominantly

               contractual” dispute pending before the appropriate forum cannot

               be converted into “a coercive mechanism for recovery”.



         o In Indus Biotech Pvt. Ltd. v. Kotak India Venture Fund, 2021

               SCC OnLine SC 268, the Appellant relies upon the proposition

               that default is “premature” where the amount payable turns on an

               unresolved contractual dispute.



         o In Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, (2008) 17 SCC 491, the

               Appellant relies upon the principle that a court cannot make out a

               case that was never pleaded.



29. Respondent No. 1, on the other hand, relies upon Torrent Power Ltd.

v. Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, 2026 SCC OnLine SC 325; Elegna Co-Op.

Housing and Commercial Society Ltd. v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction

Company Limited, 2026 SCC OnLine SC 82; Power Trust v. Hiranmaye

Energy Ltd., (2026) 5 SCC 38; E.S. Krishnamurthy v. Bharath Hi-Tecch

Builders (P) Ltd., (2022) 3 SCC 161; Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI

Bank, (2018) 1 SCC 407; Gaurav Jaiswal v. Indian Renewable Energy

Development Agency Ltd., 2026 SCC OnLine NCLAT 888; Bahadur Ram

Mallah v. ARC (India) Limited & Anr., 2025 SCC OnLine NCLAT 1924;

Indus Biotech Pvt. Ltd. v. Kotak India Venture Fund, (2021) 6 SCC 436;



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  12 of 14

and Century Aluminium Company Limited v. Religare Finvest Limited,

Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1719 of 2024.



30. On the question of balance of convenience, Respondent No. 1 is not left

without a remedy. It has already filed its counter-claim in the pending

arbitration. Its claims arising from the Settlement Agreement and the related

transactions can be pursued before the Arbitral Tribunal, subject to the

orders passed by that Tribunal. On the other hand, if the Section 7

proceedings are allowed to continue and the insolvency process proceeds

further, the Corporate Debtor may suffer consequences that may not be

capable of being adequately undone if the Appellant ultimately succeeds in

the appeals.



31. We are, therefore, satisfied that the Appellant has made out a prima

facie case for interim protection. The balance of convenience also favours

maintaining the present position until the appeals are heard. The possibility

of irreparable prejudice to the Corporate Debtor cannot be ruled out if the

insolvency proceedings are permitted to continue in the meantime.



32. In view of the above, and without expressing any final opinion on the

merits of the appeals, we order that further proceedings pursuant to the order

dated 29.09.2026 admitting the application filed by Respondent No. 1 under

Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, including further

steps in the corporate insolvency resolution process of ESPO Developers

Private Limited, shall remain stayed until the next order of this Tribunal. The

interim protection granted by this order shall not prevent the Arbitral Tribunal



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1966 & 2017 of 2026  13 of 14

from proceeding with the arbitration, including adjudication of the claims and

counter-claims pending before it, in accordance with law. Respondent No. 1

shall remain at liberty to pursue its counter-claim and all other remedies

available to it before the Arbitral Tribunal, subject to law. In the meantime,

the parties shall complete their pleadings in the appeals.



33. It is clarified that the observations in this order are confined to the

consideration of interim relief. They shall not be treated as findings on the

final rights and liabilities of the parties, nor shall they influence the Arbitral

Tribunal while deciding the disputes before it.

   1) The present appeal calls in question the correctness of



   the judgment dated 25.02.2020 passed by the National



   Company Law Appellate Tribunal [for short “the NCLAT”],



   New Delhi, in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1382 of



   2019. By the said judgment, the NCLAT, while allowing the



appeal Signature Not Verified of Respondent No. 1 herein, dismissed the Section 7

the appellant-Company herein under the Insolvency and

Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (for short ‘the IBC’) as being barred

by time.

Brief Facts:-

2) United Bank of India - the assignor, predecessor-in-

interest of the appellant-Company, sanctioned and extended

loan facility of Rs.12,26,00,000/- to M/s Kalpataru Cold Storage

Private Limited, the Corporate Debtor (CD), vide Loan

Sanction Letter dated 28.03.2013.

3) According to the appellant-Company, the first default

occurred on 31.12.2013 in the repayment of loan to the United

Bank of India.

4) On 27.02.2014, the Corporate Debtor made a payment of

Rs. 18,00,000/- to the United Bank of India.

5) On 31.03.2014, the account of the Corporate Debtor was

declared as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA).



                                                                                                                2

6) The appellant-Company claims that on 08.10.2014, the

Corporate Debtor submitted a One-Time Settlement (OTS)

proposal to the United Bank of India acknowledging the debts

due.



7) On 10.10.2014, the United Bank of India informed the

Corporate Debtor that the OTS proposal was not acceptable

and sought for an upgradation of the proposal.



8) On 16.10.2014, the Corporate Debtor requested

reconsideration of the earlier OTS proposal.



9) The appellant-Company submits that in the Balance

Sheet of the Corporate Debtor for the Financial Year 2015-16,

the loan amount was reflected as an outstanding liability. It is

the claim of the appellant-Company that the OTS proposal and

the balance sheet entries constituted acknowledgement of

debt. When the matter stood thus, on 29.03.2017, by a

registered Assignment Agreement, executed between the

United Bank of India and the appellant-Company, the debts of

the United Bank of India, pertaining to M/s Kalpataru Cold



                                                                                                                3

Storage Pvt. Ltd., were assigned in favour of the appellant-

Company.

10) It is the appellant’s further case that such

acknowledgement in the balance sheet entries were available

in the Balance Sheet for the Financial Year 2016-17 also.

11) Further, the appellant-Company submits that, on

30.06.2017, the OTS offer was repeated whereby the

Corporate Debtor agreed to offer an amount of

Rs.10,50,00,000/-

12) According to the appellant-Company, further, the

Balance Sheet for the Financial Year 2017-18, also

acknowledged the debt.

13) It was at this stage that the appellant-Company filed a

petition on 26.10.2018 under Section 7 of the IBC in C.P. (IB)

No. 1498/KB/2018 before the National Company Law Tribunal,

Kolkata Bench (hereinafter ‘Adjudicating Authority’) setting

out total outstanding debt of Rs. 21.61 crores.



                                                                                                                4

14) The Adjudicating Authority set out two questions for



consideration; (1) whether the applicant-(the appellant-



Company herein) can be said to be financial creditor on the



basis of the Deed of Assignment dated 29.03.2017; and, (2)



whether the debt was time-barred.



15) The Adjudicating Authority answered question no. 1 in



the affirmative and held the appellant-Company to be a



financial creditor. On the contention of the debt being time-



barred, it held as follows: -



       “16. However, there is one more dimension as far as case

       in hand is concerned. The financial creditor and even

       corporate debtor have produced on record the corporate

       debtor’s balance-sheet for the year ending March, 2016

       (page no.300 onwards in paper book). From the perusal of

       those financial papers of the corporate debtor, it is seen

       that corporate debtor noted that they have to pay the debt

       of United Bank of India. Their account is declared as NPA.

       In short, in the year 2016, the corporate debtor in its

       balance-sheet acknowledged the debt to be payable by

       them which is claimed herein by the financial creditor. This

       acknowledgement of debt in its balance-sheet by the

       corporate debtor in the year 2016 has brought the claim of

       financial creditor within period of limitation. It is filed well

       within period of limitation. We hold that the debt is not

       time-barred. We answer point no.2 in the negative.”



                                                                                                                5

Having found that the debt was not time-barred, the

Adjudicating Authority, by order dated 30.09.2019, admitted

and allowed the Section 7 application of the appellant.



16) Respondent No.1 carried the matter in appeal to the

NCLAT. By the impugned order dated 25.02.2020, the NCLAT

held that there was no acknowledgement in the financial

holding, the appeal of the first respondent was allowed and

the impugned order (i.e. NCLT order dt. 30.09.2019) was

quashed and set aside.



17) We have heard Ms. Vatsala Kak, learned counsel for the

appellant-Company and Mr. Shivam Singh, learned counsel

for the respondent no. 1.



18) Ms. Vatsala Kak, learned counsel for the appellant-

Company submitted that Section 7 application was not barred

by limitation. Learned counsel drew our attention to the



                                                                                                                6

sequence of events and submitted that on 08.10.2014, the CD

Corporate Debtor for the Financial Years 2015-16 and 2016-

17. It was submitted that by a registered Assignment

Agreement on 29.03.2017, the debts, together with the

underlying rights, title and interest, were assigned in favour

Learned counsel further argued that while examining an

                                                                                                                7

1963, for proceeding under the IBC, this Court has held that

such an acknowledgement cannot be construed with

“pedantic rigidity”.



19) Mr. Shivam Singh, learned counsel for Respondent No. 1

submitted that neither the audited Balance Sheets nor the OTS

letters/proposals of the CD were valid acknowledgement of

debts. Learned counsel submitted that as to whether a

defaulted in repayment of its payment to financial institutions.

According to the learned counsel, financial institutions

submitted that the balance sheet entry, unconfirmed by the

20) Learned counsel for Respondent No. 1 submitted that the

Balance Sheet for the Financial Year 2016-17 stood on a

weaker footing. Learned counsel submitted that it was not

said entry negated any acknowledgement of debt.



                                                                                                                9

21) Insofar as the OTS letters/proposals were concerned,

learned counsel submitted that before the Adjudicating

Authority, the appellant-Company relied only on the balance

22) Learned counsel contended that Section 18 of the

Limitation Act requires an unequivocal admission of a

subsisting liability and the Courts must look at the

surrounding circumstances to decide whether an

acknowledgement existed in law or not. Learned counsel

argued that acknowledgement must not only indicate the jural



                                                                                                              10

relationship between the parties, but must admit the said jural

relationship. Learned counsel submitted that Section 18

requires the acknowledgement to be made “before the

expiration of the prescribed period”. According to the

learned counsel, limitation expired on 31.12.2016 and the OTS

letters fell beyond the said period.



23) Alternatively, it was submitted that in the event of this

Court being inclined to hold that the Section 7 application is

within time, the matter may be remitted back to the

Adjudicating Authority for deciding the other questions.

Learned counsel submitted that the CD never placed its

defence on merits for consideration.



24) The question that arises for consideration is whether the

Section 7 application filed by the appellant-Company against

the CD was within time?



25) At the outset, we shall examine whether the Balance

Sheets for the Financial Years 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18

constitute acknowledgement of liability.



                                                                                                              11

2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18, as was relied upon, have been

27) At this juncture, it is apt to refer to Section 18 of the



Limitation Act, 1963, which reads as under:-



       “18. Effect of acknowledgment in writing.—(1) Where,

       before the expiration of the prescribed period for a suit or

       application in respect of any property or right, an

       acknowledgment of liability in respect of such property or

       right has been made in writing signed by the party against

       whom such property or right is claimed, or by any person

       through whom he derives his title or liability, a fresh period

       of limitation shall be computed from the time when the

       acknowledgment was so signed.

       (2) Where the writing containing the acknowledgment is

       undated, oral evidence may be given of the time when it

       was signed; but subject to the provisions of the Indian

       Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872), oral evidence of its contents

       shall not be received.

       Explanation.—For the purposes of this section,—



               (a) an acknowledgment may be sufficient though it

               omits to specify the exact nature of the property or

               right, or avers that the time for payment, delivery,

               performance or enjoyment has not yet come or is

               accompanied by a refusal to pay, deliver, perform or

               permit to enjoy, or is coupled with a claim to set off,

               or is addressed to a person other than a person

               entitled to the property or right,

               (b) the word “signed” means signed either

               personally or by an agent duly authorised in this

               behalf, and

               (c) an application for the execution of a decree or

               order shall not be deemed to be an application in

               respect of any property or right.”



                                                                                                              15

28) In Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) vs. C. Shivakumar



Reddy and Another, (2021) 10 SCC 330, this Court held as



under: -



       “139. Section 18 of the Limitation Act cannot also be

       construed with pedantic rigidity in relation to

       proceedings under the IBC. This Court sees no reason

       why an offer of one-time settlement of a live claim, made

       within the period of limitation, should not also be

       construed as an acknowledgment to attract Section 18 of

       the Limitation Act. In Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset

       Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd., (2019) 10 SCC 572 cited by

       Mr Shivshankar, this Court had no occasion to consider

       any proposal for one-time settlement. Be that as it may,

       the balance sheets and financial statements of the

       corporate debtor for 2016-2017, as observed above,

       constitute acknowledgment of liability which extended

       the limitation by three years, apart from the fact that a

       certificate of recovery was issued in favour of the

       appellant Bank in May 2017. The NCLT rightly admitted

       the application by its order dated 21-3-2019.”



                                                          [Emphasis supplied]



This Court held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act cannot be



construed with pedantic rigidity in relation to proceedings



under the IBC.



29) In Vidyasagar Prasad vs. UCO Bank and Another, 2024



SCC OnLine SC 2993, this Court observed:-



       “10. Having considered the specific facts and

       circumstances of this case, the Adjudicating Authority



                                                                                                              16

       as well as the National Company Law Appellate

       Tribunal have concurrently held that the entries in the

       balance-sheets amount to clear acknowledgment of

       debt. We agree with the findings. Further, note 3.4

       appended to said balance-sheet entry dated March 31,

       2017 mentions that “company has made certain defaults in

       the repayment of term loans and interest.” It further

       mentions of a continuing default. The entry also mentions

       long-term borrowings. The conclusions of the National

       Company Law Tribunal and National Company Law

       Appellate Tribunal that there is acknowledgment of debt

       are unimpeachable.



               10.1. Following the principles as expounded in the

               case of Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd. v. Bishal

               Jaiswal, (2021) 6 SCC 366, the Adjudicating Authority

               as well as the National Company Law Appellate

               Tribunal have examined the case in detail and have

               come to the conclusion that the entry made in the

               balance-sheet coupled with the note of the auditor of

               the appellant clearly amounts to acknowledgment of

               the liability. We see no reason whatsoever to take a

               different view of the matter. Their findings are

               fortified when we examine the matter from another

               perspective.”



                                                          [Emphasis supplied]



30) In IL & FS Financial Services Limited vs. Adhunik



Meghalaya Steels Private Limited, (2026) 3 SCC 794, this



Court, after an exhaustive consideration of the law, held: -



       “33. It was not disputed before us that entries in

       balance sheets could constitute a valid

       acknowledgement and in fact it could not have been

       disputed, in view of the categoric pronouncement of

       this Court in Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd. v.

       Bishal Jaiswal, (2021) 6 SCC 366. The only dispute was

       whether the entry in FY 2019-20 did or did not constitute

       a valid acknowledgement. Among the grounds



                                                                                                              17

canvassed was the aspect that the name of the

appellant was not mentioned in the balance sheet of FY

2019-20.



35. The other aspect which remains to be examined is the

contention of the respondent that the name of the appellant

is nowhere mentioned in the balance sheet of FY 2019-20

and as such the balance sheet of FY 2019-20 cannot be

construed as an acknowledgement of any jural relationship

between the parties. To counter this aspect, the appellant

has drawn attention to the judgment of this Court in

Vidyasagar Prasad v. UCO Bank, (2025) 17 SCC 234. In

Vidyasagar Prasad this Court, at the outset, dealt with the

earlier judgments in Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India,

(2021) 8 SCC 481, Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy,

(2021) 10 SCC 330 and Rajendra Narottamdas Sheth v.

Chandra Prakash Jain, (2022) 5 SCC 600 to reiterate that

Section 18 of the Limitation Act dealing with

acknowledgment of debt applies to proceedings under the

IBC in view of Section 238-A.



37. It will be noticed that even in Vidyasagar Prasad v. UCO

Bank, (2025) 17 SCC 234 a similar argument about the name

of creditor not being mentioned was repelled and

additionally the aspect of the proposal given by the

corporate debtor therein for a one-time settlement was

taken into account as an additional aspect in favour of

acknowledgment of debt.



39. We have independently examined the facts of the

present matter to construe whether the entries in the

balance sheet of FY 2019-20 constitute a valid

acknowledgement. As to whether a certain document in a

given case constitutes a valid acknowledgement would

depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. We

do no better than recall the observations of this Court in

Khan Bahadur Shapoor Fredoom Mazda v. Durga Prasad

Chamaria, 1961 SCC OnLine SC 147 wherein it was

observed as under: (SCC OnLine SC para 7)



       “7. It is often said that in deciding the question as to

       whether any particular writing amounts to an

       acknowledgment as in construing wills, for instance, it

       is not very useful to refer to judicial decisions on the



                                                                                                     18

       point. The effect of the words used in a particular

       document must inevitably depend upon the context in

       which the words are used and would always be

       conditioned by the tenor of the said document, and so

       unless words used in a given document are identical

       with words used in a document judicially considered it

       would not serve any useful purpose to refer to judicial

       precedents in the matter.”



40. Having said that, the legal principles as to what

constitutes a valid acknowledgment as laid down in the

precedents, have to be rigorously applied. It should

also not be forgotten that this Court in Khan Bahadur

Shapoor Fredoom Mazda v. Durga Prasad Chamaria,

1961 SCC OnLine SC 147 has held that surrounding

circumstances could be considered and that a liberal

construction should be favoured, though the process of

reasoning should not be involved or far-fetched. This

Court in Khan Bahadur Shapoor Fredoom Mazda v. Durga

Prasad Chamaria, 1961 SCC OnLine SC 147 had considered

the general tenor and context of the document. Further, as

noticed in Lakshmirattan Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. v. Aluminium

Corpn. of India Ltd., (1971) 1 SCC 67, the previous

correspondence and the surrounding circumstances were

also taken into consideration. In Asset Reconstruction Co.

(India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal, (2021) 6 SCC 366, this Court

held that a case-to-case examination will be made with

regard to entries made in balance sheets to decide the

question of acknowledgment. In Dena Bank v. C.

Shivakumar Reddy, (2021) 10 SCC 330, this Court held that

in relation to proceedings under the IBC, Section 18 of the

Limitation Act cannot be construed with pedantic rigidity.

In Vidyasagar Prasad v. UCO Bank, (2025) 17 SCC 234,

this Court affirmed the finding of NCLAT in that case

wherein NCLAT had held that the company's balance

sheet is prepared in the statutory format as per

Schedule III of the Companies Act which did not

provide for giving the specific name of every secured

or unsecured creditor.



42. Keeping all these principles in mind, if we examine

the facts of the present case, it will be clear that the

balance sheet of FY 2019-20, viewed in the background



                                                                                                     19

       of the other admitted documents, including the

       financial statements of the previous years, clearly

       constitutes a valid acknowledgment of a subsisting

       liability and indicated the existence of a jural

       relationship and an admission as to the existence of

       such relationship. We say so for the following reasons:



       42.1. The general tenor and context of the balance sheet

       of FY 2019-20 considered in the background of

       surrounding circumstances arising from the balance

       sheets of FY 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18 clearly points

       to the fact that the entry in the balance sheet of FY 2019-

       20 constitutes a valid acknowledgement and pertains to

       the same borrowing as was reflected in the balance

       sheet of FY 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18.



       42.2. Under the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 7,

       a cash flow statement is appended to the financial

       statement. The cash flow statement indicates that in FY

       2018-19 there was proceeds from borrowings of Rs

       72,30,902 and added to Rs 23,68,91,933, a figure of Rs

       24,41,22,835 is arrived at.



       42.3. More importantly, in the cash flow statement it

       was indicated that no part of cash flow proceeds was

       utilised in the repayment of existing borrowings under

       the financial activities since the amount under the head

       “cash flows from (used in) financial activities” is nil.

       This clearly indicates that the debt remained unpaid

       even in 2019-20.”



                                                          [Emphasis supplied]



31) Applying the law to the present set of facts, the following



scenario emerges. The Balance Sheet for the Financial Year



2015-16 ending 31.03.2016 clearly reflects long term



borrowings to the tune of Rs.6,17,32,832/-. Further, it is shown



                                                                                                              20

that long-term borrowings as on 31.03.2016 and borrowings

from the bank are to the tune of Rs. 4,11,62,832/-.



32) We are satisfied that there is a clear acknowledgement of

liability in terms of long-term borrowings in the balance

sheets for the Financial Years 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18.

Respondent No. 1 does not dispute that what is on record is

the correct Balance Sheet for the Financial Year 2016-17.

Hence, the argument that Balance Sheet for the Financial Year

2016-17 was not placed before the Courts below, does not

impress us. The Balance Sheets for the Financial Years 2015-

16 and 2017-18 were admittedly on record.



33) The Notes relied upon also do not carry the case of the

Respondent any further insofar as the acknowledgement of

liability is concerned. In fact, there is a contradiction in the

Notes. While Note 5 speaks of no default continuing or

otherwise as on the date of Balance Sheet, Note 29 has a

different story to tell, if the following para from the Note is

perused: -



                                                                                                              21

       “….Company’s accounts were declared non

       performing assets (NPA) earlier on certain defaults in

       repayment of loans installments and interest dues

       thereon to the Bank. A Notice under Section 13(2) of the

       SARFAESI Act,2002 has been served by Bank on

       03.04.2014 and date of declaration of NPA is

       31.03.2014, the matter is sub judice before the Debts

       Recovery Tribunal (DRT).”



34) In view of the above, we are clearly of the opinion that

Section 7 application was clearly within time. The NCLAT

clearly erred in setting aside the order of the Adjudicating

Authority. If the acknowledgements of the balance sheets of

2015-16 2016-17 and 2017-18 are taken, the Section 7

application filed on 26.10.2018 is clearly within time. The

default admittedly occurred originally on 31.12.2013 and the

account was declared NPA on 31.03.2014. The jural

relationship subsisted when the balance sheets

acknowledged the liability. The impugned judgment of the

NCLAT is dated 25.02.2020. Much water has flown on the

aspect of the entries in the balance sheets constituting valid

acknowledgement of debt in law. Even on facts, we are



                                                                                                              22

convinced that the NCLAT misread the balance sheets and the

notes appended thereto.

35) In any event, by this judgment, we are only holding that

the application is within time. As to whether as on the date of

the application under Section 7, there was any default, is a

matter which can be decided once the matter is remitted.

Before the Adjudicating Authority, we find that only two

contentions were raised viz., one with regard to the appellant-

Company not being a financial creditor and the other as to

whether the debt was time-barred. No argument was raised to

the effect that assuming the debt to be within time, there was

no default, as required under Section 7 of the IBC. However,

since the same was canvassed before us, on the special facts

of the case, we grant one opportunity to the respondent to

place his case before the Adjudicating Authority on the aspect

of default alone.



                                                                                                              23

36) For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed and

the impugned order passed by the NCLAT dated 25.02.2020

is set aside and we remit the matter to the Adjudicating

Authority to consider the merits of the plea of the respondent

on the aspect of occurrence of default under Section 7(5) of the

IBC. We make it clear that all other aspects including the

aspect of limitation in filing the Section 7 application stands

concluded by the present judgment. In view of our holding on

the aspect of valid acknowledgement in the balance sheets,

we are not considering the aspect with regard to the OTS. No

order as to costs.



                                                    ……….........................J.

                                                   [K. V. VISWANATHAN]



                     ……….........................J.

                                 [ARUN PALLI]



New Delhi;

25th November, 2026

2026 INSC 1272



                                              REPORTABLE



                        IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

                         CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION



                        CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).   OF 2026



                        (ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NO. 3249 of 2020)



SUKUMARBAI & ORS.                                …APPELLANT(S)

                                              …RESPONDENT(S)

                                      VERSUS



UNITED INDIA INSURANCE

COMPANY LTD. & ANR.



                        J U D G M E N T



VIKRAM NATH, J.



       1.               Leave granted.

       2.               The present civil appeal arises from the judgment and

                        order dated 05.08.2019 passed by the High Court of

Signature Not Verified  Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad

Digitally signed by     (hereinafter referred to as the “High Court”) in First

SHIPRA NARANG           Appeal No. 2021 of 2018, whereby the High Court partly

Date: 2026.11.25        allowed the appeal preferred by United India Insurance

18:37:23 IST            Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as the

Reason:                 “Insurance Company”) against the judgment and award

                        dated 28.08.2017 passed by the Motor Accident Claims

                        Tribunal, Latur (hereinafter referred to as the

                        “Tribunal”) in Motor Accident Claim Petition No. 197 of



                                                       Page 1 of 43

        2012. While maintaining the compensation awarded in

        favour of the appellants, the High Court set aside the

        direction requiring the Insurance Company to first

        satisfy the award and thereafter recover the amount

        from the owner of the offending vehicle. The High Court

        held that the risk of the deceased, who was travelling as

        a passenger in a private vehicle insured under an Act

        Only Policy, was not covered under the Motor Vehicles

        Act, 1988 (hereinafter referred to as the “MV Act”) or the

        terms of the insurance policy. Consequently, the

        Insurance Company was exonerated from liability,

        leaving the owner responsible for satisfying the award.

3. The controversy arising in the present appeal also bears

        upon a question of law referred for consideration by a

        larger Bench of this Court by an order dated 25.08.2022

        passed in Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 3433 of 2020.

        In the said order, a two Judge Bench of this Court

        expressed reservations regarding the interpretation of

        the expression “third party” under an Act Only Policy,

        particularly whether all persons other than the insured

        and the insurer would fall within its ambit and

        consequently be entitled to compulsory insurance

        coverage. Having regard to the significance of the

        question and the existing judicial pronouncements, the

        Bench directed that the matter be placed before the

        Hon’ble Chief Justice of India for constitution of a larger

        Bench to authoritatively determine the question of law.



                                                                                          Page 2 of 43

4. The present appeal also raises a connected question

        concerning the power of this Court to direct an insurer

        to first satisfy an award of compensation and thereafter

        recover the amount from the vehicle owner,

        notwithstanding the absence of statutory or contractual

        liability. This requires consideration of the scope and

        limitations of the extraordinary jurisdiction vested in

        this Court under Article 142 of the Constitution of India

        (hereinafter referred to as the “Constitution”),

        particularly in the context of the beneficial object

        underlying motor accident compensation legislation.



5. The second question had also arisen earlier before this

        Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v.

        Parvathneni1. By an order dated 31.08.2009, a two-

        Judge Bench of this Court expressed reservations

        regarding the power of this Court to direct an insurer to

        satisfy a compensation award despite the absence of

        liability under law, merely because it was granted liberty

        to subsequently recover the amount from the vehicle

        owner. The Bench accordingly directed that the matter

        be placed for constitution of a larger Bench to consider

        the following questions:



(i) “If an Insurance Company can prove that

it does not have any liability to pay any



1 (2009) 8 SCC 785



                    Page 3 of 43

      amount in law to the claimants under the

      Motor Vehicles Act or any other enactment,

      can the Court yet compel it to pay the amount

      in question giving it liberty to later on recover

      the same from the owner of the vehicle?”



      (ii) “Can such a direction be given under

      Article 142 of the Constitution, and what is

      the scope of Article 142? Does Article 142

      permit the Court to create a liability where

      there is none?”



       The aforesaid reference subsequently came before



a three-Judge Bench of this Court, which, by an order



dated 17.09.2013, reported as National Insurance Co.

Ltd. v. Parvathneni2, disposed of the matter having



regard to the smallness of the amount involved, while



expressly leaving the questions of law open for



determination in an appropriate case. The



constitutional question raised in the said reference thus



remained unresolved and bears directly upon the



second question arising for our consideration in the



present appeal.



6. The facts giving rise to the present appeal are as follows:

         6.1. On 15.04.2012, Suryakant Pandurang Nikam

                (hereinafter referred to as the “deceased”) was
