```text
Umesh, (2022) 6 SCC 563. We accept the main teaching of these cases.



       While generally speaking, it seems appropriate that a reviewing forum

should not re-weigh evidence only because another view is possible. The

Appellate Court may seek to understand whether the process was fair, whether

the finding rests on evidence, whether the rules were correctly applied, whether

the finding is perverse, and whether the penalty is out of proportion to the proved

misconduct. We have seen that Umesh (supra) lists these very heads, and

proportionality of penalty is one of them. Misconduct of this kind is judged on a

preponderance of probabilities and not on proof beyond reasonable doubt. We
```

```text
2. The prayer made by the Appellant before the NCLT was for

commencement of Insolvency Resolution Process against the Respondent

No. 1, who is the personal guarantor of U.N. Automobiles Private Limited,

3. It is not in dispute that when the Bank Guarantee of the Respondent

was invoked way back on 01.06.2013, in the first round of litigation when

notice under Section 13(2) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of

the “SARFAESI Act, 2002”) was issued, in an Original Application filed by

the Appellant – Bank before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, Jaipur (for short

petition before the NCLT seeking to initiate Insolvency Process against the

Respondent being a personal guarantor. The claim of the appellant having

been rejected by the NCLT, the matter is before this Tribunal.

impressed with the arguments raised by him for invocation of Bank

Guarantee. At the initial stage way back in the Year 2013, when the issue

was settled before the DRT and time for payment of the defaulted loan

amount was extended, the OA was disposed of. Once the proceedings

initiated for recovery of the loan against the borrower as well as the

guarantor in 2013 ended with settlement of the dispute with extension of

time for payment of the dues, the invocation of guarantee by the Bank at

that time will not still survive. In case there was a default by the borrower

in payment of the amount as per the settlement arrived at before the DRT,

fresh invocation was required.
```

## [judgments] 2026-11-18 | The Nasik Merchants Co-operative Bank Limited VS Shri. Kailash T Shah Erstwhile Resolution Profession for M/s. Yug Weave Tech Private Limited

- **section:** judgments
- **date (YYYY-MM-DD):** 2026-11-18
- **kind:** NCLAT Final Order /Judgement
- **exact title:** The Nasik Merchants Co-operative Bank Limited VS Shri. Kailash T Shah Erstwhile Resolution Profession for M/s. Yug Weave Tech Private Limited
- **reference number:** Company Appeal (AT)(Ins) No. 112 of 2025
- **addressed to / applies to:** NCLAT New Delhi; Coram: Hon'ble Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan (Member(Judicial)) , Hon'ble Mr. Naresh Salecha (Member (Technical))
- **official URL (detail page):** https://nclat.nic.in/display-board/judge
- **official PDF URL:** https://nclat.nic.in/display-board/view_order_pdf?fid=9910110002032025&&l=delhi&&d=2026-11-18&&order_type=J
- **local text file name:** JUD-NCLAT-0002032025-1118.txt

```text
            NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

                          PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI



                   Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 112 of 2025 &

                                   I.A. No. 499 of 2025



IN THE MATTER OF:                                           …Appellant(s)

The Nasik Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd.



Versus



Kailash T Shah Erstwhile Resolution Professional of Yug     …Respondent(s)

Weave Tech Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.



Present:           : Mr. Avinash R. Khanolkar, Mr. Mahesh Kumar T Nulolu

For Appellant(s)      & Mr. Dhanashree Patki, Advocates



For Respondent(s)  : Ms. Honey Satpal, Mr Nipun Singhvi, Mr. Aman & Ms.

                      Tanvi Gupta, Advocates for R-1



                      O R D E R

                   (Hybrid Mode)



18.11.2026         We have heard Shri Anuj Kumar Khanolkar, Learned Counsel



appearing for the Appellant, as well as Ms. Honey Satpal, Learned Counsel



appearing for the RP and perused the record.



         The instant appeal has been preferred by the Appellant, being one of the

secured creditors of the Corporate Debtor, aggrieved by the impugned order dated

12.12.2024, whereby an application moved by the Resolution Professional (RP) of

the Corporate Debtor (CD) - M/s. Yug Weave Tech Private Limited being I.A. No.

335 of 2023, has been disposed of with the directions that the pending CIRP

cost/professional fees of the Applicant/Resolution Professional amounting to Rs.

16,48,000/-, shall be paid to him within 15 days from the order.



         Learned Counsel for the Appellant submits that the Learned Adjudicating

Authority has committed a mistake by passing the impugned order, as the

Appellant was only obliged to pay such fee to the Resolution Professional which it

has ratified. In this regard, the attention of this Appellate Tribunal has been drawn



                                                                                               Page 1|5

on the 6th CoC meeting held on 02.11.2021, in order to show that in this CoC

meeting the fee of the Resolution Professional up to the month of October 2021,

has been ratified and approved for payment and therefore, the Appellant was not

obliged to pay any fee to the Resolution Professional beyond what has been

approved in this meeting i.e. till October 2021.



         The attention of this Court has also been drawn to Regulation 34 of CIRP

Regulations, 2016, and schedule II of the same in order to show that the fees of the

Resolution Professional could only be paid until the closure of the CIRP, and

therefore this aspect of the matter has not been considered by the Learned

Adjudicating Authority.



         It is further submitted that the Learned Adjudicating Authority has

committed a mistake by allowing the application moved by the Resolution

Professional and therefore, the impugned order may kindly be set aside



         Learned Counsel appearing for the RP vehemently submits that, in the 1st

CoC meeting held on 25.11.2020, the fee of the Appellant/Resolution Professional

was fixed at Rs. 1 lac in accordance with Regulation 34 of the CIRP Regulations,

2016, and schedule II of the regulations.



         She further submits and has drawn our attention towards the 6th CoC

meeting minutes held on 02.11.2021 to show that in this meeting the Authorised

Representative of the sole member of the CoC has asked the RP to reduce the

outstanding fee and the RP had informed him that all the works related to CIRP

and compliances with regard to the Corporate Debtor are to be done by him timely

and there are other works also which is to be handled by him regularly and the fee

is already less and he will continue his fee of Rs. 1 lac per month till the

appointment of liquidator by the Learned Adjudicating Authority.



                                                                                               Page 2|5

         It is further submitted that, since the aforesaid fee was never modified either

by the CoC or by the Learned Adjudicating Authority, the Appellant was obliged to

pay the same until the CD had gone into liquidation vide order dated 06.07.2022.



         It is further submitted that the reliance of the Appellant on schedule II of the

CIRP Regulations, 2016, is patently wrong, as the said schedule only provides the

minimum fixed fee, and it says that the minimum fixed fee shall be applicable for

the period from appointment as Interim Resolution Professional or the Resolution

Professional, as the case may be, till the time of either submission of application for

approval of the Resolution Plan or to liquidate the Corporate Debtor or submission

of application under Section 12A of the Code, or till order for closure of CIRP

(whichever is earlier) and since in this case the liquidation order has been passed

on 06.07.2022 the Appellant was duty-bound to pay the fees up to the period of

06.07.2022.



         We have heard Learned Counsel for the Parties and have perused the record.



         It is reflected that in the 1st meeting of the CoC held on 25.11.2020 the fee of

the Resolution Professional was decided to be fixed as Rs. 1 lac per month, plus

professional charges. It is not in dispute that the RP has continued and has

discharged his obligations throughout the CIRP. The only objection which has been

raised by the Appellant is that the RP was not having any work to do and therefore

after October 2021 the Appellant is not obliged to pay the fee of the RP, as the

Appellant has ratified his fee till October 2021.



         There are certain other objections which have been raised by the Appellant

with regard to the allegations that the RP has not performed his duties up to the

mark, and that some theft has been taken placed in the premises of the Corporate

Debtor during the tenure of the RP and the same has not been properly pursued by



                                                                                               Page 3|5

the RP. The defence of the counsel for the RP on this is that the RP had continued

the services of the same security agency which was appointed by the Appellant and

the FIR was also filed by the RP with regard to the said theft referred to by Learned

Counsel for the Appellant.



         Be that as it may, we notice that the Learned Adjudicating Authority, in the

impugned order, has taken note of the fact that, in the CoC meeting held on

21.11.2020 the CoC resolved to appoint the IRP and his fee of Rs. 1 lac per month,

plus (applicable taxes) was fixed and thereafter nothing is available on record which

may suggest that the fee of the RP was ever curtailed and made subject to any

specific function to be performed by him.



         The reference of the 6th CoC meeting, which has been given by Learned

Counsel for the Appellant, in our considered opinion, would not be of any help to

the Appellant, as in the said meeting it has only been resolved that the fee of the RP

up to the month of October 2021, is hereby ratified and approved for payment.



         We are of the considered view that once the fee of the RP has been fixed by

the CoC the same could only be altered by the CoC by considering a specific agenda

for the same or by the Learned Adjudicating Authority and not otherwise.



         We also notice that, in the 6th CoC meeting itself, when an objection has

been taken by the representative of the Appellant with regard to continuance of

payment of the fee to the RP, the RP has categorically replied that he has performed

various statutory functions on behalf of the Corporate Debtor and thereafter, we

notice that the matter has not been taken any further by the Appellant.



         Having regard to all the facts and circumstances of this case, we are of the

considered view that once the RP was appointed by the CoC and his fee has been

approved as Rs. 1 lac per month and there is no change in that fee, the said fee is



                                                                                               Page 4|5

to be paid in accordance with the eventualities described under schedule II of the

CIRP, 2016.



         In the instant case, by passing the impugned order, the Learned

Adjudicating Authority had directed that the fee up to the initiation of the

liquidation process against the Corporate Debtor i.e., till 06.07.2022 be paid to the

RP.



         We do not find any illegality or to say any irregularity in the

observations/conclusions drawn by the Learned Adjudicating Authority and thus,

in view of the aforesaid facts and circumstance, the appeal, in our considered

opinion lacks merit and is hereby dismissed.



         There is no order as to cost. The pending I.A., if any, is also disposed of.



         We further direct the Appellant to immediately pay the balance fee of the RP,

as determined by the Learned Adjudicating Authority, within a period of one month

from today.



KS/KM  [Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan]

                                     Member (Judicial)



                                       [Naresh Salecha]

                                  Member (Technical)



       Page 5|5


```

## [judgments] 2026-11-16 | In the matter of Lulu International Shopping Malls Private Limited vs. Gorinka Pratyusha and others Etc. [Civil Appeal Nos. 3110-3111 of 2026]

- **section:** judgments

```text
                                                     Non-reportable



2026 INSC 1224  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

                 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION



                Civil Appeal Nos. 3110-3111 of 2026



Lulu International Shopping Malls Private Limited    ….. Appellant



                           versus



Gorinka Pratyusha and others Etc.                  ….. Respondents



                                         J U D G M E N T



    SANJAY KUMAR, J



    1. Dismissal of the recall applications filed by Lulu International

    Shopping Malls Private Limited, the appellant, by the National Company

    Law Appellate Tribunal1, Chennai, vide common order dated 10.02.2026,



    is the source for grievance in these appeals.



    2. On 16.03.2026, this Court stayed the proceedings in Company

    Appeal (AT)(CH)(INS) Nos. 388 and 389 of 2025 on the file of the NCLAT.

    3. The National Company Law Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench2, initiated

    corporate insolvency resolution process against Manjeera Retail Holdings



    Private Limited, the corporate debtor, vide order dated 18.07.2023 in



Signature Not Verified

Digitally signed by

Deepak Guglani

Date: 2026.11.16



18:26:45 ICST ompany Petition (IB) No. 296/7/HDB/2022. The appellant emerged the



Reason:



1  For short, ‘the NCLAT’



2  For short, ‘the NCLT’

successful resolution applicant therein, upon 100% approval of its

resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors of the corporate debtor.

Thereafter, its resolution plan was approved by the NCLT, vide order dated

26.03.2025 passed in IA(IBC)(Plan) No. 08 of 2024 in CP (IB) No.

296/7/HDB/2022. Pursuant thereto, the appellant claims to have invested

₹271.52 crore in the implementation of its resolution plan.

4. While so, the respondents, viz., Gorinka Pratyusha, Srinivas Kalluri

and Rajani Kalluri, who claimed to have entered into agreements with the

corporate debtor for purchase of commercial units in Manjeera Mall, that

was to be constructed by the corporate debtor, filed appeals against the

approval of the resolution plan. Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 388

of 2025 was filed by Gorinka Pratyusha and Company Appeal

(AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 389 of 2025 was filed by Srinivas and Rajani Kalluri.

Their complaint therein was that Birendra Kumar Agarwal, the Resolution

Professional of the corporate debtor, had recorded the payments made by

them, towards full sale consideration for their units, as ‘advances from

customers’ instead of acknowledging them as financial creditors. They

contended that the orders of the NCLT in I.A. Nos. 384 and 492 of 2024

in the company petition, directing the Resolution Professional to include

their claims in the Information Memorandum, were not given effect to.

5. However, the aforestated appeals filed by them were not within time,

in terms of the limitation prescribed in Section 61(2) of the Insolvency and



                                                        2

Bankruptcy Code, 20163. Section 61(2) provided for an appeal being filed

within 30 days of the date of the order with a condonable delay of 15 extra

days and no more. In terms thereof, the appeals should have been filed

within the 30 day-period that expired on 25.04.2025 or at least within the

extendable 15 day-period that expired on 10.05.2025. However, both the

appeals were filed by the respondents on 11.05.2025, i.e., on the 46th day.

Their applications for condonation of delay on their part were, however,

allowed by the NCLAT, vide common order dated 10.10.2025 passed in

I.A. Nos. 1139 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 388 of 2025

and I.A No. 1141 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 389 of

2025, by applying Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 19634, on the ground

that the 45th day, being the last day of the extendable 15-day period under

Section 61(2), fell on a holiday, i.e., 10.05.2025, a second Saturday.

6. Aggrieved by such condonation of delay by the NCLAT, the

appellant filed recall applications in I.A. No. 183 in Company Appeal

(AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 388 of 2025 and I.A. No.232 of 2026 in Company

Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 389 of 2025. The appellant also filed I.A. No.

184 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 388 of 2025 and I.A. No. 233

of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 389 of 2025, seeking

condonation of the delay of three days in filing the said recall applications.



3  For short, ‘the IBC’



4  For short, ‘the Act of 1963’



                                 3

7. The specific case of the appellant in its recall applications was that

the decision of this Court in Tata Steel Ltd. vs. Raj Kumar Banerjee and

others5 barred the application of Section 4 of the Act of 1963 when an

appeal was filed beyond the prescribed period of 30 days under the IBC.

This Court categorically held therein that the expression ‘prescribed

period’ appearing in Section 4 of the Act of 1963 could not be construed

to mean anything other than the ‘period of limitation’ and any period

beyond that prescribed period, during which the Court or Tribunal has the

discretion to allow a person to institute the proceedings, cannot be taken

to be part of the ‘prescribed period’. Hence, as per the above decision, the

benefit of exclusion of the period during which a Court or Tribunal is closed

shall be available only when the appeal is filed within the ‘prescribed

period of limitation’ and shall not be available in respect of the period

extendable by the Court in exercise of its discretion.

8. Perusal of the impugned common order dated 10.02.2026 passed

by the NCLAT reflects that the delay of 3 days on the part of the appellant

in filing the recall applications was condoned but the recall applications

came to be dismissed. Though the aforestated decision of this Court was

specifically brought to its notice, the NCLAT opined that the order dated

10.10.2025 was passed by it on merits after hearing the counsel for the

parties and it could not be recalled on the basis of fresh evidence and



5  (2025) 9 SCC 483



                     4

material. It was further observed that submission of a precedent, giving a

ruling different from the order sought to be recalled, subsequent to the

passing of the said order, cannot be a reason to recall such order as it

would not fall within the ambit of exercising inherent powers to rectify an

error apparent on the face of the record. According to the NCLAT, the only

scope left for the appellant was to invoke remedies as were available to it

in law. Holding so, the NCLAT rejected the appellant’s recall applications.

9. First and foremost, we may note that the NCLAT was in error in

opining that the decision of this Court in Tata Steel Ltd. (supra) was

subsequent to its order dated 10.10.2025, as Tata Steel Ltd. (supra) was

decided on 07.05.2025, long before the order dated 10.10.2025 was

passed by the NCLAT, condoning the delay in the filing of the appeals by

the respondents. Further, when this Court clarifies the legal position in

relation to a statutory provision, the same would be the law of the land and

there is no question of an order contrary thereto passed earlier by a Court

or Tribunal being saved, unless such order has attained finality.

10. It is no doubt true that the NCLAT does not have the power of review

under the provisions of the IBC but it is vested with the power of recalling

its orders by exercising its inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the

National Company Law Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016. This was the

import of the 5-Judge Bench decision of the NCLAT in Union Bank of

India (erstwhile Corporation Bank) vs. Dinkar T Venkatasubramanian



                                                        5

and others6, wherein it was held that, though it was not vested with power

to review a judgment, however, in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction, the

NCLAT can entertain an application for recall of a judgment on sufficient

grounds. This 5-Judge Bench decision of the NCLAT was confirmed by

this Court in Union Bank of India vs. Financial Creditors of Amtek Auto

Ltd. and others7. This Court observed therein that it was in agreement

with the view taken by the 5-Judge Bench of the NCLAT and found no

reason to interfere with the said judgment.

11. More recently, in Greater Noida Industrial Development

Authority vs. Prabhjit Singh Soni and another8, upon reviewing the

case law on the subject, a 3-Judge Bench of this Court observed that the

law which emerged from such decisions was that a Tribunal or a Court is

invested with such ancillary and incidental powers as may be necessary

to discharge its functions effectively for the purpose of doing justice

between the parties and, in the absence of a statutory provision, in an

appropriate case, it can recall its orders in exercise of such ancillary or

incidental powers.

12. Therefore, the NCLAT was not justified in refusing to exercise its

inherent jurisdiction even when apprised of the settled legal position with

regard to application of Section 4 of the Act of 1963. More so, as the



6  (2024) 248 Comp Cas 108 (NCLAT)



7  (2024) 248 Comp Cas 126 (SC)



8  (2024) 243 Comp Cas 452 (SC)



                                    6

respondents did not even establish sufficient cause for condonation of the

the delay on their part in the filing of their appeals. Be it noted that

10.05.2025 was a second Saturday and the NCLAT was of the opinion

that the same constituted sufficient grounds to prolong the extended

limitation period to the 46th day. However, it is an admitted fact that the

appeals were e-filed on the next day, i.e., on 11.05.2025, which was also

a holiday, being Sunday. Therefore, such e-filing of the appeals could as

well have been done on 10.05.2025 itself. In any event, the application of

Section 4 of the Act of 1963 in the case on hand was not valid, given the

legal position as set out in Tata Steel Ltd. (supra).

13. It has been contended by the learned senior counsel appearing for

the respondents that the common order dated 10.10.2025 passed by the

NCLAT, condoning the delay in the filing of the appeals, was not

separately challenged and as the time to do so has expired, the said order

is not liable to be interfered with. It is pointed out that there can be no

merger of the said order with the order dismissing the recall applications

and, therefore, condonation of delay by the NCLAT is deemed to have

attained finality. However, this specious argument loses sight of the fact

that the condonation of delay in the filing of the appeals did not attain

finality, as the recall applications filed by the appellant in relation thereto

kept the issue alive and when the NCLAT, in its wisdom, refused to

exercise its inherent jurisdiction to recall such order and the same was



                                                        7

subjected to appellate review before this Court, the same can be remedied

by this Court in exercise of jurisdiction under Section 62 of the IBC.

14. On the above analysis, this Court finds that entertainment of the

appeals by the NCLAT was illegal, as the appeals were filed beyond the

time prescribed in Section 61(2) of the IBC. Further, the NCLAT erred in

failing to apply the law laid down by this court in Tata Steel Ltd. (supra).

15. The appeals are accordingly allowed, setting aside the order dated

10.02.2026 passed by the NCLAT, Chennai, in the recall applications in IA

No. 183 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 388 of 2025 and

IA No. 232 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No. 389 of 2025.

The recall applications shall stand allowed and the common order dated

10.10.2025 in IA No. 1139 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins) No.

388 of 2025 and IA No. 1141 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT)(CH)(Ins)

No. 389 of 2025 shall stand set aside. In consequence, Company Appeal

(AT)(CH)(Ins) Nos. 388 and 389 of 2025 on the file of the NCLAT, Chennai,

shall stand dismissed on the ground of limitation.



       Parties shall bear their own costs.



                                                                        .........................., J

                                                                         SANJAY KUMAR



November 16, 2026                  …..............................., J

New Delhi.                          SANJEEV SACHDEVA



                   8


```

```text
    PART A – GROUP I: APPEALS OF THE SRA ARISING OUT OF THE

    JUDGMENT DATED 05.01.2022

3. The appeals in this group raise questions of considerable importance

    in the working of the Code, namely, (i) the nature and limits of the

    jurisdiction of the NCLT and the NCLAT while dealing with a resolution

    plan, (ii) whether a resolution plan which provides for payment to

    dissenting financial creditors by way of non-convertible debentures

    satisfies the requirement contained in Section 30(2)(b) of the Code,

    and (iii) whether the CoC, having once approved a resolution plan

    under Section 30(4) of the Code, can revisit its decision while the

    approval is subject to challenge in a statutory appeal?



    FACTUAL BACKGROUND

4. The facts giving rise to the filing of these appeals, briefly stated, are



    that, the applications under Section 7 of the Code were filed by the

    State Bank of India (‘SBI’) and other creditors against thirteen

    companies of the Videocon group, including VIL. The said applications

    were admitted by the NCLT by various orders passed between

    06.06.2018 and 25.09.2018. The NCLT, Mumbai, on 08.08.2019

    directed consolidation of the CIRPs of the thirteen corporate debtors

    (‘the corporate debtors’). The Resolution Professional (‘RP’) invited

    expressions of interest on 11.10.2019. On 26.11.2019, the RP issued

    the Information Memorandum along with request for resolution plans.



                                                                                                         4

    The timeline for submission of resolution plans was extended on

    several occasions.



5. The RP received eleven resolution plans, which were opened in the 15th

    meeting of the CoC held on 02.09.2020. At that meeting, the CoC was

    informed that the fair value and the liquidation value of the corporate

    debtors, being the average of the estimates provided by two registered

    valuers, were Rs. 4,069.95 crores and Rs. 2,568.13 crores

    respectively. Two of the resolution plans, namely those submitted by

    the SRA and V Shape Investment Management Limited, were found to

    be compliant and were placed before the CoC. A proposal for

    withdrawal of the CIRP under Section 12A of the Code was also

    submitted by the Promoter on 31.08.2020. The said proposal was

    placed before the CoC for its consideration.



6. On 07.11.2020, the SRA submitted an amended and restated

    resolution plan with a total financial outlay of Rs. 2,962.02 crores.

    The resolution plan provided, inter alia, for (i) an upfront payment of

    Rs. 200 crores to the financial creditors; (ii) an upfront payment of

    Rs. 52 crores towards the admitted dues of workmen and employees;

    (iii) an upfront payment of Rs. 10 crores to the operational creditors;

    (iv) issuance of non-convertible debentures (‘NCDs’) of an aggregate

    face value of Rs. 2,700 crores, carrying an annual coupon of 6.65 per

                                                                                                         5

    cent, to the financial creditors, redeemable in five instalments, (v) the

    first instalment of Rs. 200 crores falling due 25 months after the

    closing date and the remaining four of Rs. 625 crores each falling due

    in the third to sixth years; (vi) 8 per cent equity in VIL to the financial

    creditors; and (vii) the cash balances of the corporate debtors to accrue

    to the financial creditors. Clause 3.5.1 of the resolution plan provided

    that dissenting financial creditors would not be paid less than the

    amount payable under Section 53 of the Code and would be paid in

    priority as per Regulation 38(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy

    Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons)

    Regulations, 2016 (‘CIRP Regulations’). Clause 3.5.7 of the resolution

    plan provided that “in all circumstances and in any event” payment to

    dissenting financial creditors would be made strictly as per Section

    30(2)(b) of the Code and Regulation 38(1)(b) of CIRP Regulations.



7. In the 19th meeting of the CoC held on 11.11.2020, it was resolved

    that the two compliant plans and the proposal under Section 12A

    would be put to vote simultaneously. On 13.11.2020, SBI Capital

    Markets Limited (‘SBI Caps’), the process advisor to the CoC,

    circulated a distribution calculation according to which the dissenting

    financial creditors, if any, would receive Rs. 114.21 crores. Upon

    conclusion of the voting on 11.12.2020, the Plan of the SRA was

                                                                                                         6

    approved by 95.09 per cent of the voting share. Four financial creditors

    holding about 3.077 per cent voting share dissented, namely, Bank of

    Maharashtra (1.97 per cent), IFCI Limited (1.03 per cent), SIDBI (0.053

    per cent) and ABG Shipyard Limited (0.024 per cent). The proposal

    under Section 12A submitted by the Promoter was rejected by 98.14

    per cent of the voting share. On 12.12.2020, the RP issued a Letter of

    Intent to the SRA, which was accepted by it, and the SRA furnished a

    performance bank guarantee of Rs. 296.20 crores.



8. On 16.12.2020, the RP filed I.A. No. 196 of 2021 before the NCLT

    seeking approval of the resolution plan. In Form H appended thereto,

    the amount payable to the dissenting financial creditors was

    estimated at Rs. 105.23 crores. During the pendency of the said

    application, this Court on 24.03.2021 delivered its judgment in

    Jaypee Kensington Boulevard Apartments Welfare Association v.

    NBCC (India) Ltd.1, holding that the payment to a dissenting financial

    creditor contemplated by Section 30(2)(b) of the Code can only be a

    payment in terms of money. Relying upon the said decision, Bank of

    Maharashtra filed I.A. No. 982 of 2021 objecting to approval of the

    resolution plan on the grounds that it provided for payment to

    dissenting financial creditors in NCDs and that there was a

      discrepancy between the amount reflected in Form H and the figure

      circulated by SBI Caps. A statement was made on behalf of CoC

      through its counsel before NCLT that the dues of the dissenting

      financial creditors would be paid upfront in accordance with the

      judgment in Jaypee Kensington (supra) and Section 30(2) of the

      Code.



      ORDER OF THE NCLT

 9. By an order dated 08.06.2021, the NCLT held as follows: (i) out of



      admitted claims of Rs. 64,838.63 crores, the Plan offered Rs. 2,962.02

      crores, entailing a haircut of 95.85 per cent, (ii) the operational

      creditors would receive 0.72 per cent of their admitted claims, and (iii)

      by paying Rs. 262 crores the SRA would obtain possession of all the

      thirteen corporate debtors. The NCLT, having deference to the

      commercial wisdom of the CoC, approved the plan under Section 31(1)

      of the Code. The NCLT, however, requested the CoC and the SRA to

      increase the payout to operational creditors, particularly MSMEs. The

      NCLT directed that the dissenting financial creditors be paid their

      liquidation value in cash, upfront, before any payment is made to the

      assenting financial creditors.



10. The order of approval was challenged before the NCLAT by Bank of

      Maharashtra, IFCI Limited and SIDBI by way of appeals, namely,

                                                                                                           8

      Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 503, 505 and 529 of 2021. The order

      of approval was also challenged by the Promoter as well as by others,

      including Electrolux Home Products Inc., the registered proprietor of

      the ‘Kelvinator’ trademarks licensed to the corporate debtor, by way of

      Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 545 of 2021. The appeal of the

      Promoter was registered as Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 650 of

      2021.



11. On 19.07.2021, the NCLAT, at the stage of issuance of notice, noted

      the manner of payment proposed under the Plan to the dissenting

      financial creditors, that is, deferment of the bulk of the amount in

      NCDs which was redeemable over a period of six years. Thereafter,

      considering the observations of the Adjudicating Authority and the

      “exceptional facts” of the matter, the NCLAT stayed the order of

      approval and directed status quo ante to be maintained. The SRA’s

      challenge to the said order was disposed of by this Court on

      13.08.2021 with a request to the NCLAT to decide the appeals

      expeditiously.



12. By an affidavit dated 17.09.2021, filed on 18.09.2021, the CoC,

      through SBI on behalf of the assenting financial creditors constituting

      about 94.98 per cent of the voting share, informed the NCLAT that, in

      view of the observations of the Adjudicating Authority and the NCLAT,

                                                                                                           9

      and in the larger public interest, it wished to reconsider its approval

      of the Plan, and prayed that the matter be remitted to it for that

      purpose.



      JUDGMENT OF NCLAT

13. By the impugned judgment dated 05.01.2022, the NCLAT held, inter



      alia, that (i) the resolution plan did not comply with Section 30(2)(b)

      of the Code, inasmuch as payment to the dissenting financial creditors

      by way of NCDs redeemable after a long period did not qualify as

      “payment” in accordance of order of priority; (ii) the direction of the

      NCLT to pay the dissenting financial creditors in cash amounted to a

      modification of the resolution plan, which lay within the domain of the

      CoC and not of the Adjudicating Authority; (iii) the CoC, which has the

      power to approve a plan, has also the power to reconsider its decision

      and is not functus officio upon approval of the Plan; and (iv) prior

      approval of the Competition Commission of India (‘CCI’) under the

      proviso to Section 31(4) of the Code was not shown to have been

      obtained.



14. The NCLAT accordingly set aside the approval of the Plan by the CoC

      and by the Adjudicating Authority and remitted the matter to the CoC

      for completion of the CIRP in accordance with the Code. By the same

      judgment, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal of the Promoter, holding

                                                                                                         10

      that his grievances regarding the haircut and the non-inclusion of the

      foreign oil and gas assets related to the commercial wisdom of the

      CoC, and noting that his Section 12A proposal had been rejected by

      the CoC by 98.14 per cent of the voting share.



15. Pursuant to the impugned judgment, the CoC in its 25th meeting held

      on 12.01.2022 resolved by 97 per cent of the voting share to invite

      fresh expressions of interest, and a Form G was published on

      18.01.2022. When the appeals were taken up on 14.02.2022, this

      Court issued notice and the CoC was asked not to proceed further.

       ISSUES FOR CONSIDERATION

23. We have heard learned counsel for the parties at length and have



       perused the record. The following issues arise for our consideration:

       (i) What is the nature and extent of the jurisdiction of the NCLT and



            the NCLAT in relation to a resolution plan approved by the CoC?



       (ii) Whether the NCLAT has the power to remit the resolution plan to

               CoC?



       (iii) Whether the resolution plan conformed to the provisions of the

            Code and the CIRP Regulations, namely:



            (a) Whether the resolution plan is in conformity with Section

                      30(2)(b) of the Code and Regulation 38(1)(b) of the CIRP

                      Regulations and whether NCLT could cure the deficiency in

                      the resolution plan by directing cash payment to the

                      dissenting financial creditors?



            (b) Whether the approval of the CCI was obtained under

                      Sections 5 and 6 of the Competition Act, 2002 as required

                      by the proviso to Section 31(4) of the Code?



       (iv) What is the role of the CoC during CIRP under the Code?



            (a) Whether CoC had become functus officio on approval of

                      the resolution plan?

                                                                                                           22

            (b) Whether CoC could revisit its decision?



      ANALYSIS

      IN RE: ISSUE (i)

      NATURE AND EXTENT OF THE JURISDICTION OF THE NCLT AND

      THE NCLAT IN RELATION TO A RESOLUTION PLAN APPROVED BY

      THE COC

24. Section 30 of the Code deals with submission of resolution plan.

      Section 30(2) of the Code mandates the RP to examine each resolution

      plan received by him to confirm that each resolution plan fulfils the

      requirement mentioned in clauses (a) to (f) of Section 30(2) of the Code.

      Section 30(3) of the Code requires the RP to present the resolution plan

      which conforms to the requirements contained in Section 30(2) to the

      CoC. Section 30(4) provides that CoC may approve the resolution plan

      by a vote of not less than 66% of voting share of financial creditors after

      considering its feasibility and viability, the manner of distribution

      proposed which may take into account the order of priority amongst

      the creditors as laid down in Section 53(1) including the priority and

      value of the security interest of the secured creditor and such other

      requirements as may be specified by the Board. Relevant extract of

      Section 30(2) to Section 30(4) of the Code is extracted below for the

      facility of reference:



                        “(2) The resolution professional shall examine

                        each resolution plan received by him to confirm

                        that each resolution plan—



                                                                                                           23

(a) provides for the payment of insolvency

resolution process costs in a manner specified

by the Board in priority to the payment of other

debts of the corporate debtor;



(b) provides for the payment of debts of

operational creditors in such manner as may be

specified by the Board which shall not be less

than-



(i) the amount to be paid to such creditors in the

event of a liquidation of the corporate debtor

under section 53; or



(ii) the amount that would have been paid to

such creditors, if the amount to be distributed

under the resolution plan had been distributed

in accordance with the order of priority in sub-

section (1) of section 53, whichever is higher,

and provides for the payment of debts of

financial creditors, who do not vote in favour of

the resolution plan, in such manner as may be

specified by the Board, which shall not be less

than the amount to be paid to such creditors in

accordance with sub-section (1) of section 53 in

the event of a liquidation of the corporate

debtor.



Explanation 1.-For removal of doubts, it is

hereby clarified that a distribution in

accordance with the provisions of this clause

shall be fair and equitable to such creditors.



Explanation 2.-For the purpose of this clause, it

is hereby declared that on and from the date of

in any court against the decision of the

Adjudicating Authority in respect of a resolution

plan;]



(c) provides for the management of the affairs of

the law for the time being in force;

(3) The resolution professional shall present to

which may take into account the order of

and value of the security interest of a secured



                                                                                  25

                          creditor and such other requirements as may be

                                                   xxx xxx xxx”

24.1 Section 31 deals with approval of resolution plan. Section 31(1)



       provides that if the adjudicating authority is satisfied that the



       resolution plan as approved by the CoC under Section 30(4) meets the



       requirement referred to in Section 30(2), it shall by order approve the



       resolution plan. Proviso to Section 31(1) requires that adjudicating



       authority shall before passing an order for approval of resolution plan



       under the sub-section, satisfy that the resolution plan has provisions



       for its effective implementation. Section 31(2) of the Code requires an



       adjudicating authority to reject the resolution plan if it is satisfied that



       the same does not conform to requirements of sub-section (1) of Section



       31 of the Code. Section 31(1) and (2) are reproduced below for the



       facility of reference:-



                          “31. (1) If the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied

                          that the resolution plan as approved by the

                          committee of creditors under sub-section (4) of

                          section 30 meets the requirements as referred to

                          in sub-section (2) of section 30, it shall by order

                          approve the resolution plan which shall be

                          binding on the corporate debtor and its

                          employees, members, creditors, including the

                          Central Government, any State Government or

                          any local authority to whom a debt in respect of

                          the payment of dues arising under any law for

                          the time being in force, such as authorities to

                          whom statutory dues are owed, guarantors and



                                                                                                            26

                          other stakeholders involved in the resolution

                          plan.

                          Provided that the Adjudicating Authority shall,

                          before passing an order for approval of

                          resolution plan under this sub-section, satisfy

                          that the resolution plan has provisions for its

                          effective implementation.

                          (2) Where the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied

                          that the resolution plan does not conform to the

                          requirements referred to in sub-section (1), it

                          may, by an order, reject the resolution plan.”



24.2 Section 61 provides for an appeal to the NCLAT against an order of



       the adjudicating authority. Section 61(3) provides the grounds on



       which an appeal against an order approving a resolution plan under



       Section 31 may be filed. Section 61(3) which is relevant for the



       purposes of the controversy involved in the instant appeals, reads as



       under:



                             “(3) An appeal against an order approving a

                             resolution plan under section 31 may be filed

                             on the following grounds, namely:—



                                     (i) the approved resolution plan is in

                                     contravention of the provisions of any law

                                     for the time being in force;

                                     (ii) there has been material irregularity in

                                     exercise of the powers by the resolution

                                     professional during the corporate

                                     insolvency resolution period;

                                     (iii) the debts owed to operational

                                     creditors of the corporate debtor have not

                                     been provided for in the resolution plan

                                     in the manner specified by the Board;



                                                                                                            27

                                      (iv) the insolvency resolution process

                                      costs have not been provided for

                                      repayment in priority to all other debts;

                                      or

                                      (v) the resolution plan does not comply

                                      with any other criteria specified by the

                                      Board.”

24.3 The statutory scheme contained in the Code suggests that it is a

         complete and self-contained Code. It entrusts the commercial

         decisions on the issue of revival of corporate debtor to CoC. The

         relevant statutory provisions referred to supra, namely Section 31 (1)

         & (2) and Section 61(3) suggest that the Code identifies the

         adjudicating authority and the NCLAT as adjudicatory bodies and not

         merely approving authorities. As held by this Court in K. Sashidhar

         (supra) and Essar Steel (supra), the adjudicating authority and the

         NCLAT can neither interfere on merits with the commercial decision

         of the CoC nor can rewrite or modify a resolution plan. The

         adjudicating authority while approving the resolution plan has to

         satisfy itself that the resolution plan is in consonance with the

         requirements mentioned in Section 30(2) of the Code. The NCLAT also

         can interfere with the resolution plan if the grounds mentioned in

         clauses (i) to (v) of Section 61(3) of the Code are made out. Thus, the

         Code itself, defines the nature and extent of jurisdiction of the



                                                                                                              28

       adjudicating authority and the NCLAT. Issue no. (i) is answered

       accordingly.

      IN RE: ISSUE (ii)

      POWER OF NCLAT TO REMIT THE RESOLUTION PLAN TO CoC

25. It is well-settled that an express grant of a statutory power carries with

      it, by necessary implication, every incidental and ancillary power

      required for its effective exercise.22 In the scheme of the Code, the power

      to remit a plan to CoC is not only permissible but is the only lawful

      course for the following reasons, (i) neither the adjudicating authority

      nor the NCLAT can modify a resolution plan and also cannot substitute

      their own commercial judgment for that of the CoC, and (ii) rejecting a

      plan under Section 31(2) of the Code may, by virtue of Section 33(1)(b),

      lead to the liquidation of a corporate debtor, which the Code treats as a

      measure of last resort. The appellate power conferred on the NCLAT by

      necessary implication includes the power to remit a plan. The aforesaid

      inference is further fortified by Rule 11 of the National Company Law

      Appellate Tribunal Rules, 2016, which preserves the inherent powers of

      the Appellate Tribunal to make such orders or to give such directions as

      may be necessary for meeting the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse

      of the process of Appellate Tribunal.



                   22 ITO v. M.K. Mohammed Kunhi, AIR 1969 SC 430



                                                                                                            29

26. It is noteworthy that the power to remit a resolution plan to CoC has



      been recognised by this Court in Jaypee Kensington (supra), wherein



      it has been held that in case a resolution plan requires modification, the



      adjudicating authority which would include NCLAT by virtue of the



      scheme of the Code must remit the resolution plan to CoC to consider



      the modification, so as to afford an opportunity to resolution applicant



      to modify the plan and vote upon the same. The relevant extract of the



      aforesaid decision in Jaypee Kensington (supra) is extracted below for



      the facility of reference:-



                          “170. As noticed and held in Point A (supra—

                          see paras 101 to 109), the adjudicating

                          authority has no jurisdiction to enter into the

                          commercial aspects of the resolution plan and

                          to interfere with the wisdom of the Committee of

                          Creditors. The terms as provided in the

                          resolution plan for discharging the obligations

                          towards the dissenting financial creditors were

                          clearly and directly pertaining to the financial

                          model proposed by the resolution applicant and

                          accepted by the requisite majority of the

                          Committee of Creditors. The submissions made

                          on behalf of the IRP in this regard are correct

                          that if the adjudicating authority was of the view

                          that the plan did not meet with any particular

                          requirement, it could have only sent it back to

                          the CoC to consider the proposed modifications,

                          so as to afford an opportunity to the resolution

                          applicant to modify the plan and to the CoC to

                          reconsider and vote upon the same.



                                                    xxx xxx xxx



                          172. The upshot of the discussion foregoing is

                          that though the adjudicating authority has not



                                                                                                            30

                           erred in disapproving the treatment of

                           dissenting financial creditor like ICICI Bank in

                           the resolution plan but, has erred in modifying

                           the terms of the resolution plan and in not

                           sending the matter back to the Committee of

                           Creditors for reconsideration while extending an

                           opportunity to the resolution applicant to make

                           the necessary modifications.”



26.1 Similar view has been taken in Essar Steel (supra) wherein the power



         to remand the resolution plan to CoC has been affirmed. The relevant



         extract of the aforesaid decision reads as under:-



                           “73. There is no doubt whatsoever that the

                           ultimate discretion of what to pay and how

                           much to pay each class or sub-class of

                           creditors is with the Committee of

                           Creditors, but, the decision of such

                           Committee must reflect the fact that it has

                           taken into account maximising the value of

                           the assets of the corporate debtor and the

                           fact that it has adequately balanced the

                           interests of all stakeholders including

                           operational creditors. This being the case,

                           judicial review of the Adjudicating

                           Authority that the resolution plan as

                           approved by the Committee of Creditors

                           has met the requirements referred to in

                           Section 30(2) would include judicial review

                           that is mentioned in Section 30(2)(e), as

                           the provisions of the Code are also

                           provisions of law for the time being in

                           force. Thus, while the Adjudicating

                           Authority cannot interfere on merits with

                           the commercial decision taken by the

                           Committee of Creditors, the limited judicial

                           review available is to see that the

                           Committee of Creditors has taken into

                           account the fact that the corporate debtor

                           needs to keep going as a going concern



                                                                                                              31

                           during the insolvency resolution process;

                           that it needs to maximise the value of its

                           assets; and that the interests of all

                           stakeholders including operational

                           creditors has been taken care of. If the

                           Adjudicating Authority finds, on a given set

                           of facts, that the aforesaid parameters

                           have not been kept in view, it may send a

                           resolution plan back to the Committee of

                           Creditors to re-submit such plan after

                           satisfying the aforesaid parameters. The

                           reasons given by the Committee of

                           Creditors while approving a resolution

                           plan may thus be looked at by the

                           Adjudicating Authority only from this point

                           of view, and once it is satisfied that the

                           Committee of Creditors has paid attention

                           to these key features, it must then pass the

                           resolution plan, other things being equal.”



26.2 At this stage, we deem it appropriate to deal with the alternate



         submission made by SRA that its existing plan be remitted for



         consideration in the light of decision of this Court in Jaiprakash



         Associates (supra). We are unable to accept the aforesaid submission



         for the following reasons, (i) once the resolution plan is found non-



         compliant and its approval is set aside, the matter reverts to the CoC,



         which must then exercise its commercial wisdom afresh, (ii) it is not for



         the Adjudicating Authority, the NCLAT or this Court to dictate to the



         CoC, the commercial course it should adopt, including whether it



         should consider only a modified version of the existing Plan or invite



         fresh plans, (iii) to confine the CoC as suggested by the SRA would itself



                                                                                                              32

         be an intrusion into the domain of commercial wisdom which the Code

         reserves to the CoC, and (iv) the order in Jaiprakash Associates

         (supra) was passed in exercise of the powers under Article 142 of the

         Constitution in the peculiar facts of that case and was expressly

         directed not to be treated as a precedent.

26.3 It is noteworthy that the Code was amended by the Insolvency and

         Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026 (Act 6 of 2026). By the said

         amendment, a proviso has been inserted in Section 31(2) of the Code,

         which reads as under:



                           “Provided that the Adjudicating Authority may,

                           before rejecting the resolution plan, give notice

                           to the committee of creditors to rectify any

                           defects in the resolution plan.”

         The amendment gives statutory expression to the principle laid down

         by this Court in Essar Steel (supra) and Jaypee Kensington (supra),

         namely, that where a resolution plan suffers from a defect, the

         appropriate course is to send it back to the CoC for rectification, rather

         than to reject it outright or modify it. Our conclusion in the present

         case rests on the law as it then stood. The amendment, however,

         confirms the legislative policy that the remedy for a defective resolution

         plan lies in remittance to the CoC, and the NCLAT’s order of remittance

         is in consonance with it.



                                                                                                              33

26.4 For the foregoing reasons, in our opinion, the NCLAT has rightly

         remitted the matter to CoC. Accordingly, issue no. (ii) is answered in

         the affirmative.



         IN RE: ISSUE (iii)(a)

         COMPLIANCE OF SECTION 30(2)(b) OF THE CODE & REGULATION

         38(1)(B) OF CIRP REGULATIONS AND NCLT’S CURING POWER
```

```text
                                                 Reportable



2026 INSC 1223  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

                 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION



                  CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3097 OF 2026



M/s. Ganesh Benzoplast Ltd.             ….. Appellant



                             versus



The State Trading Corporation of India  ….. Respondent



                                         J U D G M E N T



    SANJAY KUMAR, J



    1. Company Petition (IB) No. 1975/MB/2018 was filed by the State

    Trading Corporation of India (STC), the respondent, under Section 9 of

    the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 20161, seeking to initiate



    corporation insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against Ganesh

    Benzoplast Ltd., the appellant. However, by order dated 13.02.2020, the

    National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench2, disposed of the



    company petition directing the appellant to pay a sum of ₹2,18,88,421/-

    within a time frame to the STC. This amount was stated to constitute 25%

    of the principal dues of the STC. Aggrieved by this order, the STC filed



Signature Not Verified

Digitally signed by

Deepak Guglani

Date: 2026.11.16



18:27:14 ICST ompany Appeal (AT)(INS) No. 753 of 2021 before the National Company



Reason:



1  For short, ‘the IBC’



2  For short, ‘the NCLT’

Law Appellate Tribunal3, Principal Bench, New Delhi. By judgment dated

21.01.2026, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and restored Company

Petition (IB) No. 1975/MB/2018 to the file of the NCLT for deciding the

case afresh in accordance with law. Aggrieved by such restoration, the

appellant filed the present appeal.

2. By order dated 17.03.2026, this Court stayed the operation of the

impugned judgment dated 21.01.2026.

3. Ganesh Benzoplast Ltd., the appellant, is a company incorporated

in Maharashtra during the year 1986. It is involved in the manufacture and

storage of chemicals. Its infrastructure division provides storage tank

terminals for storage of petroleum products, oils, etc., at the ports in the

State. The appellant had business transactions with the STC to facilitate

supply of toluene and allied products to it in the year 2003 and for export

of its industrial lubricants during the years 2004 to 2006.

4. While so, the appellant sought reference under Section 15(1) of the

Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 19854, before the

Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) due to erosion of

its net worth, as reflected in its audited balance sheet for the financial year

ended 31.03.2008. The reference was registered as Case No. 42 of 2009.

On 06.05.2010, the BIFR declared the appellant a sick industrial unit, in



3  For short, ‘the NCLAT’



4  For short, ‘the SICA’



                           2

terms of Section 3(1)(o) of the SICA and appointed an operating agency



for formulating a Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS).



5. The DRS was circulated on 18.04.2013 with the cut-off date fixed as

31.03.2011. After statutory hearings were held, the DRS was modified as



directed and was submitted for approval to the BIFR. However, as the



BIFR ceased to function, owing to absence of a member, the appellant



approached the Delhi High Court by way of Writ Petition (C) No. 9320 of



2015 seeking approval of the DRS. The writ petition was allowed by a



Division Bench of the Delhi High Court on 04.12.2015. Significantly, the



DRS and the approved Rehabilitation Scheme (RS) provided for



unsecured liabilities being scaled down under Clause 11.11. This clause



reads as follows:-



         ‘11.11 Unsecured Liabilities

         a) The unsecured creditors would be paid at 25% of the

         principal dues in five equal annual instalment with an option

         not to accept the scaled down value of their dues and wait till

         the scheme of rehabilitation of the company has worked itself

         out/Seven years. M/s Pennar Paterson also will be treated at

         par with other unsecured creditors. Unsecured creditors also

         includes contingent liabilities, if crystallized.’



6. Annexure V appended to the DRS/RS furnished the details of the



unsecured creditors of the appellant as on 31.03.2011. The STC did not



figure in this list of 191 unsecured creditors. On the other hand, it was



shown in Annexure VI(a), titled ‘List of Contingent Liabilities of Ganesh



Benzoplast Ltd.’. The STC figured at Serial No. 6 in this list of ten



                                                        3

contingent liabilities and its claimed amount was shown as ₹11.35 crores.

Therefore, in terms of Clause 11.11 of the DRS/RS, till its liability stood

crystallized, STC could not attain the status of an ‘unsecured creditor’.

Despite it being shown as a ‘contingent liability’ in the DRS/RS, the STC

did not choose to challenge the same. The DRS had been published in

the newspapers on 09.05.2013 but despite the same, the STC never

objected to its status therein or the manner in which it was to be treated

even if it attained the status of an ‘unsecured creditor’. Even after approval

of the DRS by the Delhi High Court, vide order dated 04.12.2015, the STC

remained unmoved. The said order was challenged by a third party,

Avron Chemicals Pvt. Ltd., an unsecured creditor of the appellant, before

this Court, by way of SLP(C) No. 12096 of 2016. The SLP was dismissed

by this Court on 10.04.2018 observing that, given the facts of the case,

this Court was not inclined to interfere with the said order.

7. However, the STC deemed it fit to issue a demand notice on

20.03.2018 to the appellant under Section 8 of the IBC, claiming that a

sum of ₹24,26,44,490/- was due and payable to it. This sum comprised

₹17,00,05,876/- towards dues of export transactions; ₹3,68,62,534/-

towards domestic transactions; and ₹3,57,76,081/- for the appellant’s

failure in submitting ‘C’ Forms under the Central Sales Tax Act. The

appellant denied its liability, by reply dated 31.03.2018. Thereupon, the

STC filed Company Petition (IB) No. 1975/MB/2018 before the NCLT on



                                                        4

05.06.2018 under Section 9 of the IBC. During the pendency of the case,

the appellant handed over the requisite ‘C’ Forms to the STC on

30.01.2020.

8. In the order dated 13.02.2020 passed in the said company petition,

the NCLT noted that the STC had filed a rejoinder wherein it stated that,

as per the scheme sanctioned by the BIFR, it would be entitled to receive

25% of the principal dues in five equal instalments, treating it as

unsecured creditor. The NCLT also noted that the issue relating to

submission of ‘C’ Forms stood settled due to the submission of such forms

by the appellant on 30.01.2020. Further, the NCLT took note of the letter

dated 04.10.2019 addressed to the STC by the appellant, offering to settle

the issue by paying ₹1.75 crore, by way of compromise, in full and final

settlement of the STC’s claims. The NCLT observed that the said offer

was reasonable, as STC could only be treated as an ‘unsecured creditor’

in terms of the RS. Though the STC insisted on admission of its company

petition, the NCLT opined that payment of 25% of its dues, as offered by

the appellant, would meet the ends of justice and, accordingly, quantified

the amount payable as ₹2,18,88,421/-. Directing that this amount should

be paid within 30 days from the date of receipt of the order, the NCLT

disposed of the company petition.

9. This order was subjected to challenge by the STC before the

NCLAT, by way of Company Appeal (AT)(INS) No. 753/2021. However, in



                                                        5

the first instance, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal on the ground of

limitation, by judgment dated 20.04.2023. Aggrieved thereby, the STC

filed Civil Appeal No. 5477 of 2023 before this Court. The appeal was

allowed on 02.04.2025, holding that the STC’s appeal before the NCLAT

ought to have been treated as having been filed within time. The STC’s

appeal was restored to its original position and it was directed to be heard

and decided on merits. It was pursuant to this remand order, that the

NCLAT reheard the matter and allowed the appeal on 21.01.2026,

directing the STC’s company petition to be restored on the file of the NCLT

for decision afresh, leading to the filing of the present appeal.

10. Perusal of the impugned judgment dated 21.01.2026 reflects that

the NCLAT was of the opinion that the bone of contention between the

parties was with regard to treatment of the dues of the STC and observed

that, an unsecured creditor had two options under the RS, namely, to

accept 25% of its principal dues in instalments or, if it did not accept the

scaled-down value of its dues, wait till the rehabilitation scheme worked

itself out or seven years and agitate for its dues thereafter. The STC

contended that, if it was to be treated as an unsecured creditor, it had to

choose between the two options and the NCLT could not have forced it to

take the first option of accepting only 25% of its dues. It was brought to

the notice of the NCLAT that, pursuant to the order dated 13.02.2020

passed by the NCLT, the appellant had already paid ₹2,18,88,421/- to the



                                                        6

STC, which had accepted the same without prejudice. In that regard, the

STC contended that the appellant should have paid the 25% amount in

five annual instalments from 2015, as per Clause 11.11, but the appellant

paid a lumpsum amount only after the passing of the order dated

13.02.2020. The STC, therefore, argued that such payment was not in

keeping with Clause 11.11 and it could not be forced to accept the same.

Concurring with the STC on this point, the NCLAT observed that there was

no explanation as to why the STC’s dues were shown as a contingent

liability and why, when the appellant denied that liability altogether, the

NCLT had ordered payment of 25% of the principal dues. Holding so, the

NCLAT allowed the appeal and restored the company petition.

11. The reasoning of the NCLAT failed to take note of the fact that the

STC issued a demand notice on 20.03.2018, well within the seven year

period under the so-called second option in Clause 11.11 of the RS

sanctioned by the Delhi High Court on 04.12.2015. Further, the NCLAT

also lost sight of the fact that the options were available only to an

‘unsecured creditor’ and not to claimants under the category of ‘contingent

liabilities’. It was only upon crystallization of such a claim that a contingent

liability could be treated as an unsecured debt. Admittedly, there was no

crystallization of the STC’s claim, whereby it could call itself an ‘unsecured

creditor’. Therefore, be it viewed from any angle, at the point of time that

the STC issued a demand notice and even when it filed a company



                                                        7

petition, it did not act as per Clause 11.11 of the RS. Further, though the

NCLAT deemed it fit to wonder why the STC’s claim was treated as a

contingent liability, the inescapable fact remains that the STC itself

accepted such categorization and never challenged it. It was, therefore,

too late in the day for it to claim otherwise or raise that issue.

12. Insofar as the so-called second option under Clause 11.11 of the RS

is concerned, the NCLAT strangely refused to give effect to the decision

of this Court in Modi Rubber Limited vs. Continental Carbon India

Limited5. Therein, this Court noted that after amendment of the SICA in

1994, the BIFR was empowered to scale-down/vary the dues of creditors,

including decree holders, arbitration award holders and industrial award

holders. This Court held that, once a rehabilitation scheme is approved by

the BIFR, it would be binding on the unsecured creditors also, as there is

no difference between unsecured creditors and creditors. It was further

held that unsecured creditors did not have the option to not accept the

scaling-down of their dues as the rehabilitation scheme itself would be

rendered unworkable if this is permitted, thereby frustrating the very

objective of the SICA. This Court held that minority creditors and

unsecured creditors could not be permitted to stall rehabilitation of a sick

company by not accepting the scaled-down value of their dues as unless

and until there was a sacrifice by all concerned, including creditors,



5  (2023) 17 SCC 263



                      8

financial institutions, unsecured creditors and labourers, there could not

be revival of the sick industrial company.

13. In Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited and others vs.

Coromandel Sacks Private Limited6, this Court affirmed and applied the

ratio laid down in Modi Rubber Limited (supra). That was a case where

a holder of a decree against a sick company was not even part of the

rehabilitation scheme approved by the BIFR but, despite the same, this

Court held that, had it been part of the scheme, it would have had to settle

for the scaled-down value of its dues, as a similar approach had been

adopted in the scheme for settling the dues of other creditors and in such

a scenario, the decree-holder would not have had any other option but to

accept the scaled-down value and settle its dues.

14. In the light of the aforestated edicts, the option given under Clause

11.11 to unsecured creditors to wait till the scheme worked itself out or for

seven years and thereafter agitate their claim for their full dues was not

valid. Once the DRS was sanctioned, the approved RS was binding on all

concerned, i.e., the unsecured creditors and the unsecured creditors in

waiting, and there was no possibility of reopening the issue after the

scheme worked itself out or after seven years, thereby putting the

appellant, which stood rehabilitated, at the risk of becoming sick again.

That being so, when the STC was not even treated as an ‘unsecured



6  (2024) 8 SCC 172



                     9

creditor’ but remained a mere ‘contingent liability’ as on the date of

approval of the DRS by the Delhi High Court on 04.12.2015, the question

of it claiming a higher status than an ‘unsecured creditor’, whereby it could

agitate for the full dues claimed by it, did not arise.

15. The distinction sought to be drawn by the NCLAT, when faced with

the decision of this Court in Modi Rubber Limited (supra), on the ground

that the STC was not an ‘unsecured creditor’ but only a ‘contingent

liability’, defies logic as the STC could, at best, attain the status of an

‘unsecured creditor’, if its dues stood crystalized and upon such an event

materializing, Clause 11.11 of the RS only brought the STC on par with

the unsecured creditors listed in Annexure-V appended to the RS,

whereby it could only claim 25% of its principal dues and no more.

16. The STC’s contention that, as it was not paid 25% of its principal

dues in five annual instalments starting from the year 2015, it could not be

brought within the ambit of Clause 11.11 of the RS, is misconceived, as it

was only upon crystallization of its dues that the STC, which was shown

as a ‘contingent liability’ in Annexure VI(a), attained the status of an

‘unsecured creditor’ and was then entitled to payment of 25% of its dues

in five annual instalments. Admittedly, the STC did not initiate any steps

to have its dues crystalized and straightaway proceeded to issue a notice

under Section 8 of the IBC for its entire dues. The regime of the IBC does

not provide for determination of liability or quantification thereof, whereby



                                                       10

the STC could have sought crystallization of its dues thereunder.

Therefore, the STC was not entitled to seek payment of 25% of its dues

in five annual instalments from 2015 onwards. Despite the fact that the

STC still remained a contingent liability, the appellant addressed the letter

dated 04.10.2019 seeking closure, by offering to pay 25% of its principal

dues without the STC even resorting to crystallization of its dues. This fair

offer was acted upon by the NCLT, which directed payment of 25% of the

STC’s dues, quantified at ₹2,18,88,421/-.

17. Admittedly, the STC’s claim for non-submission of C-Forms stood

decimated by submission of such forms by the appellant on 30.01.2020.

Therefore, only the other two claims relating to export transactions and

domestic transactions remained and taking the same into account, the

NCLT quantified the amount at ₹2,18,88,421/-. No dispute has been

raised before us with regard to such quantification and the STC itself

accepted this amount on 20.03.2020, without prejudice. Viewed thus, it is

clear that nothing remained to be adjudicated in the company petition filed

under Section 9 of the IBC, as the maximum amount that the STC could

have realized, in terms of the approved RS, was already paid to it pursuant

to the NCLT’s order dated 13.02.2020. The NCLAT, therefore, erred in

overlooking this crucial fact and in allowing the STC’s appeal against the

said order and restoring the company petition for decision afresh though

there was nothing left to be adjudicated therein.



                                                       11

18. The appeal is accordingly allowed, setting aside the judgment dated

21.01.2026 passed in Company Appeal (AT)(INS) No. 753 of 2021 by the

National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi,

and restoring the order dated 13.02.2020 passed in Company Petition (IB)

No. 1975/MB/2018 by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai

Bench.



       Parties shall bear their own costs.



                               .........................., J

                                SANJAY KUMAR



                       …..............................., J.

                        SANJEEV SACHDEVA



November 16, 2026

New Delhi.



                   12
```
