```text
JUSTICE YOGESH KHANNA, MEMBER (JUDICIAL)



         The present four appeals being Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) Nos. 933,

934, 935 and 943 of 2026 have been filed by Mrs. Bindu Kapoor (Appellant) in

her capacity as suspended director of four corporate debtors. All the four appeals

have been filed against common impugned order dated 07.04.2026 passed by

Ld. NCLT, New Delhi Bench in CP(IB) Nos. 36, 32, 31 and 30 of 2026. These

four petitions were filed against four different Corporate Debtors, namely,

Imagine Estate Private Ltd (CP(IB) No.36 of 2026), Imagine Home Private Ltd.

(CP(IB) No.32 of 2026), Imagine Residence Private Ltd. (CP (IB) No.31 of 2026)

and Imagine Habitat Private Ltd. (CP(IB) No.30/2026). The common issues are

raised in these appeals and the facts of Company Appeal(AT)(Insolvency) No.933

of 2026 of Ld. NCLT, New Delhi Bench in CP(IB) No.36 of 2026 titled J.C. Flowers

Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd Vs. Imagine Estate Private Limited are taken up

while deciding these appeals. The petition CP(IB) NO.36 of 2026 was filed by

M/s J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Ltd (i.e. “Respondent No. 2 / JCF”)

seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIRP”) against

the Corporate Debtor (“CD”). It is argued Ld. NCLT has vide the Impugned Order

                                                               7



passed an entirely unreasoned order and proceeded to admit the Corporate

Debtor into CIRP, appointing Ms. Mamta Binani as an Interim Resolution

Professional (“IRP / Respondent No.1”) of the Corporate Debtor.



2. Section 7 Petition was filed by M/s JCF against the Corporate Debtor,

inter-alia, based on the following financial arrangements: (i) the CD’s

hypothecation against a loan of Rs. 105 crore availed by M/s Bliss House Private

Limited (“BHPL”) from M/s Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited (“IHFL”),

pursuant to a Loan Agreement dated 29.03.2019 (“Rs. 105 crore loan” and

“Hypothecation Deed”); and (ii) two loans worth Rs. 160 crore and Rs. 90 crore

availed by the CD from IHFL under Loan Agreements dated 05.09.2018,

aggregating to Rs. 250 crore (“Rs. 250 crore loans”), and; (iii) two loans worth Rs.

172 crore and Rs. 174 crore availed by the Corporate Debtor from Indiabulls

Commercial Credit Limited (“ICCL”) under Loan Agreements dated 07.10.2019,

aggregating to Rs. 346 crore (“Rs. 346 crore loans”, collectively referred to along

with the Rs. 250 crore loans as the “Rs. 596 crore loans”). It was alleged while

BHPL as well as the CD had duly complied with their obligations, on 09.03.2020,

IHFL issued the Loan Recall Notices (“2020 LRNs”), recalling the loan facilities

alleging an ‘Event of Default’ had occurred as a result of ‘Material Adverse Effect’

under the aforesaid Loan Agreements, without any justification or elaboration of

the alleged ‘Event of Default’.



3. Considering the dispute resolution scheme under the aforesaid loans,

arbitral proceedings were initiated by IHFL and it finally concluded on

                                                               8



08.05.2021, wherein, the Ld. Sole Arbitrator reserved the matter for the purpose

of passing the awards (“IHFL Arbitration”). After a significant delay of one (1)

year, nine (9) months and twenty (20) days, the Ld. Sole Arbitrator proceeded to

issue similarly – worded Awards on 28.02.2023. Aggrieved by the aforesaid

Awards rendered by the Ld. Sole Arbitrator in the IHFL Arbitration, BHPL as well

as the CD, preferred petitions under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act before the

Hon’ble High Court of Delhi in September 2023 (collectively referred to as

“Section 34 Petitions”)



4. On 29.03.2025, IHFL executed an Assignment Agreement in favour of M/s

JCF whereby all of IHFL’s rights in relation to the Rs. 105 crore loan as well as

the Rs. 596 crore loans were assigned to M/s JCF. It is alleged subsequently,

on 24.10.2025, M/s JCF, with an alleged malafide intent to circumvent the

aforesaid Section 34 Petitions, filed a Petition under Section 7 of IBC before the

Ld. NCLT, New Delhi seeking initiation of CIRP against BHPL which was admitted

by the Ld. NCLT, vide Order dated 21.01.2026 (“PL Admission Order”).

Thereafter, notwithstanding the fact the registered office of the CD is in Mumbai;

on 04.12.2025, M/s JCF filed the Section 7 Petition against the CD before Ld.

NCLT, New Delhi. JCF alleged the CD was an ‘obligor’ under the Rs. 105 crore

loan, and the Hypothecation Deed to secure Rs. 105 crore loan would amount to

a ‘guarantee’ enabling the Ld. NCLT to exercise its jurisdiction under Section

60(2) of IBC. Despite the CD’s vehement submissions on 07.04.2026, the Ld.

NCLT proceeded to pass the Impugned Order.

5. The learned senior counsel for the appellant rather admitted the CIRP



proceedings have been initiated against the principal borrower and the judgment



of the Ld. NCLT was confirmed till the Hon’ble Supreme Court. The impugned



order admits petitions against four different companies who had allegedly



hypothecated their assets for the loans granted to the principal borrower. It was



argued the facts of these cases are wholly different than that of the principal



borrower and the Ld. NCLT, New Delhi has no jurisdiction to deal with the



insolvency qua the guarantor(s).



6. It was argued (a) all these four companies on whose behalf the appeals



have been filed by the suspended director had its registered office(s) at Mumbai



and hence petition(s) ought to have been filed at Mumbai and (b) all these



companies are not the corporate guarantors of the loans granted to the principal



borrowers and at best these companies can be termed as hypothecators and thus



does not fall within ambit of the sub-section (2) of Section 60 of the IBC. Section



60(1) and (2) are as under: -



                 “60. Adjudicating Authority for corporate persons.

                 (1)The Adjudicating Authority, in relation to insolvency

                 resolution and liquidation for corporate persons

                 including corporate debtors and personal guarantors

                 thereof shall be the National Company Law Tribunal

                 having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the

                 registered office of the corporate person is located.

                 (2)Without prejudice to sub-section (1) and

                 notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in

                 this Code, where a corporate insolvency resolution

                 process or liquidation proceeding of a corporate debtor

                 is pending before a National Company Law Tribunal,

                 an application relating to the insolvency resolution or

                 personal guarantor of such corporate debtor' by Act No.

                 such National Company Law Tribunal.”

9. It was argued the above paras do show the plea on territorial jurisdiction



was rejected by the Ld. NCLT and the documents viz the loan agreements and



the hypothecation deeds were treated as the Corporate Guarantee(s). Reference



was made to Section 126 of the India Contract Act which defines Guarantee as



under: -



                  “126.'Contract of guarantee', 'surety', 'principal debtor'

                 and 'creditor'—

                 A 'contract of guarantee' is a contract to perform the

                 promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in

                 case of his default. The person who gives the

                 guarantee is called the 'surety'; the person in respect

                 of whose default the guarantee is given is called the

                 'principal debtor', and the person to whom the

                 guarantee is given is called the 'creditor'. A guarantee

                 may be either oral or written.”



10. It was argued the first feature of the guarantee is it has to be a tripartite



agreement, which fact was missing in the present case and no examination on



this aspect was made by the Ld. NCLT.



11. It was the submission of the learned senior counsel for the appellant the



Ld. NCLT had relied upon para 1 of the Deed of Hypothecation but had ignored

the impugned order had relied upon China Development Banks case but it



overlooked that in the cited case the Deed of Hypothecation was rather a tripartite



agreement which met the requirements of Section 126 and 127 of the Contract



Act.

         17. xxx…. We heard the counsels for the parties and perused

         1. In consideration of the Lender having lent and

19. From the aforementioned, it is clear that the Corporate

Debtors before us stood as surety for repayment of the amount

of debt borrowed by the Principal Debtor from the Lender, thus

it would not be gainsaid that the Corporate Debtors stood as

Corporate Guarantor qua the financial facility availed by the

Principal Debtor viz. Bliss House Pvt. Ltd. In China Development

Bank vs. Doha Bank Q.P.S.C. and Ors. (Civil Appeals No. 7298

of 2022 with Nos. 7328, 7407, 7615 of 2022 and 7434 of 2023)

decided on 20.12.2024 [reported as (2025) 7 Supreme Court

Cases 729], it could be viewed that a contract between a

guarantee when the same is to perform the promise or

discharge the liability of a third person in case of default. In the

said judgement, the Hon’ble Supreme Court further ruled that

going by the title, ‘Deed of Hypothecation (DoH) is a document

creating Hypothecation which means the process of using an

asset as collateral for a loan which acts as a protection to the

Lender when the Borrower does not repay the loan, however,

                                                              20



         the name of the document is not a decisive factor and only

         because the title of the document contains the word

         "Hypothecation", it cannot be concluded that guarantee is not a

         part of the document.

17. It was argued by the learned senior counsel for the appellant the loan



agreement(s) as well as Deed of Guarantee(s) are bilateral agreements and not



tripartite agreements as there are no three parties in such agreements and hence



the Hypothecation agreements cannot be read as Contract of Guarantee(s) which



infact are always tripartite agreements. It was argued Guarantee is not defined



in the IBC and hence per Section 3(37) of the IBC, its meaning has to be derived



from Section 126 of the Contract Act, quoted above.



18. The learned senior counsel for the appellant then referred to M/s PNB Ltd



Vs Shri Vikram Cotton Mills and Another, 1970(1) Supreme Court Cases 60 which



held:-



         “10. A promise to be primarily and independently liable for

         another person’s conduct may amount to a contract of

         indemnity. A contract of guarantee requires concurrence of

         three persons-the principal debtor, the surety and the creditor-

         the surety undertaking an obligation of the surety depends

         substantially on the principal debtor’s default; under a contract

         of indemnity liability arises from loss caused to the promise by

         the conduct of the promise himself or by the conduct of another

         person.:

19. It was an argument China Development Bank judgement was used out of



context as in the cited case, the Hon’ble Court interpreted tripartite agreements



which contained some other additional clauses, which are not in the present



case.

                                                              21



20. Reference was made to JC Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd Vs Vithal



M Dahake, Company Appeal (AT)(Ins) No.1801/2024, wherein the Court held: -



         “23. The Appellant submitted that the Mortgage Deeds executed

         between the Appellant, the Principal Borrower, and the

         Corporate Debtor fulfil all the requisites of a contract of

         guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,

         being a tripartite agreement wherein vide, Clause 3, the

         Corporate Debtor undertook an unconditional and unequivocal

         liability to repay the Secured Obligations. The Appellant further

         contended that the “covenant to pay” in the Mortgage Deeds

         constitutes a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the

         Indian Contract Act, 1872 and that the liability of the surety is

         co-extensive with that of the principal debtor under Section 128

         of the Contract Act, 1872 thereof.

21. Thus it was the submission of the learned senior counsel for the appellant



the judgements quoted were of tripartite agreements and were used out of context



in the impugned judgement.



22. The Respondent has rebutted each and every argument of the appellant.



23. Heard.



24. The facts do show BHPL was admitted into CIRP by the Ld. NCLT vide its



Order dated 21 January 2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 585/ND/2025. This was affirmed



by this Tribunal by judgment dated 29 May 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No.



2040 of 2025 and Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 585 of 2026 and later by the Hon’ble



Supreme Court. Hence BHPL’s admission and the underlying default has,



therefore, attained finality. This Appeal raises identical grounds as raised by



BHPL in earlier round and rejected by this Tribunal and also affirmed by the

                                                              22



Hon’ble Supreme Court. The only remaining issue is the validity of invocation of

Section 60(2) of the IBC.



25. The loan of Rs. 105 Crores to BHPL (the “BHPL Debt”) is governed by the

Loan Agreement dated 29 March 2019 (the “BHPL Loan Agreement”). Schedule I

undisputedly lists the Corporate Debtor as a “Hypothecator”.



26. Clause 1.1 of the BH Loan Agreement defines “Obligors” to include inter-

alia the Borrower and the Hypothecators i.e. the Corporate Debtor. Clause 2.1

makes all Obligors jointly and severally liable for the dues under the BH Loan

Agreement. Clause 12.2 empowers the Lender, upon an Event of Default, to recall

the BH Debt, whereupon the entire dues become immediately payable by the

Obligors, which term specifically includes Hypothecators.



27. Further, under Clause 2.2.4, the Obligors “are under an obligation to pay

from any source” upon a shortfall, payment default or Event of Default, so that

the entire dues under the BH Loan Agreement are recovered by the lender. The

Corporate Debtor admittedly executed the Deed of Hypothecation, whereby it

assumed all obligations stipulated under the BH Loan Agreement. The Corporate

Debtor executed the Deed of Hypothecation in furtherance of the BH Loan

Agreement. Under its recitals viz a) Recital A names the BH Loan Agreement in

Schedule III; b) Recital B contemplates the liability of the Obligors to repay the

dues under the BH Loan Agreement; and c) Recital D records that “Obligors”

includes the Hypothecator, a status the Corporate Debtor admits. The Corporate

                                                              23



Debtor thus consciously undertook obligations ascribed to it under the BH Loan

Agreement.



28. This is further confirmed by Clause 1 of the Deed of Hypothecation, which

reiterates the Corporate Debtor’s assumption of the obligations under the BH

Loan Agreement. Clause 5 requires the BH Loan Agreement to be read with the

Deed of Hypothecation and to prevail over it in case of inconsistency. The

obligations set out in the BH Loan Agreement establish joint and several liability

in addition to a covenant to pay any shortfall for the reasons set out below.



29. By a Loan Recall Notice dated 9 March 2020, the BH Debt was recalled

following Mr. Rana Kapoor’s arrest. No repayment was made within the 5 days

stipulated in the Loan Recall Notice, and accordingly, the default occurred on 14

March 2020. This failure to honour the notice resulted in Arbitral Awards dated

28 February 2023, which affirmed the liability of BHPL and the other group

entities. The Award in IHFL v. BHPL (the “Bliss House 1 Award”), held Imagine

Homes Pvt. Ltd. and Imagine Residence Pvt. Ltd., are jointly and severally liable

for the BH Debt.



30. The Corporate Debtor is also directly liable for loans extended to it (the

“Imagine Debt”) under two Loan Agreements dated 5 September 2018 and 7

October 2019 aggregating to Rs. 596 Crores. Clauses 12.1.8 and 12.2 of the

Imagine Loan Agreements entitled the lender to recall the loans upon default,

which it did by a Loan Recall Notice dated 9 March 2020. These defaults stand

crystallised by Arbitral Awards dated 28 February 2023. These Awards are

                                                              24



challenged before the High Court of Delhi in O.M.P. (Comm) Nos. 359/2023,

363/2023 and 365/2023, but, however, no stay has been granted and no

amount has been repaid till date.



31. By registered Assignment Agreements dated 29 March 2025 and 30

August 2025, all rights, title and interest under the loan agreements, security

documents and Awards stood assigned to Respondent No. 2 herein. By a Notice

of Demand dated 29 September 2025, the Financial Creditor called upon the

Corporate Debtor to pay Rs. 260,32,53,778.61. The said demand remained

unanswered and unpaid. Further, no monies have been paid under the loan

agreements thereafter.



32. Section 60(2) begins with a non-obstante provision which carves out an

exception to the general rule of jurisdiction under Section 60(1). It stipulates the

proceedings against the principal borrower and its guarantor are dealt with by

the same Tribunal, thereby avoiding conflicting orders and double realisation. In

this case, BHPL, the principal borrower, is undergoing CIRP before the Ld. NCLT,

New Delhi and its admission has attained finality up to the Hon’ble Supreme

Court. The CIRP of the Corporate Debtor, as a corporate guarantor, must

therefore proceed before the same Ld. Adjudicating Authority. This Tribunal by

judgement dated 1 August 2025, in S. Vasudevan v. IDBI Trusteeship Limited

CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No.362/2023, upheld proceedings before the Ld. NCLT,

Chennai against a corporate guarantor whose registered office was in Bengaluru,

                                                              25



since the principal borrower’s proceedings were pending before the Ld. NCLT,

Chennai.



33. Moreover, the Corporate Debtor and BHPL are subsidiaries of RAB

Enterprises with common ownership and promoters, forming a single integrated

group. For this reason, the Ld. NCLT, by an Order dated 12 June 2026 has

consolidated their CIRPs.



34. Section 5(5A) of the IBC defines a “corporate guarantor” as a corporate

person who is the surety in a contract of guarantee to a corporate debtor. Section

126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract of guarantee as “a

contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in

case of his default”, and provides that it “may be either oral or written”. Each

requirement is satisfied as BHPL is the principal borrower, IHFL (now

Respondent No. 2) is the creditor, and the Corporate Debtor, as an Obligor, is

the surety. Clauses 2.1 and 12.2 of the BH Loan Agreement make the Obligors,

including the Corporate Debtor, jointly and severally liable for the BH Debt, and

hence liable to pay upon BHPL’s default. A covenant to pay upon shortfall, such

as Clause 2.2.4, has been construed as a guarantee by the Hon’ble Supreme

Court in China Development Bank v. Doha Bank QPSC, (2025) 7 SCC 729. The

covenant under Clause 5(iii) of the Deed of Hypothecation considered in that case

is, in substance, identical to Clauses 2.1 and 2.2.4 of the BH Loan Agreement

read with Clause 1 of the Deed of Hypothecation. Thus the Ld. NCLT has

correctly applied China Development Bank judgement while interpreting Section

                                                              26



60(2). The Corporate Debtor’s liability is, therefore, not limited to the

hypothecated assets, Clause 2.2.4 obliges the Obligors to make good any

shortfall from any source.



35. The Appellant’s plea based on nomenclature is equally untenable. China

Development Bank (supra) reiterates the settled principle that the substance of

a document’s covenants, irrespective of its nomenclature, is decisive. Thus the

Corporate Debtor if not described as a “guarantor” is, therefore, immaterial. It is

settled law that a contract of guarantee can be recorded in multiple agreements,

so long as the intent to stand as guarantor is clearly discernible. The mere fact

that BHPL has not signed the Deed of Hypothecation is irrelevant, since the Deed

of Hypothecation itself evidences the assumption of all obligations under the BH

Loan Agreement. Read together, the BH Loan Agreement and the Deed of

Hypothecation evidence a tripartite arrangement between the principal borrower

(BHPL), the creditor (IHFL, now Respondent No. 2) and the surety (the Corporate

Debtor), constituting a contract of guarantee. The plea is all the more untenable

coming from the Appellant, who executed the BH Loan Agreement on behalf of

BHPL and the Deed of Hypothecation on behalf of the Corporate Debtor. As a

common director of both companies under RAB Enterprises, the Appellant

cannot now raise such contentions.



36. In identical circumstances, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Punjab

National Bank v. Shri Vikram Cotton Mills, (1970) 1 SCC 60, a decision cited by

the Appellant itself, held the absence of all parties’ signatures on a single

                                                              27



document does not negate a guarantee. A guarantee can be inferred from conduct,

from an oral agreement or a combined reading of several agreements.



37. Thus independently of its liability as guarantor of BHPL, the Corporate

Debtor is liable for the Imagine Debt. As held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in

Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank, (2018) 1 SCC 407, and E.S.

Krishnamurthy v. Bharath HiTech Builders Pvt. Ltd., (2022) 3 SCC 161, once

the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied on the occurrence of debt and default, it

must admit the petition.



38. The Appellant has not denied the execution of the Imagine Loan

Agreements, the disbursal or the failure to repay.



39. Thus, the appeals are not maintainable on this count alone. The Impugned

Order suffers from no illegality and thus all above appeals are dismissed.

Pending applications, if any, are also disposed of.



                  (Justice Yogesh Khanna)

                   Officiating Chairperson
```

```text
                                                 O R D E R

[Per: Justice Mohd. Faiz Alam Khan, Member (Judicial)]



         Com. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1804 OF 2026 has been preferred under Section 61

of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") by Ms. Sangeeta Aggarwal

("Appellant") challenging the order dated 31.08.2026 passed by the Ld. National

Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, Bench - II ("Ld. Adjudicating Authority") in I.A.

(IBC) No. 798 filed under Company Petition (IB) No. 651 of 2025.



2. The relevant facts with regard to this appeal are that on 06 December 2024,

Canara Bank instituted proceedings against the Appellant Ms. Sangeeta Aggarwal

under Section 95 of the Code, being CP (IB) No. 23 (AHM) of 2024, before the Ld.

National Company Law Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench ("Ld. Adjudicating Authority").

Mr. Sunil Kumar Kabra was appointed as the Resolution Professional in the said

proceedings on 22 January 2025.

3. It is further reflected that the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against

the Corporate Debtor was also initiated vide order dated 01 April 2025, passed by

the Ld. National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, Bench V, in CP (IB) No. 413 (ND)

of 2025 and Respondent No.1, Equentia filed its claim in Form C, for INR 13.40

crores, in the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor.

4. It is further evident that on 05 November 2025, Respondent No. 1- Equentia

instituted a fresh proceeding under Section 95 against the Appellant, being CP (IB)

No. 651 of 2025, before the Ld. Adjudicating Authority and vide order dated 29

January 2026, the Ld. Adjudicating Authority appointed Mr. Loveneet Handa

("Respondent No. 2") as the RP, who submitted report on 17 February 2026, bearing

I.A. No. 798 of 2026 under Section 99 of the Code, recommending initiation of the

personal insolvency resolution process against the Appellant. The Adjudicating

                                                             3



Authority by passing impugned Order initiated personal insolvency process against

Appellant Sangeeta Aggarwal.

5. It is further reflected that on 21 November 2025, i.e., subsequent to the filing

of Equentia's petition, Canara Bank withdrew its proceedings pending before the

Adjudicating Authority, Ahmedabad Bench.

6. Com. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1805 OF 2026 has been preferred under Section 61

of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code") by Sri Narain Aggarwal

("Appellant") challenging the order dated 31.08.2026 passed by the Ld. National

Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, Bench - II ("Ld. Adjudicating Authority") in I.A.

(IBC) No. 972 filed under Company Petition (IB) No. 653 of 2025.

7. The relevant facts with regard to this appeal are that on 06 December 2024,

Canara Bank instituted proceedings against the Appellant under Section 95 of the

Code, being CP (IB) No. 22 (AHM) of 2024, before the Ld. National Company Law

Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench ("Ld. Adjudicating Authority, Ahmedabad") and Mr.

Sunil Kumar Kabra was appointed as the Resolution Professional in the said

proceedings. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Corporate

Debtor was also initiated vide order dated 01 April 2025, passed by the Ld. National

Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, Bench V, in CP (IB) No. 413 (ND) of 2025 and on

15 April 2025, respondent No.1-Equentia filed its claim in Form C, for INR 13.40

crores, in the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor.

8. It is further reflected that on 07 November 2025 Respondent No.1-Equentia

instituted a fresh proceeding under Section 95 against the Appellant, being CP (IB)

No. 653 of 2025, before the Ld. Adjudicating Authority. On 21 November 2025, i.e.,

subsequent to the filing of Equentia's petition, Canara Bank withdrew its proceedings

pending before the Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority, Ahmedabad Bench. However, on

19 December 2025, Canara Bank filed a fresh petition, being CP (IB) No. 704 of 2025,

                                                             4



under Section 95 against the Appellant before the Hon'ble National Company Law

Tribunal, Bench V, at New Delhi, which is stated to be pending.

9. Ld. Adjudicating Authority vide order dated 19 December 2025 appointed Mr.

Amit Talwar, as the Resolution Professional in the Equentia's petition. However, vide

order dated 10 February 2026, Ld. Adjudicating Authority, replaced Mr. Amit Talwar

and appointed Mr. Loveneet Handa (Respondent No. 2) as the Resolution

Professional, who submitted his report on 27 February 2026, bearing I.A. No. 972 of

2026 under Section 99 of the Code, recommending initiation of the personal

insolvency resolution process against the Appellant. The Adjudicating Authority by

passing impugned Order initiated personal insolvency process against Appellant Sri

Narain Aggarwal.

10. Aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned orders the appellants/ Personal

Guarantors have filed the above appeals. Keeping in view the identical issues

involved, both Appeals are being disposed of passing this common judgment.

11. Learned Counsel for the Appellant submit that admitted facts are that, on

6.12.2024, the Canara Bank has instituted proceedings against the Appellant under

Section 95 of the Code, and an interim moratorium in pursuance of Section 96 of the

Code commenced on this date. The respondent No. 1, Equentia, has filed a petition

under Section 95 of the Code on 5.11.2025 during the existence of the moratorium

initiated by the proceedings instituted by the Canara Bank on 6.12.2024. Therefore,

the proceedings initiated by Equentia are non-est.

12. It is further submitted that the fact that Canara Bank has withdrawn its

petition on 21.11.2025 and filed a fresh petition on 19.12.2025 is of no consequence

as on 5.11.2025. The interim moratorium commenced on 6.12.2024 by the filing of

the proceedings by the Canara Bank was in force.

13. It is further submitted that the learned adjudicating authority has taken

shelter of the amendment made under Section 96 of the Code. However, the said

                                                             5



amendment is not retrospective and would not be applicable to the facts of the

instant case. Therefore, the proceedings filed within the course of moratorium

initiated by proceedings instituted earlier are nullity. Reliance in this regard is placed

on Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Limited versus Hotel Gaudavan Private

Limited, 2018 (16) SCC 94 which has been followed in Sushant Chhabra versus

Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 443 of 2026).

Learned Counsel for the Appellant have also cited Union Bank of India versus P.K.

Balasubramanian, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 293 of 2022.

14. The Learned Counsel for the Appellant further submits that the main

controversy in this appeal is pertaining to the impact of Section 96(4), which was

introduced on 26 May 2026. It says that the provisions of this section shall not apply

where an application is filed for initiating an insolvency resolution process in respect

of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor. It is submitted that the reliance of the

learned adjudicating authority on Tata Capital Financial Services Limited versus Neel

Motors LLP, Commercial Arbitration Petition No. 620 of 2021 is not correct in view

of the explanation given by the Hon'ble Bombay High Court in paragraph number 14

of the report, as it is verified that the amendment is retroactive and is not

retrospective, and therefore would apply prospectively to existing facts such as the

existing arbitration petition.

15. Elaborating further, it is submitted that a retroactive amendment applies

prospectively to events that have happened earlier. If Section 96(4) had been a pure

prospective amendment, the result would be that 96(4) would only apply to those 95

petitions filed after 26 May 2026. The import of retroactivity is merely that, even in

cases where the Section 95 petition was filed before 26 May 2026, the interim

moratorium was in force prior to the amendment.

16. It is further submitted that the judgment of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in

IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited versus Manish Jain is merely a judgment deciding

                                                             6



an application under Order VII, Rule 11. In fact, it explicitly states in paragraph

number 21 that it has not considered whether the defendant number 2 is deprived

of the interim moratorium enjoyed by it. Therefore, it cannot be relied upon by the

respondent in the instant case.

17. It is further submitted that the IBBI circular dated 21 September 2026, issued

under Section 196 of the Code, has been issued in contravention of paragraph

number 13 of the judgment of Sundaresh Bhat, Liquidator of ABG Shipyard Limited

Company Appeal (AT) (INS) No. 398 of 2021. Therefore, the petition filed by the

respondent No. 1 during the interim moratorium initiated by the filing of the petition

by the Canara Bank on 06 December 2024 is non-est and therefore the impugned

order may kindly be set aside.

18. Learned Counsel for the Respondent No. 1 and RP submits that the Appeal

rests on a single premise that the application under Section 95 of the Code filed by

Equentia Financial Services Private Limited (the “Financial Creditor”) on 05.11.2025

was barred by the interim moratorium under Section 96 of the Code, and thereby

became non-est for all time, however, the said premise no longer survives after the

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026, as sub-section (4) was

inserted in Section 96, which expressly provides that Section 96 shall not apply

where an application is filed for initiating an insolvency resolution process in respect

of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor.

19. It is further submitted that the Hon’ble Bombay High Court in Tata Capital

Financial Services Ltd. v. Neel Motors LLP & Ors., IBC Law 4165 and the Hon’ble

Delhi High Court in IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. v. Manish Jain & Ors., CS(COMM)

800/2025 have held that Section 96(4) applies to pending proceedings. The

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (“IBBI”) has, by Circular No.

IBBI/II/106/2026 dated 21.09.2026 has also clarified the effect of these judgments.

                                                             7



Thus, there was no interim moratorium when the petition was filed by the

Respondent No. 1.

20. It is further submitted that Section 96 of the Code was amended by Section

51 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026, whereby, after

sub-section (3), the following sub-section was inserted:



               “51. In section 96 of the principal Act, after sub-section (3). the

               following sub-section shall be inserted, namely: —

               “(4) The provisions of this section shall not apply where an

               application is filed for initiating an insolvency resolution process

               in respect of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor.”



21. Therefore, the Appellants are admittedly personal guarantors to a corporate

debtor, and the proceedings against them are proceedings of the very kind to which

Section 96 now longer applies. The Appellant’s contention regarding the interim

moratorium under Section 96 is, therefore, untenable in view of the express statutory

exclusion. The said amendment came into force with effect from 26.05.2026, and

from that date the interim moratorium ceased to operate in respect of applications

concerning personal guarantors to corporate debtors. The Impugned Order dated

31.08.2026 was passed after the said date.

22. It is further submitted that the ratio of the above cases is directly applicable

to the facts of this case. The application of Section 96(4) to the pending Section 95

proceedings is a prospective application of a newly introduced provision to facts that

continue to exist, and does not become retrospective merely because the application

was filed earlier. The IBBI, vide Circular No. IBBI/II/106/2026 dated 21.09.2026.

has clarified the effect of the judgments of the Hon’ble Bombay High Court and the

Hon’ble Delhi High Court regarding the cessation of the interim moratorium in

respect of personal guarantors to corporate debtor.

23. It is also submitted that the reliance placed by the Appellant on the judgment

of this Hon’ble Tribunal in Sushant Chhabra v. Catalyst Trusteeship Limited,

                                                             8



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 443 of 2026, is misplaced and that judgment

cannot be read to mean that a provision subsequently enacted by the Legislature,

expressly excluding personal guarantors to corporate debtors from Section 96, can

have no application to pending proceedings. The subsequent amendment has

materially altered the statutory position. Similarly, the reliance placed by the

Appellant on Union Bank of India v. P.K. Balasubramanian, Comp. App. (AT) (CH)

(Ins.) No. 293 of 2022, is also misplaced, and cannot override the express exclusion

now contained in Section 96(4) of the Code as interpreted by the Hon’ble Bombay

High Court and the Hon’ble Delhi High Court.

24. It is further submitted by the Counsel for the RP that the RP filed their Reports

37. We notice that before the amendment made in Section 96 of the Code with

effect from 26 May 2026, Section 96 stood as under:

                                                            12



               “96. Interim-moratorium.



               (1) When an application is filed under section 94 or section 95-



               (a) an interim-moratorium shall commence on the date of the

               application in relation to all the debts and shall cease to have

               effect on the date of admission of such application; and



               (b) during the interim-moratorium period—



               (i) any legal action or proceeding pending in respect of any debt

               shall be deemed to have been stayed; and



               (ii) the creditors of the debtor shall not initiate any legal action or

               proceedings in respect of any debt.



               (2) Where the application has been made in relation to a firm, the

               interim-moratorium under sub-section (1) shall operate against all

               the partners of the firm as on the date of the application.



               (3) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall not apply to such

               transactions as may be notified by the Central Government in

               consultation with any financial sector regulator.”



               Following Amendment has been made w.e.f. 26.05.2026;



               “(4) The provisions of this section shall not apply where an

               application is filed for initiating an insolvency resolution process

               in respect of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor.”



38. In Union Bank of India vs. P.K. Balasubramanian decided on 29.03.2023



(Supra), relied on by the Appellants, following was held:



               “12. Section 96(1)(a) provides that an interim-moratorium, shall

               commence on the date of the `Application’, in relation to all the

               debts. Section 96(1)(b) of the `Code’, also specifies that during the

               `Moratorium’ period (i) any legal action or proceeding pending in

               respect of any `debt’ shall be deemed to have been stayed; and

               (ii) the `Creditors of the Debtor’, shall not initiate any legal action

               or proceedings in respect of any `debt’. The use of expression

               ‘Creditors of the Debtor’, means that all other `Creditors of the

               Debtor’, apart from the `Creditor’, on whose `Application’, `interim

               Moratorium’, has commenced. Once `Application’ under Section

               100 is admitted, `Moratorium’, commences with respect to all

               `Debts’, under Section 101 and thereafter `Public Notice’, is

               issued and ‘Claims’ from `Creditors’, are invited under Section

               102. Section 103 provides for registering of `Claims’ by Creditors.

               Section 104 provides for preparation of list of Creditors and

               thereafter repayment Plan is contemplated under Section 105.

               Thus, when an `Insolvency Resolution Process’, commences

               against the `Personal Guarantor’, all `Creditors’ of the ‘Personal

               Guarantor’, are taken care of in the proceedings under Chapter-

               III. The Code does not contemplate multiplicity of `Applications’,

               against the same `Personal Guarantor’. This `Tribunal’, is of the

               earnest view that when the `Insolvency Resolution Process’,

               commences against a `Personal Guarantor’, `Claims of all

                                                            13



               `Creditors’, are taken care of under the scheme of the I & B Code,

               2016.”

Thereafter this Appellate Tribunal after considering various authorities opined as



under: -



               “23. From the facts noted above, it is clear that although on the

               date when Section 95 application was filed by the Catalyst

               Trusteeship Ltd. against the Appellant herein on 05.08.2025,

               interim moratorium was already operating in Section 95

               application filed Canara Bank against the Appellant. The

               judgment referred above, clearly prohibit any such institution.

               The distinguishing feature, which Respondent is contending

               herein is that even though application was filed by Canara Bank,

               prior in time and moratorium had triggered, but the application

               having been withdrawn on 10.11.2025, there was no inhibition

               in admitting Section 95 application filed by Financial Creditor

               against the Appellants herein. The real question to be considered

               and answered is whether due to withdrawal of Section 95

               application by Canara Bank, the prohibition which triggered due

               to interim moratorium shall come to an end. When application

               under Section 95 filed by Canara Bank was withdrawn on

               10.11.2025, admittedly moratorium came to an end and there

               was no prohibition and the interim moratorium no longer existed,

               but what is the consequence of withdrawal of Section 95

               application on 10.11.2025 on the moratorium, which was in

               Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. against the Appellants.



               24. The statutory moratorium which has triggered on 12.01.2025,

               continued to operate till 10.11.2025 when application filed by

               Canara Bank was withdrawn. Section 101 of the IBC provides

               that when application under Section 100 is admitted, a

               moratorium shall commence, which shall cease to have effect at

               the end of period of 180 days. Thus, moratorium comes to an end

               on the day when application is admitted or rejected. The interim

               moratorium which commences on filing an application, is a

               statutory moratorium provided by enactment. During the interim

               moratorium various actions are prohibited as enumerated in

               Section 96, sub-section (1). The statutory interim moratorium

               which triggered in Section 96, shall come to an end only when

               application under Section 95 is either rejected or admitted. The

               interim moratorium in Section 96 has statutory consequences,

               which interim moratorium although shall come to an end when

               Authority has raised the issue that application is not

               maintainable. In the reply filed to Section 95 application, the

               Personal Guarantors has relied on Section 95 application filed by

41. Perusal of the above cases would reveal that all these cases have been decided

31.08.2026, however, the earlier petitions under Section 95 of the Code were filed by



the Canara Bank against the Appellants on 6/12/2024, well before coming into force



of the Amendment under Section 96 of the Code (i.e., on 26 May 2026) and the



petitions under Section 95 of the Code, on which the impugned orders have been



passed, were filed by the Respondent No. 1, Equentia, on 05/11/2025, during the



interim moratorium commenced by the filing of the petitions under Section 95 of the



Code by the Canara Bank on 06/12/2024. Thus, it is evident that the petitions were



filed by the Respondent No. 1, Equentia, against the appellant under Section 95 of



the Code during the commencement of the moratorium initiated by the filing of the



petitions by the Canara Bank on 06.12.2024.

43. Hon’ble Bombay High Court after discussing the law laid down by the Hon’ble



Supreme Court in Rajkumar Nagpal, (2022) ibclaw.in 105 SC and Vineeta Sharma



v. Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 9 SCC 1 held as under: -



               “11. Having heard the parties and having examined the record

               and the provisions of law with their assistance, in my opinion,

               the phrase “where an application is filed” would bring within its

               sweep anything that is filed and is pending with the Adjudicating

               Authority as of that date. If the intention had been to bring within

               the sweep of Section 96(4) only filings made after the introduction

               of the provision, the legislature would have consciously used

               language to that effect. Equally, while it is arguable that the

               legislature has not used clarificatory language in the provision to

                                            17



indicate that it covers applications already filed and to be filed,

in my opinion, this provision would squarely fit within the ambit

of a retroactive application. The reading of the words “is filed” as

including those that have been filed and are pending, will not give

retrospective effect, but will have prospective effect from the date

on which the provision takes effect. Therefore, in my opinion, any

Application that is filed for initiating an insolvency resolution

process in respect of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor

would not fall within the ambit of Section 96(1) and related

provisions with effect from May 26, 2026. In other words,

anything that “is filed” would include within its sweep anything

that has been filed and is continuing to remain under

adjudication under the IBC.”



12. In Rajkumar Nagpal [(2022) ibclaw.in 105 SC]1, in near-

identical circumstances, the Supreme Court considered the

introduction of a condition in relation to restructuring of

debentures by issuance of a circular. The Supreme Court quoted

from Principles of Statutory Interpretation by Justice G.P. Singh

(14th Edn., 2016 at p. 583) as follows:



“The rule against retrospective construction is not applicable to a

statute merely because “a part of the requisites for its action is

drawn from a time antecedent to its passing”. If that were not so,

every statute will be presumed to apply only to persons born and

things which come into existence after its operation and the rule

may well result in virtual nullification of most of the statutes.”

13. Analysing the meaning of “retrospective”, “retroactive” and

“prospective”, the Supreme Court declared the law in the

following words: -



(iv) The SEBI Circular has retroactive application



98. Mr N. Venkataraman, learned Senior Counsel and Additional

Solicitor General has argued that the SEBI Circular is retroactive

in nature as it does not take away or impair any vested rights. It

operates in the future, based on events that arose prior to its

issuance. Mr Darius Khambata, learned Senior Counsel

appearing for RCFL argued that the effect of applying the SEBI

Circular to the present case will render it retrospective and not

retroactive. According to him, Clauses 22 and 23 of the Fifth

Schedule to the Debenture Trust Deed(s) vested debenture-

holders with the right to authorise debenture trustees “to sanction

any compromise or arrangement proposed to be made between

the company and the beneficial owner(s)/debenture-holder(s)”.

This sanction could be authorised by a majority of “not less than

three-fourths of the persons voting … or if a poll is demanded …

not less than three-fourths in value of the votes cast on such poll”.

The SEBI Circular, it has been urged, changed the nature of the

special majority required to sanction a compromise by introducing

the requirement of a majority of 60% of ISIN level votes.”

                                            18



*****



100. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma [Vineeta Sharma v.

Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 9 SCC 1: (2021) 1 SCC (Civ) 119] this

Court described the nature of prospective, retrospective, and

retroactive laws: (SCC p. 53, para 61)



“61. The prospective statute operates from the date of its

enactment conferring new rights. The retrospective statute

operates backwards and takes away or impairs vested rights

acquired under existing laws. A retroactive statute is the one that

does not operate retrospectively. It operates in futuro. However,

its operation is based upon the character or status that arose

earlier. Characteristic or event which happened in the past or

requisites which had been drawn from antecedent events.”



101. The terms “retrospective” and “retroactive” are often used

interchangeably. However, their meanings are distinct. This

Court succinctly appreciated the difference between these

concepts in State Bank’s Staff Union (Madras Circle) v. Union of

India [State Bank’s Staff Union (Madras Circle) v. Union of India,

(2005) 7 SCC 584: 2005 SCC (L&S) 994]:



“Retroactivity” is a term often used by lawyers but rarely defined.

On analysis it soon becomes apparent, moreover, that it is used

to cover at least two distinct concepts. The first, which may be

called “true retroactivity”, consists in the application of a new rule

of law to an act or transaction which was completed before the

rule was promulgated. The second concept, which will be referred

to as “quasi-retroactivity”, occurs when a new rule of law is

applied to an act or transaction in the process of completion….

The foundation of these concepts is the distinction between

completed and pending transactions….” [T.C. Hartley, The

Foundations of European Community Law 129 (1981).]”



Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd. v. Neel Motors LLP and Ors.,

(2026) ibclaw.in 4165 HC



“102. Many decisions of this Court define “retroactivity” to mean

laws which destroy or impair vested rights. In real terms, this is

the definition of “retrospectivity” or “true retroactivity”. “Quasi-

retroactivity” or simply “retroactivity” on the other hand is a law

which is applicable to an act or transaction that is still underway.

Such an act or transaction has not been completed and is in the

process of completion. Retroactive laws also apply where the

status or character of a thing or situation arose prior to the

passage of the law. Merely because a law operates on certain

circumstances which are antecedent to its passing does not mean

that it is retrospective.



103. In the present case, RCFL issued the debentures and

defaulted on the payments to the debenture-holders prior to the

issuance of the SEBI Circular. However, as of 13-10-2020 (the

date on which the SEBI Circular came into force), a compromise

or agreement on the restructuring of the debt owed by RCFL did

not exist. The debenture-holders were not vested with any rights

with respect to the resolution of RCFL’s debt. The existence of the

debt and the subsequent default by RCFL was the status of

                                                            19



               events, which existed prior to 13-10-2020. Once it came into force,

               the SEBI Circular applied to the manner of resolution of debt, as

               specified therein.”



                                                                              [Emphasis Supplied]”



               14. A plain reading of the foregoing would make it clear that the

               term “retroactive”, while being used differently in different

               judgements is actually a prospective application of a newly

               introduced requirement of a law to facts existing as of the date of

               the introduction of the requirement. The mere reason that some

               facts may have already been into existence but continue to exist

               would not mean that the application becomes retrospective.



               15. Applying the same principles to Section 96(4) of the IBC, in

               my opinion, a moratorium insofar as it operated in respect of

               Respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 until May 25, 2026 ceased to operate

               with effect from May 26, 2026, in respect of applications filed

               under Section 95 of the IBC. In this view of the matter, in my

               opinion, the Petition would need to be considered as not being

               barred by the moratorium under IBC.”



44. Hon’ble Delhi High Court in IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Supra) IDBI



Trusteeship Services, decided on 19-Aug-26 while considering Amendment in



Section 96 of the Code and Vineeta Sharma (supra) and State Bank’s Staff Union



(Madras Circle) vs. Union of India, (2005) 7 SCC 584” held as under: -



               “7. An interesting issue has arisen in this suit by way of an

               application under Order VII Rule 11, CPC filed by the defendant

               no.2. In that, whether a benefit granted upon a party by way of

               a provision in an enactment can be taken away by way of an

               amendment under the Amending Act without expressly being

               retrospective. Particularly, while a proceeding is pending in a

               court of law. Ordinarily, amendments are construed to be

               prospective, unless retrospectivity is expressed or implied.



               15. It needs emphasis to examine as to whether the amendment

               brought to Section 96(4) of the IBC would be “retrospective” or

               “prospective” or as postulated in the aforementioned judgements,

               “retroactive”. Before the said issue is examined, it may be

               pertinent to consider as to what transpired in the minds of the

               Select Committee on Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code (Amendment)

               Bill, 2025 while recommending amendment to Section 96 of IBC,

               which was proposed under Clause 47 of the said Bill. The

               relevant provisions like Clauses 47.1, 47.2, 47.3, 47.4, 47.5,

               47.5.1, 47.5.2, 47.5.3 and 47.6 are reproduced hereunder:”



               47.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:



               The Committee note that Clause 47 seeks to amend Section 96 to

               exclude personal guarantors to corporate debtors from the scope

               of the interim moratorium. The Committee observe that this

               amendment is aimed at addressing a persistent concern flagged

                                            20



by the Adjudicating Authority and insolvency practitioners

namely, the misuse of interim moratorium by personal guarantors

who file applications solely to obstruct or delay legitimate

recovery proceedings, a major loophole confirmed by NCLT

members to be responsible for significant value erosion. The

Committee, having considered detail submissions of the Ministry

and IBBI, underscore that removing this unnecessary pre-

admission shield is essential. The Committee observe that the

law, consistent with SARFAESI Act and Supreme Court

judgements, treats the borrower and the guarantor on the same

footing upon default, and the proposed amendment does not

deprive personal guarantors of the right to seek insolvency

resolution or bankruptcy under Part III of the Code. In view of the

above, and recognising the need to curb strategic filings and

strengthen the integrity of the insolvency process, the Committee

find the proposed amendment under Clause 47 to be appropriate

and recommend its acceptance in its present form.”



16. The recommendation brooks no ambiguity. It is apparent that

the amendment, by insertion of sub-section (4) to Section 96 of the

IBC, was brought in only to rectify the “mischief” and the

misuse/abuse of the sub-sections (1) to (3) of Section 96 of IBC.

By way of the amendment, it was sought to ensure that the

provisions of Section 96 would not apply where an application to

initiate an Insolvency Resolution Process in respect of a PG to CD

is filed by the creditor or the debtor itself.



17. It is significant to note that the Committee was sensitive and

acutely aware of the fact that though such interim protection is

critical to the resolution process, yet some other important and

critical issues which have arisen in practise, have not been

addressed. After having heard and considered the issues and

concerns of various stakeholders including the Ministry of

Corporate Affairs which voiced its concern and stated that the

removal of interim moratorium for PG is primarily intended to

prevent misuse, the Committee formed an opinion that “…..this

amendment is aimed at addressing a persistent concern flagged

by the Adjudicating Authority and the insolvency practitioners

namely, the misuse of interim moratorium by personal guarantors

who file applications solely to obstruct or delay legitimate

recovery proceedings, a major loophole confirmed by NCLT

members to be responsible for significant value erosion”. And

that, “The Committee, having considered detailed submissions of

the Ministry and IBBI, underscore that removing this

unnecessary pre-admission shield is essential”. Consequently,

the amendment to Section 96 by addition and insertion of sub-

section (4) was recommended in terms of Clause 47 of the IBC

Bill, 2025.



18. Aptly, this Court is of the considered opinion that the

Committee having noted the misuse and abuse of the provisions

in Section 96 of the IBC clearly accepted the proposal in Clause

47 of the aforesaid Bill and recommended the amendment to

Section 96 by addition and insertion of sub-section (4) solely to

rectify and remove the “abuse”, even if not the “mischief” that

                                                            21



               was being caused, and noted with great alacrity by the

               stakeholders, and appreciated by the Committee.”



               19. Learned single Judge of the Bombay High Court in Tata

               Capital Financial [(2026) ibclaw.in 4165 HC] (supra) having

               examined the aforenoted judgements of the Supreme Court read

               the words “is filed” occurring in sub-section (4) to mean even

               those which were filed prior in time but are still pending

               adjudication as on 26.05.2026, when the amendments were

               brought into force. This view, and the view taken by this Court

               are well aligned.



               20. Apropos the above, read conjointly, the aforesaid amendment

               to Section 96 of IBC by addition and insertion of sub-section (4),

               and the principles of “retroactive” legislation laid down by the

               Supreme Court, leave no doubt in the mind of this Court that the

               provisions of sub-section (4) of Section 96 of IBC by way of the

               amendment dated 06.04.2026, are “retroactive”, even though the

               Amending Act did not expressly state so. If that be so, then the

               import, purport and impact of such retroactive legislation would

               amount to “quasi retroactivity” and would be applicable to

               pending applications. It is not denied in the present case that the

               defendant no.2 is the PG to the CD (defendant no.3). It is also

               admitted that the application under Section 95 of the IBC has

               been filed by the plaintiff (creditor) and is still pending

               adjudication before the National Company Law Tribunal. Thus,

               as a sequitor, the provisions of sub-section (4) of Section 96 of IBC

               shall apply to the pending application of the plaintiff, and the

               interim moratorium enjoyed hitherto before by the defendant no.2

               (PG to CD), would be deemed to have been vacated.”



45. A Division Bench of Bombay High Court has also considered the amendment



made in Section 96 of the Code in, (2026) ibclaw.in 5435 HC, Indian Bank vs Shabbir



Abbas Patel & Ors. and held as under: -



               “The question that arises for consideration in these writ petitions

               is as to whether sub-section (4) of Section 96 of the Insolvency

               and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (IBC) introduced by way of

               amendment with effect from 26.05.2026 operates retroactively?

               In other words, whether Section 96(4) of the IBC, stating that the

               said provision shall not apply where an application is filed under

               Sections 94 or 95 thereof for initiating an insolvency resolution

               process in respect of a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor,

               applies to such applications already filed and pending or that it

               would apply only to applications filed after the aforesaid sub-

               section (4) is added by way of amendment to Section 96 of the

               IBC.”



               “2. The parties in support of the proposition that the amendment

               applies retroactively emphasize that the amendment was brought

               about to address the mischief of rampant misuse of the interim

               moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC triggered upon filing of

                                            22



applications under Sections 94 and 95 thereof. The parties

resisting such an interpretation insist that sub-section (4) of

Section 96 of the IBC introduced by way of amendment with

effect from 26.05.2026 applies prospectively i.e. to applications

filed under Sections 94 and 95 of the IBC after the amendment

has come into force.”



40. We are of the opinion that the aforesaid material, particularly

the report of the Select Committee brought to our notice, clearly

indicates that the very purpose of bringing about the amendment

for adding sub-section 4 to Section 96 of the IBC, was to address

the mischief of rampant and deliberate misuse of the interim

moratorium triggered under Section 96 of the IBC, merely by filing

of applications under Sections 95 and/or 96 of the IBC.



41. As a matter of fact, judicial notice of such gross misuse was

also taken by the Courts. It was found that the route of filing

applications under Sections 94 and/or 95 of the IBC, was being

taken, not with the purpose of triggering the procedure for

examination of applications and preparation of report by the

resolution professional, for the applications to be considered for

admission or rejection by the adjudicating authority, but only

with the sole intention of triggering and enjoying interim

moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC. It was found that the

applications under Section 94 and 95 were being indiscriminately

filed, certain papers being collected and eventually thrown into

the Registry of the NCLT, to claim that the moment such

applications were filed, interim moratorium was triggered under

Section 96 of the IBC. It came to notice that creditors had started

adopting this path at stages, when the creditors were on the

verge of completion of lawful methods undertaken for realization

of their dues.”



“47. It is crucial that the resolve of the legislature for remedying

the mischief is given its full effect, so that the mischief is

suppressed and the remedy is advanced. The Courts must

interpret such amendments to add life and force to the cure and

remedy, rather than adopting an interpretation that fails to take

forward the cure and remedy in its true spirit. The said Mischief

Rule/Heydon’s Rule has been applied consistently in our legal

system and hence, it is an accepted Rule of interpretation. We

find that the said Rule applies in the facts of the present case, to

advance the proposition that sub-section 4 to Section 96 of the

IBC introduced by way of amendment, must apply retroactively

to pending proceedings also. This would advance the cure and

remedy of addressing the mischief and it would not be

appropriate to apply the same only prospectively, in the context

of applications filed on or after 26.05.2026.



48. In this context, an attempt was made on behalf of the parties

in these cases, advancing the proposition that the amendment

ought to be applied prospectively, to claim that the applications

filed bona fide, under Sections 94 or 95 of the IBC for insolvency

resolution of personal guarantors to a corporate debtor, should

not be adversely affected and painted in the same brush as

mischievously initiated applications. We are of the opinion that

                                            23



when the legislature has acted, specifically taking note of the

rampant mischief and misuse of the said provisions and larger

and considerable public interest is involved in bringing about the

said amendment, it ought to be applied in such a manner that it

takes forward the dominant intention and purpose of the

amendment.



49. The parties whose proceedings are still pending, cannot claim

that the amendment should not apply and in the process, call

upon the Courts to go into the question as to whether such

applications for insolvency process of personal guarantors to

secured creditors, have been filed mischievously or not. As noted

hereinabove, in the context of the procedural nature of the

mechanism between Sections 94 to 99 of the IBC, such parties

cannot claim a vested right to such interim moratorium under

Section 96 of the IBC.”



“54. We find that the contentions raised by the

creditors/petitioners in these petitions, concern retroactive

operation of amendment and hence, the said contention that

literal reading would show that the amendment cannot apply

retrospectively, is without any substance. The said submission

made on the basis that use of the words ‘is filed’ must necessarily

mean that the amendment can only apply prospecti
```
