```text
                                                             2



                                                 O R D E R

                                             (Hybrid Mode)



[Per: Justice Mohd. Faiz Alam Khan, Member (Judicial)]



         CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1959 of 2026 is preferred against the order dated

04.09.2026 (Impugned Order) passed by the Hon'ble NCLT, Mumbai Bench-V

(Adjudicating Authority) in I.A. No. 456 of 2026 in CP(IB) 5l8/MB/C-V/2022,

whereby the Adjudicating Authority has recorded adverse findings against the

Appellant/SRA and directed that the conduct of the erstwhile Resolution

Professional (Respondent No. 1), the Successful Resolution Applicant (Appellant)

and Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 2), all members of the

Monitoring Committee, be referred to the IBBI for such action as it may be deemed

fit.

2. The present Appeal CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1978 of 2026 is against the order dated

04.09.2026 (“Impugned Order”) passed by the Hon’ble National Company Law

Tribunal, Mumbai (“Adjudicating Authority”) in I.A. No. 456/2026 in CP(IB) No.

518/MB/C-V/2022, whereby, while taking on record the Third Status Report on

implementation of the approved resolution plan for Sristi Hospitality Private

Limited (“Corporate Debtor"), the Adjudicating Authority erroneously observed

that the conduct of the Appellant was not in accordance with law and is referred

the IBBI.

3. Both the aforesaid appeals are presented against the same impugned order

dated 04.09.2026 and, for the sake of convenience, are being disposed of by

passing this common judgment.

4. Facts in brief necessary for the disposal of these appeals are that the

Corporate Debtor was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process

                                                             3



(“CIRP”) vide order dated 27.02.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in

C.P.(IB) No. 518/MB/C-V/2022, in a petition filed under Section 7 of the Code

by the Director of the CD, Mr. Santosh R. Shetty, and the Appellant in CA (AT)

(Ins) No. 1978 of 2026 was appointed as the Interim Resolution Professional of

the Corporate Debtor vide order dated 27.02.2023 and was later on confirmed as

the Resolution Professional. The Committee of Creditors of the Corporate Debtor

was constituted by Respondent No. 1 as the sole member holding 100% voting

share. The resolution plan submitted by Respondent No. 2 was approved by the

COC with a 100% voting share on 05.08.2023. Upon approval of the Resolution

Plan by the CoC, the Appellant/RP preferred I.A. No. 3612 of 2023 under Section

30(6) read with Section 31 of the Code before the Adjudicating Authority for

approval of the plan, and the same was approved by the Adjudicating Authority

vide order dated 12.07.2024. After approval of the said Plan, the suspended

director of the CD preferred Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1378 of 2024 and

1383 of 2024 before this Appellate Tribunal which were dismissed on 14.07.2026.

5. Appellant/erstwhile Resolution Professional and Chairman of the

Monitoring Committee of Sristi Hospitality Private Limited/ CD preferred an I.A.

(I.B.C.)/456/2026 under section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,

2016 (“IBC/the Code”), seeking to take on record this Third Status Report and to

relieve the Applicant from filing further status report on implementation of the

Resolution Plan.

6. The Adjudicating Authority however noticed that (i) The Resolution Plan

was approved by it on 12.07.2024 and was required to be fully implemented by

27.08.2024 (ii) The SRA's stated position that it would implement the Plan only

upon receipt of favourable orders from the Hon'ble NCLAT, is in complete violation

                                                             4



of settled law and the approved Resolution Plan (iii) That it is only pursuant to

the order dated 07.07.2025 of the Adjudicating Authority, the Plan was hurriedly

implemented on 30.07.2025. (iv) The Corporate Debtor was handed over to the

SRA on 30.07.2025. (v) The conduct of Chairman of the Monitoring Committee

(erstwhile RP) and other members in accepting the stand of the SRA that Plan

would be implemented only after getting favourable order from NCLAT, the

Adjudicating Authority, is not in accordance with law, while taking the third

status report on record, was of the view that conduct of the erstwhile RP, the

SRA, and the other member of the Monitoring Committee, namely, Saraswat Co-

operative Bank Ltd be referred to the IBBI for their wisdom to take such

appropriate steps as it may deem fit, directed the Registry to forward a copy of

this Order to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) for such action

as it may deem fit.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the erstwhile RP/Chairman of the

Monitoring Committee as well as the SRA have preferred the aforesaid appeals.

8. Learned counsel for the Appellant/SRA submits that the adjudicating

authority, without any cogent reason and factual matrix, has recorded adverse

remarks against the appellant without providing any opportunity of being heard

to the SRA. Reliance in this regard has been held in Defodill's Pharmaceuticals

Limited versus State of UP (2020 18 SCC 550).

9. It is further submitted that there was no occasion for the adjudicating

authority to have recorded any adverse observations/remarks against the

appellant when the appellant was not even arrayed as a party before the

adjudicating authority.

                                                             5



10. It is further submitted that the adjudicating authority, while recording the

adverse remarks, has not even considered this fact that in the clause5.7(ii) of the

resolution plan (which has been approved by the COC as well as by the

adjudicating authority), there is a clear stipulation that mere pendency of appeals

against the resolution plan would be sufficient for making the plan non-

implementable. Therefore, the very basis of recording adverse remarks against

the appellant is illegal and cannot be sustained.

11. It is further submitted that after the approval of the resolution plan by the

COC and Learned Adjudicating Authority, the terms of the same cannot be

changed or dissented to by the SRA. Reliance in this regard has been laid on

Shashidhar versus Indian Overseas Bank (2019) 12 SCC 150, JP Kensington

Boulevard Apartments Welfare Association versus NBCC (India) Limited,

(2022) 1 SCC 401 and Noida Industrial Development Authority vs Prabjit

Singh Soni, (2024) 6 SCC 767.

12. It is further submitted that the Appellant, being the SRA, was under a bona

fide belief that, having regard to the clause 5.7(ii) of the resolution plan, there is

no mandate for him to implement the plan during the pendency of the appeal

filed by the suspended director of the CD before this Appellate Tribunal. When

the learned adjudicating authority, during the course of hearing of the second

status report, revealed its willingness to get the plan implemented, the SRA,

without any further delay, deposited the money, and the RP filed the third status

report.

13. It is further submitted that when the adjudicating authority itself has

approved a resolution plan having a clause that mere pendency of the appeal filed

against the approval of the plan would be sufficient to make the plan non-

                                                             6



implementable, the same adjudicating authority could not accuse the Appellant-

SRA of non-implementation of the plan. Therefore, the adverse remark recorded

by the learned adjudicative authority in paragraph numbers 19 and 20 of the

impugned order may kindly be set aside and expunged.

14. Learned counsel for the Respondent Saraswat Cooperative Bank Limited

submits that clause 5.7 of the approved Resolution Plan specifically provides that

where litigation or legal proceedings are initiated in relation to the Resolution

Plan or the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, the SRA shall make

payment of the total Resolution Amount within seven business days from the date

on which the approval of the Resolution Plan attains finality and the approved

Resolution Plan itself contemplated the possibility of litigation and prescribed the

timeline for payment in such circumstances. The parties therefore, were required

to act in accordance with the terms of the Plan and the orders passed by this

Hon'ble Tribunal.

15. It is further submitted that the time taken for implementation cannot, by

itself, be treated as misconduct on the part of the Bank. The circumstances must

be considered as a whole, including the pending Appeals, the relevant clauses of

the Resolution Plan and the order passed by this Hon'ble Tribunal. The conduct

of the Bank ought not to be viewed in isolation from these circumstances,

considering the fact that the bank is custodian of public money.

16. It is further submitted that the respondent has acted in the capacity of

financial creditor and a member of the Monitoring Committee and its conduct

should be examined with reference to its obligations under the Code, the

provisions of approved Resolution Plan and the relevant judicial orders. The

challenge by the suspended Director to the resolution plan was pending before

                                                             7



this appellate Tribunal. Therefore, the delay in implementation, in these

circumstances, cannot automatically lead to an adverse conclusion against the

Bank. Further, the Respondent received payment against its claims upon

implementation of the Resolution Plan. No specific act of misconduct, deliberate

obstruction or violation of the approved Plan could be labelled against the Bank

as the SRA agreed to defer implementation till the Appeals were pending.

Therefore, in absence of any specific material establishing violation of plan by the

Respondent no adverse order should have been passed against the Respondent.

17. Learned counsel for the Appellant/erstwhile RP submits that totally

uncalled-for observation have been recorded by the learned adjudicating

authority. It is highlighted that clause 5.7(ii) of the Resolution Plan, as approved

vide order dated 12.07.2024 stipulated payment of the Resolution Amount within

7 days of attaining finality of the Plan if there is no litigation pending anywhere,

however Immediately after the approval of the plan by the adjudicating authority,

the suspended management filed Company Appeal (AT)(Ins) No. 1383 of 2024

challenging the order dated 12.07.2024 and in pursuance to Clause 5.7(ii) of the

resolution plan, the monitoring committee took a decision to defer the

implementation of the plan pending such appeal and when the learned

adjudicating authority had approved the plan with clause 5.7(ii), it was not open

for the Appellants to implement the plan contrary to the stipulation made therein.

18. It is further submitted that the order dated 07.07.2025 has proceeded on

the view then taken in Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd. [(2026)

5 SCC 558, judgment dated 02.05.2025. However, this judgment was recalled on

31.07.2025 in Punjab National Bank v. Kalyani Transco, 2025 SCC OnLine

SC 1634 and the matter was finally disposed of on 26.09.2025 in Kalyani

                                                             8



Transco v. Bhushan Power& Steel Ltd. [(2026) 6 SCC 431, holding that

deferment of the plan is permissible with the consent of the COC for the reasons

which may not be attributed to the SRA.

19. It is further submitted that the deferment of the plan in this case was with

due consent of the COC on account of the pendency of the appeal, as there was

no occasion for the appellants to act otherwise the learned adjudicating authority

in the impugned order has presumed that no condition whatsoever is permissible

in the resolution plan, contrary to Ebix Singapore (P) Ltd. v. Educomp

Solutions Ltd. (CoC), (2022) 2 SCC 401. It is submitted that when the

adjudicating authority has itself approved the plan with Clause 5.7(ii), the

appellant could not be made an accused of non-implementation of the plan.

20. It is further submitted that the adjudicating authority itself took cognizance

of the clause 5.7(ii) of the resolution plan in its order dated 12.07.2024, so it

could not be said that, while approving the plan, the adjudicating authority has

not taken cognizance of it. Therefore, a plan once approved by the adjudicating

authority binds all the stakeholders, including the financial creditor, the

monitoring committee, the SRA, as well as the RP-Appellant and the Appellant,

as chairman of the monetary committee, cannot violate the approved clauses of

the resolution plan.

21. It is further submitted that the only obligation on the plan was to keep the

learned educating authority and IBBI well informed about the progress of the

implementation of the plan, which has been duly complied with by the Appellant-

Resolution Professional in his capacity as Chairman of the Monitoring Committee.

The order dated 18.02.2025 of the adjudicating authority has also taken note of

                                                             9



the pendency of the appeals and also of the fact that there has been no effective

implementation of the plan till that date.

22. It is further submitted that the adjudicating authority did not have any

jurisdiction to re-examine the legality of the already approved plan, and therefore

the Impugned Order, for this reason also is unsustainable in law and there was

no justification in referring the alleged conduct of the RP and the SRA to the IBBI.

Moreover, the finding in the impugned order at Paragraph 20(d) is factually

incorrect as the Plan was fully implemented on 30.07.2025 about five months

prior to the order dated 06.01.2026 and thereafter, nothing was left to be

complied with.

23. It is further submitted that at the time of implementation of the Resolution

Plan i.e. on 30.07.2025, the Second Status Report being IA No.1662/2025 was

pending before the adjudicating authority. The application was listed on

29.07.2025, 23.09.2025 and 30.09.2025 for consideration. However, on each of

these dates, the matter could not reach for hearing and on 20.11.2025, when the

application was taken up, the Bench was apprised by the RP that the Plan has

been fully implemented on 30.07.2025 and the CD has been handed over to the

SRA and a formal separate application IA No. 456/2026 was also filed by the RP

to place on record the factum of implementation of the plan.

24. It is further submitted that the term of the Appellant as RP had come to an

end on 12.07.2024 and thereafter, the Appellant RP did not draw any

fees/remuneration services rendered by him beyond 12.07.2024 and thereafter

his term as the Chairman of monitoring committee ended on 30.07.2025, on

which day the plan was fully implemented and the monitoring committee was

dissolved. The Appellant has not drawn any remuneration/ fees as Chairman,

                                                            10



Monitoring Committee also after 30.07.2025. Thus, it is submitted that the



observations of the Ld. Adjudicating authority in para 20 of the Impugned Order



be set aside/ expunged.



25. Having heard, Learned Counsel for the parties, we think it in the interest



of justice to have a glance on the impugned order in order to assess what has



persuaded the Adjudicating Authority for taking the decision. Therefore, the



relevant parts of the impugned judgment are reproduced as under: -



              “10. It is noted that the Resolution Plan submitted by the

              SRA was approved by this Tribunal vide order dated

              12.07.2024. The Clause 10.3 and Clause 10.15 of the

              Resolution Plan stipulate as under:



                 “10.3. Binding Effect This Resolution Plan once approved

                 by the CoC and the NCLT in accordance with Paragraph

                 4 (Financial Proposal) of this Resolution Plan shall be

                 binding in accordance with its terms on the Resolution

                 Applicant, Corporate Debtor, Stakeholders, Promoters.

                 Creditors and all other interested parties and each of

                 their respective successors and assigns. Further,

                 pursuant to the Code, the Resolution Plan shall be

                 implemented by virtue of the NCLT Approval of this

                 Resolution Plan, and no further acts, deeds, things,

                 approvals or instruments shall be required for this

                 purpose.”



                 “10.15. Unconditionality The Resolution Plan is not

                 contingent or conditional except on approval of the

                 Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority.”



              11. Therefore, Clause 10.3 and Clause 10.15 of the

              Resolution Plan expressly provide that the Plan is binding

              and unconditional save for approval by the Adjudicating

              Authority, and that no further act, deed or approval is

              required for its implementation. Further, the Resolution Plan

              is not contingent or conditional after the approval by this

              Adjudicating Authority.



              12. After approval of the said Plan, the Suspended Director

              preferred Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1378 of 2024

              and 1383 of 2024 before the Hon'ble NCLAT, in which the

              Hon'ble NCLAT, vide interim order dated 23.07.2024,

              directed that “In the meantime, implementation of the Plan

              may go on which shall abide by the result of these appeals”.

              This direction from Hon’ble NCLAT was permissive and did

                                            11



not stay implementation. Accordingly, it is noted that the

Applicant being the Chairman of the Monitoring Committee

was duty bound either to get the Resolution Plan

implemented within timelines or file for liquidation in the

event of non-implementation.



14. As per Clause 9.3 of the Resolution Plan,

implementation of the Plan was required to be completed on

the 46th day from the date of approval by this Tribunal, i.e.,

on or before 27.08.2024. However, it is noted that

implementation remained at a standstill for a considerable

period of around one year, as no steps were taken by the

Monitoring Committee or its Chairman until this Tribunal,

while considering the Second Status Report, passed its

order dated 07.07.2025 in IA No. 1662/2025 calling upon

the Chairman to explain the non-implementation. It is only

pursuant to the said order, that the Resolution Plan came to

be implemented only on 30.07.2025. It is an admitted

position that the Plan was not implemented within this

stipulated timeline. Therefore, the delay in implementation

is in violation of Clause 10.3, Clause 10.15 read with

Regulation 38(3) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016, which

mandates that a resolution plan must provide for its

effective and timely implementation, and also of the

direction of Hon’ble NCLAT in their order dated 23.07.2024.



15. It is observed that the Clause 5.7.(ii) of the Resolution

Plan sought to link payment of the Total Resolution Amount

to the finality of any pending litigation. The said clause

5.7.(ii) (at Page No.43 of the Resolution Plan) is reproduced

below:



   “The Total Resolution Amount offered in this Resolution

   Plan for payment to the Stakeholders will be paid as per

   the timeline of events for implementation of Resolution

   Plan as per paragraph 9.3 of this Resolution Plan subject

   to no appeal pending before the Hon’ble NCLAT or

   Hon’ble Supreme Court or any stay granted by any

   competent Court/Tribunal on implementation of the

   Resolution Plan. In the event, any litigations or legal

   proceedings are instituted in relation to the Resolution

   Plan or matters pertaining to the Corporate Insolvency

   Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor then the

   Resolution Applicant shall make the payment of the Total

   Resolution Amount within 7 (Seven) Business Days from

   the day the Resolution Plan attains finality”



16. Further, this Tribunal, while disposing of IA No.

1662/2025 vide order dated 06.01.2026, recorded the

following detailed findings on the aforesaid conduct:

                                        12



“14. However, such a clause cannot be interpreted to

have force to override Clause 10.15 of the Resolution

Plan, which expressly provides that the Plan is

unconditional except for its approval by the Adjudicating

Authority. Also, if at all Resolution Plan is considered

conditional, then the same either could not have been

approved by the CoC or by this Authority. Any contrary

clause having effect of postponing implementation

of the plan on account of litigation is therefore

contrary to the express terms of the Resolution Plan

itself and accordingly, non-implementation of the

plan on this account cannot be termed as

justifiable.



18. As per Section 30(2) of the Code, the Resolution

Professional is required to examine the Resolution Plan

submitted by the Successful Resolution Applicant and

confirm its compliance with the provisions of the Code.

Further, under Section 30(4), the CoC may approve the

Plan after considering its feasibility and viability and

ensuring that it fulfills other requirements specified by the

Board. Further, Regulation 38(3) of the CIRP Regulations,

2016 mandates that a Resolution Plan must be feasible,

viable, and implementable, with specific timelines for

implementation. In the present case, the Resolution

Plan stipulated a specific timeline for

implementation, namely the 46th day from the date

of approval by this Tribunal. However, the Plan has

not been implemented within the stipulated period.

Such non-implementation defeats the mandatory

requirement under Regulation 38(3) of the CIRP

Regulations, 2016. The continued delay in

implementation of the plan is contrary to the

provision of the Code and Regulation as well as the

timelines expressly stipulated in the Resolution

Plan, and the Monitoring Committee, has failed to

take the necessary action



19. With regard to the Applicant’s submission in the

Affidavit dated 25.07.2025 that the Resolution Plan is not

conditional and is protected by the commercial wisdom of

the CoC, as per the terms of Resolution Plan, it is

mentioned that upon approval of the Resolution Plan, the

Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the

Corporate Debtor comes to an end and Successful

Resolution Applicant will acquire the control of the affairs

of the Corporate Debtor on the Transfer date. Therefore,

upon approval of the Plan, the responsibility for the its

implementation vests with the Monitoring Committee.

However, in any event, the commercial wisdom of the

                                            13



   CoC cannot override or contravene the provisions of

   laws.”



17. This Tribunal in the above order dated 06.01.2026, held

that clause 5.7.(ii) of the Resolution Plan, to the extent it

purported to make implementation contingent upon finality

of the NCLAT appeals, could not override the express un

conditionality of the Plan under Clause 10.15 and that the

interim order of the Hon'ble NCLAT dated 23.07.2024

imposed no impediment to implementation and, if anything,

obligated the Monitoring Committee to proceed. Further, the

continued non-implementation of the Plan within the

stipulated timeline of 46 days from the date of approval of

Plan by NCLT (46th day from approval of NCLT being the

Transfer date) was contrary to Section 30(2) and 30(4) of the

Code and Regulation 38(3) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016.

The Chairman of the Monitoring Committee was accordingly

directed to act strictly in accordance with law and take all

necessary and appropriate steps as contemplated under the

Code.



18. It is noted that when the present Application came up

for hearing on 30.01.2026, this Tribunal recorded that the

third status report placed on record did not indicate

compliance with the directions contained in the order dated

06.01.2026, and called upon the Applicant to file an

affidavit explaining such compliance.



19. In compliance thereof, the Applicant has placed on

record the Additional Affidavit dated 23.02.2026. However,

it is observed that the Applicant has failed to furnish any

cogent reason or satisfactory explanation for the inordinate

delay of almost a year in implementing the Resolution Plan,

the same having remained unimplemented from 27.08.2024

(the stipulated 46th day) until 30.07.2025. The record thus

discloses a clear case of substantial delay in

implementation of the Resolution Plan, despite the interim

order of the Hon'ble NCLAT dated 23.07.2024, which, far

from staying implementation, permitted the implementation

of Plan to proceed pending the outcome of the said appeals

(which have been decided on 14.07.2026). Despite this, the

Chairman of the Monitoring Committee took no steps

towards implementation for nearly a year, and it was only

upon this Tribunal's observation vide order dated

07.07.2025 that implementation was set in motion.

Moreover, no material has been placed on record to

demonstrate that any extension of time for implementation

of the Resolution Plan was ever sought by the SRA from, or

granted by, the Monitoring Committee. Taking into account,

the absence of any such extension, and the Hon'ble NCLAT's

                                                            14



              order permitting implementation to proceed, the SRA did not

              implement the Plan within the timeline stipulated in the

              Resolution Plan, in violation of the express terms of the

              Resolution Plan.



              20. Considering the following aspects that:



              a. The Resolution Plan was approved on 12.07.2024 by the

              Adjudicating Authority and was required to be fully

              implemented by 27.08.2024.



              b. The Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor had

              preferred an appeal challenging the Resolution Plan approval

              order dated 12.07.2024, but the Hon’ble NCLAT did not stay

              the implementation of the Plan.



              c. The SRA's stated position that it would implement the Plan

              only upon receipt of favourable orders from the Hon'ble NCLAT,

              is in complete violation of settled law and the approved

              Resolution Plan was binding upon it.



              d. It was only pursuant to this Tribunal's order dated

              06.01.2026, the Plan was hurriedly implemented on

              30.07.2025 and the Corporate Debtor was handed over to the

              SRA on 30.07.2025



               e. The conduct of Chairman of the Monitoring Committee

              (erstwhile RP) and other members in accepting the stand of the

              SRA that Plan would be implemented only after getting

              favourable order from Hon’ble NCLAT, is not in accordance with

              law.



              This Tribunal is of the considered view that conduct of the erstwhile

              RP, the SRA, and the other member of the Monitoring Committee,

              namely, Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd shall be referred to the

              IBBI for their wisdom to take such appropriate steps as it may deem

              fit.”



                                                                     (Emphasis as in the Order)



26. We notice that the resolution plan is having a clause namely clause



5.7.(ii) (at Page No.43 of the Resolution Plan) which has been reproduced by



the Adjudicating Authority in the impugned order and is reproduced below:



              “5.7.(ii) The Total Resolution Amount offered in this

              Resolution Plan for payment to the Stakeholders will be paid

              as per the timeline of events for implementation of

              Resolution Plan as per paragraph 9.3 of this Resolution Plan

              subject to no appeal pending before the Hon’ble NCLAT or

              Hon’ble Supreme Court or any stay granted by any

                                                            15



              competent Court/Tribunal on implementation of the

              Resolution Plan. In the event, any litigations or legal

              proceedings are instituted in relation to the Resolution Plan

              or matters pertaining to the Corporate Insolvency Resolution

              Process of the Corporate Debtor then the Resolution

              Applicant shall make the payment of the Total Resolution

              Amount within 7 (Seven) Business Days from the day the

              Resolution Plan attains finality”



27. The Clause 10.3 and Clause 10.15 of the Resolution Plan has been



reproduced by the Adjudicating Authority in the impugned order and we also



reproduce the same as under:



              “10.3. Binding Effect This Resolution Plan once approved by

              the CoC and the NCLT in accordance with Paragraph 4

              (Financial Proposal) of this Resolution Plan shall be binding

              in accordance with its terms on the Resolution Applicant,

              Corporate Debtor, Stakeholders, Promoters. Creditors and

              all other interested parties and each of their respective

              successors and assigns. Further, pursuant to the Code, the

              Resolution Plan shall be implemented by virtue of the NCLT

              Approval of this Resolution Plan, and no further acts, deeds,

              things, approvals or instruments shall be required for this

              purpose.”

              “10.15. Unconditionality The Resolution Plan is not

              contingent or conditional except on approval of the

              Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority.”



28. Clause 8.1 of the plan is also important and is reproduced as under:



              “8.1. Subject to (a) no stay on the implementation of the

              Resolution Plan by any Appellate Authority or any other

              Court; (b) no legal proceedings seeking an increase in the

              Total Resolution Amount or liability of the Resolution

              Applicant or for any material modification of the contents of

              the Resolution Plan having been initiated in any court or

              tribunal against the decision of the NCLT approving this

              Resolution Plan; the Resolution Applicant shall complete the

              implementation of the Resolution Plan and the Resolution

     16



     Applicant and/or Affiliates shall acquire control of the

     Corporate Debtor in the manner set out herein and the

     Corporate Debtor will make payment of amounts payable to

     the Creditors as set out in this Resolution Plan”.



29.  We also notice that clause 9.3 of the Resolution plan, which has been



reproduced by the Adjudicating Authority in its plan approval order dated



12.07.2024, provides implementation schedule and is reproduced as under:



     9.3. Term of the Resolution and Timeline of Events for

     Implementation of Resolution Plan:



     Implementation of the Resolution Plan shall commence from

     the NCLT Approval Date. Subject to Paragraph 5.6. (ii), the

     Resolution Applicant will undertake the following steps to

     implement the Resolution Plan in the indicative timeline

     provided below for the implementation of the Resolution

     Plan:



     In the event the 46th day is not a Business Day, then the

     payment will be made by the Resolution Applicant on the

     next Business Day.

                                                            17



30. Thus, it is reflected that clause 5.7 of the Resolution Plan clearly provides

that the payment to the stakeholders will be paid by the Resolution Applicant as

per the timeline provided under paragraph 9.3 of the Resolution Plan (i.e., within

46 days), subject to no appeal pending before the NCLT or Supreme Court or any

stay granted by any competent court/tribunal on implementation of the

Resolution Plan.

31. Likewise, clause 10.3 of the resolution plan would reveal that the resolution

plan, once approved by the CoC and the adjudicating authority, shall be binding

on the resolution applicant, corporate debtor, stakeholders, promoters, creditors,

and all other interested parties. Clause 10.15 provides that the resolution plan is

not contingent or conditional except on approval of the resolution plan by the

adjudicating authority.

32. We accordingly notice that clause 5.7 of the resolution plan crystal clearly

stipulated that payment to the stakeholders would only be made by the resolution

applicant according to the timeline provided. In clause 9.3 of the plan, only on

the condition that no appeal is pending before this Appellate Tribunal or before

the Supreme Court, or when any stay has been granted by any competent court

or tribunal. Significantly, this clause highlights that mere pendency of the appeal

would be sufficient for making the plan not implementable. In other words, if an

appeal has been preferred and is pending before this appellate tribunal, or if there

are any proceedings with regard to the plan before the Hon'ble Supreme Court

(even if no stay has been granted by this appellate tribunal or by the Supreme

Court), there is no foundation for the resolution applicant to make payment to

the stakeholders as provided under paragraph 9.3 of the resolution plan.

                                                            18



33. We also notice that the learned Adjudicating Authority, while approving the



plan by passing an order dated 12.07.2024 in IA No. 3612 of 2023, has not made



any observation or stipulation whereby it could be perceived that the precondition



for implementation of the plan by the SRA has been waived or changed by the



learned Adjudicating Authority and the plan appears to have been approved



without any modification.



34. Therefore, it appears that, having regard to Clause 5.7 of the resolution



plan (which has been approved by the adjudicating authority without any



modification), the SRA was not obliged to implement the plan, even if no stay



order has been granted by this Appellate Tribunal and mere pendency of the



appeal was sufficient for not implementing the plan.



35. Learned Adjudicating Authority, in its impugned order, has mentioned



that it has observed detailed findings with regard to the conduct of the RP and



SRA while disposing of IA No. 1662 of 2025 in its order dated 06/01/2026. This



IA, being IA No. 1662 of 2025, was moved by the erstwhile RP/Chairman of the



Monitoring Committee and on 07.07.2025 the Ld. Adjudicating Authority has



passed the following order: -



              “IA.1662/2025

              This IA has been filed by the Chairman of Monitoring

              Committee of the Corporate Debtor who is the ex-RP of

              the Corporate Debtor.

              It is stated by the ex-RP present in person that

              because two litigations are pending before Hon'ble

              NCLAT, the Plan despite being approved on

              12.07.2024 has not been implemented. He further

              brings to our notice that one of the Appeals is in

              respect of the IA through which the Plan has been

              approved by this Tribunal.

                                            19



The ex-RP in person also brings to our knowledge

Clause (ii) at page l0 of the Resolution Plan wherein,

it has been mentioned as under:



"In the event, any litigations or legal proceedings are

initiated in relation to the Resolution Plan or matters

pertaining to the Corporate Insolvency Resolution

Process of the Corporate Debtor then the Resolution

Applicant shall make the payment of the Total

Resolution Amount within 7 (seven) business days

from the date the resolution plan attains finality"



To a pointed query as to how this particular provision

in the Resolution Plan is not contingent and falls

within the strict timelines of the completion of CIRP

process, the ex-RP present in person submits that CoC

in their wisdom have approved the Plan.



However, to a specific query as to how such

stipulation made in the Resolution Plan passes

through the scrutiny of the applicable Regulation of

Resolution Plan being feasible and implementable, he

seeks time to address us on the next occasion.



Further, the order of Hon'ble NCLAT, Principal Bench,

New Delhi in Company Appeal No. 1378 of 2024 and

IA No. 5018 of 2024 dated 23.07.2024 is brought to

our notice wherein at the last, it has been directed as

under:



"In the meantime, implementation of the Plan may go

on which shall abide by the result of these appeals".



It is noted that this Resolution Plan was approved on

12.07.2024, and the Hon'ble NCLAT vide order dated

23.07.2024 have observed as mentioned above and,

therefore, there was no doubt about the

implementation of the Plan within the timeline

stipulated therein. However, it is as stated by the ex-

RP present in person that the Plan has not yet been

implemented. Accordingly, it is asked to him being the

Chairman of the Monitoring Committee for

implementation of the Resolution Plan, as to why it

has not been ensured that the Plan is implemented

either in view of the approval by the NCLT vide order

dated 12.07.2024 or as directed by the Hon'ble NCLAT

in their order dated 23.07.2024. Also, if the Plan was

not implemented within the time given, then why

liquidation proceedings were not initiated. Ex-RP

undertakes to file an affidavit clarifying the

aforesaid issues. List this IA accordingly for further

consideration on 29.07.2025.”

                                                            20



36. The contention of the Ld. Counsels for the appellants is that when it has

been indicated by the Adjudicating Authority that the SRA, despite having clause

5.7.(ii) in the Plan, was bound to implement the plan, in absence of any stay order

by this Appellate Tribunal, the plan was implemented at once and was fully

implemented on 30.07.2025.We find substance in the submissions made by

Learned Council for the Appellant as Clause 5.7.(ii) of the Plan clearly provides

and makes the plan implementable only on the filing of an appeal by any party

against the resolution plan (even if no stay has been granted in the appeal and

the learned adjudicating authority has approved that plan without any

modification or change. Therefore, when mere pendency of an appeal against the

plan was sufficient for the SRA not to make any payment to the creditors or any

stakeholder, the SRA or the RP cannot be held liable for the delay. Per contra, in

our considered opinion, it was the duty of the adjudicating authority to have

noticed this discrepancy, which was conspicuous on the face of it, when the

adjudicating authority was approving the resolution plan and this ambiguity

should not have been left on the discretion of the parties/stakeholders of the

resolution plan and if it was not noticed or was not modified, the stakeholders

including the Appellants cannot be held liable for the delay. The Appellants in

our considered opinion were in under a bona fide belief that they are not obliged

to implement the plan when the appeal is pending before us and as soon as they

were given green signal by the Adjudicating Authority vide order dated

07.07.2025 in the form of a query, they implemented the plan. The observation

of this Appellate tribunal vide order dated 23.07.2024, which permitted the

implementation of Plan to proceed pending the outcome of the said appeals

cannot be construed to be a mandate for the Appellants to implement the plan.

                                                            21



It only suggests that no stay has been granted by this Appellate Tribunal during

the pendency of the Appeal.

37. In our considered view the delay which has occurred in implementation of

the plan was sufficiently explained by the appellants before the Adjudicating

Authority and the same should have been accepted, more so when the plan has

been fully implemented on 30th July 2025.

38. We also notice that the observations adverse to the SRA have been made

by the Learned Adjudicating Authority, when even the SRA was not a party before

the Learned Adjudicating Authority and no opportunity has been given to the SRA

to explain its conduct.

39. In view of the reasons given herein above the Appeals filed by the Appellants

are allowed and Observations recorded by the Learned Adjudicating Authority in

Para 19 thereof in terms that "the SRA did not implement the Plan within the

timeline stipulated in the Resolution Plan, in violation of the express terms of the

Resolution Plan" , and (ii) directing the Registry of the NCLT, at Para 22 of the

impugned order, to forward a copy of the said order to the IBBI for such action

as it may deem fit, after holding at Para 20 thereof that the conduct of the

erstwhile RP, the SRA, and the other member of the Monitoring Committee,

namely, Saraswat Cooperative Bank Ltd. shall be referred to the IBBI to take

appropriate steps, is hereby set aside/ expunged.

40. The Observations recorded by the Learned Adjudicating Authority in Para

No. 20 of the Impugned Order dated 04.09.2026, to the extent of the direction

“conduct of the erstwhile RP, the SRA, and the other member of the Monitoring

Committee, namely, Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. shall be referred to the IBBI

                                                            22



for their wisdom to take such appropriate steps as it may deem fit is hereby set

aside/expunged.

41. There is no order as to costs.

42. Pending IA’s if any is also disposed of.



            [Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan]
```

```text
                                                  1



        NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

                      PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI



                Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1844 of 2026



IN THE MATTER OF:



Manoj Kumar Agarwal                                          …Appellant(s)



Versus



IL & FS Financial Services Ltd. & Anr.                       …Respondent(s)

Present:



For Appellant(s)  : Mr. Arun Kathpalia, Sr. Advocate and Mr. D. N.

                     Sharma, Sr. Advocate with Mr. Pranav Sachdeva, Mr.

For                  Sanyam Jain, Ms. Mishra Divya Santosh, Mr. P. Rohit

Respondent(s)        Ram, Ms. Khushboo Singhal, Mr. Nilay Sengupta,

                     Advocates



                  : Mr. Raunak Dhillon, Ms. Aishwarya Gupta, Mr. Jeezan

                     Riyaz, Advocates for R-1.

                     Ms. Rashmi Roy, Advocate, Mr. Sanjay Kumar Poddar,

                     CA with Mr. Manoj Kumar Agarwal, RP in person for R-

                     2 (RP).



                                                 O R D E R

                                              (Hybrid Mode)



[Per: Justice Mohd. Faiz Alam Khan, Member (Judicial)]



       The instant appeal has been preferred under Section 61 of the Insolvency

and Bankruptcy Code, 2016(the Code) against the order dated 09.09.2026

(Impugned Order) passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati

Bench (the Adjudicating Authority) in C.P. (IB) No. 12/GB/2024, whereby the

application filed by IL&FS Financial Services Limited (Financial Creditor)

under Section 95 of the Code against the Appellant, as Personal Guarantor to

Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited/Principal borrower/corporate

debtor, has been admitted and the insolvency resolution process against the

Appellant has been initiated.

                                                             2



2. Facts in brief required for disposal of this appeal, as stated in Appeal,

are that Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor),

approached Respondent No. 1, IL&FS Financial Services Limited (the

Financial Creditor), to avail a term loan facility for its working capital

requirements/general corporate purposes. The Financial Creditor extended a

term loan facility of up to Rs.30,00,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Crores only) to

the Corporate Debtor vide Loan Agreement dated 27.02.2015 Against the

sanctioned facility of Rs.30,00,00,000/-, an amount of Rs.24,44,44,456/-

was disbursed by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor on

17.03.2015. The Appellant executed a Deed of Personal Guarantee dated

27.02.2015 in favour of the Financial Creditor in connection with the

aforesaid facility. The aforesaid loan facility was also secured by pledge of

shares of Adhunik Metaliks Limited and at the time of the pledge, these shares

were stated to be valued at Rs.19.85 per share, having an aggregate value of

approximately Rs.50.00 Crores.

3. It is further stated that, according to the Financial Creditor, the

Corporate Debtor was required to repay the facility in eight equal quarterly

instalments commencing from the end of the 27th month from the date of

disbursement and the Corporate Debtor failed to repay the instalments in

accordance with the repayment schedule and committed defaults in respect

of the facility and the account of the Corporate Debtor was classified as a Non-

Performing Asset (NPA) on 01.03.2018.

4. It is further stated that Respondent No. 1 had invoked and realised

portions of the pledged securities during FY 2016–17 and FY 2017–18,

resulting in recoveries aggregating to approximately Rs.8.30 Crores, while a

                                                             3



substantial number of pledged shares continued to remain with Respondent

No.1. Thereafter, the Financial Creditor issued an alleged Event of Default

Notice dated 10.07.2018 to the Corporate Debtor and other concerned

persons, including guarantors/pledgers, granting a period of seven days for

curing the alleged default. The Financial Creditor issued a Recall Facility

Notice dated 10.08.2018 whereby the facility was recalled and the Corporate

Debtor was called upon to repay the entire facility together with applicable

interest and penalty within 48 hours.

5. It is further stated that Respondent No.1 thereafter instituted

proceedings against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 of the Code by filing

C.P. (IB) No.02/GB/2024 before the NCLT, Guwahati Bench, in respect of the

loan transaction and facility. In the said Section 7 proceedings, the Corporate

Debtor filed its Reply Affidavit dated 25.04.2024, raising, inter alia, objections

regarding limitation and the manner in which Respondent No.1 had dealt with

the pledged securities and the amounts realised therefrom and also raised the

issue of appropriation of the amounts recovered from the pledged securities

and the manner in which Respondent No.1 had maintained its accounts in

relation to the said recoveries.

6. It is further stated that the Adjudicating Authority, by order dated

16.05.2024, dismissed the aforesaid Section 7 petition filed by Respondent

No.1 against the Corporate Debtor on the ground of limitation. The said order

dated 16.05.2024 was challenged by Respondent No.1 before this Appellate

Tribunal and came to be affirmed by order dated 25.03.2025.

7. It is further stated that the above order of this Appellate Tribunal was

challenged by Respondent No. 1 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court, which, by

                                                             4



order dated 30.07.2025 passed in Civil Appeal No. 5787 of 2025 set aside the

order dated 16.05.2024 passed by the NCLT and the order dated 25.03.2025

passed by this Appellate Tribunal, and remitted the Section 7 proceedings to

the Adjudicating Authority to proceed with the application treating the same

as has been filed within limitation, inter alia on the basis of the alleged

acknowledgment dated 12.08.2020 and the exclusion of the period from

15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022, in view of Suo Moto case. Review Petition (Civil)

No. 2132/2025 filed in Civil Appeal No. 5787/2025, arising out of the

judgment and order dated 30.07.2025 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court

in the proceedings under Section 7 of the Code against Adhunik Meghalaya

Steels Private Limited, was also dismissed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court vide

order dated 30.10.2025.

8. It is further stated that Respondent No.1 issued a statutory Demand

Notice in Form B dated 20.03.2024 to the Appellant under Rule 7(1) of the

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Rules, 2019, which was delivered on 23.03.2024.

A detailed Reply to the same dated 22.04.2024 was given, disputing the

contents thereof, the alleged liability of the Appellant, the amount and the

basis on which the said amount is stated to be due and payable by the

Appellant as well as the issue of limitation.

9. It is further stated that Respondent No.1 instituted the present

proceedings under Section 95 of the Code against the Appellant, being C.P.

(IB) No.12/GB/2024, on 08.05.2024, seeking initiation of insolvency

resolution process against the Appellant as Personal Guarantor in respect of

the same financial transaction and for the same alleged claim, pertaining to

which the application filed by the Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the

                                                             5



Code. The Adjudicating Authority, vide order dated 08.11.2024, appointed Mr.

Sanjay Poddar as the Resolution Professional in the Section 95 proceedings

and directed him to submit his report under Section 99 of the Code, which

was submitted on 23.12.2024 under Section 99 of the Code, recommending

initiation of the insolvency resolution process against the Appellant.

10. It is further stated that the proceedings initiated against the Appellant

under Section 95 of the Code were barred by limitation as the personal

guarantee of the Appellant was invoked in the year 2018 and limitation had

expired much prior to the filing of the application under Section 95 of the

Code on 08.05.2024, even after excluding the period from 15.03.2020 to

28.02.2022 in terms of the orders passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court on

account of the COVID-19 pandemic and granting the further period of 90 days

as directed therein, the application filed by Respondent No.1 under Section

95 of the Code remained beyond the prescribed period of limitation, however,

the Adjudicating Authority by passing the impugned order dated 09.09.2026,

allowed C.P. (IB) No.12/GB/2024 and initiated the insolvency resolution

process against the Appellant as Personal Guarantor. The appellant has

preferred this appeal against the said impugned order.

11. Learned counsel for the Appellant, at the outset, submits that the

Adjudicating Authority has committed a manifest illegality in initiating the

process of insolvency against the Appellant, while the proceedings initiated

before the Adjudicating Authority were clearly barred by limitation.

12. It is further submitted that the crucial date for computation of

limitation was the date of invocation of guarantee and as Respondent No. 1

issued a recall facility notice on 10.08.2018 requiring the Appellant to pay

                                                             6

within 48 hours, and the application under Section 95 of the Code has been

filed on 08.05.2024, the application was clearly barred by limitation.

13. Elaborating further, it is submitted that the recall facility notice was

given by the Respondent/Financial Creditor on 10.08.2018 even if the COVID-

19 period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 is excluded, the application filed by

Respondent No. 1 under Section 95 of the Code was filed 284 days beyond

the stipulated last date of limitation as the time only till 29.07.2023 was

available to Respondent No. 1 for filing of any application under Section 95 of

the Code. In written submissions, learned counsel for the Appellant has

provided the following time flow chart in support of his submissions:



14. It is further submitted that the limitation against the personal

guarantor is required to be determined independently of the principal

borrower, and the same has no connection with the limitation stipulated for

the principal debtor and the acknowledgement made by the principal

                                                             7



borrower cannot be treated as an acknowledgement by the guarantor after a

separate cause of action had occurred. Reliance in this regard is placed on:



                  Syndicate Bank vs Channaveerappa Bileri (2006)11 SCC 506),

                  Hira Lal Chhotalal Shah vs Central Bank of India (1980 SCC



                     Online GUJ 53),

                  Dialu Mal vs Nandu Shah-Jai Lal (1931 SCC Online LAH 231),

clause operates only until invocation of the guarantee. Hence, if the limitation

against the borrower survives, then the guarantee by the Appellant can be

invoked. But once invoked and the period of limitation has expired, then

Section 18 of the Indian Limitation Act could not come to the rescue of

in the corporate debtor's balance sheet dated 12.08.2020 could not revive or

acknowledgment by the corporate debtor could extend limitation against the

and therefore the finding on limitation has attained finality and cannot be

22. It is further submitted that the issue is no longer res integra and has

been settled by this Appellate Tribunal in State Bank of India v. Bernard

John, Personal Guarantor of GEI Industrial Systems Ltd., 2025 SCC

in the Corporate Debtor’s balance sheets would extend limitation against a

Personal Guarantor also, particularly where the Deed of Guarantee expressly

provides for such effect, as their liability is concurrent and co-extensive. In

the said case, the personal guarantor had executed a guarantee containing a

the Appellant and the personal guarantee in that case was invoked in 2016.

Therefore, contention that an acknowledgment of the principal borrower

cannot bind the Personal Guarantor, where the invocation of the guarantee

preceded such acknowledgment, is wholly untenable. The aforesaid legal

position has attained finality in view of the dismissal of an appeal filed against

the above case being (Civil Appeal No. 7898 of 2026) by the Hon’ble Supreme

guarantee deed, the acknowledgment of debt dated 12.08.2020 by the

Corporate Debtor in its balance sheet is also binding on the Appellant for the

23. It is further submitted that the Deed of Personal Guarantee is a valid,

joint, several and co-extensive with that of the Borrower, and Clause 5(c)

further stipulates that the Guarantee shall remain in force until all dues are

Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union Bank of India & Anr., (2021) 8 SCC 481,

wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court recognised the co-extensive nature of a

upon default by the principal borrower and on State Bank of India v. V.

Ramakrishnan & Anr., (2018) 17 SCC 394. It is also submitted that without

SCC 456 and Amit Bhatnagar v. UCO Bank & Anr., 2026 SCC OnLine

with another entity cannot, by itself, absolve the Appellant of his liability for

hold that a continuing guarantee and a guarantee payable on demand are

mutually exclusive and the fact that the Guarantee is payable on demand

does not negate its continuing character. Further, paragraph 9 of this report

recognises that a claim may be time-barred against the principal debtor but

may remain enforceable against the guarantor, depending on the terms of the

guarantee. In the present case, Clause 5(f) expressly provides that an

acknowledgment by the Borrower binds the Appellant for limitation purposes,

Accordingly, the effect of the acknowledgment dated 12.08.2020 must be

determined in light of this express contractual provision. The Bernard John

judgment in paragraph 73, has taken into account the findings contained in

Syndicate Bank and held that an acknowledgment by the principal debtor

operates as an acknowledgment against the guarantor as well, given that their

liability is concurrent, and renews the limitation period as against both.

26. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and having perused the

record, it appears that Respondent No. 1 entered into a Loan Agreement dated

27.02.2015 with Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Pvt. Ltd. (CD) pursuant to which

                                                            13



INR 24.44 Crores were disbursed. The facility was secured, inter alia, by a

pledge of 8,10,804 shares of the Corporate Debtor in favour of Respondent

No. 1 under a Pledge Agreement dated 27.02.2015, and a Deed of Personal

Guarantee dated 27.02.2015 executed by Appellant, under which his liability

was joint, several and co-extensive with that of the Corporate Debtor. Upon

default in repayment, the Corporate Debtor’s account was classified as a Non-

Performing Asset (NPA) on 01.03.2018. Respondent No. 1 thereafter issued a

Notice of Default dated 10.07.2018 (with a copy to the Appellant, and

thereafter issued a Recall Facility Notice dated 10.08.2018 to the Corporate

Debtor and the Appellant. Subsequently, Respondent No. 1 filed C.P. (IB) No.

02 (GB) of 2024 (“Section 7 Petition”) against the Corporate Debtor under

Section 7 of the Code and an application under Section 95 against the

Appellant. The Section 7 Petition was initially dismissed as time-barred by the

Adjudicating Authority, vide order dated 16.05.2024, which was also upheld

by this Appellate Tribunal, However, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, vide

judgment dated 30.07.2025 passed in Civil Appeal No. 5787 of 2025 set aside

both orders and held the Section 7 Petition to be within limitation as the

limitation only expired on 28.02.2025, on account of the acknowledgment of

debt in the Corporate Debtor’s balance sheet dated 12.08.2020 and the

exclusion of the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 pursuant to the

Hon’ble Supreme Court’s Suo motu orders in In Re: Cognizance for Extension

of Limitation. The Review Petition filed to review the aforesaid judgment was

also subsequently dismissed on 30.10.2025. Section 7 Petition was thereafter

admitted by the Adjudicating Authority on 21.07.2026. The Adjudicating

Authority, vide order dated 09.09.2026 also, admitted the Section 95

                                                            14



Application against the Appellant, holding that the issue of limitation stood



settled by the Supreme Court’s Judgment and that the Personal Guarantee



had been validly invoked. The appellant Guarantor has challenged the same



by filing this appeal.



27. We, at the outset, are of the considered view that the rights and



obligations of the parties with regard to the contract of guarantee would



depend on the terms, conditions, and stipulations of the guarantee deed. It is



an admitted case that the Appellant had executed a guarantee in favour of



Respondent No. 1 with regard to the facility of loan granted to the corporate



debtor. For convenience, the relevant clauses of the Deed of Guarantee are



reproduced below:
```
