```text
28. A perusal of the aforesaid clauses of the Deed of Guarantee reveals that

the guarantor/Appellant, by executing the aforesaid guarantee deed, had

undertaken to make, without delay or protest and on first demand and

without recourse to the borrower, within 24 hours of the demand, payment of

the principal amount not exceeding ₹300 million only, along with interest and

other monies payable by the borrower to the financial creditor. Clause 2 of

the guarantee deed reveals that this guarantee is irrevocable and

unconditional and shall not be revoked or cancelled till the entire claim of the

financial creditor is fully met and paid by the guarantor. Clause 3 of the

guarantee deed specifies that the guarantor's obligation to pay will arise when

notice in writing is given by the financial creditor requiring the guarantor to

make payment. After such notice is given, the financial creditor may proceed

to enforce the guarantor's obligations and liabilities without first proceeding

against and resorting to any of the remedies against the borrower. Thus, it is

evident that the financial creditor was not obliged to first proceed against the

principal borrower. It was stipulated that, without initiating any proceeding

against the CD on the invocation of guarantee, the whole of the money can be

recovered from the guarantor.

29. Perusal of clause 5 (f) of the guarantee deed reveals that it is stipulated

that, for the purpose of limitation, any admission or acknowledgement in

writing given or part payment made by the borrower (in the spirit of the

repayment of the borrower's dues or otherwise in relation to the facility) shall

be binding on the guarantor, notwithstanding that the same may have been

                                                            17



made by the borrower, it shall be treated as given on behalf of the guarantor

also. Therefore, it is reflected that any admission or acknowledgment in

writing made by the principal borrower would be deemed to have been

acknowledged and admitted by the guarantor.

30. A perusal of clause 13 of the guarantee deed suggests that the parties

have stipulated that the guarantee is a continuing guarantee and is without

prejudice to, and in addition to, any other security or security documents

already held or which the financial creditor may hold thereafter on account of

or in relation to the facility to the borrower in terms of said agreement. The

guarantee thus appears to be a continuing guarantee payable on demand.

31. We also notice that in Part III of the application moved by Respondent

No. 1/financial creditor, it is stated that the account of the corporate debtor

was declared as a non-performing asset by the financial creditor on

01.03.2018. Thereafter, the corporate debtor once again defaulted in its

payments, and the Financial Creditor issued the event-of-default notice dated

10.07.2018, allowing seven days to the corporate debtor to cure the default.

32. It is further stated in Part III of the application that, despite the notice,

the corporate debtor failed to repay the amount which was due and payable

and stood in default. The financial creditor was constrained to issue the recall

facility notice dated 10.08.2018, recalling thereby the entire term loan facility.

33. In column number 4 of Part III of the application, it has been stated

that the date of default is 01.03.2018, as the account of the corporate debtor

was declared as a non-performing asset on that date. As per the norms and

guidelines formulated by the Reserve Bank of India, this date is also duly

recorded with the information utility, as is reflected in the report provided by

                                                            18



the National E-Governance Services Limited. It is further stated that the

corporate debtor once again defaulted in its payments, and the financial

creditor was constrained to recall the entire facility. The recall facility notices

dated 10.08.2018, called upon the corporate debtor to repay the entire facility

with applicable interest and penalty within 48 hours from the delivery of the

notice. It is also stated therein that the corporate debtor has continued to

acknowledge the debt in its financial statements in the balance sheet for the

financial year 2019-2020, thereby extending the period of limitation for filing

the application within the meaning of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

34. It is further stated that, while the order dated 10.01.2022, passed by

the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Suo Motu petition (C.) No. 3 of 2020, read with

earlier orders passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court between 15.03.2020, and

28.02.2022, would be excluded from the computation of the limitation period,

and, therefore, the application was filed within the limitation period

prescribed under the Limitation Act. The description of the extension of the

limitation has also been given in the tabular form, which is being reproduced

by us here below.

19

                                                            20



35. Therefore, the main contention of the Respondent/Financial Creditor is



that the limitation period has extended by the acknowledgement made by the



principal debtor in its balance sheet of the year 2019-2020. As the liability of



the Appellant is co-extensive with the principal debtor, the period for filing an



application under Section 95 of the Code is automatically extended by the



acknowledgement made by the financial creditor under Section 18 of the



Indian Limitation Act, 1963.



36. The Learned Adjudicating Authority did not deliberate on the issue of



limitation on the ground that the dispute has already been set at rest by the



Honourable Supreme Court by its judgment dated 30.07.2025 passed in Civil



Appeal No. 5787 of 2025, with regard to the Section 7 application moved by



the Respondent/Financial Creditor against the principal debtor. For the sake



of convenience, the relevant part of the judgment dated 30.07.2025 passed by



the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 5787 of 2025 is reproduced as



under: -



               “41. Keeping all these principles in mind, if we examine the facts

               of the present case, it will be clear that the Balance Sheet of F.Y.

               2019- 20, viewed in the background of the other admitted

               documents, including the financial statements of the previous

               years, clearly constitutes a valid acknowledgment of a subsisting

               liability and indicated the existence of a jural relationship and an

               admission as to the existence of such relationship. We say so for

               the following reasons: -

               The general tenor and context of the balance sheet of F.Y. 2019-

               20 considered in the background of surrounding circumstances

               arising from the balance sheets of F.Y. 2015-16, 2016-17 & 2017-

               18 clearly points to the fact that the entry in the balance sheet of

               F.Y. 2019-20 constitutes a valid acknowledgement and pertains

               to the same borrowing as was reflected in the balance sheet of

               F.Y. 2015-16, 2016-17 & 2017-18.

               Under the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 7, a cash flow

               statement is appended to the financial statement. The cash flow

               statement indicates that in F.Y. 2018-19 there was proceeds from

                                            21



borrowings of Rs.72,30,902/- and added to Rs.23,68,91,933/-,

a figure of Rs.24,41,22,835/- is arrived at.



More importantly, in the cash flow statement it was indicated that

no part of cash flow proceeds was utilised in the repayment of

existing borrowings under the financial activities since the

amount under the head “cash flows from (used in) financial

activities” is nil. This clearly indicates that the debt remained

unpaid even in 2019-20.



42. In addition to the above, it is significant to note that in this

case in the reply filed to the Section 7 application, apart from a

general objection as to the application being barred by limitation

only a bare denial was made in the following terms: - “(sic) deny

that Balance Sheet of CD can be treated as acknowledgment of

debt as wrongfully alleged or at all.”



43. In the application under Section 7 detailed averments were

made referring to a series of audited financial statements and

Balance Sheet from F.Y. 2015-16 to F.Y. 2019-20 to make out a

case that the entry in F.Y. 2019-20 constituted an

acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act by the

respondent. In any event, we have not based our finding on the

mere factum of non-denial but have construed the entry in the

Balance Sheet of F.Y. 2019-20 to conclude that the entry in the

F.Y. 2019-20 constitutes a valid acknowledgment.



44. The Balance Sheet of F.Y. 2019-20 was admittedly signed by

the board of directors on 12.08.2020. This date was within the

subsisting period of limitation for the reason that taking

01.03.2018 as the commencement of limitation, limitation

ordinarily would have continued till 28.02.2021. Since an

acknowledgment came into effect on 12.08.2020, limitation

would have stood extended till 11.08.2023. However, Covid-19

intervened resulting in this Court passing a series of orders

extending the period of limitation. The relevant order applicable

in this case is the order of 10.01.2022.



45. Parties were at daggers drawn on the aspect whether sub

Para (I) of Para 5 of the order of 10.01.2022 would apply or sub-

Para (III) would apply. Para 5 of the order dated 10.01.2022

reads as under: -



"5. Taking into consideration the arguments advanced by learned

counsel and the impact of the surge of the virus on public health

and adversities faced by litigants in the prevailing conditions, we

deem it appropriate to dispose of the M. A No. 21 of 2022 with the

following directions:



The order dated 23.03.2020 is restored and in continuation of the

subsequent orders dated 08.03.2021, 27.04.2021 and

23.09.2021, it is directed that the period from 15.03.2020 till

28.02.2022 shall stand excluded for the purposes of limitation as

                                                            22



               may be prescribed under any general or special laws in respect

               of all judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings.



               Consequently, the balance period of limitation remaining as on

               03.10.2021, if any, shall become available with effect from

               01.03.2022.



               In cases where the limitation would have expired during the

               period between 15.03.2020 till 28.02.2022, notwithstanding the

               actual balance period of limitation remaining, all persons shall

               have a limitation period of 90 days from 01.03.2022. In the event

               the actual balance period of limitation remaining, with effect from

               01.03.2022 is greater than 90 days, that longer period shall

               apply.



               IV. It is further clarified that the period from 15.03.2020 till

               28.02.2022 shall also stand excluded in computing the periods

               prescribed under Section 23(4) and 29A of the Arbitration and

               Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act,

               2015 and provisos (b) and (c) of Section 138 of the Negotiable

               Instruments Act, 1881 and any other laws, which prescribe

               period(s) of limitation for instituting proceedings, outer limits

               (within which the court or tribunal can condone delay) and

               termination of proceedings"



               46. We have no manner of doubt that sub-Para 1 of Para 5 of the

               order of this Court dated 10.01.2022 would apply and the entire

               period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 would stand excluded,

               which would mean that the limitation would, reckoning the

               acknowledgment of 12.08.2020, commence on 01.03.2022 and

               continue till 28.02.2025. Since the application has been filed on

               15.01.2024 the same is within time. Limitation, in view of the

               acknowledgment as found above, having commenced only on

               12.08.2020, the question of limitation expiring between

               15.03.2022 and 28.02.2022 cannot arise. Hence, Para 5(III) of

               the order of this Court dated 10.01.2022, has no application to

               the facts of this case.



               47. In view of the observations made hereinabove, the judgments

               of the NCLAT dated 25.03.2025 and NCLT dated 16.05.2024 are

               set aside. The appeal is allowed. The matter is remitted to the

               adjudicating authority to proceed with and decide in accordance

               with law, treating the application under Section 7 of the IBC, filed

               by the appellant, as one filed within limitation. No order as to

               costs.”



37. The aforesaid judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court records the date



of default as 01.03.2018, with regard to the principal debtor and found that



the debt of the creditor is reflected in the Balance Sheet of CD of the Financial

                                                            23



Year 2019-20, which was admittedly signed by the board of directors on

12.08.2020 and that this date is within the subsisting period of limitation for

the reason taken 01.03.2018 as the date of default and commencement of

limitation, the period would have continued till 28.02.2021. However, because

the acknowledgement by the Corporate Debtor took effect on 12.08.2020,

limitation would have extended till 11.08.2023. However, Covid-19 intervened

resulting in Hon’ble Supreme Court passing a series of orders extending the

period of limitation. The relevant order applicable in this case is the order of

10.01.2022 and sub-Para 1 of Para 5 of this would apply and the entire period

from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 would stand excluded from computation of

limitation, which would mean that the limitation period, in view of the

acknowledgement dated 12.08.2020 would commence on 01.03.2022 and

continue till 28.02.2025. The application in that case under Section 7 of the

Code was filed on 15.01.2024 the application was treated as having been filed

within time. The application under Section 95 of the Code against the

Appellant was also filed by the Respondent no.1 on 08.05.2024 i.e. before

28.02.2025.

38. It has been argued by Ld. Senior Counsel appearing for the Appellant

that the acknowledgment by the principal borrower /CD cannot be taken as

the acknowledgement by the Appellant/Personal guarantee, as the

requirement of Section 18 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, is that the

acknowledgement must be in writing, which is lacking in the instant case.

39. We, however, are not in agreement with the submissions made on

behalf of the Appellant, because the contract of guarantee executed between

the Appellant and the Respondent No. 1 would decide as to whether any

                                                            24



acknowledgement made by the principal debtor would be binding on the

Appellant/personal guarantor or not?

40. We have already noticed clause 5 (f) of the guarantee deed which

provides that, for the purpose of limitation, any admission or

acknowledgement in writing given or part payment made by the borrower

shall be binding on the guarantor, notwithstanding that the same may have

been made by the borrower, it shall be treated as given on behalf of the

guarantor also. Therefore, in view of this clause, the acknowledgment in

writing dated 12.08.2020 made by the principal borrower would be deemed

to have been acknowledged and admitted by the Appellant/guarantor also.

That being so, having regard to the similarity between the dates of default

with regard to principal borrower and guarantor and the petition by the

respondent no.1 having been filed on 08.05.2024 i.e. before 28.02.2025, was

within limitation.

41. At this juncture, we also notice that a copy of the event of default notice

dated 10.07.2018 and a copy of the recall facility notice dated 10.08.2018,

given by Respondent No. 1/financial creditor, are on record. The notice dated

10.07.2018 though, was addressed to the CD, however a copy of the same

was addressed to the Appellant, as the personal guarantor. This, in our

considered opinion, is sufficient invocation of the guarantee, as the only

purpose of invocation of a guarantee is to make the guarantor aware to pay

or discharge his or her liability as stipulated in the guarantee deed. The recall

facility notice dated 10.08.2018 is addressed to the Appellant/personal

guarantor also, apart from the CD. Therefore, there is sufficient invocation of

the guarantee by the Respondent/ Financial Creditor.

                                                            25



42. Learned counsel for the Appellant has relied on Syndicate Bank vs

Channaveerappa Beleri (Supra), in order to buttress his submission that

limitation against the guarantor must be computed with reference to the

contractual cause of action against that guarantor, once the stipulated period

had expired following the invocation, the Appellant's cause of action had

accrued, and the clock of limitation had started ticking.

43. We have perused the judgment and find that apart from other issues it

is highlighted by this judgment that the terms of the guarantee deed would

decide the nature of guarantee and no straitjacket formula divorced from the

terms of the contract of guarantee may be stipulated to fit in all guarantee

deeds. Thus, we are bound to look into various terms and conditions of the

guarantee deed. Perusal of the Guarantee Deed dated 27.02.2015 executed

by the Appellant in favour of Respondent No. 1 reveals that it is an

unconditional and continuing guarantee as Clause 13 expressly provides that

the Guarantee is a continuing guarantee and there are other clear stipulations

which suggest that it would remain binding upon the Appellant until all the

dues of the corporate debtor are discharged. It has been clearly stipulated in

clause 1 of the guarantee deed that the Appellant has undertaken the liability

of the borrower to pay all the dues within 24 hours of the first demand made,

without recourse to the principal borrower. Similarly, clause 5(b)(c) suggests

that this guarantee shall remain in force until all the dues are discharged.

44. We have already noticed the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court

dated 30.07.2025 passed in Civil Appeal No. 5787 of 2025, with regard to the

Section 7 application moved by the Respondent/Financial Creditor against

the principal debtor, wherein the Supreme Court even after taking 01.03.2018

                                                            26



as the date of commencement of limitation and taking into account the



Balance Sheet of F.Y. 2019-20 of the CD admittedly signed by the board of



directors on 12.08.2020, as the acknowledgement of the debt and after



extending the benefit of suo motu order dated 10.01.2022 found the petition



filed by the Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the Code on 15.01.2024,



within limitation as according to the Court the limitation up to 28.02.2025



was available. The application under Section 95 of the Code against the



Appellant was also filed by the Respondent no.1 on 08.05.2024 i.e. before



28.02.2025. Thus, we do not find any reason why the petition filed by the



Respondent No.1 could not be treated within limitation. The Ld. Adjudicating



Authority in our considered opinion was legally right in opining that the issue



of limitation has been set at rest by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, by passing



the aforesaid order.



45. In this regard the law laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Laxmi



Pat Surana vs. Union Bank of India, (2021) Vol 8 SCC page 481 may also



be recalled and paragraph 44 of the same is reproduced as under:



               “23. Indubitably, a right or cause of action would enure to the

               lender (financial creditor) to proceed against the principal

               borrower, as well as the guarantor in equal measure in case they

               commit default in repayment of the amount of debt acting jointly

               and severally. It would still be a case of default committed by the

               guarantor itself, if and when the principal borrower fails to

               discharge his obligation in respect of amount of debt. For, the

               obligation of the guarantor is coextensive and coterminous with

               that of the principal borrower to defray the debt, as predicated in

               Section 128 of the Contract Act. As a consequence of such default,

               the status of the guarantor metamorphoses into a debtor or a

               corporate debtor if it happens to be a corporate person, within the

               meaning of Section 3(8) IBC. For, as aforesaid, the expression

               “default” has also been defined in Section 3(12) IBC to mean non-

               payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the

               amount of debt has become due or payable and is not paid by the

               debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may be.

                                                            27



               44. In the present case, NCLT as well as NCLAT have adverted to

               the acknowledgments by the principal borrower as well as the

               corporate guarantor-corporate debtor after declaration of NPA

               from time to time and lastly on 08.12.2018. The fact that

               acknowledgment within the limitation period was only by

               the principal borrower and not the guarantor, would not

               absolve the guarantor of its liability flowing from the letter

               of guarantee and memorandum of mortgage. The liability of the

               guarantor being coextensive with the principal borrower under

               Section 128 of the Contract Act, it triggers the moment principal

               borrower commits default in paying the acknowledged debt. This

               is a legal fiction. Such liability of the guarantor would flow from

               the guarantee deed and memorandum of mortgage, unless it

               expressly provides to the contrary”.



                                                                                 (Emphasis ours)



46. In Pooja Ramesh Singh vs. SBI, in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 329 of 2023,



this appellate Tribunal observed that:



               “24. The scheme of I&B Code clearly indicate that both the

               Principal Borrower and the Guarantor become liable to pay the

               amount when the default is committed. When default is

               committed by the Principal Borrower the amount becomes due not

               only against the Principal Borrower but also against the

               Corporate Guarantor, which is the scheme of the I&B Code. When

               we read with as is delineated by Section 3(11) of the Code, debt

               becomes due both on Principal Borrower and the Guarantor, as

               noted above. The definition of default under Section 3(12) in

               addition to expression 'due' occurring in Section 3(11) uses two

               additional expressions i.e. "payable" and "is not paid by the

               debtor or corporate debtor". The expression ‘is not paid by the

               debtor' has to be given some meaning. As laid down by the

               Hon'ble Supreme Court "Syndicate Bank vs. Channaveerappa

               Beleri & Ors." (supra), a quarantor's liability depends on terms of

               his contract. There can be default by the Principal Borrower and

               the Guarantor on the same date or date of default for both may

               be different depending on the terms of contract of guarantee. It is

               well settled that the loan agreement with the Principal Borrower

               and the Bank as well as Deed of Guarantee between the Bank

               and the Guarantor are two different transactions and the

               Guarantor's liability has to be read from the Deed of Guarantee.



47. In Amit Bhatnagar vs Uco Bank and Ors (Supra) this Appellant



Tribunal in paragraph number 44 has held as under:

                                                            28



               “44. We also take into consideration that under Section 128 of

               the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of the guarantor is co-

               extensive with that of the principal debtor. The Hon’ble Supreme

               Court in BRS Ventures Investments Ltd. v. SREI Infrastructure

               Finance Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 4565 of 2021 has held that

               recovery of part of the debt or settlement with one obligant does

               not extinguish the liability of the other obligants and that the

               creditor retains the full right to recover the balance debt from the

               remaining obligants, including the personal guarantor. Thus,

               even where a Resolution Plan results in partial recovery, the

               remaining unpaid debts survive and the guarantors continue to

               remain liable for the unpaid portion as applicable in the present

               case.”



48. In State Bank of India versus Bernard John, 2025 SCC Online



NCLAT 1670, a Coordinate Bench of this Appellate Tribunal, in identical



factual matrix has held as under:



               “53. The aforesaid clauses of the Guarantee Agreement create a

               contractual bridge between the borrower's acknowledgment and

               the guarantor's liability, stipulating that any admission or

               acknowledgment by the principal borrower “shall bind the

               guarantor and be deemed made on his behalf.” This clause read

               in conjunction with Section 128 of the Contract Act, which renders

               the guarantor's liability co-extensive with that of the principal

               debtor, unequivocally extends the effect of acknowledgment to

               the guarantor as well.



               58. Therefore, each and every acknowledgment or the debt by

               the Corporate Debtor in the balance sheet up to FY 2019-2020

               has the effect of extending the limitation period.



               59. The Adjudicating Authority, in dismissing the petition,

               appears to have proceeded on an erroneous assumption that

               acknowledgment must be personally made by the guarantor and

               that balance sheets signed during CIRP are invalid. Both

               assumptions stand contrary to the settled position of law. The

               former overlooks the co-extensive nature of guarantor liability,

               while the later disregards the statutory continuity of

               acknowledgment through financial statements mandated by the

               Companies Act.



               60. Based on the above discussion, we conclude that:

                                            29



i. The Corporate Debtor's balance sheets for FY 2016-2017 to FY

2019-2020 contained clear and unequivocal acknowledgment of

debt towards the Appellant Bank.

ii. These acknowledgments, by virtue of both Section 18 of the

Limitation Act and Clauses 12 & 19 of the Deed of Guarantee,

validly extended limitation against the Personal Guarantor.

iii. The statutory exclusion of limitation from 15.03.2020 to

28.02.2022 further renders the Section 95 application, filed in

October 2021, well within limitation.



61. We therefore are of the view that the Adjudicating Authority's

finding that the petition was time-barred suffers from a clear error

of law and based upon incorrect appreciation of facts. The

application under Section 95 filed by the Appellant was well

within the limitation period.



68. The question as to whether acknowledgment of debt by a

principal borrower extends limitation against the guarantor has

been the subject of consistent judicial interpretation. The

statutory scheme under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act

provides that “the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that

of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the

contract.” This co-extensiveness implies that both the borrower

and the guarantor are liable for the same debt, at the same time,

and to the same extent, unless expressly limited by contract.



73. It is well settled that such contractual stipulations are

enforceable and consistent with Section 128 of the Contract Act.

In Syndicate Bank v. Channaveerappa Beleri, (2006) 11 SCC

506, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that acknowledgment

made by the principal debtor extends limitation as against the

guarantor as well, as their liability is concurrent. The Court held

that where acknowledgment is made by the debtor before expiry

of limitation, it renews the limitation period against both the

debtor and the surety.



75. Applying the ratio of the aforesaid Judgments Syndicate

Bank (supra) and State Bank of India (supra) to the present case,

we hold that acknowledgment of liability made by the Corporate

Debtor in its balance sheets for FY 2016-2017 to 2019-2020

constitutes valid acknowledgment not only for the borrower but

also for the guarantor. This is for three reasons:



a) Section 128 of the Contract Act makes the guarantor's liability

co-extensive, meaning that the same acknowledgment of the

same debt that renews limitation for the borrower equally applies

to the guarantor, since their liabilities are inseparable.



b) Clauses 12 and 19 of the Deed of Guarantee expressly deem

acknowledgment by the borrower to be acknowledgment by the

guarantor. The guarantor, having agreed to this term at the time

of executing the guarantee, is estopped from denying its effect.

                                                            30



               c) The ratio in Syndicate Bank v. Channaveerappa Beleri (supra)

               and State Bank of India v. Indexport Registered (supra) highlights

               the concept that acknowledgment in balance sheet made by the

               principal debtor extends limitation to the guarantor as well.”

49. Aforesaid judgment of this Appellate Tribunal was not interfered with

by the Honourable Supreme Court on an appeal preferred by the Appellant -

Bernard John and vide order dated 15.05.2026 passed in Civil Appeal No. Nil

of 2026 arising out of Diary No. 65246 of 2025 the Civil Appeal was dismissed

in timeline.

50. We, at the cost of repetition, recall that clause 5(f) of the guarantee deed

stipulates that, for the purpose of limitation, any admission or

acknowledgement in writing given or part payment made by the borrower (in

the spirit of the repayment of the borrower's dues or otherwise in relation to

the facility) shall be binding on the guarantor, notwithstanding that the same

may have been made by the borrower, it shall be treated as given on behalf of

the guarantor also. In view of this clause in the guarantee deed, we do not

have any doubt that the liability of the Appellant guarantor is co-extensive

with the liability of the principal borrower and any acknowledgement or

admission by the principal debtor would be binding on the Appellant personal

guarantor so far as the limitation is concerned and in view of this clause, we

are of the considered view that the other case laws relied on by learned

counsel for the Appellant are not applicable to the facts of the instant case.

The instant case appears to be entirely covered by the law laid down by a Co-

ordinate bench of this Court in Bernard John (supra), which has also been

approved by the Hon'ble Suprem
```

```text
                      1



        NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

                      PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI



        Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                     &



                I.A. No. 4161, 4162 of 2026



IN THE MATTER OF:



Sudarshan Aithal                                …Appellant(s)

Suspended Director of Distribution

Logistics Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.



Versus



Bank of India & Ors.                            …Respondent(s)

Present:



For Appellant    : Mr. Kunal Tandon Sr. Adv. with Mr. Sinha Shrey

For Respondents     Nikhilesh, Mr. Parth Davar, Mr. Kaustubh Khanna, Mr.

                    Swastik Verma & Ms. Faraaz Khan, Advocates



                 : Mr. Ricky Sampat, Advocate for R-1

                    Mr. K. Datta Sr. Adv. with Mr. Angad Baxi, Ms. Ratema

                    Kachwalla, Ms. Aparna Singh, Mr. Harsh Gurbani &

                    Ms. Alina Mathew, Advocates



                                                 O R D E R

                                              (Hybrid Mode)

[Per: Justice Mohd. Faiz Alam Khan, Member (Judicial)]



       Mr. Sudarshan Aithal K, Suspended Director of the Distribution Logistics

Infrastructure Private Limited, has preferred this appeal under Section 61 of

the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code), read with Rule 11 of the

NCLAT Rules, 2016, against the impugned order dated 14.05.2026 passed by

the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench – VI, Adjudicating

authority in Company Petition (IB) No. 1078 of 2025, whereby the Corporate

Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) has been initiated against the Appellant

on an application filed by Respondent No. 1/Bank of India under Section 7 of

the IBC.



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             2



2. Necessary facts required for disposal of the instant appeal, as reflected

in the impugned order, are that an application under Section 7 of the

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code), read with Rule 4 of the

Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority Rules,

2016), was preferred by the Bank of India against the CD with the facts that

the financial creditor had sanctioned a term loan of Rs. 57.50 Crore to Vikram

Logistics Limited, which later changed its name to Distribution Logistics

Infrastructure Private Limited (CD) for its container trains project, vide its

sanction reference dated 21.01.2013.

3. It is stated that in 2014, the said term loan was restructured by

sanctioning an additional term loan of Rs. 4.89 crores, and the existing term

loan of Rs. 48.01 crores were enhanced to Rs. 52.90 crores via sanction letter

dated 11.12.2014. In 2016, the credit facilities sanctioned to the CD were

again reviewed and restructured via sanction letter dated 06.10.2016 and the

existing credit limits sanctioned to the CD were accordingly reviewed with an

aggregate sanctioned limit of Rs. 68.84 crores by sanctioning a revised

repayment plan for the term loan and FITL.

4. It is further stated that the above-stated credit limits were

sanctioned/disbursed/renewed under the consortium banking arrangement,

wherein Punjab National Bank was the lead bank and financial creditor, Bank

of Baroda, Union Bank of India, and State Bank of India, as well as LNTFL,

were the other member banks. In 2021, the CD approached all existing term

lenders, including the Bank of India for one-time restructuring and agreeing



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             3



with the aforesaid request, all three members of the consortium came together

and formed a single consortium led by Bank of Baroda.

5. It is further stated that, vide sanction letter dated 22.06.2021, the credit

limits were renewed, and all banks under the consortium executed a master

restructuring agreement on 26.06.2021 and again in 2022. The credit limits

were reviewed by the financial creditor through its sanction letter dated

30.06.2022, however, thereafter, the CD did not take any steps to regularize

the account, and the default occurred on 29.12.2022. The financial creditor

classified the cash credit account of the CD as NPA on 28.03.2023. The

financial creditor issued a demand notice on 23.12.2024 under Section 13(2)

of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, however, there was no positive response from the

CD.

6. In pursuance of the notice issued by the Learned Adjudicating

Authority the reply has been filed by the Appellant. The Learned Adjudicating

Authority, after hearing learned counsel for the parties, by order dated

14.05.2026, allowed the petition filed by the financial creditor and initiated

the CIRP against the CD. Being aggrieved by the same, the instant appeal has

been preferred by the suspended director of the CD.

7. It is worth mentioning, that during the course of the pendency of the

proceedings before this Appellate Tribunal, Respondent Bank of India along

with other lenders of the corporate debtor, entered into an assignment

agreement dated June 30th, 2026, executed by the Bank of India and other

lenders of the corporate debtor. The loan has been assigned by these banks

in favour of the JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited.

Thereafter, an application has been filed by JM Financial Asset



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             4



Reconstruction Company Limited before this Appellate Tribunal for

substituting it in place of Respondent No. 1, Bank of India. The same was

disposed of by an order dated 22.07.2026 passed by this Appellate Tribunal,

and JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited was arrayed as

Respondent No. 3.

8. We have heard Shri Kunal Tandon, learned senior counsel, appearing

for the Appellant, as well as Shri Krishnendu Datta, learned senior counsel,

appearing for Respondent No. 3, and Mr. Riki Sampath for Respondent No. 1,

and perused the record.

9. Learned counsel for the Appellant submits that on 06.06.2009, the

directors of Vikram Logistics and Maritime Services Private Limited (‘VLMSPL’)

now Distribution Logistics Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (‘DLIPL’) executed a Board

Resolution approving the drawing of loan from BOB Consortium and on

27.06.2009 and 28.03.2013 common Loan Agreements were executed

between Vikram Logistics & Maritime Service (P) Ltd. (now known as

Distribution Logistics Infrastructure (P) Ltd.) as Borrower and the Bank of

Baroda consortium as lenders for credit facilities and the Punjab National

Bank, Bank of Baroda, Bank of India, Dena Bank and the Corporate Debtor;

by virtue of which a consortium of banks was formulated of which the Punjab

and National Bank was made as the lead bank.

10. It is further submitted that the Corporate Debtor had availed cash

credit facilities from two consortium of banks i.e. (A) Bank of Baroda

Consortium i. Bank of Baroda ii. Punjab National Bank 1 iii. State Bank of

India iv. Union Bank of India v. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd.

(B). Punjab National Bank Consortium i. Punjab National Bank ii. Bank of



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             5



Baroda iii. Bank of India iv. Dena Bank v. L&T Infrastructure and Finance

Company Limited.

11. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the Appellant further submits

that the assignment of the debt of the consortium of banks in favour of

Respondent No. 3 is under challenge before the Hon'ble High Court of

Bombay. The manner in which the auction of the debt has been done has

made the whole auction doubtful and under a shadow.

12. It is further submitted that during the time period from 2021 to 2025,

the corporate debtor was working alongside the banks' consortium for

resolution of the debt. On 28.03.2023, the financial creditor declared the

facilities granted to the CD as NPA. Subsequently, in March 2024, the

corporate debtor approached the banks' consortium with a proposal for a one-

time settlement so that the issue pertaining to the debt owed by the corporate

debtor against all consortium members can be settled once and for all.

13. It is further submitted that, vide its letter dated 15.01.2025, the

corporate debtor offered a sum of Rs. 580 crores to the consortium towards

settlement of the entire debt. After various discussions with the consortium

members in the joint lender forum meetings, this offer was increased from Rs.

580 crores to Rs. 590 crores and in pursuance of the aforesaid letter, the

consortium members led by Bank of Baroda accepted the revised enhanced

proposal of the corporate debtor for the sum of Rs. 590 crores. The Bank of

Baroda issued a letter for deposit of 10% of the upfront amount on

04.10.2025.

14. It is further submitted that, on the one hand, the consortium, in a letter

dated 04.10.2025, had asked the corporate debtor to deposit 10% of the OTS



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             6



offer amount, but they still sought to conduct an auction of the corporate

debtor's debt via the Swiss challenge method to ARCs, banks, NBFCs, etc.

15. It is further submitted that, in response to the aforesaid letter of the

Bank of Baroda dated 04.10.2025, the Appellant also issued a letter dated

04.10.2025 to the Bank of Baroda, acknowledging the condition of 10%

upfront payment. However, the Bank of Baroda, on behalf of all the lenders,

sent a letter dated 30.10.2025 declaring the corporate debtor as the

successful bidder in terms of the Swiss challenge process run by the

consortium (as the Corporate Debtor's offer of Rs. 590 crores were kept as

anchor bid in the auction). The CD, however, required time for payment of the

10% upfront amount from Bank of Baroda. However, the petition has been

filed by the Respondent No. 1 before the Ld. Adjudicating Authority under

Section 7 of the Code to derail the OTS procedure and when the Section 7

proceedings were reserved for orders on 10.03.2026, the Bank of Baroda

rejected the sanctioned OTS for non-deposit of the upfront amount on

16.04.2026. They initiated a fresh swiss challenge with 621 crores as the

anchor bid by the JM Financials. The JM Financial was declared the

successful bidder at ₹621 crores. However, the holding company filed its

petition before the Bombay High Court challenging this Swiss challenge and

also offered ₹625 crores towards complete settlement.

16. It is further submitted that subsequently, when the aforesaid offer of

the holding company was rejected, the holding company offered 50% upfront

with a revised proposal. However, on 06.06.2026, Respondent No. 1 rejected

the said proposal. This offer was again enhanced to Rs. 631 crores, and this



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             7



Appellant Tribunal requested the COC to deliberate. However, on 18.06.2026,

the COC rejected the offer, alleging that it is conditional.

17. It is vehemently submitted that respondent banks have not disputed

that the revised offer of Rs. 631 crores are much higher than the accepted

assignment value of Rs. 621 crores from GM Financials and the stipulations

which have been termed as conditions by the respondent bench are only

regulatory compliances under FEMA and RBI guidelines applicable to a

foreign-owned and controlled company, and are not commercial conditions

attached to the payment.

18. It is further submitted that banks have already accepted Rs. 621 crores

through the Swiss challenge, and even if the CIRP continues, they cannot

recover more than Rs. 621 crores, where the Appellant had offered Rs. 631

crores. Moreover, the 120 employees of the CD would be the only sufferer of

the CIRP process. The Appellant is willing to pay the said debt amount and

settle matter even now if given the chance before this Appellate Tribunal and

comply with the directions of order dated 29.06.2026.

19. It is also submitted that the Appellant had requested the learned

adjudicating authority to adjourn the case so that the debt may be resolved.

However, the above order has been passed.

20. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 3, J M

Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited, submits subsequent to the

Pan India advertised bid process document, the lenders executed two

assignment agreements dated June 30, 2026, in favour of the Respondent No.

3 for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 621 crores. Thus, the Respondent No.

3 has stepped into the shoes of the entire consortium of lenders and presently



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             8



holds 100% of the financial debt of the corporate debtor. Thereafter, the COC

has been reconstituted by the Resolution Professional.

21. It is further submitted that the law is well settled that an appeal against

an order of admission under Section 7 turns only upon the existence of a

financial debt and occurrence of the default. It has been admitted by the

Appellant itself that the loan accounts suffered structural delays in debt

servicing and were classified as NPA. Moreover, the CD's own OTS letter dated

January 15, 2025, refers to its acknowledgement of debt submitted to the

lenders. Thus, the debt and default have been admitted by the Appellant.

22. It is further submitted that the grounds urged in the appeal rest entirely

on alleged OTS and minority status of Bank of India. The reliance placed by

the Appellant on Vidarbha Industries Power Limited versus Axis Bank Limited

(2022) 8 SCC 352 is misconceived, since the Supreme Court in M. Suresh

Kumar Reddy versus Canara Bank (2023) 8 SCC 387 has clarified that the

said decision was rendered in its peculiar facts. Once debt and default are

established, the adjudicating authority is bound to admit the application

under Section 7 of the Code. Reliance is also laid on ES Krishna Murthy

versus Bharat High Tech Builders Private Limited (2022) 3 SCC 161 and

Saurabh Junjunwala versus Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Company Private

Limited (2025) 318 NCLAT CA (AT), Insolvency No. 648 of 2024, decided on

May 1, 2025.

23. It is further submitted that the contention that a valid contractually

binding OTS subsisted is totally misconceived. The letter dated October 20,

2025, expressly records that the offer was subject to final approval from all

the consortium lenders and that the letter does not create any binding



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                             9



obligations on lenders. Moreover, the OTS was accepted on a condition that a

10% upfront deposit would be deposited by the Appellant. However, no money

has been deposited by the Appellant, and therefore the OTS was closed on

April 16, 2026.

24. It is further submitted that the Appellant has instituted a writ petition

before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court titled Sudarshan Aithal versus Bank

of Baroda and others against the lenders, the process advisor, and

Respondent No. 3. However, the pendency of the same has been concealed by

the Appellant, while petition as well as the present appeal was verified at New

Delhi on the same date, i.e., May 21, 2026.

25. It is further submitted that repeated defaults have been committed by

the Appellant. At first, the lenders accepted the corporate debtor's offer of Rs.

590 crores as the base price for Swiss challenge, subject to an upfront deposit

of 59 crore, which was never deposited. During the course of the proceedings

pending before the NCLT, the Appellant resisted admission on the strength of

the very OTS, which it failed to perform. The OTS was never honoured. Before

this Appellate Tribunal on June 15, 2026, the Appellant represented that it is

was ready to deposit one-half of its offer of Rs. 631 crores, however, the same

was never deposited. On June 29, 2026, the Appellant recast the same offer

into two instalments i.e. 50% by July 9 and the balance by July 20, 2026.

Whereupon, this tribunal directed the Appellant to deposit the amounts

accordingly, without prejudice to the rights of the lenders to accept or reject

the proposal, but again no deposit was made on the aforesaid dates.

26. It is vehemently submitted that each of the offers of the Appellant was

considered and unanimously rejected on account of the Appellant's history of



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            10



defaults and acceptance or rejection of the OTS, otherwise also, lies within

the commercial wisdom of the lenders, which is non-justiciable.

27. It is further submitted that, in view of the amended Section 12A of the

Code (brought into force with effect from May 26, 2026), withdrawal of an

admitted application is permitted only on an application by the resolution

professional, with the approval of 90% of the voting share of the COC. In this

regard, a three-member bench decision of this Appellate Tribunal in Ayush

Prashant Aggarwal Versus Uma Export Limited (passed in CA (AT) Ins No.

1366 of 2026, decided on 24.08.2026) has been relied upon, wherein it is

held that the procedure for withdrawal of application for CIRP has now been

made more stringent. This is because Subsection 2 of Section 12A begins with

a non-obstante clause and states that an application admitted under Sections

7, 9, and 10 shall not be withdrawn prior to the constitution of the COC or

after the first invitation for submission of a resolution plan has been issued

by the resolution professional. Thus, when the CIRP has commenced, no

settlement or payment can bring the CIRP to an end. Otherwise, the

mechanism provided under the amended Section 12A of the Code.

28. It is further submitted that the object of the IBC is the resolution of the

corporate debtor and not a debt recovery tool. Therefore, the appeal filed

under Section 61 of the Code cannot be used as a forum for negotiating the

quantum and timing of settlement and to reopen a concluded RBI-compliant

public auction by relying on the price discovered therein with a deferred and

unfunded offer. Reliance in this regard has been laid on Swiss Ribbons

Private Limited versus Union of India, (2019) 4 SCC 17. It is therefore

requested that the appeal is liable to be dismissed and be dismissed as such.



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            11



29. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and having perused the



record, we, at the outset, notice that Learned Adjudicating Authority has



considered the judgments relied on by Learned Counsel for the parties and,



after considering Innoventive Industries Limited (Supra),RK Industries



(Supra),HPCL Biofuels Limited (Supra),Swiss Ribbons (Supra),Pioneer Urban



Land and Infrastructure Limited (Supra),Power Trust versus Bhuvan Madan



and others, Civil Appeal No. 2211 of 2024, decided on 18.02.2026 by the



Hon’ble Supreme Court summarized the legal position as under:



              “85. To summarize the above judgment, we observe as

              under: -



              a. The Code prescribes whenever a corporate debtor

              defaults on a debt that is due and payable, an insolvency

              process must be initiated. Section 3(12) defines “default” as

              non-payment of a debt which has become due and payable,

              and includes default in respect of a part or instalment

              thereof.



              b. When the financial creditor initiates the insolvency

              process for the purposes of admission, the Adjudicating

              Authority is only to ascertain the existence of a default from

              the records of the information utility or the evidence

              furnished by the financial creditor within fourteen days

              from the receipt of such application. At this stage, neither is

              a corporate debtor entitled nor is the Adjudicating Authority

              required to examine any dispute regarding the existence of

              such debt. This significantly reduces the scope of enquiry at

              the stage of a time-bound admission of an insolvency

              process by a financial creditor.



              c. The adjudicating authority is empowered only to verify

              whether a default has occurred or if a default has not

              occurred. Based upon its decision, the adjudicating

              authority must then either admit or reject an application,

              respectively. These are the only two courses of action which

              are open to the adjudicating authority in accordance with

              Section 7(5).



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            12



              d. The Adjudicating Authority is not required to go into the

              inability of a corporate debtor to pay its debt.



              e. The Code restricts the scope of enquiry for admission of

              an insolvency process by a financial creditor merely to the

              existence of default of a debt due and payable and nothing

              more.



              86. Applying the ratio of Power Trust (supra), we are of the

              view that the applicant has advanced a financial debt,

              which is in default, for an amount exceeding Rs. 1 Crore and

              that the Applicant has placed necessary proofs including

              the record of default issued by the information utility, which

              clearly indicates that the debt is in default and, therefore,

              this Application deserves to be admitted.”



30. Thus, the Learned Adjudicating Authority, after finding the due debt



and default, has ordered initiation of the CIRP against the CD.



31. We also notice that neither before the Ld. Adjudicating Authority nor



before us, the debt or the default has been disputed by the Appellant. What



has been agitated is that Respondent No. 1 is a minority lender having



approximately 9.4% share in the debt and illegal rejection of the OTS and also



illegal assignment of the debt to respondent No. 3. The Appellant has also



challenged the assignment by the consortium of lenders to Respondent No. 3



before the Honourable High Court of Bombay, and the said Writ petition is



stated to be pending till now.



32. Hon’ble Supreme Court in Innoventive Industries Limited Vs. ICICI Bank



and Another (Civil Appeals Nos. 8337-38 of 2017) held as under:



               “28. When it comes to a financial creditor triggering the process,

               Section 7 becomes relevant. Under the Explanation to Section

               7(1), a default is in respect of a financial debt owed to any

               financial creditor of the corporate debtor it need not be a debt

               owed to the applicant financial creditor. Under Section 7(2), an



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            13



               application is to be made under sub-section (1) in such form and

               manner as is prescribed, which takes us to the Insolvency and

               Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016.

               Under Rule 4, the application is made by a financial creditor in

               Form 1 accompanied by documents and records required therein.

               Form 1 is a detailed form in 5 parts, which requires particulars of

               the applicant in Part I, particulars of the corporate debtor in Part

               II, particulars of the proposed interim resolution professional in

               Part III, particulars of the financial debt in Part IV and documents,

               records and evidence of default in Part V. Under Rule 4(3), the

               applicant is to dispatch a copy of the application filed with the

               adjudicating authority by registered post or speed post to the

               registered office of the corporate debtor. The speed, within which

               the adjudicating authority is to ascertain the existence of a

               default from the records of the information utility or on the basis

               of evidence furnished by the financial creditor, is important. This

               it must do within 14 days of the receipt of the application. It is at

               the stage of Section 7(5), where the adjudicating authority is to

               be satisfied that a default has occurred, that the corporate debtor

               is entitled to point out that a default has not occurred in the sense

               that the "debt", which may also include a disputed claim, is not

               due. A debt may not be due if it is not payable in law or in fact.

               The moment the adjudicating authority is satisfied that a default

               has occurred, the application must be admitted unless it is

               incomplete, in which case it may give notice to the applicant to

               rectify the defect within 7 days of receipt of a notice from the

               adjudicating authority. Under sub-section (7), the adjudicating

               authority shall then communicate the order passed to the

               financial creditor and corporate debtor within 7 days of

               admission or rejection of such application, as the case may be.



               29. The scheme of Section 7 stands in contrast with the scheme

               under Section & where an operational creditor is, on the

               occurrence of a default, to first deliver a demand notice of the

               unpaid debt to the operational debtor in the manner provided in

               Section 8(1) of the Code. Under Section 8(2), the corporate debtor

               can, within a period of 10 days of receipt of the demand notice or

               copy of the invoice mentioned in sub-section (1), bring to the notice

               of the operational creditor the existence of a dispute or the record

               of the pendency of a suit or arbitration proceedings, which is pre-

               existing-i.e. before such notice or invoice was received by the

               corporate debtor. The moment there is existence of such a

               dispute, the operational creditor gets out of the clutches of the

               Code.



               30. On the other hand, as we have seen, in the case of a

               corporate debtor who commits a default of a financial debt, the

               adjudicating authority has merely to see the records of the

               information utility or other evidence produced by the financial



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            14



               creditor to satisfy itself that a default has occurred. It is of no

               matter that the debt is disputed so long as the debt is "due" i.e.

               payable unless interdicted by some law or has not yet become

               due in the sense that it is payable at some future date. It is only

               when this is proved to the satisfaction of the adjudicating

               authority that the adjudicating authority may reject an

               application and not otherwise.”



33. Learned Counsel for the Respondent No. 3 has also relied on M. Suresh



Kumar Reddy Vs. Canara Bank & Others (2023) 8 SCC 387 in order to



show that the Appellant cannot rely on the Vidarbha Industries Power



Limited v. Axis Bank Limited (2022) 8 SCC 352. Relevant Paragraphs of



the same is reproduced as under:



               “12. Reliance is placed on the decision of this Court in Vidarbha

               Industries and in particular, what is held therein in paras 86 to

               89 which reads thus (SCC p. 377)



                   "86. Even though Section 7(5)(a) IBC may confer discretionary

                   power on the adjudicating authority, such discretionary power

                   cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. If the facts and

                   circumstances warrant exercise of discretion in a particular

                   manner, discretion would have to be exercised in that manner.



                   87. Ordinarily, the adjudicating authority (NCLT) would have

                   to exercise its discretion to admit an application under Section

                   7 IBC and initiate CIRP on satisfaction of the existence of a

                   financial debt and default on the part of the corporate debtor

                   in payment of the debt, unless there are good reasons not to

                   admit the petition.



                   88. The adjudicating authority (NCLT) has to consider the

                   grounds made out by the corporate debtor against admission,

                   on its own merits. For example, when admission is opposed on

                   the ground of existence of an award or a decree in favour of

                   the corporate debtor, and the awarded/decretal amount

                   exceeds the amount of the debt, the adjudicating authority

                   would have to exercise its discretion under Section 7(5)(a) IBC

                   to keep the admission of the application of the financial creditor

                   in abeyance, unless there is good reason not to do so. The

                   adjudicating authority may, for example, admit the application

                   of the financial creditor, notwithstanding any award or decree,

                   if the award/decretal amount is incapable of realisation. The

                   example is only illustrative.



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            15



                   89. In this case, the adjudicating authority (NCLT) has simply

                   brushed aside the case of the appellant that an amount of Rs.

                   1730 crores was realisable by the appellant in terms of the

                   order passed by APTEL in favour of the appellant, with the

                   cursory observation that disputes if any between the appellant

                   and the Electricity Regulatory Commission were

                   inconsequential."



                                                                            (emphasis supplied)



               13. A review petition was filed by Axis Bank Ltd. seeking a

               review of the decision of Vidarbha Industries on the ground that

               the attention of the Court was not invited to the case of E.S.

               Krishnamurthy. While disposing of review petition by order dated

               22-9-2022, this Court held thus (Vidarbha Industries Power case,

               SCC p. 323, paras 6-7)



                   6. The elucidation in para 90 and other paragraphs (of the

                   judgment under review) were made in the context of the case

                   at hand. It is well settled that judgments and observations in

                   judgments are not to be read as provisions of statutes. Judicial

                   utterances and/ or pronouncements are in the setting of the

                   facts of a particular case.



                   7. To interpret words and provisions of a statute, it may

                   become necessary for the Judges to embark upon lengthy

                   discussions. The words of Judges interpreting statutes are not

                   to be interpreted as statutes."



               14. Thus, it was clarified by the order in review that the decision

               in Vidarbha Industries was in the setting of facts of the case

               before this Court. Hence, the decision in Vidarbha Industries

               cannot be read and understood as taking a view which is

               contrary to the view taken in Innoventive Industries and E.S.

               Krishnamurthy. The view taken in Innoventive Industries still

               holds good.”



34. We also notice that, though the Appellant has made various OTS



proposals and the same has been accepted also by the Respondent No. 1 but



the Appellant has failed to deposit 10% of the amount as indicated in the reply



given to the Appellant with regard to its OTS proposal. It is reflected that,



while the letter dated 04.10.2025 states that the Bank of Baroda has accepted



the OTS submitted by the Appellant on the condition of deposit of 10% of the



upfront amount stated in the OTS settlement (i.e., Rs. 59 crores), so that other



lenders can put up the proposal with their competent authority for internal



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            16



approvals. The said amount was required to be deposited by 07.10.2025.

However, as per the own admission of the Appellant, this amount was never

deposited. Significantly, the Bank of Baroda has written a communication to

the Appellant on 16 April 2026, in which it is informed that the Appellant was

advised to deposit ₹59 crores as 10% of the OTS offer amount and as the

Appellant has failed to deposit the upfront amount so far, the consortium of

lenders, in the JLM meeting held on 16 2026, has decided to reject and return

the OTS proposal. Thus, it is evident that the upfront amount of Rs. 59 crores

was not deposited by the Appellant, and therefore the lenders were not obliged

to accept the OTS in the absence of any such deposition.

35. We also notice that, at the stage of Appeal also, the Appellant has made

an offer that it is willing to pay Rs. 631 crores and also to deposit 50% of the

total amount of Rs. 631 crores. The said offer is recorded by this Appellant

Tribunal in its order dated 15th June 2026, and it was directed that the COC

may deliberate upon the offer made by the Appellant. However, when this

matter was taken up on 29.06.2026, it was informed that the COC has

rejected the said offer as the proposal was conditional. Thereafter, the

Appellant submits that the Appellant is willing to deposit the 50% of Rs. 631

crores within 10 days (by 09.07.2026) and the remaining 50% within the next

10 days (by 20.07.2026) and on the submissions made by Learned Counsel

for the Appellant, this Appellant Tribunal has passed the following order:



              4. Learned counsel for the petitioner in Sec. 7 petition, as

              well as the CoC, submitted that the CoC has viewed the

              conduct of the appellant and the manner in which he was

              dilly-dallying the recovery of money earlier and even after



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            17



              the commencement of CIRP. For them, it is sheer loss of trust

              in the appellant. Having stated thus, since the appellant is

              now offering ₹10 crores more than what the ARC has

              offered, we only require the learned counsel for the lender

              bank and the CoC to take instructions in the matter.

              5. In the meantime, we direct the appellant to deposit 50%

              of Rs. 631 crores on or before 09.07.2026 as first instalment

              and next 50% by 20.07.2026 before Registrar NCLAT. It is

              underscored that this order is made without prejudice to the

              right of the respondents to accept or reject the proposal now

              made by the appellant.



36. Thus, it is crystal clear that even this offer made by the Appellant before

this Appellate Tribunal recorded in order dated 29.06.2026, was not honoured

and the amount which was permitted by the Appellate Tribunal on the request

of Appellant was not deposited.

37. We find substance in the submissions made by the counsel for

Respondent No. 3 that the Appellant is guilty of repeated defaults. First, in

view of the OTS, which was treated as the base price for Swiss Challenge (Rs.

59 crore), it was not deposited by the Appellant during the course of the

pendency of the Section 7 petition before the Learned Adjudicating Authority.

The Appellant has enhanced its settlement amount from Rs. 590 crores to Rs.

621 crores, and it was also not honoured and lastly the commitment to

deposit Rs. 631 Crore in two tranches was also not honoured.



CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1056 of 2026

                                                            18



38. We also find substance in the submissions made by learned counsel for

the respondent No. 3 that any settlement or withdrawal, in view of the

amended Section 12A of the Code, is now permitted only following the

procedure provided therein. In this regard, the law relied on by the respondent

No. 3 (i.e., Ayush Prashant Aggarwal) (supra) may be recalled, wherein it has

been highlighted that the procedure for withdrawal of application for CIRP has

been made more stringent by the Amendment made in Section 12A of the

Code. It has also been highlighted that subsection 2 of Section 12A begins

with a non-obstante clause and states that an application admitted under

Sections 7, 9, and 10 shall not be withdrawn prior to the constitution of the

CoC or after the first invitation for submission of a resolution plan has been

issued by the Resolution Professional. Moreover, the financial creditor could

not be compelled to accept the OTS proposed by the Appellant, more so when,

on earlier occasions, the Appellant has not honoured the OTS and has not

deposited the 10% amount of the OTS within the time stipulated.

39. In view of the above facts and circumstances, we are of the considered

view that the Ld. Adjudicating Authority has not committed any mistake in

admitting the application moved by the Respondent No. 1 under Section 7 of

the Code. In result, the appeal lacks merits and is dismissed as such.

40. There is no order as to cost. The pending IA, if any, is also disposed of.
```
