```text
[Per: Justice Mohd. Faiz Alam Khan, Member (Judicial)]



         During the hearing on 13.10.2026, Learned Counsel for the

Respondents at the outset had raised a preliminary issue that the Appellants

being a shareholder is having no locus to file the appeal for challenging the

plan approved by the CoC as well as by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority.



2. We have heard Mr. Ashim Sood, Learned Counsel for the Appellant as

well as Mr. Abhijeet Sinha, Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the

Resolution Professional, Mr. Krishnendu Datta, Learned Senior Counsel for

the Respondent No.2 – Successful Resolution Applicant and Mr. Abhishek

Anand, Learned Counsel for the CoC, on the limited issue of maintainability

of the appeals and perused the record.

3. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1858 of 2026 has been filed by the

Appellants who are claiming to be the minority shareholders of the CD and as

per their contention, together hold approximately 20% of the equity share

capital of the Corporate Debtor, against the order dated 03.09.2026

(Impugned Order) passed by the Adjudicating Authority, National Company

Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench-I in IA (IBC)(PLAN) No. 42 of 2026 in CP (IB)

No. 291 of 2023, whereby the Resolution Plan dated 12.03.2026, as clarified

on 07.05.2026, submitted by Respondent No. 2, Shree Naman Developers

Private Limited (SRA), for Gstaad Hotels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)

was approved under Section 31(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,

                                                             3



2016 (Code), whereby the entire existing equity share capital of the Corporate

Debtor was extinguished and vests 100% of the equity in the SRA or its

Implementing Entity.

4. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1958 of 2026 has been filed by the

Appellants who are claiming to be the minority shareholders of the CD and as

per their contention holding approximately 10% of the equity share capital of

the Corporate Debtor arises out of the order dated 03.09.2026 (Impugned

Order) passed by the Adjudicating Authority, National Company Law

Tribunal, Mumbai Bench-I in IA (IBC)(PLAN) No. 42 of 2026 in CP (IB) No. 291

of 2023, whereby the Resolution Plan dated 12.03.2026, as clarified on

07.05.2026, submitted by Respondent No. 2, Shree Naman Developers Private

Limited (SRA), for Gstaad Hotels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor) was

approved under Section 31(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

(Code). The Resolution Plan extinguishes the entire existing equity share

capital of the Corporate Debtor for NIL consideration and vests 100% of the

equity in the SRA or its Implementing Entity.

5. Learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the Resolution Amount

of Rs. 1,611 crores exceed both the average Fair Value of Rs. 1,250.58 crores

and the average Liquidation Value of Rs. 1,028.33 crores of the Corporate

Debtor, and yet there is no computation under Section 30(2)(e) read with

Section 53(1) of the Code showing that the available value stands exhausted

before it reaches the equity shareholders and the objections raised by the

Appellants in this regard in IA No. 3877 of 2026, filed before the Adjudicating

Authority on 31.08.2026, were never heard, as the Ld. Adjudicating Authority

                                                             4



declined to defer pronouncement of the Impugned Order and thereafter

disposed of that application as has become infructuous.

6. It is further submitted that the claim of Omkara Assets Reconstruction

Private Limited, a secured financial creditor, on which the NIL value of the

equity rests, was never independently verified, although the amount payable

to Omkara rose from approximately Rs. 581.42 crores as on 31.03.2025 to

approximately Rs. 1,086.93 crores as on 08.07.2025, and interest on it has

been compounded monthly against the provisions contained in loan

documents.

7. It is further submitted that the Impugned Order is self-contradictory,

in as much as paragraph 92 of the same holds that avoidance recoveries

would accrue to the shareholders while extinguishing their shares, and

paragraph 101 of the same leaves the allocation of residual resolution money

to shareholders to be incorporated later through an updated Form H.

8. It is further submitted that the Appellants locus standi is based on right

to receive the surplus of the resolution amount under Section 53(1)(h) and

this right is available to them as soon as there is a surplus amount, after

settlement of dues, and the appellants as shareholders are then entitled to it.

In the instant case surplus amount remained even after the claim of the

financial creditors (other than related party creditors) are paid with interest

and therefore Appellants, as shareholders, have a right to that surplus

amount and are interested parties/stakeholders in the Resolution Plan and

fall within the definition of aggrieved person in view of the principle of Ubi jus

ibi remedium. Reliance in this regard has been laid on Sardar Amarjit Singh

Kalra v. Pramod Gupta, (2003) 3 SCC 272, para 33), Embassy Property

                                                             5



Developments (P) Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, (2020) 13 SCC 308, in order

to project that the Appellants have locus standi irrespective of the final

outcome of the Appeal.

9. It is further submitted that the Resolution Plan does not comply with

Section 53(1)(h) of the IBC, as it does not provide for the surplus to be

distributed to the shareholders. In this regard reference is given of Clause 11

of the Resolution Plan and it is submitted that Such violation of the

Appellants’ statutory right entitles them to take recourse under the law by

filing the appeal under Section 61 of the Code before this Appellate Tribunal

and the alleged modifications carried out by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority.

10. It is further submitted that Ld. Adjudicating Authority has materially

erred in altering the financial proposal of the CoC-approved Resolution Plan

by directing payments to related party creditors and such payments are

expressly barred by Clause 12 of the Plan which provides that no payment

shall be made under this Resolution Plan to any Person who is a Related Party

of the Corporate Debtor in respect of any Debt. Once a plan is approved under

Section 31(1), it binds all the stakeholders, and its terms cannot be modified

by the adjudicating authority, the CoC or the successful resolution applicant.

Reliance in this regard is laid on SBI v. Murari Lal Jalan & Florian Fritsch

(Consortium), (2025) 4 SCC 354, para 125), Mathuraprasad C. Pandey v.

Partiv Parikh, 2022 SCC OnLine NCLAT 1608, M.K. Rajagopalan v.

Periasamy Palani Gounder, (2024) 1 SCC 42.

11. It is further submitted that the Hon’ble Supreme Court has held in

various cases that that the expression “any person aggrieved” in Section 61

of the should be given wide interpretation. The law propounded in

                                                             6



Independent Sugar Corpn. Ltd. v. Girish Sriram Juneja, (2025) 5 SCC

209, GLAS Trust Co. LLC v. BYJU Raveendran, (2025) 3 SCC 625,

Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa v. AgriTech (India) Ltd., 2025 SCC OnLine

NCLAT 2062 and Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power and Steel Ltd.,

(2026) 6 SCC 431 were highlighted.

12. It is further submitted that the before filing this Appeal, the Appellants

wrote to the RP several times seeking a detailed break-up of the distribution

in terms of the Impugned order but no response was given and it is only when

this Appeal was filed the RP filed an affidavit of the SRA with an updated Form

H, disclosing the breakup and the surplus available to shareholders for the

first time. The Appellants were thus never given an opportunity to address the

basis on which the Impugned Order proceeds and even if it is assumed that

there is no modification of the Plan, as the Respondents contend, that does

not affect the Appellants locus standi as the moment there is a surplus,

shareholders can be aggrieved by its treatment, therefore appellant is having

every locus to challenge the plan.

13. Learned Counsel for the respondents submits that Appellants being

shareholders does not have locus to challenge the Impugned Order by way of

which the Resolution Plan has been approved under Section 31 of IBC. It is

admitted to the Appellants that they are equity shareholders of the Corporate

Debtor and being mere ‘shareholders’ they do not have any locus to challenge

an order approving the Resolution Plan. Ld. Counsels have relied on Prateek

Jain v. Anurag Nirbhaya, 2026 SCC OnLine NCLAT 1180 (Para 15), Shashi

Galada v. Nitin Vishwanath Panchal & Anr. 2025 SCC OnLine NCLAT

                                                             7



1397 and also judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in BYJU Raveendran

and of this this Appellate Tribunal in Park Energy.

14. It is for this submitted that the fact, that the Resolution Plan provides

for payment of surplus amount to all creditors and stakeholders including

shareholders cannot provide any locus to the Appellant to file an appeal, since

19. Section 61(1) of the Code provides that any person aggrieved by an order

subject to the interpretation given with regard to such provisions by the

courts.

25. In Clarion Health Food LLP v. Goli Vada Pav Pvt. Ltd. and Anr.,

continuation of CIRP would adversely affect its financial interests as majority

and after considering the statutory scheme and precedents held that the

appellant, being a shareholder of the company, was not the aggrieved party

within the meaning of the Code and has no locus to file the appeal. It was

further held that the appellant’s status as majority shareholder did not confer

standing to challenge admission of CIRP under Section 9 and that the Code

does not treat shareholders or investors as “persons aggrieved” for this

purpose.

18. Once again, the answer to the conclusion given by BYJU

Raveendran Judgment (supra) as contained in para 75,

would be similar to the one which has already been

answered by us in the preceding paragraphs. The Hon’ble

Apex Court in the para 75 above was dealing with the issue

of aggrieved person, in extension to the observation already

made in the preceding part of the Judgment of BYJU

Raveendran. The para 75 itself cannot be exclusively

extracted to be read, as if the reference made to the word

“any person or aggrieved person” as considered therein will

include shareholders because it was made in the context of

observation made in para 42 which limits the expression to

a class of creditors and therefore it would not automatically

be made applicable to the shareholders too, even if the

Judgment refers, the term ‘person aggrieved’, as “any

person” who would be affected by the order. The word

aggrieved person would be the person who is affected by

the order, would be a person who does not have any other

forum or a platform under law available to safeguard his

right or interest, arising from the proceedings which are

being held before the Tribunal. However as far as the

interest of the shareholders is concerned, it is protected by

the agent or the authority appointed by the NCLT i.e.,

Resolution Professional, or the liquidator, where the

liquidation has been ordered and the shareholders are

taken care of by the aforesaid two agents who are

appointed by the court under law. Therefore, the

proceedings at the behest of the shareholders, in their

individual capacity will not be maintainable as in case the

shareholders are permitted to maintain the proceedings

under the I & B Code, it would run contrary the very object

of the Code of timely resolution of insolvency, and would

rather be an abuse the process, in a proceeding where time

plays an important role to conclude the proceedings in a

time bound basis.



19. There is another logic though we have already observed

in the preceding paragraph by way of reiteration, it is once

again expressed that the sustainability of the proceedings

at the behest of the shareholder, would not be a reasonable

proposition, which should be judicially stamped in order to

provide avenue for the shareholders, to initiate and pursue

the proceeding under any of the provisions of the I & B Code,

particularly keeping in mind that the time frame is of a prime

relevance under the provisions of the I & B Code. If the said

object of permitting the shareholders to sustain the

                                            16



proceedings is permitted, that will run contrary to the very

object of the code itself, besides, being contrary to the

interest of the decision-making process by creating to a

multiplicity of proceedings which otherwise could have

stood closed. Further, when the interest of the shareholder

itself stands protected by the agents appointed by the

Tribunal and when as we have observed above, the status

of the shareholders being that of an investor, who have

profit interest only in the Company, and who do not have

any administrative interest or control in the exercise of

administrative functions of the Corporate Debtor, the

proceedings at their behest will not be maintainable.

particularly, when the said question was neither raised,

proceedings drawn under Section 61 or even at the stage of

Section 62 before the Hon’ble Apex Court. A lis decided

without specifically answering a legal question raised

affecting the issue of maintainability of the proceedings

cannot be taken as to as an answer, to a question, which

was a question of reference made before us about

maintainability of the proceedings at the behest of the

shareholders, which we answered that the petition at the

behest the shareholder will not be maintainable, which we

have quite elaborately dealt with in the preceding

paragraphs.

28. In Peninsula Holdings and Investments Pvt. Ltd. v. JM Financial

Credit Solutions Ltd. and Anr., (2025) ibclaw.in, the appeal under Section

61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 challenged the order dated

14.07.2025 by which the Adjudicating Authority admitted a Section 7

application filed by the financial creditor against the corporate debtor and

                                                            18



initiated CIRP, appointing an Interim Resolution Professional. The issue



before this Appellate Tribunal was as to whether the appeal under Section 61



of the Code filed by the appellant, claiming to be a shareholder and preference



shareholder of the corporate debtor, was maintainable in law. It is held that



the question whether a shareholder can maintain an appeal under Section 61



stood conclusively settled by the three-member Bench decision in Park



Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. State Bank of India, which laid down that proceedings



at the behest of a shareholder, being merely an investor with profit interest



but without administrative control or direct legal injury, are not maintainable



under the IBC, and the expression person aggrieved cannot be expanded to



include shareholders or investors. This Tribunal emphasized that permitting



shareholders to challenge insolvency orders would defeat the object of the IBC



by causing multiplicity of litigation and delay, contrary to the Code’s emphasis



on speedy resolution and finality and also that on admission of CIRP, Section



17 automatically transfers the management and control of the company to



the IRP; the board of directors and shareholders lose authority over the affairs



of the company, and the IRP/RP protects the interests of shareholders.



Paragraphs 36, 37 and 38 of the same are reproduced herein below: -



              “36. The issue of whether a shareholder can maintain an

              appeal under Section 61 of the IBC has been conclusively

              settled by a three-member Bench of this Appellate Tribunal

              in ‘Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. State Bank of India (2025 SCC

              OnLine NCLAT 1289)’. The larger Bench examined

              conflicting earlier judgments and laid down a uniform

              principle that the proceedings at the behest of a

              shareholder, being merely an investor with profit interest,

              but without administrative control or direct legal injury, are

              not maintainable under the IBC. The term ‘person aggrieved

              ’under Section 61 cannot be expanded to include

              shareholders or investors.

                                                            19



              37. The Judgement in Park Energy (Supra) also clarified

              that allowing shareholders to challenge insolvency orders

              would defeat the object of the IBC, which emphasizes

              speedy resolution and finality of proceedings. If

              shareholders were permitted to intervene or appeal, it

              would lead to multiple litigations and delays, contrary to the

              Code’s objectives.



              38. Once the Corporate Debtor is admitted into CIRP,

              Section 17 of the IBC automatically transfers the

              management and control of the company to the Interim

              Resolution Professional (IRP). The Board of Directors, and

              consequently all shareholders, lose their authority over the

              affairs of the company. The IRP/RP is the protector of the

              interests of the shareholders in such a situation. Thus, even

              if the Appellant had prior administrative control, that control

              ceased upon admission. The mere fact of holding 51%

              shares or being a “majority owner” does not confer a

              separate or superior locus under Section 61. The Appellant’s

              attempt to distinguish Park Energy (supra) on the basis of

              being a majority shareholder or holding preference shares

              cannot succeed.”

41. On the other hand, on the issue of the locus and

maintainability of the appeal, the appellant places its

reliance on Independent Sugar Corporation Limited Vs.

Girish Sriram Juneja & Ors. (2025) 5 SCC 209, para

24. Appellant claims that “any aggrieved person” appearing

in Section 62 or Section 61 of the Code must be understood

widely and not in a restricted person. The relevant para is

extracted as below:



“24. Once the CIRP is initiated, the nature of proceedings

are no longer in personam but rather become in rem. In light

of the same, the expression “any person aggrieved” in the

context of IBC has been held to be indicative of there being

no rigid locus requirements to institute an appeal

challenging an order of NCLT before NCLAT or an order of

NCLAT before this Court. Similarly, in the context of the

Competition Act, even those persons that bring to CCI

information of practices that are contrary to the provisions

of the Competition Act, could be said to be “aggrieved”.

Therefore, the term “any person aggrieved” appearing in

Section 62 IBC and Section 53-T of the Competition Act must

be understood widely and not in a restricted fashion.



25. In the present case, the appellant as an unsuccessful

resolution applicant whose resolution plan could have

otherwise been approved by CoC, satisfies the requirement

of being aggrieved. This preliminary locus standi objection

vis- à-vis the appellant, therefore, does not merit

acceptance.”



                                                        [Emphasis supplied]



42. We note that Hon’ble Supreme Court has interpreted

any aggrieved person to be not in a restricted manner but

widely as it says that “the term “any person aggrieved”

appearing in Section 62 IBC and Section 53-T of the

Competition Act must be understood widely and not in a

restricted fashion.” Countering the above arguments, the

Respondent brings to our notice para 197 of the same

judgement [Independent Sugar Corporation Limited

(supra)] and contends that the meaning of aggrieved person

should harmonise with the object of the Code. The para is

extracted below:



“42. In a few cases, the Courts have declined to be bound

by the letter when the letter frustrates the patent purposes

of the statute. The learned J.C. Shah, J. in New India Sugar

Mills Ltd. v. CST, noted that:



“… It is a recognised rule of interpretation of statutes that

the expressions used therein should ordinarily be

                                            21



understood in a sense in which they best harmonise with

the object of the statute, and which effectuate the object of

the legislature.”



The limitation of the purposive role of construction is that the

interpretation shall not result in legislation by the Court.

Hardship, inconvenience, injustice, absurdity and

anomalous results are avoided while construing the statute

they need be.



45. From the above analysis, we observe that:



(a) The aforesaid judgment of Park Energy Private

Limited (supra) pronounced on 22.07.20225 has no

application in the present case, where the Appeal arises out

of an order in the application filed by the Appellant under

Section 60(5) and Section 65 of the Code, and not an order

under Section 7 of the Code.



(b) Park Energy Private Limited (supra) also fails to

consider earlier judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in

Independent Sugar Corporation Limited (supra)

pronounced on 29.01.2025, wherein in the context of the

use of the term “aggrieved party” in the Code, has been held

that CIRP is a proceeding in rem and “any person

aggrieved” must be understood widely.



(c) Therefore, Park Energy Private Limited (supra) will

not apply to the present facts and circumstances where the

application by a related party creditor has been disguised

under Section 7 of the Code to circumvent the requirement

of approval of the shareholders contemplated under Section

10 of the Code, as has been noted by us separately

hereinafter.



(d) There is strong argument that the present transaction is

a collusive transaction between the Corporate Debtor and

the Financial Creditor, and the only person aggrieved are

the public shareholder like the Appellant.



46. We have noted the contentions of both sides and find

that the arguments presented by Respondent do not come

in the way of the Appellant to be considered as an aggrieved

person. The Code doesn’t bar the Appellant to file an appeal.

Section 61 of the Code clearly states that notwithstanding

anything to the contrary contained under the Companies

Act, 2013, “any person aggrieved” by the order of the AA

under this part may prefer an appeal to the NCLAT. The

shareholders are the Appellant in this case and they are

aggrieved by the order of the AA and interpreting the law in

its widest terms and not in a restricted manner, we come to

conclusion that the appellants have the locus to file an

                                                            22



              appeal and their appeal is maintainable. Even otherwise,

              we find that there are serious allegations of

              fraudulent initiation of CIR proceedings, which

              should be looked into by us. Accordingly, we further

              delve into the merits of the Appeal.”



                                                             (Emphasis in Bold by us)

Thus, a bench of three members, wherein one of us was also a member, after

considering Independent Sugar Corporation Limited (Supra), came to a

conclusion that the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the above-stated case has

interpreted the term "aggrieved person" in a wide manner and not in a

restricted fashion. It held that the judgment of Park Energy Private Limited

(Supra) would have no application to the facts of the said case, where the

appeal arises out of an order passed under Section 60(5) and Section 65 of

the Code, and not an order under Section 7 of the Code. It also held that Park

Energy Private Limited (Supra) fails to consider the judgment of the Hon'ble

Supreme Court passed in Independent Sugar Corporation Limited (Supra).

We find that the three-member bench in Park Energy Private Limited

(Supra) did not consider the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in

Independent Sugar Corporation Limited (Supra). However, in Independent

Sugar Corporation Limited (Supra), it was held that the expression “any

person aggrieved” in Sections 61 and 62 of the IBC and Sections 53B and 53T

of the Competition Act must be construed widely. CIRP proceedings are in

rem once initiated, and an unsuccessful resolution applicant whose plan

could otherwise have been approved satisfied the requirement of being

aggrieved. The preliminary objection on locus standi was rejected. Thus, it

was not a case pertaining to the shareholder(s).

                                                            23



30. We also notice that the principle laid down in Park Energy (Supra) has



been again applied in Prateek Jain v. Mr. Anurag Nirbhaya, Resolution



Professional & Ors., Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1496 of 2024,



decided on 30.09.2026, wherein a two member Bench of this Appellate



Tribunal held that an individual shareholder, merely by virtue of holding



shares, cannot be treated as a “person aggrieved” entitling him to maintain



an appeal under Section 61 of the Code, against an order approving a



Resolution Plan. The coordinate Bench of this Tribunal discussed the Larger



Bench decision in “Park Energy (Supra), M. K. Rajagopalan v. Periasamy



Palani Gounder”, (2024) 1 SCC 42 and Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa vs.



Agri-Tech (India) Limited and others (Supra) and held that the law laid



down in Park Energy will continue to bind this Tribunal. Relevant part of the



said judgment is reproduced as under: -



              “6. There had been various facets, which has been argued

              by the respective Counsel for the parties, but the moot

              question that falls for consideration before us is that except

              for the appellant, the plan thus approved, has already

              attained finality. The question that arises for consideration

              is that the appellant in the capacity of admittedly being a

              shareholder can maintain a company petition as against

              the impugned order of granting an approval to the

              resolution plan. The learned Counsel for the appellant

              submitted that the restrictions imposed by the Judgement

              of “Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. State Bank of India and

              another” as rendered by this Tribunal in CA (AT) (CH) (Ins)

              No.62 of 2023, that will not operate or create an absolute

              bar in maintaining the company appeal, at the behest of

              the shareholder, as against the impugned Order of

              granting approval of the resolution plan and in relation

              thereto, the learned Counsel for the appellant had referred

              to yet another judgement as rendered by this Tribunal in

              the matters of “Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa vs. Agri-

              Tech (India) Limited and others” as it was rendered in CA

              (AT) (Ins) No. 970 of 2025. He submitted that owing to the

              fact that the Judgement of Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. (supra)

                                            24



which has been decided by larger Bench upon a reference

being made in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No.62 of

2023 due to two conflicting views of two coordinate

Member Bench, since the same was considered in the

subsequent Judgment of Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa

(supra) and the coordinate Bench has carved out an

exception vide its Judgement of 15.12.2025 pertaining to

an exercise of fraud or collusion between the parties for

initiation of insolvency proceedings. There could still be an

exception where a proceeding in a company petition or in

a company appeal would be maintainable, even at the

behest of the shareholders.



7. We are afraid to accept this argument extended

by the learned Counsel for the appellant, and the

reason being that, so far as the matter pertaining to

the Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa (supra) is

concerned, though it apparently seems to have been

rendered by three Judges Bench, but that was a

regular constitution of Bench according to the

roaster assigned by Hon’ble Chairperson and mainly

that judgement has been rendered by Bench

constituting of three Members, will not have a

precedence over the Judgement rendered by three

Members answering a legal question, which has been

referred to be decided by a specially constituted

Bench of Park Energy Ltd. The reason being that the

Judgement of Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. will have the

precedence and the binding effect over the

Judgement of Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa, for the

reason that the Judgement of Park Energy Pvt. Ltd.

has been affirmed by the Hon’ble Apex Court, as the

SLP preferred against it, has been dismissed. In that

situation, where a ratio decidendi is based upon a

reference being answered by us in the matters of

Park Energy Ltd., that will have precedence and

binding effect over Judgement of Balkishan

Shrikisan Baldawa, which cannot be treated to have

been passed by a coordinate Bench of 3 Members,

because that Bench would be treated as to be a

Regular Bench in accordance with the roaster as

assigned by the Chairperson. Merely because of the

fact that it was constituted by the three Members,

that will not have a superseding or binding effect

over and above the ratio answered in the judgement

of Park Avenue Pvt. Ltd. (supra). Because the

constitution of 3 Member Bench in the matters of

Balkishan Shrikisan Baldawa, would be treated to

be the regular Bench, not a larger Bench constituted

                                                            25



              by special order to answer a question. And that too

              when the Park Avenue Pvt. Ltd. (supra), was carried

              unanimously by a Bench having two Judicial

              Members and a Technical Member, answering the

              limits of rights of a shareholder to traverse to the

              proceedings under the Code, alleging to be aggrieved

              person.”



                                                                       (Emphasis by Us)



31. Therefore, the Co-ordinate bench Prateek Jain (Supra) distinguishes

the law laid down by a three-member bench in Balkishan (Supra) on the

grounds that:



         (i)The judgment in Park Energy Private Limited is a judgment by a three-

         member bench on a reference made to it, as there were two conflicting

         judgments of equal strength of benches. The judgment of Park Energy

         Private Limited has been affirmed by the Hon'ble Apex Court, as the

         SLP filed against it has been dismissed.



         (ii)The judgment in Balkishan cannot be treated to have been passed by

         a coordinate bench of three members, as it was a regular bench before

         which the case was placed according to the roster as assigned by the

         Chairperson.



         (iii)The constitution of the three-member bench in Balkishan was

         comprising of two judicial members and a technical member, and also

         that the bench in Park Energy Private Limited was constituted by

         special order to answer a question.



32. Thereafter the Coordinate Bench in Prateek (Supra) after considering

the law laid down in Park Energy, M/s Clarion Health Food LLP v. Goli

                                                            26



Vada Pav Pvt. Ltd., Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No.1522 of 2023, and GLAS



Trust Company LLC v. BYJU Raveendran & Ors., (2024 SCC OnLine SC



3032 held as under: -



              “15. Exclusively, owing to the fact that, the appellant is a

              shareholder, the company appeal at his behest against an

              order of approval of the resolution plan, would not be

              maintainable, as he will not be or even treated to be an

              aggrieved person as per the judgement of Park Energy Pvt.

              Ltd. (supra). Hence, the company appeal held to be not

              maintainable at the behest of the appellant. The same is

              accordingly dismissed.”



33. We may not be in agreement, the manner in which the law laid down



by a three-member judgment of this Appellate Tribunal in Bala Kishan (Supra)



has been perceived in Prateek (Supra), however, this would not affect our view



with regard to the fact that Appellants being simpliciter shareholders are not



having any locus to challenge the Resolution Plan. So far as the distinction



which has been carved out by three members' judgment in Balkishan



Shrikishan Baldaava (Supra), we leave it the same to be discussed at an



appropriate time in an appropriate case as in the case at hand we do not find



any element of fraud or malicious proceedings.



34. Thus, it is evident from the aforementioned case laws that a shareholder

simpliciter may not be aggrieved by the approval of the resolution plan by the

COC or even by the adjudicating authority, and thus he cannot maintain an

appeal, only in the role of a simpliciter shareholder. The mere fact, as

submitted by learned counsel for the Appellants, that the Resolution Plan

provides a residual amount to the equity shareholders will not alter the legal

position. The residual interest of equity is purely consequential upon the

distribution decided by the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom.

Receipt of a residual amount does not enlarge the statutory standing of a

shareholder so as to enable him to maintain an appeal under Section 61. The

                                                            27



grievance that the residual amount might have been higher is not a ground

that may convert a shareholder into a “person aggrieved”. The limited scrutiny

that the Adjudicating Authority is required to undertake under Section 31 of

the Code is confined to examining whether the Plan complies with the

requirements of Section 30(2). That scrutiny is not open to re-examination at

the instance of a person who lacks locus under Section 61. Maintainability is

a threshold jurisdictional issue. Once it is held that the Appellants are not

persons aggrieved, this Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to embark upon

a merit’s examination of the Plan at their instance.

35. In view of the consistent view of this Appellate Tribunal in the above

mentioned cases i.e. Ravi Shankar Vedam (affirmed by the Hon’ble

Supreme Court), M/s Clarion Health Food LLP, Park Energy (As per the

Judgment in Prateek Jain, SLP filed against it was dismissed) and the

subsequent reaffirmation of this principle in Prateek Jain, we hold that the

Appellants, being only in the role of shareholders of the Corporate Debtor,

have no locus standi to maintain the present Appeals under Section 61 of the

Code.

36. The Appeals are accordingly dismissed as not maintainable. All

pending applications stand disposed of. There shall be no order as to costs.



                                                                   [Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan]

                                                                                                  Member (Judicial)



                                                                                                    [Naresh Salecha]

                                                                                               Member (Technical)

 sr


```

```text
Present :      : Mr. T.K. Bhaskar, Ms. Anusha Peri &

                                  ORDER

                             (Hybrid Mode)



[Per: Justice N. Seshasayee, Member (Judicial)]



05.11.2026: These twin appeals were preferred by the personal

guarantors who face a proceeding under Section 95 of IBC.



2. These petitions under Section 95 of IBC are filed through a

resolution professional as has been provided in Section 95 and his

appointment was eventually confirmed under Section 97 of IBC. The

resolution professional also has filed his report under Section 99 of IBC.

In his report, the resolution professional has recommended initiation of

PIRP against the appellants herein. The appellants have filed separate

replies in their separate petitions and the petitions are being heard by

the Adjudicating Authority.



3. Be that as it may. On 16.03.2025 the resolution professional

passed away and for few months this fact was not brought to the notice



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 591 & 592 / 2026          Page 2 of 6

of the Tribunal. Indeed, according to the appellants, it was they who

informed the tribunal about the passing away of the resolution

professional. It is in these circumstances, the financial creditor have

moved IA No.396/2024 proposing a new resolution professional to be

appointed. Even though, the Adjudicating Authority posted the matter

on few days in January - February, 2026, no final decision has been

taken on the appointment of resolution professional to replace the one

who has passed away. Indeed, the appellants resists the appointment

of the successor resolution professional who Bank of Baroda, the

financial creditor, has recommended, essentially because according to

him this resolution professional has been suspended by IBBI. He adds

that even though this order of suspension has been stayed by the

Hon’ble High Court of Gujarat yet he has not come clean as yet.



4. The learned counsel for the appellant would submit that without

a resolution professional to defend the action, the Adjudicating

Authority has kept that issue aside and is focusing in concluding the

hearing on the matter. Given the fact that it is the resolution

professional who has initiated the proceeding, on his demise there is

none to prosecute the petition. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority

has seriously prejudiced with the hearing on Section 95 petition without

there being anybody to represent the petitioner.



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 591 & 592 / 2026  Page 3 of 6

5. Mr. Edward James takes notice for the Bank of Baroda / the sole

respondent herein. Arguing for the respondent, Mr. P.H. Arvindh

Pandian, the learned senior counsel, would submit that the role of the

resolution professional in the context is no more than an authorisee of

the Bank of Baroda. Even in the petition filed by Bank of Baroda

through the resolution professional, and it is not the resolution

professional who has filed the petition in his name. Again, in the

verification portion, the resolution professional states that he has been

authorized by the Bank of Baroda to prefer the petition. He adds that

given the circumstances, the resolution professional is only an

authorisee of the financial creditor and he has no personal interest in

the action he has initiated. He submits that the entire exercise now

staged before this tribunal is intended to delay the conclusion of the

proceedings.



6. We have little hesitation in holding that we are least impressed by

the stance adopted by the appellants that the financial creditor has

chosen to institute the petition under Section 95 through the resolution

professional is but a statutory facility provided to it. At no point the

resolution professional claims any interest in the cause of action that

has given rise to the institution of the petition under Section 95. This

apart, the resolution professional himself makes a statement in the

verification column that he has been authorized by Bank of Baroda, and



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 591 & 592 / 2026  Page 4 of 6

Bank of Baroda also makes a statement at the opening page of the

petition that it is filing the petition through the resolution professional.



7. Secondly, a report of the resolution professional under Section 99

of the IBC is no more than recommendatory in its utility. At the end of

the day, the appellants have to defend the action proposed against them

on the strength of their defence.



8. Turning to the appointment of a resolution professional with

suspected integrity or whatever of which we do not have much clarity,

we wonder why Bank of Baroda should insist and persist with the one

whose name apparently has not been cleared by the court. There are

any number of resolution professionals, and the Bank of Baroda should

have considered the issue even when the resistance has come in the

first instance. After all, it is the stance adopted by the Bank of Baroda

that has given rise to this situation in a way.



9. The learned counsel for Bank of Baroda would now submit that

he would advise his client appropriately not to insist on someone whose

conduct has not yet been cleared by the courts of law in this country. If

Bank of Baroda propose any new resolution professional, the

Adjudicating Authority may consider the same, and if not we require the

Adjudicating Authority to appoint a resolution professional of his choice

so that situation such as this do not arise.



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 591 & 592 / 2026  Page 5 of 6

10. In conclusion, we do not find any merit in these appeals. Hence,

the appeals are dismissed.



                                                                    [Justice N. Seshasayee]

                                                                        [Jatindranath Swain]
```

```text
BEFORE THE MADURAI BENCH OF MADRAS HIGH COURT

                    RESERVED ON: 28.10.2026

      THE HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K.KUMARESH BABU

T.Kuthalingam                                                             ..Petitioner(s)



                                           Vs

4. C.Arulraj



5. M.Jayaraj



                                                                          ..Respondent(s)



PRAYER: Writ Petition, filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of

India, praying this court to issue a Writ of Certiorarified Mandamus

calling for the records to the impugned refusal check slip issued by the 2nd

respondent in RFL/Surandai/109/2026 dated 02.06.2026 to quash the

same as illegal, arbitrary and unconstitutional and direct the 2nd

respondent to register the petitioner’s settlement deed dated 02.06.2026

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                 WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



relating to the property measuring to an total extent of 24 cents in Survey

No.407B/2, Re-Surevy No.407B/2A1 Surandai-1 Village,

Veerakelamputhur Taluk, Tenkasi District and consequential direction to

the 2nd respondent to efface/delete the adverse attachment entry of the 5th

respondent relating to the above said property in the Encumbrance

Certificate within the limited time in the light of the order passed by the

Hon’ble Division Bench of this High Court in W.P.(MD)No.674 of 2023

dated 31.08.2023.



                                 For Petitioner  :Mr.I.Abrar Mohamed Abdullah

                                 For R1 and R2   :Mr.S.Venkatesh

                                                 Additional Government Pleader

                                 For R3          :Mr.C.Karthik

                                 For R4          :No appearance

                                 For R5          :Mr.A.Balakrishnan



                                       ORDER



       The present Writ Petition has been filed in the nature of a Writ of

Certiorarified Mandamus challenging the impugned refusal check slip

issued by the second respondent, dated 02.06.2026 and for a

consequential direction to direct the second respondent to delete the

adverse attachment entry of the fifth respondent relating to the subject

property in the encumbrance certificate.



                                                                                          __________



                                                                                          Page 2 of 9



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis                  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                                     WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



2. Heard the learned Counsel on either side.



       3. The learned Counsel for the petitioner would submit that the

fourth respondent had owned immovable properties, which were

mortgaged with the third respondent through execution of memorandum

of deposit of title deed. The said loan was declared as non-performing

asset and proceedings were issued under the SARFAESI Act, in which

the properties were brought under auction and the petitioner had

purchased the same by offering a valid sale consideration. He would

further submit that pursuant to which, a sale certificate was also issued

and he is in peaceful possession and enjoyment of the property.



       4. While that be so, a settlement deed was sought to be executed by

the petitioner in favour of his son and when the same was presented for

registration, the impugned refusal check slip had been issued by

indicating that the property was the subject matter of an attachment in a

civil suit. He would further submit that the properties, which were the

subject matter of mortgage by way of memorandum of deposit of title

deeds, had been sold in a public auction and that there would be a priority

of claim over the said property, which had been reiterated by Hon'ble

Division Benches of this Court and had relied upon the following



                                                                          __________



                                                                          Page 3 of 9



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                                               WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



judgments of the Hon'ble Division Bench of this Court in support of his

contentions:



       1)W.P.(MD)No.674 of 2023, dated 31.08.2023 in the case of

Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company Limited -vs.-

District Registrar, Registration Department and others;



       2)W.P.(MD)No.28500 of 2022, dated 02.08.2023 in the case of

M/s.Siva Automative Trading Private Limited -vs.- the Sub Registrar,

Othakadai Sub Registrar Office and others; and



       3) 2023 SCC OnLine Mad 8940 in the case of Cholamandalam

Investment and Finance Company Limited -vs.- District Registrar,

Registration Department and others.



       5. Hence, he would submit that the impugned refusal check slip

issued for a property which was the subject matter of the sale certificate

that had been registered with the Registration Department by relying

upon an earlier mortgage was wholly ill-founded and therefore, seeks

indulgence of this Court.



       6. The learned Counsel for the 5th respondent would submit that the

fourth respondent had borrowed money from the fifth respondent under a



                                                                          __________



                                                                          Page 4 of 9



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                                               WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



promissory note and that the fifth respondent had instituted a suit against

the fourth respondent, in which a decree came to be passed and further,

inter alia pending the suit, an interim attachment had also been made. He

would submit that the subject property was also the subject matter of

execution petition and in the said execution petition, two cents of lands

have also been sold to a third party for a full satisfaction of the decreetal

amount and in that regard, he would submit that a third party interest had

been created and the said third party also ought to have been made as a

necessary party in this Writ Petition. He would submit that therefore, the

petitioner cannot claim any exclusive right in execution of a settlement

deed in favour of his son and hence, he prays to dismiss this Writ

Petition.



       7. The learned Government Advocate submit that since there is a

pre-existing mortgage, the petitioner cannot be permitted to execute a

document, which would create multiplicity of proceeding and hence,

prays this Court to uphold the order impugned in this Writ Petition.



       8. I have carefully considered the submissions made on either side

and perused the materials available on record.



                                                                          __________



                                                                          Page 5 of 9



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                                               WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



       9. There is no dispute as regards to the mortgage created by the

fourth respondent in favour of the third respondent. The said mortgage

was supported by a deposit of title deed on various dates starting from

2009 to 2017. This had created a pre-existing right with the third

respondent. Even though the contention of learned Counsel for the

petitioner that there would be priority of right of a mortgaged property in

view of Section 26E of the SARFAESI Act, as interpreted by the Hon'ble

Division Benches of this Court in the judgments relied upon by the

petitioner, referred supra, it is further to be noted that an interim

attachment in a pending civil suit will also not extinguish a pre-existing

right created by a registered document. This is explicit from the

provision of Section 64(2) of CPC r/w Order 38 Rule 10 CPC.



       10. Hence, this Court is of the view that the third respondent Bank,

which had a pre-existing right by way of memorandum of deposit of title

deeds in support of its mortgage, read with Section 26E of the

SARFAESI Act, has priority. It is therefore discernible that the order of

attachment relied upon by the second respondent for issuing the

impugned refusal check slip is wholly erroneous.



                                                                          __________



                                                                          Page 6 of 9



https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis  ( Uploaded on: 05/11/2026 09:45:10 am )

                                                                               WP(MD) No. 19335 of 2026



       11. That apart, admittedly, when the suit had been decreed ex parte

and an execution petition had also been terminated, the sale of a portion

of the property cannot whittle out the pre-existing right with the third

respondent in view of the discussion supra. Further, it is to be noted that

the suit was based upon a promissory note executed on 01.07.2018. From

the decree of the Court below, it could also been seen that the plaint was

presented on 13.08.2018, wherein, the fourth respondent remained ex

parte. Further, it is also to be noted that the suit had been filed within a

period of 43 days from the date of execution of the promissory note and

the conduct of the fourth respondent remaining ex parte would only drive

this Court to the conclusion that the suit was filed in a collusive manner

only to defeat the rights of the third respondent. It is for the third party to

work out his remedy against the fourth and fifth respondents, as this

Court is of the view that the sale in the execution proceeding had also

been only pursuant to a collusive suit filed by the fifth respondent as

against the fourth respondent. In that regard, this Court has no hesitation

in setting aside the order impugned in this Writ Petition.



       12. Accordingly, this Writ Petition stands allowed and the

impugned refusal check slip issued by the second respondent, dated
```

```text
Heard Dr. Ashok Saraf, learned Senior counsel assisted by Mr. A Kaushik,



learned counsel for the petitioner.



2. The petitioner before this court is aggrieved by the initiation of



proceedings by the NCLT at the instance of the operational creditor namely



private respondent No. 1. The private respondent No. 1 had carried out certain



supplies of Stone chips and stone dust for an amount of ₹3,96,96,415.00 to the



petitioner. According to Respondent No. 1, the present petitioner defaulted in



releasing the payments for the supplies made by the respondent No. 1. Being



aggrieved, the private respondent No. 1 initiated proceedings under Section 9



under the IBC before the NCLT, Guwahati.



3. The learned senior counsel for the petitioner submits that in terms of the



prescribed procedure, prior to invocation of Section 9, notice(s) are to be issued



by the operational creditor, namely the private respondent No. 1. The learned



senior counsel for the petitioner submits that from a perusal of the pleadings



enclosed, it is clear that the notices as contemplated under section 8 was issued

                                                                                                            Page No.# 3/6



by the power of attorney holder and not by the operational creditor. He further

submits by referring to the relevant documents enclosed to the petition it is

clear that this power of attorney holder had issued the notice dated 15/7/2025,

which is enclosed as Annexure VI to the writ petition. The further submission of

the learned senior counsel for the petitioner is that this notice was issued by the

power of attorney holder well prior to the power of attorney holder being

conferred with such powers by due execution of a notary affidavit. Referring to

the notary affidavit enclosed to the writ petition, which is available at page 242

of the petition, it is submitted by the learned senior counsel that the notary

affidavit was executed on 14/9/2025. It is therefore submitted that on the date

when the notice on 15/7/2025 was issued purportedly by the power of attorney

holder on behalf of the private respondent No. 1, there was no power conferred

by the respondent No. 1 on the said power of attorney holder. The Notary

affidavit was executed on 14.09.2026. The learned senior counsel therefore

submits that without issuance of the mandatory notice as provided for in the

scheme of the IBC, the proceedings were initiated under Section 9 before the

NCLT.

4. The learned senior counsel for the petitioner submits that upon initiation of

the proceedings before the NCLT and upon receipt of the notice, the petitioner

had approached the authorities by filing an application seeking disclosure of all

documents including the vouchers and bills, which came to be rejected by order

dated 28th of October 2026. This application was filed in the company petition

filed by the Operational Director under Section 9, which has already been

admitted by the Tribunal. It is submitted by the learned senior counsel that a

bare reading of the orders passed by the NCLT, it is clear that the respondent

No. 1 is a student and the proprietorship firm is run by his father Mr. Tayo

                                                                                                            Page No.# 4/6



Taloom and the power of attorney holder Mr. Sonjib Gogoi. The learned senior

counsel therefore submits that the impugned order dated 28.10.2026 as well as

the order dated 28/10/2026, passed in CP (IB)/25/GB/2025, whereby the

company petition filed by the respondent no. 1 stood admitted and the initiation

of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Proceedings were ordered against the

petitioner under Section 9 of the Code, read with Rule 6 of the Insolvency and

Bankruptcy Rule 2016 is with utter disregard to the mandatory provisions of the

statute. It is submitted that where the very initiation of the proceedings is

contrary to the provisions prescribed under IBC, the NCLT Guwahati ought to

have taken into account the objections raised by the petitioner calling for the

complete documents to be placed before the Court and instead the proceedings

were admitted and thereafter the IA filed by the petitioner had also been

rejected.

5. On a pointed query by the Court with regard to the availability of adequate

alternative remedy as specified under the code itself by filing an appropriate

appeal before the NCLAT, the learned senior counsel for the petitioner submits

that where the very initiation of the proceedings are contrary to the enshrined

provisions of the IBC and thereby a question of law arises, the powers of a

constitutional Court are not curtailed in examining matters of this nature where

the Tribunal has failed to take into account the relevant provisions of the statute

particularly the fact that the proper notice as required under the IBC, had not

been issued and also in view of the fact that the relevant documents, the

vouchers on which the claims are made, are not submitted to the petitioner

under the notice nor placed before the tribunal and notwithstanding that the

tribunal proceeded to initiate the CIRP and had appointed the resolution

professional against the respondent No. 3.

                                                                                                            Page No.# 5/6



6. It is also submitted by the learned senior counsel for the petitioner that

the name of the private respondent stood altered subsequently by filing

necessary affidavit whereas the application before the NCLT was filed in the

erstwhile name of the respondent. He has referred to the judgment of Union of

India Vs. Parashtom Dass, reported in (2025) 5 SCC 786 wherein the apex court

has held that availability of alternative remedy is not a complete bar for

entertaining proceedings under the IBC Code under 226, where question of law

is required to be decided.

7. Having heard the counsel for the parties, learned proxy counsel has

entered appearance on behalf of Mr. K. Sharma, learned CGC has submitted

before the court that he is indisposed and is not available.

8. Considering the urgency expressed by the counsel to the petitioner and

upon due consideration of the submissions of the counsel for the petitioner that

the initiation of proceedings as contemplated under the IBC is hit because of

non-fulfillment of the mandatory provisions prescribed under Sections 7, 8, 9

and also in view of the fact that the production of documents as sought for by

the petitioner by filing an IA stood rejected after the company petition stood

admitted, prima facie it appears to the court that the NCLT ought to have duly

considered the IA prior to admitting the company petition and ordering the CIRP

and appointment of the interim resolution professional. In addition to the

defence projected by the petitioner as a party before the NCLT that the

procedure prescribed including issuance of proper notice under the IBC

proceedings had not been adhered to by the applicant before the NCLT.

9. Having heard the learned senior counsel for the petitioner and upon

perusal of the writ petition before this court and also upon carefully noting the

law relied upon, this court is of the view that at this stage the matter requires

                                                                                                            Page No.# 6/6



examination, keeping the question of maintainability is open to be decided at

the time of admission.

10. Let Notice be issued, returnable in four weeks.

11. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent No. 4 accepts notice,

therefore, notices are waived. However, extra copies be furnished within one

week from today.

12. Steps be taken by Speed post on respondents No. 1 to 3 within one week

from today.

13. Matter be listed for admissions on 11.12.2026. Issue notice on the interim

prayer, returnable on the same date.

14. The proceedings before the NCLT initiated under company petition and the

orders dated 28.10.2026 passed in CP (IB)/25/GB/2025 and

IA(IBC)225/GB/2026 shall remain stayed till the next date of listing.
```
