                  J U D G E M E N T

                      (04.11.2026)



NARESH SALECHA, MEMBER (TECHNICAL)

1. There are two appeals in the present case. We are taking both the appeals

together. The appeals have been filed by the Appellants i.e., Amarendra Financial

Pvt. Ltd. and Dinkar Commercial Private Limited, who are the Non-Banking

Financial Companies under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,

2016 (‘Code’) against the Order dated 16.07.2026 ("Impugned Order") passed

by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi ("Adjudicating

Authority") dismissing IA-06/2023 in CP (IB) No. 2060(PB)/2019 and IA-

05/2023 in CP (IB) No.2061(PB)/2019



       Cynosure Real Estates Private Limited, who is the Corporate Debtor, is the

Respondent herein.



                  Page 2 of 31

2. The Appellants submitted that they are Non-Banking Financial Companies

(NBFCs) incorporated under the Companies Act and engaged in extending short-

term liquidity loans. In April 2017, the Respondent approached the Appellants

seeking urgent financial assistance, pursuant to which the following amounts

were disbursed: -



   • In the appeal arising from CP (IB) No. 2061(PB)/2019, DCPL disbursed

       Rs. 2.30 crore, comprising Rs. 2 crores on 03.04.2017 and Rs. 30 lakhs on

       06.04.2017



   • In the appeal arising from CP (IB) No. 2060(PB)/2019, AFPL disbursed

       Rs. 1.70 crore, comprising Rs. 1.50 crore on 05.04.2017 and Rs. 20 lakhs

       on 06.04.2017



The Appellants relied upon their respective bank statements evidencing the

disbursements and submitted that the Respondent failed to service the debt or

make any repayment, thereby compelling them to initiate proceedings under

Section 7 of the code.

3. The Appellants contended that, in its common reply affidavit dated

09.10.2019 filed in the original Section 7 proceedings, the Respondent denied

having availed any loan and asserted that no financial debt existed and that the

Appellants were not financial creditors. According to the Appellants, this denial

was materially inconsistent with the Respondent's own financial records, which

recorded the relevant amounts under the head “Unsecured Loans.” The

Appellants submitted that the Respondent's denial of the loan transaction, despite



                                                      Page 3 of 31

the entries in its own records, constituted the foundation of the fraud and

misrepresentation pleaded in the recall proceedings.

4. The Appellants submitted that the Original Dismissal Order dated

19.04.2022 dismissed the Section 7 petitions, inter alia, on the reasoning that

mere disbursement of an amount did not constitute financial debt under Section

5(8) of the code. The Appellants thereafter filed IA-05/2023 and IA-06/2023

under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, seeking recall of the said order on the

grounds of fraud and misrepresentation, in addition to their grievance regarding

the application of law in the original proceedings.

5. The Appellants submitted that the Respondent's unaudited balance sheet

for FY 2017–18 had already been placed on record during the original Section 7

proceedings by way of rejoinders dated 24.01.2022 in CP (IB) No.

2061(PB)/2019 and 18.01.2022 in CP (IB) No. 2060(PB)/2019, respectively. The

Respondent did not dispute the authenticity of the said balance sheet or the

correctness of the relevant entries. The balance sheet recorded Rs. 24,62,80,069

under “Unsecured Loans” in Short-Term Borrowings. The corresponding

schedule contained a break-up of the unsecured loans, including the amounts

attributed to the respective Appellants. The Appellants contended that this was an

express acknowledgment in the Respondent's own financial records and directly

contradicted its sworn denial that no loan had been taken.

6. The Appellants further submitted that the Respondent's Income Tax Return

(ITR) for Assessment Year 2018–19 independently corroborated the entries in



                                                      Page 4 of 31

the aforesaid balance sheet. The ITR reflected the corresponding amount of Rs.

24,62,80,069 under “Other Loans and Advances”, as reproduced in the

Memoranda of Appeal. The Appellants contended that the identical aggregate

figures appearing in the balance sheet and the ITR, read with the detailed schedule

identifying the loans, established that the amounts advanced by the Appellants

had been acknowledged in the Respondent's own records. The Appellants relied

upon these documents cumulatively and not merely upon the bank statements

evidencing the transfers.

7. The Appellants submitted that the ITR for AY 2018–19 was discovered

and placed on record during the Rule 11 proceedings by affidavits dated

22.02.2023. According to the Appellants, the ITR had not been available in the

public domain and was within the Respondent's exclusive knowledge and

custody. It had not been disclosed during the original Section 7 proceedings. The

Appellants contended that the subsequent production of the ITR independently

corroborated the balance sheet already on record and demonstrated the material

inconsistency between the Respondent's own financial disclosures and its

affidavit dated 09.10.2019.

8. The Appellants further contended that the Respondent had not filed audited

balance sheets for FY 2017–18 or subsequent financial years with the Registrar

of Companies, as reflected in its MCA master data, which recorded its status as

“ACTIVE Non-Compliant.” They submitted that this continuing statutory non-

compliance prevented the Appellants from accessing the Respondent's audited



                                                      Page 5 of 31

financial records through the public domain and must be considered alongside the

subsequent discovery of the ITR. The Appellants accordingly alleged that the

Respondent had withheld material information concerning the liabilities which it

had itself recorded as unsecured loans.

9. The Appellants submitted that the Respondent's affidavit dated 09.10.2019

denying the existence of any loan or financial debt was irreconcilable with its

unaudited balance sheet for FY 2017–18 and its ITR for AY 2018–19. They

contended that the inconsistency was material because the Respondent's denial of

the financial-creditor relationship formed a central part of its defence in the

original proceedings, while the financial records expressly categorised the

relevant advances as unsecured loans. According to the Appellants, the

Respondent's failure to disclose the ITR during the original proceedings, coupled

with its failure to file audited financial statements with the Registrar of

Companies, must be considered alongside the sworn denial and the documentary

acknowledgment of the loans. The Appellants therefore alleged that the Original

Dismissal Order had been procured through misrepresentation of material facts,

resulting in a gross failure of justice.

10. The Appellants relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in

Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority v. Prabhjit Singh Soni &

Anr., 2024 INSC 102, wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court recognised the

inherent power of the NCLT to recall its order under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules,

2016, including where an order has been obtained by misrepresentation of facts



                                                      Page 6 of 31

or by playing fraud upon the Tribunal, resulting in a gross failure of justice. The

Appellants submitted that the Adjudicating Authority itself acknowledged this

legal position in paragraphs 5 and 6 of the Impugned Order, observing that the

NCLT possesses the inherent power of recall and that an order obtained by fraud

ought to be recalled. They contended that, having accepted the applicable legal

principle, the Adjudicating Authority nevertheless failed to examine whether the

documentary evidence in the present case satisfied the recognised ground for

recall.

11. The Appellants further relied upon Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T.

Venkatasubramanian & Ors., CA (AT) (Ins.) 729 of 2020, decided by a five-

member Bench of this Appellate Tribunal on 25.05.2023, which was affirmed by

the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Union Bank of India v. Financial Creditors of

M/s Amtek Auto Ltd. & Ors., Civil Appeal No. 4620 of 2023, decided on

31.07.2023. They also relied upon S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu (Dead) by L.Rs.

v. Jagannath (Dead) by L.Rs. & Ors., (1994) 1 SCC 1, and A.V. Papayya Sastry

& Ors. v. Government of A.P. & Ors., (2007) 4 SCC 221, in support of the

proposition that fraud vitiates judicial proceedings and that a party cannot be

permitted to retain the benefit of an order obtained by suppressing material facts.

The Appellants contended that these principles required the Adjudicating

Authority to examine the alleged false statement and the documents contradicting

it, rather than dismissing the recall applications without addressing the specific

evidence.



                                                      Page 7 of 31

12. The Appellants also relied upon United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v.

Rajendra Singh & Ors., (2000) 3 SCC 581, in support of their submission that a

court or tribunal is not powerless to recall an order obtained through fraud or

misrepresentation affecting the very basis of the claim. They contended that Rule

11 was invoked not to secure a rehearing merely because the Appellants were

dissatisfied with the Original Dismissal Order, but to remedy the alleged

procurement of that order through a materially false denial contradicted by the

Respondent's own financial records.

13. The Appellants contended that the Impugned Order dated 16.07.2026

failed to deal with the substance of the fraud pleaded in IA-05/2023 and IA-

06/2023. The Adjudicating Authority recorded that there was “nothing

whatsoever” to suggest that the Original Dismissal Order had been obtained by

fraud and observed that allegations of fraud were easy to make but difficult to

substantiate. The Appellants submitted that these observations did not constitute

a reasoned adjudication of their case, which was supported by the Respondent's

unaudited balance sheet and ITR, rather than by bald assertions alone.

14. The Appellants submitted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to refer to

or analyse either the unaudited balance sheet for FY 2017–18 or the ITR for AY

2018–19 while rejecting the allegation of fraud. They contended that the

Impugned Order did not explain why the entries recording the loans as unsecured

loans were insufficient to warrant examination of the Respondent's sworn denial.

According to the Appellants, a finding that fraud had not been established could



                                                      Page 8 of 31

not properly be returned without considering the very documents relied upon to

establish it. The failure to engage with this material, they submitted, demonstrated

non-application of mind and rendered the rejection of the recall applications

unsustainable.

15. The Appellants further contended that the Adjudicating Authority

incorrectly relied upon the Appellants' alleged inability to produce cogent

evidence in the original Section 7 proceedings, without separately adjudicating

whether the Respondent had procured the Original Dismissal Order through fraud

or misrepresentation. They submitted that the original determination of the

sufficiency of evidence and the subsequent examination of an allegation that the

order itself had been procured by fraud were distinct matters. The Rule 11

proceedings required consideration of the alleged false statement, the

contemporaneous financial records already placed on record and the ITR

subsequently produced. By reverting to the Appellants' alleged failure to establish

their case in the original proceedings, the Adjudicating Authority, according to

the Appellants, left the central issue of fraud unexamined.

16. The Appellants submitted that the aforesaid failure was particularly

material because the Adjudicating Authority had already accepted the legal

proposition that an order obtained by fraud could be recalled. They contended

that the Authority ought to have applied that principle to the specific facts and

documents placed before it and recorded reasons for accepting or rejecting the

allegation. The Appellants maintained that the Impugned Order, by declining to



                                                      Page 9 of 31

engage with the documentary evidence while rejecting the allegation in general

terms, failed to discharge the duty arising in the exercise of its recall jurisdiction

and warranted appellate interference.

17. The Appellants challenged the observation in paragraph 5 of the Impugned

Order that the bank statements showed purported transfers but were vague

because they did not disclose the nature of the transfers as loans. They submitted

that the bank statements could not properly be examined in isolation from the

Respondent's own financial records. The unaudited balance sheet for FY 2017–

18 specifically recorded the relevant amounts under “Unsecured Loans”, while

the ITR for AY 2018–19 independently corroborated the aggregate amount.

According to the Appellants, these documents directly addressed the very

question which the Adjudicating Authority considered unresolved from the bank

statements.

18. The Appellants contended that the characterisation of the transfers as

unsecured loans was not merely an assertion made by the Appellants for the

purposes of litigation, but was reflected in the Respondent's own financial

records, the authenticity and correctness of which, according to the Memoranda

of Appeal, had not been disputed. They submitted that the finding of vagueness

was reached without considering the cumulative evidentiary effect of the bank

statements, the balance sheet and the ITR. Consequently, the Appellants

maintained that the finding proceeded on an incomplete consideration of the



                                                     Page 10 of 31

record and could not sustain the rejection of their case without an examination of

the corroborative documents.

19. Without prejudice to their principal submission concerning fraud, the

Appellants contended that the reasoning adopted in paragraph 5 of the Impugned

Order was contrary to the applicable judicial precedents on the interpretation of

“financial debt” under Section 5(8) of the code. They relied upon Orator

Marketing Pvt. Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz Pvt. Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 2231 of 2021,

submitting that the definition of financial debt is expansive and does not expressly

exclude even an interest-free loan. They further relied upon BDH Industries Ltd.

v. Mars Remedies Private Limited, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 936

of 2020, decided on 07.02.2022, wherein the NCLAT held that the Code does not

prescribe the compulsory existence of an express agreement to establish a loan

and its disbursement.

20. The Appellants also relied upon Nishit B. Patel v. Good Value Financial

Services Pvt. Ltd., Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 936 of 2020, as cited

in the Memoranda of Appeal, in support of their submission that the existence of

financial debt is not necessarily dependent upon a formal written loan agreement.

They contended that the absence of such an agreement could not, by itself, negate

the existence of financial debt where the bank statements and the Respondent's

own financial records were relied upon to establish the transaction. The

Appellants further submitted that an RBI Master Circular or a regulatory Fair

Practices Circular governing the conduct of NBFCs could not, without more, be



                                                     Page 11 of 31

treated as modifying the statutory definition of financial debt under the code.

They accordingly challenged the rejection of their case on the basis of the alleged

absence of a written loan agreement, while maintaining that the documentary

acknowledgment of the loans had not been properly considered.

21. The Appellants submitted that the Adjudicating Authority erred in

observing that the burden of establishing the case rested upon the Appellants and

could not be shifted entirely to the Respondent for production of the relevant

documents. They contended that their case was not founded solely upon a demand

that the Respondent produce evidence, but upon the bank statements and the

Respondent's own financial records acknowledging unsecured loans. They

further submitted that the Respondent's continuing failure to file statutory balance

sheets with the Registrar of Companies, as reflected in its MCA master data, was

relevant to the question of why the Appellants could not access the Respondent's

financial records through the public domain.

22. The Appellants also contended that the Respondent's reply dated

09.10.2019 did not, according to their case, expressly deny receipt or utilisation

of the amounts transferred, but instead denied the existence of a loan and financial

debt. They submitted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to examine this

distinction alongside the Respondent's entries recording the amounts as

unsecured loans. According to the Appellants, the recall proceedings required the

Authority to examine whether the Respondent's sworn denial was consistent with

its own records and whether any misrepresentation had affected the Original



                                                     Page 12 of 31

Dismissal Order. The Appellants maintained that the burden-of-proof reasoning

adopted in the Impugned Order did not answer this separate question.

23. The Appellants submitted that the allegation of fraud was repeatedly

supported by documentary material during the pendency of the Rule 11

proceedings. In addition to the affidavits dated 22.02.2023 placing the

Respondent's ITR for AY 2018–19 on record, the Appellants relied upon an

Additional Affidavit dated 13.08.2024, Written Submissions dated 03.06.2024

and 09.10.2025, and a Short Note dated 27.02.2026. The Memoranda of Appeal

state that these documents were taken on record by the Adjudicating Authority

and that screenshots of the DMS portal were produced to demonstrate their

availability on the record.

24. The Appellants contended that, despite the aforesaid pleadings and

documents being available, the Impugned Order did not address their specific

case concerning the unaudited balance sheet, the subsequently discovered ITR,

the Respondent's statutory non-compliance or the alleged false statement on

affidavit. They submitted that the rejection of the recall applications without

examining these materials deprived them of a reasoned determination of the

principal ground raised under Rule 11. The Appellants accordingly maintained

that the Impugned Order was liable to be set aside for failure to consider the

material placed on record and for non-application of mind to the specific case

pleaded.



                                                     Page 13 of 31

25. Without prejudice to their other submissions, the Appellants contended that

limitation ought not to defeat the exercise of recall jurisdiction where an order is

alleged to have been procured by fraud and the material establishing the alleged

fraud was discovered subsequently. They relied upon S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu

v. Jagannath, A.V. Papayya Sastry v. Government of A.P. and Angelo Brothers

Ltd. v. Bennett, Coleman & Co. Ltd., as cited in the Memoranda of Appeal, in

support of their submission that an order procured by fraud may be recalled

notwithstanding the passage of time. They further submitted that the ITR for AY

2018–19 was not available to them during the original Section 7 proceedings and

was discovered only during the Rule 11 proceedings, while the Respondent's

failure to file statutory balance sheets continued to impede access to its financial

records. The Appellants maintained that the present appeals were filed within the

period specified under Section 61(1) of the code and that the Impugned Order did

not reject their applications on the ground of limitation.

26. Concluding their arguments, the Appellants requested this Appellate

Tribunal to set aside the Impugned Orders and allow both appeals.



                        Findings



27. These two appeals are filed under Section 61 of the Code, challenging the

common order dated 16.07.2026 of the Adjudicating Authority passed in I.A. No.

06/2023 in C.P. (IB) No. 2060 (PB)/2019 and I.A. No. 05/2023 in C.P. (IB) No.

2061 (PB)/2019, which were dismissed. Both applications were filed under Rule



                                                     Page 14 of 31

11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. They asked the Adjudicating Authority to recall its

order dated 19.04.2022, by which it had dismissed the Section 7 petitions of the

two Appellants against Cynosure Real Estates Pvt. Ltd. (the Corporate Debtor).

28. We note that the facts are almost the same and the questions are identical,

hence both appeals are decided together. We have heard learned counsel for the

Appellants on the question of admission. The Corporate Debtor has not appeared

and no notice has been issued to it. For that reason, we confine ourselves to the

question whether these appeals deserve admission. We make no finding on

whether any debt is owed to the Appellants. Dismissal at this stage does not

prejudice the Corporate Debtor.

29. It has been brought to our notice that Amarendra Financial Pvt. Ltd. paid

the Corporate Debtor Rs. 1.50 crore on 05.04.2017 and Rs. 20 lakhs on

06.04.2017, a total of Rs. 1.70 crores. Similarly, Dinkar Commercial Pvt. Ltd.

paid Rs. 2.00 crore on 03.04.2017 and Rs. 30 lakhs on 06.04.2017, a total of Rs.

2.30 crore. Both describe these as short-term unsecured loans. Both are NBFCs.

The Corporate Debtor had been incorporated on 24.03.2017.

30. We have been advised that both the Appellants filed petitions under

Section 7 of the Code on 22.08.2019. The Corporate Debtor filed its reply on

09.10.2019. The Appellants stated that the reply denied any loan and denied that

the Appellants were financial creditors. It has been brought out to us that in

January 2022, the Appellants placed on record an unaudited balance sheet of the

Corporate Debtor for the year 2017-18. A note to that balance sheet lists



                                                     Page 15 of 31

unsecured loans and shows Rs. 1,70,00,000 against Amarendra Financial Pvt.

Ltd. and Rs. 2,30,00,000 against Dinkar Commercials Pvt. Ltd. The petitions

were dismissed on 19.04.2022.

31. We note that the reasons for that dismissal are contained in para three of

the impugned order. The Adjudicating Authority recorded that no loan agreement

had been filed. The bank statement was not certified by the bank. The terms of

repayment were not shown. No proof of service was given for the Appellants’

letters dated 14.07.2017, 12.01.2018, 11.04.2018 and 30.04.2019. Not a single

document from the Corporate Debtor acknowledging the debt had been produced.

On this basis the Adjudicating Authority held that the amounts were not shown

to be a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the Code.

32. We also take into consideration the fact that no appeal was filed against

the order dated 19.04.2022. The Appellants have also declared that they have filed

no other proceeding. They filed the recall applications on 29.12.2022. On

22.02.2023 they filed an affidavit placing on record the Corporate Debtor’s

income tax return for the assessment year 2018-19. Further affidavits and written

submissions followed on 03.06.2024, 13.08.2024, 09.10.2025 and 27.02.2026.

The recall applications were dismissed on 16.07.2026.

33. We note that the Adjudicating Authority accepted that it has inherent power

to recall its orders and held that the power is used sparingly and not as a review,

and that fraud is a ground on which it can be used. It then held that there was

nothing to suggest fraud as the order of 19.04.2022 was passed after hearing the



                                                     Page 16 of 31

Appellants, on their inability to produce cogent evidence. The onus was on them.

Allegations of fraud were easy to make but difficult to prove, and bald assertions

were not enough. It also observed that an NBFC must lend only on a formal

written agreement, and referred to an RBI Master Circular on the Fair Practices

Code dated 01.07.2015.

34. The Appellants’ main complaint is that the impugned order does not

mention the balance sheet or the income tax return, and that a finding of no fraud

cannot stand without dealing with them. The appellants argued that the view on

written agreements is contrary to the law and requested that the impugned order

be set aside, the order of 19.04.2022 be recalled and the petitions be restored. In

the alternative they ask for a remand.

35. Based on the broad facts noted above, we find that three questions arise.

First, what is the scope of the recall power, and what can be examined in this

appeal. Second, whether the order dated 19.04.2022 was obtained by fraud or

misrepresentation on the Adjudicating Authority. Third, whether the way the

Adjudicating Authority dealt with the plea calls for interference or remand.



       Since all these issues are interconnected, interdependent, and interrelated,

we shall treat them as a single issue and determine them in a conjoint manner in

the subsequent discussions.

36. At first, we will deal with the scope of the recall powers of the Adjudicating

authority or, for that matter, of this appellate tribunal against an order refusing



                                                     Page 17 of 31

recall is an order of the Adjudicating Authority where an appeal lies against it

under Section 61.

37. We are of the considered opinion that the law on the power of recall is

now clear. A five-member bench of this Appellate Tribunal held in Union Bank

of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian & Ors., Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No.

729 of 2020 (reported as 2023 SCC OnLine NCLAT 283) that the Tribunal has

no power of review. It has an inherent power to recall its judgment, preserved by

Rule 11 of its Rules. That power can be used where a procedural error has

occurred, for example where a necessary party was not served. It can also be used

on other grounds, one of which is fraud played on the Court in obtaining the

judgment. The Hon’ble Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against that decision

on 31.07.2023 in Civil Appeal No. 4620 of 2023 (Union Bank of India v.

Financial Creditors of Amtek Auto Ltd.), saying that it agreed with the view of

the five-member bench. Thus, it becomes clear that the outcome of this Appellate

tribunal held by a five-member bench is now final.

38. We also know that in the case of Prabhjit Singh Soni (supra), the Hon’ble

Supreme Court dealt with the same power in the hands of the Adjudicating

Authority. It held that Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 preserves the inherent

power of the Tribunal, and that neither the Code nor the Regulations prohibit its

use. It referred to Section 60(5)(c) of the Code. It then sets the limits. The power

is to be exercised sparingly and not as a tool to re-hear the matter. Ordinarily an

application for recall is maintainable on limited grounds. These include an order



                                                     Page 18 of 31

passed without jurisdiction, an order passed without notice to a party who was

affected, and an order obtained by misrepresentation of facts or by fraud on the

Court or Tribunal resulting in gross failure of justice.

39. We need to appreciate that recall and review are different. A party who

says the Tribunal made a mistake of fact or law, overlooked a document on the

record, took a wrong view of the evidence, or has found new evidence later, is

asking for a review or an appeal. The Adjudicating Authority has no power of

review. It cannot use recall to do what it cannot do by review, even where the

error is plain on the face of the record. The Adjudicating Authority said so in para

5 of its order, and it was right.

40. We are of the considered opinion that refusal of recall is a matter of judicial

discretion, and this appellate tribunal cannot disturb the way it was exercised.

Where the reasons given are incomplete, we can look at the record ourselves and

decide whether the result is right. We do that here.

41. While dealing with such an application for recall, the adjudicating

authority needs to be cautious, keeping in consideration the fact that a petition

under Section 7 can lead to a moratorium and a change in the control of the

company. Such petitions are meant to be decided quickly. A dismissal that is not

appealed lets the company and its other creditors plan on that footing. If it could

be reopened years later on a charge of fraud that does not hold, the speed and

certainty that the Code promises would be lost. At the same time the power is

real, and a proved fraud on the Tribunal must be undone whenever it is found.



                                                     Page 19 of 31

The balance is struck by insisting on proof of the fraud. We apply that standard

in the present case which sets the boundary of the present appeals. We are asked

to decide whether recall was rightly refused. We are not asked to decide whether

the order dated 19.04.2022 was right. That order was open to appeal under Section

61 of the code. The Appellants did not file one. A recall application cannot be

used to get around the limitation for an appeal that was not filed. The prayer to

restore the petitions follows only if recall was justified. The question is therefore

narrow. Did the Appellants show that the order of 19.04.2022 was obtained by

fraud or misrepresentation on the Adjudicating Authority?

42. We are of the considered opinion that the principle is settled on this issue.

A judgment obtained by fraud on the court is a nullity, and a court or tribunal is

not powerless to recall it as noted read civil cases by the Honourable Supreme

Court where it has been stipulated that that no court or tribunal can be regarded

as powerless to recall its own order if it is convinced that the order was wangled

through fraud or misrepresentation of such a dimension as would affect the very

basis of the claim. That case concerned awards obtained on a false account of

how the injuries were caused, a fraud of a high degree that came to light

afterwards. The Hon’ble Supreme Court recalled the words of Lord Denning that

no judgment of a court can be allowed to stand if it has been obtained by fraud,

for fraud unravels everything. Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley, [1956] 1 QB 702.

The decisions, and the nature of the wrong, show what a party must establish.

There must be a false statement of fact, or a deliberate concealment of a material



                                                     Page 20 of 31

fact that the party was bound to disclose. It must have been made knowingly or

recklessly or making a representation known to be false, from which injury

follows. The order must have been obtained because of it, so that went to the very

basis of the decision. The other side, or the Court, must have had no fair chance

to expose it at the time. And, in the words of Prabhjit Singh Soni (supra), there

must be a gross failure of justice.

43. It is one settled principle of law that in such cases, the plea must also be

specific. Where fraud is alleged, the party must set out full particulars, and the

case is decided on the particulars. A general charge that the other side lied is not

enough. Thus, the Tribunal which is being requested and asked to recall its own

order on this ground must look at the specific material relied on and say why it

does or does not show fraud.

44. In the above background, in order to judge whether the order of 19.04.2022

was obtained by any fraudulent act of the Corporate Debtor, we must first see

what the Appellants had to prove in their Section 7 petitions. Prima facie, we are

of the opinion that a financial creditor must show a financial debt owed to it and

a default by the corporate debtor. A financial debt, under Section 5(8), is a debt

disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Default, under

Section 3(12), is non-payment of a debt that has become due and payable. The

application in Form 1 must carry the particulars of the financial debt and the

documents, records and evidence of default. The Adjudicating Authority has to



                                                     Page 21 of 31

be satisfied, on the material that the financial creditor produces, that a default has

occurred.

45. After examining the facts of the present case, in light of the discussion in

preceding para elaborating certain basic facts which should be met to make a

financial debt, we also find certain gaps (as noted in the order by the Adjudicating

Authority in its order on 19 April 2022), which are material in the present case.

Seen this way, the gaps noted on 19.04.2022 were gaps in proof of these very

things. The want of a loan agreement and of the terms of payment went to the

nature of the debt and the date on which it fell due. The uncertified bank statement

went to the disbursal. The absence of proof of service of the letters went to

demand and default. The absence of any acknowledgement by the Corporate

Debtor went to the admission of liability. The balance sheet and the return, even

taken at their highest, speak only to the last of these. We do not decide what the

effect would have been had they been accepted. The point is a limited one. The

order was passed on a failure of proof under several heads. The Corporate

Debtor’s reply was not the reason for it.

46. After hearing the pleadings set up before us by the Appellant, we find that

the Appellants’ case of fraud has three parts. One, the Corporate Debtor’s reply

dated 09.10.2019 was false, because its own books showed the loans. Two, the

Corporate Debtor suppressed its income tax return for the assessment year 2018-

19 throughout the Section 7 proceedings. Three, the Corporate Debtor never filed



                                                     Page 22 of 31

audited balance sheets with the Registrar of Companies, which kept the

Appellants from placing them on record. We take these in turn.

47. First, we take up the issue of reply. The Appellants describe it in two ways.

In the facts and the grounds, the Appellants submitted that the Corporate Debtor

denied that any loan was taken. In one of the grounds, the Appellant stated that

the Corporate Debtor never denied receipt or utilization of the loan amounts and

treated that as an implied admission. Both cannot be right. What the reply actually

says matters, and it has to be read as it stands and not as the Appellants summarise

it.

48. If the reply only denied that the Appellants were financial creditors, it took

a stand on how the transaction should be characterised under Section 5(8) of the

Code. That is a debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of

money. Whether a transfer of money meets that description was the very question

the Adjudicating Authority had to decide. Money paid between companies may

be a loan, an advance, a deposit or something else. A stand on that question, even

a wrong one, is a legal position that the Tribunal is there to decide. It is not a false

statement of fact.

49. If, on the other hand, the reply denied receipt of the money, it would be

false on the Corporate Debtor’s own books and on the bank statements the

Appellants had filed. But that is not clearly the Appellants’ case, and the reply

must be read to see. Even then, the answer would not change, for the reasons.



                                                     Page 23 of 31

50. The question whether the money was a loan was the matter in contest. Both

sides placed their stands before the Tribunal. The Appellants had the chance to

expose the weakness of the Corporate Debtor’s stand, and they tried to do so with

the balance sheet. When the Tribunal decided that question, it decided a contested

point on the merits. That a party’s stand on a contested point was weak does not

make the decision on it a fraud on the Court. A knowingly false statement that

the Tribunal accepted and acted on stands on a different footing, and the cases

cited above would then apply.

51. As regard the issue of the balance sheet, we note that the Appellants

themselves placed the unaudited balance sheet for 2017-18 on the record in

January 2022. That was about three months before the order of 19.04.2022. So,

the Adjudicating Authority had before it the Corporate Debtor’s denial and the

document said to contradict it. The Corporate Debtor was heard. The order

records that the Authority heard both parties and perused the documents. We are

of clear opinion that fraud on a court means that the court was deceived. A

document put before the court by the very party who now alleges fraud was not

kept from the court. If the Authority did not accept the balance sheet as proof, or

did not mention it, the complaint is that it made an error. An error of that kind,

even a manifest one, is a ground of appeal and not of recall.

52. The Appellants’ own pleading point the same way. Ground II calls the

Authority’s disregard of the balance sheet “inadvertent”. That word describes a

mistake by the Tribunal. It does not describe a fraud by the Corporate Debtor.



                                                     Page 24 of 31

The Appellants add that the mistake was “induced” by the Corporate Debtor’s

false averment. We do not see how. The Corporate Debtor did not hide the

document. The Appellants filed it and argued on it.

53. The Appellants also argued that the Authority was swayed by the denial.

The reasons for the order of 19.04.2022, as reproduced in the impugned order, do

not show this. The Authority did not say that it accepted the Corporate Debtor’s

version. It found that the Appellants had not produced a loan agreement, a

certified bank statement, the terms of the loan, proof of service of their letters, or

any acknowledgement by the Corporate Debtor. Each of these is a gap in the

Appellants’ own proof. Under Section 7 it is for the financial creditor to place

evidence of the debt and of the default before the Adjudicating Authority, which

must be satisfied that a default has occurred. The order of 19.04.2022 was passed

because that proof was found wanting. It was not obtained by the Corporate

Debtor’s reply.

54. The Appellants also argued that the Corporate Debtor never disputed the

authenticity of the balance sheet. We find that Silence of that kind does not prove

a document. In a Section 7 petition the Adjudicating Authority has to be satisfied

with the material before it. It cannot treat the absence of a denial as proof of debt

and default. Nor was the Corporate Debtor bound to say anything about a

document that the Appellants produced late, at the rejoinder stage.

55. We also find that the Appellants relied rather too heavily on what the

balance sheet proves. In this connection, we would like to refer to the ratio held



                                                     Page 25 of 31

by the Honourable Supreme Court in case of the Asset Reconstruction Company

(India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal, (2021) 6 SCC 366, where the Honourable Supreme

Court held that an entry in a balance sheet can amount to an acknowledgement of

liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. It also held that whether it

does depend on the facts of each case, including any caveats in the balance sheet

or the auditor’s report. That decision is about limitation. It does not hold that a

balance sheet entry proves that money was disbursed against the time value of

money, or fixes the date on which a debt became due and payable. The balance

sheet here is unaudited. The Appellants have not explained and elaborated the

details regarding who signed it, when it was approved, or how they came to have

it. These are matters that had to be argued in an appeal against the order of

19.04.2022. we do not find merit in the contention of the appellant on this issue;

the point was one for appeal and not for recall.

56. Now we look into points raised by the Appellant about the income tax

return. This is the only new document. It was placed on record on 22.02.2023,

after the order. The Appellants say the Corporate Debtor suppressed it. We do not

find suppression as a respondent in a Section 7 petition has no duty to volunteer

its tax returns to the applicant. The burden of proving debt and default lies on the

financial creditor, who must furnish evidence of default with the application. If a

financial creditor believes that the debtor holds a document that proves its case,

it can ask the Adjudicating Authority to direct its production. The Adjudicating

Authority has the power to do so. Nothing in the Appeal or pleadings show that



                                                     Page 26 of 31

the Appellants asked for the return, or for any of the Corporate Debtor’s books,

at any time before 19.04.2022. A party cannot be said to have hidden a document

that was never called for from it. Further, the return adds little. The excerpt in the

memoranda shows one line, “Other loans and advances”, of Rs. 24,62,80,069,

forming part of “Total long-term borrowings”. It names no lender. It matches only

the grand total of the balance sheet note. In the balance sheet the same total is

shown under “short term borrowings”. So, the return repeats a total figure, and

the two documents do not even classify it alike. The only document that names

the Appellants is the balance sheet note, and that was already before the Tribunal.

The Appellants say that two independent filings record their loans under the

specific head “Unsecured Loans”. The excerpt does not bear this out. Both

documents were also prepared by the Corporate Debtor from its own books, so

they are not independent of each other. The Appellants pleaded that the return

was within the exclusive knowledge and custody of the Corporate Debtor, and

also that they discovered it in February 2023. Both cannot be wholly true. The

appeal does not indicate how or from whom the Appellants obtained it, or what

stopped them from getting it earlier. The Appellants themselves submitted that

the return had been filed before the Corporate Debtor’s reply of 09.10.2019. They

had a copy of the unaudited balance sheet by January 2022, and do not explain

why the route by which they got it could not also have produced the return. If

they could obtain the return in 2023, they could have sought it in the two years

and eight months the petitions were pending. A document that could have been



                                                     Page 27 of 31

brought out in the original proceedings with ordinary care cannot be called

fraudulently kept back. At its highest the return is new evidence found after the

order. Discovery of new evidence is a ground for review. The Adjudicating

Authority has no power of review. New evidence can support recall only if its

non-production was itself a fraud on the Tribunal, and for the reasons above it

was not. If new evidence found later could reopen a dismissed petition, no order

under the Code would be final. Recall would become review under another name.

We are of the considered opinion that a recall must not become a tool to re-hear

the matter.

57. The Appellants argue on the question of onus that the Authority placed the

whole burden on them and ignored the Corporate Debtor’s conduct. In the Section

7 petition the burden was on the Appellants, and the Tribunal was right to say so.

In the recall applications the burden was on the Appellants again, this time to

prove fraud. They had to show that the order was obtained by it. For the reasons

given, they did not.

58. Several grounds in the appeals are really arguments on the merits of the

original petitions. The submissions that a balance sheet entry is an

acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, that a written

agreement is not needed to prove a loan, and that the bank statements were

enough, would have formed the content of an appeal against the order of

19.04.2022. They are not grounds for recall, and we do not examine them as such.



                                                     Page 28 of 31

We have looked at them only to the extent that they bear on whether any fraud

was practised.

59. The Appellants also argue that fraud can be raised at any time and that

limitation is no bar. That is correct where fraud is established. It does not help

where fraud is not made out. An unproven claim of fraud cannot be used to get

around the limitation for an appeal against the original order. We do not hold the

recall applications to be late. The point is that the Appellants chose recall over

appeal, and recall has a narrower field. A party whose petition was heard, who

filed its documents and who lost for want of proof has not suffered such a failure

through any act of the other side. The remedy for a mistake by the Tribunal was

an appeal. The position would be different if the Appellants had been kept out of

the proceedings, or if a document that they could not otherwise reach had been

withheld from them. That is not the case.

60. We are of the view that the question in a recall application is not whether

a party’s stand was creditable, but whether the order under challenge was

obtained by a fraud on the Tribunal. On the material before us, it was not. The

Appellants have not shown a false statement to the Tribunal on which the order

rested, or a concealment of a document that the Corporate Debtor was bound to

produce and that the Appellants could not otherwise get.

61. We are of the considered opinion that even the case of Prabhjit Singh Soni

(supra) does not help the Appellants. That was a case of an approved resolution

plan that did not deal, as the Code requires, with the claim of a statutory authority



                                                     Page 29 of 31

that held a charge over the corporate debtor’s land. The Hon’ble Supreme Court

allowed recall in that setting. The present case is of a different kind. There is no

resolution plan and no third party. The Appellants were the petitioners. They were

heard, they filed their documents, and they failed for want of proof. Their remedy

was an appeal.

62. The Appellants have not shown that the order dated 19.04.2022 was

obtained by fraud or misrepresentation on the Adjudicating Authority. The

documents they rely on either were already before the Authority or are, at most,

new evidence found after the order. The order was passed on the Appellants’ own

failure of proof and not on the Corporate Debtor’s reply. The Adjudicating

Authority was right to refuse recall, though its reasons were thin. The appeals do

not disclose a case for admission.

63. We state that the applicant, who wants to recall the order of the

Adjudicating authority must plead the false statement or concealment with

particulars. The applicant must show that it was made knowingly or recklessly to

the Tribunal, that the order was obtained because of it, and that the applicant had

no fair chance to meet it at the time. A document that was already on the record,

or that the applicant could have called for in the original proceedings, cannot

support a charge of fraud. A mistake in dealing with such a document is for

appeal. New evidence found later is not a ground for recall. In the present case,

we do not find any reason or cause that support the pleadings of the appellants.



                                                     Page 30 of 31

These findings apply to both Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1839 of 2026 and Comp.

App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1840 of 2026.

64. In view of above detailed examinations of facts and law, we find no merit

in the appeals. The appeals fail and stand rejected. There would be no orders to

cost and, IA if any, stand closed.

root of the institution of the appeal and the defect cannot be cured by an

6. Heard. Perused the records with the able assistance of the Ld.

Counsels.



6.1 The relevant dates in this case are not in dispute. The impugned order

was pronounced on 17.07.2026 and the appeal was e-filed on 29.08.2026

which is the 44th day from the date of pronouncement of the order. It is not in

dispute that the appeal was not accompanied by a certified copy of the

impugned order.



6.2 I.A. No. 6524 of 2026 and I.A. No. 6525 of 2026 were taken up on

16.09.2026 and thereafter on 17.09.2026 when replies on the IAs were called

for. The Appellant/Applicant filed online application for obtaining the certified

copy of the impugned order only after this, on 29.09.2026, which is the 66th

day from the date of pronouncement of the impugned order.



6.3 The Appellant/Applicant has stated that it had initially tried to obtain

certified copy through offline mode. No evidence regarding this effort has been

furnished and we are thus unable to accept this plea.



7. Before proceeding further it shall be beneficial to extract the relevant

provisions of NCLAT Rules, 2016 regarding the presentation of appeal and

authority of this Tribunal to grant exemption, as under:



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                             5



            “Power to exempt



            14. The Appellate Tribunal may on sufficient cause being shown,

            exempt the parties from compliance with any requirement of these

            rules and may give such directions in matters of practice and

            procedure, as it may consider just and expedient on the

            application moved in this behalf to render substantial justice.

            ..........

            Presentation of appeal



            22. (1) Every appeal shall be presented in Form NCLAT-1 in

            triplicate by the appellant or petitioner or applicant or respondent,

            as the case may be, in person or by his duly authorised

            representative duly appointed in this behalf in the prescribed form

            with stipulated fee at the filing counter and non-compliance of this

            may constitute a valid ground to refuse to entertain the same.



            (2) Every appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the

            impugned order.



            (3) All documents filed in the Appellate Tribunal shall be

            (4) Sufficient number of copies of the appeal or petition or

8. The appeal has been filed under the provisions of Section 61 of the IBC,



2016. The relevant sub-section (2) of Section 61 reads as under:



            “61. Appeals and Appellate Authority



            ....



            (2) Every appeal under sub-section (1) shall be filed within thirty

            days before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal:



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

             6



            PROVIDED that the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

            may allow an appeal to be filed after the expiry of the said period

            of thirty days if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for

            not filing the appeal but such period shall not exceed fifteen days.”



                                                                            (Emphasis supplied)

9. A plain reading of the provisions extracted above shows that an appeal



against the order of Ld. NCLT has to be filed within 30 days and this Tribunal



has the authority, if it is satisfied there was sufficient cause for not filing the



appeal in time, to extend the period further by 15 days but no more. The outer



limit for filing an appeal under the IBC, 2016, including the condonable



period, is thus 45 days. In the present case, the appeal was filed on the 44th



day though it was not accompanied with the certified copy of the impugned



order.



10. We now look at the judicial guidelines on the controversy in question.

The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 7882 of 2023 recently vide

judgment dated 14.10.2026 in the case of The Assistant Commissioner of

Central Tax, CGST Division v. Sreenivasa Rao Ravinuthala and another has

observed as under:



“8.  In V. Nagarajan (supra), this Court considered the



scheme of the IBC and, in parallel, examined the applicability of



the provisions of the Act, 1963 to the IBC. Instead of culling out



the excerpts, we will paraphrase the ratio of V. Nagarajan (supra)



as follows:



A.   The IBC is an exhaustive, self-contained code. By virtue



of the non-obstante clause in Section 238 of the IBC, its provisions



prevail over any inconsistencies with other statutes. While Section



238-A of the IBC applies the provisions of the Act, 1963 “as far as



            may be”, this is subject to Section 29(2) of the Act, 1963. Where a



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                7



special statute provides a distinct period of limitation, that period



governs to the exclusion of general provisions, and the IBC, being



a special law, would have an overriding effect. Section 61(1) of the



IBC starts with a non-obstante clause. Consequently, the



appellate mechanisms under the Companies Act cannot control or



relax the statutory architecture of the IBC.



B.          Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 mandates that



every Appeal be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned



Order. Section 12(2) of the Act, 1963 excludes the time required to



obtain a copy of the impugned Order. The Explanation to Section



12 of the Act, 1963 makes it clear that any time the Tribunal or



Court takes to prepare the Order before the litigant applies for a



copy cannot be excluded. If a party fails to apply for a certified



copy within the limitation period, no time can be excluded under



Section 12(2) of the Act, 1963. Applying for a certified copy is not



a mere procedural formality; it reflects the aggrieved party’s due



diligence.



C.          Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a 30-day period for



filing an Appeal, extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon



demonstration of sufficient cause, and no more. Courts and



Tribunals have no power under Section 5 of the Act, 1963, or



inherent powers to condone delays beyond the outer limit of 15



days prescribed in special statutes. The IBC’s foundational



architecture weaves speed and strict timelines to preserve asset



value, maximise recovery for lenders, and protect economic health.



Procedural rules cannot be interpreted to protract litigation



indefinitely.”



11. The question whether an aggrieved party is under an obligation to apply

for a certified copy of the impugned order, and the consequence of its failure

to do so, is no longer res integra. A three-Judge Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme

Court in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd. & Ors., (2022) 2 SCC 244,

has held as under:



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                             8



            “31. The import of Section 12 of the Limitation Act and its

            Explanation is to assign the responsibility of applying for a

            certified copy of the order on a party. A person wishing to file an

            appeal is expected to file an application for a certified copy before

            the expiry of the limitation period, upon which the “time requisite”

            for obtaining a copy is to be excluded. However, the time taken by

            the court to prepare the decree or order before an application for a

            copy is made cannot be excluded. If no application for a certified

            copy has been made, no exclusion can ensue. In fact, the

            Explanation to the provision is a clear indicator of the legal position

            that the time which is taken by the court to prepare the decree or

            order cannot be excluded before the application to obtain a copy

            is made. It cannot be said that the right to receive a free copy

            under Section 420(3) of the Companies Act obviated the obligation

            on the appellant to seek a certified copy through an application.

            The appellant has urged that Rule 14 of the NCLAT Rules

            empowers NCLAT to exempt parties from compliance with the

            requirement of any of the rules in the interests of substantial

            justice, which has been typically exercised in favour of allowing a

            downloaded copy in lieu of a certified copy. While it may well be

            true that waivers on filing an appeal with a certified copy are often

            granted for the purposes of judicial determination, they do not

            confer an automatic right on an applicant to dispense with

            compliance and render Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules nugatory.

            The act of filing an application for a certified copy is not

            just a technical requirement for computation of limitation

            but also an indication of the diligence of the aggrieved

            party in pursuing the litigation in a timely fashion. In a

            similar factual scenario, NCLAT had dismissed an appeal as time-

            barred under Section 61(2) IBC since the appellant therein was

            present in court, and yet chose to file for a certified copy after five

            months of the pronouncement of the order.



            ….



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                             9



            34. On the second question, Rule 22(2) of the NCLAT Rules

            mandates the certified copy being annexed to an appeal, which

            continues to bind litigants under IBC. While it is true that the

            tribunals, and even this Court, may choose to exempt

            parties from compliance with this procedural requirement

            in the interest of substantial justice, as reiterated in Rule

            14 of the NCLAT Rules, the discretionary waiver does not

            act as an automatic exception where litigants make no

            efforts to pursue a timely resolution of their grievance. The

            appellant having failed to apply for a certified copy, rendered the

            appeal filed before NCLAT as clearly barred by limitation.”



                                                                             (Emphasis supplied)

12. A three-Judge Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in A. Rajendra v.



Gonugunta Madhusudhan Rao & Ors., (2025) 6 SCC 618 considered two



appeals which were filed on the 39th day from the date of pronouncement of



the order of the Ld. NCLT, that is, within the outer limit of forty-five days. In



the second appeal, no certified copy was appended and an application for



exemption from filing the certified copy was filed. The appellant had not



applied for the certified copy. The Hon’ble Supreme Court held as under:



            “26. However, where the judgment was pronounced in open Court,

            the period of limitation starts running from that very day. The

            appellant is however entitled to seek relief under Section 12(2) of

            the Limitation Act for excluding the period during which the

            certified copy was under preparation on an application preferred

            by that party.

            27. In light of the above legally settled position, when the facts of

            the present case is seen, the first thing which is apparent is that

            in the absence of any certified copy having been applied by the

            appellant of the impugned orders dated 20th July 2023 passed

            by the NCLT on which it was admittedly pronounced, with Rule



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            10



            22 of the NCLAT Rules mandating filing of the appeal along with

            the certified copy. The appeals as preferred by the appellant need

            to be dismissed as they were filed beyond 30 days and no steps

            have been taken by the appellant to seek certified copy of the

            order.



            28. That apart, the second appeal, on this score alone is to

            be dismissed as there is no question of moving an

            application for condonation of delay when no application

            for obtaining a certified copy of the order has been filed.

            Exemption from filing of certified copy, as has been

            referred to above, cannot be claimed as a matter of right in

            terms of the statutory requirements of the Rules. As regards

            the first appeal, which was accompanied with the certified copy

            supplied free by NCLT the same also being beyond the period of

            limitation and the time of ten days as sought to be exempted for

            the preparation and making available the certified copy cannot be

            credited to the benefit of the appellant as the period of limitation

            commences from the date of pronouncement of the order and the

            benefit of Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act is available only on

            an application for grant of certified copy of the Order having been

            filed till the date of preparation of the said certified copy. Since no

            such steps have been taken by the appellant for applying the

            certified copy, the appeal was beyond limitation.”



                                                                             (Emphasis supplied)

13. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Ashdan Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. DSK



Global Education and Research Pvt. Ltd. & Anr., 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1682,



considered an appeal which was e-filed on the 32nd day from the date of



pronouncement of the order of the Ld. NCLT without a certified copy of the



impugned order. The certified copy was applied for only after the expiry of



forty-five days and was filed thereafter. The Hon’ble Supreme Court held as



under:



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            11



            “11. … Though the National Company Law Appellate

            Tribunal is clothed with the powers to exempt and to extend

            time under Rules 14 and 15 of the NCLAT Rules

            respectively, such powers cannot be exercised so as to

            render Rule 22(2) thereof nugatory, as pointed out in V

            Nagarajan (supra). Even if an appeal is entertained within

            the initial 30 day-period without a certified copy of the

            order, by granting exemption under Rule 14, it can only be

            for a limited period to enable due compliance with the

            mandate of Rule 22(2) by filing a certified copy at least at

            a later date and within the time stipulated by the National

            Company Law Appellate Tribunal. Such exemption cannot be

            to the extent of completely dispensing with the filing of a certified

            copy, which would annihilate the clear mandate of Rule 22(2) of

            the NCLAT Rules, which categorically uses the word ‘shall’ to

            emphasize that an appeal must be accompanied by a certified

            copy of the order impugned.



            12. Viewed thus, the fact that respondent No. 1 casually e-filed an

            appeal on 25.07.2023, with neither an application for condonation

            of delay nor an application seeking exemption from filing a

            certified copy of the impugned order, rendered its appeal

            defective. Admittedly, it was only on 25.08.2023 that respondent

            No. 1 filed an application seeking permission to file the appeal and

            an application for condonation of delay was filed much later, on

            22.09.2023. Presumably, it was at this time that a certified copy

            of the impugned order was filed without even seeking exemption

            or extension of time to do so. These aspects ought to have been

            considered by the NCLAT as the statute peremptorily

            requires proper institution of an appeal in conformity with

            all the prescribed norms and it was incumbent upon the

            NCLAT to examine and verify as to whether respondent No.

            1’s appeal was in due compliance with all such norms. More

            so, when the appellant herein had specifically raised the issue



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            12



            that such appeal was barred by limitation. The NCLAT erred in

            completely brushing aside this crucial aspect which went

            to the very root of its appellate jurisdiction.”



                                                                             (Emphasis supplied)

14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Angelwoods Apartment Allottees



Association v. M. Lalitha & Anr., [(2026) ibclaw.in 343 SC], had occasion to



consider an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC, 2016 which was e-filed on



the last day of the outer limit of forty-five days but without a certified copy of



the impugned order and without the appellant having applied for the same.



The Hon’ble Supreme Court held as under:



            “9. Given the strict timelines provided in the Code, which were

            held to be of essence by this Court (See Ebix Singapore Private

            Limited vs. Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Limited

            and another [(2021) ibclaw.in 153 SC]), we may note that

            respondent No. 1 chose to e-file an appeal against the order dated

            14.08.2024 on the very last day available to her, in terms of the

            limitation prescribed under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the

            Code. However, the filing of such appeal, without even

            applying for a certified copy of the order dated 14.08.2024,

            practically meant that there was no filing of an appeal in

            the eyes of law. As pointed out by this Court, a diligent litigant

            is expected to apply for a certified copy of the order sought to be

            appealed against before the period of limitation runs out and, by

            doing so, such litigant would be entitled to seek exclusion of the

            time taken to procure the certified copy for the purpose of

            limitation.

            10. However, as noted earlier, respondent No. 1 did not even

            apply for a certified copy of the NCLT’s order dated 14.08.2024 till

            21.04.2025, long after the refiling of the appeal on 10.03.2025. To

            make matters worse, respondent No.1 did not even choose to file



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            13



            an application for exemption from filing such certified copy at any

            point, be it at the time of filing the appeal on 28.09.2024 or its

            refiling on 10.03.2025. This was the minimum requirement for

            respondent No. 1 to have complied with, when she filed and refiled

            her appeal without a certified copy of the NCLT’s order dated

            14.08.2024. Any such application could have been considered by

            the NCLAT under Rules 14 and 15 of the NCLAT Rules to enable

            the filing of the certified copy by respondent No.1 within such

            further time as is stipulated by the NCLAT. In effect, the appeal,

            as filed and refiled, was not a merely defective appeal,

            wherein the defects could be cured, but was a wholly

            incompetent appeal that did not satisfy the essentials to

            pass muster, in terms of the requirements prescribed under

            the Code and the NCLAT Rules. However, the NCLAT totally lost

            sight of these vital aspects while considering the two applications

            filed by respondent No. 1 seeking condonation of delay in the filing

            and the refiling of the appeal. The NCLAT ought not to have

            extended such indulgence to respondent No. 1, without first

            ascertaining whether her appeal was instituted in

            accordance with the norms. We find that the NCLAT failed to

            undertake this exercise.

            11. On the above analysis, we hold that the filing/refiling of the

            appeal by respondent No. 1 was incurably tainted and the same

            ought to have been rejected at the threshold. …”



                                                                             (Emphasis supplied)

15. From a conjoint reading of the aforesaid judgments, the following view



emerges:



(i) The period of limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC, 2016 begins to



run from the date of pronouncement of the order. The time taken for obtaining



a certified copy may be excluded under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act,



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            14

1963 only when the certified copy is applied for within the period of

limitation.



(ii) The act of applying for a certified copy is not merely a technical step for

computing limitation. It is an indicator of the diligence of the aggrieved party.

This obligation is not confined to cases where exclusion of time is sought. It

applies equally where the appeal is filed within the outer limit of forty-five

days. In A. Rajendra (supra), Ashdan Properties (supra) and Angelwoods

(supra), the failure to apply for the certified copy within limitation was

nonetheless held to be fatal.



(iii) An appeal may be presented without a certified copy along with a prayer

for exemption. However, exemption under Rule 14 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016

is discretionary and cannot be claimed as a matter of right.



(iv) An appeal which is presented without a certified copy, where the

certified copy was not applied for within limitation and no exemption has been

validly granted, is not a merely a defective appeal, it is an incompetent appeal.

The defect goes to the very root of the appellate jurisdiction, and such an

appeal is liable to be rejected at the threshold.



(v) The question whether the appeal was instituted in accordance with the

prescribed norms needs to be examined first. Where no application for

obtaining the certified copy has been made within limitation period, there is

no question of considering an application for condonation of delay, as it is an

incompetent appeal.



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of 2026

                                                            15



16. We note that the certified copy in the present case was applied much

after the period of limitation, including the condonable period, and after the

IAs were taken up for hearing and replies were called for from Respondent.

Rule 22(2) of NCLAT Rules, 2016 clearly prescribes that an appeal has to be

accompanied by the certified copy of the impugned order. In the present case,

the certified copy has been applied for after the period of limitation and thus

the appeal is not merely a defective appeal but it is an incompetent appeal in

terms of the requirement prescribed under the IBC, 2016 and the NCLAT

Rules. We are not inclined to extend indulgence to the Appellant/Applicant

regarding exemption from filing of certified copy and condonation of delay in

light of the facts of this case. Since the appeal was not instituted in the

manner prescribed by IBC, 2016 and NCLAT Rules, the appeal is treated as

non-est. I.A. No. 6524 of 2026 and I.A. No. 6525 of 2026 are dismissed. In

consequence, the appeal viz. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1720 of

2026 is treated as non-est. Pending application(s) are closed. No order as to

costs.

Oral: Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Member (Judicial)



04.11.2026:  These two Company Appeals arise out of the proceedings



which were initiated under Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,



2016, which were numbered as CP(IB) No.137/BB/2022 and CP(IB)



No.138/BB/2022, against Ashok Chattaraj and M.R. Amalnath, respectively, the



personal guarantors to the debt availed by the Corporate Debtor, M/s. Siesta



Hospitality Pvt Ltd. The said applications were allowed and the Appellants were



admitted into Personal Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP) by the orders of the



Ld. Adjudicating Authority vide its orders dated 28.05.2024, which are being



challenged in the present appeals.



__________________________________________________________________________________



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 247 & 249/2024            Page 2 of 5

2. After hearing the two Company Appeals, we had reserved our judgement

on 02.07.2025.



3. The Corporate Debtor, M/s. Siesta Hospitality Pvt Ltd. too, was directed to

be admitted into CIRP under Section 7 of the I & B Code, 2016, by an order

passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority on 14.11.2014 in CP(IB)

No.13/BB/2024 and one of the suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, Mr.

Ashok Chattaraj had preferred CA(AT) (CH) (Ins) No.469/2024 challenging the

order of admission of the Corporate Debtor to CIRP.



4. During the pendency of these appeals, the parties have arrived at a

settlement and an application under Section 12A of the I & B Code was filed

before the Ld. Adjudicating Authority in the respective proceedings. The

application filed under Section 7 of the Code, was permitted to be dismissed as

withdrawn vide order dated 08.09.2026, consequent upon which the proceedings

under Section 7 of the Code, in the shape of CP (IB) No.13/BB/2024 has been

closed.



5. Subsequent to the order dated 08.09.2026 passed by the Ld. Adjudicating

Authority, the Appellant Ashok Chattaraj sought withdrawal of the Company

Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 469/2024, which has been permitted to be withdrawn

by the Coordinate Bench vide its order dated 27.10.2026.



__________________________________________________________________________________



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 247 & 249/2024  Page 3 of 5

6. Now the Ld. counsel for the appellant would submit that owing to the fact,

the settlement has already been arrived at between the parties, the matters may be

listed for passing appropriate orders.



7. The Ld. Counsel for the Appellant after prior service of the memorandum

to the Ld. Counsel for the Respondents, has placed before this Appellate Tribunal,

the fact that consequent to the settlement as arrived at between the parties, the RP

had filed applications, being IA No.536/2026 in CP(IB) No.138/BB/2022 and IA

No. 534/2026 in CP(IB) No.137/BB/2022 seeking to withdraw the Personal

Insolvency Resolution Process, against Mr. M.R. Amalnathan and Mr. Ashok

Chattaraj, i.e., the Appellants herein, in view of the settlement that has been

arrived at. She has further stated that the said company petitions have been

permitted to be dismissed as withdrawn by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority vide

orders dated 08.09.2026. Now the Ld. Counsel for Appellants would submit, that

since the proceedings CP(IB)/138/2022 and CP(IB)/137/2022 have been

permitted to be dismissed as withdrawn, nothing remains to be adjudicated in

these instant Company Appeals.



8. Owing to the aforesaid development that has taken place after reserving of



the orders passed by us and because of the fact that the withdrawal applications



have already been allowed by Ld. NCLT and because the respective company



petitions have been closed, due to the settlement that has been arrived at between



the parties, these two company appeals too would stand closed because of the fact



__________________________________________________________________________________



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 247 & 249/2024  Page 4 of 5

that once the proceedings of the company petition has been withdrawn, nothing

survives to be adjudicated.



9. Accordingly, both the Company Appeals stand closed in view of the

withdrawal and closure of the underlying proceedings before the Ld.

Adjudicating Authority. Accordingly, these two company appeals too would

stand closed.



                                             [Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma]

04.11.2026:



These twin appeals are preferred by the financial creditor in a

proceeding initiated under Section 94 of the IBC by the personal

guarantors.



2. The appellant challenges the common order of the

Adjudicating Authority in IA (IBC) No. 406/2026 & IA (IBC) No.

411/2026, which the personal guarantors have taken out, and the

Adjudicating Authority has allowed these applications.



3. Vide the applications now under reference, the personal

guarantors have sought the appointment of a valuer for assessing

the value of their immovable properties and other assets and also

to consider the repayment plan.



4. The Tribunal, vide the impugned order, has appointed a

valuer as required and also directed consideration of the

repayment plan. This order is now under challenge.



5. The only concern expressed by the appellant herein is that,

in their applications, the personal guarantors had mentioned that

pursuant to the consent of both sides made before the Tribunal on

22.08.2025, they had preferred the applications also for



Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 582 & 583/2026         Page 4 of 5

considering their repayment plan. The learned counsel brought to

the notice of the Tribunal that on 22.08.2025, the Tribunal has

not recorded any such consent as having been given by the Bank

for considering any such repayment plan. The learned counsel for

the appellant also brought to the notice of this Tribunal on how

the personal guarantors adopt every conceivable tactic to delay the

proceedings.



6. Heard Mr. Vaibhav Gaggar, for the respondent, and the

learned senior counsel defended the order.



7. The short question is, whether the appellant herein has

consented to consider any repayment plan. While keeping other

things constant, we only require that the repayment plan be

considered by the financial creditors afresh. It is underscored that

the personal guarantors might not be entitled to repeat the same

exercise at their convenience often. In other words, this perhaps

will be the last opportunity we want to give the personal guarantors

to submit their repayment plan.



8. We accordingly dispose of these appeals. No costs.



DD/PC/MS                                     [Justice N. Seshasayee]
