        THIS WRIT PETITION IS FILED UNDER ARTICLES 226

AND 227 OF THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA PRAYING TO SET

ASIDE THE ORDER DATED 14.11.2024 PASSED BY THE

HONBLE NCLT, BANGALORE IN IA (RES) NO.8/2024 IN C.P (IB)

NO.37/BB/2022 VIDE ANNEXURE-A AND ETC.,



        THIS WRIT PETITION, HAVING BEEN RESERVED FOR

ORDERS ON 13.10.2026, COMING ON FOR PRONOUNCEMENT,

THIS DAY, T.P.VIVEKANANDA J., MADE THE FOLLOWING:

CORAM: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE T.P.VIVEKANANDA



                                       CAV ORDER

        The petitioner is before this Court challenging the order

dated 14.11.2024 passed by the National Company Law

Tribunal (NCLT), Bengaluru on IA (Res) No.8 of 2024 in CP(IB)

No.37/BB/2022 at Annexure-A.



        2. The background of the impugned order passed by

the NCLT as per Annexure-A is that, the respondent herein had

filed a petition under Section 7 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy

Code, 2016 ( for short 'the IBC') before NCLT, Bengaluru, which

was registered as CP(IB) No.37/BB/2022 for initiation of

proceedings of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)

against the petitioner in respect of the debt amounting to INR

                                                        - 3 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



178,25,23,894/-. NCLT issued notice of the said proceedings.

The petitioner who was the respondent before the NCLT has

represented and submitted that the claim of the

respondent/petitioner would be settled under OTS. The

petitioner proposed a OTS for an amount of INR

117,35,25,151/-, which when accepted by the respondent

resulted in approval of the OTS proposal through sanction

letter dated 17.11.2023.



        3. Parallel to the negotiation of settlement through

OTS, the NCLT, Bengaluru passed an order on 10.01.2024

admitting the petitioner into CIRP and appointed an IRP. In

view of the fact that against the very same corporate

debtor/petitioner, another creditor Viz., Canara Bank had also

instituted proceedings under IBC, the petition filed by the

respondent came to be disposed of on 11.01.2024 granting

liberty to the respondent to file its claim with IRP in CP(IB)

No.117/BB/2023 on the ground that there can be no multiple

CIRP proceedings against a common corporate debtor. The

petitioner herein entered into a settlement under OTS with the

Canara Bank, which resulted in the withdrawal of the

proceedings in CIRP in CP(IB) No.117/BB/2023 on 16.02.2024.

In view of the termination of the proceedings of CIRP in respect

                                                        - 4 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



of Canara Bank, the respondent herein could not file its claim

before the IRP in CP(IB) No.117/BB/2023.



        4. It is the said circumstances, which resulted in the

respondent approaching the NCLT seeking recall of the order

dated 11.01.2024 and revival of CP(IB) No.37/BB/2022 under

Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016. The said

IA was numbered as IA(RES) No.8 of 2024 in CP(IB)

No.37/BB/2022. The said application was filed on 06.08.2024.

The application for revival was opposed by the corporate

debtor/petitioner herein contending that the termination of the

proceedings between the petitioner and the Canara Bank on

16.02.2024 was within the knowledge of the respondent herein.

However, the application for recall/revival was filed after 6

months of withdrawal of CIRP through order dated 16.02.2024.

It is their further contention that without there being any

liberty in the order dated 11.01.2024 to seek revival of the

petition, the application for revival filed by the respondent is

not maintainable.



        5. Upon consideration of the rival contentions of the

petitioner and the respondent herein, who were the parties

before NCLT, the Tribunal has passed an order allowing the

                                                        - 5 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



application and restoring CP(IB) No.37/BB/2022 to its original

file and directing listing of the matter on 20.11.2024. It is the

said order, which is under challenge in the present writ petition.

This Court had passed an interim order on 19.11.2024 staying

the effect of the order dated 14.11.2024 and all further

proceedings.



        6. The respondent/corporate creditor has filed the

application for vacation of the interim order on several grounds.

However, principally on the ground that the writ petition is not

maintainable, inasmuch as, the petitioner has an alternative

and efficacious remedy under Section 61 of the IBC, 2016,

which reads as follows:



                   "61. Appeals and Appellate Authority:-



                   (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary

          contained under the Companies Act 2013 (18 of 2013),

          any person aggrieved by the order of the Adjudicating

          Authority under this part may prefer an appeal to the

          National Company Law Appellate Tribunal.



                   (2) Every appeal under sub-section (1) shall be

          filed within thirty days before the National Company

          Law Appellate Tribunal:



                   Provided that the National Company Law

          Appellate Tribunal may allow an appeal to be filed after

                                            - 6 -



                                                        WP No. 30901 of 2024



the expiry of the said period of thirty days if it is

satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not filing

the appeal but such period shall not exceed fifteen

days.



        (3) An appeal against an order approving a

resolution plan under section 31 may be filed on the

following grounds, namely:—



        (i) the approved resolution plan is in

contravention of the provisions of any law for the time

being in force;



        (ii) there has been material irregularity in

exercise of the powers by the resolution professional

during the corporate insolvency resolution period;



        (iii) the debts owed to operational creditors of the

corporate debtor have not been provided for in the

resolution plan in the manner specified by the Board;



        (iv) the insolvency resolution process costs have

not been provided for repayment in priority to all other

debts; or



        (v) the resolution plan does not comply with any

other criteria specified by the Board.



        (4) An appeal against liquidation order passed

under Section 33 may be filed on grounds of material

irregularity or fraud committed in relation to such a

liquidation order."

                                                        - 7 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



        7. Apart from contending that the writ petition

challenging the order passed by the NCLT is not maintainable,

the learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the

respondent submits that the petition filed by the respondent

before the NCLT was disposed of permitting the respondent to

make a claim in the insolvency proceedings initiated by

another corporate creditor, Viz., Canara Bank and there was no

adjudication of merits of the claim of the respondent by the

NCLT. Neither the respondent nor the NCLT could have

predicted that before the respondent could make its claim in

the insolvency proceedings initiated by Canara Bank, the

petitioner and the Canara Bank would have settled the matter

under OTS. It is in the said circumstances, the respondent did

not seek liberty to file an application for restoration, if the

claim of the respondent is either rejected or not considered for

any reason whatsoever. Therefore, the respondent was well

within its right to seek revival of the petition filed by it and the

NCLT was well within its jurisdiction to entertain the application

for restoration/revival.



        8. The application for vacating stay was opposed by

the petitioner by filing statement of objections contending that,

                                                        - 8 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



        (i) mere existence of an alternate remedy under

Section 61 of IBC, this Court is not precluded from the grant of

interim order dated 19.11.2024.



        (ii) the exhausting of statutory remedy prior to

invoking the writ jurisdiction is a self-imposed restraint by the

High Court. However, the said restraint is not absolute and is

subject to the following:



        (a) where the writ petition has been filed for the

        enforcement of any fundamental rights;

        (b) violation of principles of natural justice;

        (c) where the order or proceedings are wholly without

        jurisdiction, or ultra vires of an Act is challenged.

        (iii) as the impugned order passed by the NCLT,

entertaining an application for recalling/revival of the

proceedings without there being an express provision under the

IBC and allowing the petition with the delay of 6 months in

filing the application for recalling of the order dated 11.01.2024

is without jurisdiction and nullity in the eye of law and

therefore, the petitioner need not have to exhaust the remedy

of appeal under Section 61 of IBC and the petitioner could as

                                                        - 9 -



                                                                   WP No. 30901 of 2024



well approach this Court invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction

under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.



        9. Apart from the contention regarding maintainability

of the writ petition, so also, the maintainability of the

application filed by the respondent before the NCLT for revival

of the proceedings, learned senior counsel Sri C K Nandakumar

appearing for the petitioner and the learned Additional Solicitor

General Sri Aravind Kamath appearing for the respondent have

made submission on the merits of the matter also.



        10. In addition, several submissions have been made as

regards the approval of OTS in the year 2023, part payment

made by the petitioner and the default committed, so also, the

OTS offer made in the month of February 2026 and the

correspondence between the petitioner and the respondent

from February 2026 till September 2026.



        11. The necessity of consideration of the rival

submissions of the petitioner and the respondent as regards the

legality or otherwise of the order passed by the NCLT, so also,

the arguments regarding consideration of the fresh OTS

proposal of the petitioner would have to be considered only if

- 10 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



this Court were to hold that the writ petition filed by the

petitioner challenging the impugned order is maintainable.



        12. In that view of the matter, this Court proposes to

consider the preliminary objection raised by the respondent as

regards the maintainability of the writ petition in view of the

existence of an alternative remedy of appeal before the NCLAT

under Section 61 of the IBC.



        13. In light of the serious objections raised by the

respondent with regard to the maintainability of the writ

petition, the first point that requires to be considered in the

present writ petition is as to whether the writ petition is

maintainable notwithstanding the availability of alternate

remedy under Section 61 of the IBC.



        14. As noticed supra, the order passed by NCLT

recalling its earlier order dated 11.01.2024 and restoring the

CP (IB) No.37/BB/2022 is an appealable order before the

NCLAT. Learned senior counsel for the petitioner submits that

since the order passed by the NCLT restoring the petition filed

by the respondent is without jurisdiction, therefore, petitioner

need not have to avail the alternate remedy of appeal before

the NCLAT and is entitle to invoke the writ jurisdiction of this

- 11 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



Court. In support of the said contention, learned senior

counsel has placed reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble

Apex Court in the case of Embassy Property Developments

Private Limited Vs State of Karnataka and Others1. It is

the contention that non-exercise of the power under Article 226

of the Constitution of India even in the case of availability of

alternate remedy is a self-imposed restraint by the High Courts.

It is his contention that if it is demonstrated that the order

passed by the statutory or quasi-judicial authority is with lack

of jurisdiction and in case of wrongful exercise of the available

jurisdiction the High Court is well within its power under Article

226 of the Constitution of India to adjudicate upon the validity

of the orders notwithstanding the availability of the alternate

remedy.



        15. In light of the aforesaid submission, it is necessary

to notice the facts of the case of Embassy Property

Developments Private Limited (supra). In the said case, the

question involved was whether the High Court was justified in

entertaining the Writ Petition under Article 226 of the

Constitution of India against an order passed by the NCLT



1



  (2020) 13 SCC 308

- 12 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



under the provisions of IBC, despite availability of a statutory

alternative remedy of appeal to the NCLAT. The said question

has been answered in paragraph 46 of the said judgment

holding that the NCLT whose order was questioned before the

High Court invoking the jurisdiction under 226 of the

Constitution of India did not had jurisdiction to entertain an

application against the Government of Karnataka for a direction

to execute Supplementary Lease Deed for the extension of the

mining lease. Since the NCLT chose to exercise the jurisdiction

not vested in it, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that the High

Court was justified in entertaining the writ petition filed by the

State of Karnataka, challenging the order passed by the NCLT,

directing it to execute the Supplementary Lease Deed. The

observation of the Hon'ble Apex Court is that the prayer which

has been granted by the NCLT could have been sought only

before the High Court, invoking the writ jurisdiction under

Article 226 of the Constitution of India and not before the

NCLT. It is under the said circumstances, the Hon'ble Apex

Court has held that the writ petition filed by the State of

Karnataka before the High Court of Karnataka was

maintainable. The facts and circumstances obtaining in the

present case and the judgment relied upon by the petitioner

- 13 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



are altogether different and therefore, the said judgment is not

helpful to the petitioner.



        16. Learned senior counsel for the petitioner has further

relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case

of Budhia Swain and Others Vs Gopinath Deb and Others2

and contended that the power to recall an order could be

exercised only under the following circumstances viz,



        (i) an order obtained by fraud;

        (ii) when the Court is misled by a party; and

        (iii) when the Court itself commits a mistake which

        prejudices a party.



        17. It is also his submission that a Tribunal or a Court

may recall an order made earlier under the following

circumstances:



        (i) the proceedings culminating into an order suffer from

        inherent lack of jurisdiction and such lack of jurisdiction is

        present;

        (ii) there exists fraud or collusion in obtaining the

        judgment;



2



  (1999) 4 SCC 396

- 14 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



        (iii) there has been a mistake of the Court prejudicing a

        party; and



        (iv) a judgment was rendered in ignorance of the fact

        that a necessary party had not been served at all or had

        died and his estate was not represented.



        18. Though the circumstances as stated in the

judgment relied upon by the petitioner do not specifically exist

in the present case, however, the circumstances which is cited

above i.e. there has been a mistake of the Court

prejudicing a party could be applied to the present case.

Inasmuch as, the NCLT while passing the order dated

11.01.2024 disposing of the petition filed by the respondent

permitting it to put forth its claim before the IRP appointed in

CP(IB) No.117/BB/2023 in accordance with the provisions of

the IBC, 2016 and the Regulations made there under did not

anticipate that the insolvency proceedings initiated by the

Canara Bank would get terminated on account of the OTS

between the petitioner and the Canara Bank. Therefore, it is in

the said circumstances, neither the respondent sought liberty

to revive the petition nor the Court has granted such liberty.

Therefore, this Court cannot come to a definite conclusion that

the NCLT had no inherent jurisdiction or lack of jurisdiction to

- 15 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



entertain the application filed by the respondent for recalling

and restoration of the petition filed by it, so as to accept the

contention of the petitioner that the writ petition is

maintainable since the NCLT did not had jurisdiction to

entertain the application for recalling.



        19. It is not in dispute that the IBC is a self-contained

Code. The remedy of appeal against an order passed by the

NCLT is specifically provided in the code itself. If the

jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is

exercised in the case of present nature, it would amount to

breaching the normal stream of judicial proceedings. The facts

and circumstances involved in the present case do not suggest

that an extraordinary circumstances exist for entertaining the

writ petition dehors the remedy of appeal. Whether the NCLT

had jurisdiction to entertain the application for recalling or

whether the application filed by the respondent for seeking

recalling and restoration of the petition filed by it was beyond

the period of limitation could also be a ground in a statutorily

provided appeal before the NCLAT. The said aspects need not

be gone into in a writ petition filed under Article 226 of the

Constitution of India. If the writ petition of the present nature is

entertained providing of alternative remedy of appeal under the

                     - 16 -



                             WP No. 30901 of 2024



statute would become otiose. Therefore, this Court is of the

opinion that the present writ petition cannot be entertained and

adjudicated on merits and the matter requires to be considered

only by the NCLAT in a properly constituted appeal under

Section 61 of the IBC, since the jurisdiction of appellate

Tribunal and the scope of the appellate remedy is wide.



        20. It is relevant to take note of the judgments of the

Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s Godrej Sara Lee

Ltd., Vs The Excise and Taxation Officer-Cum-Assessing

Authority & Others3 and WhirlPool Corporation Vs

Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai and Others4, wherein,

the Hon’ble Apex Court has laid down under what

circumstances, the writ court would be justified in entertaining

the writ petition despite existence of alternative remedy, which

are as follows:



        (i) where the writ petition seeks enforcement of any of

        the fundamental rights;



        (ii) where there is violation of principles of natural justice;



3



  (2025) 11 SCC 808



4



  (1998) 8 SCC 1

- 17 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



(iii) where the order or the proceedings are wholly

without jurisdiction; or



(iv) where the vires of an Act is challenged.



        This Court is of the opinion that none of the aforesaid

circumstances exist in the present case.



        21. Much of the arguments have been advanced insofar as

the request made by the petitioner for settlement under OTS and

the same is pending consideration. The said issue is outside the

scope of the present writ petition. However, by order dated

05.10.2026, taking note of the submission of learned senior

counsel for the petitioner, the respondent was called upon to

respond as to the consideration of request for OTS. In response to

the same, learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent had

submitted that the petitioner had been called upon to furnish

several documents and information for consideration of the request

for OTS, if only, the required documents and information are

furnished, the respondent would be in a position to take a decision

in the matter in accordance with the existing policy. Therefore, it is

for the petitioner to make good the requirement for consideration

of its request for OTS. No direction could be issued by this Court in

- 18 -



        WP No. 30901 of 2024



that regard. If the petitioner complies with the conditions of OTS

policy, there is no reason to believe that the respondent would not

consider the request for OTS, notwithstanding the proceeding

before the NCLT/NCLAT.



        22. In the result, the following:



                                           ORDER



        (i) The writ petition is dismissed.



        (ii) The petitioner is at liberty to approach the NCLAT by

filing a statutory appeal under Section 61 of IBC, if so advised.



        (iii) Since the petitioner is before this Court from

16.11.2024 till this day by prosecuting this writ petition, it is open

for the petitioner to seek exclusion of the time spent before this

Court by filing an appropriate application under Section 14 of the

Limitation Act.



        (iv) If such an application is filed, there is no reason to

believe that the NCLAT would not consider the same, taking note of

the pendency of this petition before this court since 2024.



        (v) In view of the fact that that interim order passed by

this Court is in operation since 19.11.2024, the same is extended

     - 19 -



             WP No. 30901 of 2024



for another period of 3 weeks from today to enable the petitioner to

approach the NCLAT and seek interim protection in accordance with

law.



        (vi) All the contentions of both the parties are kept open.



        (vii) Any observation made in this order is only for the

purpose of disposal of this writ petition. In the event of petitioner

filing an appeal before the NCLAT, the same shall be considered

without being influenced by the observations made in this order.



                  Sd/-

     (T.P.VIVEKANANDA)



                JUDGE

          NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

                        PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI

                                                  2026



IN THE MATTER OF:



Directorate of Enforcement                           …Applicant

Resolution Professional, Adel Landmarks Ltd. & Ors.

For Applicant    : Mr. Sanjeev Menon, Adv. for ED



For Appellant    : Mr. Krishnendu Dutta, Sr. Adv. & Mr. Abhijeet Sinha,

For Respondents     Sr. Adv. with Ms. Manvi Jain, Ms. Astha Singh, Ms.

                    Niharika, Adv.



                 : Ms. Shruti Munjal, Adv. for R1

                    Mr. Aslam Ahmed, Ms. Kheyali Singh, Adv. for

                    R3/ACRE



                               O R D E R

                            (Hybrid Mode)



Per: Barun Mitra, Member (Technical)



The present matter relates to I.A. 6907 of 2026 filed by Applicant-



Directorate of Enforcement (‘ED’ in short) seeking recall of the order dated



16.04.2026 passed by this Tribunal in CA(AT)(Ins)No. 460 of 2026 (hereinafter



referred to as the “impugned order”) wherein the order of the Adjudicating



Authority dated 27.02.2026 was set aside and I.A No. 1817 of 2023 filed by



the Resolution Professional (‘RP’ in short) seeking approval of the resolution



plan was revived for consideration by the Adjudicating Authority. Aggrieved



                                                                           Page 1 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

by the impugned order, the recall application has been filed with the following



prayers:



         a. Recall order dated 16.04.2026 passed by this Hon'ble

                  Tribunal in Company Appeal(AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of

                  2026;



         b. Declare that the attached properties could never have formed

                  part of the resolution plan and



         c. Pass such other orders/orders as this Hon'ble Tribunal may

                  deem fit.



2. Throwing light on the factual background of the matter at hand, Shri

Sanjeev Menon, the Ld. Counsel for the Applicant-ED submitted that the

Adjudicating Authority in its order dated 27.02.2026 had rejected the plan

approval application filed by the RP vide I.A No. 1817 of 2023 and remanded

the plan proposal back to the CoC for its consideration for re-examination in

the wake of subsequent developments including the Provisional Attachment

Order (‘PAO’ in short) dated 09.01.2026 passed by the ED provisionally

attaching some of the assets of the Corporate Debtor. This order of 27.02.2026

was challenged before this Tribunal by the Successful Resolution Applicant

(‘SRA’ in short). This Tribunal on 16.04.2026 passed the impugned order

reviving I.A. No. 1817 of 2023 before the Adjudicating Authority for passing

of fresh order in accordance with law in pursuance of which the Adjudicating

Authority passed an order on 19.05.2026 approving the resolution plan.



3. It was submitted by the Applicant that the impugned order was passed

by this Tribunal on 16.04.2026 without hearing or issuing any notice to the

ED though the order of the Adjudicating Authority which was under challenge

had been passed inter-alia on the basis of submissions of the ED. It was



                                                                           Page 2 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

added that the order of the Adjudicating Authority dealt with properties which

stood attached under PAO orders passed by the ED and the applicability of

Section 32A of the IBC on such properties. It was added that the impugned

order was passed without the Applicant being able to put forth their

arguments on Section 32A of IBC in the light of judgements of this Tribunal

in Anil Kohli v. Directorate of Enforcement in CA(AT)(Ins.) No. 389 of

2018 and in Vantage Point Asset Management Pvt. Ltd. v. Gaurav Mishra

2025 SCC OnLine NCLAТ 1652. Since this Tribunal had passed orders

without affording the ED an opportunity of hearing to field their submissions,

this amounted to breach of the principles of natural justice and therefore the

impugned order deserves to recalled. Reliance was placed on the judgment of

the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Asit Kumar Kar Vs. State of W.B. (2019) 2

SCC 703 wherein it has been held that it is a basic principle of justice that

no adverse orders should be passed against a party without hearing the party

and that an order which is passed without giving an opportunity of hearing

to an affected party can be recalled. It was further argued that it is well settled

that where an order is passed without affording a hearing to a person who is

likely to be affected by the order, such a person may seek recall of the order

by which it is aggrieved and that in this backdrop the ED-Applicant has

approached this Tribunal seeking recall of its order dated 16.04.2026. It was

asserted that the recall application is maintainable under Rule 11 of the

NCLAT Rules, 2016 which Rules do not lay down any specific limitation

period. Once the Applicant became aware of the impugned order dated

16.04.2026, it filed the recall application on 20.07.2026 which was contended

as a reasonable period of time.



                                                                           Page 3 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

4. Per contra, it was contended by Shri Krishnendu Dutta and Shri

Abhijeet Sinha, Ld. Sr. Counsels for the Respondents that while the impugned

order was passed on 18.04.2026, the recall application was filed by the

Applicant on 20.07.2026 which entailed a lapse exceeding 45 days in filing. It

was contended that though no fixed period of limitation is prescribed for a

recall application, such application must be filed within a reasonable time,

however, delay of over four months is not a reasonable period of time.

Moreover, this lapse in terms of delay is further compounded by the fact that

the affidavits supporting the recall application are dated 31.08.2026 while the

recall application was dated 20.07.2026 thus rendering the filing non-est.



5. Submission was further pressed that the statutory remedy available to

any person aggrieved by an order of this Tribunal is to file an appeal before

the Hon’ble Supreme Court under Section 62 of the IBC. However, in the

present case, no credible reason has been placed on record as to why the

Applicant did not proceed to challenge the impugned order despite having

sufficient time to do so after having acquired knowledge of the impugned

order. It was argued that the power of recall under Rule 11 of the NCLAT

Rules, 2016 cannot be invoked as a substitute for a time-barred appeal.



6. It was also contended that there is no dispute that the Adjudicating

Authority in pursuance of the order of this Tribunal of 16.04.2026 had

reconsidered the plan and approved the same on 19.05.2026. It was pointed

out that not only did the Applicant-ED not file any appeal challenging the

impugned order of 16.04.2026 despite being fully aware of the matter having

been remanded for reconsideration before the Adjudicating Authority, it also



                                                                           Page 4 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

did not take any steps to challenge the subsequent plan approval order of

19.05.2026 passed by the Adjudicating Authority. Not having challenged the

plan approval order passed by the Adjudicating Authority of 19.05.2026, even

after having participated in the proceedings remanded before the Adjudicating

Authority by the impugned order, the recall application is an attempt to

unsettle the plan approval order of 19.05.2026 which cannot be allowed as

the plan is already under implementation.



7. We have heard Ld. Counsels for the parties and perused the records

carefully.



8. The short question before us is whether there is any cogent ground

made out by the Applicant for filing this recall application.



9. For better appreciation of the matter at hand, we would like to first

notice some of the relevant dates necessary for deciding this recall application.

The Corporate Debtor had been admitted into CIRP on 05.12.2018. The CoC

approved the resolution plan of the SRA on 15.09.2022. Thereafter the RP had

filed plan approval application before the Adjudicating Authority vide I.A No.

1817 of 2023 on 20.01.2023. Much after the plan approval application had

been filed before the Adjudicating Authority, the Applicant-ED had issued

PAO order on 09.01.2026. The Adjudicating Authority did not approve the

plan approval application inter-alia on account of the PAO order dated

09.01.2026 and related developments and instead remanded back the

resolution plan to the CoC on 27.02.2026 for reconsideration and re-

examination. The order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 27.02.2026 was

challenged before this Tribunal. By the impugned order dated 16.04.2026,



                                                                           Page 5 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

this Tribunal revived I.A No. 1817 of 2023 before the Adjudicating Authority

for passing of a fresh order in accordance with law.



10. It is the case of the Applicant that they were not heard before passing

of the impugned order by this Tribunal. It was asserted that notice should

have been issued to the ED by this Tribunal as it was exercising its appellate

jurisdiction on the order of the Adjudicating Authority of 27.02.2026 which

was passed on the basis of submissions made by the ED. Having not

impleaded the ED it tantamount to denying a necessary party an opportunity

of hearing. A necessary party not being present before this Tribunal makes it

a fit case for recall.



11. When we look at the chronological sequence of events, we find that the

impugned order was passed on 16.04.2026 in which the Applicant was

undoubtedly not a party. It is also an undisputed fact that the Applicant had

become aware of the impugned order on 15.05.2026 as is evident from para

20 of the I.A No. 6907 of 2026 filed by the Applicant as reproduced below:



   “That it is submitted that since the ED was not made a party before this

   Ld. Tribunal, it was not aware of the Order of Ld. Tribunal dated

   16.04.2026 until the matter came up for hearing before the Ld. NCLT in

   the remanded proceedings”

12. The above pleading is an unequivocal admission that the Applicant was

well aware of the impugned order when the proceedings were remanded back

by this Tribunal to the Adjudicating Authority and was being heard.

Furthermore, on a pointed query made by this Bench, it was also admitted by

the Counsel for the Applicant that they had become aware of the remanded

proceedings on 16.05.2026. Thus, when it was pretty much within the



                                                                           Page 6 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

knowledge of the Applicant-ED by 16.05.2026 that the impugned order had

remanded the plan approval application back to the Adjudicating Authority,

they had ample opportunity to challenge the same by exercising the statutory

remedy available to them under Section 62 of the IBC.



13. If the Applicant on gaining awareness of the impugned order harboured

reasons for feeling aggrieved by it, nothing had stopped them from exercising

the statutory remedy of approaching the Hon’ble Apex Court as the limitation

period of 45 plus 15 had not yet expired. The Applicant-ED, instead, waited

until 20.07.2026 to file the present recall application. No credible reason has

been placed on record as to why the Applicant did not proceed to challenge

the impugned order despite having sufficient time to do so. Thus, though the

Applicant had ample opportunity to protect its interest against the impugned

order, for reasons better known to them, they had chosen not to avail of this

opportunity. Where a proper remedy such as by way of appeal was available

but was not availed, in such circumstances, filing of the recall application

tantamount to indirectly filing of an appeal against the impugned order of

16.04.2026 camouflaged as a recall. Allowing the recall in effect would mean

reopening of the hearing of Company Appeal No. 460 of 2026 which is

impermissible as the power of recall is not power of the Tribunal to rehear the

case.



14. Interestingly from the material on record, it is also clear that the

Adjudicating Authority after hearing the remanded proceedings had passed

orders approving the resolution plan on 19.05.2026. However, yet again, the

Applicant-ED did not file any appeal against the 19.05.2026 order passed by



                                                                           Page 7 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

the Adjudicating Authority approving the plan. A plan once approved by the

Adjudicating Authority and not having been challenged within the period

available for filing of a statutory appeal acquires finality and binds all

stakeholders including government authorities. This lends force and weight to

the contention of the Respondents that the present recall application is crafted

to seek review of the matter under the guise of recall.



15. The other limb of argument canvassed by the Applicant to justify their

recall application is that the impugned order so delivered was adverse to their

interests as the properties attached by the ED could not have formed part of

the resolution plan. To buttress their contention, the findings of this Tribunal

in the context of Section 32A of the IBC as contained in para 11 of the

impugned order has been attacked by the Applicant in their recall application.



16. To return our finding, we may first refer to Para 11 of the impugned

order of 16.04.2026 which is as extracted below:



“11. The next area of concern which led the Adjudicating Authority to

remand the plan back to the CoC relates to the subject property which

had come under PAO of the ED. It is the contention of the RP that the

attachment order had been issued subsequent to the approval of the plan

by the CoC. It was also emphatically asserted that the attachment was

only provisional and not final in nature as borne out from ED’s own

affidavit dated 02.02.2026. It was further contended by the RP that in

terms of Section 32A of the IBC, once a Resolution Plan is approved and

there is a change in management of the Corporate Debtor, the Corporate

Debtor and its properties stand protected from prosecution and

attachment for offences committed prior to the commencement of the CIRP.

Reliance was placed on the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in

Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power and Steel Limited & Ors. in Civil

Appeal No. 1808 of 2020 which has clearly recognized the effect of Section

32A of the IBC in protecting the assets of the Corporate Debtor from

enforcement proceedings arising out of prior offences once the Resolution

Plan stands approved and such property is covered under the Resolution



                                                                           Page 8 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

     Plan approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the IBC.

     Further, it was pointed out that this Hon’ble Tribunal in Vantage Point

     Asset Management Pvt. Ltd. v. Gaurav Misra, Resolution Professional of

     Alchemist Infra Realty Ltd in CA(AT)(Ins.) No. 1495 of 2024 reiterated that

     attachments or enforcement actions in relation to prior offences cannot

     impede the implementation of a Resolution Plan once the statutory

     protections under the IBC are triggered. We also notice that the RP had

     kept apprised the CoC of the ED proceedings. It is also the contention of

     the SRA that it had submitted its plan after conducting due diligence and

     after verifying all the information contained in the Information

     Memorandum and it was aware that as SRA it was eligible to claim

     benefit under Section 32A of the IBC which provides them protection in

     respect of properties provisionally attached by the ED. In this backdrop of

     RP having kept apprised the CoC of the ED proceedings and that the SRA,

     before submitting his plan, was also aware of the PAO on having done

     his share of due diligence, mere existence of PAO cannot be seen to render

     the resolution plan incapable of implementation. The Adjudicating

     Authority has failed to appreciate the statutory protection provided under

     Section 32A of the IBC and the binding judicial precedents governing the

     interplay between insolvency proceedings and enforcement actions. We

     therefore fail to appreciate the concern expressed in the impugned order

     of the need to remand the matter back again to the CoC on this ground.”



                                                                                 (Emphasis supplied)



17. It becomes clear from the above excerpts of the impugned order that



what was considered by this Tribunal in CA(AT)(Ins)No. 460 of 2026 was



whether the plan already approved by the CoC should go back again to the



CoC for a fresh exercise of the CoC’s commercial wisdom. The impugned order



had only set aside the decision of the Adjudicating Authority to remand the



plan back to the CoC and in doing so, the impugned order did not either stay



or set aside the PAO of the ED-Applicant.



18. A recall is warranted only where an adverse order is passed against a

party/person without hearing the party. This Appellate Tribunal in the

impugned order has merely directed the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider

the plan proposal in accordance with law and did not adjudicate either on the



                                                                           Page 9 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

sustainability and tenability of the resolution plan or the enforcement actions

qua the PAO orders. Prima-facie, no adverse order had been passed against

the Applicant-ED by this Tribunal in the impugned order, there is no

substance in the argument that the impugned order needs to be recalled on

grounds of non-impleadment of the ED while passing the impugned order.



19. The judgment in Asit Kumar Kar cannot come to the rescue of the

Applicant as the facts in that case are clearly distinguishable for in that case,

the licenses of the Applicants were cancelled without hearing them, while in

the present case, no rights of the ED were adjudicated upon nor any interest

of the Applicant interfered with by the impugned order. As the impugned order

did not contain any directions against the ED, it is a misconceived proposition

on part of the Applicant to claim to have been prejudiced by the impugned

order or that the impugned order could not have been passed without them

having been made a party therein and also heard. Hence, the reliance placed

on Asit Kumar Kar judgment is wholly misplaced.



20. Further, when we see prayer (b) of the recall application which has been

reproduced in the opening paragraph, it clearly seeks declaration that the

properties attached by the ED could not have formed part of the resolution

plan. Effectively this amounts to seeking a substantive declaration on merits

which is wholly outside the scope of a recall application. Thus, we are

persuaded to believe that the Applicant-ED under the guise of recall is seeking

a rehearing and review of the impugned order on merits together with a fresh

declaratory relief which is impermissible in the exercise of power of recall. The



                                                                           Page 10 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

present application of the Applicant is styled as recall but in essence is a

review application and therefore cannot be entertained.



21. In view of the above discussion, we are of the considered view that the

reasons for recall, as narrated in the recall application, do not fall within the

scope and ambit of recall of an order passed by this Tribunal. No cogent

grounds for entertaining the recall having been made out, we reject the recall

application. No costs.



                            [Justice Yogesh Khanna]

                             Officiating Chairperson



                                             [Barun Mitra]

                                   Member (Technical)



                                    [Ajai Das Mehrotra]

                                   Member (Technical)



Place: New Delhi

Date : 02nd November, 2026

Sheetal/Farhan



                                                                           Page 11 of 11



I.A. No. 6907 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 460 of 2026

                       J U D G M EN T

                       (2nd November, 2026)



SHARAD KUMAR SHARMA, MEMBER (J)



         These are two connected company appeals, though they are arising out

of two separate interlocutory applications being I.A. No. 4139/ND/2026 as it

stood engaged consideration in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1928 of 2026



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -3-



and I.A. No. 4138/ND/2026 as it stood engaged consideration in Company

Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1929 of 2026.

2. A few common facts, which engages consideration are that:



         The proceedings of the Company Petition, being C.P. (IB) No.

723(ND)/2020, were taken up before the Ld. Tribunal, and the Ld. Tribunal

vide its order of 28.08.2025, after recording the absence of the appellant

(who was Respondent No. 5 in the proceedings of the company petition),

directed the matter to be proceeded ex-parte.

3. By virtue of the said order of 28.08.2025, the Ld. Tribunal had

directed the matter to be proceeded ex-parte against the appellant, in terms

of its earlier order of 04.07.2023. The records of the company appeal do not

reflect, as to what proceedings took place on 04.07.2023, which has been

taken into consideration and has been referred by the Ld. Tribunal in its

order of 28.08.2025, while directing the proceedings to be taken ex-parte as

against the present appellants. This order to proceed ex-parte stands good,

having not been set aside, and admittedly, it has never even been sought to

be recalled by the appellant during the pendency of the proceedings of the

company petition.



4. At a much belated stage, a recall was preferred, seeking recall of the

order dated 28.08.2025, which was filed by the appellants herein, before the

Ld. Tribunal on 05.01.2026 i.e. almost after 4 months. What consequences

the said application reached are the facts, which are neither on record nor



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -4-



pleaded by the appellants. An order was later passed by the Ld. Tribunal on

27.04.2026, after taking into consideration the effect of the earlier order

passed on 28.08.2025, directing to proceed with the matter ex-parte and

observed that the application for recall, being I.A. No.1599/2026 that was

preferred by Respondents No. 5,7 & 8 is in the proceedings for recalling the

order of 28.08.2025. It was observed that since the application itself for

recalling the order to proceed ex-parte was barred by limitation as having not

been preferred within 30 days, as prescribed under Article 122 of 3rd

division of Part-I of the Limitation Act.



5. Hence, the Ld. Tribunal on 27.04.2026 passed an order that, since the

application for recall i.e. I.A. No.1599/2026 was preferred on 05.01.2026

seeking recall of the order dated 28.08.2025 directing to proceed the matter

ex-parte, it had declined to interfere in the application on the ground that

the applicants to I.A. No.1599/2026, seeking recall of the order dated

28.08.2025, the applicants for recall had been negligent in pursuing the

proceedings and imposed a cost of Rs. 25,000/- to be deposited in the Prime

Minister’s Relief Fund, because of the fact that the recall application was

knowingly, it has been preferred on 05.01.2026 after a lapse of a substantial

time period i.e. 174 days and was not supported with the delay condonation

application. Hence, an opportunity was granted to file a delay condonation

application.



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -5-



6. Accordingly, the appellant filed I.A. No. 4139/ND/2026, seeking

condonation of 174 days of delay, that has chanced in preferring an

application, which was for setting aside the order of 28.08.2025.



7. At this juncture, itself we make it clear, that it is surprising as to the

manner in which the appellant has taken up the proceedings for the reason

being that:



   (i) Order to proceed ex-parte was passed on 28.08.2025

   (ii) Recall was filed on 05.01.2026

   (iii) By an order of 27.04.2026, the appellant was granted time to file delay



         condonation application

   (iv) Meaning thereby, if at all any application was to be filed by the



         appellant for seeking condonation of delay, that ought to have been

         filed at least within 30 days from the date of the order, i.e.,

         27.04.2026, i.e. when the liberty was granted by the Ld. Tribunal to

         file the delay condonation application. But surprisingly the application

         seeking condonation of delay, being I.A. No. 4138/ND/2026, was filed

         by the appellant on 24.08.2026 that means almost approximately after

         four months, of grant of permission to file delay condonation.



8. That itself shows that the appellant was not diligent and vigilant too in

contesting the proceedings, despite when he was made conscious, that the

recall application of 05.01.2026, was mandatorily supposed to be supported

with the delay condonation application, and despite when he was made



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -6-



conscious of the fact by an order of 27.04.2026, he should have filed an

application for the delay condonation application as contemplated under

Article 122 of the Limitation Act i.e. within 30 days at least, and couldn’t

have waited to file the delay condonation application on 24.08.2026 that

itself would be barred by limitation.



9. In order to better elucidation, the provisions of Article 122 of the

Limitation Act are extracted hereunder:



            “122. To restore a suit or appeal or application for review or

            revision dismissed for default of appearance or for want of

            prosecution or for failure to pay costs of service of process or

            to furnish security for costs…… 30 days”

10. We have already observed, that even in the case of the appellant, if the

limitation is considered from the date of his knowledge, i.e., 16.10.2025, as

pleaded in the application for condonation of delay itself as well as in the

recall application. It would be much beyond the period of limitation

prescribed under Article 122 of Limitation Act, as extracted above, which

provides for a determination of 30 days’ delay from the “date of dismissal”,

and not from the date of knowledge. Even in those circumstances, too, the

application for condonation of delay as well as for recall would be falling to

be much beyond the period of limitation as prescribed, and since 174 days

are inordinate, it cannot be condoned.



11. Another glaring feature though earlier observed, but which is required

to be considered is that if the application for delay condonation itself is taken



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -7-



into consideration in paragraph 7, the appellant has raised the following

pleading:



            “7. That the Respondents most respectfully submit that they

            gained knowledge of the order dated 28.08.2025 only on

            16.10.2025 when the Respondents had logged in to observe

            the proceedings. However, the matter did not reach on that

            day. Thereafter, upon perusing the order sheet, the

            Respondents were shocked and surprised to note that vide

            order dated 28.08.2025, they had been proceeded ex-parte

            and it was further observed that there was no representation

            on behalf of the Respondents on several previous dates.”



12. This pleading in itself show, that the appellant got the knowledge of

the order of 28.08.2025, back as on 16.10.2025, when he logged into the

proceedings. If the appellant got the knowledge on 16.10.2025, then at least

the recall of the order of 28.08.2025 should have been filed within 30 days

and the appellant couldn’t have waited till 05.01.2026 and more importantly

what we have already asserted the date when he filed the delay condonation

application i.e. 24.08.2026.

13. If this application, which was preferred by the appellant seeking recall

of the order dated 28.08.2025, which came up for consideration before the

Ld. Tribunal and the same has been rejected by the impugned order, is taken

into consideration in paragraph 7, admitted knowledge is of 16.10.2025.

14. The Ld. Tribunal, while considering the purport and purpose of

seeking condonation of delay, has passed an order rejecting the delay

condonation application, observing thereof, that when an application for

seeking condonation of delay is to be preferred, first of all, the delay has to

be reasonably explained, and looking at the contents of the application in



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -8-



itself, the applicant was expected to explain the same in the application. As

there was no reason given in the application, as to what prevented the

counsel or the parties to appear before the Tribunal on the date when the

matter was proceeded ex parte, i.e., on 28.08.2025. Hence, the delay was

declined to be condoned. And accordingly, as a consequence of the same, an

order passed on I.A. No. 218 of 2023, was declined to be recalled.

15. Another reason, and quite validly too which has been argued and

taken into account in the proceedings before the Ld. Tribunal was, that the

counsel who was pursuing the matter on his behalf had stopped

representing him and his cause in the proceedings without there being any

prior intimation to the appellant. In fact, this ground, which has been carved

out by the appellant in the application for seeking condonation of delay,

doesn’t seem to be justified in the absence of any credible material on record

to show that when the earlier counsel had withdrawn his Vakalatnama from

the records and had stopped pursuing the proceedings on behalf of the

appellant. Besides that, even if is presumed that because of the conduct of

the earlier counsel, he remained unrepresented even prior to 28.08.2025.

There is nothing on record to show that the appellant ever made any

communications with his counsel or had carried any step as against his

earlier counsel for its professional dereliction for not pursuing the matter on

his behalf, particularly when the authority vested by the appellant continued

to operate as on the date when the ex-parte order of 28.08.2025 was passed.

There had been no pleading on record to show that appellant had ever



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

                                                            -9-



communicated with his counsel, showing his inquisitiveness towards his

case, showing his diligence to contest the proceedings.

16. It’s not the case of the appellant, that the earlier counsel ever refused

to appear. Nor is it the case of the appellant or his counsel too that, upon the

refusal of the earlier counsel, he has ever taken his no objection for engaging

another counsel as contemplated under Order III Rule 4 of CPC, which was

required by the counsel who has filed the delay condonation application, nor

is there any pleading to the said effect in the application for seeking

condonation of delay.

17. Much authenticity cannot be attached to the pleadings raised in that

context about the conduct of the previous counsel as raised in paragraph 5

of the application, since it didn’t contain any credible material or a basis, if

this could be permitted to be accepted by us for the purposes of condonation

of delay in recalling of an order. It would rather be opening a pandora's box;

invariably, any party to the proceedings could be filing a recall application on

that pretext, and more particularly when the other counsel who has been

engaged for the purposes of filing the recall application has not taken his no

objection from the earlier counsel, as required under law.

18. As the delay is inordinate of 174 days and there is no plausible reason,

which has been assigned by the appellant, and more particularly when the

application itself has been preferred much beyond the period of acquiring the

knowledge on 16.10.2025. The reasons in the application cannot be



Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1928 & 1929 of 2026

-10-



accepted, as they are being artificially created for the purposes of the present

application itself.

19. Thus, the impugned order rejecting the delay condonation application,

i.e., I.A. No. 4139/ND/2026, doesn’t suffer from any apparent error that

would call for any interference by us. In the exercise of our appellate

jurisdiction, particularly in a proceeding of I&B Code, where the statute itself

intends that the proceedings have to be completed within a specified time

frame and where the time is the essence of the proceedings.

20. The connected company appeal, which arises out of an order of

31.08.2026, is against the rejection of I.A. No. 4138/ND/2026 for recalling

the order of 28.08.2025 because of the fact that we have already rejected the

delay condonation application in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1928 of

2026, i.e., I.A. No. 4139/ND/2026. This appeal too would stand covered by

the said judgment, hence, would stand dismissed, because the consequence

of the rejection of the delay condonation application is obviously an

application to set aside an ex-parte order dated 28.08.2025 would meet its

legal death. Hence, this company appeals too would stand dismissed.



                                                    [Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma]

                                                                         Member (Judicial)



                                                              [Arun Baroka]

                                                     Member (Technical)



                                                         [Indevar Pandey]

                                                    Member (Technical)

        NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

                      PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI

                                          No. 330 of 2026

Versus

400098



Present:



For Applicant  : Mr. Gaurav Mitra, Sr. Adv. with Ms. Neeha Nagpal, Ms.

For Appellant     Asha Shah, Mr. Ajatshatru Singh Rawat, Ms. Aishwarya

                  Modi, Adv



               : Mr. K. Dutta, Sr. Adv. with Mr. Atul Sharma, Mrs.

                  Renuka Iyen, Mr. Aditya Vashisth, Mr. Arpit Paul, Adv.



                      O R D E R

                   (Hybrid Mode)



Per: Barun Mitra, Member (Technical)



The present matter relates to I.A. 7094 of 2026 filed by Applicant-Excel



Arcade Pvt. Ltd. seeking recall of the order dated 22.05.2026 (hereinafter



referred to as the ‘impugned order’) passed by this Tribunal in I.A. No. 1245



of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT)(Ins) No. 330 of 2026.



2. Making submissions on behalf of the Applicant, Shri Gaurav Mitra, Ld.

Sr. Counsel submitted that the Applicant vide Company Appeal No. 330 of

2026 had challenged an order dated 08.12.2025 passed by Adjudicating

Authority in CP (IB) No. 1068/MB/2023. This appeal was accompanied with

an application praying for condonation of delay in filing of the appeal which



                                                                                                            Page 1 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

application was dismissed by this Tribunal on 22.05.2026 on the ground that

it had been e-filed beyond the outer limit of 30 + 15 days prescribed under

Section 61(2) of the IBC. Contending that the delay was not occasioned by any

negligence/laches on their part but was due to technical glitches in the e-

filing system administered by the NCLAT Registry, their delay condonation

application ought not to have been rejected by this Tribunal. The present

application I.A. No. 7094 of 2026 is a recall application filed before this

Tribunal seeking correction of the prejudice suffered by them for rejection of

their condonation of delay application by this Tribunal.



3. Elaborating further on the condonation of delay application, it was

submitted that the 45 days outer time-period to file the appeal against the

order dated 08.12.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority was to come to

an end on 22.01.2026. The concerned counsel had readied all the documents

and thereafter attempted to e-file the appeal on 22.01.2026 but could not

succeed since the e-filing portal of the Registry of this Tribunal was

unresponsive. On account of this technical bottleneck, the counsel sent an

email to the IT Support Wing of this Registry on 22.01.2026 at 22:36 hours

along with the copy of the appeal petition with a request that the email be

treated to serve the purpose of e-filing. Though the above email dated

22.01.2026 was received by the NCLAT Registry, but the same got

quarantined by phishing protection controls of this Registry for which the

Applicant cannot be blamed or held responsible in any manner. The appeal

could thereafter be effectively e-filed only on 28.01.2026.



                                                                                               Page 2 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

4. The Ld. Counsel for the Applicant submitted that in similar

circumstances, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Regional Provident Fund

Commissioner-II vs. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors 2026 INSC 1003 had

dismissed an order rejecting the condonation of delay application beyond the

45 days period passed by this Tribunal since the delay in e-filing was on

account of technical defects in the back-end of NCLAT Registry. The Hon’ble

Apex Court further held in this case that the date on which the first bonafide

attempt was made by the litigant to e-file the appeal is what is to be kept in

mind while computing limitation period. The Hon’ble Supreme Court held that

in such special circumstances, the NCLAT ought to have invoked the higher

principle of “actus curiae neminem gravabit”. It was therefore contended by

the Applicant that in the present case too, the same precept was applicable

and limitation should have run against them only from the date when the e-

filing portal was open and functional to receive the appeal. The date of first

attempt to e-file by the Applicant should have been treated as date of

presentation of the appeal since the fault lay with the e-filing system of the

NCLAT Registry and as this was not done, hence, the recall application ought

to be allowed by this Tribunal in exercise of the inherent powers under Rule

11 of NCLAT Rules.



5. It was further submitted that the Applicant had made an attempt to e-

file the appeal on 22.01.2026 but finally succeeded in doing so only on

28.01.2026 which was admittedly 5 days beyond the 30+15 days period. It

was emphatically asserted that even during the 5 intervening days between

22.01.2026 and 28.01.2026, the Applicant had continued to make efforts to



                                                                                               Page 3 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

e-file the appeal though unsuccessfully. Towards explaining the 5 days gap,

it was submitted that there were only two effective working days as

24.01.2026 and 25.01.2026 fell on Saturday and Sunday while 26.01.2026

was a gazetted holiday on account of Republic Day.



6. It was also belaboured that this Tribunal in the impugned order had

wrongly rejected their delay condonation application by relying on the NIC

report received by the NCLAT Registry which stated that the NCLAT portal

was functional on 22.01.2026 as 70 filings were done on that day. It was

contended that this report cannot be relied upon as it does not disclose the

exact time when these 70 filings were done. Nor does the report establish that

appeals were successfully filed by others during the same time when the

Applicant also made its attempts to file the appeal but had failed. It was

contended that the fact that some users were able to e-file their appeal at

some hours of the day does not establish that portal was available to the

Applicant at the time they had attempted to e-file their appeal. It vehemently

contended that this Tribunal has not considered the absence of time-stamps

in the report of the NIC in respect of the 70 filings and that this Tribunal while

rejecting their delay condonation application had not dealt with this aspect.



7. Repelling the above arguments, Shri Krishnendu Datta, Ld. Sr. Counsel

for the Respondent contended that the recall application cannot be

entertained as it is not maintainable. It was asserted that there are limited

grounds for filing the recall application viz. when an order has been obtained

by fraud or collusion or when a necessary party has not been impleaded or

when the court has mistakenly passed an order or that the court lacked



                                                                                               Page 4 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

jurisdiction to pass such an order. Since none of these grounds have been

made out, the question of entertaining the recall application does not arise.



8. Submission was further pressed that in the present case, the delay

condonation application had been rejected by this Tribunal by way of a

detailed impugned order on 22.05.2026. This impugned order was a well-

reasoned, speaking order which was never challenged by Applicant before the

Hon’ble Supreme Court. This distinguishes the factual matrix of the present

case from that of Mamta Binani case. In the Mamta Binani case, the

aggrieved litigant had challenged the rejection of their delay condonation

application by filing an appeal before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. In the

present case when the Applicant did not file an appeal before Hon’ble Apex

Court within the prescribed limitation period, the impugned order passed by

this Tribunal dated 22.05.2026 had attained finality. It is only on realising

that the Applicant cannot appeal before the Supreme Court having turned

time-barred, the present recall application is a clever attempt to seek a back-

door entry to re-open their Company Appeal.



9. We have heard the arguments advanced by both the parties as well as

perused the records carefully.



10. The first issue before us is the maintainability of the recall application.

To answer this question, we would like to rely on the principles set out by the

judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in Budhia Swain v.

Gopinath Deb (1999) 4 SCC 396. This judgement delves into the intricacies

surrounding the powers to review or recall orders and serves as a reference-



                                                                                               Page 5 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

point in delineating the boundaries of review and recall powers. The relevant



extract from the order is as reproduced below:



   “8. In our opinion a tribunal or a court may recall an order earlier made by

   it if:

   (i) the proceedings culminating into an order suffer from the inherent lack

   of jurisdiction and such lack of jurisdiction is patent,

   (ii) there exists fraud or collusion in obtaining the judgment,

   (iii) there has been a mistake of the court prejudicing a party, or

   (iv) a judgment was rendered in ignorance of the fact that a necessary

   party had not been served at all or had died and the estate was not

   represented.

   The power to recall a judgment will not be exercised when the ground for

   reopening the proceedings or vacating the judgment was available to be

   pleaded in the original action but was not done or where a proper remedy

   in some other proceeding such as by way of appeal or revision was

   available but was not availed. The right to seek vacation of a judgment

   may be lost by waiver, estoppel or acquiescence.

   9. A distinction has to be drawn between lack of jurisdiction and a mere

   error in exercise of jurisdiction. The former strikes at the very root of the

   exercise and want of jurisdiction may vitiate the proceedings rendering

   them and the orders passed therein a nullity. A mere error in exercise of

   jurisdiction does not vitiate the legality and validity of the proceedings and

   the order passed thereon unless set aside in the manner known to law by

   laying a challenge subject to the law of limitation.”

11. It is the case of the Applicant that the recall application is warranted



since the impugned order had failed to appreciate that their attempt to e-file



the appeal within the prescribed limitation period had failed not on account



of any lapse or negligence on their part but because of system failure of the



e-filing portal which had turned unresponsive. To overcome the stalemate



arising out of the technical glitch, the Applicant had been compelled to send



the appeal petition by email but the same got quarantined due to back-end



phishing control checks put in place by the Registry. It was also contended



that while in terms of the extant NCLAT circular, an email cannot substitute



                                                                                               Page 6 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

the requirement of e-filing, in the present case, this recourse of filing the

appeal through email had to be resorted to because of the exceptional

circumstances on account of non-responsiveness of the e-filing portal of

NCLAT Registry. Furthermore, in view of the fact that in similarly placed

peculiar circumstances, the Mamta Binani judgment had restored the delay

condonation application therein, applying the same ratio, the present recall

application stood well justified.



12. Per contra, it is the case of the Respondent that since none of the

grounds for recall as outlined in the Budhia Swain judgement have been

demonstrated by the Applicant to be applicable in the present case, the

question of entertaining the recall application does not arise. It is also their

contention that it is a misconceived proposition on the part of the Applicant

to rely on the Mamta Binani judgment for in that case the rejection of the

delay condonation application was challenged by filing an appeal before the

Hon’ble Supreme Court and was not a recall application.



13. When we look at the material on record, we find that it has not been

substantiated by the Applicant as to whether and how the impugned order

can be said to have been obtained by fraud or collusion or passed without

their impleadment as necessary party or that the court lacked jurisdiction to

pass such an order or was mistakenly passed so as to justify the filing of a

recall. We also notice that in the present case, the recall application was filed

on 24.09.2026 after lapse of more than four months since the passing of the

impugned order by this Tribunal on 22.05.2026. The Applicant did not

challenge the impugned order and waited until the passing of the Mamta



                                                                                               Page 7 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

Binani judgment on 10.09.2026 and thereafter within a fortnight therefrom,

filed the recall application on 24.09.2026. The recall application not having

been premised on any of the grounds provided for in the Budhia Swain

judgement, this is clearly a camouflaged attempt to seek review of the

judgment in the guise of recall which cannot be permitted as it upsets the

doctrine of finality.



14. The Budhia Swain judgement as extracted above reinforces the

principle of finality and mandates that challenges to orders must be grounded

in expressly provided legal avenues and processes. The principle of res

judicata and the doctrine of finality is one of the edifices on which the judicial

architecture rests to checkmate arbitrary or unfounded attempts to overturn

concluded decisions.



15. The impugned order which has been sought for recall was a reasoned,

speaking order which was never challenged by Applicant before the Hon’ble

Supreme Court even after having participated in the proceedings therein

before this Tribunal. Upon an order having attained finality, any party

aggrieved by the order must exhaust his remedies within the legal framework.

The principle of res judicata is hinged on the pivotal framework that issues

once decided conclusively in a lis may not be reopened for if it were to be

otherwise, no dispute can be resolved or concluded. It is no longer open to the

litigant to undo the effect of any order unless it is established that the order

was obtained by fraud/collusion or that necessary party was excluded

therefrom or that the court lacked jurisdiction or had mistakenly passed the

order. It matters little as to whether the order passed was erroneous as long



                                                                                               Page 8 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

as lis is heard and a conclusive finding thereon has been rendered and such

finding has remained unchallenged. In the present case, the delay

condonation application stood decided on the merits and was not challenged

within the prescribed period of limitation before the next higher appellate

body, hence, the order had acquired finality. The recall application, in the

shape that it has been filed, has the characteristics of review of an order

passed on merits. We are of the considered view that allowing the present

recall application will tantamount to disturbing the foundational principles of

res judicata which we do not countenance.



16. This brings us to the second limb of argument canvassed by the

Respondent that in the Mamta Binani judgment, the Hon’ble Supreme Court

took cognisance of the fact that the litigant therein had overshot the 30 + 15

days limitation period by only one day while in this case, the Applicant has

tried to gloss over 5 days delay beyond 45 days after the initial e-filing on

22.01.2026 purportedly failed. To our minds, the plea taken by the Applicant

that there were 3 days of intervening holidays to explain the delay is a

frivolous argument since e-filing facility in the Registry remains functional

and open 24x7x365 and holidays do not come in the way of e-filing of an

appeal. The Applicant has thus grossly failed to explain the mitigating reasons

for the 5 days delay in filing of the appeal beyond the statutorily permissible

period which puts serious question marks on the claim of the Applicant that

they were steadfastly pursuing their quest for filing Company Appeal (AT)(Ins)

No. 330 of 2026 in a bonafide manner.



                                                                                               Page 9 of 10



I.A No. 7094 of 2026 in I.A. No. 1245 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 330 of 2026

17. At this stage it is also felt necessary to observe that since this is a recall

application, we are neither expected nor do we wish to enter into the merits

of the impugned order. Hence, we are refraining from looking into the

contention raised by the Applicant with regard to the absence of time-stamps

in the report of the NIC regarding the 70 filings purportedly completed on the

e-filing portal on the same day on which the Applicant had admittedly failed

to e-file their appeal. The power of recall is not the power to rehear the case

to find out any apparent error in the judgment. This lies in the scope and

ambit of a review of judgment which power to review has not been vested upon

this Tribunal.



18. In result, the present recall application lacks merit and is accordingly

dismissed. No costs.



                            [Justice Yogesh Khanna]

NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL

              PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI



Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 174 of 2026



[Arising out of Order dated 09.09.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority

Tankapani Road, Bhubaneswar,
