For Appellant



 For Respondent : Mr. Sudeep Singh, Advocate.



                              J U D G M E N T



JUSTICE YOGESH KHANNA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON



         This appeal is filed against an impugned order dated 09.09.2025 passed

by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal, Cuttack

Bench) in C.P. (IB) No.18/CB/2024. Vide the impugned order, the petition

filed under Section 7 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (for short

the “IBC”) on 10.04.2024 was accepted and M/s. SS Aluminium Private

Limited was admitted into insolvency for default of Rs.15,88,33,394.26/-.



2. As per the averments made in the application under Section 7 of the

IBC, numerous credit facilities were given to the corporate debtor from time

to time and the loan of the company was declared Non-Performing Asset

(“NPA”) on 11.05.2021. Further, the recall notice was issued on 04.10.2021

for an outstanding amount of Rs.13,48,00,000/-. Thereafter a notice dated

17.05.2021 under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, was issued and

the appellant had given the OTS dated 23.11.2021, 01.12.2021 and

13.01.2022 to the bank, but did not make any payment and ultimately on

23.12.2021, notice under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, was

issued and the proceedings were initiated against the asset of the corporate

debtor.



3. The application under Section 7 of the IBC was contested by the

appellant herein, primarily, on 2 grounds viz. (a) limitation and (b) the

procedure under the Notification dated 29.05.2015 issued by the Ministry of

Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, annexed as Annexure A-2 to the

appeal, was never followed. It was argued, as per the Notification, the banks

were obliged to identify the incipient stress in the account of the Micro, Small

and Medium Enterprises (“MSME”) and after identification of the MSME,

could voluntarily initiate proceedings under this framework, if enterprise

reasonably apprehends failure of its business or its inability or likely inability



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                        2 of 8

to pay debts and before the accumulated losses of the enterprise equals to the

half or more of its entire net worth. It was argued, it was never done and as

such the petition under Section 7 of the IBC was pre-mature and ought to

have been dismissed.



4. We have gone through the impugned order, which had dealt with the

issue of limitation and had rejected such contention saying not only there

were 3 OTS submitted by the appellant before the bank, but also on

13.07.2021, the appellant had executed an instrument of acknowledgement

of debt. It was observed by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority that on multiple

occasions, the settlement was sought by sending various OTS proposals and

thus the appellant had admitted its liability towards debt and the existence

of debt and default was purely established and the petition was within

limitation. We agree with this finding.



5. On issue b) viz. the applicability of MSMED Act, 2006 and its

Notification, the Ld. Adjudicating Authority held as under:



                 “12. The Tribunal observes that the respondent's

                 claim of MSME status under the MSMED Act,

                 2006. was raised for the first time only in the

                 Written Submissions and not in its Reply. It is a

                 well-established principle of law that grounds not

                 pleaded in the initial pleadings cannot be

                 introduced at the stage of written submissions, as

                 pleadings define the scope of adjudication. The

                 plea now raised involves disputed questions of

                 fact and has not been supported by any

                 documentary evidence. Therefore. the contention

                 of the Corporate Debtor regarding its MSME

                 status and reliance on SO 1432(E) dated

                 29.05.2015 cannot be regarded as conclusive.

                 Accordingly, the respondent's assertion that it is

                 registered under the MSMED Act, 2006, and that

                 the applicant has not followed the proceed. We

                 outlined in the Judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                                                     3 of 8

                 Court in Pro Knit (supra) fails, since the

                 respondent has never informed this Tribunal that

                 respondent was registered under the MSMED Act,

                 2006, during its reply nor has it produced any

                 MSME registration certificate to support its own

                 contention.”

6. The learned counsel for the appellant has referred to the additional

documents filed by him and referred to the I.A. No.4708/2026 filed for taking

on record the additional documents, wherein he annexed a letter dated

30.10.2023 written to General Manager, Canara Bank asking for revival of his

sick unit under Rehabilitation Scheme and such letter was duly answered on

10.11.2023, wherein the District Industry Centre, Balasore had requested the

General Manager, Canara Bank, Bhubaneswar to provide him cooperation

and re-finance for sustainable revival of the unit under Sick Rehabilitation

Scheme of RBI at the earliest. However, it was never done.



7. The said letters have been challenged by the learned counsel for the

respondent as are produced in this appeal for the first time. Nevertheless, it

was argued the MSME status of the appellant was valid only upto 31.03.2021

and thereafter the appellant ceased to be a MSME unit. It is also evident from

the record, no application was filed under Section 13(3-A) of the SARFAESI

Act, 2002, asserting, it was an MSME or intending to claim benefit of

framework. Further, if one peruse the Notification dated 29.05.2015, its

paragraph 4 says an application needs to be filed by the MSME to the

Committee for Stressed MSME, in the manner as may be specified by the

Bank for a corrective action plan and terms thereof. No such application was

ever filed when notice dated 17.05.2021 under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI

was given. Rather no reply was ever given to such notice.



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                        4 of 8

8. Even the impugned order shows, such a plea was never taken before

the Court while arguing the matter and it was only in the written submissions

the plea of it being MSME was taken for the first time.



9. In ‘Shri Swami Samarth Construction & Finance Solution & Ors.’

Vs. ‘The Board of Directors of NKGSB Co-op. Bank Ltd. & Ors.’, reported

in [MANU/SC/0997/2025], the Hon’ble Supreme Court has held:



                 “5. The Notification detailing the FRAMEWORK, more

                 particularly paragraph 1 and its sub-paragraphs, have

                 to be read together to make its terms effective and

                 meaningful. Although, in the sequence of the

                 FRAMEWORK “Identification by Banks or Creditors”

                 comes first, it is immediately followed by

                 “Identification by the Enterprise”. In terms of sub-

                 paragraph 2, any MSME may choose to voluntarily

                 initiate proceedings under the FRAMEWORK if it

                 “reasonably apprehends failure of its business or its

                 inability or likely inability to pay debts and before the

                 accumulated losses of the enterprise equals to half or

                 more of its entire net worth” (emphasis ours). The

                 obligation of the MSME does not end there. For

                 initiation of proceedings under the FRAMEWORK, the

                 application has to be verified by an affidavit of an

                 authorised person and upon receipt of a request, the

                 lending bank/secured creditor is mandatorily bound to

                 proceed in terms of the FRAMEWORK and to constitute

                 a committee to identify incipient stress in the account.



                 6. The way Mr. Nedumpara urges us to read the

                 Notification and the terms of the FRAMEWORK, if

                 accepted, would lead to the conclusion that every

                 lending bank/secured creditor under the SARFAESI

                 Act would be obliged to find out in every event of

                 continuing default, likely to give rise to classification of

                 the relevant account as NPA, whether the borrower is

                 an MSME to which the FRAMEWORK applies, whether

                 its business has failed or whether it is suffering from

                 any disability to pay its debts; and upon receiving a

                 response, to apply the terms thereof by, inter alia,

                 including the account in the Special Mention Account

                 for the claim for a corrective action plan to be

                 considered by the Committee for stressed MSMEs. This

                 could not have been the intention behind introduction

                 of the FRAMEWORK to aid the MSMEs which, for



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                                                               5 of 8

                 reasons personal to them, is unable to clear its debt

                 and require revival and rehabilitation that the

                 FRAMEWORK envisages. If indeed it is only the

                 obligation of the lending bank/secured creditor to

                 identify incipient stress in the account, sub paragraphs

                 2 and 3 of paragraph 1 would be rendered redundant.

                 An MSME, despite finding that its business is failing or

                 that it is unable to pay its debts or accumulation of

                 losses equals to half or more of its entire net worth and

                 classification of its account as NPA is imminent, it

                 would rest on its oars believing that it has no

                 responsibility and that its account will not be classified

                 as NPA because it is the entire obligation of the lending

                 bank/secured creditor to do what the FRAMEWORK

                 requires. We would read and interpret the seemingly

                 confusing terms of the FRAMEWORK harmoniously to

                 ensure that a right under the MSME Act is not

                 destroyed by the SARFAESI Act or vice versa. In our

                 reading, the terms of the FRAMEWORK do not prohibit

                 the lending bank/secured creditor (assuming that it

                 has no conscious knowledge that the defaulting

                 borrower is an MSME) to classify the account of the

                 defaulting MSME as NPA and to even issue the

                 demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI

                 Act without such identification of incipient stress in the

                 account of the defaulting borrower (MSME); however,

                 upon receipt of the demand notice, if such borrower in

                 its response under Section 13(3-A) of the SARFAESI Act

                 asserts that it an MSME and claims the benefit of the

                 FRAMEWORK citing reasons supported by an affidavit,

                 the lending bank/secured creditor would then be

                 mandatorily bound to look into such claim keeping

                 further action under the SARFAESI Act in abeyance;

                 and, should the claim be found to be worthy of

                 acceptance within the framework of the FRAMEWORK,

                 to act in terms thereof for securing revival and

                 rehabilitation of the defaulting borrower.”



10. As per judgement in ‘M/s. Pro Knits’, [2024 INSC 565], at Para 16, the



court records that the stage before the Loan turns NPA of MSME is crucial



and it is incumbent upon the concerned MSME to produce authenticated and



verifiable documents/material for substantiating its claim as being MSME. In



Para 17 the Court further records on failure to bring to notice of banker that



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                        6 of 8

the unit is MSME, then enterprise could not be permitted to thwart the action

taken in SARFAESI at the belated stage.



11. Section 7 IBC, proceedings are primarily concerned with Debt and

Default and the RBI circular which is applicable to SARFAESI Proceedings

shall not stand as hurdle to decide the present applicationas held in ‘Amit

Narang’ Vs. ‘Aditya Birla Finance Limited & Ors.’ [(Para 20) (2024] 252

CompCas 781].



12. The Adjudicating Authority had rather considered, the Debt & Default

and Form C and Form-D of the NeSL Certificate and the loan account

statements as maintained by the Respondent Bank. It found, the default

exceeded Rs.one crore and the statutory threshold for initiation of proceedings

under Section 7 had been satisfied. The Adjudicating Authority has expressly

observed, the precise quantification of the claim may be examined by the

Resolution Professional during CIRP.



13. Thus, considering the law stated above, we find no reason to upset a

reasoned order passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority; firstly as the M/s.

S.S. Aluminium Pvt. Ltd. had lost its status of MSME on 31.03.2021 and

secondly it never send a response under Section 13(3A) of SARFAESI Act for

reconstruction of its debt and thirdly it was also the responsibility of the

corporate debtor/appellant to apply in terms of notification dated 29.05.2025

at the earliest, which it never did. Thus, we are not inclined to interfere with

the impugned order. Even the letters dated 30.10.2023 and dated 10.11.2023

(supra); relied upon by the appellant, were never produced before the Ld.

Adjudicating Authority, hence no benefit qua such letters, even otherwise, be



Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 174 of 2026



                                        7 of 8

given. Admittedly the loan account of the corporate debtor was declared NPA

on 11.05.2021; was recalled on 04.10.2021 by notice and under Section 13(2)

on 17.05.2021; various OTS were given and never a benefit of the notification

was claimed; hence these 2 letters filed by the appellant would not upset the

entire proceedings under the IBC. More so, when the impugned order was

passed, delay in refiling was allowed on 13.3.2026, Form-G published on

16.03.2026, last date of EOI was 31.03.2026, submission of plan was by

18.5.2026. The Tribunal itself has recorded in its order dated 14.05.2026

that there was no stay. Resolution Plan is filed and is awaiting approval of

the Ld. Adjudicating Authority. Non-participation by the Appellant in the

Resolution process evince casual nature of appeal. The appeal thus has no

merit and is accordingly dismissed. Pending applications are also disposed

of.



                                        [Justice Yogesh Khanna]

                                         Officiating Chairperson

JUSTICE YOGESH KHANNA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON



         This Company Appeal (At)(Ins) No.1175/2026 is filed under Section 61 of

IBC challenging the order dated 19.06.2026 passed by Ld. NCLT, Mumbai

Bench, Mumbai in CP(IB)/640(MB)/2026 whereby in an application under

Section 95 of the Code filed by Respondent No.1, the Adjudicating Authority has

appointed Resolution Professional under Section 97, issued the interim

moratorium under Section 96, and has directed the Resolution Professional to

examine the application, including limitation and invocation of the personal

guarantee and to submit a report under Section 99(I).



2. It was argued by the learned senior counsel for appellant the Respondent

No.1 has no locus to file the proceedings under Section 95 of the Code as there

was no contract of guarantee executed by the appellant and Respondent No.1

and the personal guarantee was furnished only in favour of the Debenture

Trustee (IDBI Trustiship Services Ltd) for the benefit of all debenture holders and

under the Debenture Trust Deed, the power to declare an event of default,

accelerate, invoke the guarantee and initiate proceedings vest exclusively in the

Debenture Trustee, acting only on the written instructions of the majority

debenture holders representing not less than 75% outstanding debentures.



3. Respondent No. 1 (IIFL One Value Fund - Series B) is, on the admitted

record of the TDPL Committee of Creditors, only a minority debenture holder -

its voting share is 24.51% (claims as on commencement tabulated at the 20th

CoC Meeting dated 13.06.2026), whereas Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. holds

                                                               4



65.77% and Renaissance Fiscal Services Pyt. Ltd. 4.49%, the TDPL debentures

having been assigned to Rare ARC (30.03.2024) and to Renaissance

(29.06.2024). Respondent No. 1 thus cannot constitute and has not obtained the

instructions of, the Majority Debenture Holders, and the Debenture Trustee has

neither authorised nor filed the Petition. The invocation and the Petition are

therefore without authority and non-est.



4. It was argued this very objection was raised before the Ld. Adjudicating

Authority, which by its Order dated 12.06.2026, the Bench recorded that counsel

for the Personal Guarantor had taken it through the stipulations of the

Debenture Trust Deed and contended the petition is not maintainable for non-

compliance with those stipulations and reserved the matter. Yet by the Impugned

Order dated 19.06.2026 the Adjudicating Authority appointed the Resolution

Professional without deciding that threshold question of locus, instead remitting

the issue of “invocation” to the Resolution Professional’s examination.



5. It was argued the recitals to the Supplementary Debenture Trust Deed

confirm this scheme, wherein* Recital (C) records even the amendment of the

Principal DTD was effected by the Debenture Trustee acting on the instructions

of the Majority Debenture Holders a fortiori, the graver steps of default,

invocation and the initiation of insolvency proceedings could not be taken by a

minority holder acting unilaterally.



6. The Appellant submits the Adjudicating Authority ought to have

determined the threshold question of locus before setting the Section 99

                                                               5



machinery in motion, and the Impugned Order is causing serious and



irreparable prejudice.



7. Thus the issue raised by the learned senior counsel for the appellant is



whether a minority debenture holder without instructions of the Debenture



Trustee, in the manner as is given in Debenture Trust Deed, could initiate the



proceedings under Section 95 of the Code.



8. Let us see what the Ld. NCLT has to say on it. The Adjudicating Authority



vide its impugned order dated 19.06.2026 has held as under:-



         3.Further, Respondent m h1s capacity as Guarantor, executed

copy of the reply dated 20.05.2026 is annexed hereto and

marked as Exhibit-Fl.

debt as on 31.03.2026 is Rs. 206,42,01,875/- (including

·interest, penal interest and Redemption Premium) from

22.03.201

on 09.06.2026 under Section 95 of the Insolvency and

Bankruptcy Code, 2016, seeking initiation of the Insolvency

resolution process against the Respondent m his capacity as a

Personal Guarantor to the Corporate Debtor.

9. Though the Counsel for Personal Guarantor tried to make his

case for non-maintainability of the Petition, however, the same

cannot be gone into and adjudicated at this stage. In this

regard, we refer to judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in

Dilip B Jiwrajka Vs. Union of India & Ors. (Writ Petition (Civil)

No. 1281 of 2021) dated 09.11.2023, wherein the constitutional

validity of Sections 94 to 100 of the Code was upheld and, inter

alia, held as follows:



         "(i) No judicial adjudication is involved at the stages

         envisaged in Section 95 to Section 99 of the !BC;



         (ii) The Resolution Professional appointed under Section

         97 serves a facilitative role of collating all the facts

         relevant to the examination of the application for the

         commencement of the insolvency resolution process

         which has been preferred under Section 94 or Section 95.

         The report to be submitted to the Adjudicating Authority

         is recommendatory in nature on whether to accept or

         reject the application."



10.Accordmgly, having regard to the facts and circumstances

of the present ca e, and considering that at this stage only the

appointment of a Resolution Professional under Section 97 of

the Code is required, no adjudication of the merits of the matter

         and contentions raised by the Respondent can be dealt, at this

H Volume III, a recall notice dated 23.12.2024 by IIFL One Value Fund, Series

individual Financial Creditor.



11. Reference was also made to the Debenture Trustiship Deed dated



22.03.2018 wherein the only exceptional clause is Clause 2.1 as under:-

         (b) to take whatever action shall be required to be taken

12. It is argued none of the above i.e. (a) to (d) were pleaded in the petition and



none of the conditions (a) to (d) as stated in later portion of Clause 2.1 are



applicable. Further he referred to Clause 9.2(a) (ii) as under: -

                  Transaction Documents or under the Law;



13. Further he referred to Schedule 3 of the Debenture Trustee Deed which



reads: -

14. Thus it was argued before invoking the personal guarantee the meeting of



debenture holders ought to have been called for and its quorum ought to have



been 51% in value and thereafter a Resolution ought to have been passed in such



meeting for invocation of the guarantee by majority of 75% or more in value,



which was never been done in this case.



15. The Ld. Counsel for the appellant argued in Dilip B Jiwrajka Vs Union of



India & Ors Writ Petition No.1281/2021, the questions which were before the



Court were whether any debt or whether relationship of debtor and creditor could

                                                              12



be examined by the Insolvency Professional at the threshold and it was only in

these two circumstances; those being mixed question of facts and law, the Court

held it cannot be dealt with at this stage and has to be seen at the stage under

Section 100 of IBC.



16. It is further the submission of the learned senior counsel for the appellant

he is not arguing about merits and rather is challenging the locus of the

Respondent to initiate the proceedings under Section 95 since the appellant has

not given any personal guarantee to the Respondent but has given the personal

guarantee to Debenture Trustee. Hence these proceedings ought not to have

been initiated at the first instance and the issue of locus and limitation can be

very well be looked into at the initial stage itself.



17. The learned senior counsel for the appellant then referred to the judgement

Pawan Gupta Vs Charm Investments Pvt Ltd & Ors, Company Appeal (AT)

(Insolvency) NO.374/2026 decided on 29.05.2026 to support this view.



18. Further, the Ld. Sr. Counsel for the appellant referred to the judgement in

Prabhaben Ravjibhai Harkani Vs Bank of Baroda & Ors Company Appeal

(AT)(Insolvency) No. 1002 decided on 7th August, 2026 which held:



         “45. The above decision shows that appointment of a Resolution

         Professional is not an essential requirement in every case under section 94.

         The Adjudicating Authority, where it finds, on the admitted facts and the

         applicable law, that the application is not maintainable, it can reject an

         application under Section 94 before appointing the RP. The order cannot be

         said to be invalid merely because a Resolution Professional was not

         appointed. The validity of such an order has to be examined in the facts of

         each case.

         49. In view of the above findings, we are of the view that the Adjudicating

         Authority has rightly rejected the application filed by the Appellant under

                                                              13



         Section 94 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. We do not find

         any factual or legal infirmity in the Impugned Order dated 21.04.2025

         calling for interference by this Appellate Tribunal. Accordingly, the appeal is

         dismissed. There is no order as to costs. Pending IA’s if any are also

         disposed of.”

19. To suggest his argument the learned senior counsel for the appellant even



referred to Supplementary Trust Deed dated 24.06.2021 which contains the



following clauses:



         “c) The definition and all references to the “Debenture Holders’ Nominee” in

         the Principal Debenture Trust Deed shall hereby stand deleted and replaced

         and be deemed to mean “Majority Debenture Holders’ (as defined

         hereinafter).

         e) Any determination under the Debenture Documents including with respect

         to the materiality or reasonableness of any matter, proof or the occurrence

         of any event, circumstance, change, fact, information, document,

         authorization, proceedings, act, omission, claims, breach, default or the

         satisfaction of any conditions or otherwise shall be made by the Debenture

         Trustee (acting on the instructions of Majority Debenture Holders) which

         determination shall be final and binding on the Obligors.”

20. And to the definition of Majority Debenture Holder as under:-



         “Majority Debenture Holders shall mean Debenture Holders holding an

         aggregate amount expressing not less than 75% (Seventy five percent) of the

         nominal value of the Debentures outstanding for the time being.”

21. Thus he argued in the recall notice dated 23.12.2024 though it was



mentioned the debenture trustee is enforcing the right to invoke the present



guarantee but in fact it was invoked by the Financial Creditor viz the Respondent



herein and not by the debenture trustee. He further referred to Malvika Hegde



Vs IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited and Another 2025 SCC OnLine NCLAT 422



wherein this Tribunal had dismissed the petition under Section 7 of the IBC



only on the ground it was not filed in accordance with the terms as contained in



the Debenture Trust Deed.

                                                              14



22. Heard



23. We have also heard the learned senior counsel for the Respondent also



and we are of the considered view the issue of locus and maintainability cannot



be adjudicated prior to the stage of Section 100 of the IBC and our this view is



supported by the law laid down in Dilip B Jiwarajka V. Union of India & Ors



(2024) 5 SCC 435, wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court held:-



         “Para 86.6 No adjudication is involved at the stages envisaged in Section 95

         to Section 99 of the IBC” and “no judicial determination takes place until the

         adjudicating authority decides under Section 100 whether to accept or reject

         the application.”

24. Further in Bank of Baroda Vs Farooq Ali Khan (2025) SCC OnLine 374 it



was held:-



         9. The Adjudicating Authority, by its order dated 16.02.2024, has followed the

         procedure envisaged under Sections 95 to 100 of the IBC, and has also relied on

         the afore-stated principles in Jiwrajka (supra). It specifically observed that

         respondent no. 1’s objections regarding limitation and waiver of the guarantee will

         be considered once the resolution professional submits his report. This is the correct

         approach as the appointment of a resolution professional at the very threshold is

         statutorily mandated under Section 97 of the IBC. As has been held by this Court

         in Jiwarajka (Supra) the Adjudicating Authority does not adjudicate any point at

         this stage and need not decide jurisdictional questions regarding existence of the

         debt before appointing the resolution professional.

25. In Canara BANK Vs Uma Kumari Singh 2025 SCC OnLine NCLAT 1514 decided



by three judges bench, this Tribunal held:



         “Para 9-11. We have heard Counsel for the Parties and after examining the record,

         are of the considered opinion that there is an error committed by the Ld. Tribunal

         in dismissing the application, in all the three cases, filed by the Bank on the first

         the date of hearing on the ground of limitation because it has been concluded by

         the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Dilip B Jiwrajka (Supra) that no judicial

         adjudication is involved at the stages in Section 95 and 99 of the Code.

         10.Thus in view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances the present appeals

         succeeds and the impugned order passed in all three appeals are hereby set aside.

         The application filed under Section 95 are hereby restored to its original number.

         The matter(s) are remanded back to the Learned Tribunal to decide the same in

                                                              15



         accordance with the law. The parties are directed to appear before the Tribunal on

         23.09.2025.



         11.Before parting, we would also like to add that the Respondents shall have a

         right to raise the issue of limitation when the Tribunal would exercise its

         adjudicatory jurisdiction.



26. In CL Sharma V Bank of Maharashtra 2024 SCVC OnLine NCLAT 279 this



Tribunal held:-



         “11.The law declared by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the above

         judgement (Jiwrajka) is very clear. The Adjudicating Authority

         should consider the issue pertaining to jurisdictional fact at the stage

         of Section 100 and there is no adjudication contemplated at the stage

         when RP is appointed under Section 97 sub-section (5). The

         conclusion recorded in paragraph 86(iii) clearly lays down the

         aforesaid. The submission of the Appellant(s) that applications were

         barred by time, ought to have been considered at the time when

         Adjudicating Authority appointed the RP, thus, cannot be accepted.



27. In Central Bank of India Vs Deepen Arun Parekh, this Tribunal held as under:-



         36. We are of the considered opinion that Adjudicating Authority committed error

         in considering the objection raised by the Respondent on the merits of the

         application under Section 95 filed by the Central Bank of India at the stage when

         RP was not even appointed. The Adjudicating Authority proceeded to enter into

         adjudicatory issues, which can be taken by the Adjudicating Authority only at the

         time of hearing of Section 95 application under Section 100, as is now the law

         declared by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Dilip B Jiwrajka’s case, as noted above.



28. Further in Prabhaben Ravjibhai Harkani Vs Bank of Baroda, Company Appeal



(AT) (Ins) No.1002/2025 decided on 07.08.2026 this Tribunal held:-



         This judgement applies to applications filed under Section 94 of the IBC i.e.

         applications filed by the debtor itself. It will not apply to applications filed under

         Section 95 of the IBC i.e. applications filed by creditors/personal guarantors.



         This judgement itself recognizes that different procedures apply to proceeddings

         under Section 94 and Section 95.



         39. The learned counsel for the appellant has also relied upon the judgement of the

         Hon’ble Supreme Court in Di8lip Jiwrajka V Union of India (2024) 5 SCC 435 to

         contend that once an application under Section 94 is filed, the Adjudicating

         Authority is required to appoint a Resolution Professional before examining the

         application on merits. It is, therefore, necessary to consider whether the said

         judgment has an application to the facts of the present case.



29. Thus in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and also



three judges bench of this Tribunal, we are not inclined to interfere with

                                                              16



impugned order of the Ld. NCLT and dismiss the appeal filed by the appellant as

per settled law viz the adjudicatory process shall start only after the report is

filed by the Resolution Professional per Section 100 of the IBC.

30. The appeals are accordingly dismissed. Pending applications are also

disposed of.
